Mr. NIXON: I should like to say a
few words against the adjournment of
the House. I know it is usual to adjourn
Parliament at this time of the year, but
at the same time there are a lot of things
that should be attended to before the
adjournment. For one thing, there is the
Sittings of the House
Sittings of the House
18 JANUARY 1944
Report of the Select Committee on
Health Services for which everyone in
Northern Ireland is waiting. I know
that it is to be put on the Order Paper
for this day week, but I think that very
much more than that should have been
done in respect of that Report before
Parliament adjourns until we do not
know when. I think that that Report
should have been attended to. I do not
see why it has been held up. I think
that Parliament should have sat a few
days to deal with it, because the reference
states that the Committee has to report
to the House. Of course, it is for Parliament to state when that Report can
be presented to the House.
Ulster is a
There are other things.
small place, but we have one city of
which we are proud, and that city is
Belfast. If we had not Belfast we would
have nothing. There has been a libel
published on Belfast by a Minister, and
the sooner it is brought here the better.
I am not going to debate that Bill or
to anticipate what is in it, because I
would not be allowed to do so, but when
a Minister, or anyone else, takes upon
himself to libel the city of Belfast the
sooner that libel is brought to the Table
of this House and thrashed out the better.
We have got too much of that. As I
say, I am not going to anticipate the
Bill. Everyone knows the Measure to
which I refer, and which, in effect, means
that the representatives of the electors of
the city of Belfast are men of such
character that they cannot be trusted. I
say that their character individually is
as good as, and in some cases better
than, the people taking it on themselves
to libel them. I am not going to go any
further on that, but I say that when that
libel was published it should have been
brought here at an early date and
thrashed out. It might then have the
same result as the last libel that was
brought here, we would see who were
the honest men and who were not the
honest men.
The
Then there is another thing.
Prime Minister in a debate here some
time ago promised us. a day to discuss
the questionable activities of the Electricity Supply Board, or the activities in
connection with that Board, whatever
they are. I am not going to go into
that matter now, but I am going to say
that that promise should have been
honoured.
There is another thing that is not
occurring in any Parliament under the
British Constitution except this Parliament. There are two Cabinet Ministers
drawing salaries without any authority
whatever from this House. The Minister
of Finance promised last summermonths and months ago that he would
bring forward a Supplementary Estimate to put the matter in order, but he
has never done so. I have not seen a
Supplementary Estimate dealing with
that subject tabled in this House. If
Ministers can take money without any
authority from this House the sooner it
is closed and a dictatorship set up the
better. I think Parliament should have
been kept open until the Minister of
Finance came forward to this Table with
the Supplementary Estimate; in fact, it
should have been done at the time. What
are we coming to at all when two right
hon. Gentlemen can come in and take
money without this House voting it?
We are supposed to go step by step
with the Imperial Parliament, but this
would not be allowed in the Imperial
Parliament; no, not for five minutes.
It would not be tolerated anywhere but
here. We are not going to tolerate it.
As far as I am concerned, I was out
absolutely to help the Prime Minister.
The Prime Minister got a vote to extend
the life of this Parliament almost unanimously on condition that there would be
no contentious legislation, but that libel
of a Bill to which I referred a while ago
for me at all events is the breaking point.
We find the Government back in the
same old rut again. This is the parting
of the ways for a lot of people outside as
Iwell as for me.
The supreme authority in this House
sits on the Back Benches. I appeal to
you to assert yourselves and put this
House on the same footing as any other
House and to uphold the city that is the
capital of Northern Ireland. At the
same time, if anyone who is a public
representative does anything wrong put
your foot on him. When men who are
drawing salaries without the authority of
this House have the audacity to consent
to a Bill like that in respect to a public
body that get nothing for their services.
it is about time it was stopped, no matter
what the result may be.

Mr. HENDERSON: I agree with the
other speakers that this House should
not adjourn, and I do so owing to the
housing situation that exists throughout
Northern Ireland. It is quite true that
the Minister of Home Affairs has at least
tried to do something, but the condition
that prevails is absolutely horrible.
could not exist in any other community
than Northern Ireland. This Government
has brought in legislation to build 750
houses when we should have at least forty
or fifty thousand. But for us to adjourn
while tens of thousands of people are
living in hovels is a disgrace. I feel very
much about this and I do not think the
Cabinet realise the situation that exists.
It is a case of passing the buck. It is
nobody's darling, and they want rid of
it. I want to protest against any adjournment because of the position of the people
whose homes have been devastated by
Hitler's airmen.
There is a lot of talk about securing
sites by members of the Corporation and
by the Government. There is a site of
40 acres up the Malone Road that could

houses. The old aerodrome that was

Mr. LOWRY: This is an amendment

service, whether in the armed forces or

no person is damnified by reason of being

other persons as may from time to
time be
be appointed by the said

CLAUSE 3 (Sale of adulterated or
impoverished milk).
(1) Any person who sells or offers
or exposes for sale adulterated or impoverished milk shall be guilty of an
offence under the principal Act which
may be prosecuted before a court of
summary jurisdiction; and for the purposes of this provision milk shall be
deemed to be adulterated or impoverished if, when tested in the
prescribed manner, it has been found
to be mixed with any other substance,
or any part of it has been found to be
abstracted, so as, in either case, to
affect injuriously its quality, substance,
or nature.
(2) Where a person who has been
convicted of an offence in relation to
milk under the foregoing provisions of
this section or under section three,
section six or section nine of the Sale
of Food and Drugs Act, 1875, is the
holder of a milk licence, or a licence
under section two of the principal Act
for the sale of milk of Grade A, Grade
B or Grade C, the Ministry may
revoke or suspend the licence.

improved this Bill. The Minister would

Milk Bill-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Nixon]
High Court, and with the decisions of the
courts. I hope we will hear no more of
Ministers bringing in Bills to put any
official or any Ministry over the liberties
and rights of the citizens of Northern
Ireland. I want to have the courts above
the Ministry in a matter of this kind
where someone's living is at stake. All's
well that ends well.
Lord GLENTORAN: As my hon.
Friend, the Member for Antrim, has just
said, when this Bill was going through
this House I tried to pour oil on the
troubled waters. I did so for the very
good reason that I had been associated with
this milk improvement scheme for two or
three years, and I found how satisfactory
it was to have the control of licences an
administrative matter and not a judicial
matter. This Amendment does not to
any great extent interfere with the line
I took that day, because this is a case
where the people concerned asked to have
the right to go to a court of law. I have
again and again spoken in this House in
favour of the principle that every man in
this country should have the right to go
to a court of law. I supported that
principle when it was raised in connection
with the Planning and other Bills, and so
long as I am in this House I shall stand
for that principle, because it is the only
principle that will enable democracy to
live.
The relations between the farmers and
the Ministry of Agriculture have been
very happy during the past seven or
eight years on this question, and there is
no doubt that the Ministry have, to a
quite extraordinary extent, improved not
only the quality but the quantity of milk
produced in this country. I therefore
hope that the Ministry and the farmers
will carry on as they did before. I trust
that the farmers will not lightly go to the
courts, and that the Ministry will not
feel, "Well, we are sick of this fellow.
We will push him into going to court."
That might happen on either side, and it
is a dangerous thing. I am quite sure
the Ministry will not adopt such an
attitude, but there is the danger that the
Ministry might push a man to have recourse to the courts.
On the other point as to whether we
in this House should or should not accept
Amendments from the Senate, I have
always been a great supporter of the
Senate, but I have never seen a Government having such an admiration for the
other House as has this Government. It
takes all the law and the prophets from
the Senate. The care and trouble the
Members of the Senate take over Bills is
quite exceptional, and that is all to the
good. The Senate is part and parcel of
Parliament, just the same as is this House,
and there is no reason why we should not
take Amendments from the other House.
I have great admiration for the Senate.
I have had to appear before them, and, in
my opinion, no point should be raised on
that question. I approve of this Amendment, and I hope the House will accept it.
Mr. McGURK: I rise to support this
Amendment. At the time the Bill was
before this House it was the opinion of
Members on this side, and of back
benchers on the Government side, that the
word "Court" should have been inserted
instead of the word "Ministry." I am
very pleased that the Senate has passed
this amendment. I believe it amounts
to the same thing as the amendment
moved in this House, but it is in better
terms. It perhaps gives the farmer a
better chance than did the amendment
which we supported in this House. It
enables him to go to a Court of Quarter
Sessions, and thus gives him three.
months' grace. We are not casting any
reflection on the farmer or on the
Ministry of Agriculture. In the
majority of cases we find that the Ministry
officials meet the farmers as fairly as possible. It was so in the time of the last
Minister of Agriculture, and it is the
case with the present Minister. I hope
that the same harmony will exist in
regard to this Bill and that the Ministry
will not use their
power against the
farmer in any vindictive spirit if he does
not carry out their orders. I am very
pleased to support this amendment, and
I hope that the carrying out of the
measure will be satisfactory to all concerned, both Ministry and farmers.

that protest against the

Members look a little farther ahead they
might not be so sure.
Question put, and agreed to.
Senate's Amendment:
Clause 4, in page 4, line 21, after the
word "milk" ("production of milk")
insert the words "for sale."
Resolved, "That this House do agree
with the Senate in the said Amendment."
-(Rev. Robert Moore.)
Ordered, That a Message be sent to
the Senate to acquaint them that the
House agree to the Amendments made
by the Senate to the said Bill without
any amendment.
Adjournment.
Resolved, "That this House do now
adjourn."—(Sir Norman Stronge.)
Adjourned accordingly at Twentyfive Minutes to Four o'clock
until Tuesday next at Twelve
noon pursuant to the Resolution
of the House of this day.

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS,
Mr. SPEAKER: I wish to impress
upon the hon. Member for Woodvale who
has eleven questions on the Order Paper
that we shall have only ten or twelve
minutes before the interruption, and that
if he wants to get through he should not
ask many supplementary questions.
Mr. NIXON: I know that.
Dungannon Rural Cottage Rents.
1. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state if the
Dungannon Rural District Council increased the rents of 78 houses owned by
the Council; whether such increase was
made with the approval of the Minister;
what is the percentage of such increase;
and whether the Rent Restriction Act
applies to these houses.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Mr. Lowry): The answer to the first two
parts of the question is in the affirmative.
With regard to the third part, the increases in rents of the 78 cottages range
from 1s to ls 5d per week, representing
percentage increases varying from 25 per
cent. to 42 per cent, although it should
be borne in mind that the largest percentage increases were in respect of cottages, the rent of which was only 3s per
week.
The revised rents of the cottages now
range from 4s 3d to 4s 9d per week.
I would point out to the hon. Member
that last year the Rural District Council
incurred a loss of over £800 on their
cottages, and, furthermore, the Council
is embarking upon a scheme of repair of
cottages which will cost £15,000.
When sanctioning the increase, the
Ministry stated that increased rents
should only be charged where the cottages were in a reasonable state of repair, and also required that no increase
should be imposed in any individual case
if hardship to the particular tenant would
result.
With regard to the last part of the
question the Rent Restrictions Acts do
not apply to labourers' cottages built by
rural district councils.
Mr. NIXON: In view of the Minister's
answer, would he take power by Act of
Parliament to see that even labourers, as
he almost put it, are protected the same
as anyone else?
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
25 JANUARY 1944
Mr. LOWRY: It has been the policy in
connection with the Rent Restrictions
Acts ever since they were first brought
into force that they should not extend to
houses built by local authorities, the
reason being that the rents of such houses
rarely ever are economic rents.
Mr. NIXON: Why does the Minister
of Home Affairs himself consent to the
raising of rents at the present time?
Cabinet Ministers.
SALARIES OF MINISTERS OF
FINANCE AND AGRICULTURE.
2. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of

that he would bring forward a supplementary Estimate to cover the salaries of
the Ministers of Finance and Agriculture,
and whether this has been done.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Major
Sinclair): Yes, sir, I have informed the
House on earlier occasions that Supplementary Estimates would be introduced
covering the provision of salaries both for
myself as Minister of Finance and for the
Minister of Agriculture, and these
Estimates will be included in the usual
Spring Supplementary Estimates, which
will be laid before the House in the
normal way, but, of course, statutory
authority for the payment of these
salaries already exists.

to take this question.

The authority which the hon. Member

Mr. NIXON: Is the Prime Minister
aware that notwithstanding the answer

has no authority, to authorise any
Minister to have the use of a motor car

Mr. NIXON: I am asking the right

Mr. SPEAKER: The hon. Member is
giving information under the guise of a
question.
Mr. NIXON: According to the Prime
Minister's statement he was not aware of
this, and I was asking him if he was
aware of it. Is it not a fact that he has
no more right, without the authority of
this House, to use a public car with the
services of a policeman than any man
standing at the corner, and that to do
so is a species of larceny?

War Workers.
RIGHT TO IMPROVE
POSITION.
3. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Labour whether he imposes restrictions or
exercises his authority to prevent war
workers from bettering their conditions
by transferring their services from one
firm to another, whether the conditions
in the firm of J. Mackie & Sons in so far
as pay, bonus, etc., are as good as conditions in other similar firms.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Grant): Cases arise from time to time
where it is necessary in the national interest to direct workers, especially skilled
workers for whom the demand exceeds
the supply, to remain in a firm where
the need for their services is more urgent
than in other employment to which they
may wish to transfer. I am naturally
anxious that no worker should be prevented from bettering his conditions, but
the hon. Member will realise that furtherance of the war effort must, in all
circumstances, be the primary consideration.
With regard to the second part of the
question, I am advised that the rates of
pay and conditions of employment in the
firm of Messrs. James Mackie & Sons,
Ltd., are regulated by appropriate agreements between associations of employers.
and workers.
Mr. NIXON: With reference to the
Minister's statement that he has power,
which he exercises, to prevent workers
from bettering themselves, is it not a fact
that he has compelled workers to work
at 30s a week when they could get £3 or
£3 10s; and is it not a further fact that
the Minister when he got the opportunity
took a better position himself? In view
of that fact why does he not give the
workers the same privileges?
Mr. GRANT: No one in this House
knows better than the hon. Member that
where it is possible for me to exercise any
sympathetic treatment towards this type
of workers I have never hesitated to do
so, but in view of the national emergency
and in consideration of the claims that
are made I must exercise my powers in
this case to see that the national effort
does not suffer. In the case of agriculture, in which Members on all sides of
the House point out that farmers are
compelled to grow more food, we have to
exercise discretion to see that the labour
is provided in order to gather in the
harvest, even though the agricultural
labourer may suffer financially.
Mr. NIXON : In regard to the
Minister's attempt to switch this question
on to agriculture, is it not a fact that war
workers at a certain industry have been
refused permission by the Ministry to
take up work in other war factories where
they could get more wages, and why it is
that it is the working people who have to
suffer all the time in the national interest?
POWER OF DISMISSAL.
6. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Labour whether it is a fact that a firm
engaged on war production can dismiss
any employee by alleging that he is unsuitable for the work; whether a worker
in a firm so engaged can leave that firm
and take up work in another firm by
alleging that the firm which he leaves or
proposes leaving is unsuitable.
Mr. GRANT: The Ministry of Labour
can direct any worker in Northern Ireland to take up, or return to, employment with any employer.
So long as such a direction is in force,
the employer cannot dismiss the worker except for serious misconduct-in which
case the worker has a right of appeal to
a local appeal board.
If the directed person or the employer
feels aggrieved by a direction, he can
apply for it to be withdrawn. The application is first considered by a national
Royal Assent
Oral Answers

25 JANUARY 1944
service officer of the Ministry of Labour,
and if either party objects to his decision
there is a right of further appeal to a
local appeal board.
Except by the issue of directions, the
Ministry of Labour has no power, under
the existing Orders, to compel a worker
to remain with a firm, or a firm to accept
or retain a worker.
Mr. NIXON: Is it not a fact that a
worker was dismissed in Mackie's on the
ground that he was unsuitable, that he
appealed, and that the tribunal who
heard the appeal said they could do nothing without asking Stewart Mackie,
who was not here at all; and is it not a
fact that when Stewart Mackie came back
he would not have the worker, and that
led to a sit-down strike? Is it not also a
fact that the Minister was on the job,
and if he had authority he failed to
exercise it?
Vacancies on Municipal Bodies.
BELFAST CITY COUNCIL.
4. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state the
total number of Aldermen and Councillors
constituting the Belfast City Council; the
number of such who were co-opted; and
whether it is proposed to amend the law
so as to fill all vacancies by by-elections.
Mr. LOWRY: The total number of
aldermen and councillors constituting the
Belfast County Borough Council is sixty.
Since the last election of members held on
15th May, 1939, nineteen members have
been co-opted to fill vacancies and there
are at present two vacancies remaining to
be filled.
The answer to the last part of the
question is in the negative.
Mr. NIXON: Are we supposed to go
step by step with Great Britain, and is it
not a fact that in Great Britain vacancies
in councils are filled by election, thereby
giving the people an opportunity of
having a say in them?
Mr. LOWRY: No. The hon. Member
is quite wrong. The two statutes are
similar. The English statute is 2 & 3
Geo. 6, chapter 115, and our statute is
4 Geo. 6, chapter 2. Precisely the same
conditions of law prevail in both countries.
I may add that when the Northern Ireland statute was passing the Second
Reading on 27th February, 1940, and the
Third Reading on 5th March, 1940, the
hon. Member never raised his voice or
voted against it. I had the curiosity to
observe that.
Mr. NIXON: With regard to the
Minister's statement that things here in
regard to local government are exactly the
same as in Great Britain, is there any
part of Great Britain where the public
representatives were suppressed and
administrators put in to do their duty?
Is there any part of Great Britain where
an official out of a Ministry has been
shoved in at £50 a week with super
powers to do the work of a council? If
the Minister wants to follow Great
Britain, why does he not follow it? If
he does so he will have a stronger supporter in me.
Mr. LOWRY: In so far as a question
emerges from the observations of the hon.
Gentleman, in reply I would say that
what I said was that the statutory position
with respect to elections during war time
is precisely the same in England as here.
Mr. NIXON: In reply to the Minister's
supplementary statement, is it not a fact
that he only follows Great Britain when
it suits him, and when it does not suit
him he does not follow Great Britain.
POSITION IN GREAT BRITAIN.
7. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state if all
vacancies for Councillors and Aldermen
arising in Municipal bodies in Great
Britain are filled by the ordinary democratic procedure of by-elections.
Mr. LOWRY: The answer is in the
negative. Local elections have been
suspended in Great Britain since the outbreak of war.
Mr. NIXON : Were any councils
suspended in Great Britain for not
pleasing the Ministry?
Mr. LOWRY: It is not necessary there.
Mr. NIXON: No.
Prorogation
Oral Answers

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Police.
ADMISSION OF MARRIED MEN TO
THE R.U.C.
9. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether members of the
Special Constabulary who are married
are eligible for admission to the Royal
Ulster Constabulary.
Mr. LOWRY: Married men, whether
members of the Special Constabulary or
not, are not normally eligible for recruitment to the Royal Ulster Constabulary.
It is possible, however, subject to my
approval, to vary the qualifications laid
down for candidates so as to permit of the
recruitment of a married man under 35
years of age who is in possession of qualifications which make his acceptance desirable in the interests of the Force.
Mr. NIXON: Is it not a fact that it is
the policy in Great Britain to revive the
dwindling population? That being so,
why does the Minister adhere to this old
rule not to admit trained men of the
Special Constabulary to the Royal Ulster
Constabulary?
Mr. LOWRY: It is possible to vary the
qualifications in approved cases.
Mr. NIXON: How often has it been
done, if it is possible?
PAY OF R.U.C. SPECIAL CON-
STABULARY AND HARBOUR
POLICE.
10. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he will grant the
Royal Ulster Constabulary, including
Harbour Police and Special Constabulary,
an increase of pay comparable to the increases recently granted to the officers of
that Force.
Mr. LOWRY: The pay of the rank and
file of the Forces referred to is at least as
favourable as that of equivalent ranks in
corresponding Police Forces in Great
Britain, and no increase of pay in
Northern Ireland, or so far as I am aware
in Great Britain, is at present in
contemplation.
Home Guard.
RECOGNITION OF SERVICES.
11. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether the time has
arrived to show practical appreciation of
the work done by the Home Guard by
giving them a money grant.
Mr. LOWRY: I do not consider that
the time has arrived, or indeed that it is
ever likely to arrive, when it will be desirable or necessary to pay members of the
Home Guard.
This Force was formed and has been
maintained on the basis of voluntary, unpaid, part-time service to the country in a
grave emergency, and I believe that I
interpret correctly the wishes and the
spirit of the volunteers in saying that it
should be continued on a purely voluntary
basis.
Mr.
NIXON : Has the time not
arrived to put the Home Guard under the
control of the War Office? Is it not a
fact that the controlling authority here,
which includes the Minister of Home
Affairs, knows nothing whatever about
military matters ? I refer particularly to
the political control.
PROROGATION.
A message was delivered by the acting
Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod, as
follows:
I am commanded by the Senate to
inform this honourable House that the
Proclamation of His Grace the Governor
of Northern Ireland proroguing this present Session of Parliament is to be
communicated in the Senate forthwith.
and, further, I am commanded to invite
this honourable House to hear the said
Proclamation read.
The House went, and, having returned,
Mr. SPEAKER (standing in the
Clerk's place at the Table): I have to
report that the House has this day attended in the Senate, when the Proclamation proroguing this present Session of
Parliament was read by the Speaker of
the Senate as follows:
BY HIS GRACE THE GOVERNOR
OF NORTHERN IRELAND
A PROCLAMATION
For Proroguing the present Parliament
of Northern Ireland
WHEREAS it is provided by section
eleven of the Government of Ireland Act,
1920, as modified by and in pursuance of
certain enactments amending the said
Prorogation
Prorogation
25 JANUARY 1944
Act, that the Governor of Northern
Ireland shall, in His Majesty's name,
summon, prorogue and dissolve the
Parliament of Northern Ireland:
AND WHEREAS it is desirable that
this present Parliament of Northern
Ireland should be prorogued to the first
day of February, one thousand nine
hundred and forty-four:
NOW I, JAMES ALBERT EDWARD,
DUKE OF ABERCORN, KNIGHT OF
THE MOST NOBLE ORDER OF THE
GARTER, KNIGHT OF THE MOST
ILLUSTRIOUS ORDER OF SAINT
PATRICK, Governor of Northern Ireland, by this Proclamation do publish
and declare His Majesty's Pleasure that
the said Parliament be, as from the
reading of this Proclamation in the
Parliament of Northern Ireland, prorogued to Tuesday, the first day of
February, one thousand nine hundred
and forty-four.

AND I do hereby further declare His
Majesty's Royal Will and Pleasure to be
that the said Parliament shall on the said
first day of February, one thousand nine
hundred and forty-four, assemble and be
holden at Stormont for the despatch of
divers urgent and important affairs, and
the Senators and Members of the House
of Commons of Northern Ireland are
hereby required to give their attendance
accordingly.
Given this twenty-fifth day of January,
one thousand nine hundred and fortyfour.
(Signed by his own hand),
ABERCORN.

time. The officers came into my cell at
dinner time. Officer A said to me that
my plate was very dirty. I said I
would use it. He then said, "Half of
you fellows must have been reared in a
pigsty. Did you live like this outside?
You must have been reared like pigs.'
At this I said, "I am sure I was better
reared than you.' As soon as I had
said this he wheeled round and struck
me twice on each side of the face with
the back of his hand. Although the
blows hurt me at the time they did not
mark me. On the following Friday I
complained to the Board of Visitors
about the incident, but they would not
believe it. They said as I was not
marked they could not believe it.

They happened, and they are happening

A warder called Mr. B approached

Upon my refusal to take off my clothes
Mr. A said to me, "We will soon see

After that he pulled me from the bed

He then trailed me by both feet along

Officers B and C did not in any way

locked up in my cell until the following

before the medical officer, who examined
me, the marks were on me,
nevertheless no action was taken.

I say
no. It would not be tolerated in Britain.

I want to say that prison medical officers
are perhaps just like all other medical
officers they accept decisions in reports
from persons who are perhaps concerned
in those reports. I think that a review
of the medical officers in the prisons might
be worth while. I would also say that if
the health of these men and women, who
are interned or who are prisoners because
of political actions, deteriorates in any
respect, I think a change is called for in
the medical service, a service which is set
up for the purpose of looking after the
health and strength of the men while they
are incarcerated. I know that the food
in the jail is anything but good. I have
seen the food and I have tasted it.
have watched it being cooked, and I must
say that I cannot recommend it. Over a
period of four months, while I was there,
the cooking and the serving of the food
improved considerably, but I understand
that they have now gone back to their
former condition.
I
It is badly cooked and served in dirty
vessels. Searching of the cells usually
takes place before dinner and supper,
and the warders hands are anything but
clean after searching dirty and sweaty
clothing and mattresses, yet they will
leave such searching and commence to
serve out the food without bothering to
wash their hands. We must object to a
Vote on Account to people who are so
careless about the health of others that
they would start to handle food with
hands that have been used to search
things that are likely to be covered with
many millions of germs and other
dangerous things. Surely, there should
be some little consideration for the health
of these interned people, and surely the
warders should at least wash their hands
before doing this work. More hygienic
methods could be introduced into the
prison service so far as the food is concerned.
In England and Scotland there are 26
dishes served up to the prisoners every
month. The same used to apply in Northern Ireland when it was under the
Imperial Authorities. In Belfast there
are six different dishes in the year.
Surely the medical officer should realise
that he is responsible to those men, and
that all men cannot take the same dish.
There are men interned in Belfast, because of political convictions, who should
not on medical grounds be taking some of
the food provided, but they have to take
it, because if they did not they would not
get anything else. Here is a quotation
from the Report of the Scottish and
English Prisons: "There are twenty-six
different diets in any one month," but in
Northern Ireland there are only six diets
which prisoners can have in any one year.
Another question I want to raise is
that these prisoners are entitled to
liberty and they are entitled to
letters and to visits. For the first year
a prisoner is allowed one letter and a
visit once every three months. On these
occasions only certain relatives are
allowed to visit. The decision as to whom
they shall be rests with the police. One
man is allowed to visit his son but is
prevented from visiting his brother.
Physical contact between the visitor and
the prisoner is not allowed, not even a
shake of the hands being permitted.
Public events are not allowed to be discussed by the visitor and the prisoner,
and the visitor must confine himself to
personal affairs.
These visits last for twenty minutes
under the supervision of the warder, who
sits between the visitor and the prisoner.
Even clergymen have been subject to such
conditions. Why are those strict and
rigid regulations applied to Northern
Ireland and not applied elsewhere? I
think these people are being made the
victims of political persecution. I think
this Government has got so hard-hearted
and so afraid of being removed from
office that they are oppressing their
political opponents because the Government think they are likely to bring their

or a job in Northern Ireland. We were

One reason was that there was a

I certainly challenge the right of this

simply on an Executive decree, a mere
fiat of a Minister. These men are held
when there is no apparent danger to the
public safety from their release. You
find the conditions very peculiar. I see
from the reports in the papers that if a
man places what is called a tricolour flag
over a coffin he is liable to arrest and to
a term of imprisonment, and yet that flag
flies high over Whitehall.
The Prime Minister goes there. The
British authorities take no exception to
it. How is it that it is lawful in Britain,
that it is not objected to in Britain, and
yet here in Northern Ireland a humble
peasant or a labourer in one of our towns
is liable to be sent to jail if he is in
possession of that flag? Is that in accordance with a sense of justice? It can
never be justified or even excused, it can

These men are men who come from decent

I raised in this House some time ago

There have been many committals in the

main denominations here in the North of

Coming to the Ministry of Health and

People are living in hovels. In Belfast

are
rent will be in the region of £1 a week

Mr. WARNOCK: As I said a very
wide field was covered on some matters.
Some of the matters were of importance
and I want to deal with them. I think
the first matter dealt with by the hon.
Member for Pottinger related to the

of internees in the main in Belfast

community, but they have been forced
upon this Government by circumstances
beyond their control and by circumstances
not of their own seeking.
Ever since the constitutional position
of Northern Ireland was established some
25 years ago we, unfortunately, had in
the country a body of people who were
bitterly opposed to its Constitution and
who sought by every means in their power
to destroy it. I think the first duty of
any Government is to defend its constitutional position. The attacks which
were made upon the Government of Northern Ireland were characterised by a
violence and severity which is almost unknown in any civilised community. They
were met and they were defeated by firm,
resolute, but, I believe absolutely fair
government.
It is suggested that at the present time
there are a number of persons deprived
of their liberty in Northern Ireland by
reason of their political views. Certainly
I would be no party to any such proceedings. When a man holds particular
political views and is prepared to advance
those political views in a constitutional
manner he will get the fullest and
greatest liberty to do so; but when, in
order to force upon the community views
which are destructive of the Constitution
under which we operate, he seeks to have
recourse to violence in order to destroy
that Constitution, then the Government
is not only entitled but absolutely bound,
in defence of its Constitution, to take
measures to put an end to those insurgent
or revolutionary ideas. The Government
of this country has done it firmly, resolutely and fairly. Speaking as the
Minister responsible for the maintenance
of law and order in this country, the
policy of firm, resolute and fair government will, so far as I am concerned, be
maintained so long as the threat to our
Constitution exists.
It was suggested by the hon. and
learned Member for Central Belfast that
the internment of certain persons who
constitute a threat to the security of this
country is due to partition It is a very
interesting argument, but it has not the
merit of truth. Partition does not
operate in Eire in the same way. The
latest figure I have of the number of
people who are interned in Eire as constituting a danger to the Government of
that country is 477. We have nothing
like so many as that; in actual fact the
number in Northern Ireland is 232. The
last figure which I have from Eire is 477,
almost double the number of persons
whom we have interned in this country.
The conditions of internment there are
vastly more rigorous than those in operation in this country.

and the Roman Catholic people, for whom
the Member for Central Belfast speaks,
say their teachers must teach Roman
Catholic children the Roman Catholic
catechism and religion. It does not matter
what the Minister says or wants, they will
have to get that, and there must be no
compliment about it.
The right hon. Gentleman shaped extremely well at the start of his Ministerial
career, and he answered any questions
without any reservation or qualification.
I myself thought he was going to be a
good Minister until this question arose. I
do not know what he was doing in 1930,
but I think he was in Parliament, and
that was the time to raise the point he
has raised. He should not go back now
and pretend that in 1930 the Attorney-
General was wrong, and that the
Attorney-General in 1935 was wrong. I
am not a lawyer, and therefore I do not
know whether they were wrong or not,
and I do not care either. It is not my
business to ascertain whether they were
right or wrong, it is not the Minister's
business, and it is not anyone's business,
because if you started to do that there
would be no end to it. If a Government
passed a Bill that was not popular and
another Government repealed that Bill I
could understand it, but in the case of
the Education Acts they were popular
with the people, they were Acts the people wanted, and with which they were
satisfied, and why the Minister should
pretend that they violated the Constitution
and make a laughing stock of Parliament
is a thing I cannot understand.
The Minister was a strong supporter
of the Government at that time, but I was
not a supporter, although I supported the
Education Acts, and I supported the
Government when I thought they were
right, and condemned them when I
thought they were wrong. I would hesitate before I would pretend that in 1930
the Government were acting contrary to
the Constitution and to the Act of 1920.
I think it is a ridiculous position to take
up. The Attorney-General of that day
is not the Attorney-General of to-day. It
is not the business of the Attorney-
General of to-day to go back and tell us
whether the Attorney-General of 1930 was
or was not right. That is not his business
under any circumstances. It is his business to refer us to anything that arises at

I feel that if it had not been for the war
the Government would have considered

These men in the prisons may not be the

amongst them. I feel that prisons to-day

Government should take the prisoners
away to a big estate, where the men
might become good citizens by learning
to perform agricultural and other duties.
When a man goes into prison he does not

I am a visitor at the prison, and I have

is room for reform in the prisons of
Northern Ireland. The right hon.
Gentleman, the Minister of Home Affairs,
has told us that it is much needed. I do
hope that when the war is finished, and
when we can turn attention to reform of
many classes, that this reform is one that
will not be lost sight of.
The hon. Member for Central Belfast

Oral Answers
Oral Answers
15 MARCH 1945
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Tuesday, 1st February, 1944.
The Seventh Session of the Fifth Parliament of Northern Ireland appointed to
meet on 1st February, 1944, in the
Eighth year of the Reign of King George
VI., was opened by the Governor (His
Grace the Duke of Abercorn, K.G.,
K.P.) in person.
The House met at Ten Minutes before
Twelve of the Clock, Mr. SPEAKER
(Right Hon. H. G. H. Mulholland) in
the Chair.
Brigadier-General
H. G. Young,
C.I.E., D.S.O., acting Gentleman Usher
of the Black Rod, was announced.
Addressing Mr. Speaker, the Acting
Gentleman Usher said:
His Grace the Governor of Northern
Ireland commands this Honourable
House to attend immediately in the
Senate.
The House went, and having returned,
The Sitting was suspended until Two
of the Clock, and then resumed.
Paper Presented.
Ministry of Labour:
National Health Insurance (Arrears)
Amendment Regulations, 1943. (By Act.)
SESSIONAL ORDERS.
ELECTIONS.
Ordered, That all Members, who are
returned for two or more places in any
part of Northern Ireland do make their
Election for which of the places they will
serve, within one week after it shall
appear that there is no question upon the
Return for that place; and if anything
shall come in question touching the
Return of Election of any Member, he is
to withdraw during the time the matter
is in debate, and that all Members returned upon double Returns do withdraw
till the Returns are determined.
Resolved-That if it shall appear that
any person hath been elected or returned
a Member of this House or endeavoured
so to be, by bribery, or any other corrupt
practices, this House will proceed with
the utmost severity against all such persons as shall have been wilfully concerned
such bribery or other corrupt
in
practices.
WITNESSES.
Resolved: That if it shall appear that
any persons have been tampering with
any Witness in respect of his evidence to
be given to this House, or any Committee
thereof, or directly or indirectly hath
endeavoured to deter or hinder any person
from appearing or giving evidence, the
same is declared to be a high crime or
misdemeanour; and this House will proceed with the utmost severity against
such offender.
Resolved: That if it shall appear that
any persons hath given false evidence in
any case before this House or any Committee thereof, this House will proceed
with the utmost severity against such.
offender.

King's Speech
ROYAL ULSTER CONSTABULARY.
Ordered: That the Commissioner of
the Royal Ulster Constabulary do take
care that, during the Session of Parliament the passages through the streets
leading to this House be kept free and
open, and that no obstruction be permitted to hinder the passage of Members
to and from this House, and that no
disorder be allowed in the precincts of or
in the passages leading to this House,
during the Sitting of Parliament, and
that there be no annoyance therein,
or thereabouts, and that the Serjeant-at-
Arms attending this House do communicate this Order to the Commissioner of
the Royal Ulster Constabulary aforesaid.
VOTES, PROCEEDINGS AND
RECORDS.
Ordered, That the Votes, Proceedings
and Records of this House be printed,
being first perused by Mr. Speaker; and
that he do appoint the printing thereof;
and that no person but such as he shall
appoint do presume to print the same.
PRIVILEGES.
Ordered, That a Committee of Privileges be appointed.
OUTLAWRIES BILL,
"for the more effectual preventing
Clandestine Outlawries," was read the
First time.
KING'S SPEECH.
Mr. SPEAKER: I have to report that
the House has this day attended in the
Senate to hear His Grace's Speech on
behalf of His Majesty to both Houses of
Parliament, of which I have for greater
accuracy obtained a copy. The Speech is
as follows:
Members of the Senate and of the
House of Commons.
Since I last addressed you the Forces
of the United Nations have been
enabled, by God's Providence, to assume
the offensive in all theatres of war with
results which justify high hopes for the
future. Northern Ireland, as part of
the United Kingdom, is willingly and
proudly contributing to the mighty
effort of the Allies and I feel confident
that our people, in company with all
other freedom-loving peoples, will
maintain their whole-hearted efforts to
bring about that complete and final
victory which we are resolved
achieve.
to
The happiest relationship continues
to exist between my Government and
the various arms of the Allied Forces
in Northern Ireland, and I have noted
with deep satisfaction the many manifestations of good feeling between the
members of those Forces and the civil
population.
Two years ago my Government
extended cordial greetings to the
American Troops on their landing in
Northern Ireland These were the
vanguard of mighty Forces which have
since crossed the ocean to take their
share in the battles against the enemy
on this side of the Atlantic. Many of
them are now in our midst, and we
welcome them as the representatives of
a great Ally whose friendly co-operation and goodwill have been abundantly
shown In many branches of our
common war effort. I trust that in
the years to come our comrades-inarms from the United States will
treasure the memories of their stay in
Northern Ireland as an abiding proof
of the respect and friendship of our
people for their great Nation.
I rejoice to learn of the gallant
exploits of Northern Ireland units on
the fighting fronts and have noted
with pride that many volunteers from
this part of the United Kingdom,
serving in all branches of the Forces
and in the Merchant Navy, have been
awarded decorations for bravery and
devotion to duty. The demand for
more recruits remains urgent, and it
is my earnest hope that our young men
and women will answer the call in
ever-increasing numbers.
The Ulster Home Guard, under the
guidance and direction of the military
authorities, has become a well armed
and well trained Force. .I am confident that its members can be relied
on to meet with efficiency and devotion
the calls that may be made on them.
The Civil Defence Services are being
maintained in constant readiness to
deal with attacks which the enemy may
launch against us. I am glad to
know that the risk of loss of life and
King's Speech

property has been reduced by greatly
improved fire-fighting facilities.
Our farmers have made a splendid
response to the appeal for increased
food production during the past year.
It is due to their efforts, supplemented
by the help of unemployed industrial
workers and volunteers from the towns,
that such a large crop has been safely
gathered in, notwithstanding the unfavourable weather during the harvesting season.
Although the area under the plough
is not to be increased during the
coming season, my Government confidently hopes that the more extensive
use of artificial fertilisers will result in

is still a pressing need. A greater
acreage of flax is essential to meet the
increasing demands of our wor
factories; and I have no doubt that
our farmers will make an even larger
contribution in the present year.

substantial increase in the production

I observe with satisfaction that

harmonious relationships between

unemployed is welcome evidence of the

absorption of available

which local authorities have
perienced, through the operation of

date. At the request of my Government Sir Francis Floud recently
examined the scope of the duties of the

The transition from war to peace
conditions will create intricate problems
affecting the entire community. I am
therefore gratified to learn that my
Government continues to devote unremitting attention to the framing of
post-war policy. On a number of the
wider issues involved in the formulation
of plans for the future my Ministers are
maintaining the closest contact with the
Imperial Government. Every endeavour is, therefore, being made to prepare for the reconstruction period and

to ensure the development and
expansion of our industries within the
economic structure of
of the United
Kingdom.
Some post-war questions will, however, fall within the jurisdiction of the
Parliament of Northern Ireland, and I
have learned with satisfaction that
many sudh matters have already
received detailed attention from my
Ministers. It has been found possible
to make a start in dealing with the
housing problem, and I am confident
that, so far as the supply of building
material permits, further progress will
be made in this direction. The Report
of the Select Committee on Health
Services has now been issued and will be
of value in the moulding of future
policy in matters relating to the physical
well-being of our people.
The development of Social Insurance
and other Social Services is closely
engaging the attention of the Imperial
Government. Any action taken as a
result of those deliberations will have
its counterpart in Northern Ireland in
pursuance of the frequently expressed
policy of my Government to maintain
equal standards with Great Britain in
these matters.
Also prominent amongst the matters
which are receiving consideration is the
position of the linen industry, into
which an expert Committee is conducting an investigation.
The education system of Northern
Ireland is under comprehensive review
by my Ministers, whose earnest resolve
is to bring about a marked advance in
the provision of educational facilities.
A White Paper dealing with this most
important matter is being prepared and
will be laid before you in due course.
I rejoice to learn that law and order
have been well maintained and I desire
to commend the skill, efficiency and
high sense of duty displayed by the
Royal Ulster Constabulary and the
Special Constabulary under difficult
war conditions.
I pray that the blessing of Almighty
God may rest upon your deliberations.
Debate on the Address.
Lieut.-Colonel PANTER (in morning
dress): I beg to move:
That a humble Address be presented
to His Grace the Governor of Northern
Ireland as followeth :
Your Grace,
We, His Majesty's most dutiful
and loyal subjects, the Commons of
Northern Ireland, in Parliament
assembled, beg leave to offer our
humble thanks to your Grace for the
Speech which your Grace has addressed
to both Houses of Parliament.
It is indeed a great honour to my constituents and myself, who represent
historic Mourne, to be entrusted with the
task of moving the Address in Reply to
the Gracious Speech, more especially at
such an epoch in our harmonic naval,
military, and air force onslaughts, which
are characteristic of our tenacity of purpose, and our determination to see this
business through to the end.
No doubt you will allow me to refer
back to the 19th of December, 1939, when
I was privileged to second the Vote of
thanks in reply to the Gracious Speech on
that day, and when I ventured to suggest
to those assembled in this House the
following:-
"I should like to make it crystal
clear that none of the difficulties which
I have mentioned must be allowed to
dismay us. It is probably a platitude
to say that difficulties are made to be
overcome. The stress and ever-increasing strain of War has forced us to carry
out in days, an organisation that in
normal times would have taken us as
many months, if not years. It is
inevitable that there should be loose
ends and pieces, in some cases
anomalies, and in others even abuses.
This war has been described as a war of
mental attrition, but I prefer to think
of it as a test of patience and of faith,
and I am convinced that if our whole
population are quietly patient and
steadfastly unshaken in their belief,
both in the justice of our cause and
ultimate victory, not all the armies,
nor all the propaganda, nor all the
intrigue in the world, can possibly
defeat us."
That was December, 1939, and I can
see no reason why those views should be
changed to-day. The winning of the war,
as the Gracious Speech implies, must be
our first and most important objective,
and, in fact, our patience and faith, to

a
which I have already alluded, have since
been rewarded by the unstinted, everincreasing, and overpowering contribution
afforded to us by the armed forces of the
United States of America, some of whose
members. we welcome in this House to-day.
And I might add that it is my fervent
wish, that the friendship which has
sprung up between us will become
guiding light to all nations, and may conceivably prove to be one of the methods
whereby ignorance of each other can be
abolished and misunderstandings resulting
in war banished for ever. Our patience
and faith have also been rewarded by the
crushing defeats being meted out to the
Nazis by our Russian Allies, and last, but
not least, by the expulsion of the enemy
from North Africa-(hon. Members:
Hear, hear)—the invasion of Europe from
the south, the capture of three great
inlands, the advances in Italy, the U-boat
and Scharnhorst successes, and the breaking up of the Berlin-Rome axis.
These have been some of the changes in
our fortunes, but knowing the crafty
Hitlerite Hun I realise that it would be
folly and madness for anyone of us to
relax for a moment. The enemy is still
strong and determined. War is full of
surprises, so we cannot afford to indulge
in any illusions as to the magnitude of
the task ahead, nor should we minimise
the imperative necessity of the nations,
who march together in war, particularly
the British Empire and Commonwealth,
the United States of America and Russia,
standing as firmly as a rock together
when victory embraces our allied
arms.
The Gracious Speech, as well as dealing
with the successful prosecution of the
war, which is the first preoccupation of
the Government and country, alludes to
preparations for post-war life, so let us
hope that we can look upon the coming
session as a dual purpose session, because
if we do not make adequate preparations
now we shall surely be caught as unprepared for peace as we were for war.
The whole tone of the Gracious Speech
signifies "There is no road back to
yesterday and to-morrow starts to-day";
indeed a good omen, and together with
our inspired, determined and vigorous
Bridgehead leadership let us strive for
active and concrete results without undue
delay or friction.
As men and women return from war
service and industries they cannot expect
to find the transitional period easy, but
they will at least expect and have been
officially promised food, homes, and
employment.
I realise that this Speech should be
non-controversial, but I assume that this
does not eliminate enthusiasm and constructive candour, such as a suggestion
for a thoroughly satisfied agricultural
community, of which my constituency is
entirely composed. We all know only too
well that the farmers, through their own
exertions, were instrumental in saving
the country during a grave period in the
last war, but what happened after?
Poverty and distress.
Mr. HENDERSON: Shame!
Lieut.-Colonel PANTER: Take the
position of the farmers to-day, they have
again put their shoulders to the plough
and come to the rescue. If we owed them
a debt of gratitude in 1918, how much
greater is our indebtedness to-day? I am
one of those who do not believe that the
farmers are in search of some mythical
Utopia, but I am convinced that fair
prices, security, and definite assurances
about the future, present no difficulties.
We know the amount we produce, and
the amount we consume, we also know
that starving Europe will require any
surplus including cattle for the next five
or six years.
From such data it should not be difficult for experts to draw up a six-year
plan, it is indeed a golden opportunity.
We have an Imperial House consisting
of all parties, and in the post-war period,
each Government of whatever party it
might be formed, would be tied to a
policy which they themselves sanctioned,
whilst in the coalition Government the
farmers would thus be assured of their
ever present and ever increasing value to
the State. This is merely an example of
one of the many problems that will no
doubt confront us, and what I have expressed to-day is my interpretation of
the theme of the Gracious Speech, which
is both inspiring and creative.
There is a nobility of spirit abroad
to-day, there is an eagerness amongst the
men and women of the country. Let us
then unleash these forces so that with a
spirit of unity and strenuous endeavour
we may plan, prepare, and erect, an

reason, but had to depend solely upon

It is natural, too, that the Gracious
Speech should contain references-and

in the war. In 1940 and 1941, when
France was overwhelmed and Italy was
against us, when Belgium, Holland and

-and when the aim of the enemy was

one step alone, remained-the invasion of

might well have been attempted. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)
The triangulation of the three great
ports on the Clyde, Mersey and Lagan has

I think it is fair to say, and also true to
say, that Ulster in this war has an
importance entirely out of relation to
its geographical area and to its
population. But apart from our straand
tegical position
its value has

When we come to consider post-war reconstruction, perhaps the most clamant

leeway to make up. Over a great many

do not know how far the writer is in the

The present permission to the Belfast

Another point in the King's Speech
refers to the Estimates for public
services. I am going to suggest, and I
think it is the first time it has been
suggested in this House, that it is time
to establish a loan development fund to
carry out the reconstruction of the
Province. We cannot depend entirely on
grants made by the Imperial authority
from the Imperial Contribution; we must
make an effort ourselves to create a liquid
capital fund to finance schemes of reconstruction. We cannot depend on private
enterprise, its day is past. We do not
live in the nineteenth century. We live
in 1944, and we know the risks of the
individual now are too great for him to
invest his money because big monopolies
cause fear and trembling to the small
investor. Monopolies decide all our lines
of production. Therefore, if we are to
have methodically planned reconstruction
.
the Government must have control over
the liquid resources of capital, to direct
it into essential channels and not leave
it in the hands of private individuals.
A loan development fund is necessary and
important. We cannot go ahead with a
post-war programme depending on grants
from the Imperial Contribution. We in
this part of the world can raise this loan
development fund and keep it for the
requirements of our people and use it
when the necessity arises. All talk about
reconstruction and planning is nonsense
without the liquid resources to do the
job.

The Speech makes that declaration, and

for the children of England. This will

A good deal of controversy has been

of providing, equipping, and repairing

One of the most serious problems which

now crying out for 70,000 teachers. We
are also crying out for more teachers. If
you want more teachers you must make
the profession attractive by raising the
present sorry scale of salaries to an attractive figure so that you will get the
best class or type into the profession. If

get the type of boy and girl who will be

operating in the profession.

All those who passed through college and

We must have many more teachers

There should be parity also with the

The PRIME MINISTER (Sir Basil
Brooke): I know that it is conventional
to congratulate the Mover and Seconder
of the Address, but I think it is particularly appropriate on the present
occasion because the two hon. Gentlemen
are hon. and gallant Gentlemen. They
played their part in the last war most
gallantly, and I think it is significant
that in the year 1944, when we see such
great events unfolding before us, that
these two gentlemen should have moved
and seconded the Address of humble
thanks to His Grace the Governor in such
an extremely able and eloquent way.
It is only right that I should refer to
the first portion of the Gracious Speech
where His Grace mentions the British
Forces and the Forces of the United
States. Since 1939 we have been glad to
welcome our own soldiers in our midst.
We were glad to offer them what
hospitality we could, and we were glad
to co-operate in any way we could. I am
sure I am expressing not only my own
feelings as Prime Minister but the feelings
of the members of the previous Government when I say that nowhere could we
have found a greater anxiety to help us
in what was not altogether an easy task,
and also to co-operate with us in our
schemes in an adequate way. I do wish
to express my gratitude to the General
Officer Commanding the British troops,
our own troops, for the way they have
worked into the scheme of things.

In addition to that we have had our
friends the Americans amongst us.
want to say that the welcome and
hospitality which has gone out to them
has been given with a heart and a half.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I think
hon. Members will realise that when
soldiers are away from home, and have not
their home ties, and when public opinion
is not so strong as in their own country
there may be trouble occasionally, but I
can say quite truthfully that it would be
impossible to find strangers who worked
in better and behaved better than the
American troops we have amongst us
to-day. When we look at the campaign
which has just opened in Italy—it has
been completed in North Africa and
Sicily-I know from personal contact that
the co-operation between the British and
American troops has been of the highest
order; in fact they are not two armies,
but one army working for one
purpose.
I should like to feel that the presence of
so many of these gallant men from the
States in this country has helped to
remove misunderstandings we might have
had about each other, because when we do
not know another nation we are perhaps
inclined to think the worst of them.
Introducing them into Ulster first perhaps has helped them to understand and
to realise that the differences between us
are really very small indeed. I like to
think this point was referred to by the
Mover and Seconder of the Address-that
this land of ours has been able to help in
training and making efficient not only
British troops but also the American
soldiers, and that our bases, ports and
aerodromes have done something to defeat
the threat of the U boat in the Atlantic,
and, perhaps, helped to protect American
troops on their long journey across the
sea.
This year may be a momentous one. I
do not think we ought to be carried away
by the feeling that there is necessarily
going to be victory in 1944. In a war of
this kind nobody can say what will
happen. It may be 1945 or 1946. As we
see the picture, we believe that 1944 will
produce victory. Not only the military
forces but the civilian forces of the great
nations are working to that end. The
climax is being reached, and it is a
striking fact that in spite of five years of
war the democratic form of Government
has succeeded in carrying through and
making good during a very difficult
period. Without in any way wishing to
lecture the House, I should like to look at
the responsibilities which are incumbent
upon us all. The hon. Member for
Pottinger mentioned that criticism is
essential to democratic government.
Freedom of debate is also essential.
I would draw the attention of the House
to the fact that the last four or five debates which we had in the last Parliament
were of an extremely high order. Previous
to that I had spoken to hon. and right
hon. Gentlemen about this matter. I suggested that hon. Members should move
amendments to Clauses in Committee
stage with a great deal more freedom than
was done previously. Members of the
House may not realise the method by
which Bills are prepared. First of all
they are probably debated in the Ministry
or the particular Department concerned.
When I was Minister of Agriculture we
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
1 FEBRUARY 1944
A
used to have strong debates on various
clauses. The Bill then comes before the
Cabinet, and the wording of the Clauses,
or the Clauses themselves, are very often
merely a matter of opinion. I see no
reason why hon. Members should not, if
they think it right, move the deletion of a
Clause or an amendment to it, provided
it does not cut across the principle of the
Bill.
Perhaps hon. Members feel that if they
move an amendment to a Bill they are
giving the Government notice to quit. I
do not think it is necessarily notice to quit.
The Government is the best judge of when
that moment arrives, and it will take such
action as is necessary. I think it is necessary to keep Parliament alive. Sometimes
the accusation goes out that these Bills
are purely Civil Service Bills. They are
none the worse for that, because we have
the best civil servants in any part of the
United Kingdom. By having closer debates on the Committee stage we will
improve the whole standard of debate and
cause a greater interest to be taken in our
political affairs.
I do not wish to follow the hon. Member for Pottinger in his ramifications in
regard to certain articles which have
appeared in the Press. The Members of
the House are the best judges as to what
is to happen to the Government. If this
House decides that the Government has
got to go the Government will accept the
challenge with pleasure, but the Government is not going to be influenced by any
outside party. It is within the rights of
Parliament to deal with this Government
and its fate. The Government is not
ashamed of what it has done and what it
intends to do, and it will deal with all
matters to the best of its ability.
I think the hon. Member for Pottinger
has turned over a new leaf, because he
has expressed anxiety at the opinions expressed by people in England which are
not in favour of this country.
No doubt
it was mixed up in the criticism of the
Government itself, but the impression it
left was that this country was a very poor
place to live in. I am glad to see he now
resents anybody attacking this country. I
think it is most unfortunate that in the
process of attacking the Government—it is
always there to be attacked and must
justify its existence
should
tarnish the fair name of Ulster or the
gallantry of its people.

anyone
We are now in the fifth year of war, and
it is necessary for us all to think and think
deeply. When I say that, I mean not
only the party which happens to be on
all
this side of the House, but that
Members should think of how we can get
over the difficult times which lie ahead.
Somehow or other we have to find a better
way of life for our people. I think
democracy which has stood the test of the
most ghastly war in history should also
be able to stand the test which will come
as peace draws closer. We in Ulster have
earned the right to deserve a victorious
peace.
The Gracious Speech has mentioned the
efforts which this very small part of the
British Empire has played towards the
winning of the war. Our main industry
is agriculture, and surely no man can say
that the farmers of this country have not
done a magnificent job in connection with
the difficult times we have been through.
New methods have been put into practice;
mechanisation has developed to a considerable extent; there has been a
tightening up of the whole industry, but
without the efforts of the men and women
on the farms, people who have had to
stand the extremely inclement weather we
have experienced for the past two years,
such an increase in our agricultural output could not have been obtained. They
were not down-hearted; they got on with
the job of saving the crops.
Hon. Members should realise that this
eternal question of flax is still an important one. If I could take up a farmer
and if he had to come down by parachute
I am sure he would feel much safer if he
had one made from Ulster flax. He
would jump with more confidence than if
he had a parachute made from a substitute material. It is hard for them to
realise that the crop they are growing is
essential for victory.
The Gracious Speech states that there
will be no increase in the Tillage Order,
but nevertheless it is hoped that the more
extensive use of fertilisers will help production. As the farmers have COoperated so well during the war, I would
ask them also to do their best when peace
comes along.
On the industrial side we have reason
The
to be proud of our contribution.
shipyards and factories have done a truly

magnificent job.
That work has been
acknowledged by responsible Ministers on

We have had difficulties to face.
One cannot move from peace to war without upsetting many of the things which
have been in existence for, perhaps, 100
years. However, all these difficulties
have been got over by a realisation of the
urgency of the situation.
I want to remind hon. Members that
the most potent factor in removing such
difficulties has been the Production
Council, which is composed of representatives of the employers, trade unions, and
officers of the various Supply Departments. As an adjunct to that Council
we
have established Joint Production
Committees in most of the engineering
factories. I think I am right in saying
that in Northern Ireland we have probably more of these Production Committees for the number of engineers employed
than in any part of the United Kingdom.
They have made for efficiency by pointing
out difficulties to the management, and
they have removed many sources of discontent which might have boiled up into
a strike. They have also helped welfare
work which is of the utmost importance
at the present time.
I realise we all realise-that after five
years of war everybody is a little bit
weary and just not perhaps on the tips of
his toes as he was before. Men and
women have been working on the same
machine for perhaps four or five years,
and therefore small grievances, perhaps,
assume undue proportions. But I would
ask all those engaged in industry to think
very carefully before they strike. The
machinery is there. These upsets and
troubles can be dealt with. The trade
unions are looking after the interests of
their men.
The men themselves have
some responsibility with a great sense of
the importance of looking after their own
people, so that I might appeal to them
when dealing with grievances of any type
dealt with by trade unions to take their
advice and if possible submit those grievances to the proper tribunals, rather than
take the matter into their own hands
straight away.
So far as housing is concerned we have
had a debate on that already. We realise
that the limiting factor is material. For
these 750 houses the amount of steel
necessary would roughly build a ship.
The amount of steel that would be required to be used in those houses in peace
time it is a little reduced now-would
build a ship of a thousand tons. The
timber bottle neck is the other shortage.
Hon. Members will realise that bridges in
Italy have to be built and piers have to
be built, and you cannot use unseasoned
timber for building houses of the sort we
want. I hope the House realises that the
subsidy that has been obtained for Northern Ireland houses is the highest subsidy, or rather equal to the highest that
exists in any part of the United Kingdom.
Hon. Members have referred to the
Report of the Select Committee. I
would like if I might to congratulate the
very
able Chairman and his Committee on
the fine Report which they have issued.
It is a fine piece of work, and I can
assure him the Government will consider
it most sympathetically.
So far as the post-war position is concerned the Ministries here are in close
touch with their opposite numbers on the
other side. In addition to that I have
had the pleasure of meeting Lord Woolton
and discusisng with him the various
problems with which he is faced and with
which in a minor degree this Government
is faced. I can assure the House that Lord
Woolton realises our position and he is
prepared to allow us to have a representative on any of the conferences or meetings if we desire, and he will keep us
fully informed of any movement in the
situation which comes before him. As to
education, a White Paper I hope will be
issued and a full debate can take place.
I need say very little more. We hope
that before this Session is over we may
have to try to solve some of the many
difficult problems that we will have to
face, but I do not think that Utopia will
arrive by any scheme of an armchair
critic. It will be worked out by men who
will have to think very deeply. It will
have to be worked out by people with
patience who see that the new world cannot come in a night. But I think that
as we have taken our share, and I think,
considering our size, a good share, a
creditable share, in victory which I
believe will be coming, so I think we can
face the struggle for peace in an equally
fine and satisfactory way. When I say
peace I do not just mean the
of
peace

tranquillity. I mean the peace whereby
men and women can live a happier and
a better life where there is greater final
prosperity in the nation.
Mr. NIXON: I should just like at the
outset to congratulate the Mover and
Seconder of the Address. I did not hear
all the Mover said, but certainly the
Seconder spoke extremely well. I would
also congratulate the Prime Minister on
what he said. Now at the outset I should
like to point out for the benefit of some
of our friends who perhaps do not understand this document headed "The King's
Speech" and which is read to us by His
Grace the Governor that they have no responsibility for the document at all and
that we, the freely elected Members of this
House, can criticise it, vote for it or
reject it or do what we like with it. It
is only a statement of the policy of the
Government and we can agree with it in
so far as we agree with that policy. And
I particularly, as one perhaps of the
greatest critics of the Government in this
House, agree absolutely with all the Prime
Minister said and all he did to cultivate
the very best of relations with out great
ally here in Northern Ireland, the members of the U.S.A. Forces and also of
course never forgetting our own men. We
never do that.
•
me
I would say that I have far more kinsmen in U.S.A. than I have in this
country, and in the part of the country
I come from two-thirds of the people at
least that were at school with
emigrated to U.S.A. They were received
with kindness and they got work and they
did well. We can like the U.S.A. Forces
for their own personality. I hear nothing
but what is good about them. Of course
we know there is an odd thief trying to
get money from them for nothing. We
know that, but it is up to the police
authorities to arrest them and the magistrates will know what to do. Mr..
Churchill got for us as allies the two
greatest nations in the world, Soviet
Russia and the U.S.A., and in our own
interests and in the interests of the peace
of the world it is up to us in our own
little way to do our best to cultivate their
friendliest relations.
The Prime Minister so far as his speech
is concerned touched on nothing that one
could criticise. He touched on nothing
that I do not agree with, and I should like
to be able in what may be the last year
of the war and what will be the seventh
year of this Parliament-I should like
that the Prime Minister would give me
the privilege of being able to agree with
his policy until the end of this Parliament. But judging by some of the things
that appear in the latter part of the
King's Speech I am going to be deprived
of that privilege. And again that is all
coming from the same source.
A great
many people think they can laugh at me
and think I am done. It may take ten,
fifteen or twenty years, but I will turn
the laugh into a grin sooner or later. It
has always happened. I know there are
scores of people who think they can floor
me like that, but then after a few trials
they give up. It is not for the like of
that I come here at all. I do not want
that, but I am not going to allow any
Member or Minister no matter who he is,
no matter how well I like him, to drown
my personal opinion of what is right and
what is wrong in regard to matters of
policy. Most of you know what I am
driving at.
We come to the question of houses.
Everyone agrees that something about
housing will have to be done and done
quickly. And I think everyone that is
reasonable will agree with the Prime
Minister that it is very difficult to get
material, but I say the Government is not
doing all that should be done or that
could be done. Sometimes there is a
controversy about whether houses should
be built of concrete or of bricks. I cannot see why that should be controversial
at all in a country where you can have any
amount of bricks if you would only allow
people to make them. Concrete is not as
suitable for building as brick, and every
brickyard in Belfast is full of bricks and
the brickmakers are idle. It was brought
up here before, and we got no satisfaction,
that the Government should buy the
bricks and dump them in a suitable place
and allow the brickmakers to employ men
making more bricks and have them
available when the time comes. Sometimes you ask for constructive criticism.
Constructive criticism is suggesting to the
Government what might reasonably be
done within the resources in their power.
The Government might reasonably give
consideration to that suggestion, and that
is a thing they have not done. And then
when the time comes for building the
Government will be the way they were

before-importing bricks to Northern
Ireland in shiploads, whereas they could

at hand.
Now, I leave that for the moment to

my
Who should be consulted about this?
Who bans this? Who in the Cabinet has
any knowledge of housing? Certainly
not the Prime Minister himself, and not
the Minister of Home Affairs. I am sure
they would be the first to say they know
nothing about it, and if they would not
say it I would say it for them. The
Minister of Finance I know does know
