Government go asking officials for their
opinion on everything. Why not take
the opinion of Members of this House
sometimes? That has been urged here
more than once, but it has been shelved.
And we have one of the usual visits to
England, running round looking at
houses. We were told some few months
ago before some political meeting that on
the suggestion of the Minister of Home
Affairs the Parliamentary Secretary went
to London by air to inquire into the question of houses and to examine houses, and
then he was to come home and report to
his chief. That all happened. Some
people thought he would bring a house or
two home in the aeroplane. He came
back and he reported to his chief. Then
there was another race round England
which has just concluded. And all the
time people want houses.
The thing we never inquired about or
were told about is, what will be the probable rent of the houses that are to be
built? That is one of the most important
subjects. Sometimes we have lectures
from architects who have been brought
over from England. I notice that one of
the things these noble architects condemned was petrol pumps alongside the
road. I wonder where they would be
put if not along the roads on which
people would be driving. The architects
are very artistic, and their noble sense
would be hurt by a petrol pump.
If
one was driving his car and ran out of
petrol he would be very glad to see a
pump. As long as we have people like
that conducting the policy of housing we
will have no houses.
The Member for Pottinger suggested
that the post-war position of Ulster so
far as the Boundary is concerned is hardly
safe or reliable and that the people across
the water were not too sure of it. If we
are not then that is our own look-out.
Personally I do not accept that. At all
events I want to tell the Prime Minister
something I have been thinking about.
I have a lot of connections in London.
It is a place I used to go to frequently.
What I say now does not refer to the
Prime Minister. There is no respect in
London or any other place for a crawler
who goes with his hat in his hand to
some civil servant and says,
If you
please, sir, will you give me that?"
There is no respect anywhere for that
class of individual.
""
The late Lord Carson never went that
way. The way to take those people is to
say that we in Northern Ireland are a
Government with certain powers and we
will let no person from Great Britain
interfere with those powers. We would
not even listen to him. There is only
one way this Parliament can be interfered with. We hear a lot about the
Atlantic Charter. I agree with the
Atlantic Charter, and the right of the
people to select any Government they
want. I wanted more men of my point
of view elected on this Government, but
so long as this Government are elected I
will make my. protest here and do my
best both inside and outside and accept
the ruling of the majority.
The Prime Minister did not mention
coal. A lot of people are criticising the
Prime Minister for the statement he made
regarding the surrender of coal due to
Northern Ireland. But what makes the
people of Northern Ireland particularly
bitter at the present moment is that the
German and Japanese Embassies in
Dublin are burning English coal. They
are doing that now, when there are
soldiers' wives and soldiers' mothers in
Northern Ireland with only coke or slack
in their grates. We are entitled to resent
that and the Prime Minister and the
other Cabinet Ministers have a right to
talk to the Imperial Government on that
subject the way I am talking to them
now. There is no use in going over
crawling while the like of that is going
on. It is about time this crawling
stopped. There is too much of it. One
of the things that pleased the Prime
Minister in regard to the Mover and
Seconder of the Address was that they
were hon. and gallant Members; that

they were ex-Servicemen.
As I stand
here and look across the Table I am in-
T clined to wonder why he did not give the
ex-Servicemen a better show in his
Cabinet, because the most useless men he
has in it are the men who are not ex-
Servicemen. I am not referring to the

now for a little bit.
t

On the last day the House met I had
down a question to the Minister of Labour
regarding work in war factories and regarding his policy of refusing to allow
men or women engaged in them to better
themselves. The Minister in his reply
stated something like this. He said that
I knew that his Ministry were very
favourably inclined to help people in that
matter. Speaking about administration,
what the Minister said is freely admitted,
but I want the right hon. Gentleman always
to remember that there is a line drawn between administration and policy. Administration is how the officials and the
Minister interpret and carry out the rules,
regulations, orders and laws of the Department. Now, no one pays more tribute to the
administration than I do, but I can pay
a tribute to administration and at the
same time be dissatisfied with the policy,
which is another thing altogether.
policy is quite different. from the
administration.
The
No later than yesterday I had with me
a man who was born in Court Ward,
Belfast. The Minister knows where that
is. He had with him his wife and child.
He is not in the Army because he was
rejected when he went to join. He went
to the shipyard where he always worked,
but they refused to allow him to work in
the shipyard because he was not an ex-
Service man. It is not his fault that he
is not an ex-Service man. That is policy.
I can be dissatisfied with that, but it is
not essential that I object to the general
principle. Sometimes the Minister gets
up and he knows he is the last speaker.
He makes a statement calculated to make
the public believe that some of us are
against the policy of giving the preference
to ex-Service men all other things being
equal. We are not. I do not want the
Minister to do that again. He did it
before.
I could point out to the Minister that
his favourable policy to ex-Service men
is not always carried out. For instance,
it was not carried out in appointing the
chief of the Fire Service, nor was it
carried out in appointing the Chairman
of the Assistance Board. I could go a
bit farther but will not do so. My whole
object in going so far is this. So far as
the administration of the Minister's Department is concerned, I would not say
anything against it, nor would I allow
anybody else to say anything against it.
It is very considerate and the officials are
very kind and courteous to everyone who
comes out here. But if the Minister
makes rules he cannot stand over, then
that is another question.
There is another matter the Minister is
being blamed for, and I will put it up to
the House. I represent the most Protestant constituency in Ireland, and I am
proud to represent it. I stand for
Protestants, but I do not attack people of
other religions. As I say, I stand for
Protestants and I put them first. I remember that the late Lord Craigavon,
referring to the Boundary, said that so
long as we are here in Ulster, so long
would the Protestants in the Free State
be welcome to Ulster. At the present
time the residence permits of Protestants
who found work in Northern Ireland are
being cancelled wholesale. I spoke to the
Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry
of Home Affairs about it, and he said it
was the Minister of Labour who had
insisted on that policy.
I want to make it clear that I am
talking for Protestants. If other people
want to talk for Roman Catholics they
can. I am not blaming them. The Table
is here for them. I am talking for Protestants and we know that this is being
done, and being done wholesale. I know
it is actually done in the name of the
Minister of Home Affairs. I know that
the letters that are sent are headed,
"Ministry of Home Affairs." The Prime
Minister is listening to what I am saying.
He knows that everything I am saying is
correct. That is the promise that was
made by the late Lord Craigavon subsequent to the breaking of the Covenant
and the betrayal of the people of Cavan,
Monaghan, and Donegal. I have taken
on myself to point out publicly what has
happened. I came across one man from
East Donegal. He came down here and
got work. He took a house, was married,
and had two children. His residence

permit has been cancelled. I leave that

Now there is the Local Government
Officers Bill, in other words the John
Dunlop Bill. I did not think we would
get anything like that again. I thought
there had been enough about it. No
matter what the Lord Mayor or a few
councillors say, I am not going to accept
a dictatorship for Belfast. The only city
you have in Northern Ireland of any size
is Belfast. The Corporation of Belfast
consists of 47 official Unionists, three
Independent Unionists and the balance
Labour and Nationalist. That is a total
of 50 Unionists and ten non-Unionist.
You look upon them as so corrupt and
dangerous that they are not to be trusted
to buy what councils all over the United
Kingdom buy. They are nominated by
the same committees that nominate yourselves apart from the co-opted members
the Unionist members elect.
I think the Prime Minister in his
speech said something about being proud
of Ulster and of upholding it. I know
the previous Prime Minister often told us
never to slight Ulster. I never slighted
or ran down Ulster. Do you know any
better way to run down or slight Ulster
than to come into this House and by
Act of Parliament suggest that 47 official
Unionists out of a Council of 60 are not
to be trusted as such Councils are trusted
in England? Is it a wonder that the
people are getting doubtful of the future
position of Ulster if 47 official Unionists
out of 60 are men who cannot be trusted?
Who are these men? One of them belongs to your own party, the Member for
Windsor who sometimes sits here. He was
one of the members of the Corporation
who had to go into court to vindicate his
character. Although I do not agree with
him politically, I say that if I got a commission to find a decent, respectable,
honest, honourable man, I would say,
"Yes, the Member for Windsor is."
But
he and others I could mention are not to
be trusted. John Dunlop is. Not alone
that, but there is a special clause going to
be put into the Bill to indemnify him
against any mistakes he may make. A
councillor will be surcharged if he makes
a mistake. He will be prosecuted if he
does what is wrong, but if this Bill passes
John Dunlop cannot be prosecuted. In
other words, the King can do no wrong,
John Dunlop can do no wrong. I do not
think the House is going to agree to that
at all.

We will go a little deeper into it.
Whiteabbey was the excuse for all this.
Mr. Dunlop, Dr. Armstrong and Mr.
Gillespie were appointed to hold the inquiry, although the Minister of Home
Affairs took it on himself to contradict me
when I said that there was
special Act of Parliament, which
most of you will remember, passed
in 1938 to enable an inquiry of
this sort to be held by an inspector. Mr.
Dunlop was the identical man who passed
everything that happened in Whiteabbey.
There was one remarkable thing he never
inquired into, although the Attorney-
General did so. He never followed up
allegations about bribery. He dismissed
that, but the Attorney-General took that
up and issued a warrant which stands
and has not been executed because the
person charged in it with bribery was out
of the country. The then Minister of
Home Affairs was his solicitor. In view
of that you would think that the Government would wait until the inquiry by a
judge and jury was over. You would
think they would wait until the person
accused in the warrant and his colleagues
at home stand together in the dock.
the
Whatever the decision will be the one
service in Northern Ireland that we all
admire is the judiciary-his Majesty's
judges. That is one service that is not
criticised any place at home or abroad.
I never heard anything imputed to it
anywhere except that you get the law as
it is made when you go before his
Majesty's judges. The least the Government might do in this particular case is
to wait for the result of this particular
case unless it is that they want to raise

they will get plenty. If you want
dictators let the Administrators
tinue.
con-
Nobody has ever said they were
not decent men. I say they are decent
men, and of the three men who held the
inquiry Mr. Dunlop is now Town Clerk,
Dr. Armstrong is in charge of Whiteabbey, and Mr. Gillespie would be
Deputy Town Clerk only he was convicted
of roguery in the meantime.
I told you some years ago that the
whole of this legislation was to make John
Dunlop town clerk. Some of you did not
believe it. You know what you were told
at the party meeting and who told it to

you. You know that what you were told
was wrong. You know that well enough.
What do I want? I want to appeal to
the Prime Minister to exercise his
authority. I do not want to be going
against the Government at the present
time. The Prime Minister does not kick
up any rows, neither does the Minister
of Finance. It took me a while to make

Affairs a man that walked in with his

Prime Minister and said, "I will not
serve under you." Why did he do that
if he thought things were all right? How
can he get up and defend it after doing
that?
I did not know at the time, I confess,
why these gentlemen tendered their resignations. I know that they never gave
a public explanation, but I also know they
suffered in silence. People have said they
tendered their resignations and got jobs
on their own conditions. That was not
their motive. I am not referring by any
chance to the man who sat on the fence
and saw how things were going and came
down on the winning side. I am referring
to the Attorney-General, the present
Minister of Finance, the Parliamentary
Secretary of the Ministry of Commerce,
and I think the Parliamentary Secretary
of the Ministry of Education. I did not
know their motives at the time, but I
know them now. I know that they suffered
in silence. I know that they could have
vindicated themselves more in the eyes of
the public than they chose to do. I am
quite satisfied they could if they had been
let alone. I am quite satisfied no matter
how big the man may be or how well I
like him, if he tries to floor me I will
bring in Motions which he will hate to
vote for.
As to the question of Ministerial
salaries, I should like to congratulate the
ex-Minister of Finance on his ability in
showing how people with big salaries dodge
income-tax. He and the Member for North
Armagh seem to be masterpieces of
that thing judging from this report, the
sum total of which is, if it passes, that
every Cabinet Minister except two is
going to get £100 in his pocket by dodging
the income-tax. The reason those two are
not getting is, that I do not think they
are liable to income-tax except on their
salaries. If they are liable to income-tax
they are going to get £100 in their
pocket. The Prime Minister is certainly
entitled to something substantial for
entertainment, and I congratulate him on
the good use he is putting the money to.
He could not do a more laudable thing
than to give entertainment to people who
are in the forefront and in the conduct
of affairs; I do not mean that part of the
question at all.
There is another part I take serious
objection to. I am a very good attender
in this House. At one time I did not
come for seven months. I have the
honour to be the only Member of the
House that had his allowance stopped
for non-attendance. I was ill, but I
subsequently recovered. According to the
proposed regulations, if a man does not
attend for four months he is to get
nothing. He must have one-third attendance out of four months. There is hardly
a Member but that might happen to. A
civil servant gets six months. Do not let
anybody take away your liberty or right
as an M.P. Do not turn yourself into a
slave.
The Government did not bring this in.
I know that well enough. This was the
lever used to get at the Nationalists who
do not attend. I do not care how you get
at them, and I do not care whether they
attend or not. Get at them in any way
you like, but let the other Members alone.
To punish the majority to get at the few
is not the British way of doing things. I
appreciate what the Prime Minister said
about moving amendments to Bills. That
policy was carried out, and the debates
were very good. I think it did a lot of
good, and I appreciate the attitude which
the right hon. Gentleman has taken up on
the matter.

It is a good thing to know that.
man can do so, but it is an admission by

Then we have juvenile delinquency. I

The juveniles are no worse to-day than

Then I come to Rent Restrictions,

That is a good one.
We
cannot criticise that until we see what it

I would appeal to the Prime Minister
to preserve his own policy of upholding
Ulster and its honour. He is not upholding it by treating 47 Unionist colleagues in the city of Belfast as rogues.
That is not upholding it at all. I was
in the City Hall one day and the mayor
of a London borough was present. There
was a debate. With the usual pomp we
get from London he proceeded to
criticise the debate
""
which had taken
place in the Council. I said that it was
better here than across the water, and he

The Lord Mayor of Bradford is after
getting six months for stealing the carpet
off the floor. That was stooping very
low, because he had to stoop to get it.
I told the gentleman in question that

you take his advice you will not go far

King's Speech
Debate on the Address
2 FEBRUARY 1944
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Wednesday, 2nd February, 1944.
The House met at Two of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.

ORDER OF THE DAY.
KING'S SPEECH.
Motion for an Address.
Order read for resuming adjourned
Debate on Question (1st February):
That an Humble Address be presented
to His Grace, the Governor of Northern
Ireland, as follows:
Your Grace,
We, His Majesty's most dutiful and
loyal subjects, the Commons or Northern Ireland, in Parliament assembled,
beg leave to offer our humble thanks to
Your Grace for the speech which Your
Grace has addressed to both Houses of
Parliament.-(Lieut.-Colonel Panter.)
Question again proposed.

desire to pay a well-earned tribute to my
hon. and gallant Friends who are responsible for this Motion for an Address
in Reply to the King's Speech. I am
sure that we were all impressed with the
way in which they performed what is
looked upon as a very important but at
the same time difficult and delicate
Parliamentary duty. I am sure we are
also impressed by their earnestness and
their desire to be helpful.
I feel now that I should say candidly
that it is true that months
some

with Ulster courage those difficulties and

referred very appropriately to the Home

The Gracious Speech refers to our contribution to the war effort, and to the
fact that there are thousands of Ulstermen serving in the Forces of the Crown
and also in the Merchant Service. The
King's Speech also refers to the fact that
our farmers and their labourers are doing
a big job in providing the food and raw

Reference is also made to the fact that
our employers and their workpeople are
working together in harmony to provide
the weapons of war and the ships which
are required to bring us victory. All
these and other things are mentioned in
the Gracious Speech, and I congratulate
the Government upon it.
I appreciate the fact that the Government have not, as it were surrendered to
a certain clamour that is prevalent and
made promises which they might not be
in a position to fulfil. The Government
have stated quite bluntly what their intentions are, and in carrying out their
aims they can depend upon the loyal

true that on occasions some of us may
feel it necessary to express doubt about
the desirability of certain Bills. Suggestions for improving them may be made,
but such suggestions from this side of the
House are not put forward with any
desire to place difficulties in the way of
the Government or to embarrass them;
they are rather put forward with the
intention of helping the Government in
order that it may do what is best for the
people who owe allegiance to it.
The hon. and learned Member for St.
Anne's mentioned housing and health
services as the most important matters
requiring serious, earnest and immediate
attention. I want quite frankly to put
forward my views in connection with both
these important matters. As regards
housing there are ways of giving effect to
what is the desire of us all-that comfortable homes should be provided.
hear a great deal about the necessity for

anyone who will say that timber, iron and
other building materials which are required for our war effort should be used

for any other purpose until victory is

The land can be taken, but this is not

As regards our health services I should
like to say that I am happy that one of
the last acts of the late Government was
to bring into being the Health Committee. It was composed of interested
and earnest men who have produced a
report which-I think we all realise this
-will be of great help to the Government
in arranging that our standards in Northern Ireland as regards health shall not
be allowed to remain for long behind the

Britain. I venture to hope that without
unnecessary delay the Government will
let this House and the people know what
their intentions are in this connection. A
great many of the difficulties which
existed in the past have been cleared

local authorities will require to play their

Britain.
The Government have arranged that
funds will be available to the local autho-

Mr. HENDERSON: Might I take this
opportunity of saying how great a pleasure it was for me to be here yesterday to
listen to the speech delivered by the
Mover of the Address in Reply to the
Gracious Speech from the Throne? It is
not my intention to flatter the hon. and

Member of this House I never heard a

which was more to the point. I trust
that the Members of this House will hear

Member. To the hon. and learned
Member, who seconded the Address, I
also wish to offer my felicitations, but
not in such a strong manner as to the
hon. and gallant Member who moved it.
The hon. and learned Member is, like
myself, a revolutionist.
So far as Independent Unionism is concerned there is no necessity for us to
apologise for any break in our ranks. We
are standing four square, but there is a
split in the ranks of official Unionism.
The ex-Prime Minister, the right hon.
Member for Mid Down, has pointed out
that there is no split in the ranks of the
official Unionists, that they are united.
So far as the well-paid Government is
concerned that may be true, but so far as
the Unionist people of the country are
concerned it is entirely wrong. The
Unionist thought in this country which
is not turning towards Socialism is turning towards Independent Unionism. The
more speeches that are delivered by the
right hon. Gentlemen on the other side
of the House the stronger the Independent Unionist Party will become. There
is no necessity to worry about who will
run the country.
The right hon. Gentleman who is the
Member for Willowfield has referred to
the people that were sniping at the Prime
Minister. That is what I was sent here
for-to snipe, to hit hard and clean. I
have never hit below the belt. If I had
done so I might have a job on the other
side of the House. I always like to play
the game as cleanly as possible, at least
as cleanly as politics will allow one to
play it. It is not a game you can play
with extraordinary honesty.
Take the Prime Minister. He has
gallivanted all over the Empire. He has
been north, south, east and west. Is this
the manner in which they produce the
King's Speech across the water? In my
opinion this document is an insult to the
King. More economy. You have no call
to start economising in paper in so far
as
the Gracious Speech is concerned.
There are a thousand and one other ways
in which you could economise. I will try
to point them out. The Prime Minister
has wasted valuable time as well as taxpayers' money going across the water.
The Minister of Finance followed on his
heels. Not satisfied with that the Minister
of Labour followed after him and they
were all supposed to be doing something
for Ulster. Tell us what you have done
for Ulster. You have done absolutely
nothing.
I am one hundred per cent. with the
Prime Minister, the ex-Prime Minister
and every hon. Member on the other side
of the House in so far as our efforts to
bring about the termination of the war
are concerned. There is no one prouder
than I am. On every occasion I have the

going to be any peace in the world, that

America. We had a quarrel with America
once, but nevertheless we are brothers and
sisters and we speak the same language.
They have come hear to help us to defend
our freedom, and the best is not too good
for them. Therefore, I agree with the

Nothing. The men and women of this
country are anxious to work in the production of munitions of war, and with all
this speechmaking and blowing of
trumpets unemployment is rampant in
Ulster again. I think there are almost
3,000 more on the unemployment register
now. That is deplorable. If these
gentlemen had stayed at home it might
have been better. The Government should
be honest about this matter.
This Government brought men from
neutral Eire that have taken no part in
the war. You brought men from Southern
Ireland and gave them the jobs which you
should have been given to Ulster people
who are the backbone of this Government,
and which for the last 20 years you have
looked upon as the salt of the earth. You
were shipping boys and girls to England
who should have been kept along with the
fathers and mothers. You cared naught
about them. Now trouble has arisen, and
these men and women are unemployed.
Your own kith and kin who are 100 per
cent. loyal to the Empire are idle, but the
people you brought to Northern Ireland
are in employment here. The tactics
adopted here are everything but clean. I
make no apology for saying that. I have
always said in this House that as long as
one solitary man or woman of Ulster is
idle I protest against anyone being
brought here from England, Scotland or
Wales or the Free State. That is why
you are returned here-to get work for
the people. This Government, whether
the old guard, as it was christened by the
young ruffians, or the young ruffians
themselves, is just the same. There is no
change in the situation. The one crowd
is as bad as the other. The blood transfusion has not taken on. (An Hon.
Member: It was not the monkey glands?)
The monkey gland would be no use to
them. It would take an elephant gland
to be any use. It is not my intention to
punish them by giving them the monkey
gland. The men in charge of the zoological gardens at Bellevue would be
trying to capture them. The position is
too serious.
Might I take this opportunity of congratulating the hon. Member for the
University, who was the first to speak
about the health situation in Northern
Ireland. He deserves great credit. I
raise my hat to him. But his report will
go just the same way as the other report.
It is all right when a war is on, but when
you have the power you will do the same
with this report as you did with the last.
Is there anything new in that report? I
say no.
We on this side of the House for
the past 20 years have been pointing out
to you the unhealthy situation. We were
laughed at and sneered at and shouted
down. But thank God we have been delivered by a Member on your own side of
the House who has substantiated 100 per
cent. of everything we said. The report is
a volume costing two guineas or £2. The
man who would give 40s for it should be
in a lunatic asylum.
That Report is absolutely useless and I
will tell you why. You have deliberately
kept out of it the question of housing and
a water supply. The Public Health Committe did not deal with the principal
matter concerning a good public health
service. How can a public health service
function without a water supply? The
small towns and villages throughout
Northern Ireland are a disgrace to civilisation and this Government have nothing
to be proud of. You should hang your
heads in shame. It is only now after
being in office for 20 years you are talking about these reforms. The village
represented by the right hon. Member
for Mid Down has a water supply just
the same as existed at the time of Adam
and Eve. I know the Speaker will forgive me.
Being a Member of Parliament I love
to go down to the seaside. I go down at
the week-end. My wife and married
daughter live there and I try to forget
about this Parliament. If it were not
for going down there at the week-end I
would be in a mad house. Take Millisle.
Is there any difference in Millisle? The

Mr. HENDERSON: I usually get the
protection of the Chair. The present
housing situation is absolutely ridiculous.
What is taking place to-day? Does the
Minister of Home Affairs realise that
millions of bricks are being stacked up
and not used while there is all this
blethering about erecting concrete houses.
If you want to build houses you have in
Northern Ireland the best perforated
bricks to be found in any part of the
Empire. The Ulster brick manufacturers
do their job well. They have millions of
bricks stacked up with no market for
them. One man told me last night that
there were eight rats below the wooden
floor in his house and that no rats could
live in these concrete houses. I agree,
because they would be frozen to death in
such houses. The majority of the brick
manufacturers are friends of the Government, and if you take them into your
confidence I am satisfied they will produce
millions and millions more bricks in
addition to those they have in stock.
When you begin to build houses for the
people you will have no scarcity of
bricks.
I wish the Prime Minister would give
me the power to appoint a committee to
go into this question of housing. If he
gave me the power to appoint on that
committee Members from both sides of
the House I can assure him that I would
have 1,000 houses erected inside the next
nine months. I would ask no payment
for that. If ever there was a time for
a proper inquiry to be held into the
question of housing it is now. Have the
Government had a solitary conference
with the building operators who will
be building houses? No, they never
consulted them. Have they ever consulted the people about the supplies of
materials that are supposed to be scarce,
and are available? There is as much
timber in Northern Ireland as would
supply at least 5,000 houses.
Is it any
wonder that Members rise in angry protest when statesmen say it would be
impossible to do this? They do not understand the meaning of the word "statesmen." I am satisfied there has been
neglect in regard to this matter of housing
the working people. You need not worry
whether there is a division in the ranks of
the Unionist Party or not. If you go on the
way you are doing you will be exterminated at the next election. I am sure the
hon. lady Member knows that. She comes
in contact with people who are practically
turning red owing to the neglect shown.
I need not ask the Minister of Agriculture to do anything, as he is too busy. He
and the ex-Minister of Agriculture have
worked wonders. They inoculate pigs
and look after the hens, the ducks, the
stallions and the bulls. In fact, if there
is the least sign of tuberculosis in an
animal it is destroyed. But we do not
want to destroy mankind. What we
want is proper sanitary houses, with water
supply and other necessary requirements.
These houses can be built if you had the
guts to start a scheme, but you have not
the guts to do it. You are standing idly
by. It must be admitted that the youth
of a country is the wealth of that country.
The real thing that counts is youth;
money does not count. If you have not
a healthy youth, your money does not
count much. What the people are now
coming through is enough to make the
angels weep.

As an
innocent I fell for his ways, for he is a

he started this revolution I would be with

converts in one of the hon. Members for

Mr. HENDERSON: And we will meet

It will not need the hon. and learned
Member for St. Anne's to start this revolution. I have a battalion for him
already. If there was a meeting of protest against the Government called in
Belfast it would be well attended. But I
have stopped that kind of thing. I have
never taken part in anything of a political nature since the war started. I
have tried to be a builder. I have never
attacked the Government outside, but if
I were to call a meeting to-night in any
part of Belfast I would get 40,000 people
to come without the least trouble. Will
anyone say I could not get that crowd?
However, I would like much better to get
them into houses. I could get them out
to protest and overthrow the Government,
but I do not want to do that now.
I say you can get ample material for
houses. You want to take the brickmakers into your confidence.
You are
going to give £390 for the building of
these houses that are being talked about,
but nothing is being done. I say, get in
touch with the brick manufacturers and
start to get the bricks made. Is there
any reason why you should not now put
in the foundations for these houses? Is
there any reason why you cannot put in
the water, gas and electricity supplies? I
say no. The foundations and everything
can be ready. I have told the Minister
responsible that if he does not do something he is heading for trouble.
The
Member for Oldpark, who is the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Home Affairs, knows that his constituency
was practically wiped out. They were
hard working, decent people, who worked
in the textile industry in the mills of
that locality, and now they are scattered
to the four winds of heaven, and are
never thought about. These people are
waiting and praying for homes for themselves and their children. I have no call
to tell this to the hon. Member for Oldpark. He knows what the people of his
own constituency are saying about the
neglect of the Government.
My contention is that you can get all
the steel you want, and I would keep the
steel rails you are lifting in Belfast.
There is too much carry on about the two
or three tons of steel needed. How much
would be needed to make the eaves,
spoutings, and the few other things? For
one thousand homes it would not be
great. You can get all the green timber
you require, and I know a certain place
in Northern Ireland that will dry that
timber for one thousand homes inside a
fortnight or three weeks. You could get
the timber dried, but you are not concerned about it. Then there is the
question of sites. It is said the local
authority cannot get any land in Belfast,
and that it will need Parliamentary
powers to get land outside the city
boundary. If land is needed, pass the
legislation immediately, but I contend
there is ample land. There are the sites
of the blitzed houses, and 40 acres are
available at Malone, where can be built
between 800 and 900 houses. The
Corporation have it at their disposal now,
and I suggest that the Minister of Home
Affairs takes action now; otherwise I am
afraid that, law-abiding citizen as I
am, I will be necessarily compelled to
become a greater revolutionary than Joe
Stalin was.
In regard to the Select Committee on
Health Services and the report they published, in view of conditions in the city
of Derry I suggest here and now that
you appoint Administrators. The shocking statements that were made by the
public health officers for Derry, and the
evidence of the analyst concerning the
revolting conditions existing in that city,
would justify the Government in putting
in Administrators immediately. I stand
for democracy, but if these men
supposed to be democrats and yet allow
the people to die in a wholesale manner
for a number of years without giving
them the proper medical and social
services which mankind requires, I say
exterminate them and let this democratic
Government put in two democrats to rule
Derry.

I would not give one hang for it so long

taste of fresh milk, and so long as the
byres were clean and the people attending

If the Minister
of Finance thinks that I am going to stand
here and make speeches in this House and
that that is the end of it and I will go no
further, he is mistaken. If a start is not

hornet's nest about your ears that will

the law, but as sure as I am standing here,
if you do not do something there is going

you compel the people to live. I want to
say, practically in conclusion, that when
the old guard were in they were no worse
and no better than the new guard or the
young ruffians. You are just the same,
full of empty promises. You promised
the people during the last war-
Mr. ANDREWS: We were not here
during the last war.
Mr. HENDERSON: Shortly after the
last war.
One Member of this House
said we would be far better off under
British rule. I know personally I would
much prefer it, and it would stop a lot of
trouble about the border. If the right
hon. Gentleman agrees with me we can
go back to Great Britain and save
the hundreds of thousands of pounds
necessary to pay the Civil Service
here. It would also save unncessary expense in the opening of this
Parliament when we try to imitate Great
Britain. It would be far better if we sent

House of Commons, and that would save

place here for two or three months in the
year.
I notice that the Prime Minister, with
great enthusiasm, spoke about the loyalty
and devotion of His Majesty the King's
Fighting Forces, and the great job of
work they are doing in many foreign
lands. We all agree, but I am going to
stand up here and give a warning. About-
50 of the ex-Service men of the last war
are in the Workhouse on the Lisburn
Road next door to where I live. Their
breasts are full of medals. When it comes
to the turn of the present men to come
home the Government will have to carry
out their promises; otherwise their lives
as politicians will come to an end. You
need not make any mistake about it.
Things are changing very rapidly. I
have friends in every branch of His
Majesty's Forces, and when these boys.
come home they will want things different
to what they were the last time.
I have a brother who takes part in
convoy work. He came home one day a
short time ago, and he said: Tom, we
have great fun in the ships." Do you

I represent is the greatest constituency in

everywhere. My brother said to me,

The Prime Minister of this country has

absolutely no right to do so, and I want

has a Coalition Government.
Such a
farce. Does not the Prime Minister know
that that is not altogether the truth? We
have no Coalition here. We have not the
semblance of a Coalition. Does the
Minister of Labour, who is a member of
the Unionist Labour Association, represent official Labour in this city? He does
not. Does the Minister of Public Security, who used to be a Labour man,
represent Labour to-day? I say no.
There is no representative of recognised

the House. Official Labour does not

Northern Ireland representing Unionist

The trade unions never put these
Ministers forward as candidates. Therefore, as far as the official Labour ticket
is concerned, the Prime Minister had no
right to make that statement. As far as
looking after the interests of the working
classes is concerned I have no fault to find
with the two Ministers I have mentioned,
but I cannot look upon them as official
representatives of the Labour party of
Northern Ireland. They are nothing of
the sort, and I appeal to the Prime
Minister not to make such a statement
again. It may not have been deliberately
done, but it was misleading.
I am not going to detain the House,
although I could go into scandals that
have taken place under this Government,
and drag in the Bann drainage scheme.
I could show you where you have lost
hundreds of thousands of pounds in connection with that scheme. Your electrical undertaking activities are a thing
that would require another inquiry, and
I am afraid the present Prime Minister
would not come out of such an inquiry
with flying colours. I hope I shall have
an opportunity of moving a Resolution to
have an inquiry into the Prime Minister's
conduct in so far as it concerns the
electrical station that was erected under
his direction. You cannot filch any more
of the citizens' property away from them.
They will not stand your tactics of putting in control of the electricity undertaking men who do not understand the
technicalities of that undertaking, and
who try to sell it. I think the Prime
Minister would be well advised to leave
the Belfast electrical undertaking alone;
otherwise I am afraid he will get his
fingers burned. I warn him that as soon
as the war is over I am going to move
that we take immediate action to have a
sworn inquiry into the station he erected
under the guise of an electrical undertaking in one of the most unsuitable
places in Ulster. You ought to be
ashamed of yourselves..
I appeal to the Prime Minister to make
a new start from to-day. You have used
other people by taking them over to your
side of the House and paying them a
Cabinet salary. I am prepared to give you
free my lifetime's experience in the building trade and the engineering trade,
without any Cabinet salary. I will also
give you the benefit of my 25 years'
municipal experience. As a member of
the Belfast Corporation I know something
about housing, and I am prepared to
place my services at the disposal of the
Prime Minister. But he does not want
them. The right hon. Gentleman does
not want anybody who knows anything
about housing to assist him at all. To-day
you are talking about building houses at
the end of 1944. I tell you that you
could have a thousand houses erected in
six or nine months.
In the meantime, on behalf of
thousands of homeless people, and young
people who have got married and have
no homes, I ask you to hold even a private
inquiry and I will bring you a few
experts from the building trade operatives
and the employers to show you how you
can get something done. Will you please
see if you can get 400 or 500 Nissen huts
to house people whose homes were
destroyed by Nazi airmen and who are
living in sheughs, and pigsties, and byres
in the country. When you hear statements made that nothing will be done
before 1944 it makes you see red. The
wrath of these people will be worse than
terrible if something is not done before
then. There is a Member of this House
who has known brickmaking all his life,
and why not take him into your
confidence and let him tell you all about
the manufacture of bricks.
It has been stated definitely that 40,000
houses are needed in Ulster. I say that
60,000 houses are needed, and at the
present rate of progress there will be
another battle of the Boyne
the Boyne fought
before they are forthcoming. Spend less
time across the water, unless you have
some motive in going there. Many people
have suggested to me why you are taking
these trips across the water, but I do not
believe what they say. I say, stop these
trips to London. They have done you no
good, because unemployment is rising.
To give employment to our people who
are idle you should start building houses
at once, and then you will have the
blessing of every homeless person in
Ulster.
The Prime Minister has been eloquent
in praise of ex-Servicemen, but I would
like him to take a walk with me. I live
at 53 Lisburn Road, and I would like to
take him to see 50 or 60 ex-Servicemen
wearing medal ribbons who, I am told,
are now in the workhouse next door to
me. After the last war it was stated that
you were going to erect a home, or

hospital, on the lines of the Chelsea
Hospital in London, for those ex-Servicemen who had no home to return to. Now
is the time to lay the foundation stone of
such a home or hospital where these men

hope that before the next King's Speech

Mr. ELLIOTT: Those of us who expected from the two hon. and gallant
Members who moved and seconded the
Address speeches of a very high order were
not disappointed, and I should like to add
my congratulations to those of previous
speakers on the way in which they discharged the duties assigned to them. The
Gracious Speech is a somewhat lengthy
document, and yet I cannot see that any
part of it is unimportant. The reference
in it to our American allies and to their
co-operation with our own British troops
is very appropriate, and I feel confident
that, as the two hon. and gallant Members
have already stated, the co-operation and
companionship which will be formed in
time of war will, I am sure, lead to that
further co-operation and goodwill between
these two great nations that will be so
necessary and so important in the days of
peace.
Right in the foreground of our programme must be the winning of the war,
and I would like to emphasise here the wise
words of our Imperial Prime Minister,
Mr. Winston Churchill, that belief that
the war will soon be over is vain and
foolish, and that there must be no relaxation of effort either on farm or in factory
because of the fact that the way to victory
is now more apparent. Now is the time
for us all to unite and give that knock-out
blow which will clear for ever the Nazi
menace from the world. In that spirit
let us face this new Session, reassuring the
Prime Minister and the Government that
we who sit behind them are with them in
this matter 100 per cent., and in whatever
efforts they think necessary to carry us to
victory full and complete they can count
on our whole-hearted effort.
•
A fitting tribute was paid by the hon.
and gallant Member who moved the
Address, to the agricultural community
and the part they have played in this
great struggle. Despite broken pledges
and circumstances over which even
Governments have no control, they will
continue to play their part. I would
refer further to the agricultural position
were it not for the fact that at an early
date my Colleague in the representation
of County Tyrone (Mr. Lyons) and I intend to bring the agricultural position
before this House by a Motion placed on
the Order Paper.
There is one other important matter in the
Gracious Speech to which I wish to refer,
and that is housing. I am in complete
sympathy with the suggestion made by
the hon. and gallant Member for St.
Anne's that the housing question could
best be solved by some central Housing
Commission or Committee. There should
be more co-operation in the planning and
building of new houses, and the best plans
that can be produced for the housing of
our people ought to be made available for
every area in Northern Ireland. While
I am not objecting in any way to the fact
that the first move in housing is to be in
this city of Belfast, where I know the
position is very acute, I want to state,
as other county representatives have done
when this subject was debated in this
House some time ago, that the housing
shortage is also very acute in our rural
areas. Plans ought to be made now, and
arrangements ought to be made now, so
that when it is possible to do so the work
of building may be commenced and not
held up by technicalities and other formalities that ought to be dealt with at the
moment.
I could not follow very well the hon. Member for Shankill in the charge he made
against the Government in regard to the
housing programme. I think the record
of the last Government and of the Government before that, as far as providing
houses for the people is concerned, is one
of which they need not be ashamed. The
Government inside the last twenty years
have done a great deal to provide houses
for the people, and I have no hesitation
in saying that had it not been for the
intervention of the war a great deal more
would have been done to solve the housing
problem. The hon. Member for Shankill,
who has made such serious charges against
the Government of neglecting to provide
houses, seems to overlook the fact that he
himself is, I understand, chairman of the
Improvement Committee of the Belfast
Corporation. Three months ago the

administrators?

I want to emphasise that in rural Northern Ireland we are very badly fixed so

I want to bring one pathetic case in
my own County of Tyrone forward so
that it may receive consideration by the
Government. It is a case in which I hope
the Government will take immediate
action. In my own county, at Victoria
Bridge, there is a man who served his
country in the last war and who served
in the present war until he was invalided
out of the Army on medical grounds.
That man has a wife and a small son and
daughter and he has been turned out of
his home in Victoria Bridge although
there are three empty houses quite convenient to the one from which he is being
displaced. Is there any law that the
Government can put into operation to
compel those houses to be opened to that
man? What is his record? He served in
the last war, and he served in the present
war until he was discharged on medical
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Elliott]
grounds. He has five sons serving in the
present war, and yet he and his wife and
two small children are turned out of their
house because a farmer wants it for one
of his men.
I have every sympathy with the man
who wants to get his house for his workman, but I have no sympathy with any
Government or any person who has a
house available and yet closes the door
and says, "I will not allow that man to
occupy one of my houses." There ought
to be some legislation whereby an empty
house could be commandeered for that
man. It is not fair that he and his wife
should be separated and their two children
sent somewhere else while there are three
empty houses in the neighbourhood. I
hope the Government will take action to
put such a state of affairs right. That has
happened in my own county and I am
ashamed of it. I am ashamed to say I
come from a county where such a state of
affairs is allowed to exist.
If there is no legislation to remedy
that state of affairs I hope it is not too
late for the Government to make some
regulation whereby a house that is empty
can be made available for a man who
served in the last war and in this war
until discharged on medical grounds, and
whose five sons are to-day fighting for
King and Country. While they are
fighting their father and mother and
sister and brother are left on the roadside or to the kindness or compassion of
some of the neighbours to take them in.
I do not want to say anything more
about that. It is a case which makes
one's heart bleed. If that is the treatment that is going to be meted out to
ex-Servicemen when they come home
there will be another revolution, and I
will be in it, because when ex-Servicemen
come back from the war I want to see
they are treated, not as they were dealt
with after the last war, but as men who
went out to fight, and, if necessary, to
give their lives for King and Country.
They will have to be treated better this
time. So far as I am concerned I will
give all the support I can to any legislation or to any Government that will give
these people what they deserve when they
come back home.
One other matter the hon. Member for
Shankill referred to was the Bann drainage scheme. I want to say that the hon.
Member for Shankill is entirely wrong in
his ideas and his views about the Bann
drainage. He seems to think that the
Government could have saved hundreds
of thousands of pounds if they had not
bothered with the scheme. I am here
from County Tyrone to say that the Bann
drainage scheme was the best scheme the

A Ministry of Health should have been

in putting that recommendation into
effect. I will give such a Ministry my

Mr. THOMAS CAMPBELL: As the
last speaker this afternoon I will
be as concise as I possibly can
in my remarks. Regarding the housing
problem I would summarise it in
one sentence. This war is costing
£13,000,000 a day and yet there
millions of people in Great Britain and
there are tens of thousands of people in
Northern Ireland who are living in houses
which are not homes, but hovels where
children are languishing and withering,
and the luckiest of those children are those
who die early.
With regard to post-war reconstruction
there is not a very clear cut programme
on the part of the Government, yet I
think it is a well known fact that on
the day after peace is signed there will
be 30,000 people out of employment in
the factories in Northern Ireland alone.
They will be coming back in swarms and
multitudes and we have no provision
made whatever with regard to that grim
emergency.
The Gracious Speech makes mention of
the contribution of Northern Ireland to
the effort of the Allied Forces, and to the
gallant exploits of the Northern Ireland
units. That commendation is almost
superfluous. The Northern Irishman is
fighting as he always has fought with
traditional courage. During the course
of this debate I regret to say that rash
and mischievous statements have been
made by some Members. The hon. and
learned Member for St. Anne's made a
very able speech. I admired his ability.
He pictured an encampment, as he called
it, of a large British Army with their
faces to the Border, with bayonets fixed
and batteries pointed towards the Border
ready to foil any attempt to complete,
what he was pleased to call, the encirclement. of Great Britain through an invasion of Ireland. I venture to say that
irresponsible talk of that type, reckless
and wanton, is calculated to do harm
and to create bitterness against the people
of this country.
If any invasion of Ireland had been
attempted or essayed the invaders would
never have reached the Border. They
would have had to fight their way through
towards the Border, and they would have
met with resistance on every stretch of
the Irish coast and on every acre of every
Irish county through which they would
have had to pass. Before reaching the
Border they would have learned by bitter
experience what a brave people can do,
in defence of their liberty. There
would have been no trouble at the
Border, because they would have
been encountered by an
army second
to
none in courage, in discipline, in
efficiency and in equipment; an army
backed up by an united people. Both
army and people, before that army of invaders could have reached our Border,
would have fought with resolution in
defence of their country.
It is very largely to speeches of that
type that the neutrality of Eire can be
traceable to-day. When we consider that
the misrule of this country by its powerful neighbour has been going on for seven
or eight centuries, and is aggravated today by Britain riveting partition on this
country, it is a matter rather for wonder
that Eire, far from showing any un-

Debate on the Address

2 FEBRUARY 1944
I want to speak for a moment on the
reference in the Gracious Speech to the
Health Services in the Province. The
impression is going abroad that the Report
will be pigeon-holed. That Report is one
of paramount importance to the health of
the population here in Northern Ireland,
and its recommendations, I submit,
should be implemented by legislation at
the earliest available date or at least in
the immediate future. The evidence
given to the Committee revealed an
appalling neglect of health services, an
appalling disorganisation of health
services, and I would almost say an
appalling want of organisation of health
services. Northern Ireland has a shockingly high maternal and infantile death
rate and a dismal record of safeguards
of the health of the masses of the
population. These dreadful conditions.
must not and ought not to continue.
Sweeping remedies are required without delay, and I do say that the public
conscience of all classes in our community
will be outraged by any unnecessary
delay in putting into legislative effect the
main recommendations of the Committee.
The Government must act, and act
quickly, and if they do not I feel perfectly
convinced that an indignant public will
not be put off with inaction and unnecessary delay.
Motion made, and Question, "That the
Debate be now adjourned," put, and
agreed to.-(Mr. Lowry.)

Milk and Meals for School Children.
1. Mr. BROWN asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Education whether she can now give the
House the detailed information promised
as to the comparative positions in Northern Ireland and Scotland in the matter
of milk and meals for elementary schoolchildren, showing in each case the
numbers of pupils receiving (a) milk; (b)
meals; (c) both milk and meals; and (d)
the numbers receiving neither; and the
respective numbers of schools concerned
and the proportions of both scholars and
schools benefiting by such schemes
otherwise in the two areas.
or
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mrs. Parker): I regret
that I am not in a position to supply
recent statistics regarding the provision
of meals and milk to school-children in
Scotland, as no figures have been published since those relating to February,
1943. At that time 16.4 per cent. and
67.2 per cent. of the children attending
schools in Scotland were receiving midday dinners and milk respectively. These
figures are for all types of schools and
separate statistics for public elementary
schools are not given. As stated in my
reply to the hon. Member on 7th
December, 1943, the percentage of
children in attendance at public elementary schools in Northern Ireland who
were then receiving meals and milk was
4.5 and 33 respectively.
Agriculture.
POTATO PRICES.
2. Lieut.-Colonel GORDON asked the
Minister of Agriculture whether he has
any statement to make in regard to the
recent negotiations with the Ministry of
Food for the purpose of obtaining an increase in main crop potato prices in
Northern Ireland.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Rev. Robert Moore): I welcome this
opportunity of giving a brief account of
the negotiations. The position is that
for several months past prolonged discussions regarding main crop potato prices
in Northern Ireland have taken place
between my Ministry, the Ministry of
Food, the Ministry of Agriculture and
Fisheries and the Treasury. I am
satisfied that growers in this area are
entitled to an increase, having regard to
the prices which are paid to growers in
other areas in the United Kingdom. The
strongest possible representations in support of this view were made by my
Ministry. The whole question was made
more awkward and delicate by the decision
of the United Kingdom Government to
the effect that recent increases in wages
must be borne mainly by farmers.
I regret, therefore, to have to state
that it has now been finally decided by
the Imperial Authorities that no change
will take place in the price of Northern
Ireland main crop potatoes for the 1944
season.
Mr. BROWN: Are we to take it from
the Minister that he is prepared to allow
this great injustice and discrimination
against the farmers of Northern Ireland
to remain ? Is he absolutely satisfied that
this injustice is to continue?

21. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of

became of his Ministry's scheme to allow
a dozen experimental dwelling-houses to
be erected in Belfast by six applicants

houses each; whether any such applications were, in fact, received other than
the application of the hon. Member for
Ballynafeigh; and, if so, how were they
dealt with by his Ministry, and how
many, if any, of the other five pairs of
proposed houses have been erected or are
to be erected; whether the two houses
being erected by the hon. Member for
Ballynafeigh are now almost completed;
and whether a start has yet been made
with the erection of the proposed 750
subsidy houses in Belfast, and, if not,
why.
Mr. LOWRY: Five applications to
build experimental dwelling-houses have
been received by my Ministry. These applications have been examined by a special
Technical Sub-Committee of the Housing
Committee of the Planning Advisory
Board, and also by the Technical Officers
of my Ministry. The report of these
technical experts on the proposals indicates that none of the proposals shows
sufficient promise to justify the Ministry
in facilitating the promoters to build the
dwelling-houses.
The two houses being erected by the
hon. Member for Ballynafeigh are at present in course of erection, but some time
must elapse before they are completed.
With regard to the 750 subsidy houses
to be built in Belfast certain difficulties
regarding the particular materials to be
used for the building of the houses and
respecting suitable sites for the houses
have required special consideration, but
these difficulties have now been
mounted, and so far as sites are concerned
the Government is introducing legislation
which will empower the Belfast Corporation to acquire compulsorily land for
housing purposes.

be unprepared,' but unless

allowed to
war agriculture was

whose son is to-day probably in the
Appenines fighting with others. Why
should the hon. and learned Member for
Central even dream that the Minister
would try to insult the American Forces ?
I do not want to see the House of
Commons dragging such foolish things into
debate. On the contrary the House
should try to make Ulster a decent place
for people to live in.
In the Gracious Speech reference is
made to the linen industry and a proposal
to set up a special committee of investigation. If the Government can set up a
special committee to study the linen
industry surely they can set up a special
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Minford]
committee to study agriculture in order
to ensure that the farming industry will
get a fair crack of the whip after the
war and not go back to the decadent condition it got into after the last war. I
am not speaking for one party or another
party, but I am speaking for all the
people of Northern Ireland when I appeal
to the Government to give agriculture a
chance and place it on the same basis as
agriculture in England because we are
part and parcel of the British Empire.
Nothing more do I ask, and nothing less
will I take.
Lieut.-Colonel HALL-THOMPSON: I
should like to join with other speakers in
congratulating the Mover and Seconder
of the Motion for the Address. I regret
that the hon. and learned Member for
Central should be absent from the House,
because I take strong exception to his
criticism. I am glad to see that the hon.
and learned Member has now come into
the House. I was saying I take strong
exception to his criticism of the speech.
made by the hon. and learned Member
for St. Anne's who said:
I think it is a confident assumption
that had it not been for the assistance
of the Ulster Bridgehead and for the
presence on that bridgehead of a large
British Army with their faces towards
the Border, their bayonets fixed and
engines running, the plan of the enemy
to complete the encirclement of Great
Britain might well have been attempted.
With that I thoroughly agree. The
hon. and learned Member for Central is
a man for whom, outside this House, I
have the greatest respect. I admire his
ability and his integrity, but I strongly
resent many of the speeches which he
feels called upon, for some good reason
known to himself, to make in this House
at least once a year.
I think that when
he spoke last week it must have been one
of those occasions, because, in addition to
other criticisms, he says of this speech of
the hon. and learned Member for St.
Anne's:
I venture to say that irresponsible
talk of that type, reckless and wanton,
is calculated to do harm and to create
bitterness against the people of this
country.
May I, speaking as one with some little
knowledge of this subject, and as one who
was one of those forming that bridgehead,
•
say that every word which the hon. and
learned Member for St. Anne's spoke is
perfectly correct. In my opinion, had
there not been a British Army in
Northern Ireland ready to defend the
whole of Ireland, Ireland would have
suffered exactly the same fate as befell
Poland, Belgium, Holland, Greece, and
other countries that were invaded one at
a time. I believe, therefore, that, indirectly, to have Ulster available as a
bridgehead played a most important part
in the defence of this country and the
whole of the United Kingdom during the
the great crisis that existed from late 1939
to 1941.
With reference to other matters mentioned in the King's Speech, the public
at the present time are most interested in
housing, health, education, the removal of
post-war restrictions, and the development of post-war agriculture. I am glad
to say that not one of these subjects has
been neglected in the King's Speech, but
before speaking about them, I should like
to refer back to what I have said already.
In connection with the compliment paid
to the Ulster units in the Speech and in
regard to the recruiting which has taken
place, I still regret the fact that the Royal
Ulster Constabulary have not been
allowed to join up. There were good
reasons for that decision during the crisis,
when, perhaps, they were doing a greater
and better service here than they might
have been able to do in another place,
but I think that time is now past and that
the restriction on the members of the
Royal Ulster Constabulary joining should
be removed. If they now wish to join
they should be permitted to do so.
I should also like to see the proper
authority being approached with the
object of obtaining permission for Ulster
volunteers to wear flashes on their arm
to indicate their territorial origin. One
sees numerous flashes-
-someone has said
the men look like Christmas trees-and
seeing that that is permitted, particularly
in the case of Canadian, Australian, and
other Imperial troops, I think the permission might be extended to those individuals who are not fortunate enough to
find themselves serving in Ulster units, as
it would be a great matter of pride to
them to be able to show that they were
representing a country that had not got
conscription and were serving entirely as
volunteers.

To come back to the question of
housing, health, and education, to talk
about the necessity for housing is beating
a willing horse. Everybody in this House
knows there is a clamant necessity. The
Ministry know it just as well as every
Member who has spoken to-day or any
other day, and they have shown they are
perfectly aware of it and are perfectly
anxious to do all in their power. I do
not think that any reasonable person can
insist that there are ample materials,
outside bricks and cement, available
for building houses at the present
time. There still definitely is a shortage
of steel and timber, and until those two
materials are available we can only deal
with the matter in a piecemeal way. A
small contribution has already been made
by the Government in so far as a grant
of £390 per house has already been
promised, and permission has been given
to one local authority to erect 750 houses.
In connection with health, I was very
glad to hear the Prime Minister give such
a cordial reception to the Report of the
Select Committee on Health Services. It
is not for me to say much about that
Report as I was Vice-Chairman of the
Committee, but they thoroughly investigated the whole subject and held 67 meetings. The Report covers 768 pages.
am very pleased to know that it will be
dealt with at the earliest possible
opportunity.
I
We are looking forward now to what I
hope will be weeks rather than months
till we see this White Paper on Education.
Though I am one of those who believe in
the three R's, I would rather see a firstclass tradesman with a good technical
education in employment than a fourthclass unemployed black-coated gentleman.
I still feel that in the matter of education
we cannot afford to be one whit behind the
educational systems prevailing in the rest
of the United Kingdom, and therefore
this matter of improving our educational
services and bringing them up to the very
high standard contemplated in the Butler
Bill is a matter which, I hope, will be
dealt with in a thoroughly vigorous and
expeditious manner.
As far as agriculture is concerned, I
hope that once the war is over we shall
not continue to try to grow in Ulster what
the Ulster climate is not suitable for. Any
person who tries to save grain, as I have
done during the last three or four years
on a very small scale, knows that unless
you are in the forunate position of
having a large staff and very up-to-date
machinery you cannot successfully grow
and save grain, but our climate is ideal
for developing our milk, cream, butter,
eggs, vegetables, pigs, and cattle trade,
and, last but not least, that thoroughbred stock to which the noble Lord has
referred.
Judging by recent bloodstock sales
there will be a tremendous demand immediately after the war for good bloodstock. To my mind there are not as
many thoroughbred horses in Northern
Ireland as there should be. Those of us
who wish to get the services of horses of
the very highest quality have to send our
mares down to the South of Ireland. We
do not want to do that, and it should not
be necessary. I think there is scope here
for the Government to assist the proper
kind of people to purchase two or three
high-class thoroughbred sires, and to see
that they stand at convenient places in
Northern Ireland.
We have heard
a good deal about
Beveridge and security. I am in agreement with the majority of the recommendations made
Sir
by
William
Beveridge on that subject, but I think it
would be much more important if we had
a report from Sir William Beveridge, or
some other person equally competent, on
employment. We cannot get security
except indirectly through employment.
One of the post-war problems which, I
think, will be most difficult will be that
of getting people, when they come back
from the Army and munitions, into
constant remunerative employment.
I hope in doing so all unnecessary restrictions will be removed at the earliest
possible moment. Of course when I speak
of unnecessary restrictions I do not refer
to such restrictions as exist on food,
building materials and other things which
are bound to continue for some considerable time. In the interests of private
enterprise and initiative, however, I
think unnecessary restrictions should be
removed. I hope the Board of Trade
will not make the mistake they have
made during the last few weeks in their
removal of the restrictions on austerity
clothing. To my mind, speaking as an
individual, it would appear that the re-

of cases in which he is interested and

Mr. NIXON: I have cases from outside

The hon. Member had also something
to say about residence permits. This is
a thorny question. I want to say something definite about it because there are
some people-I am not referring to any
particular persons in the House, although
they are on both sides-who speak with
two voices on this question. On the one
hand they say that I ought at least to
agree that permits should be given to
certain people to come into Northern
Ireland, because they are a certain type
of people who would make good citizens.
On the other hand, when they are
making political speeches, they denounce
the Government Department for allowing
people from this part I am referring to
to come into Northern Ireland. Hon.
Members cannot play both ways with me
on this question.
The Order, as it is made, is not a matter
for me to administer. The Ministry of
Home Affairs act as agents for the
Imperial Home Office on this question.
Then it is put up to my Department
whether the person should be allowed to
have a residence permit or not. Invariably and in all cases, as far as I am
aware of, if my Department discovers
that we have an unemployed person in
Northern Ireland who could fill that
position we will never agree to recommend
that a permit should be given to people
coming in from Southern Ireland or any
other place. That is the policy of the
Ministry. I want to remind hon.
Members of that, because I have heard
speeches in this House by hon. Members
who ask, "What are you doing for the
unemployed people of Northern Ireland?
The Government should provide work for
them." Then you are met quietly here
or somewhere else or you receive a letter
saying, "Here is a very decent fellow.
You can give him a permit and let him
in." They cannot play that game. It is
the policy of this Department, and I hope
hon. Members will bear that in mind and
not write me letters, so that I will not
have the trouble of replying to these
particular appeals.
I want to make it quite clear that we
do not wish to cause hardship to any
workers from any part of the country,
but, after all, our first duty is to the
people of Northern Ireland.
Now at
this particular time our unemployed
register is rising again and it would be
indefensible for my Department to recommend to the Ministry of Home
Affairs that they should, at such a time,
issue residence permits to workers coming in from a neutral State when we
have our own unemployed people in
Northern Ireland. Going on from that, I
should like to congratulate the right hon.
Gentleman the Member for Mid-Down
for the helpful and constructive speech
he made. His example might very well
have been followed by some of the other
speakers.
I am sorry the hon. Member for
Shankill is not here to-day. But he, in
his usual breezy style, discussing the visit
of different Ministers to London, stated
that instead of gallivanting over there
they would have done better to stay at
home. We all know the hon. Member is
not serious in this statement, because he,
with other Members on previous occasions and rightly so-has suggested that
Ministers should go to the other side to
put up Ulster's case and to see, as far as
they possibly can, that the claims of the
people of Northern Ireland for equal

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Grant]
treatment are not overlooked. Then after
having accused Ministers of gallivanting
on the other side he proceeded to tell the
House about the deputations, of which
he had been a member, that had travelled
as far afield as Germany; but he did not
tell us what benefits the people of Belfast
received from those visits. He also commented-as did other Members on the
fact that the unemployment figures were
rising. Perhaps I should just explain
at this juncture the causes of the rise.
There has been an increase of 4,700 persons on the register from the October,
1943, figures. Those are the latest available figures. And I would also remind
the House that those October, 1943,
figures were the lowest ever recorded in
Northern Ireland.
But the increase in the January figures
is due to seasonal slackness in the farming industry, and is made up as follows:
-1,693 normally insured agricultural
workers and 1,533 non-agricultural
workers suspended from harvesting gangs
—making a total of 3,226. To that must
be added those paid off at Millisle aerodrome-about 1,000. That accounts very
largely for the increase in the unemployment figures.
I should perhaps refer to the fact that
Members in this House on both sides in
the early days of the harvesting were
seriously alarmed lest the farmers might
not be able to gather in the harvest. But
even with unfavourable weather this year
I think it must be admitted that a good
job of work was performed. This gang
system that was brought into being
through consultations between the
Ministry of Agriculture and my Ministry
went all over Northren Ireland and my
Ministry has received from many sections
of the farming community expressions of
gratitude for the help rendered in this
direction. Hon. Members cannot during
the harvest time warn the Government
that they must find labour to bring in
the harvest, and then, when the Government makes provision of the ingathering
of the harvest and after they celebrate in
the churches that all is safely garnered
in, and when these men are paid off,
raise the question of the unemployment
figures in the House. We could probably
have found employment for the majority
of these people in other parts of the
country and the farmer would have
suffered the loss of that labour when they
most required it.
Notwithstanding the increase in the
present figure since October last, it is
almost 5,000 less than the figure on the
same date last year. And I think it is
only right to point out that as a result
of war
conditions a large number of
people have been attracted into industry
who were not formerly in the industrial
field.

they have a policy that will provide work

Mr. GRANT: It is unfortunate that I
now have to deal with some of the points
raised by the hon. Member who has just
left the House. It is well within the
memory of every hon. Member of this
House that the Labour Party were returned to power in Great Britain on the
promise that they would solve the unemployment problem-in fact one of their
most prominent leaders wrote a book
entitled Fifty-three Positive Remedies for
Unemployment-yet after a period of
office and power, when their back benchers
got a bit impatient and wondered when
all these positive remedies would be produced and asked the Minister of Labour
of that day, Mr. Shaw, when they were
going to get them, the only answer they
got was, "You can't take rabbits out of a
hat."
I referred to the fact that our Government or party is not prepared to give
pledges it cannot carry out, but the other
people fooled the country, and when they
got into power they could not deliver the
goods. That is why I was dealing with
that particular point. In my opinion,
the duty of any government, no matter
what political party it may represent, is
to do everything it possibly can in the
best interests of the people who sent it to
power.
Now, I want to say something which I
hope will not cause any feeling. The hon.
and learned Member for Central Belfast
stated that there was not a very clear-cut
programme on the part of the Government
with regard to post-war reconstruction,
and he painted a gloomy picture of the
people who would be out of employment
in the factories in Northern Ireland alone
in the days after the declaration of peace.
It is easy to talk glibly about post-war
reconstruction and clear-cut programmes.
That is a problem that every country in
the world will have to face up to after the
war, and yet when members of this
Government visit London-I want to
assure hon. Members that going to London
in these days is no picnic-to discuss most
important matters in connection with
post-war policy, they are accused of
gallivanting and are told it would be
better if they stayed at home. However,
the Government do not pay attention to
all the advice it gets from certain hon.
Members on the other side. I can assure
the hon. and learned Member that we all
realise the seriousness of this question,
and no efforts will be spared in grappling
with the problem.
The same hon. and learned Member also
took exception to some things which the
hon. and learned Member for St. Anne's
mentioned. He said that irresponsible
talk of that type was calculated to do
harm. Most members of the House will,
I think, agree with me that the speech
made by the hon. and learned Member
himself was not exactly the type one would
use at a peace conference. However, as
they both belong to the same profession
and are probably accustomed to this sort
of thing, I think it would be better for
an ordinary layman like myself just to
leave it to them.
There are, however, one or two other
points he dealt with which I feel I would
like to mention. He said that in this
war there was no particular reason to
brag and boast of the volume of the contribution of the Six Counties to the
fighting forces. He gave some figures,
