HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Grant]
and went on to talk about Eire's contribution-a territory at which, he said,
pin-pricks were constantly being levelled.
The hon. Gentleman compared figures of
recruiting in the last war with those of
the present war, but I would remind him
that during the last war there was no
division in Ireland between North and
South, and, with the usual enthusiasm
of Irishmen, recruiting was carried on in
the early stages on a very large scale.
As time went on there was a great shortage of manpower for essential war work,
and hundreds of thousands of men had
to be brought back from the trenches.
In the present campaign different
methods were adopted. Many occupations
were reserved so that recruitment for the
Forces would not interfere with war industries. As a matter of fact officers of
my Ministry have been in the recruiting
establishments in Northern Ireland since
the beginning of the war, and they have
to see to it that men in reserved occupations are not allowed to join His
Majesty's Forces. We have to realise
that men and women are required at
home to provide the fighting forces with
the necessary munitions of war. Large
numbers of Ulstermen and women were
in the Services and the Mercantile
Marine before the war, but no official
figures of these categories are available.
the
Immediately prior to the outbreak of
war, however, 4,365 men joined the
Royal Air Force Auxiliary Force, the
Territorial Army and the Army Supplementary Reserve in Northern Irelandno figures are available for
R.N.V.R.-and from the commencement
of hostilities up to the end of December
last 27,932 men and 6,407 women from
Ulster joined the Forces in the Northern
Ireland recruiting areas. These are the
actual figures. The hon. and learned
Member gave figures about recruiting in
Southern Ireland, but I have not the
foggiest idea what authority he has for
them. I am not going to discuss that
particular question; I will approach the
matter from a different angle.
The position is, of course, different in
Southern Ireland. Being a neutral
country it is not playing any part in
making munitions of war. It has not
large shipyards, aircraft factories and
munition works. It is not engaged in
any war industries of the character that
I have mentioned. Personally I yield to
no man in my admiration of the gallant
men and women from Southern Ireland
who did not agree with their Government's policy of neutrality, but nobly
came forward and offered their services
in the cause of liberty and freedom. I
would, however, remind the hon. Member
that many of those who came from Southern Ireland to enlist in His Majesty's
Forces were not actuated by reasons of
loyalty and belief in the cause for which
the war is being fought, but because
there was no employment for them in
their own country and the fighting services offered at least the opportunity of
a livelihood. In spite of all the hundreds of thousands that the hon. Member
has on this and other occasions mentioned
as being in the Services and employed on
munitions work in Great Britain, the
unemployment figures in the South are
still over 70,000.
Earlier in his speech the hon. and
learned Member referred to the misrule
of that country by its powerful neighbour as going on for seven or eight
centuries, and he stated that it was
aggravated to-day by Britain riveting
partition on this country. Surely it is
the hon. and learned Member who is
adopting the policy of pin-pricking.
The neighbouring country to which he
refers is actually responsible for providing
most of the necessities of life, and he is
bound to admit that without that neighbouring country Ireland, both North
and South, could not exist.
The hon. and learned Member dealt
with Northern Ireland's contribution to
the war, which he regarded as far from
satisfactory. He stated that he would
like to mention one fact that if a very

a number of hefty young men who seemed
to have no concern at all about the war,
and he would be rather struck with
amazement to see young men, stalwart in
health and strength, queuing up outside
the cinemas and crowded dance halls
during a great war. I do not want to
accuse the hon. and learned Member of
suggesting that all these people were constituents of the hon. and learned Member
for St. Anne's, but he had something of

Mr. CAMPBELL: Thank you. I wish
to refer to the banning of this book
called Orange Terror. The ban was imposed on the very day that the Prime
Minister had broadcast a B.B.C. postscript on "Our Great Democracy". The
original title of the 21 articles comprised
in Orange Terror was "The Real Case
Against Partition". Was it banned for
its present title, or was it banned for its
contents? When you look at its pages it
does strike you with amazement that any
banning took place at all. It has a map
of Ireland. It indicates on that map by
shadings the areas of this country for
and against partition-29,821 square
miles against, and 2,526 square miles for.
Is that another reason for banning a
book of this kind? It indicates that even
in this area of Northern Ireland the
majority, judged by square miles, is
against partition, almost 100,000 being
in that category. The book gives the text
of a resolution of the Grand Orange
Lodge of Belfast of December, 1921, in
these words:-
That any member of the Orange
Institution found frequenting Roman
Catholic public houses is guilty of conduct unbecoming an Orangeman, and
a charge to that effect may be brought
against him and dealt with according
to our laws.
It
Is that a reason for banning this publication in Northern Ireland? It has the
facsimile of the introduction card of the
Ministry of Labour in which was written
in one word why employment was refused
to a Catholic worker-"Religion".
gives an account of the riots which have
disgraced Belfast from cycle to cycle and
of the educational difficulties and disabilities of the Catholic minority. Is that
a reason why the banning order should
have been issued? It gives statesmanlike arguments why partition should end.
The majority of the contributors to
this booklet are gentlemen of the highest
eminence. Among them is the respected

Bishop of Down and Connor. Another is
Lady Yarrow, widow of Sir Alfred

Dean of Belfast, whose personal friendship I was proud to have. Another is an
Ulster Protestant gentleman who was the
first Minister of Finance in the Irish
Free State. Another is an Ulster

I
myself in a very humble way am proud
to be in that goodly companionship. The
writers differed as to the approach to the
repeal of partition but their scholarly
essays gave food for deep thought.
We have gone, I submit, a long way
towards a totalitarian State when this
arbitrary ban can be imposed on a work
of this restrained literary and political
quality. In this booklet not one line can
be read which directly or indirectly
wounds the religious susceptibilities or
feelings of any man or is in any way
offensive to those feelings and susceptibilities, but very different publications
are tolerated, if not condoned, in this
area, the vilest of the vile, the effluvium
of sectarian sewers, reeking with offence
to the Catholic community. They go
unchecked. They can circulate as free as
the wind. They back the Government,
and through backing the Government
create no disaffection. The Minister cannot face the logic of facts. A great
English poet has asked, "Who ever knew
truth put to the worse in a free and open
encounter?" Truth here is not met by
argument, it is met and countered by
the meat-axe and the bludgeon.
I charge the Government with seeking
to drive young Irishmen into the ways of
desperation, to be there entrapped by
agents provocateurs and spies and consigned to penal servitude. I charge them
with doing so in order to break the
Nationalist spirit in this area. If this
booklet tends to create disaffection, the
American Declaration of Independence
tends tenfold more. We should be the
veriest slaves if we passed by as negligible
this banning of a grim, but true, history
by distinguished and cultured writers, of
pogroms, persecutions, and bigotry. This
banning is a futile weapon. It is the
futile weapon of a foolish and panicky
Executive. It will recoil on them. People
may not publish Orange Terror here, but
it can be published in London, Dublin,
Liverpol, Glasgow, and Edinburgh.
can circulate very freely, without restraint
or restriction of any kind everywhere
beyond this bridgehead of democracy.
It
The Minister deserves the thanks of the
publishers in one aspect, for he has given
a big impetus to the circulation. Thousands who never heard of Orange Terror
are now in full cry for the booklet. It is
selling like wildfire in Britain and Eire.
In the Six Counties it had achieved a large
measure of popularity during the four or
five months that elapsed between the first
publication and the issue of the ban. For
four long months the Minister lay asleep
like Rip Van Winkle. Then for some
mysterious reason he suddenly became
wide awake and lurched blindly at this
booklet. For the Minister to act in this
way leaves nothing to be wondered at on
the score of audacity. This suppression of
the freedom of the written word is a
measure to introduce which is degrading
and to put in force which would be disgraceful, and is unworthy of any but a
totalitarian tyranny masquerading in
shreds and patches of democracy.

The Betting Laws.
1. Mr. THOMPSON. asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he is satisfied
that the laws in regard to betting and
gambling are being properly enforced,
and whether he is prepared to take any
action with a view to the stricter enforcement of these laws.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Mr. Lowry): I am satisfied that the
police are taking all possible steps within
their power in this regard, but as some
abuses may have arisen by reason of the
stress
of war-time conditions, I am
arranging to set up a Committee to consider the whole matter.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Arising out of the
reply of the right hon. Gentleman, may I
ask whether it is a fact that before these
betting places are raided the police
notify the people concerned that they will
raid them on a certain day and that the
subsequent proceedings are all staged?
Mr. LOWRY: I can assure the hon.
Member there is not a scintilla of truth
in the suggestion.
Mr. NIXON: Absolutely correct.
Mr. THOMPSON: I beg to thank the
Minister for his reply stating that he is
going to set up a committee. Does he
mean this committee will be a Government
committee?
Mr. LOWRY: No. It will be a committee, as I hope, representative of the
interests involved in this matter.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is the intention of
the right hon. Gentleman to set up a
committee for the purpose of going into
the pros and cons of betting in Northern
Ireland with a view to having registered
betting offices in the city of Belfast and
throughout the country?
Mr. ELLIOTT: Further arising out of
the reply of the right hon. Gentleman
before he flatly contradicts the suggestion
that I have made, will the right hon.
Gentleman make further inquiries and
find if it is not the case?
Mr. LOWRY: In reply to the last
question there is no need to make inquiries. I know it to be the case. With
regard to the hon. Member for Pottinger,
I cannot possibly anticipate the recommendations of the committee.

of Mr. Dunlop and the other officials who
held an inquiry into alleged irregularities
at Whiteabbey Sanatorium included a

Mr. LOWRY: As the then Parliamentary Secretary to this Ministry pointed
out in reply to a Motion moved by the
hon. Member on the 25th April, 1939,
the reports furnished by inspectors to

Water Supplies.
BALLYGOWAN, COMBER,
NEWTOWNARDS AND BANGOR.
4. Mr. ANDREWS asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he is aware of
the great disappointment which exists
owing to the fact that a start has not yet
been made on the scheme for the provision
of a water supply for Ballygowan,
Comber, Newtownards and Bangor, and
whether he can state the reason for the
delay.
Mr. LOWRY: As my right hon.
Friend is doubtless aware the scheme
under which it was hoped that it would
be possible to provide water for the places
mentioned was not primarily one promoted by the sanitary authorities for the
purpose of providing the public in these
places with water. The purpose for which
the scheme was prepared being no longer
necessary, the project was abandoned.
The local authorities interested in the
water supply to the localities mentioned
are considering the possibility of preparing a scheme of their own to supply those
places, and I have arranged to discuss
their proposals with a joint deputation
which I am meeting on 21st February.
Mr. ANDREWS: I am glad that my
right hon. Friend is conferring with the
local authorities in the matter and I hope
the promise of a Government grant will
be honoured.

the
Mr. LOWRY: Apart from

Ireland there will be any shortage of

an Order made under the Defence Regu-

The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF

assure the hon. Member
that any increase agreed to in Great

TUBERCLE BACILLI.
17. Dr. LYLE asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether, having regard to
the fact that it is not proposed under the
provisions of the Milk Act to pasteurise
"accredited" or grade "B" milk, he is
aware that figures recently collected by
Sir William Savage, as reported in the
British Medical Journal of 22nd January
last, show that the proportion of samples
of "accredited" milk found to contain
tubercle bacilli was almost consistently
higher than that of ungraded raw milk,
and whether he can state if this is due to
the fact that cows from T.T. herds which
have reacted to the tuberculin test are
frequently purchased by the owners of
herds which supply "accredited" or grade
"B" milk.
Rev. ROBERT MOORE: It is intended to require the pasteurisation of
all grade "B" milk sold in the Belfast
area except where it is the production of
a single herd. In this case the milk will
require to be bottled on the farm. I do
not feel that I would be justified in requiring such milk to be pasteurised as
this would interfere drastically with the
ability of a producer to retail his own
milk. As the hon. Member is aware,
however, all grade "B" herds are subject
to inspection by my Ministry and in the
future special attention will be given to
those herds from which unpasteurised
grade "B" milk is sold.
Dr. LYLE: Is it not a fact that as
regards the herds supplying "accredited"
or grade "B" milk, tuberculosis of the
udder, which is the cause of tubercle
bacilli in the milk, cannot be diagnosed
by veterinary surgeons until it is in an
advanced condition, and as a result milk
is provided which is filled with tubercle
bacilli.

OLD AGE PENSIONS.
Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Labour whether he can state the number
of old age pensions reduced to 6s, 4s, etc.,
in Northern Ireland for the year ending
31st December, 1943; whether it is a fact
that this branch of his Ministry is very
drastic in its work; and will he make a
survey of the system in operation, as
considerable uneasiness exists among
pensioners.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Grant): The rate of pension payable
under the. Old Age (Non-contributory)
Pensions Act depends on the means of
the pensioner, as assessed in accordance
with the provisions of the Act. The
assessment is made in the first instance. by
the pension officer, and a pensioner who
is not satisfied with the decision has a
right of appeal to a Pension Court and,
in certain cases, to the umpire.
I cannot see that any objection can be
taken to this procedure, which appears to
me to be entirely fair and reasonable. In
point of fact, while the special review of
pensions conducted during 1943 led to the
rate of pension being reduced in 296
cases, it resulted, on the other hand, in
the rate being increased in 516 cases.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Rent Restrictions (Defective Tenancies)
Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Mr. LOWRY: This is a short Bill
which I think will receive the support of
all sections of the House. It seeks to
deal with a question which has received a
certain amount of publicity by reason of
the fact that a number of cases to obtain
possession of dwelling houses on agricultural holdings have come before the
county courts, and the courts have been
compelled to give decrees for possession.
Under Section 30, sub-section (1) of the
Northern Ireland Land Act, 1925, an Act
passed by the Imperial Parliament, any
letting of a portion of land or house and
land is void unless the proprietor has
already obtained the consent of the
Ministry of Finance. This Section was
designed to prevent lettings prejudical to
the security for the advance made by the
Ministry of Finance to enable the tenant
to purchase the holding.
This position then arises. This letting
being void, the owner of such a house can
eject the tenant on the title, and the suggestion, which seems to be supported by
some cases, is that where these houses
have been let, certain people, seeking the
opportunity of obtaining a rent far in
excess of the value of the premises, and
relying on their own wrong, so to speak,
eject the tenant and get vacant possession
with a view to letting it at a higher figure
still. At one time similar things were
done under Sections 10 and 8 of Deasy's
Act, the Landlord and Tenant Act of
1860, where there was a Section forbidding either assignment or sub-letting.
I am sure it will be recognised by the
House that a man who has a house on
his farm ostensibly for the purpose of
housing an agricultural labourer should
not be allowed to let in breach of Section
30 of the Act of 1925 and eject the tenant
on the title, and then proceed to let the
house at a still higher figure.
What this Bill proposes to do is this.
In the case of a house of that character,
although the letting is void, for the purpose of protecting the tenant who has
been admitted it is provided that it shall
be treated as premises to which the Rent
Restrictions Acts apply, notably Section
2 of the most recent Act, the Act of 1943.
That will prevent oppression, and at the
same, time it will prevent a man who has
let a house of this character at a reasonable rent turning out the tenant-relying
on his own wrong—and letting the house
at a higher rent. It also protects the
very strong interest the. Ministry of
Finance has in holdings of this sort. I
beg to move.
Question proposed, "That this Bill be
now read a Second time."

Mr. MINFORD: There is another side
to this question that should not be lost
In my district three people
sight of.
were given notice to leave their houses,
and the judge gave a decree, for eviction.
The reason was that the rents were only
ls 6d and 1s 9d per week, and under the
Rent Restrictions Acts the landlord has
the right to close a house if the cost of
doing the necessary repairs would not
give him an economic controlled rent.
There are at the present moment quite a
number of landlords and tenants who
would like to come to an agreement, but
they cannot do so because of that provision that the rents must be controlled,
and the landlord may close the house if
he is asked by the rural council to spend,
say, £100 on repairs and the controlled
rent of, say, 1s 6d a week would then
become uneconomic. That has been the
difficulty in many cases.
I am speaking on behalf of the workers,
who have asked me to bring this matter
to the attention of the Ministry of Home
Affairs: I hope that this little Bill,
which I welcome, will prevent such a
thing occurring in the future. The present Rent Acts do provide that where the
owner thinks the controlled rent of a
house is not economic he may close the
house entirely, although the tenant may
want to pay more rent, and the landlord
may want to do the necessary repairs.
That results in an injustice to the working classes of Northern Ireland as well as
to the landlords.
Major SINCLAIR: I should not like
the House to get the impression that this
practice regarding these tenancies has been
widespread, or that it has been spread
over a great number of years. It came

The reason for the delay was that there

ment of the 18th century, under the

practice operated very unfairly in cases
where the fire was accidental, and accordingly, in the year 1707 in England, and
in the year 1715 in Ireland, Acts of
Parliament were passed to give relief in
such cases.
The Act of 1715 was very informative
as to the need for the amendment of the
law. It was entitled "An Act for Preventing Mischief that may happen by
Fire," and it says:
"Whereas by the common law of this
Kingdom every person or persons in
whose house, chamber or out-house, ny
fire should accidentally happen, was
compellable to make recompense and
satisfaction for all damages suffered or
occasioned thereby, to the impoverishment and utter ruin frequently of such
persons; for remedy whereof, be it
enacted by the King's most excellent
Majesty by and with the advice and
consent of the Lords spiritual and temporal and Commons in this present
Parliament assembled, that no action,
suit, or process whatsoever, shall be
had, maintained, or prosecuted against
any person or persons, in whose house
or chamber any fire shall from and
after the twenty-fifth day of March in
the year one thousand seven hundred
and sixteen accidentally begin, or any
recompense or satisfaction be made by
such person or persons for any damage
suffered or occasioned thereby; any
law, usage, or custom, to the contrary
notwithstanding."
This Act of 1715 applies as existing law
in Northern Ireland, and until recently
no one appears to have questioned the
scope of the protection which it gave to
persons in whose premises accidental fires
occurred. A year ago, however, an
action at law came before the Supreme
Court in Eire, and by a majority the
judges held that the word "house"
meant only dwelling-house and did not
include business premises. Inasmuch as
there could be no assurance that judicial
opinion in Northern Ireland would not
take the same course if a case should
come before the courts here, the Government have considered it desirable to
clarify the law and make it plain that the
protection assumed to have been given
by the Act of 1715 with respect to
accidental fires shall apply to all buildings and also to land and not merely to
dwelling-houses.
The Bill forbids the institution of legal
proceedings against any person in or on
whose building or land any fire has
accidentally begun, in respect of damage
caused by reason of such fire, subject,
however, to the proviso to Clause 1 (1)
which excludes certain classes of cases,
for example, cases of negligence.
With this explanation I think hon.
Members will have no difficulty in grasp
ing the intention and meaning of the Bill,
which is framed ir simple terms. I beg
"That the Bill be now read a
to move,

House, therefore, in the interest of the

for Northern Ireland potatoes, pigs,
poultry and eggs, with a view to placing

population to the pre-war level, and
further that in the opinion of this House
the present position entailing lack of
confidence is calculated to prejudice the
immediate war and post-war effort, and
that an early statement of the broad outline of post-war policy would be of
immense value in restoring the confidence
of the agricultural community and so en-

In moving this Resolution it is not
necessary for me to dwell at any length
on the effort that is being put forth by
the agricultural community to assist the
nation in the present struggle in which it
is engaged. Glowing tributes have been
paid to the agricultural industry by those
best able to judge, and members of the
agricultural community have played, and
will continue to play their full part in
bringing this struggle to a satisfactory
and victorious conclusion. When the
farmers were urged to increase production,
not only were they urged, but a demand
was made on them for increased production, and the farming community have
responded nobly to the demand then made
on them. They have given of their best,
and they have produced more than it was
anticipated they would be able to do.
Farmers, however, have long memories,
and the farmers who are veterans to-day
were those who were in the front line of
farming in the war of 1914 and 1918.
When that war broke out in 1914 an
appeal was sent forth to the agricultural
community that it was necessary for them
to go to the plough; that it was necessary
for them to produce food for the nation
if it were not to go under. They were
promised, if they would do so, not a
land fit for heroes to live in, but that the
farming industry would never be allowed
to get into the same state of decay in
which it was then. Agriculture previous
to 1914 was in a state of decay and bankruptcy, and it is a peculiar thing that it
takes a war to bring the agricultural
industry into its own. The 1914-18 war
passed away, and the British nation were
victorious. But no sooner was the last
shot fired than all the promises that had
been made by the politicians of those days
to the agricultural community were
treated like scraps of paper, and not one
of them ever materialised.
Not only was agriculture allowed to
revert to the state in which it was previous to the war of 1914-18, but, when
the war was finished and was won, an
agricultural depression set in, and never
in the history of agriculture in Northern
Ireland was the same state of depression
felt in the industry as there was after the
war of 1918. So the agricultural community in the intervening years between
the end of that war and the beginning of
the present war were allowed to carry on,
but many of them lost their farms, and
many of them went out of the business
altogether. The fertile land of Northern
Ireland became in many cases a wilderness. Unfortunately for the nation, but
rather fortunately for the agricultural
community I think, another war has
come upon us. In 1939 the dogs of war
were unleashed, and it was only then
that the Government of Great Britain
realised that they again wanted the farming community. In spite of the broken
pledges, in spite of the broken promises,
when the agricultural community were
asked to put forth a mighty effort to produce food for the people the response
again was magnanimous.
The Imperial Minister of Agriculture,
Mr. Hudson, in order to induce the agricultural community to give of their best,
and with the consent of the members of
the Cabinet of Great Britain, fixed prices
for agricultural produce based on the
wage which was fixed by the Agricultural
Wages Board, and which had to be paid
to the agricultural labourer. With that
promise went the assurance given by Mr.
Hudson that these prices are fixed now,
but if any new advance takes place these
prices will be revised on the ground of
the increased cost of production.
agricultural community were again soft
enough to believe the promises of the
politicians. The promise was not made
good, and when the agricultural community approached Mr. Hudson about
his broken pledge he made the usual political defence in the Imperial House of
Commons, which was the most peculiar
defence I have ever heard made to any
such pledge.

The defence was, "Well, right enough
you were promised an increase in costs
corresponding with any increase in the

there is an increase in the cost of produc
tion, but you have done rather better
than I thought you would do. If you
have lost something on the swings you
have made it up on the round-abouts and
you must be satisfied with the prices we
have made." In other words, he says to
the farmers of Great Britain and also the
farmers of Northern Ireland, through
our own Ministry of Agriculture, "You
have been over-efficient. You have produced rather more than we thought you
could produce. You have done better
than we thought you could do, and for

the greatest possible sympathy for the

But coal miners are not told,

Let us take the munition factories. Did

which the workers were told that the

expect you to produce so many shells, but

was being installed. When one of the

"" That seems to be the

""
It is about time that agriculture was
lifted out of the maze in which it has been
for so long; it is time agriculture was not
looked at by some people with an inferiority complex as a debasing occupation; it is time that agriculture got its
proper setting in the industrial life of the
community. It will never get that setting
until the agriculturists and the agricultural workers are placed on the same
footing as those engaged in any other
industry. What is a country without a
virile race? I think it was Goldsmith
who said:
Il fares the land, to hast'ning ills
a prey,
Where wealth accumulates, and men
decay.
Many of the social evils with which
we are confronted to-day can be cured
only by the return of many of our good
people to the land. Last week I listened
with great pleasure to the noble Lord,
the right hon. Member for Bloomfield,
declaring that he and the hon. and learned
Member for Iveagh were strong believers
in large families If we are to bring up
large and also intelligent families the best
place to do that is in the country. Every
empire which has gone to ruin owes its
downfall to neglecting agriculture. I
should be very sorry to see our Empire
toppling to the ground, but until the
people in authority in Great Britain see
to it that agriculture gets its proper
setting, and that the man who tills the
ground and faces all the attacks of wind
and weather is at least compensated for
the work he does, I see very little hope
of prosperity either in Northern Ireland
or in Great Britain.
Why should a farmer not get a similar
return on his invested capital to that of
any other business man? Farm capital,
farm brains and farm labour are worthy
of a proper return, and they should get
it.
Farm workers should not for all time
be kept on the bottom rung of the ladder;
they ought to be paid for their labour in
connection with agriculture as well as
those engaged in any other industry.
Comfortable cottages should be provided
in rural areas for our farm labourers.
When speaking on the question of agricultural cottages a few days ago I was
twitted by the hon. Member for South
Armagh because the rents in Dungannon
rural district were raised. On the spur
of the moment I replied that the rents
of the cottages had been raised by 1s a
week, but I find I was wrong. The amount
by which the rents of these cottages was
raised was in some cases ls 2d per week,
and in other instances 1s 3d per week.
What are the rents of the cottages in
the Dungannon rural area? As the
representative of that area, I say that
some of the best cottages that are to be
found in Northern Ireland can be found
in Dungannon rural area, but they were

ticularly when many of the ratepayers

that is to be, a proper place will be found
for agriculture, that it will be taken out
of the slough of despond in which it has
rested for so long, and that it will be

We are told by some people who do not
really understand the agricultural position at all-perhaps they do not want to
understand it-that the agricultural community are a spoiled lot, that they are
never done asking, asking, asking, that
they are never done receiving, receiving,
receiving, and that they are never
grateful for anything they get. We are
told that the farmers get a subsidy for
flax, a subsidy for potatoes, and a subsidy
for wheat. Who gets the subsidy?
Unfortunately it passes through the hands
of the farmers, but surely these subsidies
are not for the benefit of any farmer?
These subsidies are paid by the Government in order that cheap food may be
provided for the people.
No farmer wants a subsidy; what he
does want is an economic price for his
produce. He wants a price that will
enable him to keep himself, his wife, and
his family in decency, and one which will
enable him to pay his labourers a decent
wage.
The farmer does not want a subsidy, but
if the Government decide that there must
be cheap food for the people I am afraid
there is no other way of doing it. I am
one of those who believe that you will
never put any industry on a safe and sure
foundation by paying subsidies. I hope
the day of subsidies will soon be over
and that we will come to the time when
a farmer will receive an economic price
for his produce, a price which will enable
him to play his full share in the industrial
life of the community. Agriculturists
can play a great part to-day, and they
are prepared to play a great part in the
building up of the Empire.
I should like to pay a tribute to the
Prime Minister in spite of the injustice
he did to the Pigs Marketing Board. I
believed then he was wrong, and I still
believe it. But owing to the Prime Minister and his officials bringing into operation
the marketing schemes they did before
the war they put Northern Ireland, so
far as agriculture is concerned, on the

map, and we have been put in a position

We can go on with our marketing

of our climate we are an exporting

I am proud of the industries of Northern Ireland. I am proud of our linen,
tobacco and shipbuilding industries, but
in spite of the pride I feel in all these
the greatest industry we have in Northern Ireland is agriculture. There is more
wealth drawn from agriculture than from
all of these three and there are more
people employed in agriculture to-day, I
understand, than there are in all the
other industries put together. And if
agriculture goes down how are we to carry
on the linen business, the tobacco business, or even the shipbuilding business?
Everything depends on a sound, solid
agriculture, and I am pressing on the
Government the necessity for making
immediate efforts to restore confidence to
the farming community.
Farmers, as I said before, will play
their part. They will do the job if they

Does he think farmers are all fools? If

Farmers to-day are getting their eyes

They are not going any longer to be

They are going to see that they get a fair

They have no confidence in the future.

A promise is a promise. The promise
made to the farming community that the
prices would be revised when any extra
cost occurred in regard to production was
a straight promise if ever one was made
to the agricultural community, and no
politician no matter how expert can give
the impression to the farming community
that they have not again been let down.
The farmers to-day have no confidence.
They have no faith in their work to-day
compared with what they would have had
if the pledge made and given in all
sincerity had been honoured. They were
prepared to work morning, noon and
night in order to deliver the goods. The
time has passed when the farming community, as I said before, can be any
longer dragged by a political machine.
They are going to stand on their own feet
and demand the justice they deserve. A
farmer and his wife and family are no

better things from the consuming public

play and a fair deal. Something must be

and restore that confidence which is necessary for agricultural prosperity, so that
farmers can continue the good work in

industry one which the people should be

The Government will have to do something to restore that lack of confidence
which exists amongst the whole farming
community if they want prosperity in the
industry. If they do not do that then
instead of Northern Ireland being the

Denmark of the United Kingdom, and

Of course the Imperial Government
insist that the consuming public must be
protected and food prices kept down;
therefore prices are fixed at a low level
and subsidies are in some cases paid to
the farmer which would make it appear
that agriculture was subsidised, whereas
it is the consumer, who alone enjoys the.
benefit of the subsidies. Why I say the
consumer alone benefits is that the prices
of farm produce are so tied down that
where subsidies are applied the amounts
are determined in relation to the increased
costs of production, based on production
costs and prices of the pre-war period.
This may sound somewhat involved, but
the point I want to make is that it is
wrong to base farm prices on a period
when the agricultural community were
just recovering from the greatest depression that ever hit the industry.
Agriculture in Ulster does not get the
consideration which it deserves from the
Imperial Government. It is at all times,
whether in peace or war, by far the most
important of our industries in Northern
Ireland, but such is not the case in
England, where agriculture ranks very
low in the general scheme of things.
Prices for all our commodities are fixed in
London, whether by the Ministry of
Agriculture or the Minister of Food I
care not, but when a protest goes forth
from Stormont that certain prices are unremunerative, as in the case of potatoes,
the result is usually a flat negative. Now
potatoes are one of our two sale crops,
and we have not got anything approaching parity with English farmers in the
price of that commodity. In spite of
the fact that the Ministry of Food have
begged us to increase the acreage and
produce more potatoes they persist in
keeping the price down to an impossible
level. Even with his better prices for
potatoes the English farmer is very dissatisfied with the present level of prices.
Flax, the other sale crop I mentioned,
is grown in this country entirely for sale,
and the farmer who for any reason fails
to market his flax has left on his hands
a product that he can do nothing with.
Fortunately, while the war is on, he
usually has no difficulty in disposing of
his fibre, but the price is not sufficiently
remunerative owing to the uncertainty of
the yield and quality. Now, as regards
pigs-
Mr. HENDERSON: They are the
boys!
Mr. LYONS: The rearing and fattening of pigs has been sternly discouraged
for the past three or four years owing to
the shortage of feeding stuffs. Now, this
has of necessity, combined with the low
price for pork, led to the wholesale.
slaughtering of sows in many districts.
The number of sows at present, compared
with the pre-war period, is only 39 per
cent. of that total, and I personally have
reason to think that that figure quoted
by the Ministry of Agriculture is too
high. Something must be done at once
to encourage the rehabilitation of the
pig industry. My suggestion is, add 10s
per cwt. to the price of pork and the
farmers will do the rest. Now, before I
leave the subject of pigs, I should like to
mention another point which is generally
missed. I have not the slightest doubt
that the farmers of Great Britain and
Northern Ireland could supply all our
requirements of pork and bacon. There
is no need for any pork or bacon to be
imported into this country. It is known.
that the importation of bacon in the past
has frequently led to the introduction of
serious diseases, I refer particularly to
foot-and-mouth disease and swine fever.
Both these diseases, when they occur,
cause a serious dislocation in the business
of farming, and they are the cause of
considerable expense to the. Government
in stamping them out and putting our
livestock into a healthy condition once
more. I think that this is a very
important point, and on that account I
would suggest that the importation of

Poultry stocks have been reduced to a

and the low return for eggs, but I insist

To come back to the matter of subsidies,
we have often been told that we have
parity in prices with Britain in everything except potatoes. Now, let us look
into that. Admittedly we have parity in
certain respects, but take our cereal
crops, wheat and oats. England has
always grown a considerable acreage of
wheat. Ireland, especially in the north,
has never been a wheat growing country.
I understand that we grow approximately
3 per cent. of our cereal crops in the
form of wheat, whereas at the present time
England has approximately the same
acreage under wheat as she has under
oats. We know that the wheat subsidy
of £4 per acre applies to both countries
alike, but when it is not produced in
Northern Ireland we do not get any
benefit.
The farm economy of the Northern
Ireland farmer does not prompt him to
grow wheat extensively, for this reason.
The farmer here is dependent on his straw
for feeding his cattle, but Irish cattle will
not eat wheat straw. I do not know
whether English cattle will, but I know
they will not in this country. Therefore,
the farmer here finds himself with this
wheat straw a drug on the market and
fit for nothing except returning to the
land in the form of manure. The English
farmer, on the other hand, is in a much
better position. He has been accustomed
to growing wheat and producing an excellent crop. He is not troubled with the
problem of what to do with his wheat
straw, as he has an excellent and ready
market for it because in England there
are factories producing paper pulp from
straw, in other words, making paper from
it. The English farmer can sell his straw
at approximately £5 per ton, which is a
sound economic price. If we were in that
position we would probably grow quite a
lot of wheat and enjoy the benefits the
English farmers get.

Mr. BROWN: As a matter of administration I would like to refer to the fact
that a report appears in the Belfast News-
Letter to-day announcing the possibility
of impending Government changes in the
Cabinet. I would like to ask the Prime
Minister whether there is any substance
in that statement or not. I am not going
to debate this at length. It will be dealt
with in time. I merely want to say in
passing that the people of Northern Ireland have never become reconciled to the
inclusion of two clergymen in the Cabinet.
I am not going to debate that now, and
the only reason I mention it is that this
reference in the paper has to do with one
of these clergymen. This matter will be
coming up for debate at the forthcoming Presbyterian General Assembly,
and the whole thing will be rehashed, as
to whether it is right or not that two
clergymen should be in the Cabinet. My
opinion is that the country has never
become reconciled, and never will become
reconciled, to the presence of two clergymen in the Cabinet, but the reasons are
so many and so obvious that I am not
going to tire the House dealing with
them.
I want to know whether that statement is correct. Hon. Members of this
House should know when changes in the
Cabinet are contemplated, and they
should also know if such forecasts are a
fact, and, if so, what the proposed
changes are. I am sure
the Prime
Minister, with his usual courtesy, will be
able to make, an announcement on the
matter and tell us whether this is correct.
If I were asked to suggest other changes,
I could do so, but I am not going to.
Mr. SPEAKER: The hon. Member
for South Down is far too modest.
(Laughter.).
Mr. BROWN: I am not even likely to
be asked to give them, and I will not
trouble the House with suggesting them.
In view of this particular reference in the
paper to-day, and in view of the fact
that we are going to have this matter
thrashed out in detail at the Presbyterian
General Assembly in June, it is a matter
which should bring an announcement
from the Prime. Minister at the earliest
possible moment, because I believe the
House is certainly entitled to this information. I am sure the Prime Minister,
with his usual courtesy, will be able to
tell us what the position is, and what the
position is likely to be in the immediate
future.

QUESTIONS.
New Derating Grant.
1. Lieut.-Colonel GORDON asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he can
state (a) what is the total figure of the
provisional new additional grant made
available by the Government in respect of
derating in rural areas in Northern Ireland in the financial year commencing on
the 1st April, 1944; (b) on what general
basis has this additional grant been
allocated and what other factors are taken
into consideration in fixing the allocation;
(c) what sum has been allocated to each
of the unions and rural district councils
in Northern Ireland in the financial year
1944-45; (d) why is a lower percentage on
the basis of the Consolidated Grant
allocated to certain unions and rural
districts than to others; and (e) in fixing
the sums to be allocated to the unions and
rural district councils are estimated credit
balances taken into account.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Mr. Lowry): With reference to the hon.
and gallant Member's question-(a) The
total amount of the provisional new
additional grant made available by the
Government in respect of derating in
rural areas in Northern Ireland in
respect of the coming financial year is
£148,348.
(b) In the allocation of the additional
grant the extent to which hereditaments
in the particular area are derated, the
provisional estimate of the particular
local authority for the coming financial
year as compared with that of previous
years, the extent to which the consolidated
grant, which relates to payments of derating grants in a previous year was
insufficient to meet the derating loss for
that year the credit balance of the local
authority and the current poor rate
payable in the area are all taken into
consideration.
(c) The sums provisionally allocated to
each of the unions and rural district
councils in Northern Ireland in respect
of the financial year 1944-45 are contained
in a lengthy schedule of which I am sending the hon. and gallant Member a copy.
(6
""
""
""
(d) As was explained in a circular issued
by the Ministry to all local authorities
on 9th December, 1943, the consolidated
grant payable to a particular local
authority consists of deficiency contribution payable as standard grant and
supplemental grant in accordance
with the provisions of the Local Government (Finance) Act (N.I.), 1936, plus
the particular local authority's share of
theextra-statutory grant payable in
the financial year 1942-43. The new
additional grant bears no special percentage relationship at all to the consolidated grant for any particular local
authority, because the consolidated grant
which, as pointed out above, is based on
a certain year, was insufficient to meet
fully the derating loss in many cases in
that year and the new additional grant
was calculated with a view to meeting this
deficiency.
(e) The answer is in the affirmative.
I may add that before the allocation of
the new additional grant was settled the
officials of the county councils were consulted informally, and each indicated.
satisfaction at the allocation and at the
same time expressed his keen appreciation
of the Government's action in making
this generous additional grant available
to rural authorities.

Housing.
BALLYMONEY RURAL
LABOURERS' RENTS.
2. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he has received
a resolution from the tenants of the
labourers' cottages in the Ballymoney
rural district, protesting against the proposed action of the Ballymoney Rural
Council to increase the rents of labourers'
cottages built under the Labourers Acts
of 1883-1935 by 50 per cent., and will he
state what action he is prepared to take
in the matter.
Mr. LOWRY: I have received the resolution from the tenants of labourers'
cottages in the Ballymoney rural district
to which the hon. Member refers. The
increase in rents sanctioned by my
Ministry amounts to 1s 6d per week and
is in respect of the cottages erected just
before the outbreak of war under the
Council's last labourers' cottages scheme.
The new rents will amount to 4s 6d per
week, a very small figure in view of the
accommodation provided and the quality
of the cottages. When giving its sanction the Ministry made it clear to the
Council that increases in rents of other
cottages would not be sanctioned until
the cottages were put into a proper state
of repair and, furthermore, in respect of
the increases already sanctioned the
Ministry requested the Rural District
Council to take into account cases of
hardship and to impose no increase if
severe hardship would be involved. I
would also point out that the Council propose to spend £40,000 on repair of cottages. I propose to inform the tenants
who have forwarded the resolution to
this effect.
Mr. NIXON: With regard to the
Minister's statement on the rents of these
houses being raised, is it not a fact that
a private owner of house property cannot under any circumstances raise the
rent, whether it is economic or is not
economic, and why should a council be

5. Mr. JOHN BAILEY asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he can
state if it is a fact that large numbers
of people who are in Northern Ireland on

Mr. LOWRY: I have no information
as to whether persons from Eire who come
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Lowry]
within the ambit of the Residence in
Northern Ireland (Restriction) Order,
1942, are buying up farms and house
property in Northern Ireland.
The issue of residence permits does not
confer any right on the holders to remain
in Northern Ireland after the war, and
in this connection I cannot do better than
quote from the statement made in the
Imperial House of Commons by the
Home Secretary and Minister of Security
on the 18th October, 1942, on the question of the control of persons who come to
Northern Ireland whether from Eire,
Great Britain or elsewhere.
Mr. Morrison stated on the occasion
referred to that "the immediate object
of the scheme is to deal with war conditions, but it is also contemplated that
the scheme will be of value on the termination of hostilities for the purpose of
facilitating the reinstatement in employment of demobilised men from Northern
Ireland who joined His Majesty's Forces
as volunteers. At such a time it will be
right to give to the demobilised volunteers preference in the labour market of
Northern Ireland over these newcomers,
and for this purpose to have power to
terminate the permits granted to persons
who are in employment. It is accordingly contemplated that the scheme will
be kept in existence for a reasonable time
after the end of the war, and if the
Defence Regulation should expire before
the demobilised men have had reasonable
opportunity of being absorbed into employment, it will in the view of the Government be right that the necessary
legislation should be introduced in the
United Kingdom Parliament for a
temporary prolongation of the system."
Health Services.
LONDONDERRY ANTE-NATAL
CLINIC.
7. Dr. LYLE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he is aware that
the only ante-natal clinic in the city of
Londonderry is run as a charity, without
remuneration, by a philanthropic doctor,
and will he impress upon the Corporation
of that city the necessity for a municipal
clinic to which the mothers may resort
without incurring the stigma of receiving
charity.
Mr. LOWRY: The matter of antenatal clinics in Londonderry is being investigated and will be considered in connection with the improvement of the
health services generally in the city.
There is no question of the "stigma of
receiving charity" attaching to expectant
mothers who have the good sense to seek
ante-natal advice and treatment at this
clinic which is operated in the City and
County Hospital, which, as the hon.
Member knows, is not a poor-law institution, and which, furthermore, is subsidised by the Londonderry Corporation to
the extent of £2,750 per annum.
That there is no such stigma as is
visualised by the hon. Member is evidenced by the progressive popularity of
this clinic over a period of years, as
shown in the evidence tendered by the
City Medical Superintendent Officer of
Health to the Select Committee, the
number of attendances annually having
increased from 430 in 1939 to 1,290 in
1943.
As I have mentioned, the matter of
ante-natal clinics is being investigated,
but no matter what decision may be
reached in the matter of providing additional clinics, I would deprecate any
action which would detrimentally interfere with the obviously useful work
which is being done in this hospital on
a voluntary basis and which is clearly
appreciated by the public.
Dr. LYLE: Arising out of the reply
of the right hon. Gentleman is it no
concern of his that his constituents in
Derry are being pauperised by being
granted this charity or service which is
their right to obtain and which, if in
Belfast or any city in England and
almost any urban or rural district in
England, they would obtain as a right?
Mr. LOWRY: I am by no means
aware that my constituents are in need
of this care, but in any event it is not a
charity, and primarily the matter of designing and organising public service
belongs to and is vested in the local
authority. Whenever they make a move
or any suggestion comes from that quarter or any other it has never been turned
down since I have been associated with
this Ministry.

a
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL: (Mr.
MacDermott): I have been unable to
identify the statement of the Ministry of
Food official to which the question refers.
But I am informed that this Ministry,
while recognising test purchases as
normal part of the machinery of enforcement, has instructed its employees most
definitely that in no circumstances should
they, when making a test purchase, use
persuasion or pressure to induce a shopkeeper to break the law.
I am not aware of any convictions
obtained by disregard of these instructions, and I do not consider that inspectors
who discharge this unpleasant, though
still necessary, duty in accordance with
such instructions can fairly be regarded
as agents provocateurs or as breaking the
law themselves.
I have read in Hansard the proceedings
of 12th March, 1941, to which the hon.
Member refers. I do not know of any

then alleged which do not appear to have
been considered such as to warrant
criminal procedings.

incident to which the hon. Member refers

of evading the law to the shopkeeper concerned, but he need not take it. I cannot
see any way of enforcing these regulations
without resorting to this system of test
purchasing, unpleasant though it may be.

will, of course, progressively decline as
the years pass by. The settlement I have
outlined, when approved by Parliament,
must be regarded as final, but I am
satisfied that to have been able, after the
lapse of so many years, to re-open this
question and rectify the position of
teachers so substantially is no mean
achievement. I am grateful to the
Chancellor of the Exchequer and the
Financial Secretary for their sympathetic
and helpful approach to what has proved
to be a complicated and thorny problem.
Representations have also been made.
to me in regard to the devaluation, for
pension purposes, of the non-contributing
service of secondary and certain other
classes of teachers. At present I am unable to say more than that the matter is
receiving my sympathetic consideration.
Hon. Members will recollect that in
November last I announced an extension
of the existing Lump Sum Scheme which
had the effect of awarding a lump sum
in respect of service since 1st February,
1922, to pensioners who have retired on
or after that date. The House will be
aware that strong representations have
since been made to me that these concessions did not go far enough and I
found some force in the arguments put
forward, particularly in the cases of those
teachers whose retirement took place in
the early twenties. I consequently continued negotiations and I am glad to say
that I am now in a position to announce
a further very substantial concession
=which I am confident will commend itself
to the House, and to those who will
benefit therefrom. Subject to the
approval of Parliament, the arrangement
which I announced in November will be
extended so that pensioners who retired
since 1st February, 1922, will not only
receive a lump sum in respect of their
service subsequent to that date but also
in respect of one-half of their service
before it. The date before which
half service will count varies in
the case of certain classes of teachers
other than elementary teachers.
Furthermore, while contributions at
the rate of 11 per cent. per
annum of the teacher's retiring salary
will be made for the years after 1st February, 1922, no such deductions will be
made for the previous years. The
estimated immediate cost to the
Exchequer is £280,000, a figure which is
inclusive of the concessions contained in
the scheme which I announced in
November.
Had the payment of such lump sums
been authorised in each year since the
setting up of this Parliament they would
have formed a charge on the years in
question. Their payment now in bulk
cannot be regarded as a legitimate charge
on the revenue for 1944-45 and I therefore propose that this expenditure should
be met from the capital of the Teachers'
Superannuation Fund. Legislation will
be introduced at a later date to give
effect to this proposal.
Teachers retiring in the future will also
benefit under the scheme now announced.
The extra cost involved in their case is
estimated at £100,000 spread over about
18 years, the cost in the financial year
1944-45 being £11,500: the latter amount

ADJOURNMENT MOTION.
RESIGNATION OF MINISTER OF
EDUCATION.
Prime Minister's Statement.
The PRIME MINISTER:
I beg to
move, "That this House do now
adjourn."
I am obliged to the House for having
given me this opportunity to make a
statement on a matter which has been the
subject of considerable agitation and
speculation since the Minister of Educa
tion resigned. I think I should say that
it is not normally necessary for the Prime
Minister to give any reason why he
appoints a colleague or why he asks a
colleague to resign. On this occasion the
right hon. Gentleman in a statement
which he issued to the Press last week
stated that his views as to the need forand this is the quotation-"handing on
to the children a Christian view of man
and his responsibilities" were strongly
opposed, and the Press and many people
have naturally come to the conclusion
that there were differences of opinion between the Minister and the Government
on this matter. I wish to state categorically that that is not the case. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)
I
The Government have already announced that a White Paper will be published as soon as possible setting out the
proposals for educational reform. Naturally the question of religious instruction
will be included in the general survey of
our whole educational system, which is
now being undertaken by the Ministry of
Education as a necessary preliminary to
the preparation of the White Paper.
should like the House to listen particularly carefully to this because this is one
of the main arguments. The ex-Minister
had not reached the stage of discussing
the question of the policy of his Ministry
with me.
So far as I am concerned I
know nothing about the policy or the
future policy of the Ministry of Education, so there can be no difference between
the Minister and myself on that score.
It is obvious also that if he had not discussed the matter with me he did not
discuss it with or put it before the
Cabinet. The Cabinet were never asked
to consider any question of policy with
regard to religious education. Therefore,
so far as any complaint or allegation is
made that the Government and myself
take different views from the Minister of
Education that falls to the ground, as we
have not even discussed it. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)
The House would, no doubt, like to
know the reason why I asked the Minister
to resign. It has always been my view
that a Minister should keep in the closest
Resignation of Minister-
Prime Minister's Statement
22 FEBRUARY 1944

יס
I.
possible touch with all the activities of his
Department. As long ago as August last
year I discussed this with my right hon.
Friend, but, unfortunately, he did not
find it possible to attend at the Ministry
in Portrush as frequently as I considered
necessary. It is the duty of each Minister
to weld the Ministry together, so that he
has a perfect team working in co-operation
with him and with the Government. I did
not consider that that team spirit had been
created in this Ministry owing to the unfortunate fact and I admit the difficulty
-that the Ministry is at Portrush and
the Minister lived here; but, without
constant attendance at his Ministry, I do
not consider it is possible to produce that
team spirit. The duty must fall on the
Prime Minister, if he considers that
sufficient attention is not being given to
the Ministry, to act, and in this case I
considered that it was my duty to act and
request the late Minister of Education to
hand in his resignation. I frankly say
that the position with the Ministry and
the Minister was entirely unsatisfactory.
Whilst I believe that the House will
accept the assurance that I have given
them that there has been no difference
either between myself and the Minister
or between the Government and the
Minister, there may be a suggestion that
there has been a difference between the
Minister and the Parliamentary Secretary.
I, therefore, took the trouble to inquire
from the Parliamentary Secretary whether
there had been any difference of opinion
on this matter. Exactly the same argument
holds good so far as the Minister and his
Parliamentary Secretary are concerned,
because the Ministry had not reached the
stage where any question of policy could
be discussed. I am satisfied that no
difference did occur, and that that was
not the reason for this resignation. I do
not think it is possible in a Ministry for
everybody to agree. In fact, I think it
would be an unhealthy sign if all heads
of Departments of the Ministry agreed
and all became yes-men to what the
Minister said. Perhaps I have been un-
Efortunate, but it never happened in any
Ministry I have had the honour of leading. We discussed matters and we may
all have had a great deal of difference,
but it is only by difference and debate
that we can arrive at a proper solution
of the problem.


This I want to say, if there had been
any serious difference between the Minister
and his Parliamentary Secretary it was
the duty of the Minister to report the
matter to me. No such report reached
me, and I knew nothing about it until
the last interview I had with the right
hon. Gentleman. I should like here to
say very definitely that the Government
are fully aware of the need for handing
on to our children a Christian view of
man and his responsibilities. We are a
Christian people, we want our children
brought up in the Christian way, and we
shall never attempt to force upon anybody an educational system which does
not allow, in the fullest possible measure,
for the teaching of religion which I, personally, hold to be of supreme importance
in the education of the young.
It is most unfortunate that this matter
of religious education should have been
brought up. It did not arise and I can
give, the House a complete assurance on
that when the question of asking the
right hon. Gentleman for his resignation
came up. The House will, I hope, in a
short time receive the White Paper, when
the public and this House will be able to
discuss the policy of education. It is
impossible now to go into a policy of that
sort. This is not the time, but I am
here merely to state quite definitely that
it is not a case of any difference between
myself and the ex-Minister; it is not a
case of any difference between the Cabinet
and the ex-Minister; and it is not a case
of any difference between the Parliamentary Secretary and the ex-Minister.
It is because the ex-Minister was unable
to give, sufficient attention to his Ministry.

I want to warn the right hon. Gentleman the Prime Minister that the people

Republics every day in the year. There

We
do not know who are going to form the
Government here this day four weeks.
There is only one solution of the whole
problem and that is the solution I have
put forward within the last three weeks
both in this House and in London.
I have certainly been abused by the
newspapers for putting this solution forward. In the London Parliament I
advocated the refusal of permission to
this Parliament to have an extension of
its life because I believed on that occasion
that I was going to do something useful,
something that would help to secure for
Northern Ireland a stable Government.
I was misrepresented in the Press. I
came to this House and attack on me was
prepared from that side of the House for
the speech I made at Westminster. Unfortunately for all that preparation, I
made a different speech in this House, but
one meaning the same thing. The, politicians on that side of the House were not
alive to that road of travel by a politician
who is, I suppose, as long in service as
they are. I said in this House that the
life of this Parliament should not be
extended and in the British House I said
that Part II of the Bill should be
deleted.
Here is the reorganisation that I suggest. It is not a reorganisation of the
Ministry of Home Affairs or of the
Ministry of Public Security, nor the transfer of police to the Ministry of Public
Security and the transfer of something
else to the Ministry of Home Affairs. In
a way I sympathise with the Prime
Minister, because he has a very bad working team. He has a combination of
misfits from other parties who could not
find a tenth place in those parties. I
know it is not possible for him to clear
them all away together. They might
become back benchers and organise. a
revolt to overthrow the Government. I
suggest that we proceed to have a general
election so as to clarify the air and learn

to take note of, and that is the very
thing this Government does not do. They
care nothing about what the people outside do. But you will care in the near
future, because if you were not afraid of
the people outside you would immediately
respond to the call for a general election.
It has been suggested to me that the
right hon. Gentleman may pass out

position held by himself and his colleagues. I want to tell you the people

We want to decide what form of government we require in this part of the
country. We, the people, must get the

I can assure the Prime Minister that it

will be sent back. I know one. or two
in this House who think they are sacrosanct from any interference at the next
general election. But I can assure the

Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: I have no

Member has said he has put down a
Motion on this subject for debate next

The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-

Agriculture.
A FLAX AGREEMENT
1. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether his attention has
been drawn to proceedings at the last
Ballybot (County Armagh) Quarter
Sessions arising out of an agreement in
connection with the growing of flax and
the supply of flax-seed therefor, which
were dismissed; whether he is aware that
during, these proceedings it was stated by
the solicitor for the defendant, Mr.
Daniel O'Hare, of Messrs. Fisher &
Fisher, solicitors, Newry, that the agreement between the parties was one which
he would advise no client to sign, and
that with this remark His Honour County
Court Judge J. H. Robb, K.C., agreed;
whether he is aware of the further fact
that during the same proceedings the
solicitor for the plaintiffs, Mr. Cullen,
of Messrs. R. M. Cullen & Son, solicitors,
Portadown, stated that the agreement in
question was one prepared by the North
of Ireland Flax Processors' Association
and approved by the Ministry of Agriculture for Northern Ireland and also by
the Ulster Farmers' Union and that his
clients had no option but to use it;
whether he can state why his Ministry
approved of an agreement that has now
been held to be defective and condemned
by a county court judge; and what steps
his Ministry propose to take in the
matter.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Rev. Robert Moore): The answer to the
first part of the question is in the affirmative. The case in question related to the
1942 contract-now two years out of
date. Under that contract the processing firm provided the farmer with seed,
the cost of which was to be deducted
from the first payment made by the firm
to the farmer. The processing firm did
not take the grower's flax and proceeded
to seek payment for the seed. The court
held that the processing firm was not
entitled to recover the cost of the seed
from the farmer as the firm, not having
made any payments, could not deduct
the value of the seed.
I am not aware that the agreement was
defective, and I would not propose to
take any steps in the matter, even if it
were competent for me to do so.
Mr. BROWN: Surely the Minister
deems it to be part of his duty to protect
the interests of the farmer in this matter?
Surely when a county court judge has
held that this agreement is defective it is
the duty of
Mr. SPEAKER: The hon. Member
knows supplementary questions should be
short questions of fact.
Mr. BROWN: I propose to carry out
your directions. Would the Minister
not think it incumbent upon his Ministry
to protect the interests of the farmer in
this matter by seeing that there is an
agreement provided that is not defective
such as this one is?
Rev. ROBERT MOORE: As far as I
can judge from the issue the farmer was
protected.
Mr. BROWN: Surely if the farmer is
protected-
Mr. SPEAKER: The hon. Member is
carrying on a debate.

RELIGIOUS INSTRUCTION.
9. Mr. BROWN asked the Prime
Minister whether his attention has been
called to the letter in the Belfast Press
of 24th instant stating that under the
Education Bill now before the Imperial
Parliament the British Government propose to provide that instruction in the
Christian faith will be given (subject to
a conscience clause) to all boys and girls
in England and Wales at public elementary, preparatory and secondary schools,
and whether he can give the House an
assurance that the Government intend
adopting precisely the same policy in
regard to all public elementary, preparatory and secondary schools in Northern Ireland.
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir Basil
Brooke): I have seen the letter to which
the hon. Member refers; I have also seen
the Education Bill which is being debated
in the Imperial House of Commons.
As I informed the House last week,
future policy with regard to education has
not yet been considered by the Cabinet,
and I have no intention, therefore, of
committing the Government to a hasty
and perhaps ill-judged pronouncement in
the precise terms that the hon. Member
desires. The question of religious instruction will certainly not be overlooked in
the White Paper which is being prepared
in the Ministry of Education and which,
of course, will form the subject of debate
in this House. I would remind the hon.
Member that last week I made a special
reference to this important matter and
lest he or any other person-should be
in doubt as to the attitude of the Government I say, here and now, that we do
not propose under any circumstances to
whittle away the present provision for
religious instruction in our Education
Acts; we are determined to maintain it
and even to extend it, so far as we properly can and so far as we are satisfied
that it is for the good of our children
that we should do so.
Mr. BROWN: Can the Prime Minister
-I ask the question courteously-give me
a plain answer to a plain question? Is
Ulster going to keep step by step with
England and Wales in this matter of
Christian instruction in schools or not?
Does he not think that is a question to
which the Ulster people require and
deserve an immediate answer?

Civil Service-Number of Officials.
14. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Finance whether he can state the total
number of civil servants at present employed by the Government of Northern
Ireland, including those on agency
services; how
many of these are permanent, and how many temporary
officials; how many of those described as
temporary officials have been in the employment of the Government (a) for over
twenty years; (b) for over fifteen years;
(c) for over ten years; and (d) for over
five years; whether temporary officials are
deprived of pension and certain other
rights; and whether it is fair that those
in the employment of the Government for
many years are still ranked as, temporary
officials and therefore denied the same
rights enjoyed by permanent officials in
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Brown]
the employment of the Government for
shorter periods.
Major SINCLAIR: The total number
of persons at present employed in the
Civil Service of Northern Ireland including prison officers and industrial and
subordinate staff is 7,417. This figure
includes those engaged on agency services
and also those absent with H.M. Forces;
of the total, 2,290 persons have established
status and 5,127 are temporary employees.
The number of temporary staff who have
served for over 20 years is 48; between
15 and 20 years is 67; between 10 and 15
years is 177; and between 5 and 10 years
is 537. Thus 829 persons have over five
years' service, but about 40 per cent. of
these are employed in subordinate and industrial posts which have never either in
this or the Imperial Service had an
established grading.
Under the Superannuation Acts temporary officials do not enjoy the same
privileges as officers of established status,
the position being that, subject to the
fulfilment of certain statutory conditions,
the latter receive a pension and lump sum
allowance on retirement, while the former
receive a gratuity only. There are certain
other differences in the conditions of
service affecting annual leave and sick
leave privileges.
With regard to the final part of the
question I would point out that the paramount consideration in filling established
posts must be the efficiency of the Service,
and that this involves not only the selection of officers for such posts on a competitive basis, but also requires that due
measures be taken to ensure a graduated
age distribution. Neither of these objects
could be attained if established status
were conferred automatically upon the
completion of a prescribed period of
service.
So far as practicable, however, the
claims of temporary officers to established
status have always been kept in mind in
our Service. Thus, on the clerical side
the established grade of male clerical
assistant is recruited exclusively from men
who have served in a clerical capacity for
at least five years; and a proportion of
the vacancies arising in the established
grades of elerk (male) and clerical assistant II are filled by selection from recommended officers who have served in a
temporary capacity for at least two years
and four years respectively. On the
technical side vacancies in the established
ranks are filled so far as possible by selection from serving temporary staff and
when it is deemed expedient to fill particular vacancies by open competition,
serving officers are considered pari passu
with candidates from outside. In the
subordinate ranks all established messenger posts are filled by selection from
the temporary employees in that grade.
