PERSONAL STATEMENT.
Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry
of Education.
Mrs. PARKER: With your permission, I desire to make a personal statement, in view of the deliberate attacks
which have been made upon me, since this
House met on February 22nd. I do so
with the greatest reluctance and distaste,
but, for the sake of my personal reputation, I cannot allow these misrepresentations to pass uncontradicted.
In the statement issued by the late
Minister of Education to the Press at the
time of his resignation, he was reported
as implying that I had strongly opposed
his views on religious policy. In the
statement made by him in the Senate on
February 24th he switched his attack on
me to another issue that of the personnel
of the Youth Committee. I propose to
answer both of these accusations.
On February 22nd, in this House, I
stated very definitely that there had
never been any controversy on religious
policy between me and my Minister;
secondly, that there was never any unpleasantness or controversy on any subject
between me and my Minister, and that
our relations had always been absolutely
friendly. I also stated that there had
been no discussions on religious policy in
connection with educational reconstruction, because only the broad outline had
been prepared by the officials ready for
discussion, and that discussion had never
taken place owing to recent events.
Consequently, there could have been no
disagreement as to future. policy. In any
case, in the broad outline, curricula
which would cover religious instruction
were not included. This is the truth and
cannot be controverted.
To this I would like to add that no one
could be more conscious than I am that
religious teaching is essential for every
and any child and young person and that
the earlier a thorough grounding is given
the better.
Now, as to the personnel of the Youth
Committee. Professor Corkey stated that
he was presented with a list of 12 names
selected by me from a longer list compiled by the Ministry, that he made
alterations in this list, and that I expressed "strong indignation" at his
decision.
Personal Statement-
Mrs. Parker
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mrs. Parker]
The true facts are as follows: A list of
17 suitable people with their respective
qualifications was prepared by the officer
in charge of the Youth Welfare Branch
of the Ministry. In accordance with
recognised procedure, this list was passed
to the Permanent Secretary of the
Ministry for his observations. In a
minute addressed to the Minister he
narrowed down the list of 17 names giving
his reasons for each recommendation and
his general views. As the Minister had
decided-long before this stage that I
was to be chairman of the new committee
-and as I had been in the closest touch
with this work for a long time—the
Permanent Secretary's minute to the
Minister together with the original list
of 17 names was passed to the Minister
through me.
The memorandum bore a covering note
addressed to me as follows:
To Mrs. Parker: "Please see underneath memorandum I have addressed to
the Minister and on which you may
wish to offer observations."
After careful consideration I prepared a
separate minute. I endorsed the general
principles laid down by the Secretary and
made my suggestions, giving pros and
cons. My suggestions differed in two or
three instances from the Secretary's but
were taken out of the original 17. All
three documents were then passed to the
Minister for his final decision.
On two or three subsequent occasions
when the different suggestions were being
discussed by the Minister and the officials
I was asked to be present and we went
into them in a perfectly friendly manner.
No "strong indignation" was ever expressed by me. Indeed, nothing transpired
about which I felt any indignation,
although I did not necessarily agree with
all the final decisions. My sole idea and
that of the Ministry was to get the best
possible working committee, consisting of
people most interested in and with the
greatest experience of youth work as a
whole.
The documents referred to are on the
Ministry's file and there can be no questioning of the facts which I have stated.
What I have just told the House may
serve to show how events have been distorted. I give the House my solemn
word of honour that there never was
friction or controversy between the ex-
Minister and myself on any matter. When
he took up office he told me he would be
guided by me and rely upon me to give
him advice based on my six years'
experience of the work of the Ministry.
Whilst realising that this was, of
course, merely a courteous indication of
his wish to be friendly, I told him that
I would help him in every possible way
and that he could count on me. I told
him at the same time, that the principal
suggestion I could make was that he
should keep in the closest possible touch
with his Ministry and the senior officials
in Portrush. On the same occasion he
asked me what suggestions I had to offer
as to educational literature which he
should study. He mentioned The Times
Educational Supplement and I agreed
that this was valuable, but I urged him
to gain a thorough knowledge of our own
present educational system in Northern
Ireland as embodied in the Northern Ireland Education Acts. This is different
from the English one in many particulars.
At that time, Professor Corkey did not
appear to be conversant with these details
and I felt that it was essential that he
should become so before we embarked on
reconstruction. Since that day I have
proffered neither advice nor opinion unless
I was deliberately requested by Professor
Corkey to do so on any specific matter.
I
T
It has been suggested that I made
accusations against my Minister, and it
has been stated that I resigned because of
differences of opinion between us. The
answer involves some past history. When I
the air raids on Belfast took place in
1941 the Government of the day decided
to move the headquarters of the Ministry
from Belfast to Portrush. The term
"headquarters" means the senior as well
as junior officials and all documents. The
only officials remaining in Tyrone House
were the Minister's private secretary, two
inspectors and since July, 1943, the
principal officer in charge of the youth
welfare activities who has returned there
with his staff. The location of the Ministry in Portrush presents the most difficult
and tiring problem to me as well as to
others on account of my Parliamentary
and other duties, but I have been obliged
to face it since 1941. For a considerable
time before the appointment of the late
Minister we had been anxious to return
if accommodation could be found.
Nothing was available.
Eventually

1.
matters reached a stage last August when
it seemed absolutely imperative that headquarters should go to the Minister as the
Minister did not find it possible to
go to headquarters. At that time I
approached the Prime Minister to urge
him to bring about our early return. He
had already heard of the urgent
necessity for this move and understood the
reasons. As a result of his sympathetic
response we hope to be in new quarters
in Belfast, at any rate, before the end of
1944, if not earlier.
After the August interview and when
six months had elapsed, and before the
building of the new headquarters was
started the Prime Minister questioned me
as to whether the necessity for our return
was as vital as it had appeared to be in
August or if the situation had improved.
After hearing my reply, the Prime
Minister said that, if my statements
could not be verified, he would have to
call for my resignation. I did not resign, nor was my resignation called for,
because the statements made in reply to
his questions were substantiated.
To sum up there has been no clash
or controversy between me
and
Professor Corkey on religious policy
or on any other matter. His statements regarding the selection of
the Youth Committee are utterly misleading to use a mild form. I did not
resign because there was no reason for me
to do so, and I have never made difficulties
on any subject in our official conversations.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)

MEMBER'S
MOTION.
PRISON WARDERS.
Mr. NIXON: We are coming now to
a case of six ordinary humble men earning their living who were dismissed without trial, and dismissed without being
informed why they were dismissed. In
accordance with the Atlantic Charter and
general British justice I am submitting
this Motion to-day. The humble subject.
of His Majesty has the same right as the
highest subject, and that is the right of
trial, the right of charges being framed
against him, and the right to be heard.
Another part of the Motion, which I beg
to move, deals with the necessity for a
public sworn inquiry and investigation
into these recurring escapes from His
Majesty's prisons. The wording of the
Motion is:
That in the opinion of this House the
dismissal by the Minister of Home
Affairs of six Protestant warders without trial on a secret report which the
Minister is unwilling to produce but
which relates to the escape of prisoners
from Belfast Jail, is a violation of the
rights of free and loyal men and tends
to discourage loyal Protestants from
taking service in H.M. Prison. Further,
the House thinks that these everrecurring escapes should be the subject
of a public sworn inquiry by one of His
Majesty's Judges.
own
When the Minister came to the conclusion and made the decision that these
men should be dismissed he was in a very
peculiar position, because on his
showing he was not the Minister of Home
Affairs at all. He stated in this House—
and I will read it later on-that the
decision to dismiss these men was taken
six weeks before his Parliamentary Secretary came into his present office. Both
the Minister and his Parliamentary
Secretary came into their present offices
on or about 7th May, 1943, and he took
the decision to dismiss these six men on
or about 26th March, 1943; that is, if
you accept the Minister's statement as
being true. What was his own personal
position at that particular time? At that
particular time, or about that particular
time, the present Minister of Home Affairs
was Parliamentary Secretary.
Mr. LOWRY: No.
Mr. NIXON: Well, we will read it
later on, and I say "Yes."
Mr. LOWRY: I say you are wrong.
Mr. NIXON: Imagine my being contradicted by a Minister who stated here
the other day that he thought the
Hibernians had the Orange Hall in
Portrush. There is not a man in this
House or in the North of Ireland who
would believe him. He never thought
anything of the kind. His statements
in this House are continually misleading.
I ask the Members of the House, and
some of them have sons at the front or
relatives in the various Services, how
would they like it if their sons came home
and stated they were dismissed, and when
they asked, "What are you dismissed
for?" they received the reply, "I do not
know, daddy. I was not told."
But the Minister, at the time he states
he took that decision, had tendered his
own resignation. He had done so, not
on ordinary grounds but on extraordinary
grounds. By tendering that resignation
he had suggested, as he stated, he would
not serve under the then Prime Minister
for something that was wrong, according
to him. I do not know what the something was. That was the man who took
the decision to dismiss these six officers.
Then he waited till June. I do not know
the date they were dismissed, but somewhere in June. He announced it on the
9th of June. Why did he wait? Was
he afraid that the then Prime Minister,
who belongs to a family that has produced
judges distinguished throughout the world
for their sense of justice, would not allow
him to dismiss them? Was that what
made him wait? How could the Parliamentary Secretary take the decision which
he states he did take, and which he has
the effrontery to deny here to-day? Now
he made a statement in this House on the
26th of August about this matter:
Mr. Lowry: I suppose it is a commonplace. in matters covering such a
wide field and of such importance that
common courtesy, apart from the possibility of giving information, demands
that the Minister responsible should be

I perused the evidence and the

Remember, he was acting as Parliamentary Secretary because on or about

decided that he would dismiss these six

How did he know he was going to be

was to tender his resignation? I often

Gentleman made up his mind to do a

A prison warder is entitled to the same
justice as anyone else. No matter what
position a man is in he is entitled to his
living, and if it is anything in connection
with the Government with which he is
deprived of his living I will bring it to
the Table of this House.
This kind of thing seems to be the
general policy of Ministers. The other
day a good Presbyterian living on the
Ballygomartin Road was dismissed from
his job in the Ministry of Agriculture in
order to make room for a man from
Dublin. That could not be denied,
although an attempt was made to justify
it. I am bringing this forward now in
an endeavour to stop for all time the
antics of the Minister of Home Affairs
and anyone who feels inclined to do this
kind of thing.
The prisoners escaped from Belfast on
the 15th January, 1943, and from Derry
on the 20th March, 1943. You have
heard the time he decided to dismiss
them, but you may not have heard the
bogus excuses he put up here at first. He
told us that in Derry they dug a hole
about twelve feet deep, and then burrowed about 50 feet. They got rid of
the clay and nobody knew what they were
doing. Could you dig down twelve feet
here and then burrow for twenty or
thirty feet to the outside of the building
without some official noticing it? They
must have eaten the clay they took out,
because there is no other way in which
they could have got rid of it. I should
say that that is as good a story as the one
about the Hibernians getting Portrush
Orange Hall. One story is as good as the
other, if not better.
It is rather unfortunate that the
Minister of Home Affairs has no personal
experience of discipline or of a disciplined
force. The Minister of Finance, the
Prime Minister and the Minister of
Public Security have such experience.
You always get more justice from a man
who understands discipline and has been
under it himself than from a man who
knows nothing whatever about it.
The Minister of Home Affairs came in
here from Derry as the result of a byelection, and his progress has been pretty
rapid. The Parliamentary Secretary at
that time, the hon. and learned Member
for St. Anne's, resigned, and the present

knows that the men who escaped know

The most ridiculous things are being put

The prison may be familiar to some
persons, of course through their professional activities, but not to others.
Shortly, it consists of three tiers, a
ground one, one somewhat higher up, and
a third higher up still. It is almost up
to the roof of this chamber. The cells
are arranged along each side.
had to the second tier, A2 as it is called-

Access is had to the corridors which surround the cells which are, of course,
fastened up as in any prison by a very
strong wire. Now, two of these dismissed
men were on duty in A1, two in A2 and

Now, it was the plain duty of these
men from the moment they entered in
until they went out to get their breakfast at 8-30 to be responsible for the safe
custody of every one of the convicts under
their charge.
Their first duty on coming on duty was
to check up and confirm what the night
guard had reported that 115 convicts
were there safe. They did that and, of
course, found them safe and correct. The
next job after that check was what is
called first slops. The cells are unlocked
and certain matters are emptied out into
receptacles which are carried by four
prison orderlies. The officer unlocks.
The orderlies come in between him and
the class officer who comes behind and relocks the doors. The next step is service
of breakfast. Much the same process is
carried out and was carried out on the
second tier and on the top tier, except
that there only one cell door is unlocked
at a time, and the number of convict
orderlies is two instead of four as there
were on A1 and A2. Now, breakfast
began to be served about five to eight,
and was completed at ten past eight. The
next step, about ten minutes later, is what
is called second slops and the men then go
off duty. They are relieved by the stores
staff, the people in charge of the stores,
while these men get their breakfast and
go on duty again at ten to ten. They
were out of the wing at half-past eight
o'clock and they reported that everybody
was safe and secure in that place as it had
been their duty to do.

going in daylight with a man not caring

That is what happened that morning.
And the clear negligence that emerges

floor had no other duty to perform except

him-keep him under observation till he

These two convicts, Maguire and Steele,
made their way up the stairs. There
were two officers on duty in A2. One
man escaped from them, Donnelly, and
whatever they were doing that prevented

going up from their proper floor, it could
could not have been the close look they

Donnelly joins the party and goes to the

McAteer, McAteer would not have got

was a trap-door in the room, which led

past. The four betook themselves to the

First of all they had to make their way
up. If all the plans had been made,
even if the roof of the prison had been
away altogether, if the Belfast Fire
Brigade had been there with their ladders
-all these aids would have been of no
consequence. If the men in A1, A2 and
A3 had been doing their duty these men
could not have taken advantage of whatever aids were there for them. Now the
first duty of any warder is the safe
custody of the prisoners. That is not a
thing that demands experience, although
these men could not plead want of experience.
Now I have accounted for five of them.
There is the sixth man, and the negligence charged against him is this, that
he saw the presence of the table and the
ladder underneath the trapdoor without
making sure that the trapdoor was
securely locked. That was done by a
man in charge, a principal officer of four
years, who had eight and a half previous
years' experience in that wing as class
officer. Can there be any doubt about
the negligence of the six men in question
on that morning?
I come
now to the action that was
taken. I heard about it-of course I
admit that on the 15th January I was
just Parliamentary Secretary, but I could
take this step-a few minutes before 9
o'clock and I was in my office at 9.30.
The Assistant Secretary, the Prison.
Inspector responsible, was at the jail at
10.30 ready to start a sworn investigation into the matter. He was somewhat
delayed because naturally the police were
on the spot and they had to have first
preference, but an inquiry on oath started
that day. Some 20 men, including those
six, who might be able to throw any
light on the matter were invited. They
made their statements by means of question and answer, and they signed them.
That was done on the 15th, 16th, 18th
and 20th January, and as speedily as the
matter could be furnished to me I read it.
I came to the conclusion 'that perhaps
the ordinary investigation by the Prison
Inspector-the matter was very serious,
because at least two of these criminals
were of a desperate character-was not
sufficient and that the matter required
the most searching examination. I had
no doubt about the ability and knowledge

very experienced

It has been charged against me that an
Indian judge was not a suitable person
to investigate the truth in Northern Ireland. It is commonplace and anyone who
knows the history of India, especially in
regard to matters about litigation, knows
that on the subject of corrupt perjury
they are second to none. We have many
somewhat skilled operators of that sort
in our own courts, but they are a bad
second to certain of the inhabitants of
India. Therefore as to the competence of
this Tribunal to find out the truth I had
no doubt whatsoever. They investigated
this matter. They sat on the days that
have been mentioned-seven full days
examining 37 witnesses. They had the
assistance of counsel in the matter.
The hon. Member for Woodvale says
that to employ counsel or solicitors before
a formal charge is made against one
would be taken as an admission of guilt.
On turning the matter over I came to the
decision that it was desirable, because it

gave
depositions in the matter-that these six

I seems to me that the hon. Member

Prison Officers' Association what is in

or not it exists. However, that request

The right hon. and learned

He, too, had a great interest

that
interest,
here desperate and
dangerous criminals had escaped, and the

They had taken the trouble to arrest these

Although Section 11 makes no provision whatsoever for the representation
either of prison officers or anybody else I
agreed to it. A complication was thereby introduced, because the procedure required that the presiding Judge should
examine the witnesses coming before him.
The Attorney-General's counsel crossexamined, and then counsel for the
prison officers certainly could not be
denied the right of cross-examining. It
is a chance for which advocates pray, but
which very rarely happens-an opportunity of cross-examining their own witnesses. As the hon. Member for
Woodvale will recollect that gives counsel
an opportunity of leading his own client
through his story, and an advocate can
be trusted to put as good a story as
possible into the mouth of his client.

The proximate cause of the escape was
the failure of those men to do their duty
t and the failure of the principal officer
in charge of the wing to take care that
facilities to get into the roof space, to

were not furnished to the inmates of that
wing. For seven days counsel for those
six men laboured courteously and with
skill and persistence, but those six men
were too tightly enmeshed in the coils
of their negligence for anybody, be he
the angel Gabriel out of heaven or the
devil out of hell, to free. them for those
coils. That could not be done, although a
great fight was made for them. It would
occur to anybody who had never even
been inside a prison in his life that the
first duty of a warder is not to let a
prisoner escape. This is a case of res ipsa
loquitur, but it does not rest there. The
admission of these six men to the presiding judge and his colleagues, their answer
to the cross-examination of counsel for
the Attorney-General and even the crossexamination, if you will so call it, of
their own counsel time and again con-.
victed them out of their own mouths.
Mr. NIXON: Why not publish it?
Mr. LOWRY: The hon. Member never
listens to anything I say. I explained at
the beginning of my observations why it
is not possible to publish it. The reason
is that too much is known already about
the interior of our jails, and to publish
it or to follow the suggestion that has
been made that I should show it to some
person or another would only facilitate
further attempts at escape.
I have just one other word on the
justice of the decision arrived at. On
29th November of last year I had a
letter from the Prison Officers' Association relative to these six dismissed men,
these supposedly oppressed men, and
what was the purport of that letter? The
association never questioned for one
moment the justice of the decision. Four
men they passed over in complete silence
and as to the other two they put forward
a plea for clemency. There was never a
suggestion that an injustice was done,
that these men did not get a fair chance,
that they did not know what they were
charged with. They asked for clemency.
I was sorry in all the circumstances that
it was not a matter for clemency. The
offence had been too grave and the consequences far too serious for me, after
a full and impartial investigation, to
advise that conduct of this sort could be
tolerated, and with regret the Prison
Officers' Association's secretary was informed that the decision must stand.
That secretary is the area secretary. He
is one of the officials in Belfast Prison,
and doubtless has a committee to guide
him. He writes on behalf of that great,
most numerous association.
He is a
prison officer of very considerable standing, and if the association are ready to
acquiesce in and accept the justice of the
decision, which was arrived at, I do not
think that the most enthusiastic amateur
jailers or authorities on prisons could
have one piece of evidence to suggest that
natural justice was not observed in every
particular. I do not think that this
House will pay very much attention to
this Motion which has been brought forward and supported in the way in which
it has been.

Question put: "That in the opinion of
this House the dismissal by the Minister
of Home Affairs of six Protestant warders
without trial on a secret report which the
Minister is unwilling to produce but which
relates to the escape of prisoners from
Belfast Jail, is a violation of the rights of
free and loyal men and tends to discourage loyal Protestants from taking
service in H.M. Prison. Further, the
House thinks that these ever recurring
escapes should be the subject of a public
sworn inquiry by one of His Majesty's
judges.'

ADJOURNMENT.
A Belfast Strike.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That this House do now adjourn.".
(Sir Wilson Hungerford.)
Mr. HENDERSON: I gave notice to
the Minister of Labour that on the
Adjournment I would raise the question
of one of these strikes that none of us
want to hear about. From information,
which I believe is very reliable, and
having a thorough knowledge of the
engineering trade, I know the conditions
under which the men are being worked.
I know also their great grievance as far
as wages are concerned as compared with
men in other parts of the engineering
works where they are employed. I believe
the Minister of Labour we have now is
putting his heart and soul into his work
and is creating a very favourable impression with many of the trade unions
Sinclair, Major Rt. Hon. John
Maynard

throughout Northern Ireland. I believe
the time is now opportune for him to
show what he can do to bring about a
settlement of this dispute which may have
far-reaching effects and may spread to
other departments engaged on war work.
I feel that something will have to be
done. At the moment when we are expecting to hear of the second front being
opened it is deplorable that there should
be a strike in Belfast. Before you realised
it half the shipyard might be in it. I
see the Prime Minister smiling and yawning, but it is not very creditable to him
as Prime Minister and leader of this loyal
Province that we should allow these

number have given notice that they are
going out. The numbers may ultimately
run into tens of thousands. I appeal to
the Minister of Labour to do everything
he can possibly do to bring about an early
settlement of this dispute. If he brings

men belonging to the big firm were overhauling one engine room. The men

I know machinery for settling these

They are right on that day if they vote
for members of the. Government.
not going to say anything to aggravate

CLASS I. No. 2.
Houses of Parliament.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
That a supplementary sum not exceeding £1,000 be granted to His Majesty
for the service of the year ending 31st
March, 1944, to pay the salaries and
expenses of the Senate and of the House
of Commons."
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Major
Sinclair): In this Estimate provision
is made under Sub-head B for the
payment of additional war bonus under
the awards of June and November,
1943, and as this item recurs in
quite a number of Votes, and, indeed,
is responsible for most of the unusually
large number of 25 Supplementary Estimates in this book, I think it as well to
inform the Committee on this first
Supplementary Estimate of what these
awards generally consisted.
The June award increased the rates of
war bonus and also brought within the
Scope of the payments salaries up to, but
not exceeding £850 per annum. The
former limit was £500 per annum.
A
distinction between the rates of bonus
payable on differing salaries was still
maintained, the bonus, as regards people
of over 21 years of age, diminishing as
the salaries increased.
The November award, which did not
affect persons below the age of 21,
abolished the distinction in rates of bonus
which I have just mentioned and established a flat rate in respect of all salaries
not exceeding £850 per annum. The
new rates of bonus, which are payable
from the 1st November, 1943, are 19s
per week for men and 15s,6d per week
for women.
Comparable awards have
been made in the Imperial Civil Service.
In Subhead C, the additional sum of
£200 required for travelling is mainly
due to the sittings of two Committees,
those on Health and Ministerial Salaries.
Mr. BEATTIE : I take this opportunity of directing the attention of the
Committee to the ever-increasing cost of
this Parliament. I think the time has
now come-it should have been arrived
at long ago when the cost of what I
might describe as this Parliamentary
machine should be substantially reduced.
The CHAIRMAN: The hon. Member
knows that on a Supplementary Estimate
he cannot discuss policy or anything that
would require legislation. No one knows
that better than he does.
Mr. BEATTIE: I am quite aware of
that, and it is not my intention to discuss this Estimate to the extent of indulging in policy. I feel that when we
are curtailing the spending power of the
people we should at least do something
as an example to those outside. I do
not intend to oppose the extension of the
bonus to the officers of this House, but
it is my intention to direct the attention
of the right hon. Gentleman to the
anomaly he has created in this part of the
world as compared with Great Britain. In
the British House of Commons the higherpaid officials do not receive a bonus, but
in this House they are included in this
£800 which is being voted.
I do not know that we should give the
higher-paid officials preferential treatment. It is quite true that the officers
of the House who are not classified in the
higher grade are justly entitled to receive a bonus to meet the increased cost
of living, but my opinion always has
been that the higher-paid officials of this
House are too highly paid. Their pay
Supplementary Estimates-
Houses of Parliament
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Beattie]
is not in relation to their responsibilities.
The right hon. Gentleman, I know, is
only following the precedents set by his
predecessor step by step. There was,
however, a reason for setting a high
figure on the value of these higher-paid
men at the beginning of the life of this
Parliament. The Parliamentarians of
that time depended to a very great extent
on the support and knowledge of those
officials. With the exception of one or
two-you,
Sir Robert, were an experienced man-all who came into the political life of Northern Ireland at that
time were amateurs. We have paid for
that knowledge and experience, and I say
that it is now time that we closed that
account. Compensation has been given
to the higher-paid officials to an extent
which, as I have already said, was
exorbitant.
I come to the second part of the
Estimate, the £200 for the expenses of
Members of the House who travel to
attend such committees as that on Health
Services. I am opposing that. My reason
for doing so is that for at least twelve
years I attended every committee of this
House. I was a member of every committee and I never received any opposition, the reason for that being that at
that time there were no fees attached to
committee work. When fees were introduced it was never intended that they
should not include travelling expenses. The
two guineas were to cover all expenses,
attendances at committees and the provision of transport to and from the meetings. Now two guineas plus travelling
expenses is given. That was never the
intention of the right hon. Gentleman
who introduced this to the House.
As the two guineas was to cover everything it is my intention in the very near
future to ask the House to revert to the
status quo, to bring this matter back to
what you would call a sound foundation
and so get the best elements in the House
to act on the committees without either
fee or reward. I certainly will not omit
those travelling expenses which would be
incurred by a Member of the House
attending any committee so that he should
not be out of pocket. It is a crying-out
scandal to introduce into this Estimate
something that, I think, is an anomaly
and that will now become a precedent for
the Members who are hand-picked by the
Government, and some of whom are taking
the rightful places of Members sitting on
this side. They have no Parliamentary
authority behind them, because we on
this side are as much entitled to representation on these committees as any
member of the Unionist Party sitting on
that side of the House.
The precedent and practice of the
British House of Commons will have to
be adhered to. As a Labour movement
and party we have been ignored in this
House and have been excluded from all
committees We did not grumble or cry
out when we were selected without any
fee. We did the work. I was appointed
on those committees as a representative
of the Labour Party at that time and I
remained on them until last year when
something came over the minds of the
Government who thought I would serve
them better by being off the committees
than by being on them. I never attended
a committee with the object of getting
paid for the work performed. If I had
done so I do not think the £200 would
have covered payment for my services. I
have been responsible for much economy
in the finances of Northern Ireland, and
I have also been very much responsible
for getting rid of the red tape that prevailed and the over-riding authority of
civil servants over the Prime Minister and
other Members of the Government. My
voice is only one voice. It is quite true
that the overwhelming majority in this
House would be opposed to me on a vote,
but that cannot be said for the overwhelming majority I claim to represent
in this House. That being so I say that
my voice represents more than one single
vote, and I put forward my case on
behalf of those people who feel that there
is extravagance going on. The Minister
of Finance is over-generous in the paying
out of money. I listened to a debate on
how the Government was using public
funds for the purpose of keeping intact
their position as a Government. Members
may have read it.
The CHAIRMAN: I do not like to
interrupt the hon. Member, but we cannot go into a discussion like that. We
are dealing with this one particular item
of £200, and the hon. Member must
confine himself to that.
Mr. BEATTIE: It is the £200 I am
coming to. I was giving an illustration of
how the Government were keeping intact

CLASS I. No. 2.
Cabinet Offices.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That a supplementary sum not exceeding £5,430 be granted to His Majesty for
the service of the year ending 31st March,
1944, to defray the Salaries of the
Department of the Prime Minister, the
Salaries of the Cabinet Secretariat, and
other expenses in connection therewith,
including the expenses of the Privy
Council Office and the Office of the Agent
for Northern Ireland in Great Britain.'
Major SINCLAIR : The principal
reason for the increase in this Vote is the
transfer from the Ministry of Commerce
to the Cabinet Offices Vote of the ex-
""
penses of the office of the agent of the
Government of Northern Ireland as from
1st April, 1943; a full year's provision
for the office in this Vote is, therefore,
required. The consequent saving in the
Ministry of Commerce Vote effected by
the transfer does not, however, exactly
correspond owing to the recent appointment of the Honorary Director of Information Services and other staff changes.
This transfer has been brought about for
administrative reasons, the activities of
the London office under present conditions being regarded as more germane to
the Cabinet Office than to the Ministry
of Commerce.
The only other item to which I think
it is necessary to draw attention in this
Vote is the provision for publicity in the
new Subhead D1. I feel that no one
will question the importance of bringing
home to the British public and to our
Allies the role which Northern Ireland
plays as part of the United Kingdom.
Most members will have seen a pamphlet
"The Ulster Bridgehead"-which was
issued recently for the purpose and the
cost of which is to be borne on the Estimate for Stationery and Printing. The
£100 included in this Estimate is required in the main to cover postage and
incidental expenses arising from the distribution of this pamphlet.
Hon. Members may have expected to
find included in this Supplementary
Estimate provision for the payment to
the Prime Minister of an allowance to
meet the contingencies of his office following the statement which I made in the
House on 11th May last to the effect that
it was proposed to grant an allowance of
£500 per annum and that an Estimate
for the item would be brought before the
House in due course.
It has now been decided to make provision for such an allowance at the rate
of £500 per annum with effect from the
Prime Minister's appointment in May,
1943, but as a decision had not been taken
at the time this Supplementary Estimate
was printed, Parliament will be asked to
give effect to this proposal with retrospective effect when considering the Estifor 1944-45. I apologise for
referring to a service which is not provided for in this Supplementary Estimate, but in view of the retrospective
character of the proposed allowance I felt
that it was only fair to the Committee to

Mr. BEATTIE: I was delighted to see

The CHAIRMAN: I do not see where

Mr. BEATTIE: That is quite true,

If there is a privilege for one there must

The CHAIRMAN: I took the Minister

Mr. BEATTIE: Out of courtesy you
let him refer to it. Out of courtesy you
might allow me to give him an idea to
work upon, and that is that when he is
building up the total Estimate he will
give consideration to the sum of money
that has been paid out to those who failed
in their duties in their respective offices.
That is one of the points which I think
are worth noting on that bit of paper
you have before you. As to the travelling and subsistence expenses, which
includes the upkeep of a car for the Prime
Minister, may I say that I am very hot
on motor-cars, so much so that I see the
tall man going about town now in a
10 h.p. car which is more economical and
less expensive to the public purse. That
should have been done five years ago.
The Prime Minister's car, perhaps, comes
into a different grade. What about the
amount of travelling that car is doing on
a Sunday and also the amount of travelling it does on work which does not come
within the Prime Minister's official
duties? Perhaps I live too close to the
main road that this car travels on so often.
I think there should be a limit to the
use of cars.
The Estimate includes £180 as increased
cost of travelling by car by the Prime
Minister. Certainly if he is travelling to
Colebrooke two or three times a week
you are going to have another £180 or
more put on to the cost. Is there any
more reason for his not travelling to his
home by train at the week-end than there
is for compelling the Minister of Home
Affairs to travel to Portrush by train?
I have seen this car, and I have not seen
the Prime Minister in it. I have checked
up the number of passengers in it several
times on the road. I have seen other cars,
but they will come in their turn. No one
should use this car except the Prime
Minister. If the Prime Minister is not
present in the car it should not be on
the highway. I claim that I will not
curtail the Prime Minister's doing
journeys which he is called upon to make
within the ambit of the Six Counties. I
will approve of any supplementary
estimate for that purpose, but I am not
going to stand for the car being used for
purposes outside the official duties I know
it is being used for.
I believe the increase in the Supplementary Estimate is due to the misuse of
this car at the present time. I told the
ex-Prime Minister and the previous
Prime Minister that as long as they used
the car for official duties I was with them.
It mattered not to me what the cost was
in those circumstances. Their duties must
be performed and the car was essential
for the performance of those duties. I
will always give support to that. I have
done so up to the moment, but I never
found the official car of the Prime
Minister going about in the same way as
I have seen the official car being used in
the past eight or nine months. I hope
some note will be taken of this by those
who give authority for the use of this car.
Let them see it is not used for any purpose other than that of official duties.

the
Then we have heard about
pamphlet called "The Ulster Bridgehead." I should not like to express to
you what some people in London thought
about that penny-halfpenny pamphlet.
Certainly it was no credit to those who
put it forward as a publication. I should
be inclined to say that there were better
brains and people with more foresight in
Northern Ireland than would appear
from the pamphlet known as "The Ulster
Bridgehead." A more impoverished or
skimpy production I never saw in my life.
Instead of bringing the position of Ulster
before the Empire and the world in a
manner worthy of the people of Ulster
one would think that the production came
out of a workhouse, and that it was put
forward as a competitive document for
the best offer. The thing was scandalous
and unbecoming to the ability and standing of the people of Ulster, and to none
more so than the working classes. They
are the people who are doing most for
the war effort here. How much do they
get? I could have got children among
the junior infants to present a better
record of Ulster's value in the war. I
hope that in the near future something
will be produced that cannot be smiled at
by those who read it, something that will
be a credit to this part of Ireland.
Then we have a Supplementary Estimate in regard to the office of the agent
in London. I want to tell you quite
candidly that this position is looked upon

put in the forefront the last man you
should have thought of getting was a

its value, and the value of the commodities that could be got here, and how
serviceable these things had been to other
countries in the past. The industrial
value of Ulster to other countries is a
matter of primary importance and it

people always run away from home to

CLASS 1. No. III.
Government Hospitality.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That a supplementary sum not exceeding £500 be granted to his Majesty for
the service of the year ended 31st March,
1944, as a grant in aid of the Government
Hospitality Fund."
Major SINCLAIR: I had hoped, when
presenting the Estimates last year, that
the sum of £500, together with the £196
already in the fund at the beginning of
the financial year, would have been
sufficient to defray all expenditure incurred under this heading, but such has
not been the case. Expenditure to date
has totalled over £750, and it is anticipated that altogether a sum of £950 may
be expended in the current year. It is
necessary, therefore, to ask for a further
sum, and I have put down £500 to be on
the safe side. Any unexpended balance
will, as usual, be carried forward to next
year.
The Ministry of Commerce, as might
have been expected, made the heaviest demands upon the fund in connection with
the visits of Ministers from Great
Britain who were concerned with our war
production programme. I refer to Sir
Stafford Cripps, Mr. Oliver Lyttleton,
and Mr. Hugh Dalton. There were also
the visits of Prince Bernhard of the
Netherlands and Mr. Herbert Morrison,
the Armistice Day Luncheon given to
repatriated prisoners of war, and the
recent luncheon given to Representatives
of the Allied Forces in Northern Ireland.
This latter entertainment provided the
greatest single charge upon the fund, the
expenditure amounting to £107, but I
trust that hon. Members will regard the
occasion as a memorable one. I make
no apology for coming back to the Committee in this way, as I regard the giving
of State hospitality in proper cases as a
Government duty. We are privileged to
have had so many distinguished visitors
in our area during the period covered by
the Estimate. I beg to move.

get something in reply about the inci-

Major SINCLAIR: I think it will

Finance Votes together, and with your
permission I propose to do this.
The No. 1 Estimate includes provision
for a salary payable to the Minister.
This is made necessary because, as the
Committee is aware, my predecessor in
office elected not to draw any remuneration. The provision is very largely offset
by the saving in the salary of Financial
Secretary, a position which is not filled.
at present. Hon. Members will notice
the salary is based on the existing scale,
namely, £1,716 13s 4d. It is not proposed that any alteration should be made
in the salary scales, for although the
Government are grateful to the Select
Committee which recently examined the
salaries of Ministers and analogous
questions they felt that this is not the
time to introduce proposals which under
present conditions might appear to, and
indeed do, constitute an avoidance of
income-tax. While, therefore, as I say,
the Government are grateful to the Select
Committee for the care with which they
have examined the matters referred to
them, it has been decided not to ask
Parliament to proceed, in wartime at
least, with the changes that Committee
have suggested.

offset by additional agency fees shown

scheme.

ence of works of this kind-acquired outside the Government service had made
it unnecessary for the Ministry to utilise
at very much greater cost the services of

The remaining £55 of the £430, provided for in this Supplementary Estimate,
is by way of recoupment of the surtax

The saving of £3,000 shown under
Sub-head A(7) is largely due to the reduction in the Agency Service carried out
in connection with war damage claims for
the Board of Trade.
The increase in the work of the Ulster
Savings Certificate Branch has necessitated
extra staff. This increase in work is, of
course, reflected in the higher rate of
purchase of savings certificates which is
now being achieved.
The heavy increase in the staff provision under Sub-head K(2) is due to
work on the new Electoral Registration
Scheme created by the Imperial Act
entitled The Parliament (Elections and
Meeting) Act. As in the case of Subbead H, the increase is covered by Agency
Fees received from the Imperial Departments concerned.
The deficiencies under Sub-head L are
due, in part, to the return of certain
officers from the Services and also to a
reduction in certain of the Agency
Services carried out for Imperial Departments, such as the war damage work for
the Board of Trade to which I have
already referred.
The other deficiency of £3,000 is due to
the fact that the emergency drainage.
schemes as proposed for 1943 were not all
put into effect, the largest scheme in particular (River Maine) not having been
undertaken. There is a consequent reduction in the fees which it was expected to
receive from local authorities in respect
of the staff engaged on this work.
In No. 2 Vote (Valuation and Surveys)
the increase in the valuation staff is due
to additional work being carried out for
the War Damage Commission, as the more
badly damaged properties which had been
left over in favour of the numerous and
smaller cost of works claims are now being
dealt with. Owing to a reduction in the
cost of the annual revision of valuation
payable by counties for the five-year
period ending in 1946, there is a deficiency of £4,000 in the amount expected
to be received from local authorities this
year.
The Public Works and Building Vote
does not require a very lengthy explanation. The £20,000 required for National
Fire Service accommodation arises from
the fact that it was only after the preparation of the original estimate that
the cost of meeting requirements became
accurately known; in addition some work
allowed for last year had to be carried
forward to this year.
Supplementary Estimates- HOUSE OF COMMONS
Ministry of Finance
[Major Sinclair]
The new drawing office in the Law
Courts has been erected on the roof of
the Central Hall. This accommodation
was urgently needed, and as no suitable
accommodation was available in the
vicinity at a reasonable price, there was
no alternative to adding in this way to
the accommodation at the courts. I may
add that this solution commended itself
to me as the more economic proposition,
bearing in mind the saving in site costs,
foundations, and so on, and the obvious
convenience.
At Baronscourt forestry centre the
machinery hitherto in use was worn out,
and the opportunity was taken to replace
the oil driven plant by electrical driven
machinery, which will meet the increased
requirements of the centre. The work
comprises box making in addition to other
saw mill activities.
The administrative offices in Court
Chambers have been occupied for some
time by staff of the Ministry of Commerce
and when an opportunity of purchase
arose it was thought desirable to take it
in view of the convenience of these offices
to the Law Courts. An annual saving of
rent of £670 is thereby effected.
The purchase as a Remand Home for
Girls of the premises known as Slievenafailte, Whiteabbey, meets the long felt
want of a building of this kind. There
will, of course, be a sum necessary for
adaptation of this building, but this will
not fall due until the next financial year.
The savings mentioned are due to the
fact that it was decided in view of altered
conditions that we should not purchase
all the additional repair materials for
which provision had been made, and to
the fact that the delivery of a certain
amount of equipment required in connection with emergency water supplies has
been delayed, and its cost will, therefore,
not fall to be met this year.
As regards the new store at Sprucefield, it was decided that the needs here
could be met by a building of a simpler
structure than that originally planned,
and the modifications resulted in the very
substantial saving of £6,000 on a total
cost of about £15,000.
While the additional sum required for
the Public Records and Ancient Monuments Vote is very small, I think it is
perhaps worth mentioning that the
Deputy Keeper of Records, in addition
to his other duties, is now acting as
historian of the official record of Ulster's
war effort, which work he is carrying out
under the direction of a War Committee
under the chairmanship of the Vice-
Chancellor of Queen's University. This
work, of course, requires a good deal of
time and labour, and it was necessary to
secure the services of a part-time
assistant.
In the Miscellaneous Expenses Vote
the only item to which I wish to draw
attention is the purchase of the tabard of
the Ulster King of Arms. As will be
remembered, the abolition of this office
in Dublin took place recently, and I am
sure the Committee will agree that this
historic coat should find a permanent
home in Northern Ireland. At present it
is being displayed in the Belfast Museum,
but arrangements have been made for it
to be kept in this building. I beg to
move.

I do not know for the life of me how
you expect Northern Ireland to hold out.
Through all the Estimates there was not
one word about a few pounds to try to
provide shelter for the thousands of
people with no homes. There was talk
about a drawing office on the top of the
Law Courts. Money can be found for
anything at all except for sheltering the
people. The other day a woman from
Oldpark, who has a big family, told me
she would live in an air-raid shelter if
she could get one. Here we have a drawing office, the Bann drainage nine years
overdue, and so high a salary to the man
in charge for prolonging it that he has
now to pay super-tax-at least he should
pay it, but the Minister is so anxious
about his pocket that he is trying to
relieve him. What is this little bit of a
place turning to? What kind of notions
have you?
Is it necessary for the war
effort, for instance, to prolong the agony
of the Bann drainage? Is it necessary
for the war effort to endeavour to relieve
this overpaid gentleman of his super-tax?
Is it necessary for the war effort to start
building a drawing office on the top of
the Royal Courts of Justice? I often
wonder if you have the war effort
as much at heart as you pretend. I am
beginning to wonder about it. One would
imagine that while the war is on savings
would be effected in every direction,
but no. That fellow will never be got
out of the Bann as long as he is drawing
a salary on which he has to pay super-tax.
Then we hear about the hard-headed
Ulstermen. When that phrase
was

The next item is housing, £6,020. I
may tell the Committee that, in the
autumn of 1942 the Housing Committee
of the Planning Advisory Board suggested
that as an essential step in the investigation of the future housing needs of
Northern Ireland a survey of the existing
housing accommodation should be made.
The Board, being in agreement with this
view, requested the Ministry to undertake
such a survey on its behalf. Preliminary
estimates revealed that it would be a very
lengthy and costly undertaking to make a
complete survey, but further investigations suggested that the practical results
desired could be achieved by the restriction of the survey to carefully selected
samples. On this basis, with the agreement of the Board and the Ministry of
Finance, the Ministry undertook the
survey.
It was decided to divide the survey
into two sections, the first dealing with
the structural conditions and characteristics of the houses, and the second with
the number and composition of their

ORAL ANSWERS TO
QUESTIONS.
B Special Constabulary Uniform.
1. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he is aware of a
circular issued to men of the B Special
Constabulary setting out the following
conditions:-
"N.C.O.'s and men who wish to have
an issue of cloth on payment in order to
have their uniform made up at their own
expense may apply through the official
channels and each case will be considered
on its merits."
I understand that their Government issue
would have to be returned in place of
this uniform.
"I am applying for a free issue of a
Police Manual to each S.D.C. I understand members of the Force may be
allowed to purchase a copy on application
through the official channels at a cost of
5s per copy."
Whether he will state what has been the
past practice regarding the supply of
uniforms and Police Manuals.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Mr. Lowry): No instructions have been
issued to the men of the B Special Constabulary on the matters referred to by
the hon. Member. The B Special Constabulary authorities in Belfast have,
however, had the matters under consideration and the County Commandant,
following a staff conference, issued an
explanatory memorandum, which was not
intended for general circulation. The
wording in the memorandum is similar
to that in the hon. Member's question.
The matters have not yet been referred
to the Ministry, but if and when they
are, they will receive due consideration.
The practice in regard to the supply of
uniform to the rank and file of the Special
Constabulary is to provide necessary
garments in the made-up state at Government expense.
An official issue of the Manual has been
made to every Royal Ulster Constabulary
establishment, while, in addition, any
member of that Force who wishes to purchase a copy for his own personal use,
may do so at a cost of 5s. No issues of
this volume have been made to the Special
Constabulary.

Shortage of Houses.
3. Mr. THOMAS CAMPBELL asked
the Minister of Home Affairs whether he
can state if the minimum shortage of
houses in Northern Ireland is 100,000,
and whether it is a fact that the erection
of a small type of house for employees
at the
central electrical generating
station cost about £970 each.
Mr. LOWRY: The figure of 100,000,
stated to be the number of houses
required in Northern Ireland, is based
upon the preliminary results of the
housing survey carried out on behalf of
the Planning Advisory Board. It is incorrect to regard this number as the
minimum number required at the present
time. The figure should rather be regarded as representing the number of
houses required to bring up the standard
of housing accommodation in Northern
Ireland to a highly satisfactory level,
having regard to modern standards.
The answer to the last part of the
question is in the affirmative.

Billeting Restrictions.
4. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of
Home Affairs whether the Senior
Billeting Officer, Banbridge, has prohibited Mrs. Lavery and family of three
from making a one-day visit to the city
of Belfast for the purpose of having professional advice on matters appertaining
to the health of her family, and can he
state under what regulation the billeting
officer prohibits these people travelling
for the period of one day on any business
matter.
Mr. LOWRY: For obvious reasons it
would be impossible to operate the official
evacuation scheme if persons accommodated in reception areas at the cost
of public funds were free to return to
the evacuation area without the knowledge or consent of the billeting officer.
Once a family has been evacuated it
should not return to the evacuation area,
even for a short visit, save in exceptional
circumstances and with the prior approval
of the billeting officer. There should not
be, normally, any necessity to visit
Belfast for the purpose of having professional advice on matters appertaining
to the health of a family, since the
Ministry has made arrangements for all
forms of medical and hospital treatment
to be available in the reception area, and
if for any reason it is considered that a
visit to Belfast is essential, arrangements
should be made in consultation with the
Ministry.
In the case of Mrs. Rose Lavery, who,
with her three children, is billeted with
Mrs. Conlon, Drumnagally, Banbridge,
an inspector of the Ministry who visited
the billet found that Mrs. Lavery had
left the billet the previous day to visit
Belfast and had not returned though she
was expected to do so the same day. She
had not taken the children with her, but
the householder stated that for some time
past Mrs. Lavery had been the habit
of going frequently to Belfast for an
afternoon and has often taken the
children with her.
The Ministry instructed its billeting
officer at Banbridge to warn Mrs. Lavery
that visits to Belfast must cease, and that
if she again leaves the billet without the

Erne Laundry, Enniskillen.
7. Mr. BEATTIE (for Mr. Agnew)
asked the Minister of labour whether
he can
state if the recommendations
suggested were carried out by the owner
of the laundry at Enniskellen in order to
comply with the Factory Act; whether he
can state what the conditions were like
when the inspection took place; whether
the wash-house was kept in proper order
to ensure the safety of the workers employed; whether the floor of the washhouse is on occasions covered with water
through which workers have to walk, and
whether this is injurious to the health of
the girls and women employed.
Mr. MAGINESS: A reasonable
interval of time will be allowed before
inquiry is made at the Erne Laundry Co.,
Enniskillen, as to whether the recent recommendations of the Inspector of
Factories have been carried out.
The working conditions at the recent
inspection were, as I have informed the
hon. Member in answer to a previous
question on the same subject, on the
whole fairly satisfactory.
In regard to safety in the wash-house,
the automatic locking devices on the lids
of two hydro-extractors were inoperative.
and the low shafting of the washing
machines was not protected; the firm was
asked to have these matters put right
without delay.
The wash-house floor is wet when work
is in progress, but has a good surface
suitably sloped and with run-off gulleys;
suitable protective clothing for the
workers is supplied and worn.
Mr. THOMPSON: Is the Parliamentary Secretary aware that the owner
of this particular laundry service is at

HOUSING BILL.
Order for Second Reading read.
Mr. LOWRY: The part of this Bill
which is of the most immediate importance
and interest is its provision to enable
local authorities to which it relates to use
the vesting order procedure for the
purpose of acquiring land for housing
schemes. This procedure has been in
operation since the passing of the Local
Government Act (Northern Ireland),
1934, and has worked satisfactorily in
cases where it is necessary to acquire land
compulsorily for public health purposes
or in connection with roads, but it has
not been applicable to land acquired for
housing. It has the great advantage of
enabling the local authority, once a vesting order is made, to enter on the land
almost immediately, leaving the question
of the compensation to be paid for the
land to be arranged for subsequently,
either by agreement, or, if agreement cannot be reached, by arbitration in the
usual manner.
as
I feel sure it is unnecessary for me to
urge upon hon. Members the desirability
of these powers being afforded to local
authorities as soon as possible. It is
vitally important that and when
materials become available local authori
ties should be in a position to get on with
their housing schemes without delay, and
this, of course, they cannot do if elaborate
procedure has to be followed before they
are in a position to enter upon land. The
procedure proposed is, as I have mentioned, by no means new. It has
operated satisfactorily where land was
required for public health and road
widening purposes, and it causes no hardship that could
could be considered unreasonable upon anyone.
The remaining provisions of the Bill
cover matters to which reference has been
made very frequently in this House in
the past, that is to say, the provision of
750 houses in Belfast, and the possibility
of further war-time building in other
parts of the Province. It is only right
that I should make it perfectly clear that
at the present time no authority whatever
has been obtained for the granting of a
subsidy in respect of more than the 750
houses which are about to be built by the
Belfast Corporation nor anything in the
nature of a definite promise for a further
Housing Bill-

La
release of materials, and the immediate
object of the Bill in this respect is therefore to provide statutory authority for
the arrangements that have been made in
connection with the Belfast houses. As
has been stated on many occasions, however, the Government is not without hope
that as money becomes available and the
supply of essential building materials
becomes easier it may be possible, later
on, to arrange for some further war-time
building, and the Bill, therefore, has
been drafted in general terms so that
fresh legislation on almost identical lines
will not be called for whenever this extension of building becomes possible, or
if it should be necessary to alter the
amount of the subsidy.
It will be noted that in the Bill provision has been made for.the payment of
subsidies to housing associations as well
as local authorities, in which respect the
Bill follows the precedent of previous
legislation. Further provisions of the
Bill in regard to housing schemes which
it covers also follow the usual lines. The
for schemes must be submitted to the
Ministry of Home Affairs for approval,
and grants may be made upon such terms
and conditions as may be prescribed
under the regulations. Grants under the
Bill will be payable in respect of houses
erected in pursuance of a housing scheme
where the scheme was approved by the
Ministry and the works commenced on or
after 1st April, 1944, and before the 1st
January, 1947. It will be seen, therefore,
that there is nothing in the Bill of a
controversial character. As legislation
which is obviously necessary as
a first
step to providing houses for our people I
feel it will have the sympathetic
consideration of the House.

There is just one matter in the definition Clause to which I wish to direct the
attention of hon. Members. Some questions have aready been directed to me as
to why "local authority" does not include
a rural district council. I should like to
point out that there is a very elaborate
code with regard to rural housing in
existence since 1883, a matter of 61 years.
The rural authorities have got accustomed
to working this particular code. It is,
perhaps, a little bit slower than what is
proposed here, but I think, on the whole
that those who have had experience of
it will agree that it is more suitable for
rural conditions than vesting order procedure. In any event there are at the
present time no fewer than thirteen
schemes that have been sanctioned and
are only awaiting the supply of materials.
I think it would be a pity to start up
a new method of housing and a new procedure in the rural districts when the
members of the councils and their officials
are thoroughly conversant with the procedure they have been operating for over
sixty years. Therefore, this is not any
omission but has been done with a great
deal of deliberation. The monetary provisions of the 1939 Act do not differ by
one half per cent. from the £390 subsidy
which is now available, so that from the
monetary point of view there is no
placing of the rural authorities in a worse
position. That is the only difference. I
may add that under the 1939 Act rural
councils are in exactly the same position
as they will be under the Bill at present
before the House. I beg to move.
Question proposed, "That the Bill be
now read a Second time."

of housing. I gather that the right hon.
Gentleman and the Cabinet are throwing

authorities. I understand from information received that the houses are going to
cost roughly £1,000, and that it would
be utterly impossible, even with the grant

could pay.
The Members on this side of the. House
at least, know that in regard to county
or rural councils adopting schemes of any

extortionate, the tenants having to pay
from 12s to 15s and £1. I believed that

each! None at all. Although the Government may give a subsidy of £390 per
house, the Corporation or the Government will have to increase the amount by
£100 or £150 to enable the houses to be
let at 11s or 12s per week. If that is not
done working class people will be asked
to pay 15s or £1 as they were when the
last housing scheme subsidy was in being.
Take the houses built on the Cherryvalley site. What happened in connection
with them? Those beautiful houses were
built for working class people. What
happened? It is now a kind of paradise
for civil servants. Only civil servants are
living in them. The people for whom the
houses were erected were not able to
pay the rent of £1 a week. The Minister
should deal in a serious way with the
question of housing. The only body that
will benefit by this Bill is the Corporation. It is quite true to say that powers
have been conferred upon the Corporation to enable them to take land outside
the city boundary. Could the Corporation go five miles outside the boundary
of Belfast in order to secure land for the
building of houses? In Belfast alone
some 40,000 houses are needed. This Bill
will not solve the problem. It refers
to only 790 houses while 40,000 are
needed.
Last night I had the pleasure of accompanying two American officers. We were
in Library Street and I took them across
to a place which the hon. and learned
Member for Central Belfast knows very
well-Carrick Hill. I did not try to hide
the black spots in the city from them.
One of the troubles with Belfast people
is that they are inclined to show off the
bright spots. I brought these Americans
to a house in Hamill Street where they
were enthusiastically received. I also took
them up some of the little entries off
Millfield, the sight of which would make
angels weep or darkies blush. Belfast
has many bright spots, but I showed
these men the dark places-places like
the Black Hole of Calcutta. I took them
there so that they could see the sights.
They were shocking. One of them told
me that the working class people here
should get the same amenities as are provided for people in other countries.
I think these officers are stationed in
County Antrim. For safety reasons I
must not name the place. If I did Hitler
might get to hear about it. As I stated
they are stationed in County Antrim, and
they were shocked to find that there was
no water in the camp other than what is

know that I am speaking to an audience

I contend there is enough timber in

15,000 to 20,000 houses. You can get
up-to-date machinery for drying timber
if you are anxious to do it. Therefore,
the question of timber should be forgotten
at the present time. Then there is the
question of steel. I notice that one of

our Members in the British House of

cannot solve the housing problem in a

and it would only cost £40,000 to supply
the whole of County Down from it.
That is the first step you should take,
and the second step which the right hon.
Gentleman should take is to start the
18,000—or half of them—who are idle at
the moment on this housing. You have the
quarries for the stone and you have the
the Magheramorne Cement Co. at Larne,
which can give you all the cement you
want. It will not hinder the war effort,
because it can be taken from Larne to
any part of Northern Ireland without
occupying shipping space. You have the
stones and you have enough sand. The
Member for Woodvale could tell you
many stories about sand that would be of
great interest to the people of Northern
Ireland. You have the stone, you have
the sand, you have the screenings, you
have the cement, and what is more you
can get in Northern Ireland all the pipes
for your drainage system. Why not go
for a comprehensive scheme extending
from one part of Ulster to the other?
Get your land sewered and drained, and
put in your foundations. If the Minister
of Labour were here I would suggest that
he should bring back to Northern Ireland
the
men he exported like cattle to
England-the skilled craftsmen like the
joiners, the plasterers, the bricklayers,
the painters and everyone connected with
the building trade. Now is the time to
bring them back. I say here and now
that this Government should be ashamed
of the shocking conditions that exist in
our country.
I am against dictators, who are murderers, but if there were for a time a
housing dictator in Northern Ireland he
would be received with pleasure. I believe if the Minister of Home Affairs became a little dictator or a big dictator in
regard to the problem of housing, the s
citizens of Northern Ireland would be
delighted to rally round him. But he is
too weak. He is not going about it in
the right way. This passing the matter
to the local authorities is like passing the
buck, or like trying to get rid of the
problem. They will dabble at it for two
or three years, and nothing will be done.
Times have changed, and the whole
system of municipal and parliamentary
government and the administration of the
affairs of the country are changing. In
fact after this war you will find the poli
tical situation changing so rapidly that
it will resemble the turning of night into
day.
But there will be no change in the
politicians adorning the Front Bench,
Because the Prime Minister is quite satisfied to sit there as Prime Minister and
live in the lap of luxury at the taxpayers'
expense, without paying much attention
as to whether the Minister of Home
Affairs is doing his job or not. I feel
rightly or wrongly that this measure is
not going to bring the relief expected,
because I believe that before any of these
houses are erected two or three years will
have elapsed. I say go ahead now and
get the foundations cut and the water
and the gas and electricity laid on, and
let the Government do the job themselves
with the assistance of the manufacturers
and the men who will build these homes.
Only then will the people of this country
get the homes they are justly entitled to
and homes let at reasonable rents.

Bill should be brought in to enable every
man and woman and child to live in
houses which are fit for human beings.
I know that housing in my constituency
is very bad. I have sat for sixteen years
in this House and I have always proclaimed the want of houses and the bad
housing conditions in my constituency;
and, in fact, throughout Ulster. Surely
in the year 1944 it is time that a Bill
Housing Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Minford]
should be brought in which would be
comprehensive enough to bring in houses
worthy of Ulster men and women.
How can you expect a man to go about
his daily work if he leaves behind a discontented wife and little children? Remember that the houses which we have,
not only are bringing misery to our men
and women but disease to our children.
I speak as a father of a family when I
say that nothing is as dear to a man as his
wife and family. Let us rise to the
occasion and put an end to bad housing
conditions in Northern Ireland and not
try to do it bit by bit by bringing in Bills
year after year. Our Ulster men and
women are worthy of having the same
conditions as the men and women have in
Great Britain. I demand nothing more
for them, and I will take nothing less.
Before the Committee stage is reached
the Government should take advice of the
back benchers, and instead of bringing in
Bills year after year they should bring in
a comprehensive Bill that will give to
every man, woman and child in Ulster a
house worthy of Ulster people.
Mr. NIXON: I might say as a preliminary that the public seem to take an
interest in the debate; in fact, everyone
seems to take an interest in it except the
Cabinet, and they are conspicuous by
their absence. I presume they are celebrating their bloodless victory. The last
speaker suggested that people could not
sleep unless they had good houses. I can
prove that some people can sleep anywhere
-Hush! hush! Do not wake him.
(Laughter.)
Mr. MAGINESS: Is it the sleep of
the just?
Mr. NIXON: I shall endeavour to
keep close to the terms of the Bill. I
am sorry the Minister of Home Affairs
has left the House before I got up. I
hope he will return. I do not know what
has happened to him.
Mr. BEATTIE: He has got a headache.
Mr. NIXON: I shall cure him. He
should take a sleep on his bench and then
he would be all right. This Bill is to
pretend to the people that there are going
to be houses. It is to give more power to
the Minister of Home Affairs. The Bill
is only intended to fool the people. It is
a remarkable fact that we read in Clause 1
that it is to come into force on a very
appropriate day, the 1st April. And the
1st April is All Fools' Day. The
principal object of the Bill is to confer
more power on the Minister, and in that
Clause there is something about what the
Minister may do. There is no restriction
on the Minister. The Ministry get on so
well that when they come to Clause 6 it
is stated that they may make regulations
prescribing anything. It does not matter
what it is.
But we shall go back to the beginning
of the Bill. Sub-clause (4) of Clause 1
states:
Grants under this section shall be of
such amount, not exceeding the sum
of three hundred and ninety pounds
in respect of each house, as the Ministry, with the approval of the Ministry
of Finance, may from time to time
determine.
What is wrong with the Clause is that
the amount is to be fixed by the Minister.
When we had subsidised houses before
now, the subsidy was fixed and everyone
got the same amount, but according to
this Clause the Minister may give one
£50, another £100, and so on up to a
certain amount. I object not to the grant
of money, but to discretion being given
to the Minister as to the amount he will
give. I say that this House should fix
the amount of the subsidies.
Why should
the Minister of Home Affairs have power
to give one
more than another!
That is exactly the power that this Clause
contains. We know that in 1938 there
were extracts taken from the books of the
Minister, and published in pamphlets for
political purposes, stating what some
people got in the shape of subsidies for
houses, which was a most improper thing
to do.
man
We come to Clause 2. Hon. Members

the Minister is given a discretion to give
anything he likes. Clause 2, sub-clause
(1), says:
A local authority seeking to obtain a
grant under this Act shall prepare and
submit to the Ministry a scheme (in the
- Act referred to as a "housing scheme")
