showing the nature of the works proposed to be executed by the authority
and containing such further information as the Ministry may require.
Why not prescribe the information
that any person going to build is to give
to the Minister? It states here that he
must give "such further information as
the Ministry may require." This Ministry has been a dictatorship ever since it
was set up. We know from the hon.
Member for Ballynafeigh the obstacles
that can be put in the way of anybody
who wants to build houses. We have that
proved here, and it cannot be denied.
Why should the Minister be able to put
additional queries until he blocks the
whole thing.
The Ministry of Home
Affairs have no concern except for powers
for themselves. That is well known, not
only in regard to this matter but to
every other thing.
Then we come to the next sub-clause:
The Ministry may approve the
scheme or any part thereof without
modification or subject to such modifications as it thinks fit.
There is no power left in the hands of
the local authority at all. The. Ministry
may approve of the scheme, or they may
approve of part of it, or they may modify
it, just as they think fit. That should
read, "That they might approve or disapprove of any part of it that does not
comply with the regulations or the specifications laid down for building," and not
"as they think fit."
When a specification is made out if a
builder does not comply with it the work
is rejected and he has to do it over again.
No one in the world would take a contract on the condition that the work can
be rejected on any grounds that the
Ministry or anybody else think fit. In
no other part of the world would such a
thing be put up.
It might happen in
England having regard to the way some
Cabinet Ministers are talking about setting up a post-war dictatorship. We are
fighting against dictatorships.
I will
pause until the Parliamentary Secretary
digests the note that has been handed to
him by one of the officials.
I now come to the next Clause. It
reads:
The submission of a housing scheme
under this section by a local authority,
and the approval of such scheme by the
Ministry, shall not affect the liability
of the authority to comply with any
of the provisions of the Housing Acts
applicable to any of the works proposed
to be carried out under the scheme.
It is very difficult to understand that
having regard to the peculiar position in
which some of the local authorities are
placed at the present time to the disadvantage of the tenants. We know
that at the present time no landlord can
raise the rent, and very properly so,
above what it was in September, 1939,
but a local authority can.
Local authorities in Northern Ireland have done so
with the approval of the Ministry. I
cannot see why that is not remedied here.
I now come to Clause 3. There are
seven lines and a few words in it. In
those seven lines the Ministry is men-
'tioned no fewer than four times. It
says:
Where a housing association has
submitted to the Ministry a scheme for
the provision of houses for the working
classes and the scheme is approved by
the Ministry, then, if the scheme is
carried out within such period as may
be specified by the Ministry, the
Ministry shall, subject to the provisions
of this section, make or undertake to
make grants in respect of the houses
erected in pursuance of the scheme.
The whole of that refers to the Ministry.
The Ministry may approve or disapprove
of it on any grounds they think fit; not
on any grounds laid down by Act of
Parliament, or on any grounds in connection with the specification, but on any
grounds that the Ministry think fit.
Now I come to the next sub-clause. It
reads:
--
A scheme submitted by a housing
association under this section shall be
in such form and contain such particulars as the Ministry may require.
Why is the form not made out? Why
is Parliament not informed of the particulars which the Ministry will require?
Is there any special reason why this
Parliament should trust the Ministry of
Home Affairs with unlimited powers and
allow it to make forms and to require
conditions which no person would apply,
and which, in the words of the hon.
Member for Ballynafeigh, would defeat
the Bill. The sub-clause goes on:
Housing Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Nixon]
Every such scheme shall provide a fair
wages clause complying with the
requirements.
...
A fair wages clause is included. We agree
with that. That is laudable and should
be in every Act of Parliament which has
to do with building or other work carried
out at public expense.
I am not going outside the scope of the
Bill. There is a lot one could say outside
the Bill, but I shall have an opportunity
of dealing with that in a more comprehensive way in the near future. We know
that the Ministry have not made any
effort to provide accommodation for the
thousands of families who are homeless
since 1941. We know that there are
vacant shops, but nothing has been done
to turn them into temporary dwellings
for the people. We know that 250 huts
were erected by the Government for war
workers, and we also know that the huts
were not used by them. We know that
the Ministry refused to give those huts to
homeless people. I know a blind man
who was lying on the roadside, yet the
Ministry refused to give him one of those
huts. As I hope to deal with these things
in a different way very shortly I do not
think I will labour them. If I did it
might put me out of court when I bring
in a Motion at an early date.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: The main
Clause in the Bill now before the House
is Clause 5. It gives power to local
authorities to acquire compulsorily land
on which to build houses for the working
classes. At a recent meeting of the
Unionist Council-it was reported in the
Press-the Minister said he understood
that this Bill was going to be opposed. I
do not know who gave him that information because there is not a single local or
urban authority in Northern Ireland that
can build houses until it gets the land.
The Bill now before the House has been
brought forward with the object of
enabling local authorities to obtain land
on which to build houses. I do not think
anybody here is going to quarrel with
that at all. It would be utterly futile for
anybody in the Opposition or anywhere
else to accuse the Government of not
getting on with the work-everybody
knows the delay is caused in connection
with the acquisition of land-and at the
same time
oppose this Bill which is giving
the necessary power.
There are some matters in the Bill on
which I should like some information.
In introducing the Bill the Minister said
that the procedure for obtaining land on
which local authorities could erect houses
was very cumbersome and slow, and that
this Bill was designed to expedite matters.
The procedure, as I understand it, is that
the local authority tells the Ministry that
they want certain land on which to build
houses. The Ministry then give a vesting order, and the local authority can go
on with the work. The price to be paid
for the land is to be arrived at by agreement, and, if agreement cannot be
reached, then by arbitration. If the
owner of the land is not satisfied with the
price fixed by the arbitrator he is at
liberty to go to the county court. I think
that is a very fair method. The point
with which I quarrel is that the Minister
said this Bill will apply only to urban
districts and county boroughs, and not to
rural district councils.
The Members for rural constituencies in
this House and the Government, too,
know perfectly well that the need for
houses in the rural areas is just as great
as anywhere else. The point is that in
the cities and urban districts the dwellers
are to have certain powers expediting the
acquisition of land, but the rural district.
councils are not to be given those powers.
The Government are quite satisfied that
they should continue in the old way of
obtaining land for the working classes,
because they know how it worked in the
past. But what was the procedure in the
past? If you could not come to an
agreement you had two arbitrators and
an umpire, and it was a very costly and
expensive proceeding, sometimes taking at
least two years. I think I am right in
saying that in one case known to the
Member for North Down it took two
years to acquire land under this procedure. Yet here we are bringing in a
Bill to expedite all this housing business
and obtain land for the sites of the houses,
but the rural councils are just as they
were under a cumbersome procedure.
I do not understand that at all, and I
would like the Parliamentary Secretary
to explain it again, as I am not quite
satisfied with the Minister's explanation.
It is not good enough that the rural
districts have to go along in the same old
way. Again, under this Bill this subsidy

We are told that under

, same procedure throughout the whole
Site country, and the quickest way of acquirdit ing land under these vesting orders

icht quarrel with the process under this Bill

Mr. ELLIOTT: Hear, hear.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: I want an
explanation as to why the rural districts
are being treated as beings apart, and
why they do not come under the scheme?
It has been said here that 100,000 houses
are required. In the past 25 years, out
of the houses built in Northern Ireland,
10 per cent were built by the local
authorities, and 90 per cent. by private
enterprise.
Mr. THOMPSON: Hear, hear.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: No one can
expect that we are going to get 100,000
houses from the local authorities alone.
Under the powers they have been given
they can build a certain number. I do
say that unless the Government encourage
private enterprise they will not get these
houses. You have heard what the Member for Ballynafeigh has done with a
couple of houses. Anyone who is going
to build houses will want security for
their enterprise. They will have to let
these houses at a profit. After all is said
and done, you can invest your money in
stocks and shares, and you can also invest
it in housing, but no
one is going to
invest his money in housing unless he
can get security and a return for his
money. This talk about the Government
providing houses will never come to anything unless private enterprise is brought
in.
We will be just where we were
before. There will be this shortage.
There is another point. In the. rural
districts you will find any number of farm
houses requiring improvement, as well as
labourers' cottages which are now occupied
but have had nothing done to them for
•
the past five years. These houses are not
good houses, and they are not bad houses.
They could be improved, and it seems to
me that as well as talking about new
houses, we should remember that we have
houses which can be improved by the
expenditure of a little money. There
should be grants made. The farmers are
now working overtime and the labourers
are working overtime, and when this war
is over we do want to see the rural community able to put their own houses in
order. Under the present system of taxation, under which we pay 10s in the £
under Schedule D; not as it used to be,
under Schedule B, which is the valuation,
there will be very little money left to do
these improvements. I do hope the
State is going to consider making some
grants for improvements through local
authorities where existing houses can be
improved.
I hear of all these Planning Commissions, and I also hear a lot of talk about
green belts. I am told that some of the
plans provide for a green belt right round
Belfast, and that to get that green belt
they are going to pull down some houses
already there. I do not know whether
the story is true or not, but if it is, I say
it is damn well mad. There is another
subject which has to do with the Bill,
and it is a technical point. In the Bill
you get a Vesting Order under Clause 5.
Perhaps the Parliamentary Secretary of
the Ministry of Home Affairs will take a
look at it. Does the Vesting Order
secured by a local authority apply only
to the area covered by that local
authority, or can that local authority go
into someone else's territory under this
Vesting Order and acquire land? If the
Belfast Corporation want to go a bit outside into someone else's area, does this Bill
give them power to go outside their own
boundary? Does the Bill give, the Bangor
Borough Council authority to go outside
its boundary to get this green belt I have
been talking about? I do want to stress
again that you are setting up in Northern
Ireland two systems for obtaining land,
and it is all wrong. You should have one
system, and it should be the best system.
Mr. BEATTIE: It was not my intention to take part in this debate, but in
view of the developments that I see arising
I think it is necessary that I should make
one or two comments in regard to the
Housing Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS

[Mr. Beattie]
housing of the people. I have already
made my contribution to the housing
situation in Northern Ireland, and I feel
that I have not yet learned of anything
that is more advanced than the housing
policy of the party of which I am a.
member. That is Labour's housing plans
for the homes of the people. I do feel
that in this Bill there are many anomalies; anomalies of the kind that are likely
to lead to so much dissatisfaction that
the housing question will be in the pigeon
hole for a further period of time. We
have those who are interested in land;
we have those who are interested in the
commercialisation of housing; and we
have those who are interested, in an
indirect way in the proceeds which come
through housing and land, necessary for
the accommodation of the working people.
Mr. ELLIOTT: And we have the
homeless.
Mr. BEATTIE: And last, but not
least, we have the homeless people, the
people whom the right hon. Gentleman
believes he has now domiciled in an area
known as a prohibited area, or an area
from which they cannot move without his
authority. They are those who suffered
by the blitz on this city. I say here and
now that to start with a subsidy for the
purpose of encouraging private enterprise
to build homes to let for the working
people is only lost time. I believe that
the first duty of the State is to see that
the people receive homes of a kind that
are going to be for the betterment of
family life, for the benefit of the health
and welfare of the children, and not
homes such as those erected in our day
and generation by private enterprise with
only three or four feet entries at the back
between each house, and a frontage of
somewhere from 15 to 20 feet. Some
people would not house their prize cattle.
in such places.
We in the Labour movement are not
concerned about the rents of houses. We
are not concerned about the price of homes.
We believe that the first duty of the State
is to give homes to the people; homes that
will give them the protection necessary
for good health; the maintenance of
family ties, and the protection of their
own children so that they can be taught
all those things that go to make up good
citizenship. I do not believe we are ever
going to make that great step forward in
the development of the mentality of the
people of Northern Ireland, and more
especially the mentality of the present
Government, to enable them to strike out
on the road to progress, the road to
success. We would never have been on
the way to winning this war if we had
left the organisation and the winning of
the war to private enterprise. We had to
co-ordinate all the Services and get them
united and fitted into the places where
they would best fit so as to achieve that
final victory of which we are assured in
the near future. If it took that united
effort on the part of the nation, a policy
of each for all and all for each, to ensure
the winning of this war, it will take the
same united effort, the same co-operation
and the same determination to provide
houses fit for heroes to live in.
I do not intend to be disrespectful to
the churches when I condemn all slum
property ownership, whether that ownership is vested in the churches or anyone
else. It is a standing disgrace to this
Province of ours to know that the church
has been so inveigled into the position
of slum ownership; that the most ancient
and primitive methods are still existing
in some of the homes of our people; and
that that particular property belongs to
the churches. I am out to condemn slum
ownership of that kind. This Bill is only
tinkering with the real issues that should
be faced, and they will not be faced
until we in this House sit down as a combined unit and accept our responsibilities
for the housing of the people, and until
we lay down the principle, in which I
think the majority of the Members of
this House believe, that not only do we
need houses, but we require the immediate
appointment of a Minister of Health. A
Minister of Health should be the regulating factor in deciding how the people
should be housed, and he should be the
one to decide whether or not a house is
fit for human habitation.
I do not care whether land is available
or not. I have heard about the difficulty
of getting sites for the erection of homes
for the people, and we all know that
even in our generation, land within the
city boundary has increased in price by
from 500 per cent. to 600 per cent. Land
in this very district that you could have
purchased, when I was a boy, at a reasonable figure is to-day unpurchaseable

When the Member for Antrim was
speaking I was going to ask him if he
was in favour of the taxation of land
values. I knew he would not be. The
property and the land-owning classes in
our Province would not stand for it, and
the Government would not introduce it.
I claim that the problem of housing is
far greater and more important than this
House seems to realise. We must and
we shall have proper homes for the
people, erected in a manner that will
bring the amenities of the home into these
houses. In our day and generation we
have had new houses built in Ballymacarrett. The noble Lord, the Member for
Bloomfield, knows that two people could
not dress in one of the rooms, and the
children could not play in the kitchen or
in one of the bedrooms. They have got to
go into the public street so that their
parents can get on with their work. We
want homes that will accommodate the
children. Homes are not merely places
to sleep in but places where the life of
our future citizens should be moulded.
We have been told that there is no
Christian teaching in our schools, and
that apparently parental control has
gone. Why has it gone? Anyone looking
at the homes in which our people have to
live will wonder how the inmates have
existed at all. While I do not want to stop
the erection of one single home, I say the
voices that have sounded in this House
to-day point the road which this Bill is
going to travel, and I claim that that
road is the wrong road if it is the road
of private enterprise. We must take control. We must pay for the homes, and
the burden must be carried by the community. We are not again going to allow
the rampant house building that went on
before and after the last war.
I remember the development that took
place in East Belfast. Houses were
erected by the hundred. If you went
into those houses to-day, after only about
two-thirds of their life has expired, you
would think they were built in the days
of the Ark. At the moment they are not
fit for human habitation. I will give the
Minister or his Parliamentary Secretary,
if they wish it, a book containing the
ideal housing plan that has been presented
in England, and I will show how the
working class there, who have rallied together for the defeat of Nazism and
Fascism, the class that is now fighting for
the four freedoms, are being treated in
the matter of housing. In this book there
is set out that great Socialist planning
scheme for homes for the people, and in
it he will find the ideal homes required by
those who need them.
In this scheme the ladies have been
very prominent, because, after all, the
ladies should be taken into consideration
in the erection of the home. It is the
workshop of the woman and she is never
consulted. She is presented with a building which in her mind is not an accommodating building. She is presented with
difficulties in its erection that she herself
would never have thought that man
could invent. Therefore, I ask the right
hon. Gentleman and the Parliamentary
Secretary to keep a tight grip on the
housing of the people of Northern Ireand, and not allow it to drift into the
hands of private enterprise, because it
only caters for the commercialisation of
houses, and the commercialisation of
houses does not fit in with the ideal
which this House has expressed so often,
that is, to house the homeless at rents
suitable to the paying power of those who
live in them.
My last point is this. I have stated it
often. We have three or four grades in
the community. We have the labourers,
the semi-skilled men and the tradesmen
who make the middleman, and, I think,
these are about the grades we cater for
at the moment. Each one has not the
same buying power to take a home equal
to his requirements. The man with the
low-buying power may have the largest
family. I say here that the buying power
of the individual is not the factor in the
erection of houses. The man who has not
got the buying power and has got the
family should be accommodated in
accordance with his requirements. Private
enterprise cannot do that. It will not
Housing Bill—
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Beattie]
do it. The only power that can carry
that into effect is the State, and the first
thing the State must do to put it into
effect is to nationalise the land and bring
in a national scheme of housing and foot
the Bill for its erection. If they do that,
I think they will meet the requirements
of the housing situation in Northern
Ireland.
Lord GLENTORAN: I am very glad,
as the Member for Bloomfield, that this
Bill is brought forward. But, whilst I
am glad, I do not think the Bill can do
very much, because I do not think the
materials are in the country to get on
with it, nor have we got the labour. At
the same time it is a start, and it gives
me hope. I am glad that it gives me
hope, because after the last speech I
listened to I would never have any hope
at all for my people in East Belfast. I
would remind the House of this fact, that
previous to what we may call the
nationalisation of houses, that is, houses
being built by the State or by urban
district councils or city councils, and these
restrictions being brought in, the effect of
which is we need 100,000 houses here-
Mr. BEATTIE: That is due to the
right hon. Member's neglect.
Lord GLENTORAN: No. When private enterprise had its own way there
were 10,000 houses vacant in Belfast.
Now, when there is this communistic idea
we need 100,000 houses. Further, when
the jerrybuilder built houses, he had to
build houses the people liked, or he could.
not sell them or let them. Now, when
the State is building houses you have got
to live in them whether you like it or
whether you do not, and from what I
can see, the people do not like council
houses. They would very much sooner
have houses built by private enterprise.
Nobody knows better than the hon.
Member for Pottinger that these houses

Mr. BROWN: This question of
housing is Northern Ireland's No. 1 problem and it must be approached as its
No. 1 problem. I am not satisfied that it
is being approached as such. I think this
Bill is in the nature of a piece of mere
window dressing. My chief objection to
it is that, while it makes reference to
certain grants being afforded certain local

reference is made to the rural district
councils. It will be contended that the
rural councils have powers to acquire land
Housing Bill-

compulsorily. They have, but all the same
it is wrong to preclude the rural districts
from the operations of this Bill. It means
that the rural districts are going to get
nothing at all except that the Government give them power to build houses and
the necessary grants for doing so.
In my own area and other areas rural
district councils had plots selected for
labourers' cottages. They were paid for,
the foundations were cut, and the councils
were ready to go ahead with the schemes.
The war came, and the Government would
not allow the local authorities to proceed.
They had those plots left on their hands.
I protest most strongly against the exclusion of the rural district councils from
any consideration in this matter. In this
whole matter of housing I am asking for
nothing more than what is being done in
England, Scotland and Wales. I realise
that the war effort comes first, but if
Great Britain can get the materials for
building then Northern Ireland should
and could get the materials too.
Thousands of houses have been built
across Channel since the war started and
not one has been built here. In the rural
areas in England there was a scheme for
the erection of 3,000 farm workers'
cottages. It is stated officially by the
Ministry of Health that at the end of
January last 244 of these had been
finished. We have not erected one in
Northern Ireland and do not propose to
erect one.
How long are we going to stand for
this? We cannot stand it much longer.
It is gross discrimination against the interests of agriculturists. Why cannot we
get the materials required? It is
absolutely preposterous to say they cannot be had. As to employment, we have
too many people unemployed. There are
roughly 18,000 unemployed which is the
same number as when the Government
took office ten months ago. Surely these
unemployed could be put on to the work
now and let the rural councils proceed
with the schemes they had ready at the
start of the war. We are getting neither
fair play nor the shadow of fair play,
and we are not keeping step by step with
Great Britain in the matter. That we
should do so is all I ask.
The same thing applies to housing in
the urban and city areas. We have not
kept step by step with Great Britain.
There have been hundreds and thousands
of houses erected across the Channel, but
not one has been started and finished here
since the war commenced. I congratulate

a very important and essential feature of

and completely excluded it from this Bill.
Mr. BEATTIE: Rightly so.
Mr. BROWN: The hon. Member for
Pottinger and I do not agree. I think

who have protested against the exclusion

in this matter.
Then there is the question of the

from going ahead as they would otherwise

It is a very important matter and one on
which we should have some information.
I therefore hope that as well as this Bill
we shall have a measure making some
provision for the rural areas, because it
is highly important, as the noble Lord

Mr. WARNOCK: I have not got a

I welcome the Bill, which is a timid,
hesitating approach to a very big problem.
I feel that if the Bill represents the
distance which the Ministry have got
they have rather failed to seize a very
great opportunity.
The first thing I want to speak about
is the Clause which provides for the compulsory acquisition of land. That is an
absolutely essential provision in the Bill.
But there must, in my view, be a ceiling
fixed for prices. The public cannot be
held to ransom by landowners whose
land has appreciated in value not by
reason of anything that they have done,
but by reason of the public demand for
sites in the city. I hope that between
now and the Committee stage the Government will very seriously consider the
fixing of a ceiling for the price of land
to be compulsorily acquired for housing
purposes.
It seems to me that one thing is quite
inevitable, that as the field of choice
narrows for the selection of sites in the city.
every site that is left goes up in price, and
while the earlier sites may have been
acquired by arbitration at prices which
C were not unreasonable, as the demand
increases and the supply lessens naturally
the law of supply and demand will assert
itself and the arbitrator-I have complete faith in the persons who are on
the panel-must make his award according to the evidence before him.
The
evidence before him will inevitably be
that as you take up pieces of land here
and there, and leave a smaller lot, these
will increase in price and the arbitrator
will be forced, if he acts on the evidence
given before him-and he has no right to
do anything else and cannot do anything
else to give awards which are vastly in
excess of the real value of the property.
He will have to award fictitious values
which are created entirely by the demand.
That is a vicious principle, and I think
that a ceiling must be fixed by statute,
and by this statute, for the acquisition of
land in this city. The public must not
be held to ransom.
Our economic system
is such that the working-class people of
this country are never in possession of
sufficient funds to enable them to provide
their own houses. Their houses must be
provided for them, either by capitalistic
enterprise or by the. State, and in the
event of provision by the State, the State
is entitled to acquire the land at prices
which are fair and reasonable, and the
public should not be. compelled to pay
fictitious values.
If I had time, and if I had known that
this Bill was coming on to-day, I could

better form. I do commend these views
to the Ministry and to the Government.
I believe they are the views of the people
of the Province. I believe they are sound

would not care if they did not commend

There is one other glaring omission.

have places of their own or we are going

AFFAIRS (Sir Wilson Hungerford):
For the benefit of my hon. Friend, the
Member for Woodvale, I should like to
say that the absence of the Minister of
Home Affairs is due to illness. He got
out of bed to come up here to-day to
move the Second Reading of this Bill.
Unfortunately he is still suffering from
the effects of influenza, and he had to go
home right away. It was not due to any
discourtesy that he went away; I am sure
hon. Members will realise that.
This debate has covered a very wide
field; in fact a great many things were
said to-day which would form the ground
for another housing debate. A great deal
of the matter discussed this afternoon
was debated on a Motion which came
before the House in October last.
Mr. NIXON: There is a Motion.
Sir WILSON HUNGERFORD: I am
merely pointing out that a great many
of the points were raised last October.
This Bill is a very simple one. There are
really only two points in it, and no one
wants to go outside these at the present
moment. The first object of the Bill is
to legalise the payment of the £390 which
is being given in connection with the erection of the 750 houses. The second object
of the Measure is to expedite the
machinery whereby the local authorities
may acquire the land. I will yield to no
one in my desire for houses. I represent
a constituency which was badly knocked
about in the last blitz. I know the position there, and I know the position in
the other constituencies throughout the
city. I am anxious and willing to do anything I can to help on the Bill.
Hon. Members will recollect that some
time ago I ventured to decry the delay
that was taking place in the erection of
the 750 houses, and some people were a
little bit annoyed about that. One of
the reasons why the houses were not
erected was because land could not be
acquired. This Bill is being introduced
to get over that difficulty. Those are
the only two points that one can deal
with to-day. A good many other matters
have been introduced which will, as the
hon. Member for Woodvale stated, come
up for discussion on a Motion.
This is a very simple Bill. It does not
deal with the post-war problem, but with
war-time houses. It will only operate
•
is
until the 1st January, 1947. As the
Prime Minister explained to the House
in October last the Government
anxious to get on with housing. The
question of materials is the one outstanding feature which debars them from going
on at the present time. We know there
is very little hope of material being made
available at the moment. The short
supplies available must be given to the
local authorities, because they are in a
position, when costs are so high, to subsidise the building of these houses and
thus enable them to be let at a rent
which the workers can pay. It is not a
question of private enterprise being
blocked out.
The hon. Member for Ballynafeigh
talked about some friend of his who
could erect 1,000 houses and another who
could erect 500. The Government would
be willing to let them do so, but there is
not the material, and so long as the
Government have to deal with the local
authorities such material as is available
must go to them. Many interesting
points were brought out in the debate,
and several of those I would like to deal
with. The hon. Member for South
Armagh objected entirely to housing
companies. I am afraid that he did not
read the Clause very carefully, because
it is not a housing company to which we
propose to give a subsidy. It is a housing association. There is no question of
their making money at the expense of
the people who are going to take those
houses. If I might refer him to Clause
7, he will see what we define as a housing
association, and that prohibits their
making any money, and prohibits a payment of any dividend to their members.
I am sure that my hon. Friend realises
that we were looking after the interests
of the workers.
If I might draw his attention to what
we really mean; a short time ago the
Council of Social Welfare, with a grant
from a very charitable lady, was able to
erect a certain number of houses in
Belfast, and these were let at extremely
low rents. That is why we want to encourage associations of that type to take
advantage of any money there might be
to build houses. Several Members raised
the point of the local authorities, and
why the rural areas were excluded from
this Bill. They are not excluded, because
Housing Bill-

[Sir Wilson Hungerford]
under the Housing of the Working Class
Act of 1890, and under the Labourers
Acts, they have these powers already,
and we do not know of any case where
there has been delay in obtaining land.
Where there has been any delay it has
been found that it was a case where the
rural district council did not wish to use
their compulsory powers,
and were
rather anxious to acquire land by agreement, but they are not excluded because
their name is not in the Bill as it stands

the Parliamentary Secretary, may I ask
if the rural district councils will get
corresponding benefits simultaneously
with the other local authorities when they
come to get benefits under this Bill with
regard to the release of materials and so
forth?
Sir WILSON HUNGERFORD: The
point the hon. Member makes is an
altogether different one. The point the
Member for Antrim made was that they
were excluded from the power of acquiring land. They have that power at
present under the Labourers Acts. The
hon. Member for Woodvale raised a
point on the second portion of Clause 1
whereby the Government would deal
with grants not exceeding £390. That is
a Clause put in so that when more money
is made available, even if the amount is
not so much as that received from the
Treasury, we will not have to lose any
time coming to the House with a new
Bill but we will be able to agree on the
amount of money which will be given
to the local authorities.
Mr. NIXON: That does not meet the
point.
Sir WILSON HUNGERFORD: That
will help us to get on with the matter.
There are no new powers given to the
Ministry in this Bill from what they
originally had, and there is no special
direction given to the Ministry to alter
the amount of subsidy between one local
authority and another. Subsidies are
fixed from time to time by the Ministry
in conference with the Ministry of
Finance, and these, so long as they are
in force, apply to all. The hon. and
gallant Member for East Down raised a
question on Clause 5 with regard to the
Vesting Order for the compulsory acquisition of land for the purpose of the
Housing Acts. As it is at present, one
local authority can go into a neighbouring area to acquire land, but only by
the consent of that authority. That is
how the matter stands at the moment.
It is not necessary for me to go into
the question of private enterprise versus
local authorities. I think my hon.
Friend, the Member for East Belfast,
and the noble Lord, the Member for
Bloomfield, will be able to settle that
matter very well between themselves. We
will leave that to them in the meantime.
I am sorry the hon. Member for St.
Anne's was not here when the Minister
introduced the Bill. I know the points he
raised will be carefully considered, and
anything that is required to meet the
points raised will be brought in on the
Committee stage. But the Government
are not behind in this matter. The
Government are most anxious to get
houses. We recognise the position as
keenly as any people do, but with the
present uncertainty regarding materials
we cannot go out for a big scheme.
Nothing would please me more than to
be able to announce that the Government had given authority for the erection
of one thousand houses or a proportion
of them.
The hon. and learned Member did
raise the point as to whether we were
thinking of prefabrication. There has
not been any plan or any notice that
has appeared with regard to any means
whereby houses can be erected quickly
that this Ministry has not endeavoured
to find out everything there is about it.
I know about the houses in Sweden, but
there is no hope of getting the timber
here at the present time. We have seen
various schemes of prefabrication, and a
short time ago I had the opportunity of
seeing a new system of quick construction which I am happy to think might
well be applied in Northern Ireland,
because it utilises bricks in building. I
would be very loth to suggest to the
Government the bringing in of any
scheme of prefabrication using an imported material, which would mean that
our brick yards in Northern Ireland
would be allowed to go into decay.

Mr. THOMAS CAMPBELL: I do
not rise to say anything that calls for
reply on behalf of the Ministry, but I do
rise to direct the attention of the House
to the spirit in which this Bill has been
met here to-day. There has been allround agreement on the broad underlying
principle of the Bill. It has not been
welcomed with any great enthusiasm, and
certainly it has not been decried or condemned. To my mind it is a very poor
measure. It is merely nibbling at the
fringe of a mighty problem. I would
remind the House of this fact; that the
slums which we had 20 years ago in the
cities of Belfast and Londonderry are
still there to-day. Hardly a brick of
those slums has been removed, hardly a
pillar of those houses has been taken
away, and the poorest sections of the
community are the sufferers. Sooner or
later the time must come when the slums
that infest and poison the. air will disappear once and for all, and once and for
ever.

Mr. BEATTIE: I gave the Minister
of Home Affairs notice that I would raise
on the Motion for the Adjournment this
very important question of the hunger
strike in Belfast Prison. I regret that
the Minister has been taken ill, and I
hope he will soon be restored to health
and strength, and to his accustomed place
in this House. However, the Parliamentary Secretary is in the House, and I
am satisfied that he will be able to deal
with the matter if I outline the facts to
him. In my question I asked the Minister
to set up at once an inquiry into the.
cause of the hunger strike now taking
place in H.M. Prison, Belfast, and his
answer was in the negative. I am one of
those who believe that where there is an
injustice being done, no matter on what
class of the community that injustice is
being imposed, I, in my individual capacity as
representative of the
working class in this House, am
a
entitled to ventilate the matter.
Accordingly I have taken this opportunity
to draw the attention of the Minister and
the Parliamentary Secretary to many
things which I believe have caused the
hunger strike in H.M. Prison, Crumlin
Road, Belfast.
I feel that freedom of conscience and
self-expression are the keynotes of our
democracy, and that in standing for
them we stand for what is most precious
I think these
in the world to-day.
principles should be inculcated into the
mind of every Member of this House and
into the minds of everyone outside. I
care not what these men's crimes may
be, or what they have been incarcerated
for.
That is no concern of mine. All I
am concerned about is to see that the laws
applicable, to the prison and to these particular inmates are properly carried out,
and I am going to show this House that
the administration of this prison is far
from being correct.
In the first place, the cells of the men
are searched almost daily. Not only
that, but the men are stripped periodically and their persons subjected to the
indecent searching of the warders, who
accompany the searching with vulgar and
Belfast Prison Hunger Strike 492
Belfast Prison Hunger Strike HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Beattie]
obscene language. The Governor promised that men would be stripped only
once every three weeks. Yet men are
being stripped and searched twice and
three times every week. It should be
noted that all these searches are without
result. In other words, these searches
are taking place three, times a week without result. Under the code governing a
penal settlement, it is a place for men
who have been sentenced to three years
or over. It includes men sentenced for
political offences, criminal offences,
capital offences, sex crimes, and every
other sort of crime that comes under the
law. That penal settlement is the home
of those people during the period of their
sentence.
I must first and foremost say here that
I protest strongly against men of that
type being placed in a sort-term prison.
Crumlin Road Jail is a short-term prison,
and therefore. it is not suitable for the
class of person I am speaking of. It is
against the cramped nature and unsuitability of this prison that I make my first
complaint. This searching is a violation of
the code laid down in the King's Regulations for the treatment of these longterm prisoners. One search in a week is
quite ample. When there is no result, why
do they search the men twice more? In
most of these long-term prisons, such as
Peterhead, where we used to send our
long-term prisoners, the conditions were
quite satisfactory. For that accommodation we had to pay at least £137 10s
per head. Then we brought them into
our jail on the Crumlin Road, which was
unsuitable, and where. the accommodation was not in accordance with the
King's code laid down for the treatment
of these men.
Many classes of people are confined in
this particular prison, and the associations are not always congenial. There
are approximately 120 prisoners in "A"
Wing at the present time. About onefourth of these are lads whose ages range
from 17 to 21. These boys are in that
long-term prison for a period of years.
They are forced to associate with thieves
and men who are in prison for sex crimes,
and they must listen to their filthy and
degrading talk. I do not know whether
many of the Members of this House have
ever taken an interest in prison life. I
am one of those who have gone into the
question of what was best for the reformation of those who had been led astray
outside, and I have taken an interest in
prison life. I certainly agree that the
conditions under which these boys of from
17 to 22 or 23 have to associate with
other types of men are not such as are
laid down by the Regulations for the
guidance of prison officials regarding the
treatment that should be extended to
youths of this type.

Now I want to draw attention to the
food. The food rations are considerably
less than the authorised allowance. It is
badly cooked, almost cold, and is given
to prisoners in vessels which bear visible
traces of the previous meal. Cocoa and
tea have been served in tins with considerable pieces of porridge or
turnips stuck to the bottom. Frequently
during the past few months, when the
orderly came into the Wing with the

This meant that the food was cold when
brought back. Well, now, you would
have thought that if the humanitarian
touch had been there at least this process of search would not have taken place
at the hour when the prisoners were to
receive their food. Some have suggested
that this was done deliberately.
not know whether that is true or not. It
often happens that some of the men cannot eat their porridge. The reason for
this is that they cannot digest the halfcooked inferior meal.

Now in the British prisons to-day and

I am going to call upon someone now.

There are two shoe shops, one tailor's

There are two other shops in which
mats are made. These are very unhealthy
owing to the fact that the men are continually breathing into their lungs the
fibre particles which are floating through
the air. In my young days I worked in
the Belfast Ropeworks and I know the
difficulty of working in a room when
particles of that kind are floating through

be taken out or carried out for fresh air
and given a tonic to restore us before
resuming our work. But here in the
jail, where conditions should be at least
in accordance with the Factory Acts, we
find that they are not.

Another right to which prisoners are
entitled does not exist. It is usual to
supply men on hunger strike with warm
water.
It is done in Britain, in Eire, and

It is being denied to the men at present
on strike. In every hunger strike that has
taken place throughout the world that is
the one thing that has been maintained,
but in Northern Ireland, which is a
different place from any other throughout
the world, they have denied the men
warm water. The men are. left without
water from 7-30 a.m. to 10-30 a.m., from
12 noon to 2-30 p.m., and from 3-45 p.m.
to 5 p.m.
All water during those hours
is removed from the cell. Water does not
cost you very much. What justification
can the Minister give for allowing things
like this to happen?
I give another instance. One of the
prisoners, partially crippled in one leg,
has during the past three years been
allowed a bucket of hot water daily to
bathe his leg, but on 29th February an
official put colouring stuff in the water in
case. he would use it for any other purpose. He put colouring stuff into the
water the man was going to bathe his
crippled leg with. Nobody knows what
that colouring stuff was. What sort of
conduct or treatment certainly not
Christian treatment-is taking place in
this particular jail? The men are closely
confined in separate cells, and no one but
the prison chaplain and the prison officials
is allowed to see them. Officials have
been using jeering, insulting, and filthy
remarks about the men on strike. During
the period of intense coldness the cells
were barely half heated and the men
suffered terribly from cold.

I should like to explain that there seems
to be some misapprehension about the
lay-out of this thing. The convict wing
has been set apart for long-term prisoners.
It is a building by itself, and it has its
own workshops and recreation rooms.
Therefore the prison regulations are not
violated in any way. According to our
reports the food is not badly cooked, and
is up to the standard laid down for this
class of prisoners. A new recreation
room is being prepared and I hope it will
meet the case. I repeat to both hon.
Members that the complaints as set forth
will be investigated.

party Committee-

sorry to say he is not a member of it. It
was very difficult to give the members of
that force adequate training in the use
of rifles. The only time we could get on
to a rifle range was, generally speaking,

time we could get on in the evenings.
There are very few ranges to accommodate the various members of the Home
Guard. That being so it was decided
that a number of Nissen huts should be
I employed as rifle ranges. That item

when out on a Sunday morning or an

The members

Mr. BEATTIE: I could give an idea to

because the Party of which he is a member
thrive by having these places in a flourishing condition with plenty of occupants.
The whole point is this. The pay and
allowances of prison officers amount to
£64,500. We are six counties with a
population of a million and a quarter,
and, according to the original Estimate,
the cost of pay and allowances of officers,
including uniform, was £64,500. The
revised estimate brings the total to
£69,500. What sort of an area or a
community do we live. in when we are
spending that amount of money on prison
officers alone in order to keep a percentage
of the population incarcerated in prison?
I do not think any country in the world,
having regard to relative population, can
show as high a percentage of people in
prison as we have in these six counties.
In saying that, I include America and
Sing Sing Prison..
We seem to have a mania for putting

who speaks or votes against them, or who

Party, should be in jail because they are

Supplementary Estimate of the

There is nothing very secret about
that, but I did not think it was right to
have criminal lunatics confined in public
mental hospitals. Criminal lunatics are
lunatics who commit a crime owing to
their mental condition, and when they
are indicted the first indictment the jury
has to try them on is to ascertain if they
are a mental case, and if they are, and
the crime is proved, they are committed
to a criminal lunatic asylum during the
pleasure of His Majesty.

CLASS III. No. 7.
Grants to Local Authorities.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a supplementary sum not exceeding £10 be granted to His Majesty for
the service of the year ending 31st
March, 1944, to provide for grants to
local authorities, etc., in respect of

in respect of housing grants, and for

""
Sir WILSON HUNGERFORD: Under
Section 41 of the War Damage Act, 1941,
damage to highways by enemy action was
excepted from the General Scheme and
the Imperial Treasury was authorised,
after consultation with such associations
of local authorities as appeared to be concerned, to make a scheme under which
the cost of war damage to highways would
be borne between the Government and
the Highway Authorities. This scheme
was embodied in the War Damage (Highway) Scheme, 1943. Without wearying
the House with details, the basis of the
scheme is:
(1) The Imperial Treasury bears the
same proportion of cost of damage
to highways as it bears to the cost
of damage to immovable property
under the War Damage Act;
(2) The contribution payable by the
Highway Authorities is divided
into four interim instalments and
one
final instalment, and the
Treasury has certified that the proportion of the amount of the interim instalments to the total cost
of the damage shall be taken as
one half, i.e., one half shall be
levied off the Highway Authorities;
(3) Power is also taken to recoup
Highway Authorities up to 50 per
cent. of the amount of each instalment. In Great Britain the
amount so recouped is charged on
the Road Fund. As, however, the
basis of filling the Road Fund
differs with Great Britain and
Northern Ireland, it was agreed
that the cost of recoupment in
Northern Ireland should fall on
the Exchequer and Section 4 (b)
of the Exchequer and Financial
Provision Act, 1941, was passed
by Parliament to enable Northern
Ireland Road Authorities to be
recouped out of the Exchequer at
the same rate as Highway Authorities are in Great Britain.
It will, therefore, be seen that as a.
result of the contribution in the first
instance from the Imperial Exchequer
and, secondly, the recoupment to the
Highway Authorities in respect of their
contributions the net amount to be borne
Supplementary Estimates-
Emergency Services
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Wilson Hungerford]
by the Highway Authorities is in the
neighbourhood of 25 per cent. levied in
five instalments. The amount of each
interim contribution chargeable on the
Highway Authorities as a whole is levied
on each contributing authority in the
proportion which the rateable value of
that Authority bears to the rateable value
of the United Kingdom. It was originally
hoped to recover annually one instalment
only, but owing to various difficulties it
was found impossible to put the scheme
into operation until the present year. To
make up leeway contributing councils
have been asked to pay two instalments
in the present financial year, two more
will be paid in the year 1944-45, and the
final instalment will not be demanded
until the final position has been ascertained. The gross amount leviable in
Northern Ireland on contributing authorities in the present financial year is
approximately £7,000, and the estimate
of £3,500 is designed to provide the
money to recoup the contributing
councils in Northern Ireland 50 per cent.
of their contributions and place them on
the same basis as in Great Britain.
For simplicity it was arranged with the
Inland Revenue Authorities only to
demand on contributing authorities the
net amount of each interim instalment,
the Government agreeing to pay direct
to the Inland Revenue Department in one
single payment an amount equal to the
total amount due to be recouped to the
several contributing councils in respect of
those instalments. I beg to move.

CLASS III. No. 8.
Emergency Services.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That a supplementary sum not exceed
ing £10 be granted to his Majesty for
the service of the year ending 31st March,
1944, to provide for emergency services."
Sir WILSON HUNGERFORD: This
Estimate recalls the two unofficial strikes
affecting transport in the months of
February, March and April last year.
It will be remembered that in February,
1943, certain drivers and conductors in
the employ of the Transport Department
of the Belfast Corporation ceased work.
The effect was that all the petrol omnibuses and the vast majority of the trolley
buses in the city were not in operation.
In the interests of the war effort the
Government decided that
effort
every
should be made to provide alternative
transport facilities for the conveyance of
workers to essential war factories which
were normally served by the vehicles then
immobilised. Whereupon the Government authorised the Minister, who was
the Minister of Home Affairs, to ascer
tain if the military authorities could provide for the necessary transport, and with
the ready co-operation of the General
Officer commanding at the time, it was
found possible to convey the workers to
the factories so that
war production
should not be interrupted on account of
the strike.
Where military transport is used in
such circumstances, it is the normal
policy, as laid down by the War Office,
that the military should raise charges in
respect of the provision of transport
appropriate to
Co
the type of vehicle
employed. The charge raised by the
military amounted in this case to £1,194,
Imper
577 Supplementary Estimates-

9 MARCH 1944
Emergency Services

and payment was made in full in
accordance with the prior agreement
reached with the military authorities.
In the following month the employees of
the local carriers in Belfast organised an
unauthorised strike. Once again the
Government was concerned to ensure.
that, in the interests of the war effort of
the Province, production at essential war
factories was not impaired and that the
distribution of essential commodities was
maintained.
Subject to the same conditions, the aid
of the military was again forthcoming to
haul essential traffic, mainly to and from
the docks. The day following the outbreak of the strike, the Ministry of Commerce decided that traffic at the docks
would have to be cleared to store, and
that it would be necessary,
to arrange for
the loading and unloading of ships, particularly as the dockers had joined in the
strike in sympathy with the carters.
Accordingly that Department asked the
G.O.C. direct to make available military
personnel for this purpose. The G.O.C.
readily acquiesced, although the personnel
would not be accustomed to this class of
work.
as
Military assistance therefore extended
to the following:-(1) The provision
of motor vehicles; and (2) the supply
of military personnel-(a) to drive, load
and unload the vehicles at the docks and
business premises; and (b) to load and
unload ships and to move traffic as required round the sheds. Military
vehicles and personnel were always in
readiness to carry out the work
required. The charge, as calculated by
the military, amounted to £9,434, which
is made up as follows:
:-(1) Cost of transport, including supply of vehicle crews
and labour used in connection with loading and unloading vehicles, £5,496; (2)
cost of labour employed at the quay sheds
and in loading and unloading ships,
£3,938 total, £9,434.
The Government agreed to defray this
sum from public funds, subject to the
recovery, so far as it was possible to do
so, from those bodies who would otherwise have been responsible for the services of such sums as would normally be
appropriate. Consignments were handled
by the military not only at the instance.
of certain Northern Ireland Departments,
but also of Imperial Departments represented
in Northern Ireland. The
haulage of the. majority of items took
place either from or to the docks, a great
number of which had already been consigned "carriage paid" through the
shipping companies. The shipping companies would also normally have been
responsible for the loading and unloading
of ships. The military accounts in respect
of these services have therefore been submitted to those companies for recoupment
of normal costs. As their financial affairs
are, subject to scrutiny by the Ministry of
War Transport, the matter has been
placed before that Department by the
companies for the necessary authority to
make such payments as would normally
have been incurred. As indicated in the
note to the Supplementary Estimates,
receipts will accordingly be brought to
account in the next financial year. I beg
to move..

granted to His Majesty for the service of

marginal land grants, agricultural credits,

As regards the scheme of grants for
the improvement of agricultural holdings
hon. Members will be glad to learn that
the farmers are as keen as ever to improve their holdings, and, in so doing, to
help not only themselves, but the nation
as a whole. Despite the limitations
imposed by seasonal work and weather
conditions, and even though it was again
found necessary this year to suspend the
receipt of applications from the end of
January, the number of applications received was so great that the provision in
the autumn Supplementary Estimates is
inadequate to meet the grants payable
before the end of this month. A further
increase of £15,000 has, therefore, been
provided for in the present Estimates. I
mentioned that no new applications are
being received after the end of January,
but I should like to make it clear that
the scheme has not been closed. Applications for grants for flax dams, bog
roads and water supplies will continue to
be accepted and dealt with and new
applications for all schemes will be resumed at the beginning of November of
this year. In the meantime it will be
appreciated that tillage operations in
preparation for the coming harvest must
take first place in our efforts and the
efforts of our farmers.
The second item of £18,000 is for
marginal land grants. This scheme has
been introduced to assist production
which is unremunerative to the producer,
but which will increase the supply of
foodstuffs or other raw materials required for the war effort.
It is

estimated that the cost of the additional

Hon. Members are already aware of

An additional sum of £13,200 is required for the purchase of four new areas
for forestry-two in County Londonderry, two in County Tyrone. The importance of the work of afforestation,
whether in peace or war, is widely appreciated.
Hon. Members are already familiar
with the scheme for the recruitment of
unemployed industrial workers to assist
in harvesting. The scheme provided for
the payment of the workers from the
time they reported for work until the
time of their return to the starting point;
the farmers were, however, charged only
for the time spent by the workers on the
farm. When bad weather intervened, of
course, the workers had to be paid without any return from the farmers. The
workers, moreover, were paid at the
highest of the minimum wage rates laid
down by the Agricultural Wages Board,
but the farmers were charged only at the
rate appropriate to their particular district. When the. original Estimate was
introduced to this House the scheme received warm support. In view of the
success which despite the unfavourable
weather-attended the scheme in the
earlier months of the harvest season, it
was decided to extend it to the end of
November SO as to ensure the safe
lifting of the potato crop. The extension
was fully justified by the fact that
October and November were, by far, the
busiest months of the season. To meet
this extension an additional sum of
£21,500 is now required, which is to
some extent offset by an estimated increase in receipts amounting to £5,500.
Against the net cost of the scheme may be
set the saving of urgently needed crops,
which would certainly have been lost to
the community if the scheme had not been
in operation.

Lord GLENTORAN: Before coming
to the point that originally I intended to
raise, as this is a new Vote perhaps I
might say a word or two about the items
put forward in it. In the first place I
would like to say, with reference to the
destruction of foxes and other species of
vermin, that I do not think there is very
much hope, if there is any hope, that
the Government are going to be able to
deal with this matter successfully the
way they are now doing it. I am quite
certain that if they are going to deal with
the influx of foxes into this country-and
they are increasing at an extraordinary
rate as well as with the increase in rats,
the only way to deal with them, particularly foxes, is to have, as they have
in Scotland, trained catchers who do
nothing else but catch foxes. The vast
majority of the foxes that are caught in
Northern Ireland under the. Government
scheme are what I call easy foxes, and
the real root of the fox difficulty is such
that the ordinary amateur simply cannot
deal with it.
Therefore, I am quite satisfied—and I
have seen this and I know what I am
talking about, as I have had actual experience of it-that the only way the
Government can deal with a fox menace
of such an increasing nature is to get the
county councils in the various counties
to agree with them to employ professional
fox catchers, whose duty will be to kill
foxes during all that period when you
can kill foxes, and to kill rats in the
intervening period. I am quite certain
that it is full-time work. In England
not only have they one vermin catcher in
each county, but generally they have a
group of vermin catchers, and each deals
with a separate district in that county.
In Ulster up to ten or fifteen years ago,
and certainly 20 years ago, foxes were
never heard of in County Down. Now
we have foxes wherever we go, and they
are being particularly destructive,
especially amongst young lambs on the
hills and among poultry of all kinds, and
that will get worse unless firmer steps
are taken. My belief is that the only
way in which a serious menace to our
food production can be dealt with is by
the employment of proper fox catchers in
each area under the county councils.
I am glad to see that so much money is
being spent on the erection, reconstruction, and renovation of scutch mills. I
think it is a very wholesome sign to see
so much money spent on that, because,
if what one hears is true, we will have
to depend for a considerable period after
the war on our own flax. At one time I
thought, and a great many people also
thought, that once the war was finished
we would be getting our flax straight
away from Russia and Courtrai as if
nothing had happened. We have now
got to grasp the fact that there has been
such destruction on the Continent and
such terrific destruction in Russia that
all lands where this flax was grown have
been destroyed, and that the people in
those countries will be so hungry when
the war is over that they will have to
put their full efforts into growing food
for themselves and their families. They
will not be able to allocate the land or
give the time to the growing of flax for
export to Ulster.
I, therefore, believe that for a considerable number of years after this war
our linen industry will have to depend
to a very considerable extent on the flax
we grow in this country, and, therefore,
I think that the money spent in making
scutch mills efficient and on other things
such as tank retting is really well spent
money. I now come back to the remarks
I originally intended to make, because I
am very worried to see the amount that
is being saved on livestock. The hon.
Member for Pottinger asked me if I was
going to make some reply to the charges
against Ulster stock which I think were
made on the wireless by a Mr. Green.
Mr. Green is a great enthusiast for improvements, and the first charge he made
was a general charge which he made
against England too. As well as that, the
particular area of the country where Mr.
Green saw the cattle was certainly not
the area which you would take anyone

to the extermination of

and
Rev. ROBERT MOORE: I think hon.
Members will recall that in the Agriculture (Destruction of Vermin) Bill
which my predecessor put through the
House, roughly speaking one and a half
Supplementary Estimates-
Ministry of Commerce
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Rev. Robert Moore]
years ago, it was left to the County Committees of Agriqulture to frame their
own schemes for the destruction of foxes,
and the amount of money the Ministry
contributed depended upon the schemes
the different county Committees formulated. Of course, if this House wants to
have brought in a compulsory measure,

The hon. Member for Woodvale suggested
that a bonus should be given for the killing of foxes, but I understand that that
is what most of the county committees
do. I understand they have increased
the bonus very considerably in County
Derry.
Mr. NIXON: I know, but it is too
small.
Rev. ROBERT MOORE: With regard
to the point raised about the saving of
£2,000 under the milk scheme, the explanation of that is quite simple.
Perhaps hon. Members do not realise that
my Ministry buys the milk from every
producer, and if it is up to liquid
standard a certain price is paid. All that
milk does not go for liquid consumption,
great as that consumption is, and a
quantity bought at liquid prices but not
put into liquid consumption is used for
manufacturing purposes. It is sold at a
price different to the price at which we
buy it. In this case it just happens that
there was less milk of that kind bought
at liquid prices and transferred to manufacture than was anticipated, and therefore we sustained less of a loss, and that
amount was saved. It did not affect the
producers' price in any way. We buy all
milk. If it is sold for liquid consumption there is a certain price for it, and
if any part is not sold for liquid consumption it is sold for manufacture, and
there is a manufacturing price which is
lower than the liquid price.
With regard to livestock, the saving
there was due not to any niggardliness
on the part of the Ministry, but simply
to the fact that there was a shortage of
bulls and boars up to the premium
standard. Therefore, the premiums were
not paid, and there was a saving there.
Mr. McGURK: There is one point I
would like to mention to the Minister
regarding the grading of milk. He talked
about liquid and manufacturing prices.
There is a lot of dissatisfaction at the
present time regarding the grading of
milk. Some milk is for liquid consumption and some for manufacture. I know
the farmers are dissatisfied regarding the
grading of their milk. They think a lot
of milk that is going for manufacture
should be graded for liquid consumption,
and there is a difference of 6d in the
price. I am sure that the Ministry will
consider the matter and if there is any
cause for complaint it will be remedied.
Question put, and agreed to.

The
PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
COMMERCE (Mr. Maginess): In presenting these Supplementary Estimates
for the Ministry of Commerce in
respect of Salaries, Fisheries, Harbours
and Commercial Services, I propose to
deal first with the salient points in the
figures as set out in the printed copies in
the hands of hon. Members, and then to
comment briefly on one or two matters of
particular interest which arise therefrom.
Under Vote I the gross Supplementary
Estimate of £8,237 has been arrived at
after making allowance for savings which
include the provision already made in the
main Estimates for 1943-44 in regard to
the Office of the Agent for Northern
Ireland in Great Britain, the adminis
tration of which has been transferred as
from 1st April, 1943, from the Ministry
of Commerce to the Cabinet Secretariat.
Deducting additional receipts appropriated in aid amounting to £7,387,
which are enumerated in further detail
under subhead K, we arrive at the net
total of £850.

Supplementary Estimates
Supply
9 MARCH 1944


Directing attention firstly to the subheads under Vote I it will be seen that
subheads A.2 and A.3 are in respect of
staffing arrangements including additional posts in the production branch, the
flax factories and fisheries branches and
the raw materials branch; additional
clerical staff has also been necessary in
the compilation of a household coal consumers' register. The branch dealing
with post-war reconstruction, whose work
is closely connected with the development
of industry during war time, has also
been strengthened.
Subhead D.1 includes provision for the
Weights and Measures Services. By
arrangement with the Board of Trade
provision was made in the main Estimates for an expenditure of £155 in connection with the quinquennial verification.
of standards and beams. The verification of the standards and beams has been
carried out by officers of the standards
department. The local standards were
found to be in good order, but the scale
beams were not so satisfactory, and their
overhaul and repair by a firm of specialists
was considered necessary. Further expenditure will be provided for in the
1944-45 Estimates.
With regard to subhead F I may mention that ex pansion of my Ministry's
services and extended use of the telephone to transact urgent Government
business with the minimum of delay
accounts for the increase in the additional
sum required for telephones.
Under subhead G, it will be realised
that advertising in connection with those
services which directly affect the man in
the street is most essential; I would, in
this connection, like to voice my appreciation of the co-operation of the Press,
who I know have their hands full in
war time with the difficulties of dealing
with this side of public relations.
Subhead K covers receipts appropriated
in aid. It is anticipated that, owing to
the development of wartime control
schemes, the sums recoverable from
Imperial Departments will be larger than
those shown in the main Estimates. We
are, of course, responsible to the Imperial
Departments concerned as their agents
in operating these various wartime controls. Credit is also taken under this,
subhead for the recovery in connection
with a new agency which we have undertaken since the main Estimates were
drafted, in respect of work arising out
of the functions of raw material officers.
In the matter of the agency relating to
flax factories, capital expenditure on
erection and equipment has been incurred
at a higher rate than was anticipated
when the main Estimates for the current
financial year were being drafted; I
should explain that the agency charge in
this connection is calculated as a percentage on the capital expenditure, and not,
as in the case of other agencies, on the
basis of staff units employed.
Turning now to the sub-heads in Vote
2, under which the Supplementary Estimate of £73,000 in respect of fisheries,
harbours and commercial services will be
accounted for, I should like to refer in
particular to the following: Subhead C
is mainly in respect of the construction
of electricity high tension lines to ensure
adequate stand-by supplies. Of this expenditure 50 per cent. is being met out
of borrowed moneys and the balance
ranks for a grant under the Civil Defence
Act (Northern Ireland), 1939.
Under subhead F the grant in aid of
flax development is a carry-over of the
position of the agreed annual grant which
was not taken up during the year 1942-
Subheads J, K5, and L are selfexplanatory, and I think I may say the
same of the remainder. I beg to move.

The MINISTER OF FINANCE
(Major Sinclair): The Resolution which I
am now privileged to move will enable a
subsidy of £390 per house to be paid
from the Exchequer in respect of houses
which may be begun before 1st January,
1947, and, as hon. Members are aware,
the approval of Parliament to the proposal is of special importance at the present time in view of the decision to allow
materials to be made available to enable
a 750 house programme to be proceeded
with in Belfast without delay. I make
no apology in regard to the basis of this
subsidy seeing that it represents the
highest figure payable at the present time
in Great Britain in respect of urban
housing.

My right hon. Friend, when moving
the Second Reading of the Bill, alluded
to the possibility of further wartime
building in other parts of the Province
and this will depend upon the case which
can be made out for the release in war
time of an additional quantity of essential building materials. Meantime the
programme is limited to the 750 houses
for Belfast and the call upon the Exchequer in that connection will amount
to some £300,000. The rate of subsidy
is substantially higher than the subsidy
payable at the present time in respect of
housing in England and Wales, and is
equal to that payable in Scotland which
includes £100 per house to take account
of increased building costs in war time.
I am satisfied, therefore, that the
subsidy of £390 per house is essentially
fair in relation to that which is payable
in other parts of the United Kingdom.
I need not point out that this Resolution and the Bill on which it is based
provides for a war-time situation, and it
must not be assumed that the much
larger post-war housing programme will
necessarily attract the same rate of
subsidy. I beg to move.

ORAL ANSWERS TO
QUESTIONS.
Labour.
SUPPLEMENTARY PENSIONS.
1. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Labour whether he can state if it is a
fact that some supplementary pensioners'
allowances have been reduced in Northern
Ireland despite the fact that an increase
all round was anticipated; whether his
Department is following step-by-step
policy in this matter; whether he will
make a statement on the position of
supplementary pensioners in Northern
Ireland and state whether they are
receiving the same treatment as in
Britain.
SECRE-
The PARLIAMENTARY
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
COMMERCE (Mr. Maginess): I have
been asked by my right hon. Friend to
reply.
Where necessary, alterations both by
way of increases and decreases are made
in the amounts of supplementary pensions
where the circumstances of the recipients
have altered, and accordingly the reductions which have taken place in some
cases have been due to improvements in
the pensioner's circumstances.
The answer to the remainder of the
question is in the affirmative.
Mr. AGNEW: Can the Parliamentary
Secretary inform the House what was the
cause of the reduction in the allowances?
Mr. MAGINESS: As I have said, it
is due in some cases to the pensioner's
circumstances.
UNEMPLOYMENT IN ARMAGH
AREA.
2. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Labour whether he can state the actual
number of unemployed in Armagh Exchange area for the week ending 4/3/44;
what chance the unemployed of Armagh
have of obtaining local work; whether his
only solution of unemployment is sending them to Britain; and whether the
prosperity of Northern Ireland is best
assured by work at home.
Mr. MAGINESS: I have been asked
by my right hon. Friend to reply.
I am unable to give the hon. Member
the information asked for in the first
part of his question.
•
As regards the remainder of the question, it has always been the policy of the
Government to secure as much employment in Northern Ireland as possible;
and, in fact, as the hon. Member is
aware, more employment has been created
here than ever before. It is not, however, possible to have full employment in
every locality, especially during the
present emergency, and when people cannot obtain work in their own district
they should be prepared to accept it
wherever they are needed.
Education.
STRABANE TECHNICAL SCHOOL
RAILINGS.
3. Mr. BROWN asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the. Ministry of
Education whether her attention has
been drawn to the report in the Belfast
Press of 6th instant stating that at a
meeting of the Strabane and Castlederg
Regional Education Committee a letter
was received from the Ministry of Education stating, in connection with the
removal of iron railings from Strabane
Technical School, that the Committee's
solicitor had been conducting correspondence on the Committee's behalf with the
Ministry of Finance, and asking in what
circumstances it was considered necessary
to refer the matter to the solicitor;
whether the report shows that the chairman of the Committee (Captain J. C.
Herdman, D.L.) said he was very much
astonished at the tone of the letter from
the Ministry and took great exception to
it; whether it was decided by the Com-
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Brown]
mittee to write a letter of protest to the
Ministry and to express the resentment
of members of the Committee; and
whether she can state by whom the
Ministry's letter was signed and on whose
authority it was issued.
The
PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mrs. Parker): I have
seen the statement in the Press to which
the hon. Member refers.
The letter under reference, to which no
reply has yet been received in the
Ministry, was issued on the authority of
the Ministry and was signed by an
Assistant Secretary.
I might say that the Ministry's letter
drew the attention of the Committee to a
circular letter issued by the Ministry of
Home. Affairs to local authorities generally, pointing out that it is not competent for such authorities to instruct their
solicitors to carry out work of a non-legal
character which should properly fall
within the province of their officials, and
that it is the duty of the auditor to
examine such items and to take such
action as he may consider right.
So far as my Ministry is aware, no
legal issues were involved in the removal
of the railings in question, and the Committee were asked to be good enough to
state in what circumstances it was considered necessary to refer the matter to a
solicitor.

Mr. MAGINESS: I have been asked

A general appraisal of the industrial
needs and potentialities of Northern

Armagh, of which the Government is

cumstances of individual localities.

attention of the Government.
