move, "That in the opinion of this House
the Government should make strong and
pressing representations to the Imperial
Government for an immediate and adequate grant from the Exchequer towards
the Health Services of Northern Ireland
and to point out that these services are
not in parity with but are very inferior
to those which exist in Great Britain, that
rating authorities can no longer stand any
further demand upon their resources and
that the urgency of the matter is of vital
Health Services-
Northern Ireland
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Thomas Bailie]
consequence to the health and well-being
of the people of this country."
The Motion is one which I believe, can
be discussed with due regard to the vital
issues that are involved. I make no
apology for introducing this Motion this
afternoon, because I believe it is a Motion
that very directly affects the health and
well-being of the people of this community. Now, as I say, it would be my
personal desire to present this Motion
to-day in as uncontroversial a manner as
I can. I merely want to present my point
of view, and to ask Members of the House
simply for their verdict. After I have
discussed my point of view they will see
whether they agree with me or not.
The Motion is really a very simple one
and one that I believe I can present
without any undue elaboration. Since I
became a Member of this House, I have
made repeated references to my deep
conviction, and impression, and disturbance of mind by reason of the fact that
I believe I consider in common with a
great many Members of this House-that.
we here in Northern Ireland are very far
behind England and Scotland and Wales
so far as our health services are concerned.
That impression, which I held and still
hold, has been very much accentuated and
emphasised by reason of the fact that I
was a member of the Select Committee
on Public Health and had personal opportunity of knowing, through that Committee and the evidence brought before
it, just the exact conditions that do exist
here in Northern Ireland. Therefore, I
should like to think that no difficulty
exists in enabling Members of this House
to arrive at the conclusion that our health
services not only have been but are to-day
very inferior to those across the water. I
should be very much surprised if anyone
here in this House this afternoon will
disagree with that contention.
I
I could take up very considerable time,
which I do not intend to do, by mentioning in detail the various services which
are seriously in arrear. I could refer to
the very serious lack of sanatoria.
could mention the fact that here in
Northern Ireland we are faced with the
urgent and vital need for an additional
500 beds in our sanatoria. I could refer
to the unsatisfactory character of certain
existing sanitary institutions. I could
refer to the need for schools for mentally
defective children, the need for more
ante-natal clinics, the need for adequate
provision for orthopedic treatment, the
need for an advance, a
very great
advance, in our midwifery services and to
the rehabilitation and training of our
disabled persons, and more important
than these all, certainly equally
important, is the terrible need for adequate and satisfactory hospital accommodation in this country. These that I
have referred to are rather the institutional or medical side of the question, but
what about the public health or preventive side. of our need? Hospital and
institutional treatment is all to the good,
but I venture to suggest that provision of
preventive conditions is infinitely better.
I want to ask the Members of this
House are they satisfied that the conditions in our rural areas in Northern Ireland are such as they should be. I
venture to suggest that very much on the
contrary they are distinctly appalling. I
could take Members of this House to
villages and small townships in different
districts throughout Ulster which represent and would represent a disgrace to
the Middle Ages. In many places the
number is legion. There is no sewerage
system. There is no water supply, and
there is no system of public cleansing,
and there are no qualified sanitary
inspectors. Is it any wonder that, as a
Member of this House who is qualified to
speak on the subject said in the course
of the last few weeks, men, women and
children here in Northern Ireland are
dying unnecessarily? I feel in this matter
because I happen to know a good deal
about the subject.
I could speak of housing conditions, but

within the scope of my Motion, and at

Member for Woodvale. I suggest there is
no use in talking about housing if we do
not at the same time talk about the necessary water supply and sanitation. Public

of water supply is notorious, particularly
in many places I could mention. For the
city of Belfast we are here at the moment
considering paying £300,000 by way of a

disease. I anticipate that one of the main
objections, if any objection is made to
my Motion, will be based upon my use
of the word "immediate". I know that it
will be argued that the war effort must
come first. I seriously suggest here to-day
that a great deal can be done in this
matter without seriously interfering with
the war effort.
Seven hundred and fifty houses are
being built in the city of Belfast.
£16,000 we are informed is going to be
spent in building a centre for the educational executive work, also in the city of
Belfast. Can no money be made available for essential health services throughout Northern Ireland? Is the need for
the one not as great as the need for the
other? Is the need for hospitals and
sanatoria not as great as the need for
building an education office at £16,000
in Belfast? Before we teach the children
I venture to suggest it is infinitely more
important to make these children healthy
in the first instance for that teaching.
Millions of bricks are lying unused in the
brickyards, and scores of brickmakers are
on the dole. Why cannot we use these
materials and why cannot we use these
men to some extent at least in improving
our health services?
I have heard it advanced, and it may
be said to-day that the present position is
due not to the Ministry of Home Affairs-
I do not
want to be controversial in
making that statement-but that it is
due to the local authorities not carrying
out their functions. I want to say that
it may be true of some of these local
authorities, but it is not true of all the
local authorities. The consequence of the
present regulations is that there is a wide
variation in the standard provided in
different parts of Northern Ireland. There
are authorities which have carried out
their functions and there are authorities
which have failed to do so. In the case
of those who have carried out their functions may I suggest that these authorities
are absolutely at the end of their financial
resources? A great deal of the difficulty
is attributable to the fact that too many
of these regulations are purely of a permissive nature. Certain of these authorities have refused to carry out their functions because there is no obligation to do
so. I am not in favour of a dictatorship,
but I do say that in the matter of public
health these functions should
mandatory and not merely permissive.
be
I think I might condense what I want
to say by making one statement of my
own personal opinion. And that is, we
here in Northern Ireland are a distressed
and depressed area. We are not step by
step with Great Britain. We are, I
suggest, hopelessly behind, and if you are
going to march step by step in the future,
then I suggest there is a big lag behind
that has got, in the first instance, to be
made up. In sporting parlance we are
very much behind scratch. We need to
go up a long way to arrive at the starting
point from which we may venture in the
future to go step by step with Great
Britain. I think we are entitled to goor the Government is entitled to go to the
Imperial authorities and say to them,
"We hope to share with you in the new
order of advancement in our health,
social and other services. But before we
can proceed with you we need your help
to pull up the arrears. That very
simply is the proposition that I venture
to make with all seriousness to this House.
We are lagging so far behind that without this help we must, in my opinion,
remain behind. We are paying on the
basis of equality and parity.
""
This is, as I may say, roughly the substance of the case I want to put very
briefly before the House this afternoon.
There is, in my view, not merely a
financial but a moral obligation upon the
Northern Ireland
Health Services-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Bailie]
Imperial Parliament to come to our help
in these matters. I have said before,
and I now repeat, that the provision of
health and hospital services is a vital part,
and it should be regarded as a vital part
of our war effort. If we save the life of
a soldier on the battlefield and at the
same time sacrifice the lives of his wife
and children at home, then surely our
war effort is incomplete. The battle
against disease, I think, is one which at
all costs must be carried on no matter
what else is, through the necessities of
war, put on one side. We need not
merely buildings, concerning which there
is difficulty. We need equipment and
we need facilities. We need training for
our nurses. We need training and
qualifications for our sanitary inspectors.
We need nursery schools. In fact, we
need a thousand and one things of this
kind to bring us up to the condition of
parity with conditions in Great Britain.
The position is one which I regard
personally with all seriousness. I hope
that every Member will agree that the
position is very serious. Our boards of
governors, our rating authorities, our
rate-aided hospitals and voluntary hospitals cannot sustain any further demand
upon their resources. In my own area—
I am speaking for the Ards District
Hospital-we have reached the end of
our tether. We cannot meet any further
demand. Our rates are heavily burdened.
Yet in spite of that position the need
increases and the call is clamant for
expansion. All this is because our
services of almost every kind are hopelessly in arrear. If ever a just claim
existed for an Imperial grant, that claim
exists in connection with our health and
hospital services. I bring this Motion
to-day with only one object, not to
criticise the Government, not to indulge
in any unnecessary criticism, but rather
to assist the Government and the responsible Minister in presenting this
claim.
I do not think my Motion will
embarrass the Government. On the contrary I think it will strengthen it in its
prosecution of the case, and enable the
Minister to go to the Imperial authority
and say, "Here is a Motion passed by
the House concerning the health conditions which exist throughout Northern
Ireland and showing the present urgent
need for a grant." I have not alluded
to the need for a Ministry of Health or
the appointment of a Minister of Health,
because of the fact that there may be
divided views on that important subject.
I have purposely refrained from introducing anything of a controversial
character. I have merely endeavoured to
set out what I believe is an urgent need
to enable us, when this unhappy conflict comes to an end, to stand upon the
same threshold and look forward to a
step-by-step advancement into fresher
fields of health and healing for our
people.

seeing that when this Government was

I should like to deal with one or two
points in the Health Committee's report
which were not dealt with in the able

Down. One is the position of the poorlaw service in Northern Ireland.
For
some years before our present Government
was set up here, the Local Government
Board was endeavouring-and succeeding
-to redress grievances and anomalies in
the poor-law service. They were getting
the salaries of dispensary doctors raised
to a more appropriate level than then
existed. The aim which they set themselves was to get uniform salaries, rising
from £250 in the course of 20 years by
graduated increases to £350. They succeeded in this in the case of a good many
unions in Southern Ireland, and in the
case of two unions at least in Northern
Ireland. In other unions they got increases which did not amount to that
a full sum of £350, but which still were
substantial amounts on the salaries that
previously existed. In other cases they
found that Boards of Guardians absolutely refused to move in the matter. Just
thabout that time, before the functions of
the Local Government Board were taken
over by this Government, they had begun
to use compulsory powers, and they had
in one instance in Northern Ireland issued
a sealed order to a Board of Guardians
compelling them to pay what they thought
should be the salary.
em
Those salaries, once fixed by compulsion or by agreement between the doctors
and guardians, were sanctioned by the
Local Government Board as permanent,
and it was held that a Board of
Guardians in future appointments could
not reduce those salaries. I want to
emphasise that. Since that time, since
our Government was formed, and the
functions of the Local Government Board
as regards the poor-law service were taken
over by our Ministry of Home Affairs,
nothing whatever has been done. Absolutely nothing has been done to reach the
aim which the Local Government Board
had in mind the fixing of a uniform
maximum salary of £350 a year for dispensary doctors. Not only has nothing
been done, but our Ministry of Home
Affairs has actually permitted Boards of
Guardians to reduce those salaries that
were fixed by agreement and declared to
be permanent by the Local Government
Board. In the case of the Strabane
Board of Guardians, which fixed the commencing salary at £200, rising by £5 to
£300, the Ministry of Home Affairs
actually permitted that Board of Guardians to reduce that sum of £200 to £175,
and the maximum salary to £275. That
is an extraordinary thing for a Ministry
to do, seeing that the grievances and discontent-the justifiable discontent-of
the service was well known to them.
It is an unfortunate thing to have a
service which looks after the health of
about 50 per cent of the population of
this country seething with discontent and
a sense of injustice. It must necessarily
have an effect upon the way they perform
their duties, not that those duties are not
well performed. They are, and always
have been, well performed, as is shown by
the fact that complaints for neglect of
duty are almost unknown. I would
appeal to the Minister of Home Affairs
and to the. Ministry to complete the work
of the Local Government Board in bringing up the salary to the figure that was
fixed by the Local Government Board 25
years ago. It is a reasonable figure.
believe that in spite of the altered value
of money to-day that figure would satisfy
the service, but with less than that it will
never be satisfied.
I
When this Government was set up the
existing members of the poor-law service
were given the status of civil servants.
They were given an absolute right to
pensions and the right of appeal to the
Civil Service Commission if not satisfied
with the pension granted. But not one
of the poor-law medical officers appointed
since 1920 has an absolute right to a
pension. He may be granted a pension
by the board of guardians, but he has to
go to that board of guardians and ask
for that pension. I would ask the
Minister to-day in all justice to those
men, to put all poor-law medical officers
on the same level as regards pensions.
Another matter which was not referred to
by the mover of the Motion, but came
before the Select Committee on Health
Services, is the work of the registrars of
births and deaths in Northern Ireland.
Health Services-
Northern Ireland
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Dr. Lyle]
I am going to make a rather startling
statement, and one that can be either
confirmed or refuted by another hon.
Member present in the House. If he refutes my statement I will apologise to
the House for making it, but I do not
think I will have to make any apology.
That statement is that your vital statistics
in Northern Ireland so far as mortality
rates are concerned are fallacious and
indefensible. That is a very sweeping
statement to make, and I make it with a
full sense of its gravity.
The offices of the registrars of births
and deaths in rural districts are open on
two days of the week for two hours on
each such day. Take a district in which
the office is open on Mondays and
Fridays. If a person dies on Monday
the death cannot be registered on that
day. That person has to be buried and
is buried before the death is registered.
That cannot happen in Belfast, but it
happens day and daily in the rural districts. As a result the deaths in rural
districts are not registered for some considerable time after they take place, and
in many cases they are never registered.
Furthermore, in the rural districts a very
large proportion of the deaths are registered under the heading "Cause unknown. No medical attendant."
Some years ago the Registrar-General
issued a circular to registrars of deathsthis may be contradicted, but it is true
because I was a registrar of deaths and I
received the circular-advising them not
to use the words "Cause unknown," because it did not look well and did not fit
in with accurate statistics. We were to
try to ascertain from the person giving
the information about the death what
the probable or possible case of death was
and put in some definite cause of death.
What, I ask you, is the effect of that
upon your vital statistics? All registrars
of deaths in rural districts know that as a
result many deaths are registered under
a wrong heading. We know that the
tuberculosis death rate is far higher than
that shown by the Registrar-General. I
say that because deaths from tuberculosis
are registered as probably from bronchitis or something else, or are written
down as "Cause unknown." That is a
fact.
There is another very grave implication
in that, and that is that the door is
open to numerous cases of undetected
crime. People are allowed to die who
should have got better, or they are has
tened on their last journey by those who
want to get rid of them. I also suggest
to the House that there is another hon.
Member in the House who can either confirm or refuse to confirm what I have
stated. If he refutes it I will apologise
for the statement I have made to the
House. I do not think I will need to
apologise. I think the hon. Member will
confirm what I have said that deaths in
suspicious circumstances are often not
investigated and that they are registered
as from probably such and such a disease
or as "Cause unknown."
I hold that the registrar's office should
be open every day in the week, and that
no person should be buried until the
death has been registered. You cannot
do that because the remuneration of the
registrar is the same now as the amount
fixed 90 years ago when the service was
inaugurated. The remuneration of a
registrar of births and deaths in a rural
area would amount to only £10 or £20
a year.
Out of that sum he has to provide an office, and pay a deputy or assistant registrar.
Mr.
BEATTIE: Shame!
Dr. LYLE: Need I say any more on
that point? I also hold that every death
for which no medical certificate is forthcoming giving the cause of death should
be investigated by a coroner. In the old
days when coroners were paid for each
inquest they were investigated, but nowadays they are not, because coroners are,
as a rule, paid salaries which would not
defray their travelling expenses if they
investigated all the cases they should.
There is just one other question that
was before the Select Committee to which
I should like to refer the appalling unsanitary conditions in the city of Derry.
First of all we have the River Foyle. The
crude sewage of Strabane and Lifford
flows into the Finn and the Mourne,
where they form themselves into the
Foyle. As the river proceeds along the
sewage from St. Johnston and Carrigans
flows into it. That comparatively small
quantity of sewage might be dealt with
by the action of the water without injurious consequences, but it must be
remembered that the sewage of the whole
of Derry flows into the river with the
result that the lower end of the River
Health Services-

Foyle and the upper end of Lough Foyle
are nothing more or less than a cess
pool surrounding the city of Derry.
Two-thirds of the houses in Derry have
no baths. There are no public baths
except two or three slipper ones. The
back passages in Belfast, or mews as they
are called, come under the jurisdiction of
the Belfast Corporation and are as well
looked after as streets, but in Derry they
are nobody's baby at all. They do not
belong to anybody, and the Corporation
takes nothing to do with them. All the
surrounding rubbish, including human
excreta, is deposited in the back pasasges,
and they are cleansed only when the inhabitants of the houses adjoining find it
impossible to get along them. That is an
dappalling state of affairs to exist in the
In twentieth century in a country which is
supposed to be civilised.

The Motion goes on in a manner which

I doubt very much whether the hon.
Member for North Down, after full

authorities free for the. future from

cardinal consideration of which I would

riot.
The local authorities should be very

idle task to start to apportion the blame

if one bears in mind the difficulties in the

pressing representations to the Imperial

concern of our people are a matter for

the

kind?

have your

separate purposes, one of which must be

declaration is not yet forthcoming. I
think there should be no more delay in
bringing into being the suggested Ministry of Health. The Select Committee,
which represented all the interests in the
House, went into every detail, and I
cannot see the slightest cause for any
further delay in regard to the setting up
of a Ministry of Health. It is an
Cate
Health Services-
Northern Ireland
14 MARCH 1944

essential and an immediate necessity.
That being so, I hope we will have a
declaration from the Government that
this will be done.
In my opinion this Motion does not go
far enough. There is a great lack of
parity between Northern Ireland and
Great Britain in regard to education,
housing, and other matters, and especially so in regard to public health. No
further time should be lost in remedying
that state of affairs. We are part and
parcel of the United Kingdom, and as
such we pay £32,000,000 a year to the
Imperial Exchequer. There should not
be a moment's delay in regard to the
setting up of a Ministry of Health.
The hon. Member for Antrim has
reminded me about the land annuities,
but I do not want to bring you to your'
feet. I will reserve that for another
occasion. When we contribute £32,000,000
to the Imperial Exchequer-I do not
begrudge one penny piece that is spent
in helping to win the war-we should put
ourselves in the same position as they are
in across the Channel. That is really what
the Motion asks. No one can deny that
so far as public health is concerned there
is a great lack of parity between Northern Ireland and Great Britain.
I was astonished at the statement made
by the hon. Member for the University
that our vital statistics are fallacious; in
other words that they are false. The socalled explanation of that fact does not go
far enough. If that statement is correctit has not been denied so far as I knowit is a matter which requires immediate
attention. It is a very important matter
if, as the hon. Member suggests, the
statistics are false. This matter should
receive immediate attention even to the
extent of setting up a commission under a
high court judge to inquire into it.
So far as public health is concerned a
very good case has been made out for the
setting up of a Ministry of Health. It
has been sought to remove the portion of
the Motion which says:
.
that rating authorities can no
longer stand any further demand upon
their resources and that the urgency of
the matter is of vital consequence to
the health and well-being of the people
of this country.
Does any person seriously contend that
this is not a vital concern? If it is a
vital concern every hon. Member must
object to the leaving out of that part of
the Motion. As no one has stated that it
is not a matter of concern why do we
get this change in the Motion? Does anybody deny that the local authorities can
no longer bear the burden? That is
another matter that will have to be
tackled. The Local Government Acts are
years and years out of date, and the whole
matter of local government will have to
be investigated from top to bottom.
We are acting and operating under
Acts wholly archaic and we must have a
complete overhaul of the whole machinery
regarding local government. Certainly,
in my opinion, the local authorities cannot bear any more burdens than they are
bearing at present, and it is the duty of
the Government to come forward and
bear these burdens in the respect set out
here and in other respects which I do not
propose to go into. There, is a great increase in the rates all over the country.
Some years ago we had the Revaluation
Act, which substantially increased the
valuations with the result that the rates
were greatly reduced by many local
authorities, for more money was coming
in as a result of revaluation. The position to-day is that the rates have gone
far beyond what they were before the
increased money began to come in under
the Revaluation Act. I am told by the
hon. Member for Queen's University that
in Derry the rates are 20s in the £. Who
is going to suggest that Derry is in a
position to bear more burdens in the way
of increased rates?
Take the rates all over Northern
Ireland, and the position is equally
grave.
I tell you that the ratepayers
cannot bear more burdens in these
matters, and it is the duty of the Government to step in, and step in at once,
because the matter of public health is of
the most urgent importance. The Motion
talks of strong and pressing representations. We are told that strong and
pressing representations are made every
day. With what result? I am sick and
sore and tired listening for six years in
this House to statements that strong and
pressing representations are being made,
I want to see results. It is jam yesterday, jam to-morrow, but never jam
to-day. We want jam now.

Mr. MINFORD: And every day.
Mr. BROWN: We are told that representations are made every day. We
want to see some results, and we intend
to see some results. The mortality rates
all over Northern Ireland are such as
would shock a normal assembly into
immediate action. There is the position
regarding cancer and all other serious
diseases. If we examine our figures we
find the position much more serious than
elsewhere. That alone should shake this
House and the Government into instant
action in this matter. We certainly cannot allow matters to rest where they are,
and I think we should have a pronouncement on the subject right away. To
allow that Report of the Select Committee on Health Services to go into a
pigeon hole is 'something that this House
cannot and should not stand for.
In my
opinion this House should not for one
moment allow that two guinea volume to
be put into a pigeon hole. The whole
country wants something done about a
Ministry of Health, and wants its done
at once. I cannot see why in the wide
world that cannot be done. There is no
problem more important than this except it be the allied problem of housing.

ORAL ANSWER TO
QUESTION.
North Down Water Supply.
Mr. ANDREWS asked the Minister of
Finance whether he can state the amount
of the Government grant which he proposes to give to the North Down Water
Scheme and to other schemes of the kind
in Northern Ireland, SO that local
authorities may be in a position to make
arrangements for carrying out such
necessary work without delay.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Major
Sinclair): I would preface my reply to
the right hon. Gentleman by reminding
him that in war-time borrowings by local
authorities for public health and other
services are strictly controlled by the
Capital Issues Committee whose function
in relation to the country, as a whole, is
to ensure that capital expenditure is
limited to those schemes which
definitely necessary at the present time
for the maintenance of essential services.
From my experience with applications to
this Committee it is extremely doubtful
whether approval would be given unless
the North Down Water Scheme as an
essential war-time scheme and unless the
No.
of
Vote

12345
SERVICE
are
approval of the Capital Issues Committee were forthcoming, then it would
not be possible to obtain the requisite
allocation of the necessary materials for
the purpose of such schemes.
The right hon. Gentleman may be
assured that the Government is fully
alive to the claim which has been made,
that if the undoubted leeway in the provision of water supplies is to be made
good after the war, then Exchequer
assistance will have to be given in order
to lighten what might otherwise prove
to be a very heavy rate burden. He will
not, however, expect me to make any
definite announcement on this subject at
this stage and until the Government can
see somewhat more clearly the priorities
which will govern the post-war activities
of our local authorities.
Mr. ANDREWS: Owing to the unsatisfactory nature of the reply, I regret
that I will have to take an early opportunity of raising the matter, possibly on
the Vote on Account.

Mr. ANDREWS: There are two
matters in this Vote on Account that I
wish to refer to. I understand there
were two sums included, one an amount
of about £18,000 for the erection of a
building for the Ministry of Education
and the other a substantial sum-I really
have not heard the amount definitelyfor the erection at the Royal Courts of
Justice of a drawing office. Now these
two schemes will undoubtedly require
both iron and timber, and it seems
strange to me and to those I have the
honour to represent that these materials
which we are told are so urgently required
for war-time purposes should be used for
the erection of these buildings. Again we
are told that they cannot be used for
housing, even in Belfast, except to a
very limited extent, and that housing
schemes cannot be carried out in our
country districts during the war, or only
to a very minor extent. I should like to
ask my right hon. Friend the Minister
of Finance for an explanation as to why
these two schemes to which I have referred are considered so urgently necessary.
The other matter which I have already
told the Minister of Finance I intended
to raise was what I considered his
unsatisfactory answer to the question
I asked to-day in reference to what
is known as the North Down water
scheme. This scheme has been under
consideration for many years, and
a Government grant was promised as a
relief scheme grant many years ago.
At that time our local authorities were
not prepared to do their part. Now, I
am glad to know, they are strongly in
favour of the scheme, as also are the
people throughout the districts affected,
especially in Comber, Bangor, Newtownards, Ballygowan, and elsewhere.
The excuse, I understand, for not
going on with this scheme is the abandonment some time ago of the airport scheme
which was to be brought into being close
to this North Down water main and to
which there were to be very substantial
grants from the Air Ministry. All that is
asked at the present time is that as the
grants from the Air Ministry are not
available the Northern Ireland Exchequer
should meet the liability. I know that
the scheme has already been prepared,
that plans have been drawn, that contracts have been placed, and that way.
leaves have been acquired. I understand
that even the pipes were ordered and were
almost ready for delivery. I wonder will
there be a claim for damages in consequence of these contracts being
cancelled. Whether or not that may be
so, I feel that a scheme of this kind
which is so urgently required should be
proceeded with.
I do not see the reason for the delay.
If it could go on when the airport
required water it appears to me that it
ought to go on when the people of this
large district require it very urgently. I
would ask the Minister to think again
in connection with this matter. I would
ask him even to develop his persuasive
powers, and, if necessary, be
a little
stronger in his representations to the
Treasury across the water. I have had a
good deal of experience in my time in
dealing with the British Treasury, and I
always found them to be most willing and
anxious to be helpful and at times
remarkably generous to Northern Ireland.
Examples of that generosity can be found
in the Re-insurance Agreement, in the
large financial assistance given to our
transport undertakings, in the arrangements that were made as regards
time expenditure, and also in connection
with the possibility, not now the probability, of there being at any time an
unbalanced Budget.

а

Marriage (Declaration of Law) Bill
[Senate].
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Mr. Lowry): The one object of this very
brief Measure is to afford protection to
Ministers of religion who on grounds of
religious belief and as a matter of conscience object to solemnize the marriage.
of divorced persons or of persons coming
within certain prohibited degrees of
relationship and who are legally entitled
to marry. It is difficult under existing
law to say definitely whether clergymen
are legally bound in certain events to
solemnize such marriages. The Bill now
before the House removes these difficulties and makes it clear that no clergyman
shall be under any legal obligation either
to solemnize such a marriage or to permit
his church to be used for that purpose.
Dealing with Clause 1, the Matrimonial
Causes Act (Northern Ireland), 1939, in
addition to introducing new grounds for
dissolution of marriage, substituted a
judicial for a legislative system of divorce.
Prior to the passing of the Act, as will
be within the knowledge of many Members of the House-because some of them
I have seen acting on Joint Committees on
Divorce Bills-it was only possible to
obtain a dissolution of marriage by virtue
of a private Act of Divorce following a
decree a mensa et thoro. Now either of
the parties is entitled to marry again as
soon as the decree of divorce has been
made absolute. If the clergy of any
religious denomination are bound by the
civil law to solemnize the marriage of any
party whose former marriage has been
dissolved under the provisions of the Act,
the effect of this Clause will be to release
all clergy from the obligation.
For a long time protection has been
afforded in Great Britain for certain
marriages within the prohibited degrees;
this protection will now be provided here
under Clause 2 of this Bill. Section 2 of
the Marriage Act, 1835, lays down the
prohibited degrees of consanguinity or
affinity within which persons may not
legally marry. There are two cases of
persons who though within the prohibited
degrees are nevertheless legally entitled
to marry. First, a man may marry
deceased wife's sister by virtue of the
Deceased Wife's Sister's Marriage Act,
1907, and, secondly, a man may marry his
deceased brother's widow by virtue of the
Deceased Brother's Widow's Marriage
Act, 1921, as amended by the Deceased
Brother's Widow's Marriage Act (Northern Ireland), 1924.

his
It may be that these marriages,
although justifiable under the civil law,
offend against ecclesiastical law and prac
tice. This Clause makes it clear that no
clergyman shall be compelled to solemnise
the marriage of persons coming within
these two degrees of relationship.
Bill is really for the protection of tender
consciences, and I am sure it is a matter

Constabulary Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Mr. LOWRY: This Bill prolongs the
operation of the Constabulary (Acquisition of Land) Act, 1924. It has been
renewed from time to time, and is shortly
to expire. The House will remember
that this Act gave power to the Ministry
of Home Affairs to acquire lands compulsorily for the use as accommodation of the
Royal Ulster Constabulary, limited to a
period of five years from the passing of
the Act. The power, however, was
further extended until the 28th May,
1934, by the Constabulary Act of 1928,
and further extension until the 28th May,
1944, was made by the Constabulary Act
of 1933, when it was anticipated that the
programme of barrack building would
have been completed and the necessity for
compulsory powers of acquisition of land
for this purpose would no longer be required. The war intervened, which made
it necessary to suspend the operation of
the barrack building programme, and some
considerable time must necessarily elapse
before the scheme as a whole can be completed. The Bill now before the House
will extend the Ministry's powers until
the 28th May, 1954. Although the
powers conferred by the Act are only
invoked in exceptional circumstances, it
is nevertheless most desirable that this
should be available so long as the building
scheme is in progress. I beg to move.
Question, "That the Bill be now read
a Second time," put, and agreed to.
Bill committed to a Committee of the
Whole House for to-morrow.

ORAL ANSWERS TO

Belfast Prison Hunger Strike.
2. Mr. THOMAS CAMPBELL
asked the Minister of Home Affairs
whether any prisoners in Belfast jail
have been on continuous hunger-strike
for the last 23 days, and if so, how
many; and what information the Minister
can give regarding their present condition
after such a prolonged period of want
of food.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Mr. Lowry): Three convicts in Belfast
prison have been on hunger-strike since
the 22nd of last month and the condition
of these men is only what could be expected after such a prolonged period
without food.
.
The Government cannot accept any
responsibility for the actions of these men
whose present condition is solely due to
their own voluntary abstention from food.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Is this trickle of
information all the information the
Minister has to give the House on the
present situation in which men's lives are
in the balance? Are these men in hospital, or is each in his separate cell? Are
they refused the use of warm water?
Mr. LOWRY: I think I have answered
the question put by the hon. and learned
Gentleman, which was how many
prisoners have been on continuous
hunger-strike for the last 23 days. I
have given that information.
As to
where the prisoners are, one is in hospital,
the rest are in their cells. The number
is steadily dwindling, though a question
of this sort may stimulate a few more
foolish men to continue their malignant
and criminal practice.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Arising out of the
peevish answer of the Minister, may I
ask him, in view of the extreme nervous
and physical prostration of these three
men, will he allow their immediate relatives or their own doctors to see them?
Mr. LOWRY: The medical treatment
is entirely satisfactory. Their own relatives at an appropriate time, for
example when death is imminent, will be
duly notified.
Mr. CAMPBELL: In view of the
gravity of this matter I propose to raise
it on the Motion for the Adjournment.

regarding post-war educational reforms
stating that "the preparation of a White
Paper by officials of the Ministry of

whether he has seen the statement published in the Belfast Press of 7th instant
of the joint sub-committee of the

that before any White Paper is published
in Northern Ireland the procedure as to
prior consultation with various interests
that was followed across the Channel
should be followed in Northern Ireland,
and whether he will consider the advisability of setting up an unpaid Joint
Select Committee of the House of
Commons and the Senate to hear evidence
from all interested parties and make recommendations on the whole subject of
Northern Ireland's future educational
development.
.
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir Basil
Brooke): Yes, sir. I have received the
resolution of the Ulster Teachers' Union
to which the hon. Member refers. My
reply to the Union was published in the
Press on the 10th instant, and I feel that
I cannot do better than repeat the concluding paragraph, which reads as follows: . -
It has always been the intention that
there should be full and frank discussion with educational interests before
the White Paper is published; that the
White Paper itself will be open to
debate and discussion, and that the
projected Bill will not be brought

Mr. THOMAS CAMPBELL:
Minister of Home Affairs to-day informed
the House that there are three prisoners
in Belfast Prison who have been undergoing a voluntary fast for a period of
almost four weeks. I intend as a matter
of public duty to refer to that very painful position. I shall endeavour to do so
as briefly as I possibly can, and I hope
not to say an unnecessary word.
As a
public representative the position seems
to me to be one of gravity, and I have
felt bound as a matter of duty to come
here, and, after hearing the statement
of the Minister, to draw attention to the
position which, as we are all aware, has
an abnormal and urgent aspect.
I do not intend to go beyond those
three cases. The matter of hunger
striking generally was discussed on a
recent occasion-I think it was last week
-in this House on the Adjournment, and
to-day I limit myself entirely to the
position which evolves from the statement
made by the Minister this afternoon.
Those three men, having regard to their
prolonged fast, must be in a state of
extreme physical and nervous prostration.
The agony they are suffering must be
beyond the power of words to tell.
Having regard to the strength, or rather
to the weakness of human nature and the
human frame, the human frame cannot
stand that strain very much longer. No
matter what we may say about them and
why they are in prison, these men deny
that they are criminals. Rightly or
wrongly they have principles. They cling
to those principles, and they say that
they are proud to be suffering for those
principles. They claim that they should
not be classified and branded as criminals,
and, from what one can glean from the
statement made by the Minister a few
days ago in this House, they resent being
degraded by being graded and associated
with criminals.
same
You may condemn their views, you
may challenge their principles, you may
say that their tendencies are subversive
and revolutionary. You are entitled to
say that, but, on a broad view,
when you do say that, you must
say the
of thousands of men
who in the countries on the Continent

among

English attitude was different towards

I put
Mr. LOWRY: I should like in the
first instance to point out that this is the
only part of the British Empire in which
this method of trying to defeat the law
has never succeeded. This hunger striking
has a rather interesting history so far as
the British Empire is concerned. The
first time it was ever tried was in the
year 1875 in the Fiji Islands. The person
who did it was an Indian coolie. I think
it was yesterday that the hon. and learned
Member referred to the Oriental practice
of sit dharna whereby a creditor tried to
coerce his debtor to pay by sitting and
starving himself to death on his door
step. The supposition there was that this
would soften the heart of the debtor, or
that some evil would befall the man who
would not pay his debts if he caused the
death of his creditor
I am bound to say that this sit dharna
had quite a wonderful effect. It was introduced, as I said, in the Fiji Islands
in the year 1875. It was then taken up
on a large scale over 30 years during
the suffrage agitation, when what was
known as the Cat-and-Mouse Act was
passed to try to deal with the situation,
and prisoners were taken in and out of
jail. In this country-in Dublin-well
over 20 years ago an attempt was made
to combat the matter by forcibly feeding
the persons concerned. Experience proved
that that was a wholly unsatisfactory way
of dealing with the matter, because it led
to the application of force, and the
doctrine of reasonable and necessary force
is a difficult one to superintend.
When this Government was set up the
policy was to allow a man to commit
suicide if he were so minded. I think
that, as a practical way of dealing with
the situation, and also from a moral
standpoint, that is the proper attitude to
take up. The practice now is that when
men go off their food they are supplied
with milk. It is perfectly obvious that
these men would not be so well to-day if
they did not drink milk. The sustaining
qualities of the milk supplied is a sort of
tribute to the Ministry of Agriculture.
It is true that three of the men are not
just as well as the other thirteen. The
number now is reduced to sixteen; at
one time it was as high as thirty-two.
The numbers are rather illuminating. It
started with nine, and in a very short
time three of them dropped out. There
was then a debate on prison administration in this House, and the number
jumped to ten, then to twenty-eight, then
to thirty, and finally to thirty-two. Every
time a question was asked in this House
it acted as a sort of stimulus to these
criminals. My experience, and the experience of those who have had professional dealings with criminals—the
hon. and learned Member, from his professional dealings with criminals, will
confirm me in this-is that they are the
vainest of mankind. Vanity, next to
criminality, is the strongest characteristic
of criminals. When notice is taken of
them in the Press, in this House, or anywhere else it stimulates them, and they
think they are of great importance, and
that the whole world is trembling about
their fate. That is why I have so
frequently deprecated in this House any
allusion to those criminal outcasts and
the fact that they do not like to associate
with other criminals.
Let me tell you this. One of the
Visiting Justices appointed by the Grand
Jury was approached by convicts-they
have every right to approach the Visiting
Justices and they complained bitterly
that they should be confined in the same
wing with the very people for whom the
hon. and learned Member raises his voice.
There are degrees of social distinction
even in "A" Wing of the Belfast Prison.
I am bound to confess that my sympathy,
such as it is, is entirely on the side of
those people who approached the Visiting
Justices. To my mind the real criminals,
the dangerous ones, are those who selfstyle themselves political criminals.
The suggestion that there is some sort
of excellent political crime is the greatest

ey
Some sort of analogy is sought to be
drawn between the people who
are
engaged in the underground movement on
the Continent and these rapscallions.
Really, I wonder how anyone could
solemnly put that forward as an argument. It would be laughable, if it were
not so serious, to compare Frenchmen, or
Dutchmen, or Belgians, or Norwegians,
or Czecho-Slovakians, who are rightly
struggling to be free from a great
tyranny, with these people who are not
suffering under any disability or any
tyranny, and who with gun, bomb,
murder, and so forth try to make their
position good, to the great danger of this
community and the United Kingdom.
No, the policy that has been observed
from the start of the setting up of this
Government will be observed to the end,
and if these men deliberately add to
crimes which they have committed another
felony, namely, the felony of suicide, the
Government cannot stop them and will
not stop them. They must take the consequences, here and hereafter.

QUESTIONS.
Belfast Corporation Transport Workers'
Conditions.
en
2. Dr. LYLE asked the Minister of
Labour whether he is aware that the incidence of peptic ulcer and other digestive
disorders is abnormally high among the
employees of the Belfast Corporation
Transport Department; whether, owing
to the absence of canteen provisions for
vehicular crews, the men are compelled to
snatch hurried meals from cafes
route; whether the hygienic conditions.
and the standards of lighting, heating,
sanitation and ventilation in depots and
repair shops are below those required by
the Factories Act (Northern Ireland),
1938; whether a report submitted to Dr.
C. S. Thomson, Medical Superintendent
Officer of Health for Belfast, by a
member of his staff in December last was
to the effect that lavatories in depots were
in an unsatisfactory condition and
whether he is prepared to take the necessary steps to have these conditions
improved.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Grant): I have no information about the
complaints mentioned amongst the employees of the Belfast Corporation Transport Department, and I have no power
to deal with the question of canteen
facilities for vehicular crews.
In premises occupied by the Transport
Department and coming within the
provisions of the Factories Act (Northern
Ireland), 1938, the working conditions
are, on the whole, satisfactory. There is
room for complaint, however, at the Falls
Road workshops, though I am glad to
say that plans have been prepared for a
new shop which, if completed, would
provide excellent working conditions and
welfare amenities. These plans are at
present receiving the active consideration
of the Belfast Corporation.
With regard to the last part of the
question, I have no knowledge of a report
furnished to Dr. Thomson, the Medical
Superintendent Officer of Health for
Belfast, by a member of his staff about
unsatisfactory depot lavatories. It is,
of course, for Dr. Thomson to deal with
such matters.
The hon. Member is no doubt aware
that a centralisation scheme for the
maintenance and repair work of the
Transport Department was considered by
the Belfast Corporation, but that it was
found necessary to postpone the question
until after the war.
Dr. LYLE: I would ask the Minister
if he has never seen the conductor of a
tram or bus stop the vehicle and dart
into a restaurant and come out of it again
with a few sandwiches for himself and
the driver and one or two tins presumably
containing tea, and if he does not consider some better arrangement than that
should be made for meals for these people.
Mr. GRANT: I have seen instances
of what the hon. Member has mentioned
here to-day. My sympathies are entirely
with the men in question, but unfortunately I have no power to help them.
Bann Drainage Scheme.
4. Mr. HENDERSON asked the Prime
Minister whether he can state the date of
starting the Bann Drainage contract, the
total contract price, the total amount paid
up to date and whether this contract is
now completed.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Major
Sinclair): I have been asked by my right
hon. Friend to reply.
The amount of the contract which was
entered into in connection with the scheme
for the drainage of the River Bann formed
portion only of the total expenditure involved, and I am replying to the hon.
Member's question on the assumption that
he desires to know the total cost of the
scheme.
The work was started in the last week
of July, 1930. The total expenditure up
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Major Sinclair]
to date is slightly over £890,000, and this
covers not only the amount paid to the
contractors but also the cost of certain
direct labour works carried out by the
Ministry, the provision and maintenance
of the necessary craft and vehicles, the
cost of salaries of the site staff, their
offices, equipment, etc., and the sum of
slightly over £120,000 in respect of land
and fisheries compensation. Some amounts
in respect of fishery compensation remain
to be paid, but these cannot be determined for some time. The scheme was
completed on 31st January, 1942.

Stormont Castle-Civil Servants'
Entrance.
5. Mr. HENDERSON asked the Prime
Minister whether he is aware that civil
servants employed in Stormont Castle
have been prohibited from entering by
the main entrance and, if so, has this
prohibition his approval.
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir Basil
Brooke): The departments occupying
Stormont Castle recently notified their
staffs that, as the number entering by the
main entrance had become unduly large,
the side door should normally be used. I
entirely approve of this arrangement.
Education.
RELIGIOUS INSTRUCTION.
6. Mr. HENDERSON asked the Prime
Minister whether he can state if the Government intends to provide for religious
instruction in all schools in Northern
Ireland so that the children will not be
at a disadvantage in this matter when
compared with children attending similar
schools in England and Wales.
The PRIME MINISTER: The intentions of the Government in this matter
were set out in my reply to a question by
the hon. Member for South Down (Mr.
Brown) on 29th ultimo. I have nothing
to add to that reply.
Mr. HENDERSON: Would the right
hon. Gentleman tell the House if the
children of Northern Ireland are going
to be kept step by step with those of
Great Britain in this matter?
The PRIME MINISTER: As I have
already told the House, this is a matter
for the House. The House will decide
the whole of this question when the
White Paper is laid before it. It is for
the House to say and not for me.
Mr. HENDERSON: In view of the
fact that the right hon. Gentleman is
Prime Minister of the country is he going
to give the House a lead in this matter?
Mr. BROWN: Will the Prime
Minister tell us why he has not answered
the challenge issued by the Moderator of
the General Assembly of the Presbyterian
Church in Ireland calling upon him for
a statement of the Government's intention in this matter?
Mr. SPEAKER: That does not arise
on the question.

21 MARCH 1944

CONSULTATIONS BEFORE ISSUE
OF WHITE PAPER.
7. Mr. HENDERSON asked the Prime
Minister whether he can state why in the
official communication given to the Press
and published on the 10th instant
enumerating the various bodies with
which the Ministry of Education proposed to consult before issuing the White
Paper on Education no mention whatever
was made of the churches or religious
bodies although consultation with
religious bodies had occupied a foremost
place before the issue of the White Paper
on education in England.
The PRIME MINISTER: The hon.
Member will observe that the official communication to which he refers states that,
before drawing up the White Paper, the
Ministry of Education will ascertain "the
views of the various bodies able to speak
with authority on every aspect of our
educational system." The hon. Member
may accordingly rest assured that consultations with the churches and religious
bodies will take place in due course.
8. Mr. HENDERSON asked the Prime
Minister whether he can state on what
date the Ministry of Education was first
informed or became aware that "it had
always been the intention that there
should be full and frank discussion with
educational interests before the White
Paper was published" and how and by
whom this information reached the
Ministry of Education.
The PRIME MINISTER: The procedure outlined in the letter sent to the
Ulster Teachers' Union
on the 9th
instant represents the policy invariably
followed by the Ministry of Education
before formulating proposals for any
major change in the educational system
in Northern Ireland.
Mr. NIXON: Arising out of all these
questions, would it not have been wise to
postpone this matter for five minutes
until the new Minister of Education takes
his seat there?

10. Mr. BROWN asked the Prime
Minister whether he can state if the
Advisory Council to advise the Ministry
of Education on educational matters,
provided for in Clause 1 of the Education
Act of 1923, was duly set up and if so
whether he can state when the Council
was last summoned by the Ministry and
when it last met; whether he can give
the names of the members who first constituted this Council; whether there have
been any changes by death or otherwise
in the membership since then or since the
Council last met; whether such vacancies,
if any, have been filled, and by whom;
and whether he can give the names and
addresses of all the members at present
forming the Council.
The PRIME MINISTER: As the
answer is very lengthy I propose, with
the hon. Member's permission, to have it
circulated in the Official Report.
Mr. BROWN: In the meantime will
the Prime Minister tell us, in view of the
fact that the Act distinctly stipulates that
this Council must be summoned or called
at least twice a year, why the Ministry
of Education have been allowed to break
the law and break it most flagrantly for
many years by absolutely ignoring this
Statute passed by Parliament ?
The PRIME MINISTER: I think if
the hon. Gentleman puts down a specific
question I may give him an answer.
Mr. BROWN: Is it not a fact I have
put down a specific question, and will the
Prime Minister not give me a specific
answer?

Mr. JOHNSTON: I beg to move,
That this House desiring to promote a closer association between the
Parliament of Northern Ireland and the
Congress of the United States of
America, directs Mr. Speaker on its behalf to invite the delegation of Congress
during their stay in. Great Britain, to
visit Northern Ireland as the guests of
this Parliament and thus further
advance the cordial relationships which
have been strengthened by the presence
of the United States Forces in this
area."

I think it is right and proper that we
should invite the delegation of Congress
of the United States to visit this Parliament for many reasons and one particularly, and that is that the beginning
of the Congress in America was largely
the performance and work of people from
Northern Ireland. In the .revolutionary
war of the eighteenth century it was the
people from this country who were the

739 Congress of the United Statesstrongest supporters of Congress, and
were, as it were, the spearhead of the
American revolution of that date, and
among them were the authors and
founders of the American Constitution.
It is our people who were the pioneers of
the westward movement over America.
It was they who blazed the trail from the
Atlantic to the Pacific, and were
primarily the founders of the great Union
of North America and of the United
States which now stretch from the
Atlantic to the Pacific.
Therefore it is with the greatest confidence that I move this Motion, seeing
that members of Congress are coming
back again as it were to their homeland
and to the place of their origin. Again
they will be coming to see their own
troops whom we have welcomed in very
large numbers, and who have come into
our life in many ways. We have welcomed
them and we support them and we are
going to fight side by side with them until
victory is won. I am sure the delegation
will be received by the whole population
with enthusiasm and that this House will
welcome them in accordance with this
Motion. I cannot stop here without saying something about the peace and the
war. We have fought side by side now
for some years in this present war and
we hope to bring it to a successful conclusion. It is after the war that we might
lose. Unless the people of the United
States, unless Congress and ourselves stick
together after the war, we will be in
great danger of losing the peace, and to
lose the peace might be nearly worse than
losing the war, because it is the peace
that we must win.
One thing that has been burned into
our consciences is that this civilisation of
ours could not stand the third shock of
another great war. If we are to win the
war and lose the peace I think that what
we have fought for and died for will be
in vain. I should like to impress on the
American people when they are over here
the necessity of our two countries sticking
together during the peace and ensuring
that what we have fought for is not
thrown lightly away. I am looking forward, and I am sure the House is looking
forward, to this delegation, and I am
hoping that our two countries will march
safeguard the future of mankind. (Hon.`

Mr. NIXON: I have the greatest possible pleasure in seconding the Motion so
ably proposed by the hon. Member for
North Armagh. There is nothing more
important in the world to-day than good
relations between Britain and our great
Ally, the U.S.A. I remember well in the
dark days of 1940 and 1941 I sat up every
night and all night trying to hear what
they were saying in America, and I was.
never discouraged by anything I heard.
The hon. Member who has spoken
referred to the part that Ulstermen
played in laying the foundation of that
great Republic. I did not intend to refer
to it, but I might be permitted to say
that a kinsman and namesake of mine,
John Nixon, publicly read the first
Declaration of Independence in America
-(Hon. Members: Hear, hear) and I
would do the same in the same circumstances. But the circumstances we are
now living in here are very different,
because I can come into this Parliament,
although in a minority, and say what I
want to say-and I do not hesitate to do
it-under the protection of Mr. Speaker
-(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I might
also at this stage congratulate the Prime
Minister on what he has already done in
the direction that this Motion tends. I
remember the arrival of the U.S.A.
Forces, and I was very proud that day
I saw them in Belfast, and I should like
at this stage to pay tribute to the courtesy
and kindness and politeness of the
American soldiers in our midst. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) I meet as many
of the common people as any person, and
what pleases us all is their manners. Their
manners are extremely good. I know that
in Northern Ireland there are many
things they could criticise if they wanted
to, but never do you hear any criticism.
You never hear an unpleasant word.
Last night I was speaking to a member
of the Royal Ulster Constabulary since its
inception. He is a member of the Royal
Ulster Constabulary, who has the Mons
Medal, and who served in the war under
General Alexander, of whom he has a very
high opinion. I was asking him about the
American Forces. He is meeting with
them every day and he has nothing to say
about them except what is good. And so
long as Ulster is Ulster we will always be
glad to see them here. The enemies of
the U.S.A. are my enemies. I was born
and brought up in Cavan, an Ulster
county that is now in Eire. I always

The PRIME MINISTER: I need add
very little to what has been said by the
Mover and Seconder of this Motion. I
think both of them expressed the opinion
of the House and the opinion of the

(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) The
Seconder made reference to the fact that
I had done something to promote the good
feeling and hospitality which I know
exists between Ulstermen and the Forces
of our friends and Allies the United
States, and I did that for two reasons. I
have retained the chairmanship of the
Hospitality Committee in my own hands,
because I considered it of the verv utmost
importance. I have been supported ably
by men and women all over Ulster who
have done everything they could to make
our friends happy and feel at home, but
I want to say in addition to that it takes
two to make a success of an arrangement
of that sort. I have the privilege of
reading the reports of Hospitality Committees from time to time, and it would
gratify any hon. Member in this House
to see the extraordinary spirit of goodwill
and kindliness which exists not only on the
part of those responsible for hospitality,
but also on the side of our guests.

It is an agreed thing, I believe, that
Ulster is playing a very important part
in the object we have in view, that is a
better understanding between the two
countries; but, I think, what we must
abolish from our minds is the idea that
there will be no differences between us.
There are bound to be differences just as
there are differences in families, differences
on points of view; but there still remains
the feeling in the family that the good
of the family matters just as in the House
there are different points of view, but still
the main object of the House is the betterment of the country and the betterment
of our people. And so in the world you
are bound to have differences. America
is a continental country; we are a maritime
country. America is a vast country where
there must be divergencies of views. We
are a more or less compact country and able
to absorb the different races which go to
make the British race. America is successfully moving towards that goal. So
there are bound to be differences. I think
we can improve the position by recognising
that we can agree to differ, and that whilst
those differences in a minor degree might
have an effect on our relations if we did
not know each other better, we must put
up with those differences. Unless we can
get together, then I see ahead a poor
peace and perhaps a further disastrous

In the first place I want to say very
definitely that this is not an issue between
the Ministry of Finance and the Treasury
as some hon. Members seem to think.
The position briefly is this. If a local
authority or a number of local authorities wish to initiate a scheme which
requires them to exercise their borrowing
powers, and schemes for the supply of
water do require such borrowing, their
first step in war time, after the preparation of their plans and the approval of
them by the Ministry of Home Affairs,
is the approach, with that Ministry's
blessing, to the Capital Issues Committee
sitting in London who alone can authorise
the borrowing, in war time, of money by
local authorities or any other similar body
or even by private concerns.
The House must realise that the
borrowing of money in war time is controlled just as are so many commodities
and no amount of intervention by this
Government will affect that control any
more than we would succeed in increasing
the tea ration or the number of clothing
[coupons for Northern Ireland citizens.
Furthermore, that control extends to
borrowing in
banks or from
any
form whether from
Government
our Own
Loans Fund. It is a restriction on capital
borrowing whatever the source, and the
completeness of this control will
be
evident from the fact that even the
borrowings of the Northern Ireland
Government itself come under the
Committee's review.
The first thing the Capital Issues Committee, presided over by Lord Kennett,
requires to be satisfied about is the need
for the proposed expenditure in relation
to war purposes or, alternatively, that it
is an essential service despite war time
considerations. So far no approach has been
made by the local authorities concerned in
the North Down water scheme to the
Capital Issues Committee for the necessary borrowing powers and therefore,
even if I were able to announce to-day a
to
Government grant
generous
the
scheme, it would not of necessity lead to
its immediate execution as the balance of
the outlay would still have to be found by
a loan, the issue of which would be governed by the conditions I have outlined.

I appreciate that local authorities,
who I believe fully understand the
present position, would like to know in
advance what, if any, Government grant
they may expect towards this and similar
schemes-which incidentally will,
doubt, have to conform to some general
plan for Northern Ireland-so that they
can make their plans against the time
when the control, which is almost an
embargo, on local authorities' borrowings
is raised, and, as I have said, I hope to be
in a position to make a statement in the
near future on this particular aspect of
the problem. But no matter how early
I may be able to indicate a rate of grant,
it seems to me it can only facilitate the
preparation of schemes, the execution of
which will be undertaken as soon as possible after the war.
I appreciate also that hon. Members
interested in this project are bound to be
disappointed that it has had to be temporarily abandoned owing to the fact that,
because of the closing down of an aerodrome, its wartime character disappeared.
The position, of course, is that at the
instigation of our Government, local
authorities were prepared to meet the
extra expenditure necessary to convert a
purely wartime supply, inadequate for
civilian needs, into one which would be
of lasting benefit by the installation of a
larger pipe than purely service requirements demanded. This was a commonsense proposal which would save the
nation money in the long run, and as
Consolidated Fund Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Major Sinclair]
such might have commended itself to the
Capital Issues Committee. It was indeed
a proposal on much the same lines as we
have seen in our electrical development,
where advantage has been taken of war
industrial and other requirements, including in this case standby precautions, to
increase substantially our generating
capacity with an eye to the electrical
development of the Province after the
war.
As regards our general relations with
the Treasury which this question brings
into relief, while for my own part I am
quite willing to bear the gentle strictures
of the right hon. Member for Mid-Down,
I feel it would be wrong of me to allow
the impression to gain ground that our relations with the Treasury have worsened
in the least degree, or that we are less
financially independent than in the past.
In this respect the position remains the
same as it was when the financial administration of the Province was in the care of
the right hon. Gentleman. Any consultation which may be found desirable and
necessary arises from our acceptance. of the
principle of a parity of services unless
special conditions over here warrant a
departure.
Generally speaking, within the limits
covered by the term "comparable services," the discretion of the Ministry of
Finance cannot be called in question, and
I am satisfied, and hope the House will
be too, that the degree of consultation
which is called for from us under the
arrangements which my right hon. Friend
was able to make during his tenure of
office, is reasonable and is one to which no
right thinking person could possibly
object. The very fact that we are part
of the United Kingdom requires from us
a continuation of the closest possible
co-operation with the Imperial Treasury.
I fully endorse what the right hon.
Member for Mid Down has said in regard
to the general aura of sweet reasonableness which surrounds the approaches of
my right hon. Friend, the Chancellor of
the Exchequer, to the proposals affecting
Northern Ireland which have been developed with him from time to time, and
I am glad to be able to inform the House
that consultations with the treasury about
the pattern of our post-war financial relations are being carried out in an atmosphere of helpfulness and understanding.
I beg to move.

I am not going to discuss the matter at

In connection with the Ministry of
Education there is one thing I want to
call attention to. I think we have
developed in the Ministry a bureaucratic
domination about which we will have to
do something. There has certainly been
an increasing tendency towards bureaucratic domination in the Ministry, and,
in my opinion, the proof of it is this. We
have the Education Act of 1923 which
provides for the setting up of an Advisory
Council to advise the Ministry on all
matters of education. There are several,
provisions in regard to this Council and
the final provision is that the Council
shall be summoned by the Minister and
shall meet twice each year and at such
other times as the Ministry may consider
necessary. That is definitely set out in
the Act. In reply to a question put by
me to-day the Prime Minister said that
the original Council was set up in 1925,
and consisted of a number of persons,
some of whom are dead. He said that the
Council was reconstituted in 1928 and he
gave the names of the members. He also
stated that it was last reconstituted in
1932 and he gave the names of the members again. It last met in November,
1932, and the Prime Minister went on to
make this statement in his answer:—
The Council legally ceased to exist
in February, 1935, on the termination
of the three-year period for which it
was reconstituted in February, 1932.
Since that date there has been no
Advisory Council.

that the Government had no

Therefore, under the Act the Minister

by repealing that "Act.
Yet we are told now that the Council

Apparently bureaucracy is going to run

I say it is quite wrong for anyone, to tell

to exist, for it cannot legally cease so long

Apparently the bureaucrats, these mighty
and majestic nabobs in the Ministry of

contempt, and they are going to defy us
and the Acts of Parliament which we

Personally, I will not submit to any Act

of Parliament of this House being defied.
People are prosecuted day and daily, and

turned out by the square yard day and

consideration.
new

The Member for South Down inspired

He told us how far we are behind Great

It is not true.
over
The other night a gentleman, one of
those so-called experts that come
here from across the water at a big salary,
gave a lecture in Belfast, and it was the
same old story: Belfast was a small hell
and nothing was right. I see very
fine men and women and very fine
girls in Belfast. The Minister of
Agriculture smiles when I say that. I
do not know where the gentleman who
gave the lecture was brought up, but
three like him would not make one man.
He was a most miserable wretch, and was
certainly a very bad advertisement for
what he was talking about.
We were told to-day that we should
go step by step with England in the
matter of religious education. No, we
will not. There are no Anglo-Catholics
in Northern Ireland that I ever heard of.
We have our own religious education in
accordance with what our belief may be.
I would not change it for the Anglo-
Catholic religion, not by a long way,
under no circumstances. They can have
it for themselves in England if they want
to. I do not believe the people know
exactly what they are talking about when
they advocate going step by step. I never
very much religious fervour in
England. It is to be found in some places
like the south of London and Wales, but
not in the majority of places.
saw
I do not want to follow in that direction. I want our own religion, whatever
that is I do not care what it is-taught
in the schools. I do not want to go step
by step until I know where I am stepping
to and what I am stepping on. I do not
want to shout a thing because everybody.
is shouting, without thinking what it is
about. I do not want Lord Halifax's type
of religion at all. I am utterly opposed to
it. He could get a meeting composed of
16,000 people in the Albert Hall in
London. I know the telegram that was
sent from that meeting which was presided over by the then Bishop of London.
I also leave that at that.
We should carry on our own traditions
and not always be running down our own
bit of country. It is not necessary to run
it down. We can hold our own for our
numbers in any part of the world. In
other places no men rise higher than
Irishmen. The present Prime Minister of
Australia I know by his name-Curtinis an Irishman, but I am not so sure about
the Prime Minister of New Zealand. I
think he is Scottish. If we carry on and
do our own business in our own way
without always looking across the water
we would get on far better.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

The House met at Two of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
ORAL ANSWERS TO
QUESTIONS.
Belfast Prison.
HUNGER STRIKE
1. Mr. THOMAS CAMPBELL asked
the Minister of Home Affairs whether he
can state the present condition of the
three men in Belfast Jail, who have been
on hunger-strike for the past month; and
whether these three men have taken any
milk since their hunger-strike began
".
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Mr. Lowry): I have nothing to add to
the reply which I gave to the hon. and
learned Member on the 16th instant.
With regard to the last part of the
question, milk is provided for these men,
and whether they take it or not is a
matter entirely for themselves.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Can the Minister
say whether or not the men in fact have
taken the milk?
Mr. LOWRY: To the best of my knowledge. No one has actually seen them
take it, but the milk is placed in the cells
and in the course of time the receptacles
are removed minus the milk.
DEMAND FOR POLITICAL
TREATMENT.
2. Mr. THOMAS CAMPBELL asked
the Minister of Home Affairs whether he
can state if before the hunger-strike in
Belfast Jail began many complaints were
made to the Governor of the conditions in
the jail and of the victimisation of certain
prisoners; whether these circumstances
were the primary cause of the strike;
whether the following statement was delivered to the Governor in advance of the
strike: "In furtherance of our demands
for political treatment and in protest
against our continued victimisation and
against the intolerable conditions existing
in Belfast Prison we the Irish Republican
Prisoners declare a hunger-strike"; and
whether he will institute an impartial
inquiry into the conditions in the jail.
Mr. LOWRY: The answer to the first
part of the question is in the negative.
The request or demand for so-called
political treatment is one which the Government will not concede, and I am fully
satisfied from reports which I have received that there is no justification for a
formal inquiry into the conditions in the
prison.
Education.
NUMBERS OF PUPILS IN
ELEMENTARY SCHOOLS.
3. Mr. THOMAS CAMPBELL asked
the Prime Minister whether he can state
the number of enrolled pupils in the
public elementary schools to-day compared with the number, in the year the
Ministry of Education was established;
the number of Catholic pupils enrolled at
that date and the number enrolled to-day;
and the corresponding enrolment as
regards Protestant pupils.
The MINISTER OF EDUCATION
(Lieut. - Colonel Hall - Thompson): The
total number of pupils enrolled in public
elementary schools on 31st December,
1922, in the first year of the Ministry was
198,385, of whom 68,959 were Roman
Catholic and 129,426 were Protestant. It
is not possible at this stage to give the
corresponding figures on 31st December,
1943, but on 31st December, 1942, the
corresponding figures were 184,755,
71,200 and 113,550.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Does the right hon.
Gentleman regard it as a matter of no
consequence that there are to-day almost
14,000 fewer children in the elementary
schools in Northern Ireland than there
were when the Government took up office
20 years ago?
Lieut.-Colonel HALL-THOMPSON: It
suggests to me that the income of the
average person in Northern Ireland has
benefited to such an extent that the
secondary schools are now overcrowded.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Does the right hon.
Gentleman say there is an influx of
14,000, or anything like it, into the
secondary schools of Northern Ireland?'
Lieut.-Colonel HALL - THOMPSON:
No, sir.

7. Mr. THOMAS CAMPBELL asked

the number of pupils now receiving instruction in Irish in the elementary and
the secondary schools.
Lieut.-Colonel
HALL-THOMPSON:
The number of pupils receiving instruction in Irish in public elementary schools
on 31st December, 1943, was 12,021.
In the present school year Irish is being
taught in 30 recognised secondary schools.
There are 5,158 pupils on the rolls of

body in the matter of housing in this

have the honour to move is:
That in the opinion of this House
the Government should take immediate
steps to provide accommodation for the

that no time should be lost in putting
brick yards in production, preparing
sites and matters necessary to the building on a large scale of houses at a rent
which working people can afford to pay,
and generally to take a more active
and practical interest in the whole
question of housing.

with the notorious housing scandal of

air attack on the city of Belfast. Most

the Government have done in the matter
is to set up various committees.
