After listening to the speech of the hon.
Member for Shankill the thought struck
me, as no doubt it struck others, that the
question of the housing of the Ulster
people is one that should be above party
politics. It is a human question we are
studying. We are trying to bring homes
and happiness to the people, and yet the
hon. Member tries to draw a red herring
across the path by bringing in politics.
The Housing problem should not be the
shuttlecock of party politics. Why should
it? No Member has been more critical
than I have been during the last sixteen
years, but I am surprised that the hon.
Member should make the statement that
the Government has done nothing in this
matter. That is wrong; it is not true. I
have figures here showing that the Government gave.almost three million pounds in
subsidies towards building houses up to
the time the war broke out. It might
enlighten the hon. Member to know also
that almost 37,000 houses were built
under the Government's subsidy scheme.
It is wrong for any Member of Parliament to come here, at a time when we are
fighting the greatest war in history for
freedom and liberty, and attack the
Government for doing nothing in this
matter. Instead of doing that he should
be trying to help the Government to carry
out its great obligations. He knows perfectly well that as regards steel and

greatest scheme of social reconstruction
in the history of our time. It is
going to involve the expenditure of
£50,000,000, and in my view it is far
too big a task to be handled by 50 or 60
different authorities.
"
One other figure I intended to give,
but it slipped me for the moment. The
Minister of Finance was good enough
to-day to get for me the figures of the
number of people, who have been married.
since the beginning of 1940. There have
been 43,575 marriages in Northern Ireland since the beginning of the war. We
know that there. are numbers of those
young married people who are living
under conditions which are far from ideal
and which are not conducive either to
the continuance of married happiness or
to the proper upbringing of the children.
The vast majority of them-amongst the
working people certainly-in the city are
being forced to live with their parents-inlaw. I have never urged, I do not urge
and do not believe in any large scale
building programme during the continuance of the German war. I think
can employ our time between now and
the happy days when that war comes to
an end very much better than by hastily
building. We can employ our time very
much better by making careful and
detailed preparation so that when that
day comes we shall be able to make an
immediate start.
we
Under our present system the responsibility for housing rests upon somewhere
between 60 and 70 local authorities. I
cannot give the exact figure, but I know
it is about 60. Only two or three of
those authorities, like the Corporation of
Belfast, the Corporation of Derry; and
the Borough of Bangor, have got a
technical staff adequate to handle this
problem. The great majority of the
authorities in smaller local and rural districts employ engineers-perfectly competent gentlemen-but they are generally
engineers who are carrying on a private
practice and who do the local authority
work in their spare time.
I yield to no man in my admiration for the work of the local
authorities in this country. I think if
you take local government over the
United Kingdom it is probably the
highest achievement of democracy anywhere in the world. Our local government services throughout the United
Kingdom have brought our people to a
pitch which has not been attained anywhere else. I want to make it perfectly
clear that in anything I say to-day no
criticism of any local authority is meant
or intended. I believe they do their work
admirably, and I believe they do it much.
better than it can be done under any
other system, but I think the job we are
giving them is too big for them.
never
If you put this housing burden upon
the local authorities, and if the machine
breaks down through having imposed
upon it a burden which it was
designed to bear, the blame will not rest
upon the machine, but on us who put
upon it a burden which was far too great
for it. The scheme involves an expenditure of £40,000,000, £50,000,000 or
£60,000,000. It involves the employment of very large numbers of skilled
workers, and we shall certainly for some
years to come have a very definite shortage of skilled workers in certain trades,
such as bricklayers, plasterers, plumbers,
and electricians. Many of them are still
in the Forces. Many of them will not
be back for years.
We do not know the
date of demobilisation, but it is almost
inevitable that we shall have during the
early years of reconstruction a shortage of
skilled labour. It involves the acquisition of considerable tracts of land. I
gave the figures for Birmingham. For
50,000 houses alone they required 5,800
odd acres.
It will involve the purchase of an unbelievable quantity of building materials.
Here again during the early years difficulties of supply will meet us on every hand,
and, to use a popular phrase, it is almost
inevitable that we shall have bottlenecks
of a very serious character. The result
will be that for years, if there is not
central direction to designate priority,
you will find local authorities in various
parts of the country starting their housing schemes, and when they get to a
certain stage they will be held up by the
lack of some essential parts for building.
Building will stop and costs will increase.
Speed is one of the first essentials of cheap
Housing
Housing
22 MARCH 1944
1.
building. To my mind, for the supply
and direction and flow of material for
these schemes some central direction is
absolutely essential. I honestly believe.
that if we do not have it within three
or four years our whole scheme will be in
a state of chaos.
The scheme will involve-and again I
call Birmingham to aid the making of
at least 100 miles of road. Surely the
central direction of some road-making
plant and equipment is essential. You
cannot start to have over 50 different
road-making authorities in connection
with your sites. Then we come to what
is perhaps the most important thing of
all. We have moved thousands of miles
from the building which we know has
given rise to the sordid conditions of
housing in this country. We have got
clean away from it. Architecture, some
form of aesthetic design, has at last come
into its own. Over the whole housing
schemes of Birmingham, involving
50,000 houses, in no single case has the
density of 15 houses to the acre been
exceeded, and the average density runs
to about 11 houses to the acre. There is
no doubt in my mind that unless we get
skilled direction and government in this
matter we shall have all sorts of different
plans and designs, differing according to
the lights of the various local authorities,
and we will not get anything like uniformity of practice.
Some of our local authorities will start
to build houses, and they will be 15 to

years behind the times when they are
built. I think there is the strongest case,
and I am putting the case now, for the
creation of a central authority. I do not
suggest that the Ministry should make
the decision now or that the House
should be asked to vote upon this. I am
trying to make the case for the establishment of some central, directing authority,
not to build houses at all, but to coordinate the efforts of local authorities
and guide them along the paths that they
ought to travel, to give them encouragement, advice and assistance, and,
generally, to see that the scheme which
we shall ultimately produce is worthy of
the money we spend on it, and is the last
word in housing. We are going to build
for 60 or 70 years. This country cannot
afford another housing scheme like this
for at least 60 or 70 years, and it is of
vital importance that we should start off
with the most up-to-date type of house
in design, plan, and layout, and not start.
off our houses, as I said a minute ago,
with a design 15 or 20 years behind the
times.
It was suggested in the speech of the
mover of the original Motion that the
question of brickworks should be looked
into. It is part of a much larger scheme.
I have asked in this House, and much
better informed people than I have
asked, a question to which no reasoned
answer has yet been given.
At the present moment no local authority will
acquire sites, because the finance has not
been settled, but any central authority
could be absolutely certain that a very
large building programme is coming all
over the Six Counties. If we have a
central authority, that central authority
should be empowered on behalf of the
local authorities to acquire immediately
a considerable number of sites upon which
preparatory works could be begun now.
The question I asked, and I ask now
for a reasoned answer to it and the
House is entitled to receive a reasoned
answer is, what is the difficulty in here
and now selecting a number of sites for
future building operations, laying out the
roads, and providing the essential services, in order that when the day comes
when building can be begun we can begin
there, and not begin by putting the bulldozer on the land and waiting for seven
or eight months before beginning to lay
the foundations. The time between now
and the end of the German war could be
usefully employed in the preparation of
a considerable number of sites. I personally cannot see, and have never heard
any answer to that question.
If you set up a central housing authority that authority can acquire the land.
It can have finance found from Government sources in the meantime, and so
soon as building schemes begin there can
be an allocation of the cost as between
Government and local authority, but the
original finances can be provided by the
Government. I would like to know what
the answer to that is. Everybody wants
to see a start really made with this
scheme. There is no question about that.
We have here what they have not got in
England. We have a pool of labour. It
differs from week to week, but it is avail-
Housing
Housing
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[MB. Warnock]
able for this purpose. We have many of
the materials which will be required for
this purpose, though not all, but we have
the materials which will be required for
road making. I venture to suggest that
the House should get from a responsible
Minister some indication as to why the
preparatory work should not
be commenced at once.
There is one other matter. When I was
speaking on the Housing Bill some little
time ago in this House I suggested, in
regard to the acquisition of land, that a
ceiling should be fixed to the price, and
I suggested the 1939 valuation. I intended, as I indicated to the House,
moving an Amendment when the Bill
next came before the House. Unfortunately on that day I was engaged in
a lawsuit at the court, and judges do not
like you getting up and saying, "Pardon
me, but I have another engagement elsewhere." The result was that I arrived in
this House ten minutes after the Bill had
been passed. Since I spoke in the House
I have received ample confirmation of
what I then said. I indicated then that
if you have five sites within the city, and
the local authority buys one, it
immediately puts up against itself the
price of the other four sites. When it
buys the second site it puts up the prices
of sites three, four and five, and when it
buys the third site and leaves only two,
it virtually creates a monopoly of those
two.
In 1923, when the Birmingham Corporation bought sites, it was able to buy
those sites at a capital cost of £15 per
house. In 1930 they had to pay £32, or
more than 100 per cent. more. I have
the exact figures here, and the price was
£15 in 1923, and £32 in 1930. Birmingham did what we are going to by buying
up sites A, B, C and D, and pushing the
price of D up by 110 per cent. Why
should we do that? Establish your
central authority, designate throughout
the country the land you want for your
housing schemes, and say that that is
housing land, and the price to be paid for
it is the price prevailing now. Do not
start buying up land around the Malone
Road and Ballygomartin and find yourself left with only five or six sites which
the valuer must value at the then price.
The arbitrator must make his award on
the prevailing value of the land, and he
cannot take into consideration the fact
that we ourselves have put up the price.
You can buy land to-day by arbitration at a reasonable figure, but as the
supply gets less and the demand increases
the price will go up, and the landlord
will get a figure that does not represent
anything he has done to increase the
value of the land. He gets a price that
has been created, and fictitiously created,
by the demand of the local authority.
That is a vicious principle, and this
Government ought to bring in legislation
at the very earliest moment to ensure that
a landlord gets a fair price for his land,
and nothing more. I would have moved
an amendment to the Housing Bill had I
been here, but unfortunately I arrived
a few minutes too late.
I have only two other matters I want
to deal with. The first is that I would
far rather see housing provided by private
enterprise, if possible. I believe we will
get a certain number of houses built by
private enterprise, but the economic
system under which we live is such that
the ordinary working man cannot build
his own house. But in so far as private
enterprise fails to provide houses-and it
has failed in the past, and failed miserably the State, must take upon itself the
obligation. My central. housing authority
would not interfere in any way with
private enterprise, except that it might
help private enterprise on the question of
materials. It would not have any
authority over private enterprise, or interfere with it in any way. It would
deal only with houses to be provided out
of public funds. I want to make that
quite clear.
What will ultimately turn out to be
one of its most important functions is
this. I am not being critical of many of
our smaller local authorities when I say
that they are composed very largely of
the small shopkeeper people who have
small ideas on money, and I can visualise
a great deal of difficulty-and I appreciate the difficulty in getting the
smaller local authorities to embark upon
housing schemes of a considerable size
which will necessarily involve considerable
additions to the rates. I think that is
perfectly natural, but if we assume that
houses have got to be built, then your
central authority will have to take upon
itself this function of directing, or, if
-
Housing
Housing
22 MARCH 1944
necessary, taking over housing in areas
where the local authorities are unwilling
to accept the burden.
Take, for example, the. Bincastle urban
district council. It decides, as it is
entitled to decide, that it will build
eight houses, and 80 are necessary.
Under the present system, I do not
know how they could be forced to build
80 houses. Is this House and the Government prepared to say that only eight
houses are to be built? If it is not,
how are the additional 72 to be provided?
It appears to me that it will be necessary
to have some authority which shall lay
down at least the minimum number, and
that it will be prepared to undertake to
build that minimum number if the local
authority is not prepared to do it.
I could go on, but I would only weary
the House in giving arguments in favour
of the establishment of some such authority. I recognise that there are arguments the other way.
I have done nothing more than try to open for discussion a subject which is worthy of discussion. I do not suggest that because I
put these views forward there is not
another side to the question. I think we
ought to hear the other side. The reasons、
why there should not be a central direction should be indicated, and I hope hon..
Members will think about this question.
We are going to undertake an enormous
adventure. We are going to put it into
the hands of 50 or 60 different authorities, and unless we have some central
authority directing and co-ordinating
their efforts I would be very much afraid
that within a short time we will get into
a state of chaos. Therefore I recommend
to the House the idea of some central
authority to guide and direct the efforts
of the local authorities.

Well, what are the facts? I know the

1s a week. You never hear what happens

Then they came to me and showed me the

people at a cheaper rate. Thus, the

on a balanced basis. The more houses
built, it is reasonable to assume, the
nearer we arrive at a solution of the
problem. One thousand houses at 25s a
week without subsidy or 17s with subsidy
free are certainly better than no houses
at all.

The type of house that I suggest can
be built now, similar to the two which I
have almost completed, can be built with
the materials that are now available. I
wish the Government would tell
whether the materials really are available
for the 750 houses proposed to be erected.
Is the material available for 1,000 houses?
I should like to have this matter cleared
up. For the type of house I suggest most
of the materials can be procured in
Belfast. The system of the houses has
been devised with a view to effecting saving in materials, of which there is a
shortage, and of which there is likely to
be a shortage for a year or two. Timber
has been eliminated except for the doors.
Only 7 cwt. of steel per house is
needed against one ton in the ordinary
house. In 100 houses of my type 125
standards of timber are saved, and 50
tons of steel would be saved compared
with a normal house of the same size.
Expressed in words of war effort, the
cargo space saved would
would equal the
victualling of an army of 15,000 men for
two weeks in addition to supplying each
man with uniform. The walls of the
houses are 11-inch cavity brick. All
floors will be covered with cork tiles. One
will be unaware of the concrete floors
which have been so much criticised. The
loss from fire even in air raids would be
small. My two houses have saved the
war effort in cargo space the equivalent

vacancies occur in any of their Departments in Northern Ireland the positions
will be filled through his Department by

Grant): My Ministry was not asked to
submit candidates for the vacancy in
question.
With regard to the last part of the
question, in submitting candidates for
vacancies notified by Imperial Departments in Northern Ireland my Ministry
gives a preference to ex-Service men.
Mr. MINFORD: Should the right
hon. Gentleman not make inquiries as to
why a request should not be made to him
by the Ministry of Food when Northern
Ireland appointments are being made?
Mr. GRANT: Invariably the Divisional
Food Office has co-operated very closely
in the past with
past with the appointments
register of the Department, and has taken

HOUSING.
Resumed Debate on Amendment.
Order read for resuming Adjourned
Debate on Amendment to Question
[22nd March], "That in the opinion of
this House the Government should take
immediate steps to provide accommoda-
Housing
Housing
HOUSE OF COMMONS
tion for the wants of thousands of homeless people, that no time should be lost
in putting brick yards in production,
preparing sites and matters necessary to
the building on a large scale of houses at
a rent which working people can afford
to pay, and generally to take a more
active and practical interest in the whole
question of housing."-(Mr. Nixon.)
Which Amendment was: To leave out
all the words after the word "That" and
insert:
"This House views with concern the
large number of persons in the Province
who are inadequately housed, that it
supports the Government in all steps that
it is taking to alleviate the situation and
it impresses upon the Government the
vital necessity of further developing such
measues in the widest and most effective
manner possible, with the object of
securing, at the earliest possible moment
and on a large scale the provision of
houses at a rent which working people
can pay."-(Mr. Minford.)
Question again proposed, "That the
words proposed to be left out stand part
of the Question.'
""
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Mr. Lowry): Before I begin to deal
with the several observations in the
speeches of the Mover and Seconder of
the original Motion and the Mover of
the Amendment I. should like to state
once more in very broad terms the extent
of this problem and to touch in some
measure on what are the causes of the
problem. Before the war started, the
shortage of houses in Northern Ireland
was 50,000 in comparison with England
and Wales, taking a population basis.
In England and Wales there
11,400,000 houses, and
houses, and in Northern
Ireland there were 320,000 houses. As I
were
say, on a population basis the shortage
was 50,000 houses, therefore there ought
to have been 370,000 houses in Northern
Ireland.
Those figures really relate to the period
from about 1937. Of course obsolescence
was going on in housing, and then we
have some immediate and particular
causes, namely the influx of people into
Belfast, and the fact that more people
are in daily employment-I do not speak
of an ephemeral matter like strikes-than
at any other time in the history of Northern Ireland. Then came the air raids
in April and May, 1941. There was also
an increase in Belfast's population. Of
the 23,000 by which the population had
increased between 1926 and 1936, 98 per
cent. was in the city of Belfast alone, so
it is clear that so far as this city itself
is concerned the problem was formidable
even before the war and before the air
raids.
As to the cause of this, there was a
great difference in the aid given in
England and Wales and Northern Ireland between the two wars: The reasons
for that are doubtless far more familiar
to Members of this House who were Members long before I was than to me, but
I will take just one date beginning in
1930 that deals with the difference in
Government aid. In Great Britain in
1932 the subsidy for urban housing was
£7 10s house
per per annum for 40 years;*
there was a slum clearance of £2 5s per
person displaced for 40 years; agricultural housing was £11 per house per
annum for 40 years. In Northern Ireland there was an urban subsidy of £25
per house; there was nothing for slum
clearance, and there was nothing with
regard to agricultural housing. The
figures differ for England and Wales,
except that the serious back of urban
housing had been broken by 1933 The
grants for slum clearance, for flats and
for agricultural housing continued down
to 1937. In 1938 there was nothing for
urban housing, but slum clearance went
from £5 10s to £6 10s per house per
annum for 40 years In 1938 agricultural
housing was provided for here by 40 per
cent. of the loan charges.

I am not seeking to put the blame on
anybody, either central Government or
local authorities, in this matter, because
I venture to say that there must have
been some good and sufficient reason. I
should think that it was financial
stringency alone that permitted Northern
Ireland to fall so far behind. Of course,
it eventuated in certain results which to
my mind were inevitable. Between 1918
and 1938 in England some 308,000
slum dwellings were demolished; the
corresponding figure in Northern Ireland would have been about 8,000.
Some 4,000,000 houses were built in
England between the two wars. Here
there were roughly 40,000 built between
Government-aided schemes-as the Member for Antrim mentioned yesterday be-
Housing
Housing
23 MARCH 1944
tween 37,000 and 38,000-and a further
3,000 or so under the Soldiers' and
Sailors' Trust. To deal with that shortage is the problem with which we are
confronted to-day.
Again let me say I am not seeking to
apportion blame to anybody. Those who
were Members of the House long before
I became one must know the circumstances far better than I do, but I think
the real reason was financial stringency,
that the Government of the day
thought perhaps it was far more
important to keep people alive by unemployment benefit, by relief schemes and
so forth than to endeavour to tackle this
very difficult problem. Yesterday an
appeal was made by the noble Lord, who
is the Member for Bloomfield, and by
the hon. and learned Member for St.
Anne's. They could see no reason why
the Motion of the hon. Member for
Woodvale should not be accepted. The
Member for St. Anne's is quite well
aware of what an innuendo means, and
it is obvious that no Government, especially when the question of its guilt was
concerned, could say "Amen" to the concluding words of the Motion "and
generally to take a more active and
practical interest in the whole question of
housing."
I hope to satisfy the House that this
Government have taken an active and
practical interest in housing and that in
so far at any rate as these concluding
words in the Motion are concerned this is
a matter in which we could not acquiesce.
I have no doubt that the hon. and learned
Member for St. Anne's was not just
thinking of what the innuendo was, but
I am perfectly certain had he been asked
to put a very serious implication on it in
another capacity he could have done so in
a way that would have made my hair
stand on end.
Another matter as to the immediate
cause was the failure of the evacuation
scheme after the two severe air-raids. I
am not speaking of people who left the
city in April and May, 1941, and provided for themselves, but of those for
whom the Government as agents for the
Ministry of Health were responsible. At
one time the number was 67,800 persons
for whom the Government were paying.
They were provided with places in which
to live. The scheme was a failure.
There were many causes operating to
make it a failure. One thing that seems
to be certain is that you will never get
urban bred people inured to living in the
country. One of the commonest complaints was not about the question of
convenience to the church or the school,
but to the serious drawback to country
residence that you had to go three miles
to a picture house. Those who are members of the Advisory Defence Committee
know that from time to time I reported
a gradual return to the city until to-day
there are fewer than 10,000 people outside Belfast under the Government's
evacuation scheme, and of that 10,000
more than 6,000 are people who left
Great Britain; so that of the 67,800 for
whom we were once responsible we are
responsible for fewer than 4,000 to-day.
-
When one remembers the complete destruction of nearly 4,000 houses, one can
see that when that vast population comes
back here again there is bound to be overcrowding, a terrible shortage, terrible inconvenience and most unhealthy conditions. But I do feel that if these people
had been content to put up with the want
of amenities and going to a picture house
the problem would not be so acute as it is
at the present moment. As to what the
Government that is, the previous
Government did endeavour to do, I may
say it was under their auspices that the
Planning Advisory Board was set up. I
know that the word planning seems to
rouse the worst passions in mankind that
can be stirred up, but experience has
shown-and I refer not to matters of
housing or such like but to everything in
this connection-that unless there is
planning there is going to be waste and
there are going to be perhaps not very
good results at the end.
The hon. Member for Woodvale,
alluded, as he has alluded more than
once in this house, to the serious housing
scandal in Belfast that occurred over 18
years ago. I took an active part in that
investigation, and I have no hesitation in
main
saying that the
cause of that
scandal was not the dishonesty of one
official in particular or the dishonesty of
a number of tradesmen, merchants and
others, but the opportunity that arose
through the fact that the Belfast Corporation, confronted with a sudden
emergency after the war of supplying
houses, had not a well-laid systematic
plan; they had not the staff or the
Housing
Housing
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Lowry]
machinery, and the consequence was that
when people saw the opportunity of enriching themselves, well, they did not
resist the temptation and did so. That
to my mind was the main cause not the
iniquity of two or three persons, but the
very fact that the Corporation were not
prepared for the functions that were
taken up by them, and that they endeavoured to do in a hurry with improvisation and with an inadequate staff
what should have been tackled only after
serious and careful preparation.
Mr. NIXON: Mr. Megaw gave the
decision and he knew all about it.
Mr. LOWRY: The hon. Member says
Mr. Megaw, afterwards Mr. Justice
Megaw, gave the decision. I, too, took
a very active part in that matter, and
although that end of the matter is not
stressed very often, counsel who appear
in a case and afterwards appear for other
individuals who are involved, get a sidelight that never emerges at all in what
transpires in the investigation. It does
seem perfectly plain that if there is not
good planning and foresight there must
be waste. In order to prevent anything
like that happening in the future the
Planning Advisory Board was set up, and
despite all sneers to the contrary it has
done, and is doing, good work. The
Planning Commission, whose function is
very much misunderstood, are technical
men, and what is sought to be evolved is
a plan for the entire Province into which
every local authority shall fit its plan.
Already it has made a most valuable
report on the subject of water. No
similar survey has yet been made across
the Channel.
True it is that just last week the
Association of Water Providers issued a
most valuable document, and I am very
glad to say that speaking of Northern
Ireland therein they recommend the
adoption of certain of the Commission's
suggestions, but subject to and in accordance with the report of the Planning
Advisory Board. In addition to that
there is a committee whose report I am
expecting any day-two reports in fact
will be out in the near future, one on
housing and another on the location of
industry and transport and roads. The
Water Report does not appear to me to
have interested either Members of this
House or of the local authorities as it
ought to have done. It has been
published almost completely in the newspapers and it is out a considerable number
of weeks now.
I wonder that anybody
can dispute the question of planning at
this time of day.
That is the manner in which it is sought
to tackle this great problem—in a
systematic fashion. One of the most
valuable things carried out is a survey
of the housing position in the Province
at the moment. I know this is a thing
that has excited the derision of the
hon. Member for Woodvale. It
falls into two stages. Some of the
visitors doubtless were employees of the
Belfast Corporation, because the work
was divided into halves in urban districts.
The urban districts carried out the survey
and the matter of accommodation and
the state and condition of houses was
looked after by this Ministry. A similar
survey was made through selected slices
of the rural districts. The urban districts
have been fully reviewed. The position as
revealed in Belfast is very disquieting, as
one would expect knowing all that has
gone before. On standards of overcrowding alone, the percentage of overcrowding in the city of Belfast is 26.8.
The percentage of overcrowding for
England and Wales, including London,
is 7. Taking comparable cities the
city of Manchester has 0.4 per cent.,
the city of Leeds 0.25 per cent., and
Nottingham 1.1 per cent. And yet the
chief architect of the Ministry was criticised because of a speech which he made
in Belfast and which was reported in a
few lines. How could anyone do otherwise with almost 27 per cent. of overcrowding?
That survey is going to prove of the
very greatest value as I shall clearly
demonstrate before I sit down. The fact
that no detailed statement on housing
policy has been made is not because we
have failed to take an active and practical interest in the matter. It is a matter
of the very greatest difficulty with the
changing. position so far as the war is
concerned from day to day to make a
pronouncement that can be carried out to
its last detail when dealing with the local
authorities. Remember that this problem
will fall naturally into three parts. There
is first the question of war-time housing;
Housing
Housing
23 MARCH 1944
secondly, emergency housing; and thirdly,
the post-war programme. The war-time
housing is a small scheme that we have
endeavoured to initiate at the present
time. It deals with a limited number of
houses which are of a permanent character,
and will always serve a useful purpose,
but
are designed in accordance with economy
standards. They have been christened
austerity houses. But it is quite clear
that you cannot during war time have
houses of exactly the same, type as you
could have pre-war or, as one would hope,
post-war. Emergency housing is the provision of purely temporary housing,
offering shelter and comfort that are
tolerable for a short time. Such housing
cannot be permitted to remain for more
than a limited period. I know that after
the last war
one municipality entered
very largely into this emergency housing
and created a most frightful slum.
Now and again I hear suggestions made
about utilising Nissen huts for a temporary purpose. In the last three years
we have had good experience of Nissen
huts. Nissen huts for evacuation purposes were built in different parts of the
country to take the first brunt, supposing
there was another air raid. They costthe money was provided by the Ministry
of Health-£750,000. They have been
up now a matter approaching three years,
and although they have not been subject
to the wear and tear that they would have
been, the matter of their maintenance in
good condition is a serious item. And as
an emergency measure we do not think it
desirable, or possible, or practicable.
Certainly the places where they have been
put up were far away from anywhere,
because we were guided therein by the
advice of the Air Ministry. Furthermore, hon. Members may have observed
that on a similar question, and in similar
circumstances, the Minister of Health in
England, and the Secretary of State, in
Scotland have with one voice condemned
the proposition.
Emergency housing is a difficult problem. First of all there is the financing
of it. It must be cleared away. I should
not give it a life. of more than five years.
It must be cheap to provide, and it should
be so placed that any roads, water or
sewers will be used for permanent
housing. At the best it presents this
great difficulty, that very low rents must
be charged for it. It is therefore impossible to make it pay its way, and there
would be grave risk, in fact certainty, of
serious financial loss falling upon the
local authority before expenditure on
proper housing came to be made.
These three forms of housing, whether
war-time housing, 'emergency housing or
post-war housing, must all be considered
together and an endeavour must be made
to work them in and interlace them so
that the greatest possible provision can
be made at the most reasonable cost.
Although it may seem to hon. Members
quite an easy thing, it is by no means
easy. Post-war housing must, as far as
possible, be provided with sewers, water,
etcetera, and if this is to be done at a
reasonable cost, the principle must be to
bring the houses to the services rather
than bring the services to the houses.
This means planning. What is to be.
done? How are the local authorities to
be encouraged? There is a circular ready
in draft, and I am only waiting for one
piece of information before it is issued.
The obvious things, like preparing sites,
streets, sewers, supplying water, gas, or
electricity, or both-really obvious things
like that do not come from that side of
the House with all the novelty and pleasure of surprise. I have been thinking
of very little else for the last two years.
But one cannot make promises.
The first thing a local authority asks
in these matters is "How much??' and it
is no good trying to feed local authorities
with airy promises. Far too many
promises, in my judgment, have been
made elsewhere, and if only one-tenth of
them are realised, then you will see this
brave new world. It is repeatedly urged
that even if there are no materials for
building houses the Government. might
encourage and assist local authorities to
acquire land and get ready, so that as
soon as materials do become available
houses would be put up with the least
possible delay. I understand it seems to
hon. Members that we have been ignoring
that, since no steps have been taken. That
is very far from the case. Action on
these lines is not as simple as it may
seem. There are many matters concerning which local authorities feel they have
to be given information before we can
proceed. We have been placing ourselves
in a position to give that information..
Housing
Housing
HOUSE OF COMMONS
!
[Mr. Lowry]
I regret that one most important aspect
of the matter remains unsettled. I hope
it will be settled one way or the other
shortly.
This outstanding question is the amount
of the subsidy that local authorities may
expect to receive for post-war housing
schemes. If this were determined there
is the further question of whether some
part of it might be paid in respect of
sites. I am unable to give the exact percentage, but this much I will venture to
say here and now. So far as one can
reasonably judge one could, I think,
safely hope that any subsidy would not be
less than the subsidy already arranged to
be given to the city of Belfast for its
small war-time programme, and I hope it
will be more. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.)
Mr. BROWN: For country as well as
the towns?
Mr. LOWRY: In the circular which
we have prepared and which is ready but
for one particular, I had hoped it would
have been possible to name the subsidy
with definiteness, but that is not possible although everything points to a
quick decision being arrived at. But I
think one can safely say this, that for
the acquisition of the site, for sewering,
for providing roads, and for the necessary amenities you may reckon that you
will get a fair percentage of the ultimate
subsidy. Now there is fair material upon
which to go. As to the site, taking it
over all and having it fixed, levelled and
sewered, streets made, water, gas, electricity laid on, two committees at
different times have sat on that one of
them was called the Hay Committee and
the other is easily remembered, the May
Committee and their figures were very
much alike something between £60 and
£70. Now I should think an offer for this
purpose of 15 per cent. to 20 per cent.
of the subsidy paid on account ought to
encourage the local authorities to take
steps which will place them in a position
to go ahead.
Hon. Members may have noticed that
quite recently the Minister of Health in
England envisaged a programme of
300,000 houses in the two years after the
war. Our calculation based, on population is that our share for that time would
be 10,000 houses, 5,000 a year. I may
say nothing like that was done in the
years after the last war. How we think
of approaching that is this. Using the
survey that is made we could go to each
urban authority and point out to them
what the survey disclosed as their shortage. I take, for example, that go-ahead
town of Lisburn, which is most active in
this matter, I am very glad to say. Their
shortage would appear from this to be
1,326 houses. We should consult with
the urban council there and ask how this
coincides with their views and from their
own knowledge of the problem and then
we should endeavour to scale the 10,000
houses which we think should be done in
two years, assuming that perhaps
Lisburn's share might be 550, and so on
for the various places, and in this way
invite them to provide sites for the houses
they may think they would be able to put
up in two years after the war, reckon
the percentage of the subsidy to meet
the initial cost of the sites and putting
them in condition.
In the meantime there is this question
of the emergency house. Some say it is
a very good one. It has not yet been
passed by the Ministry of Health, as I
understand, in England. Naturally from
the point of view of health it will have
to be considered, and this House will
have to consider emergency houses being
put up, and removed later, on these
sites which had been drained and on
which other amenities had been provided.
But, of course, there again who ought
to pay for the emergency house? I think
it is plain the local authority ought not
to be asked to pay for something which
is more or less in the nature of Jonah's
gourd, although it did not last for five
years. That is one way of approaching
the emergency problem. Of course it
will depend on a great many considerations. I do not contemplate that the
problem will be by any means easy.
Yesterday my hon. and learned Friend
raised a couple of points which I find of
very great interest indeed, and which I
propose to deal with now. One was the
possibility or desirability of setting up a
housing commission. Whether he contemplated that they would do and be
responsible for the actual building, or
merely settle priority I was not exactly
clear. On the question of a housing
commission I can see some strong arguments that can be urged in its favour.
Housing
Housing

E
But I take leave to remind the House
that recently when I was suggesting setting up a sort of overriding authority
over local authorities with regard to
planning I was immediately held up as
the enemy of democracy and the fathergeneral of bureaucracy.
Mr. WARNOCK: You did not get
away with it.
Mr. LOWRY: As my hon. and learned
Friend reminds me, I did not get away
with it. The matter was modified,
although curiously enough a further
examination of the Act will show that
more power was put into the hands of the
Ministry in consequence. I am wondering
whether the hon. and learned Member for
St. Anne's has undergone a great change
of heart since then. On this question of a
housing commission, there is one thing I
can see plainly, and that is that it would
have to depend to a large extent on circumstances. Even if the materials became freely available this programme is
bound to be somewhat gradual, but at the
same time the point is worthy of consideration.
There should be control, co-ordination
and the prevention of undue competition
between local authorities. Care should be
taken to see that people will not be asking for things for which they are not
quite ready. When supplies are available
they should be placed through a particular controlling channel. As at present contemplated on the other side of the
water, that will be the duty of the Office
of Works. The actual construction of
houses, where they are to be put up, and
the question as to who is going to settle
the rents, are matters which it would be
very difficult to take out of the hands of
the local authorities.
I was astounded at the moderation of
the hon. Member for Shankill yesterday.
He started off by saying that 100 per cent.
should be borne by the State. He then
came down to 60 per cent., and, finally,
was becoming quite reasonable because he
suggested 50 per cent. I believe if he
had spoken for an hour or two longer he
might have brought the figure down to
25 per cent.
The central fund must bear its share of
the financial burden, and the local
authorities will also have to bear their
share. My hon. and learned Friend, the
Member for St. Anne's, gave some
interesting figures about Birmingham. It
is true that Birmingham did a great job
of work, but one must realise that it has
a population almost equal to that of the
whole of Northern Ireland, and that the
valuation is about three and a half times
that of Belfast. It will be a comfort to
the ratepayers of Belfast to know, even
this year when the rates have gone up
slightly to 11s 10d in the £, that the rates
in Birmingham are 17s in the £. They
ought to have good houses when the rates
are 17s in the £. I am certain that if
Belfast cared to embark on something
that would bring the rates up to 17s in
the £ it would not want any money from
the Government, but I do not think the
people would take that point of view.
One knows that 1d in the £ in Belfast
produces nearly £12,000. It is by far
and away the strongest local authority
in that respect. I have no doubt that
when the time comes they will be ready
to bear a fair share of this great undertaking.
It is true that after the unfortunate
business in 1925 housing came under a
cloud in Belfast. I think one of the
reasons was what was brought to light
during that time. I am convinced that
this is a warm-hearted and generous community. There is one thing, however,
they will insist upon-getting value for
their rates. If they can feel assured that.
the housing rate is being well and wisely
spent you will find them as ready and
eager to play their part in providing
houses as the people in any other place,
in the United Kingdom. Matters of
finance in regard to this housing business
will require very serious consideration,
and I think that the local authorities
ought to know where their houses should
be situated, the types of the houses, and
especially the rents that can be paid by
those for whom the houses are intended.
That brings me to the second point
raised by my hon. and learned Friendwhat I am inclined to style his glossary
or paraphrase of the Uthwatt Report.
The recommendation of the Uthwatt
Committee was that the Government
should forthwith declare as a general
principle that the payment for compensation in respect of the public acquisition
of land should not exceed sums based on

the values at the 31st March, 1939. That

or roads directly

a
serving the property that have come into

Mr. LOWRY: From the many inquiries I have made, I cannot find that

I think that useful information might be

which, if
upon
necessary, legislation can be based.
There are a number of considerations
that occur to me, and I am merely putting
them forward for the consideration of the
House. If the better times one hopes
are coming to farmers, better times that

it be fair, right, or reasonable to ask a

have not got as much land as would sod

Major SINCLAIR: I had not intended
to take part in this Debate, as I felt that
I had already outlined the financial position when the previous Motion on housing
was before the House last November.
However, I feel I cannot allow the statement on finance by the hon. Member for
Antrim to go without a reply. The hon.
Member started with the fallacious
assumption that, while financial stringency and the consequent difficulty of
producing a balanced Budget in the later
inter-war years were a reason for the
Government not proceeding as actively as
it might with the construction of houses,
that state of affairs did not exist to-day,
as there was an abundance of money
available. I find it difficult to follow the
hon. Member's reasoning.
The United Kingdom, of which I believe the hon. Member will acknowledge
that we form a part, is spending money at
a daily rate far in excess of anything that
was thought possible before the war. In
order to meet that colossal and abnormal
expenditure we, in common with the rest
of the United Kingdom, are being heavily
taxed, and at the same time exhorted to
save to the uttermost. While, therefore,
from the purely parochial point of view
-and I should not like to ascribe such a
view-point to the hon. Member-we may
appear to have money to burn, yet when
we remember our Imperial connections
and obligations, it is easily seen that we
are in no better position to-day to spend
money on local amenities which have no
connection with the war, than we were in
the nineteen-thirties.
I do not suppose hon. Members, such as
the hon. Member for Antrim, realise
what harm their attitude in these, debates
can do to Northern Ireland. It is difficult to persuade any thinking person outside our area that we are whole-hearted
in our determination to bring the war
to the speediest possible conclusion when
we suggest, as hon. Members so frequently do, that part of the money raised.
here by special taxation for the financing
of the war should be spent on improving
services which, while admittedly backward, have been in much the same
condition for many years and, in some
cases, at least are no worse in 1944 than
they were in 1924. I am not, of course,
suggesting that applies to housing.
I have. referred to what the hon. Member for Antrim said about the inter-war
years, and the cause then for curtailing
expenditure. on various services, which
were admittedly below the British
standard, in order to balance our Budget.
I am glad to be able to inform the House
that under the arrangements made with
the Treasury within the last few months,
that pre-war position will not again arise.
Housing
Housing
HOUSE OF COMMONS
.
[Major Sinclair]
It has been definitely established that,
allowing for any circumstances peculiar
to Northern Ireland, as distinct from
Great Britain, the standard of social services-and I use that term in its widest
sense, to include housing, health services,
etc. shall not only be raised to the
British level, but shall be kept there, and
that ways and means will be found to
enable this to be done. The machinery
for achieving this is now under discussion.
A natural condition to this is that the
share of the new necessary expenditure,
which falls on the rates, shall be comparable to that borne by ratepayers across the
water. That is a great step forward for
Northern Ireland, and I hope hon. Members on both sides of the House will
appreciate the significance of what I have
said.
But that arrangement has been reached
not because of the utterances of hon. Members on inter-Exchequer finances, but in
spite of them. All these suggestions about
keeping back money out of the Imperial
Contribution (though how you can keep
back something you have never had is
beyond me) do Northern Ireland far more
harm than hon. Members realise. Let us
recognise that all the money which can
be raised at present is urgently required
for the prosecution of the war.
Let us
think imperially, and not parochially, and
then, having played our full part without
reservation, we may look forward to
sharing to the full in whatever advances
in social services the post-war finances of
the United Kingdom can afford.

and learned Member pointed out that

The Government cannot escape
their

the people. With all my heart, and soul
and spirit I deplore the present situation,
but the Government cannot escape responsibility. They should get a move on and
do something at once.
The whole question of housing is one
that we should lay at the door of bureaucracy. I will tell you why. In the year
1909 there were '10,000 to 12,000 vacant
houses in the city of Belfast. After 1909
Mr. Lloyd George introduced his Tax on
Land Values Bill. That was really the
start of bureaucracy that killed the enterprise which was putting up the houses. A
department was set up at Westminster to
collect that tax. That department actually cost four to five times more than the
tax it collected. That was only the start
of the trouble. The question of land
values was one reason why private enterprise was driven out of the field in which
it was doing so well. It was doing so well
that we had a surplus of 10,000 to 12,000
houses in the city of Belfast alone.
Then the Rent Restrictions Acts were
passed. It is admitted now that these
Acts are inequitable in many respects.
Committees have been set up to see if they
could be amended so that justice, and fair
play might be meted out to all parties. I
am not denying the need for some control
over rents, but these Acts have not given
fair play to all parties.
Then we had the Valuation Act, which
was mentioned by the hon. Member for
Woodvale. That was another matter
which helped to kill private enterprise.
In the period between the two world wars
the vast majority of the houses erected
were built by private enterprise. Something like 3,000,000 houses were built
across the water by private enterprise as
against 1,000,000 by the local authorities.
It will thus be seen that by far the
greater number of houses were provided
by private enterprise.
This bureaucracy has been continued,
and we have the buck passed from one
Ministry to another. The Ministry of
Home Affairs have a certain responsibility
in the matter. The Ministry of Commerce deal with the release of materials,
and the Ministry of Finance have also a
say in the matter. That is absolutely
wrong. There is a lack of that co-ordination suggested by the hon. and learned
Member for St. Anne's. He suggested
the setting up of a central housing
authority. I think something will have
to be done along those lines. Whether it
should take the form of a Central
Authority or a Ministry of Health,
Housing and Reconstruction I do not
know, but it should take some form. We
want some authority to deal with this
matter.
On the question of the post-war period
the Minister of Home Affairs told us that
the local authorities are going ahead and
getting plans ready, but he did not tell
us one word about the policy of the
Government regarding the essential question of the location of industries. The
Northern Whig in a recent leading article
told its readers that Belfast is already
too big, and that to increase it in size
would disturb the balance between town
and country. It is time the Government
told us what their policy is. Are they
going to make Belfast bigger?
The
Northern Whig says that would be a
bad policy. Are the Government going
to redistribute industry and see to it that
the provincial areas get their fair share?
It is time we had some pronouncement
on that question. Can the local authorities make any plans until that is done?
I say it would render the position very
difficult for them. The number of houses
to be provided in a certain area would be
governed by the fact as to whether or
not that area was to remain an industrial
one.
We are not keeping step by step
in preparing for the post-war period.
The bulldozers are already at work
across the water preparing the sites for
the post-war building programme, but
not one sod has been turned here. When
I asked a question in this House as to

whether we were going to keep step by 1
step with Great Britain in this matter

Is anything necessary? Why is something not

not think the people will tolerate the present conditions much longer. We heard
much talk in this House yesterday about
the Belfast Corporation and Memel
Street. I do not remember ever being in
Memel Street. God knows I do not deny

I do say there is a most urgent and
pressing need for houses in city, town
and country, and this House, when it is
discussing housing, should not make it a
Belfast question. It is not a Belfast
question at all. It is a Northern Ireland
question, because the need for houses all
over is absolutely urgent and absolutely
clamant, and one that cannot and will
not be denied. Again there is the question of keeping step by step with Great
Britain. Across the water they have
3,000 houses for agricultural workers
erected or almost erected, yet here no
one can build, although there are cases
where rural councils have almost 500
sites that are paid for and prepared and
ready if the Government will only say the

cottages almost completed in England,
should allow the local authorities, who
have sites in hand and the ground prepared, to go ahead and build, particularly
in view of the fact that they were ready
to build when war broke out and the
schemes had to be stopped. The Government should place those local authorities
on the same basis as pre-war in regard to
subsidies for houses.
We are told that another solution of
the problem is the introduction of a Bill
for the requisitioning of premises. Anybody who knows anything about the
country knows that practically all the
vacant premises in the country have been
requisitioned and used for a certain purpose and are not available. This talk of
requisitioning is simply another piece of
window-dressing and will produce next to
nothing. Any premises that I can see
seem to be premises that have been requisitioned already and are being used
for a certain purpose, and that decision
cannot be altered. I hope some premises
will be made available by this method,
but I do not think that will help to
anything like the extent of the number
required. I want to conclude as I started.
I hope the Government will get a move
on in this matter, because it is a matter
that will really brook of no delay, a
matter on which something must be done
and done at once.

Main Question, as amended, put, and

Resolved, "That this House views with
concern the large number of persons, in
the Province who are inadequately
housed, that it supports the Government
in all steps that it is taking to alleviate
the situation and it impresses upon the
Government the vital necessity of further
developing such measures in the widest
and most effective manner possible, with
the object of securing, at the earliest
possible moment and on a large scale the
provision of houses at a rent which working people can pay."

The Strike Negotiations.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That this House do now adjourn.".
(Sir Norman Stronge.)
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: I should like
to ask the Government what is the business for next Tuesday. I do this because
on the Order Paper there has appeared
for the last two months the Belfast
County Borough Administration (Amendment) Bill, Second Reading. That has
been there from day to day, from week
to week, and from month to month. I
gather that this Bill is to be dropped. If
this House gets Bills put into their hands
they should deal with them or the Government should take them off the Paper. I
am raising this because it is an interesting point. We come here and get a Bill,
and whether it is discussed or not depends
on whether the members of the Corporation can agree. I raise the point, because it does not seem to me to be in the
best tradition of Parliamentary business
to put a Bill on the Order Paper if there
is no intention of going on with it.
Major SINCLAIR: The business for
Tuesday next is the Clogher Valley Railway Bill, Second Reading, and there will
be a Private Member's Motion at the
usual time, 3-30. I have taken a note of
what the hon. and gallant Member said
on the other matter.
Mr. NIXON: That is a very nice reply
from the Minister of Finance about this
Bill that is flung at the House from time
to time. I am not going to discuss the
Bill, which is dear to the heart of the
Minister of Finance and a few more
Members. It is more important to them
than a lot of things. I think the Government have any amount on their hands if
they look after the strike of nearly
19,000 people. Instead of that this Bill
is before the House nearly every day.
The Minister of Labour gave us to understand at least I understood him the first
time this was raised-that the strike was
over. That was the impression I got.
Since then it seems to be spreading. I
was reading a resolution which was passed
by the men calling for more speed in
conducting these negotiations. I know
some negotiations are allowed to hang fire
and drag on. I have nothing to say but
for a settlement. That is all I have to
say.
Yet we have a Bill on the Order
Paper day after day that nobody wants
except three men, and a strike like that
drags on. We must try to do something.
If the Government cannot do anything
they should get the House to help them.

Mr. GRANT: I am not suggesting in

Not when the strike was on, but long
before it started I went specially to
London, and I was not gallivanting on
that occasion. I went specially to see

out to him that from my own observations I was convinced something would
have to be done. He did not say "No"

I want hon. Members to understand
that the negotiating machinery has got
nothing whatever to do with the Gov-
The
ernment in any shape or form.
negotiating machinery is the machinery
approved by the National Federation of
both employers and employees; it is
national machinery. If an application
is made in any district for an increase in
wages above the ordinary district rates
the application has to go through certain
machinery. It is very slow, I admit, but
that is not the fault of the Government.
In their executive capacity the trade
unions are very loath to have any interference with this machinery-they value
it very highly-from Government circles
or from anyone else. When a local application is made to a firm the first thing
that happens is that what is known as a
workers' conference is arranged between
the representatives of the firm and the
trade union concerned. Then, failing
agreement and I must confess they
nearly always fail to agree-there is what
is called a local conference, which is a
conference of the employers of the area
with the representatives of the men.
Failing agreement there it has got to go
forward to central conference in York.
This central conference in York is composed of representatives of the executive
committees of the trade unions and the
employers' organisation, so that the
matter is entirely in their own hands,
and the Government cannot speed up
this machinery.

On the occasion when the Prime

of the strikers, but of the confederation,
we promised that if they would take this
themselves with their own
up
organisation we were prepared to give

their executive committee would have to

The question of the National Arbitration Tribunal is a different matter
altogether. That is a matter the Government is interested in, but a question in
dispute does not go to the National
Arbitration Tribunal until such time as
the negotiating machinery between the
employers and the workers has failed. In
the case of this particular decision that
The Strike Negotiations
Adjournment
23 MARCH 1944
is being awaited from the National
Arbitration Tribunal there has not been
any delay, because within a few days of
the application being made for the matter
to go before the Tribunal a date was
fixed, the 29th of this month, for the
hearing of that claim. Therefore, from
the Government point of view there has
been absolutely no delay in setting aside
a date for the hearing of this claim before
the Tribunal. All the delay has been in
the ordinary negotiating machinery
between the employers and the trade
unions.
There is another strike at present, and
that is a strike that everybody in the
country detests and abhors. It is the
strike in connection with Messrs. Short &
Harland's aircraft factory. The men
employed there have made no claim for
anything against the firm. That is my
information. They walk out, and they
say it is a sympathetic strike.
Mr. THOMPSON: Who is at the back
of it?
Mr. GRANT: They have no grievance
with the firm about wages or conditions,
but they simply walk out and say they
are out on a sympathetic strike. The
Prime Minister expressed the views of the
Government and, I am sure, the views
of the Members of this House and the
large majority of the people in the community, in that admirable speech he made
the other night. I only want to add this;
that I am prepared to accept any suggestion that any Member of this House
or anybody outside can make to help to
bring this regrettable stoppage to a conclusion. I am bound to say I feel satisfied
in my own mind that the Government
have done everything they possibly can
not only to settle this strike but to prevent any other strikes.

Tuesday, 28th March, 1944.

ORAL ANSWERS TO
QUESTIONS.
Agriculture.
FORD-FERGUSON TRACTORS.
1. Mr. JOHN BAILEY asked the
Minister of Agriculture whether he can
state if it is a fact that advertisements
refusing to take any further orders for
Ford-Ferguson tractors have been issued
by his Ministry; whether this is an
attempt to compel farmers to take some
other make of tractor not as suitable for
conditions in Northern Ireland; and
whether in the event of there being a
short supply of these Ford-Ferguson
tractors allocated to Northern Ireland he
will have strong representations made to
the Imperial Government or the United
States of America for a further supply,
as many thousands of these tractors are
still urgently needed in this area.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Rev. Robert Moore): It is a fact that,
because there was a very long waiting
list of applicants for Ford-Ferguson
tractors, and because supplies would not
be available to meet the demands of these
applicants for a considerable time, an
advertisement was issued recently by the
Ministry to the effect that until further
notice applications for Ford-Ferguson
tractors could not be accepted. While
the advertisement stated that certain
other makes of row crop tractors were
available it was not intended, in any
way, to influence applicants in their
choice. The purpose of the statement was
purely to provide information for applicants for Ford-Ferguson tractors whose
demands could not be met, so that, if
they so desired, they might obtain
alternative makes to enable them to carry
out tillage work this season. My Ministry has constantly made very strong
representations to the appropriate authorities with regard to the allocation of Ford-
Ferguson tractors to Northern Ireland,
and is continuing to do so.
Mr. HENDERSON: Can the right
hon. Gentleman state how many of the
tractors issued by his Ministry to farmers
for agricultural work have been directed
to constructional work in connection with
Government contracts?
Rev. ROBERT MOORE: I do not
think there are any at the present time.
There was a time when that was done,
but we stopped it.
BANBRIDGE AND NEWRY
POTATO-DRYING FACTORIES.
2. Mr. JOHN BAILEY asked the
Minister of Agriculture whether, in view
of the fact that the potato-drying
factories at Banbridge and Newry have
not been operating for some time, he has
any statement to make as to when they
may be reopened or with regard to their
future prospects.
Rev. ROBERT MOORE: My predecessor, the noble Lord, the Member for
Bloomfield, made it abundantly clear at
the time of their erection that potato drying factories in their present form were
uneconomic and could not, unless heavily
subsidised, continue to operate post-war.
With this opinion I concur. The justification of potato drying factories in the
present emergency lies in the fact that
potatoes constitute one of the most important food reserves that can be built up
in the United Kingdom, and that if the
surplus crop is to be preserved it must
be dried. When, however, the crop can
be utilised in the fresh state, there is no
point in continuing the operation of the
factories. It is impossible for me or
anyone else to say when the drying
factories will re-open. It depends upon
a number of factors which cannot be
estimated. I would merely repeat that
in their present form they are purely an
emergency measure without an economic
future.
With regard to the Newry potato drying factory, I am glad to be able to state
that as a result of negotiations between
my Ministry, the Ministry of Food and
Messrs. Chivers & Sons, Ltd., of Histon,
Cambridge, this firm is taking over control
of the existing potato factory on behalf
of the Ministry of Food and is adapting
it for production of a new product to be
made from potatoes. This product is in
Oral Answers

factory will provide considerable employment in the Newry area. It is likely that

MILK COLLECTION IN COUNTY

3. Mr. LYONS asked the Minister of

recent Order altering the routes of milk
collecting lorries in Co. Tyrone seriously
curtails the service to the farmers, particularly in backward areas and inflicts
unnecessary hardship on an already overburdened community, and whether this
disservice is peculiar to Co. Tyrone.
Rev. ROBERT MOORE: The answer
is in the negative. Certain changes have
been necessary in the milk collection
routes in certain parts of Co. Tyrone
owing to the state of the roads. No unnecessary hardship has been occasioned
by these changes which have all been
made with due regard to the interests of
farmers in the area. In some cases the

nearer the farms than those formerly in
existence.

RESIDENCE PERMITS.
4. Mr. THOMAS CAMPBELL asked
the Minister of Home Affairs whether he
state the number of instances of
refusal of renewal of residence permits
in the past six months to natives of Eire;
how many of these persons come here for
essential war work which would otherwise
have been unperformed; and whether any
exodus from Eire by State compulsion of
Northern Irish workers has been in
force across the Border, and on what
basis the refusals in this area proceed.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Mr. Lowry): Some 1,475 natives of Eire
have been refused renewal of residence
permits in the past six months. So far as
I am aware none of these persons came
here for essential war work which would
otherwise not have been performed.
I am not aware of any exodus from
Eire of Northern Ireland workers.
The issue of permits or of renewals of
permits in Northern Ireland is governed
solely by the nature of the employment
of the persons concerned and whether the
presence of the people is essential for the
furtherance of the war effort.

ACTION AGAINST A PRISON
WARDER.
5. Mr. THOMAS CAMPBELL asked
the Minister of Home Affairs whether
he can state if it is a fact that at the
Belfast Quarter Sessions on 29th September an internee in Belfast jail, Eric
Hughes, a minor, was given a decree for
£12 for injuries inflicted on him with a
belt in the jail by James Sloan, a warder,
and if this warder is still in the Belfast
prison service.
Mr. LOWRY: A decree for £12
damages was made at Belfast Quarter
Sessions the 29th September last
against Prison Officer James Sloan for
assault against Eric Hughes, who was
not an internee.
The prison officer is still in the Belfast
prison service.
Mr. THOMAS CAMPBELL: Is he
still retained to encourage the others?
Mr. LOWRY: No. He is retained
because the county court judge found
that he committed the assault under the
greatest provocation, and in view of his
unblemished long service in the prison he
was reprimanded and cautioned as to his
future conduct, which, in my judgment,
entirely met the necessities of the case.

women who will be demobilised from His

Government of Ireland Act, on the

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
CLOGHER VALLEY RAILWAY
COMPANY (WINDING UP)
BILL.
Order for Second Reading read.
Major SINCLAIR : The Clogher
Valley Railway Company was established
under a Provisional Order made in 1884
under the Tramways and Public Companies (Ireland) Act, 1883, and this Order
provided that payment of interest at the
rate of 5 per cent. on the paid up share
capital of the company should be guaranteed by certain baronies in the counties
of Tyrone and Fermanagh. The Order
also provided that in the event of the
baronies being called upon to fulfil their
guarantees the Government would contribute, subject to an over-riding limitation, half of the cost so borne by the
counties. From a financial point of view,
this undertaking was never a success, and
in no one year was sufficient earned by
the company to pay the interest on its
capital.
From the outset the burden had to be
shouldered, in part, by the ratepayers of
the contributing baronies, and, in part,
by the Government. The share capital
of the company was £123,310 and the
sum which had thus jointly to be found
in each year amounted to £6,166. In
succeeding years, apart from one brief
hiatus, the only happening which broke
the monotony of the regularity of these
dividend payments was the gradual shifting, under the Local Government Act of
1898, and by reason of the derating of
agricultural land in 1929, of the greater
part of the responsibility for the fulfilment of the guarantees from the shoulders
of the ratepayers to the broader and less
complaining back of the Government.
In 1926 the county councils of Tyrone
and Fermanagh, as they were empowered
to do by the Order of 1884, took over the
management of the railway and became
the owners of the line. The company,
though it now had no say in the management of the railway, still remained in
being and the payment of the share dividends continued.
The railway's affairs, however, prospered no better at the hands of the county
councils than under the company and
eventually it was decided to discontinue
its operation. As the House will re-
T
895 Clogher Valley Railway Bill-

28 MARCH 1944
Second Reading
•
member, in 1941 the Clogher Valley Railway and Roads Act was passed, and the
railway, as such, came to an end. The
line has been taken up, the property sold,
and the employees pensioned off, or
otherwise compensated, but the position
of the company with its share capital of
£123,310 and its guaranteed dividends
at the rate of 5 per cent. is unaltered.
All that the 1941 Act did was to complete the process to which I have referred
and enact that 100 per cent. of the
deficiency in the company's ability to pay
dividends should be met by the Govern-
⚫ment.
The position has, therefore, to say the
least of it become increasingly anomalous
in recent years and not one in which the
Government willingly acquiesced, but my
Ministry was advised that if steps were
taken to wind-up the company the existence of the guarantees would entail
difficulty in deciding what compensation
should be paid to the shareholders and
the Government were in any case naturally averse to any suggestion of the compulsory acquisition of the share capital.
For some time past, therefore, the policy
of the Ministry has been to purchase the
shares, by voluntary negotiation with the
holders, at a price below, or not exceeding, their par value, and this has been
carried out by making use of the ordinary
powers of investment which are held on
behalf of Government funds, the particular fund to which recourse
was had
being the Land Purchase Sinking Fund.
It was not until a very recent date that
any noteworthy progress was made towards the realisation of this policy, but
early in this year we reached the position
of owning 99 per cent. of the share
capital, the purchase of these shares having been effected at an average price of
£9 5s Od for each £10 share. Holding,
therefore, virtually the entire share
capital, there remains no further reason
why the company should not be wound
up, and the share capital extinguished,
and these are the formal purposes which
are proposed to be effected by this Bill.
It will be seen that provision is
made for
of
payment
compensation to the few remaining private
shareholders, with whom the Ministry has been unable to make contact,
at a rate not exceeding the par value of
the shares. The Land Purchase Sinking
Fund, which has performed such useful
work, will also be reimbursed in full for
its outlay, so that, in general, the financial
proposals contained in the Bill relate to
internal Government book-keeping.
The passing of the measure will result
in the Exchequer being relieved from an
annual drain of £6,166. The immediate
cost of obtaining this relief will amount
to about £115,000, and I am satisfied
that this sum represents an economical
price in relation to the extinction of
shares of the nominal value of £123,310,
carrying interest at 5 per cent. One most
satisfactory feature is that the acquisition
of the shares has been effected on a
voluntary basis and without resort to any
question of compulsion upon the shareholders. I beg to move.
Question proposed, "That the Bill be
now read a Second time."
