AGRICULTURAL POLICY.
Order read for resuming Adjourned
Debate on Motion [February 15]:
That in the opinion of this House
strong representations should be made
to the Imperial Government with regard to the effect of the present price
structure on Northern Ireland agriculture, in view of the fact that apart
from potatoes and flax Northern Ireland has no sale crops, and this House,
therefore, in the interest of the agricultural industry, urges that consideration should be given to a fair price for
Northern Ireland potatoes, pigs,
poultry and eggs, with a view to placing the production of such products on
an economic basis, and in particular
permitting a gradual expansion of the
pig population to the pre-war level,
and further that in the opinion of this
House the present position entailing
lack of confidence is calculated to prejudice the immediate war and post-war
effort, and that an early statement of
the broad outline of post-war policy
would be of immense value in restoring
the confidence of the agricultural community and so ensure the continuation
of the maximum effort.-(Mr. Elliott.)
Question again proposed.
Rev. ROBERT MOORE: I feel that
a good deal of the interest in this Motion
has already evaporated. Nevertheless,
it might appear that the Government had
no interest in the matter if I, as Minister,
did not say something on the question. I
recognise that my text is not unlike the
experiment of Faraday trying to galvanise
a dead frog, but I will probably not be
just as successful as he was. I do not in-
Agricultural Policy-
Adjourned Debate
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Rev. Robert Moore]
tend to cover the ground that was covered
by hon. Members who spoke to the Motion.
I would somewhat deprecate some of the
statements that were made, I am sure in
all good faith, by hon. Members, but
there were references made to Mr.
Hudson and the controversy between Mr.
Hudson and the farmers in England that
I think were unfortunate.
When the war started I was in a very
different position from that which I
occupy to-day. I was then President of
the Ulster Farmers' Union, and it fell to
me to voice the unanimous decision of the
representatives of the farmers in regard to
the whole national situation which had
arisen over the war. Things were pretty
black from the national and international
points of view at that moment, and speaking in that capacity for the representatives of the farmers I made no conditions
and I laid down no terms as to prices or
anything else, but I offered, on behalf of
the farming industry, that whatever
sacrifices were called for from the community generally the farmers would contribute their full share.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Hear, hear.
Rev. ROBERT MOORE: I think I
can claim that that pledge has been
honoured in the letter and in the spirit.
The emotions at that time were running
pretty strong, and since then 4 years
have passed, bringing with them changing fortunes each year. The emotion
that swept the country at that time has
settled down to what I might describe as
a spirit of persistent, determined resolution. There I leave it, but in the meantime factors emerged that were never
thought of when the war began. It soon
happened that the farmers saw their
workers drifting away from their employment to go into other forms of National
Service where they could obtain very
much more attractive wages. The result
was that the farmers found it much more
difficult to do what was required of them.
They found their costs steadily mounting
up, because the wages of their own
workers were not the only increase that
they had to contend with.
The consequence of all this was that it
was found necessary to review the prices
of farm commodities more than once. In
those reviews of farm prices the only consideration that was kept in mind was not
the total increase of the industry's costs
but the national necessity to spurt up production in this or that commodity which
was the most urgently needed, and so
an added incentive was given in certain
commodities that was not given in certain
other commodities. The net result has
been that as time went on the whole
balance of our agriculture has become
more or less upset and lopsided.
There was another factor at work.
That was that we were steadily achieving
parity with Great Britain in practically
every agricultural commodity. The maincrop potato prices are an outstanding exception. But the fact that they are an
outstanding exception goes to prove my
contention that we were gradually achieving what we never had, namely, parity of
prices with the farmers in Great Britain.
We have to keep those different factors
in mind in trying to adjudge the situation to-day. I will go back to this question of main-crop prices later.
I think that one hon. Member in the
previous Debate referred to flax prices,
and it was contended that we here in
Northern Ireland were getting only 258
per stone whereas in Eire growers were
receiving £2 per stone. I do not think
that that is quite accurate. We in Northern Ireland are receiving from 25s 8d
to 30s 8d per stone, plus an acreage payment of £10. I am not absolutely certain
of the price to a penny in the Free State,
but I understand it is about 31s 6d, and
there is no acreage payment there. It is
only fair to remember that, because the
Northern Ireland farmer so far from
being in a worse position in regard to
flax prices is actually in a better position.
Mr. MINFORD: What is the yield per
acre?
Rev. ROBERT MOORE: It varies in
the Free State, I have no doubt, as it
varies in Northern Ireland, but from
what I can gather the yield for the 1943
crop in Northern Ireland, taking it all
in all, must have been very satisfactory,
because it looks as if it is going to be
almost a problem to find enough seed to
satisfy all the people who apparently
want to grow flax in Northern Ireland in
1944. I think that fact speaks for itself,
be they speculators or be they what they
may.
I want now to say a word about maincrop potato prices. I know there is a
Agricultural Policy-

TE
good deal of heart-burning on that point.
I should like to say that every consideration, every fact and factor, that would
weigh in the interests of the North of
Ireland producer was put forward by us

But there were other things that outweighed our arguments, and I should like
to specify two of them. First of all, there

has steadily crept up.
Mr. MINFORD: Not this year.
Rev. ROBERT MOORE: I am speaking of up to now.
""

eternal."
Rev. ROBERT MOORE: Hope may
materialise even in 1944 in regard to all

they would not allow us to brush aside.
Whilst our farmers were crying out that
it was not paying them they were planting more potatoes. The other fact was
this. A Statistical Committee set up by
the British Treasury to inquire into the
relative well-being of farming in Northern Ireland as compared with Great
Britain for the period 1938-39 up to 1943,
when it had investigated the whole position as to the actual financial improvement of the farmer in Northern Ireland
as compared with that of the farmer in
Great Britain over those years came to
the conclusion that having regard to the
industry as a whole we had done slightly
better than the farmers in Great Britain.
Those two points, the continued increase
in the acreage and the findings of the
Statistical Committee really proved the
twin rocks between which we came to

know there are other considerations,
other countervailing points, that can be
advanced to rebut the findings of that
committee, and I think we advanced them
all and we emphasised them all, but
figures are not easily got round, and there
the matter rests.
I should like to go back for a minute
to the question of the disbalance or
unbalance of our whole farming structure. It was partly created by those
incentives that were given to boost the
•
production of certain commodities that
were urgently wanted in the national
interest. For instance, I might point
out, just as an illustration, that when
one of those price reviews was being made
after we had had an increase in wages,
it was proposed not to give any increase
in the price of fat pigs. It was only after
strong and urgent representations had
been made on the point by Northern
Ireland and by Scotland that a very
slight increase in the price of pigs was
actually given in that review of farm
prices. The result has been that a section of the industry, that pre-war was
worth somewhere round about £4,000,000
per annum, has fallen steadily until
to-day the pig population is only between
one-third and one-quarter of what it was,
say, in '1938.
Take the case of poultry. The. Motion,
if I recollect aright, refers in particular
to pigs and poultry. It became the
policy of the Ministry of Food definitely
to discourage the fattening of poultry,
partly because of the difficulty of obtaining supplies of food and mainly perhaps
because the Ministry of Food wanted to
encourage all it could the production of
eggs. Here again this disbalance of the
industry comes in. In the wisdom, or
otherwise, of the Ministry of Food a flat
price for eggs was fixed for the year.
Those who have taken any interest in
these matters in the past know that in
Northern Ireland we had for years
specialised in winter eggs production.
That was the period of the year when
imports from Denmark and other parts
of the Continent were lowest, and prices
were highest. That was the principle
round which the whole industry came to
be built. Now their flat-rate price. has
blown that to the four winds, and all the
years of instruction, and all the propaganda that were carried on by my
Ministry are in grave danger of being
lost.
There is another side of this matter,
however, which we cannot in fairness
overlook, and that is the price of milk.
There is no comparison whatever between
the price the producer is receiving for his
milk to-day and that which he received
pre-war, and whilst our small producers
have been hit, and are still being hit very
hard, in regard to pig production and in
certain poultry matters, and are perhaps
Agricultural Policy-
Adjourned Debate
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Rev. Robert Moore]
not getting all they are entitled to in the
main-crop potatoes, here is a matter in
which they are being much better treated
than they were pre-war. The production
of liquid milk is no longer the preserve of
the favoured few, the few farmers who
happen to be situated in proximity to the
the city of Belfast, the city of Derry, or
some other consuming centre like them,
because the smallest farmer in the most
remotest district of the Six Counties can
to-day command the full liquid price for
all the milk he produces. Wherever else
we have failed, in that matter we have
achieved parity with Great Britain. I
think that is a fair picture of the situation without any exaggeration.
A question was raised about the future
policy of the Government-I take it the
Imperial Government was meant-in regard to agriculture. It is only fair to
say that at the present juncture any
Government sitting at Westminster, being
there, you might say at the very heart of
the whole Allied Forces, must find itself
in a very awkward and difficult position
in trying to make. a worth-while public
pronouncement on the future of agriculture. Personally, I have long held
the view that whatever our personal
opinions may be, whatever our sympathies
may be, whatever our personal prejudices
may be, in regard to how agriculture
should be helped, unless the ultimate plan
for agriculture is a plan that can be
fitted into the great general scheme of
things after the war, it may thrive for a
little while, but from the start it is really
doomed to failure. It will only be when
the Imperial Government in consultation
and in conference with the other members
of the Commonwealth, and with the
United States and with the powers on the
continent of Europe-it will only be
when they have come to a real conclusion
in regard to the future general structure
of trade and commerce and all the rest
that it will be possible to make a real
public pronouncement on how agriculture
is going to be fitted into that general
picture. I say that because it is only
right one should say it in fairness to the
Government at Westminster.
On the other hand, I am satisfied that
the fact that there has been no such pronouncement, that it has had to be delayed
year after year up to the present time,
has had a very deleterious effect and has
shaken the confidence of the farming
community throughout the whole United
Kingdom, and I believe there is nothing
that would do so much or go so far to
restore the confidence of the farming
community if, just as the Motion points
out, it were possible for the Imperial
Government in a reasonable time to state
at least the broad general lines of the
policy that is going to be implemented
for agriculture after the war. Now that
has, to my mind, a tremendous bearing
on the
cry about prices, and if agriculture is going to be neglected, if it
going to go unregarded and uncared for
after the war, if it is going, one might
say, to be left like nobody's child on anybody's doorstep, then nobody could blame
the farmer to-day for insisting that so
long as what he produces is recognised as
being necessary he should get his pound
of flesh, that he should get the last halfpenny he can in the way of prices for his
products. To my mind, whilst that is
all true and I do not blame him-on the
other hand, I think it would change his
outlook tremendously and modify some of
his demands and end some of his complaints if the Imperial Government could
see their way to make a pronouncement—
even of a very general kind, without committing themselves to details at the
earliest moment possible.
I do not think I need detain hon.
Members beyond that, but I would like
to say this about our own Government.
Hon. Members will be aware that there
was a Committee set up by my predecessor to inquire into certain matters
relating to agriculture here in the Six
Counties. From what I have said they
will realise that the general outline of
post-war policy is a thing for the
Imperial Government, and therefore the
main points are things that do not really
come under our jurisdiction. That does not
mean there are not a great many
local
internal matters here that we can deal
with, and it was to deal with those that
the Committee, under the presidency of
Lord Justice Babington, was set up by my
predecessor. I think hon. Members will
agree that we were most fortunate in
getting a gentleman of the character and
the ability and the enthusiasm of Lord
Justice Babington to act as chairman of
such a Committee. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) And on the other hand,
or
I

have talked on several occasions with
Lord Justice Babington and he speaks in
the highest terms of the personnel of his
Committee. He has very high hopes as to
the value of the work that that Committee is doing.
The Committee has been given the
widest possible terms of reference. It is
dealing with rural housing, with the
maintenance of land fertility, the improvement of livestock, the electrification of the
countryside, with the marketing of agricultural products and a large number of
other matters. I have referred to this
simply to show that this Government cannot be accused of being in any way behindhand in the efforts it is making to be
ready to help all it can in the future
well-being and the development of the
agricultural industry. I do not suppose

think, without any exaggeration and
with some insight and real understanding
of the whole case, I have put the matter
for this Motion before the House. All
I want to say is that I, on behalf of the
Government, am quite prepared to accept
the Motion, and I do so now.

SUPERANNUATION (TEACHING

Order for Second Reading read.
Major SINCLAIR: Though all the
four matters dealt with in this Bill relate
to teachers' superannuation, they are in
themselves quite separate and distinct.
With
In Clause 1 it is proposed that as from
the 1st April, 1945, superannuation payments to teachers will be a direct charge
on the annual Votes of Parliament instead of being paid, as is the present
case, out of the Teachers' Superannuation
Fund. For a long time now this fund
has not been able to meet the cost of
these payments and the deficiency, which
has progressively increased from year to
year, has had to be met annually by
voted money. Thus in the year ended
31st March, 1943, the total payments
from the fund amounted to £244,000,
and towards this the Exchequer had to
contribute £130,000 as compared with
only £32,000 fifteen years ago.
increasing benefits the tendency towards
an increasing deficiency must continue,
and in the view of the Government the
time has now arrived when we should
fall into line with the practice in Great
Britain, and make the entire cost of
these superannuation benefits a direct
charge on voted moneys bringing-(a)
contributions paid by schools and teachers
towards their superannuation, as well as
(b) the income of the fund from its investments to the credit of the Vote by
way of an Appropriation-in-Aid. In this
way Parliament will be presented with a
complete gross and net picture instead of
at present allowing the payments to be
hidden in the accounts of the fund.
Hon. Members will appreciate that the
Superannuation Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Major Sinclair]
position of the individual teachers will be,
if anything, strengthened by this change.
in accounting practice. It is not proposed to do away with the fund, but to
let its corpus remain static while using
its income in the way I have just
mentioned.
Clause 2 calls for little further explanation than that already given in the
memorandum circulated with the Bill.
The House may, however, like to be reminded that lump-sum payments for
teachers in Northern Ireland were first
introduced under a scheme formulated
in 1936, and under the Teachers' Superannuation Act (Northern Ireland), 1936,
it was provided that the contributions
towards these lump-sum payments should
form part of the capital of the Teachers'
Superannuation Fund for a period of not
less than seven years from 1st July, 1936.
In 1940 it was agreed with the teachers
that the lump-sum benefits already
granted should be extended by allowing
the years between 1922 and 1936 to
reckon, and that, in return, teachers who
elected to enjoy these additional benefits
should pay
additional contributions. A
further condition was that payment in
respect of these years should not be made
until after the war, and the Superannuation (Teaching Services) Act (Northern Ireland), 1941, provided that the
additional contributions should not be
drawn upon for a similar period.
As I stated, when announcing the last
concession on 22nd February, it is proposed to make immediate payments of
all the lump sum allowances now due,
and to enable the cost to be met it will
be necessary to release the contributions
at present locked up in the fund. As
I also stated on 22nd February, the lump
sum payments to be made this year will
probably cost in the neighbourhood of
£280,000, and if the total of the accumulated contributions now to be realised
does not reach this figure, the Clause
empowers the Ministry to obtain any
further sum required by realising portion
of the capital of the Teachers' Superannuation Fund.
Clause 3 is more a matter of machinery
than anything else and is merely a reenactment of Section 2 (3) of the Teachers'
Superannuation Act (Northern Ireland),
1926. This section of the 1926 Act made
provision for the Ministry of Finance
to keep statistics and accounts in respect
of the payment of teachers' pensions,
and it is now thought fit to enact that
if there should be a change in the
Ministry which pays teachers' pensions,
that that Ministry, and not the Ministry
of Finance, should also keep the statistics.
I come now to Clause 4. The Teachers'
Superannuation Act (Northern Ireland),
1926, gives the Ministry of Finance the
power to reduce a State pension where
it is known that the recipient of the
pension is also in receipt of a pension
from another source. Briefly, such other
source is defined in the Act as being
either moneys voted by Parliamentwhether directly or indirectly-rates, or
any fund under Government control. For
some time past, however, the Board of
Education in England has enjoyed wider
powers in this respect, and it is desirable
that the Ministry of Finance should also
have the power to take into account pensions payable under superannuation or
pension schemes which do not come within the categories to which I have just
referred. This will enable the Ministry.
if the circumstances demand, to ensure
that the benefits of the State pensions
scheme will not inure to the undue advantage of those who are also receiving substantial benefits under other schemes for
the same period of service. Actually the
Ministry has never had occasion to require such a power, as any question of
the actual amount of a pension paid by
another body to supplement the award
under the Teachers' pension scheme has
been settled satisfactorily in discussion
between that body and the Ministry,
and it is only sought now to meet any
very exceptional cases which may arise
in future. I beg to move.

HOUSING (REQUISITIONING OF
PREMISES) BILL.
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Mr. Lowry): This Bill is being introduced to assist in providing housing
accommodation for an unfortunate section
of the community who are at present
unable to obtain suitable homes or who
have no homes at all. As hon. Members
are aware there is an acute shortage of
housing accommodation throughout the
Province and yet instances occur of houses
lying vacant for considerable periods.
The Bill empowers local authorities to
requisition premises for the purpose of
providing accommodation for persons who
are homeless or inadequately housed. The
consent of the Ministry of Home Affairs
will be required before requisitioning can
take place. In addition, the Bill provides
that a local authority may, with the
approval of the Ministry, adapt premises
or carry out works of repair or alteration
in order to make the premises reasonably
suitable for housing purposes.
The premises to which the Bill applies
are dwelling-houses, whether furnished or
unfurnished, which are not being used for
residential purposes, and other buildings
-not being residential buildings-which
are unoccupied. A local authority may,
therefore, with the sanction of the
Ministry, if it thinks fit, requisition
houses or shops or other premises which
can suitably be converted into dwellings, or may requisition large houses and
convert them into flats suitable for two
or more families. In order to give the
owner of the premises an opportunity of
letting the premises to a bona fide tenant
the local authority will in practice give
the owner a notice in writing of their
intention to take possession of the
premises within 30 days for bona fide use
as a dwelling-house. If within that period
the owner of the premises lets them to
a bona-fide tenant the local authority
will not requisition the premises. The
object of making vacant premises available for the housing of the homeless will,
however, have been achieved without the
actual necessity of requisitioning.
The local authority will be required to
charge for the accommodation provided,
a rent which is reasonable, having regard
to all the circumstances. The local
authority will thus be allowed to charge
less than an economic rent to workingclass tenants in appropriate cases. Any
loss which may be incurred by the local
authority as a result of operations under
the Bill will be recouped in full by the
Ministry. Where premises are requisitioned compensation will be payable to
the owner in accordance with the provisions of the Schedule to the Bill. Any
dispute regarding the amount of compensation will be referred to the county
court for determination.
This is a matter that has been under
consideration from time to time since
August, 1941, but on advice that was
received from those best qualified to
judge, it was thought an undesirable step
to take by reason of the fact that a great
many of the shops, for example, were in
extremely vulnerable areas in the city.
The position was reviewed from time to
time. At one time it was thought this
might be done under the Defence of the
Realm Regulations, but on investigation
it was found it was not practicable to
deal with the matter in that fashion, and
consequently this legislation has been
introduced for a purpose which, I am
sure, will commend itself to all the Members of the House. I beg to move.
Question proposed, "That this Bill be
now read a Second time."

ADJOURNMENT MOTION.
THE BELFAST STRIKES.
Statement by the Minister of Labour.
Motion made and Question proposed,
"That this House do now adjourn."
(Sir Norman Stronge.)
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Grant): For the information of the
House I want to give an outline of the
course of events which have come to the
knowledge of my Ministry in relation to
the present deplorable strikes in our
shipbuilding, aircraft and engineering
industries. They mainly involve the
members of one trade union-the
Amalgamated Engineering Union-but in
three different firms, and concern the
question of the rates of wages of time
workers as laid down in the National
Agreements.
HARLAND & WOLFF.
On the 23rd February Messrs. Harland
& Wolff reported that a deputation of
shop stewards had informed the firm
that the fitters in certain departments
"had decided to give 48 hours' notice to
cease work in the event of no action being
taken in connection with their recent
application for an increase in wages."
This application had previously been
made by the union on a national basis.
On inquiry to the Trade Union my
Department was informed that a meeting of the District Committee of the
union was being held to consider the
position. On the 25th February the men
ceased work, and I had a request from
the Trade Union to receive a deputation
of the men's representatives. I met
them that afternoon and was informed
that their claim was for a rate of 38 per
hour. They asked me to try and
arrange a conference between them and
the firm. This was subsequently arranged
and there were joint meetings between
the firm and the Trade Union representatives both on the 29th February
and on the 1st March.
I understand that as the outcome of
the meetings the firm submitted proposals
in writing for the settlement of the dispute
on the basis of an additional allowance
of 6s per week during the initial stages
of the extension of the piece-work
system. These proposals were rejected
at a mass meeting of the men. The union
informed the firm of the men's decision.
This was followed by an extension of the
strike in other departments. On the 6th
March I again met a deputation of the
men's representatives and arranged for
a further joint conference of the parties
on the following day at which both the
Flag Officer, Rear-Admiral Bevan, and
I were present. On this occasion the
men's representatives reiterated their
claim for a time work rate of 3s per hour,
to which the firm were unable to agree
in view of their obligations under the
National Agreement, and the firm again
offered a system of piece-working as the
appropriate solution of the difficulty.
The Trade Union representatives undertook to put the firm's views before another meeting of the men.
Meantime the position had been reported to the national bodies in England
by the respective parties, and as a result
two Executive Officers of the Amalgamated Engineering Union arrived here
on the 13th instant. They met representatives of the firm and the Admiralty
on the following day, and after further
negotiations the firm's offer of an
allowance of 6s was increased to one of
88,
but on the 17th instant the
Executive officials informed me that this
revised offer had again been rejected at
a mass meeting of the men at which a
ballot vote was taken. The Executive
officials returned to England that evening. I would add that the United
Kingdom claim for an increase of 10s on
the basic time-rate is still before the
Statement by Minister of Labour 952
The Belfast Strikes-
30 MARCH 1944
I
Engineering Employers' Federation for
consideration.
SHORT & HARLAND.
The strike was extended to Messrs.
Short & Harland on the 14th instant
when some thousands of workers came
out in sympathy with the claim of the
fitters in Harland & Wolff. In this case
the firm stated "that no applications for
wage increases or changes in conditions
or representations of any kind from
Trade Unions or shop stewards, either
written or verbal, had been made upon
them." I myself have had no representations on behalf of the workers in
this matter. The National Agreements
also apply to this firm.
JAMES MACKIE & SONS, LTD.
The employers state that a demand,
coupled with a threat of strike action,
was submitted on the 18th March for a
rate of 3s per hour: This was followed
by a strike on the 21st instant. Here
again the position is covered in the terms
of the national agreements.
I think I am safe in saying that no
strike of recent times in our area has been
the subject of so much comment as that
which is taking place at present. Opinions
have been expressed for and against the
action of the men, and I as Minister of
Labour have to be particularly careful
to deal with the matter in a strictly
impartial way. My responsibility when
a strike takes place is to use every means
at my disposal to bring the parties together in the hope that a settlement will
be effected. If I were to express an
opinion in regard to the merits of the
matter in dispute, I would become a
partisan, and as such I would destroy
the neutral position which I must maintain.
Without going into the merits of the
matters at present in dispute, I think I
am entitled to say that a strike could
not have taken place at a time more
prejudicial to the fight that we are waging on all our battlefields, and which we
will wage in the immediate future, with
the utmost intensity, at the new battle
front to be opened in western Europe.
In this new offensive ships and aircraft
will be of paramount importance, and
Northern Ireland was looked to for a
much needed contribution. I am sorry
to say that already an appreciable number of ships which required urgent repair
has had to be sent to other yards whose
capacity is already taxed to the utmost.
The strike in our aircraft factory, where
there is no dispute about wages, has also
reduced very considerably the output of
aircraft this month.
This is a mechanical war, and the
greater preponderance we have in the
weapons of war the more rapid will be
our success and the more we will safeguard the lives of our fighting men. I
say our fighting men, and I do not mean
merely the British soldiers and sailors
and the troops of our great Allies, though
we all know that their lives are at stake
also. But for the moment I am thinking
of our own men-the fathers, the sons,
the brothers and the sweethearts of our
people here in Northern Ireland. I
think, too, I am entitled to say that
when the history of this war comes to be
written, and when the contribution that
Northern Ireland has made to the war
effort is recorded, one dark spot-and I
hope the only dark spot-will be the
holding-up of the output of essential
munitions at this most imperative time.
I may be asked how the men, assuming they are suffering under a grievance,
could secure the conditions they seek
without recourse to strike action. My
answer is that over a long period of years
men in the trade union movement have
fought for and secured the right, by
collective bargaining, to negotiate with
employers and their organisations in
these matters.
I
Far-seeing labour leaders realised that
mob law was not the best means of securing their legitimate claims, and where
men have joined together in trade unions
to engage in this collective bargaining,
they are undermining their own strength
if they fail to have their grievances dealt
with in their constitutional manner.
know how easy it is at a time when men
are suffering under a supposed sense of
injustice for evilly disposed persons to fan
that feeling into open revolt against their
elected leaders. Indeed,. I fear that this
has been the position in the present strike,
and I would appeal to my fellow-workers
-for I still regard myself as such-to
place their accredited representatives in
a position in which they can resume
negotiations through the bargaining
machinery that has been established by
joint consent for that purpose. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.).
Statement by Minister of Labour 954
The Belfast Strikes-
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Grant]
Much as I am concerned about the
interruption to the flow of essential war
material, I cannot but be concerned also
about the effect that this strike may have
on the post-war position. It has been
contended by those who have taken the
control of the men away from their
legitimate leaders that they are fighting
in order to establish better conditions for
the skilled men who will be returning
from the Armed Forces when peace is
declared.
But I should like to point out that since
recruitment started in Northern Ireland
my Ministry, in conjunction with the
Service authorities, have been insisting.
that skilled men who are required to
engage in the production of the munitions
of war would not be recruited for the
Services, in other words, they were a
reserved occupation. Apart, therefore,
from those in the technical branches of
the Army, the Navy and the Air Force,
there will be very few skilled men returning to the engineering industry. Indeed, I
feel that the strikers are doing a disservice
to the men who will be demobilised from
the Armed Forces, as well as to themselves, for everything that tends to place
Northern Ireland in a disadvantageous
position in production, as compared with
other parts of the United Kingdom, will
have the effect of lessening the amount of
work that will be available here for men
in the Forces when they return to civil
employment.
It has been a policy accepted by all
classes of our community that social conditions here should be identical with those
in Great Britain: surely it is not
unreasonable to contend that wage conditions on a United Kingdom basis should
also apply. If we force wages above this
level, orders will not be placed here.
It is for this reason that I think
national wage negotiating machinery is a
principle that should find common
acceptance, and any effort to depart from
this common policy will injure and not
benefit our workers. It has been stated
that this machinery is slow in its operation; but just as its form was devised by
both employers and workers, so its timetable can be speeded up by the common
consent of these parties.
There is a further aspect of this dispute
to which I feel I should refer, and that is
that, as a result of the action of the men
who have left their work, a very considerable number of their fellow-workers
have had to be discharged by the
employers because of the upset that the
strike has caused to the balance, of production. These workers, who have been
rendered involuntarily idle, are not only
being thwarted in their desire to continue
in the production of essential
materials, but they and their families are
suffering financial loss through the action
of the strikers.
war
Even now I would ask the men to accept
the advice of the trade union leaders and
leave all questions of wage adjustment in
their hands. By doing so, they will
show that they are mindful of the nation's
needs of the moment and that they are
prepared to take their place again in our
shipyard, aircraft and engineering works,
and make the contribution that they
alone can give to their kith and kin who
are fighting for them in this battle which
will, we hope, establish for all time man's
right to a full and free life.
I think I have said enough to show that
this strike is not the concern only of the
men and the employers. It has far-flung
implications, and I am making this statement in order that Members of all parties
may express their views. I feel that it is
a matter on which public opinion should
not only be informed, but should express
itself, and I know of no better place in
which this can be done than in this
assembly of the elected representatives of
our people. (Hon. Members: hear, hear.)

Mr. BEATTIE: I want to give this

knows the piece-work system better than

Since I was 14 years of age I worked on

& Wolff's. I know the dangers that surround piece-work, and I know the difficulties, the pitfalls and the obstacles that
would be placed in the way of a ship's
fitter applying himself to the straight
piece-work system. I want to tell this

That very
offer was made years ago and was accepted

and it had to be given up.
Let me give in my own way the point
of view of the men on strike. I know I

Mr. NIXON: You were made a J.P.
Mr. BEATTIE: That is not a decoration; it is something that Labour is entitled to receive. If Labour has got one
J.P. out of all the J.P.'s that were
appointed, Labour is badly represented

If the hon. Member would call upon me

But let me get down to the real position.
I want to tell the right hon. Gentleman

the shipyard fitting outside engine works,
the Victoria outside repair departments
and plants refuse to accept the principle
of piece-work. I am going to give you a

Two of these departments tried to work
the system for a number of years, and
both had to repudiate it in disgust. It is
their considered judgment that the nature
of engineering work aboard ship is totally
unsuited to the system. I do not know
whether hon. Members recognise the difficulties of engineers and other men working aboard ship during the final
construction. I certainly have watched,
and worked with, ships' fitters, and I cannot see how it would be humanly possible
or practicable to apply the straight piecework system to those men's work.
It cannot be done with other trades.

has got to be considered is the changing

Anyone who understands engineering
knows that there are many varieties of

The outside engine works repudiated it

to operate the system again under any
circumstances. No matter what the

and practice to be wrong.
The system has the effect of negativing the principles of trades unionism, and
the firm deals with each man as an individual through the medium of the
rate-fixer leaving him. open to intimidation. I think that can be
borne out by the experience of these men
who have had to stand victimisation and
attacks from time to time in putting
themselves in the position of challenging
the authority of the rate-fixer or foreman.
Much time has been lost in that respect.
The organisation was built up for the purpose of collective bargaining, and the men
in this year 1944 are not going to give
up that right either in the workshop or
outside. During the depression weak
members are inclined under duress to lend

even
charge non-existent jobs in order to

operates in any yard in Great Britain,
let alone Ireland, I am prepared to hear
in what districts this system of straight
piecework pays. Very few, if any, shipyards on the other side operate P.B.R. on
engineering work on board ship.
P.B.R. in any establishment where skill
and accuracy is required tends to
encourage the individual to skimp the job,
quality suffers, price tends to follow and
the good worker suffers. P.B.R. is a
method devised by the employers to increase profits, and experience has shown
that many employers do not interpret the
spirit of agreements justly when they
have the power to do so. The original
P.B.R. Agreement definitely states that
the prices shall be so fixed that the man
of average ability shall be enabled to earn
at least 33 per cent. We must dwell for
a moment on that. If a man does not
earn 33 per cent. he can be graded as
an engineer not of average ability. This
figure was decreased in December, 1932,
to 25 per cent. Then in 1943 it was raised
to 27 per cent. That means that 33}
per cent. is to be the minimum and there
is no maximum stated.
During all the years that the firm of
Harland & Wolff operated this system
they made this the maximum and men
were graded downwards to the flat rate.
The men consider this unjust. Furthermore, according to the 326 award P.B.R.
workers were to get 20s transferred from
the cost of living bonus to the basic rate
and P.B.R. raised from 25 per cent. to
27 per cent. on basic rate. Employers
generally refused to calculate P.B.R.
wages on the new basic rate, and it took
a strike in Barrow to force the Arbitration Court to redefine the award and
prove what to anyone who could read
English and had a sense of honesty was
quite obvious from the first. Even yet,
months after the award has been clarified
there were men working in the engine
shop on P.B.R. based on the old rate of
49s 9d. The men consider this dishonest.
The 20s was defined to be applied to the
basic rate of 49s 9d, making a total of
69s 9d. At the time this statement was
handed to me there were men who were
not getting the benefit of that rate of 20s.

The men ask a flat rate of 3s per hour.

At the moment the men have, a basic rate

£4 11s 3d. I have a number of pay

They are out of Harland & Wolff's. To

having advanced, the men are paying

mentally and physically much better off
during the years of depression.
Think for a moment of a firm like Harland & Wolff making all preparations for
reorganisation. May I say they have
made plenty. They have made-sometimes at the expense of the war effort-a
beautiful corner in which to carry out
their building of ships and other things
to which they will apply themselves after
the war.
I believe I am not far wrong in that.
If they are to be allowed to reorganise

to do so to keep the wages down to a
certain level and to keep the noses of the
working class to the grindstone, then I
say that is asking for butter and jam on
their bread, but giving neither butter nor
jam to the working classes. I do not
stand for that. If it is good and wholesome for employers to commence
organising for after-the-war conditions, it
is good and wholesome for the working
classes, in view of the experience of the
last war, to be alive to their own interests
after this war.

Some point has been made about the
strike being unofficial, but every member,
who is either on the streets or in sympathy with the men, is a member of some
union. We must appreciate that the
members of the. Engineering Union,
whether they are turners, fitters, or
machine men, are engaged on work which
requires very great skill, patience and
courage. Acccording to the 326 Award,
a fitter on P.B.R. is entitled to 27 per
cent. on his basic rate of 69s 6d and a
cost-of-living bonus of 15s 6d, which is
equal to £5 28 6d. Even if he were
allowed to earn the total 27 per cent.,
this would be equal to only £6 5s. Many
of the lesser skilled tradesmen can easily
earn £10 to £12 per week. That is the
limit of the earning power of the skilled
engineer.
We have been told that this is a war

I am here to-day to present the case to

not ashamed of what I am doing here.

of their wives and

in other trades. That being so, they

Coming now to my finale, might I say
I have telegrams here from outlying
districts asking me to do all that is
humanly possible in this House to-day to
avert the greatest disaster and the
greatest tragedy that ever happened in

we have had everything that, any country
could have. Here we have this presenting itself to us to-day. It is not confined
to the Six Counties. This whole position,
as it appears to me now, is this, that it is
not an internal affair concerning ourselves,
but it must be taken on the broad basis

not show any feeling for one side as
against the other. What we must do is
be the medium through which these two
parties can come closer together than they

do

Mr. ANDREWS: It has been suggested that I should endeavour to express
my views for what they are worth in
connection with this important matter
which we are discussing to-day. I hope
to do so very briefly, and at the same
time frankly and helpfully. For sixteen
years I was Minister of Labour in this
part of the United Kingdom, and during
that time I had opportunities of learning
very definitely the difficulties and disappointments that often occur to the
person who occupies the position, but I
am happy to say that during my term
as Minister of Labour my direct relations
both with the employers and the members
of the trade unions were very happy, and
I think I may add mutually helpful.
We are up against a very serious position at the present time. We have large
numbers of our fellow-workers walking
the streets because of this dispute. We
have always recognised the loyalty, the
industry and the craftsmanship of our
workers. I am quite certain that I am

speaking for great numbers of them today when I say that they are very unhappy about the situation. They would
rather be working. They recognise how
necessary it is that they should be working. Circumstances have produced a very
different position. It is not my duty today to go into the question as to whether
the wages they are being paid are
sufficient or not, or whether the conditions under which they work are
what they should be, but I want to say
very definitely, because I feel it is my
duty to say this, that I do not think
that these unofficial strikes are justified
under existing conditions. Our country is
engaged in the greatest struggle that the
world has ever known.
We have our fellow Ulster citizens to the
number of many thousands fighting for the
freedom of all mankind and fighting for
us to-day, and surely it is the duty of
each one of us to get on with his job
to the greatest possible extent whatever
that job may be. It is a time, in my
opinion, when we should be careful that
we do not allow personal considerations to
be more prominent in our minds than the
national interests and what is more desirable for the national welfare. In my day
as Minister of Labour trade union leaders
were in a position to speak for those
whom they represented,
and when
negotiations took place and a settlement

Some of our trade unionists object to

have these unofficial strikes.

The best that can be done in my opinion
in the interests of all concerned is that
as
Ulster standards should be the same as
the standards in Great Britain.
I have always held that view as regards

my
I hold the view that the employees have
the same right to have their trade union
as the employers have to have a trade
association. It should be the privilege of
those two bodies, through their appointed
representatives, to meet from time to time
to discuss and settle matters of common
interest to their particular industry. In
many industries this arrangement has
worked excellently for years. That
has happened more especially through the
machinery of the various trade boards.
Wages have been fixed in a friendly way
and working hours and conditions of
labour have been arranged. In most cases
relationships have been of a friendly
nature.. This is as it should be, if any
measure of goodwill and friendship in
industry is to be permanently built up.
We must have team work. The day
should have passed for ever when they
should be any need to call in the strike
weapon. When there is a desire for
understanding and goodwill this cruel

Both parties should be prepared to set up
machinery and appoint delegates from

agreement and goodwill.
When any set of individuals outside
the appointed leaders step in and try to
undermine or usurp the power of the
appointed leaders nothing but chaos can
result. We must have agreements made
by trade organisations loyally accepted
and agreed to by both parties if we are to
arrive at real and lasting decisions. I
would appeal to-day to all employers to
honour their agreements, face the facts,
and be prepared to produce the evidence
for their decisions. To the employees
I would say, honour your agreements with
your trade unions and your leaders
appointed by the unions, and do not be

matter how willing they are, no body of

I trust that a fair figure will be arrived.
at at an early date, a figure that will

Adjournment
Mr. BEATTIE: I realise that, and I

The PRIME MINISTER: Taking it
by and large, the House will agree if
there is machinery there let us use that
machinery and not undermine it. I need
not go into the arguments any further.
I am tremendously proud of the work
done both by the employers and the employees. We all regret these disputes,
but unfortunately they do arise at various
times. To my mind the tragedy is that
they should arise at the present moment.
It is a very difficult thing for people either
in or outside this House, except they
have been in it themselves, to visualise
the position, where men may be depending for their lives on supplies of
machinery, be they ships or aeroplanes,
and how unpleasant it is to be short of
supplies or food. One can read where
men in an isolated position are being supplied by aeroplanes. If there are not
sufficient aeroplanes obviously they cannot be supplied.
One can see the position of troops being
asked to land upon open beaches without
aeroplane cover. If they had another
ship, another aircraft carrier, their lives
would be safe. I have not experienced
the necessity of aeroplane cover, because
that was not a thing that arose in the last
war, but I feel sure that if the loyal
working men in this country could only
realise the necessity of their output, and
also the importance of the negotiating
machinery, which we would all like to see
used and accelerated, perhaps they would
think again and realise that by doing
their work they would not only be saving
the lives of many others, but raising their
own prestige.

HOUSING BILL.
Order for consideration of Senate's
Amendments read.
Resolved, "That the Amendments
made by the Senate in the Housing Bill
be taken into consideration forthwith."
(Mr. Lowry.)
CLAUSE 5 (Vesting orders for com
pulsory acquisition of land for purposes
of the Housing Acts).
In any case where a local authority
have power to acquire otherwise than
by agreement any land for the purposes
of the Housing Acts, the authority
may apply to the Ministry for an order
vesting such land in them and the
Ministry shall have power to make such
order; and the provisions of section.
twenty-two of, and the Second Schedule to, the Local Government Act
(Northern Ireland), 1934, shall apply
as if the purposes for which the authority may acquire land thereunder included the purposes of the Housing
Acts, and the authority shall for those.
purposes be the local authority within
the meaning of the said section twentytwo.
Senate's Amendment: Clause 5, page
5, line 14, at end add the following proviso:
Provided that before making any
such order in pursuance of the power
conferred by this section, the Ministry
shall have regard to the effect which
the order, if made, would have on the
user, value and amenities of lands in
the immediate neighbourhood of the
land proposed to be acquired.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Mr. Lowry): When this Bill was before
the Senate certain criticisms were made to
the effect that the making of a vesting
order by the Ministry might affect injuriously the owners of land in the immediate neighbourhood, and such owners
would have no means of making their
objections known to the Ministry. This
Amendment has, therefore, been introduced in order to place an obligation on
the Ministry to have regard to the effect
on land in the immediate neighbourhood
which the making of a vesting order
would have. In addition to that safeguard there is the power to hold an
inquiry. As this seemed to be an Amendment which would meet certain criticisms
the Government have no hesitation in
agreeing with it. I beg to move, "That
this House do agree with the Senate in
the said Amendment.'
Question put, and agreed to.
Senate's Amendment: In page 5, line
14, at the end of the Clause add a new

• MINISTRIES BILL.
Order for Second Reading read.
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir Basil
Brooke): The Ministries Bill, the Second
Reading of which I have the privilege of
moving in the House to-day, gives effect
to the main recommendation of the Select
Committee on Health Services. The
Government are in full agreement with
the Committee that the time has come to
concentrate all these services
in one
Department under a Minister specially
charged with their supervision. I feel
sure I am only voicing the feelings of
every Member of the House when I express our appreciation of the comprehensive way in which the whole field of
health services has been reviewed by the
Committee, under the able chairmanship
of the hon. Member for the University
(Mr. Stevenson).
As will be seen from Clause 1 of the
Bill, the proposed Ministry will be responsible for the administration of health,
housing and local government services.
The health of the community is one of
the major responsibilities of any Government, and this Government have had no
hesitation in agreeing with the Committee
that these matters are of such importance
as to warrant the undivided attention of
one Minister and one Department.
health services cannot be divorced from
Our
housing conditions. We fully recognise
that the most up-to-date methods for the
prevention and cure of illness must be
made available, to the greatest extent
possible, for those who unfortunately require medical attention, and to this end.
the new Ministry will apply itself.
But there is also the other side, and
that is, paradoxical though it may seem,
the creation of conditions which will
lessen the need of the community for
these services. It is the opinion, not only
of the Government but also of all who
have the welfare of our people at heart,
that the only method by which the general
standard of health can be improved and
maintained is by the provision of better
housing conditions. Health and housing
are inseparable, the former improves or
worsens in direct ratio to the upward or
•
downward trend of housing facilities.
These two important matters, which are
so vital to the country, are closely linked
with our system of local government. The
complex code of public health legislation,
built up over many years, with extensions
of the original structure devised to meet
new conditions as they arose, relies to a
great extent for its administration on
local authorities. Housing, too, is one of
the most important functions of local
government, and in the years which lie
ahead will assume even greater importance. All these services are interdependent and the Government consider,
therefore, that the responsibility for
health, housing and local government
should rest with one Department.
The need for such a new Ministry is, I
feel sure, generally agreed, but the
necessity for creating an additional
Government Department would not, I
imagine, be so readily admitted. The
Government have, therefore, decided to
abolish the Ministry of Public Security
and to add its functions to those of the
Ministry of Home Affairs, which will, of
course, under the Bill give up the functions which are to fall within the sphere
of the new Ministry of Health and Local
Government. But here I should like to
utter a word of warning. The abolition
of the Ministry of Public Security does
not mean that the necessity for our Civil
Defence Services no longer exists. The
need is as great as ever, as the recent
raids on many centres in Great Britain
clearly indicate.
The Ministry of Public Security has
done a fine job of work, so too have all
those the great majority in their spare
time-who have helped to maintain the
present efficient standard of our. Civil
Defence Services. I know the Ministry
of Home Affairs will be able to rely on
the same keen spirit of co-operation for
the safety of the community, and it is
scarcely necessary for me to urge that
only with the sounding of the last "All
Clear' can we slacken our efforts in this
most important work. And here I should
like to pay a special tribute to the present
Minister of Public Security and to his
predecessors in that office who had a
difficult task, and, I am sure, everyone
will agree that they carried it out in a
magnificent manner.. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.)
Ministries Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[The Prime Minister]
One other matter to which I should
like to refer is the machinery referred to
in Clause 4. As the House is aware, the
Government invited Sir Francis Floud,
a distinguished civil servant, who has a
very wide experience in the Imperial
Service of the complex questions of administration, to help in reviewing the
present distribution of duties between the
various Ministries. Conditions have
materially altered since our Departments
were first established, and the whole question of the re-allocation of functions is
being examined. This Clause had, therefore, been inserted to facilitate the
transfer of services between Departments
where it is thought expedient for
administrative reasons to effect such readjustments of responsibility.
I feel sure that this Measure will mark
an important stage in our progress
towards the creation of better conditions
of health and housing throughout the
country, and that it will commend itself
to the House as a whole. I beg to move.
Question proposed, "That the Bill be
now read a Second time."

sccial services are going to be before we
make a definite transfer from one Ministry to another.
The hon. Member for the University
also referred to a rumour that the staff
of the Ministry of Home Affairs which
have been dealing with health services
were to be transferred holus-bolus to the
new Ministry. There is no truth in any
such rumour, because the question of
transfer of staff has not yet been developed. I should hesitate to agree with
the hon. Member in the sweeping statement he made that we should sacrifice the
officers of the Ministry of Home Affairs,
who have many years' experience of
health services behind them, and try to
divert those activities into a completely
new channel. There are a great many
officers in the Ministry of Home Affairs
who are steeped in this business of health
.
services and local government and, in my
opinion, it would be criminal folly to
scrap that knowledge gained over the
years.
The hon. Member for South Down
referred among other things to the question of the Minister's salary. He suggested that the fact that it appeared in
the Bill as £1,300 was misleading to the
public. There is, of course, no such idea.
The £1,300 is paid to all Ministers as
heads of departments, and the balance of
their salary is made up by a share of the
pool of £2,500 which is paid to them as
Members of the Cabinet. That £2,500
has already been voted and, consequently,
it does not need to appear in any Bill,
and, in fact, it could not appear in this
Bill. The £2,500 is divided according to
the number of Ministers employed, but
it cannot in any case exceed £500 per
Minister.
It is perhaps necessary for me to point
out to the House that the setting up of
a new Health Ministry is not of itself a
cure for all the ills which we have to
meet and from which we suffer. I wish to
assure hon. Members that the Government are very much alive to the situation
and to the fact that money is going to
be at the bottom of all improvements.
We are now taking steps to ensure that
exceptional Exchequer treatment will be
accorded to local authorities towards
bringing into parity with Great Britain
those services which are below the
standard in Great Britain. Hon. Members will I know forgive me if I remind
them that in war time any exceptional
financial expenditure which has not
already been undertaken cannot be undertaken without prior consultation with the
Treasury and with their agreement. These
negotiations are at present going on. I
might also remind the House that already,
in spite of the fact that money cannot be
diverted from the war effort, a certain
amount of additional Exchequer assistance has been agreed to as the county
councils will be the first to testify.
Before developing that point I should
like to remind hon. Members that the
Public Health Act laid the responsibility
for the initiation and development of
health services in the main on local
authorities. No one can claim that the
authorities have done all they might have
done in that direction. In 1936, as hon.
Members are aware, the standard derat-
Superannuation [Money] 1016
Ministries Bill

ing grants were stabilised, and, consequently, no more money was paid by
the Government in excess of the 1936

the last Government we were quite

being done in Northern Ireland in war
time although they were themselves not

in Great Britain, which were stabilised in

there was undoubted preponderance of

definitely not on the same level as in

of Parliament, have been

a certain portion of the

for, with the result that considerable
capital expenditure is necessary in order
to raise the standard of these services to

I now revert again to the speech made
by the hon. Member for North Down.
He stressed the need for sanatoria. It is
not possible under present conditions to
treat adequately the tuberculosis patients
in Northern Ireland until we have this
capital assistance for sanatoria where
they can be treated. That is the first
step towards the treatment of tuberculosis, which I realise as much as anybody else is particularly rife in our Province. Had that capital expenditure
been met years ago clearly the cost of the
work would have been much lower than
it will be after the war, and it is here
that the exceptional financial assistance
to which I referred a week or so ago in
another connection is essential if the cost
of these works is not to lay too heavy a
burden on local authorities in the future.
Whatever form that assistance may take
-I am hopeful that I will be in a position to make a definite statement on the
subject in introducing the Budget next
month due regard will have to be paid
to all the circumstances, the amount
already accomplished in the areas of the
different local authorities and the amount
already borne for these services on their
rates, so that while aiming at uniform
services for the Province as a whole
those who went ahead more vigorously in
the past will not be at a disadvantage as
compared with their less go-ahead neighbours. That, however, is more a matter
for my right hon. Friend the new
Minister of Health and Local Government.

Major SINCLAIR: While this Resolution now authorises the payment out of
voted moneys of all the charges which
formerly fell upon the Teachers' Superannuation Fund, it does not mean that
the net cost to the Exchequer will be any
greater than it would have been under
the present system. It is simply a matter
of different accounting machinery. Instead of the payments being made from
the fund and the fund being assisted by
the Exchequer, in future payments will
be made direct from the Exchequer which
in return will be assisted by the income
of the fund and the teachers' contributions. I beg to move.
Mr. BEATTIE: As this is the Money
Resolution I should like to draw the
attention of the right hon. Gentleman to
a great hardship which might arise if
provision is not made in regard to a
certain section of teachers who did not
participate in the 1922-1936 lump-sum
arrangement. They claim that this
Money Resolution in some ways reverses
the conditions operating at the time that
lump-sum payment was granted. Through
their organisation they asked me to put
before the Minister the right of the 60
odd teachers who opted out to repay to
him the amount of money owing and to
give them the privilege and opportunity
of carrying on in continuity. That may
mean some financial adjustment, but it
will not be of a nature that will upset the
calculations of the right hon. Gentleman.
He will be receiving a reward in return
for the position he will establish because
he will bring all teachers under the lumpsum conditions from the date which has
been set out-1922-1936.
I asked him before about the matter but
the right hon. Gentleman had not an
opportunity of replying. I would ask
him to review the question in regard to
this small number of teachers and, in
view of the changed conditions in regard
to the lump sum, to reconsider their position and allow them to come in under the
lump sum payment on repayment of the
necessary sum. I have been requested by
the teachers' organisation to put this
matter before the Minister. The reason
the 60 odd members opted out was
because of the conditions of payment. The
conditions of payment were, of course, for
after the war. Now that the conditions
of payment have been changed and the
whole scheme has been revised, they feel
that if the Government have the right to
change their mind on the question of the
lump-sum payment they have also the
right to have their position reviewed.
They are willing to pay whatever percentage they are entitled to pay in order
to participate in the lump-sum payment
between 1922 and 1936. I would ask the
right hon. Gentleman to give the matter
his sympathetic consideration.
Dr. RENSHAW: I should like to
thank the Minister of Finance for the
way in which he has met the teachers with
regard to this question of the lump sum.
With a small deputation I had the
privilege of interviewing the Minister
with regard to this matter, and I wish to
I thank him for the courtesy with which
he received us on both occasions, and also
for the generous way in which he met us
with regard to the question of the lump
sum. There is one little matter in connection with pensions-he is not treating
'the pensioned and the pensionable
teachers alike. The pensionable teachers
after the 1st April this year will receive
certain specific treatment, whereas the
pensioned teachers, especially those who
retired some years ago, will lose a certain
fraction calculated to be somewhere
between one-ninth and two-ninths. I
think one of our morning papers
mentioned this matter.
I should like the Minister to look into
this matter and give it as generous treatment as he did in connection with the
lump sum. I am sure he will realise the
justice of the claim of these teachers as
they were teaching at a time when teaching was a calling and not a profession,
and when salaries were very small. I
mean by that that they had such an urge
to teach that they taught no matter what
the payment was. Since that time teaching has been raised to the dignity of a
profession, and the salaries are moving
in the right direction.
These teachers for whom I am pleading
to-day were teaching at the time when
salaries were purely subsistence allowances
and they went out on pensions which were
much smaller than those on which the
teachers of to-day are retiring. Some of
them, indeed, were on miserably small
salaries, and how they eked out an
existence I do not know. I think that if
1019 Superannuation [Money]-

Committee
the Minister looks into this matter he
will find it is a very small sum when
compared with the sum he has already
dealt with, and about which he has been
so magnanimous. I do hope that he will
view this other matter in the same light,
and wipe the slate clean so far as these
grievances by the pensioned teachers are
concerned.
Mr. NIXON: I only want to add my
voice to what has been said by the hon.
Member for Queen's University. The
Minister of Finance himself knows there
are anomalies in the pensions. They are
not so very big so far as the State is
concerned, but they are very serious for
the people affected. If anyone suffers at
all through light salaries in the teaching
profession, it is the elderly teachers who
have retired before 31st March, and yet
these are the teachers who are going to be
left out of what we may call the new or
amended scheme. From the financial
standpoint, or from any other standpoint,
it is wrong.
Furthermore, from the standpoint of
the Exchequer it is not worth while considering, because the outlook of life for
any person who has come to a certain age
is not very much. In proof of that, I
think there are only three or four Members on the Government side who entered
the first Parliament of Northern Ireland.
I only mention that to show it is not
worth while saving a few pounds at the
expense of the older people who have
retired. And it is wrong. The same
thing applies to some of the secondary
teachers. If a teacher retired on 31st
March he would get credit for one-third
of his past services prior to 1922, with
the result that he would receive a pension
of only £191. However, if he retired
after 31st March he would get £225.
There is something wrong about that. I
may not have explained the thing adequately, because I am not quite familiar
with it, and I have not the time to look
into it. There is an undoubted discrepancy which could be corrected.
Perhaps it is too much to ask the
Minister to make up his mind on the
subject now. I always find that by sleeping on a matter like this and thinking it
over, a better judgment is given. I do
not want the Minister to plead finance
involved. The finance in this case is not
worth talking about, and if the Minister
has nothing good to say on the subject at
the moment, I would recommend him to
keep it an open subject. I hope he will
not say anything that will bring me to
my feet again, because I do not want to
make speeches this afternoon. However, if he rejects this appeal on financial
grounds I will have to get up again. Is
it just, or is it not just? That is the
question. Is it just when a teacher who
retired on 31st March receives substantially less than the teacher who retired
the next day? The Minister knows it is
not just, and nothing that is not just
should exist. Let him do justice. I will
leave it there for the present, and I hope
that before the Minister speaks he
will weigh well if he can come to a
decision this afternoon, and if he cannot
give a decision this afternoon, I hope he
will defer his decision. I have seen good
coming from a deferred decision.
Mr. BROWN: I rise to support the
pleas made by the hon. Member for
Pottinger, the hon. Member for the
University, and the hon. Member for
Woodvale for the removal of certain
anomalies and disparities in this matter.
The Government should not have a
moment's hesitation in acceding to the request put forward. The sum involved is
very trifling. I am very pleased that the
Minister of Finance has gone a considerable way in this matter, because I was
one of those who supported the claim of
the teachers. I hope he will go the whole
way urged by the Member for Pottinger,
the Member for the University, and the
Member for Woodvale. I do not think
there is really anything to prevent him
doing so, and I hope he will see the
justice of the pleas that have been made
this afternoon.
We are getting well away from the
time when teachers were paid £30 a year
and lived under conditions referred to by
Oliver Goldsmith. We are living closer
to the time envisaged by Lord Wavell,
the new Viceroy of India, who said that
the world would be a better place when
teachers were paid a little more and
lawyers a little less. I agree with Lord
Wavell in that. I would like to express
my thanks to the Minister of Finance for
what he has already done, and I would
appeal to him most strongly to take into
consideration the views that have been
advanced, and in my opinion most reason-

ably and most convincingly advanced. I
hope he will have no hesitation in falling

Major SINCLAIR: In the first place,
let me say I should like to thank hon.
Members for what has been said about
what has been done for retired teachers
in the matter of lump-sum payments. I
have listened to the eloquence of hon.
Members pleading the question of pensions
for secondary teachers, but I must point
out to the Committee that pensions do
not arise on this Bill, which deals entirely
with lump-sum payments. The hon.
Member for Pottinger raised a point
which he also raised on the Second Reading, and, as he said, I did not have the
opportunity then of replying to it. That
was with regard to those teachers who had
the option in 1936 whether they would pay
contributions towards the lump sum or
not, and exercised that option to the extent of deciding they would not pay contributions, and would not, therefore,
enjoy the lump sum benefits. The hon.
Member was slightly in error when he referred to the 1936 scheme as being the
deferred scheme for paying lump sums
after the war. That was a different
scheme which came later, in 1940.
Mr. BEATTIE: I did not mean that
at all.
Major SINCLAIR: The position there
is that those teachers who in 1936, and
again in 1940, decided that they would
not qualify by contributions for lump
sums, are not now eligible for grants in
respect of service prior to 1922, which is
also now being included in the lump sum
payments. It was represented to me that
that would be a considerable hardship in
that the teachers, who were contributing,
were not being asked for contributions for
their years of service prior to 1922. In
consequence of that the lump-sum payment for those years was in the nature of
a free gift, and I felt it was only fair that
those who decided not to qualify for the
lump-sum payments in the ordinary way
by contributions should share in that free
gift, and that has been arranged.
Mr. BEATTIE: To clarify the position
a little bit better, it is those 14 years
between 1922 and 1936 to which I am
referring. When the decision to grant a
lump sum was brought in it was a sort
of lottery principle. It was decided that
the teachers should pay 1 per cent. for
the 14 years. I tried to the best of my
ability to get one hundred per cent. of
teachers included in the scheme. Unfortunately there was a small minority who
said they were not prepared to contribute
because, it was a lottery, and there was no
information as to the date of payment.
The old principle of the date of payment
has now been rearranged and the
Minister has changed his mind as to the
date of payment. The date of payment
was a contentious point in connection
with the refusal of a very low percentage
of teachers to contribute.
The Minister has now taken the opportunity of reversing his opinion as to that
date, and I think it is reasonable and
fair that he should allow those who were
opposed to the principle of the payment
to change their opinions, too, and should
permit them to come into the scheme.
These teachers will enjoy the privilege of
the 50 per cent. payments for the years
prior to 1922, without payment. What
they want to do is to link up the 14
years between 1922 and 1936. In other
words, they are now prepared to fall in
with the views of the majority of teachers
for continuity of payment of 1 per cent.
from 1922 right up to the date of retirement. I think the right hon. Gentleman
is not so unreasonable or so stiff as not
to concede the request which I am
making.
I have stated there are only about 40
teachers affected. There may be fewer at
the moment. I did all that one man
could do, and my organisation did all
that any organisation could do to try to
get these people to realise that, whilst
the date of payment was in doubt, the
principle embodied in this lump sum payment was good and would be beneficial at
some future date. It is not I who am
asking the Minister to do this. I am only
the medium here to-day of all primary
teachers in Northern Ireland who have
taken this step, and who are being helpful
to the Minister of Finance and the
Minister of Education in other spheres.
They have asked for the Minister to help
now, and I want the Minister to be

ADJOURNMENT MOTION.
THE BELFAST STRIKE.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That this House do now adjourn.".
(Sir Norman Stronge.)
Mr. BEATTIE: I have endeavoured
since I came into the House to get in
touch with the Minister of Home Affairs,
They have created a position which, I
think, is uncalled for, a position very
damning and very destructive of our war
effort in this city. It is likely to lead to
a very serious disorganisation of our war
effort, and I should have liked the right
hon. Gentleman who is responsible for
this law to have been in his place in the
House.
I am given to understand that
serious developments might take place
because of his attitude, and I was going
to make an appeal to him, as all reasonable people would be inclined to do, on
behalf of the five men who have been
made the victims, and are at the present
moment in Crumlin Road Jail. Their
presence there is likely to bring forth
something that will have a very serious
effect on war production.
As my interests are primarly concerned
in production for winning this war I am
prepared to go to any extent or do any
thing I can do to safeguard and protect
that productive element which is equipping us so well, that at the moment we
are on the road to victory. I do not want
anything to enter in that would mar
or destroy that position which we and our
Allies are now enjoying. I understand
that representations have been made to
the responsible Minister that the sentences
on these five men were very cruel and
harsh and not in keeping with the charge
preferred against them, and that the men
should be immediately released in order
to bring out the best that is in every
individual, so that this great production
about which we have heard so much may
be maintained. That is that point.
My next point is in reference to the
Minister of Labour. I notice in the
paper that he has agreed to call a composite conference. I want to ask him why
it was necessary to meet deputations
before he was able to come to a decision
The Belfast Strike
The Belfast Strike

that he would be the medium through
which the conference would be called, seeing the proper place for him to make that
decision was here last Thursday on the
representations which I made and which
were ably supported by Members on both

refused at the instigation of the Prime
Minister. We see now that the authority
of this House has been undermined-I
am not concerned so much about my
authority being undermined because if
what we have got in the papers is true, the

The
I am not concerned with whether the
Minister or the Prime Minister thinks
that the proper policy to adopt.
representatives that the Minister did

that good will result from the meeting,
and I trust that wiser heads on both sides
will see the reasonableness of the claim
which the men in Harland & Wolff's have
made and are continuing to make. In my

so far as an early settlement is concerned.
I am satisfied that the right hon."
Gentleman, the Minister of Home Affairs,
has provoked the men. He, and he only,
by referring the matter to the Attorney-
General, has provoked them. In his
personal capacity he hates and despises the
working class. On Thursday I referred

Why did the right hon. Gentleman not
put forward the Member for St. Anne's
(Mr. Warnock) as Crown Prosecutor to
prosecute these men? He had to get Mr.
Fox, a substitute for the Crown Prosecutor. I am leaving the Attorney-
General out. He gave his decision on the
cases referred to him by the right hon.
Gentleman. I have no complaint against
the Attorney-General. He did the job
that was referred to him.
Five men, one of them not a member

You have Mr. Baxter, Mr. McBrinn, Mr.

I say the democratic rights of the people
have been badly injured, insulted and

the community, of national production,
and of winning the war.
Those two right hon. Gentlemen must
be asked to give up the reins of office at

nearly had a conflict previous to this in

Allies by the "fumigation" incident.
That certainly was a very dangerous
thing to say. Things like those do not
raise the prestige of this country, and
other matters carried out by those two
authorities do not raise the prestige of
this country, such as questions affecting

Labour goes down to Eire and brings in

He is now reacting on these men and

I demand here and now that these men

is solely on the shoulders of the Government. That is the demand. The other

used the opportunity

When he raised this matter yesterday,
