The hon. Member for Pottinger intervened to say that they were not appealing, and it is true that they said that last

thought when I spoke in the House yesterday that they might change their minds;

In these circumstances I think it becomes a matter of public interest that the
reason for this prosecution should be
made plain without more ado, and that
the lie should be given to the suggestion
that any high-handed or Gestapo methods
were used in connection with these five

Mr. BEATTIE: No.
There
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL:
is nothing to support that. Of the five
men charged only one made a statement,
and that one made his statement voluntarily, and indeed with alacrity. The
case against these five men did not depend
upon statements made to the police; it
depended upon their own open and deliberate activities.
It is material to glance for a moment
at the situation that faced me.
And may
I say at once that the responsibility for
this prosecution is mine and no person
else's? The Executive, under our Constitution, has no right to direct a prosecution or to tell the Law Officer what
to do, and in this case there was no effort
on the part of my right hon. and learned
Friend the Minister of Home Affairs, or
on the part of anyone else, to tell me
that pressure should be brought by way
of prosecution to bear on any person who
had gone on strike. In fact, the papers
on which I was bound to act, and which
came to me direct from the police, did
not pass through the Ministry of Home
Affairs or any other Ministry.
But what was the position with which
I was faced? I propose to set it out as
shortly as I can, and to leave hon. Mem-
'bers here and the public outside to make
up their minds. I wish to inform them
that the question to be decided is not the
liberty of the five men, but whether we
are to have the rule of law or anarchy.
It is quite apparent to me from what has
happened in this case, and from what
happened before the strike, that those
responsible for it not only issued a challenge but issued a challenge which they
hoped would be taken up.
.
The present strike at Short & Harland's
was not the result of any grievance
against the firm on the part of those in
its employment. They ceased work without making any claim or request in so
far as their wages or working conditions
were concerned. They acted in concert.
They withdrew their labour in such large
numbers as to cause a serious hold-up in
the supply of essential war equipment and
to make the prosecution of all the individuals concerned quite impracticable.
There can be no doubt that these two
factors and the illegal nature of the
strike were fully appreciated by those who
organised this particular stoppage at
Short & Harland's. This stoppage was
deliberately planned. On 5th March the
following resolution at a meeting of
Belfast shop stewards was passed and
published:
That the members of the Shop
Stewards' Movement are in full
sympathy with the men on strike in
the shipyard, and demand that the
The Strike in Belfast
The Strike in Belfast
5 APRIL 1944

Government, who are their employers,
force their management in the shipyard
to meet the claim of the strikers in the
true spirit of arriving at a speedy
settlement. Failing that the Shop
Stewards' Movement will place the full
strength of the workers of Belfast behind the men on strike.
I say nothing as to the merits of the
dispute at the shipyard. But the strike
there was not only unofficial in the sense,
that it was not sponsored or supported by
the trade unions concerned; it was illegal
and plainly contrary to the terms of the
Northern Ireland Conditions of Employment and National Arbitration Order,
which was made in 1940, and is identical
with the corresponding Order in Great
Britain, made by the Minister of Labour
after consultation with the trade unions
and the employers' associations. This
resolution, which I have read, therefore
amounted to a threat of direct action in
support of a clear breach of the law and
regardless of the attitude of responsible
trade unionism.
Further, it is important to observe that
it depended for its effect on the very circumstances which make this whole matter
one of extreme gravity-namely, the
approaching crisis in the battle with
Germany and the urgent need for supporting our armed forces with the full
weight of our industrial effort. It constituted a challenge to constitutional
methods and the rule of law, which could
not but cause me most serious concern.
But the hope that wiser counsels would
prevail and the difficulty of obtaining
sufficient evidence as to those responsible
for the resolution made proceedings at
that stage inadvisable. The threat thus
made was some days afterwards implemented by the mass stoppage at Short &
Harland's.
The men who were prosecuted last
Monday for taking part in this stoppage
were not picked upon at random. Men
do not strike in concert in large numbers
and
in such circumstances without
leaders, though they may not fully understand or share the motives of their
leaders. The defendants who were convicted were beyond all question leaders in
this strike.
Mr. BEATTIE: McAteer.
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL:
including McAteer.
I am
Mr. BEATTIE: He was not a leader.
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL: They
held meetings and exhorted the
strikers not to go back. They made
every effort to sustain the strike
and to prevent a drift back to work.
They warned those attending the meetings not to drift back to work. On the
evidence presented to the court, it is plain
that they were out to manifest their power
by promoting a strike which they knew
to be illegal and which they knew would
result in a weakening of the effort which
the waging of war now so urgently
demands.
In these circumstances the conduct of
the men concerned could not be overlooked. In my opinion, to do so would
have been contrary to my duty and to the
due administration of the law which is
essential to stability and good government in this country. The Resident
Magistrate who heard the case with a
fairness and impartiality which was
acknowledged by the men themselves,
came to the conclusion that they had
broken the law "deliberately, callously
and calculatedly." I think that that
finding at least shows that I had before
me a plain prima facie case which
warranted the decision at which I arrived.
In conclusion, I must observe again
that in a case of this kind, so far as I
am concerned, the matter for consideration is not the rights or wrongs of a trade
dispute.. The choice here was between
letting things drift from bad to worse and
refusing to countenance a deliberate
breach of the law, fraught with grave
consequences which were well known to
those who were prosecuted. To have
taken the first course would have meant
encouraging mob law and putting a
premium on anarchy. The course which
was adopted may be used in an attempt
to cause more trouble by those who are
ready and willing to reduce the national
effort at this juncture. But in my view
it was the only course open to me compatible, with the discharge of my duty,
and I venture to think that, viewed dispassionately, and in perspective, that
opinion will have the support of all
responsible citizens at this time.

I feel I am in duty bound to say that
at the present time this strike is a real
tragedy, and I believe if the Prime
Minister now rises to the occasion something good might come out of the evil
that has been done by sending these five
men to prison. Any time I heard them
addressing meetings they were always
pleading for increased production to bring
about the destruction of Hitler, and
despite all their pleadings to help industry they are in prison now. I believe
some good would come out of such a conference as I have suggested, and as far
as I am concerned I am at the Prime
Minister's disposal. We want to get the
shipyard workers and the aircraft workers
back to their jobs so that we will have
increased production and get Hitler
defeated as soon as possible. After that
we can start with the greater job of
rebuilding Ulster and making it a better
place in which to live.

I hesitate to enter into a debate on

These men only now realise or think

official representatives of the
the trades

in the streets of Belfast from 26,000 to

People are getting concerned about this

I can remember those prosecutions were

The MINISTER OF FINANCE
(Major Sinclair): This is a necessary
Resolution on the Ministries Bill, the
purposes of which have already been explained to hon. Members on the Second
Reading.
It may, first of all, be desirable to
explain the necessity for the segregation
under two heads of the charge on public
funds in the Resolution. There is already
a general statutory provision under
Section 4 of the Administrative Provisions
Act (N.I.), 1925, under which the administrative expenses, including the salaries
and remuneration of staff, of all Departments of the Government are charged on
public funds and it is only therefore
technically necessary to apply this provision to the administrative expenses of
the new Ministry of Health and Local
Government. Specific provision is, on the
other hand, made in the Bill for the
annual salaries of the Minister and Parliamentary Secretary.
The Vote on Account for the current
financial year was framed on the basis of
the Departments now existing, and
revised Estimates will accordingly require
to be submitted to Parliament in due
course in order to give effect to the new
proposals.

The
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL:
intentions underlying Clause 4 have been
rather misapprehended judging by the
debate yesterday. That Clause has,
broadly speaking, a two-fold object. First
of all it is designed to implement the
previous Clauses, particularly Clause 1.
It will be understood that the setting up
of a new Ministry is a complicated operation. The new Ministry will have to
deal with and administer functions under
a great many different Acts of Parliament, and it is essential to feed the
general provisions of Clause 1 by a series
of Orders in Council which will transfer
the various functions and enable the new
Ministry to act. Clause 4 goes further
than that. The second object is to enable
the Government by the ordinary means
of Order in Council to take the executive .
steps needed to provide for any necessary
adjustments between the various departments existing for the time being. There
is nothing new or novel about the form of
this Clause; it has been adopted by this
Parliament before.
I should point out for the information
of hon. Members that it is not a Clause
giving what one might call delegated
legislative power. It is a Clause dealing
with what are essentially executive functions-executive functions with regard to
the allocation of duties amongst the
various departments of the Government.
In the ordinary course this is a matter
for the Crown. Under the Government
of Ireland Act such executive functions
were exercised by the Crown, though, of
course, subject to any Act of this Parliament.
It is quite obvious that even when,
the new Ministry gets all its statutory
functions dealt with and is equipped
legally for its task there will be quite a
number of consequential modifications to
be made with regard to other Ministries.
It may well be, following on the recommendations of the Floud Report, that as
the result of the setting up of this new
Ministry, the abolition of the Ministry
of Public Security and the modification
of the Ministry of Home Affairs, it will
be expedient, in view of the Government,
to alter the balance of other functions.
I
Take the question of roads. From one
point of view roads are a matter of local
government; from another point of view
they are undoubtedly connected with
public transport. Again from another
point of view they involve traffic
rules and regulations for road vehicles,
and it might be said from that
aspect that they concern the Department responsible for law and order.
It is felt that the Government should not
be rigidly bound in these matters, but
that they should be free and able to make
such amendment as may be necessary.
would suggest that these executive
matters be left to the Government. Of
course any Government can abuse their
powers, but the whole nature of this Bill
goes to show that the Government are not
anxious to abuse their powers, but rather
to implement the various recommendations which Members of this House have
put forward from time to time. I would
point out that the more executive power
that is taken away from the Government
the less power Parliament has to criticise
the Government for the exercise of their
executive functions.
It is necessary in this Clause to implement what has gone before. It is also
necessary in the public interest that the
Government should be free to fashion the
best instruments for doing the job. If
this House at any time thinks the
Government have mis-allocated their
functions, it can make its views felt very
clearly.

pass an Act of Parliament in regard to
every single one of these particular functions. I take it from the speeches I have
heard that the chief anxiety of Members
is that it should not be presented with a
fait accompli by the Government in the
shape of a transfer of some function from
one Ministry to another which was not
contemplated by the terms of this particular Measure. I may say that is
entirely reasonable, and it is not the
desire of the Government that the House
should be kept out of consultation in the
exercise of its powers, though I again
stress that executive responsibility must
remain with the Government.
One suggestion has been made that this
Clause be limited to matters of health and
housing. There is a very real and substantial difficulty there. In the first place
matters of health and housing have
attached to them all sorts of things which
are not technically health and housing
functions, and it would be difficult,
technically and administratively, to carry
out Clause 1 if Clause 4 were limited in
that way. What I was endeavouring to
do while hon. Members were speaking was
to find some way of meeting the substance of the points which have been put
forward so clearly by the various Members who have spoken, and I think I have
hit on
a form of amendment which I
should like to submit to the Committee
and which, I think, may meet its views.
I have referred to an Amendment on the
Report Stage, but I am reminded that, if
no amendments have been put down, the
Report Stage is automatic, and I think
it would be better that I should put before
the Members who have raised the point
an Amendment to be submitted in
another place.
What I would propose, therefore, is to
add to Clause 4 a sub-clause which will
provide that before any Order in Council
is made it should be put before the
House in draft form so that hon. Members
if they object to it will have the opportunity of debating it and if they so
determine an opportunity of preventing
its becoming a fully-fledged Order in

Newry Potato Processing Factory.
The following question stood on the
Order Paper in the name of Mr. Brown:
1. To ask the Minister of Finance
whether he can state the amount which
has been or will be paid to the Newry
Urban District Council in respect of, or
in lieu of rates in the case of the potato.
processing factory in Newry; whether he
can explain the present position generally
in this matter and what it will be in

Number of Motor Accidents.
Mr. ANDREWS asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he can state the
number of motor accidents in Northern
Ireland during the year 1943 and the
number of deaths; the numbers for the
city of Belfast; the numbers in the same
areas for the present year up-to-date;
and whether he will undertake to consider
means by which the position can be substantially improved.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Mr. Lowry): The number of accidents
involving motor vehicles in Northern Ireland during the year 1943 was 1,065
resulting in 138 deaths. The figures for
Belfast for the same year were 477 and
48. In the first two months of 1944 the
figures for Northern Ireland were 205 and
26, and for Belfast 81 and 10.
I may say that the total number of
road accidents during 1943 was the lowest
since 1930.
Since the outbreak of war the Ministry,
through the Press, the cinema and the
wireless, has constantly directed the
attention of road users to the increased
dangers due to the black-out. Special
lectures on road safety have been given
to school children, and, in co-operation
with the Ministry of Education, teachers
have been asked to include instruction on
safety measures as a regular part of the
school curriculum.
Mr. ANDREWS: I am grateful to my
right hon. Friend for his reply. I should
be also grateful to him if he would look
into the matter further.
Mr. LOWRY: This matter is constantly engaging attention, and with the
right hon. Gentleman's permission I propose to write him giving full information
on this topic since statistics were first kept
on the subject.
Mr. ANDREWS: Thank you.

Repair of a Belfast Building.
Mr. BROWN asked the Prime Minister
whether it is a fact that his Department
or any other Government Department has
issued a licence for the reconstruction of
29 Linenhall Street, Belfast, whether the
purpose of reconstruction is to provide
Written Answers
Adjournment
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Brown]
motor-car show rooms; whether the reconstruction involves the erection of a
wooden staircase and a two-tons hoist;
and whether in view of the restrictions
in regard to motor-cars he will state how
he justifies the issue of valuable and
essential materials for such a purpose.
Mr. MAGINESS: I have been asked
by my right hon. Friend to reply.
A licence was granted by the Ministry
for the repair of the building to which
the hon. Member refers. This building
had suffered slight damage by fire. The
licence was not granted for the purpose
of providing a motor-car show room, but
in carrying out the repairs the owner was
permitted to make limited adaptations to
the building to render it suitable for
carrying on the work of a tyre service
depot. The licence was not intended to
cover the erection of a wooden staircase
or a hoist, but I understand that a staircase has been erected and a hoist shaft
has been constructed with a view to the
installation of a hoist as and when the
supply position makes it possible for the
owner to obtain a suitable hoist. The
question as to whether the terms of the
licence have been observed is being
investigated.
With regard to the last part of the
hon. Member's question, the licence was
granted on the understanding that the
building would be used by a tyre service
depot approved by the Tyre Control for
the conduct of business for which suitable
premises were not available.

Bank Holiday on Twelfth of July.
1,
1. Mr. THOMPSON asked the
Prime Minister whether he is aware that
the Belfast banks were open on the 12th
July last year, when all shops, warehouses
and factories were closed; whether it is a
fact that many of the banks had not a
single customer and the majority only two
or three; and whether he will take steps
to see that the 12th of July is in future
proclaimed a bank holiday, and thus ensure that the employees of the banks enjoy
this holiday with the rest of the Province.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Mr. Lowry): I have been asked by my
right hon. Friend to reply.
The 12th of July last year was not
officially proclaimed a bank holiday, but
steps are being taken, in pursuance of the
Bank Holiday Act, 1871, and other
relevant statutes, with a view to appointing the 12th of July next as a special day
to be observed as a bank holiday and as a
public holiday in Northern Ireland.

Gentleman also take steps to have the
First of May declared a general holiday
in Northern Ireland?
Mr. NIXON: Is it not a fact that the
12th of July was declared and proclaimed
a bank holiday at one time? Who
allowed that bank holiday to lapse in
1940? Who was the Prime Minister in
office in 1940 who did not keep it up?

The ATTORNEY-GENERAL
leave of the House): I think there is a
misapprehension as to the meaning of
this term statutory period." It is a
period inside which either House has the
right to take certain steps, and the
statutory period is computed in respect
of each House, and accordingly for this
House the statutory period reckons the
days on which this House sits. In another
place the statutory period reckons the
days on which that House sits and not
when this House sits. In other words,
the sitting days for Members of this
House have regard to the days on which
this House sits, and the sitting days of
the Senate have regard to the days on
which that House sits.

TRADE BOARDS BILL.
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Grant): This Bill proposes two amendments to the Trade Boards Act (Northern
Ireland), 1923, under which our present
system of Trade Boards was established. I
hope both amendments will commend
themselves to the House, but before dealing with them in detail it may help any
hon. Members who may not be familiar
with this subject if I say a few words
Trade Boards Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Grant]
about what trade boards are and what
they do.
We have in Northern Ireland eighteen
trade boards and each board consists of
equal numbers of representatives of employers and workers in a particular trade
with an independent chairman and, in
some instances, two other independent
members, appointed by the Ministry of
Labour. The board have statutory powers
to regulate the wages of the various
classes of workers in the trade by fixing
the minimum rates at which they must
be paid. They meet from time to time
to consider whether rates should be fixed,
varied or cancelled, and when they settle
on any proposals they give notice to all
interested
and allow time for
persons
objections to be lodged and considered.
When the board reach a final decision
they notify the Ministry of Labour of the
wage-rates they have fixed and the
Ministry, unless there is any point to
refer back for further consideration,
makes an Order giving the force of law
to the board's decision.
Workers who are employed in trades to
which this system applies fall into two
broad classes-time-workers, that is to
say, people who are paid so much an hour
or so much a week, and piece-workers
who are paid according to their output,
say, so much for a garment or for a
dozen articles or whatever the customary
unit may be. For all classes of timeworkers in the trade the board must fix
appropriate general minimum time-rates,
and for men and women on piece-work
they must fix minimum rates on a time
basis by which the yield, to an ordinary
worker, of the piece-rates paid by an
employer can be judged.
In addition to these duties the board
are given certain powers, including one to
fix general minimum piece-rates so that,
in the case of a job which is more or
less standard throughout the trade, they
can, if they like, actually lay down the
minimum rate to be paid for it. The
existing law, therefore, contains provision
for securing that the piece-rates paid to
a worker in a trade board trade shall be
adequate but, unfortunately, that does not
always in practice mean that the worker's
earnings are adequate. If, for example,
a worker, even of ordinary skill and experience, is put on to work which is new
to her, her earnings for a time may be
unduly low until she has become familiar
with the operations and worked up her
speed. Some employers recognise this
and voluntarily make allowance for it,
but others, I am sorry to say, do not.
I had recently a case brought to my
notice in which some stitchers who were
experienced in one end of the makingup industry, in which they were able to
earn about £2 a week, were transferred to
another where at first they could carn
only about 10s or 15s, although the actual
piece-rates on which their earnings were
based were satisfactory when tested by
their yield to employees familiar with
the work. Transfers to new work are
more necessary now than in peace-time
as many firms have frequently to switch
over from their normal products to a
different type of article urgently required
for war purposes. To give a board power
to remedy this type of hardship the Bill
proposes, in Clause 1, to enable them to
fix guaranteed time-rates.
If the board so decides, then workers
engaged on piece-work, while entitled
to whatever they can earn on the piecerates, will be protected by the underlying
guarantee of a minimum sum for each
hour spent on the job. The incentive
given by a piece-rate to work hard, produce more and earn more money will remain, but the worker will be safeguarded
to a reasonable extent if it should happen
that his or her output is below normal.
It will be seen from the clause that the
guaranteed time-rate must not be fixed
at a higher point than the general
minimum time-rate. This is only fair,
as otherwise piece-workers would be in a
preferential position and getting the best
of two worlds. I should like to emphasise
to hon. Members that sub-section 2 of
Clause 1 makes it clear that a board need
not fix a guaranteed time-rate to apply
indefinitely, but that they can limit its
operation to some specified period if they
think that is all that is required.
The second object of the Bill is dealt
with in Clause 2. It is a comparatively
minor point relating to procedure. I
mentioned earlier that if a board propose
to fix new rates or change existing ones
they must, before coming to a final decision, send out notices of their proposal
and allow time for objections to be
lodged. Now it happens fairly frequently
that no objections are lodged and a
further meeting, which involves extra
travelling and a loss of time and money,
2 MAY 1944
Trade Boards Bill-
Second Reading
is therefore unnecessary. The Amendment put forward will enable the board,
if they wish, to decide at the meeting
when they settle on their proposals that
if there are no objections within the
statutory time limit the rates they have
proposed will then become automatically
fixed and can be sent on to the Ministry
for confirmation.

titled to at least the minimum time rate
that applies to the trade in general. This
is to give that power to the board. I am
rather surprised that the board did not
take the power of themselves, because it
is really the custom, and there is precedent
for it set up by all recognised authorities
from the employers' side and from the
trade union side. Perhaps they find it
necessary to give the power to the trade
board, and I am not one who is going to
make any objection to the power being
given.
These two Amendments will, in my
opinion, make a definite improvement in
our trade boards legislation, and I recommend them to the House for favourable consideration. As I have explained,
the first is to extend the powers which a
trade board have under the present law
by enabling them, if they think it desirable, to fix for piece-workers what are
described as guaranteed time-rates. The
second is to enable a Board-again if they
think it desirable-to cut out what is,
in some circumstances, an unnecessary
meeting.
Hon. Members will notice that in both
cases I used the words "enable” and “if
they think it desirable," and I want to
stress that this is purely an enabling Bill.
I beg to move.
Question proposed, "That this Bill be
now read a Second time."
Mr. BEATTIE: I must say that the
extension of the trade boards does fall in
with the wishes of the party which I have
the honour to represent in this House.
I think they have fathered the trade
boards for many years, and when we get
a glimpse of brightness in regard to
workers' conditions being regulated by
the voice of representatives of these
workers, we cannot reasonably make any
objection. The extension of these trade
boards to cover other classes of workers,
which we would like to see covered, would
certainly be a boon and a benefit to those
other trades.
But with regard to the extension asked
for in this Bill, and particularly in regard
to the Clause dealing with a guaranteed
minimum rate for piece-workers, I do not
see that it required an Act of Parliament
to do that. It has been the law for some
considerable time. It may not be legally
so, but it is the law which has operated in
all firms that the piece-worker who is
getting it rather hard during the week
and cannot make the time rate-a clear
understanding has always existed—is en-
I do feel that the Bill is a step forward,
and if it is only half a step and it is in
the interests of the working classes and
the industry in which they are employed,
I would support it. I am one that always
tries to bring his side to review a Measure
in the light of the circumstances in which
it has been introduced. I am waiting for
the day when all trades and all workers
will be regulated by trade boards and will
be allowed a guaranteed minimum wage,
a wage that will be commensurate with
the standard of life and the amenities for
which workers are clamouring at the
moment, and which have been denied to
them in the past. I believe we will have
to legalise certain rates for certain industries and guarantee to the workers that
no man, woman, boy, or girl will work
below the standard which is adequate to
meet the requirements of the life which
they should live and be allowed to live.
I believe it has been the right hon.
Gentleman's desire to move forward a
little from his predecessors, but he is
moving at a slow rate. Perhaps he may
claim that it is surer going slowly than
going fast, but I would ask him to review
all industries in Northern Ireland and in
the city of Belfast in particular, to see
if he cannot bring every trade and calling
in which any man, woman, boy, or girl
works and receives wages, under control
to the extent that these workers will be
guaranteed at least a wage, commensurate
with the labour which they have applied.
I welcome the measure, and I must say
the right hon. Gentleman has my support
in every respect, and I hope he will
continue developing this kind of law
meantime.
Mr. THOMPSON: As one who has
been associated with trade boards practically since they were set up, I also
should like to express my full apprecia-

tion of both these clauses. I did think

Health Services.
FAMILY ALLOWANCES FOR
TUBERCULOUS PATIENTS.
1. Dr. LYLE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he is aware that
for a considerable time past in Great
Britain the families of tuberculous
patients in hospitals or sanatoria have
been in receipt of family allowances, and
whether he will provide identical treatment for families of tuberculous patients
in Northern Ireland as recommended by
the Select Committee on Health Services.
The following question stood on the
Order Paper:
2. Mr. STEVENSON: To ask the
Minister of Home Affairs whether
the Government has given consideration to
the recommendation of
the
on
Parliamentary Select Committee
Health Services to pay family allowances
for the benefit of persons suffering from
pulmonary tuberculosis to enable them
to leave remunerative employment and
undergo treatment for the disease.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Mr. Lowry): With the hon. Members'
permission I propose taking this question
and No. 2 together, as they relate to the
same subject.
I am happy to inform the hon. Members that this matter has received the
sympathetic consideration of the Government, which has decided to grant maintenance allowances similar to those
granted in Britain for a like purpose.
It is recognised that when facilities for
diagnosis and treatment are available it
is important that those who give up work
temporarily for treatment should be able
to do so without financial anxiety as to
the maintenance of their dependants.
The Government has, therefore, approved
of a scheme for the payment of certain
allowances, conditional on the patient's
undergoing a course of treatment prescribed by the tuberculosis officer, conforming to any advice given to him for
preventing the spread of infection, and
attending at the dispensary for examination as required.
The persons who have been primarily
in mind for the purpose of these arrangements are persons gainfully occupied and
with dependants, whose source of income
necessarily ceases when treatment is
undertaken either in an institution or at
home, but allowances will also be payable
to persons without dependants, whose
source of income necessarily ceases when
approved treatment is undertaken at
home; an applicant whose sole income is
unearned will not qualify for maintenance allowances.
The allowances are payable to persons
already under treatment as well as to new
cases, including those discovered as
suffering from the disease by the new mass
miniature radiography unit, in addition
to those detected by ordinary clinical
examination. Allowances will not be
payable in respect of chronic active cases,
that is, persons in whom the disease is
stabilised but still active in spite of treatment, the reason for this exclusion being
that in such cases the chances of cure are
remote and the object of the scheme is
to promote recovery to working capacity.
The approved allowances, to be paid in
the first instance by the local authority
(county or county borough council) and
subsequently recouped in full by the
Government, will take the following
forms:
-
.
(1) A standard rate of maintenance
(described as "maintenance allowances') payable without inquiry into
means.
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Lowry]
The maintenance allowances should meet
the needs of the ordinary case, but for
cases of special difficulty there will also be
available on application :
(2) additional payments (described
as "discretionary allowances") at the
discretion of the authority and after
need has been established, towards
meeting exceptional commitments in
the way of charges incurred for high
rent or rates, hire purchase instalments,
insurance premiums and school fees;
and
(3) special payments to meet certain
special circumstances.
The allowances will be continued until
the patient is in a position to resume fullscale employment, but they will be
adjusted from time to time having regard
to his earning capacity or part-time employment pending his complete recovery.
Full particulars of allowances have
been communicated to local authorities,
and allowances will be paid in due course
when such authorities have set up appropriate machinery for dealing with applications.
Dr. LYLE: In regard to the answer of
the right hon. Gentleman, in which he
states that chronic active cases will not
receive family allowances, is it not desirable, and has it not been recommended,
in the Report of the Select Committee on
Health Services that these cases should
be isolated in order to prevent the spread
of the disease to heathy people and would
it not be desirable in that case that these
allowances should also be paid to these
chronic active cases, and that they should
be sent to some institution, or induced to
go to some institution, where they would
not be a danger to the community in
which they live?
Mr. LOWRY: The immediate object
of the allowances is to restore the earning
capacity of those gainfully occupied. The
allowance which the hon. Member contemplates is not within the similar allowances that have been sanctioned and are
being paid in Great Britain.
Mr. NIXON: As a question of fact,
is it actually recommended that chronic
cases of tuberculosis should be isolated?
Mr. LOWRY: No doubt it is recommended, but it is very largely a question
of accommodation.
Mr. NIXON: I should like to know
where it is recommended.
Does the
Mr. THOMAS BAILIE:
Minister not consider it harsh and unchristian that chronic cases should be
bereft of any benefit under the scheme?
Dr. LYLE: Arising from the replies
of the Minister, is it not actually more
important to prevent the spread of this
disease to people who are not affected by
it than to cure those already suffering
from it?
Mr. LOWRY: I have no doubt that
the preventing of the spread of the
disease is a matter of the highest importance, and it is hoped that the payment
of these allowances will do a great deal
towards preventing the further spread of
the disease.
Mr. NIXON: Is it not a fact that any

WRITTEN ANSWER.
Requisitioning of Land at Kilkeel.
Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether his Ministry has
requisitioned or taken over land. at
Kilkeel from the Provincial Building
Estates Ltd., and, if so, on what terms;
why they have done so in view of the
fact that the lands have been under
potato crops for four years and that now
about two-thirds of them are lying
derelict with nothing but weeds; whether
it is a fact that three inspectors with three
motor cars visited the lands on Thursday
week; whether he can state who is responsible for the stones and soil carted off
the land; and why the whole field was
not taken as half an acre is now wasted;
and whether he will inspect the place and
see the present state of this land which
forms some of the best in the Mourne
district.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Rev. Robert Moore): At the urgent
request of allotment holders in Kilkeel
my Ministry has requisitioned land from
The
Provincial Building Estates Ltd.
land has been used for allotments for the
past four years and the owners had
refused to renew the letting for this year.
The land has been let by the Ministry
to the Kilkeel Plot Holders Association.
The rent compensation which the owners
will receive for the requisitioned land will
be determined under the terms of the
Compensation (Defence) Act, 1939.
Arrangements have been made for the
cropping of a portion of the land, about
one-third, which has not so far been
taken up as allotments and I understand
that this area has been sown with oats.
Work is proceeding on the remainder of
the area which is let to allotment holders.
Two officials in one motor car visited the
lands at 8 p.m. on Thursday, 27th April.
A third official travelling by car
engaged on other duties in the district on
that day awaited their arrival.
The Ministry's responsibility does not
extend beyond the area requisitioned on
the 29th March, 1944; the portion not
requisitioned was not required and provides access to flax dams situate at the
end of the field. I do not consider any
useful purpose would be served by accepting the hon. Member's invitation to visit
this allotment site.

That the Regulations made by the Ministry of Labour on the 30th day of December, 1943, under Sections 33 and 46 of the
Unemployment Assistance Act (Northern

The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Grant): The Motions standing in my
name ask for the approval of the House
to the Supplementary Pensions and Unemployment Assistance Regulations which
3rd
were presented to Parliament on
January, 1944, and are now in full
operation.
The Supplementary Pensions Regulations embody in a single document the
rules which, for the time being, govern
the grant of supplementary pensions, and
the Unemployment Assistance Regulations do the same for unemployment
assistance. In the process of consolidation the opportunity was taken to make
some changes with a view to simplifying
the regulations and effecting improvements in the general standards of supplementary pensions and assistance. These
improvements are identical with those
introduced in Great Britain. The
schemes, therefore, remain the same
throughout the United Kingdom.
.
Scale rates have been fixed to meet
needs other than rent, and, so far as the
rent is concerned, the ordinary householder receives under the regulations a
rent addition equal to the rent which he
is actually paying, so far as it is reasonable having regard to the general rents
in the locality. Where the applicant is
living as a member of someone else's
household the rent allowance granted is
his due proportion of the rent paid by
the householder calculated on the basis of
the number of persons in the household,
but not less than 2s 6d nor more than
7s Od.
The scale rates remain the same
throughout the year and have been fixed
to take into account the winter allowances
which were formerly paid. Rates for
women have been made the same as the
corresponding rates for men and the distinction between the rate for a wife who
is a pensioner and one who is not has
been dropped. Differentiation between
town and country dwellers has been
abolished. Rates for children have been
improved. More favourable treatment
has been accorded to the earnings of the
applicant or of the husband or wife of
the applicant.
For instance, under the old regulations
the rule for supplementary pensions was
-ignore the first five shillings or, subject to a maximum of eight shillings, one
half of the weekly earnings, whichever
is the greater. The new rule introduced
by these regulations is-ignore for sup
plementary pensions purposes the first
10s 6d of the weekly earnings.

House of Parliament, I beg to move,

Ministry of Labour on the 30th day of
December, 1943, under Sections 33 and
46 of the Unemployment Assistance Act
(Northern Ireland), 1934, be hereby
approved."

ORAL ANSWERS TO
QUESTIONS.
Fires at Flax Mills.
1. Dr. RENSHAW asked the Minister of Public Security whether he can
state the number of fires at flax mills
during the past 12 months and the quantities of flax and tow destroyed by these
fires, and what special fire-watching precautions are taken where flax is either
stored or undergoing manufacturing
processes.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Rev. Robert Moore): I have been asked
by my right hon. Friend to reply.
There were 24 fires at scutch mills
during the 12 months ended 30th April
this year, but it is impossible to state the
actual quantities of flax fibre and tow
fibre destroyed in these fires. I can, however, inform the hon. Member that the
straw and fibre destroyed represented the
produce of 118 acres.
Fire-watching precautions are not compulsory, but I am satisfied that the existing Regulations made under the Scutch
Mills and Flax (Fire Insurance) Act provide as adequate precautions against fires
in scutch mills as in all the circumstances
it seems reasonable and practical to impose. Furthermore, having regard to the
longer scutching season and to the greater
number of mills now operating, the
number of outbreaks does not seem
abnormal.
Labourers' Cottages in Fermanagh.
3. Mr. THOMAS CAMPBELL asked
the Minister of Home Affairs whether
any scheme of agricultural labourers' cottages has been received from any rural
district council in Co. Fermanagh since
the Northern Government came into
being, and if so, the nature and date of
such scheme; whether it is a fact that not a
single cottage for an agricultural labourer
has been put up in that county since the
year 1912; whether shortly before the
first Great War all schemes in hand were
then suspended; whether it is a fact that
when a scheme is presented to a council
the formula is to adjourn it for six months
and adjourn it at the end of each six
months for another six months; whether,
as a result, labourers are living in old
shacks and damp and unsanitary places;
whether
labourers have gone away
many
from the county so that its quota under
crop has had to be fixed lower in proportion to the arable acreage than in any of
the other counties of Northern Ireland;
and whether it is a fact that a chairman
of the West Tyrone Unionist Association
wrote to the chairmen of the various
rural councils in Co. Tyrone and Co.
Fermanagh advising them to be careful
in the matter of such cottage schemes as
most of the applicants would be
Nationalists.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Mr. Lowry): Each of the rural district
councils in Co. Fermanagh has submitted
a scheme for the erection of labourers'
cottages under the Labourers Acts. These
schemes were submitted prior to the outbreak of the present war. The Enniskillen scheme provided for 62 cottages,
the Irvinestown scheme for 27 cottages
and the Lisnaskea scheme for 11 cottages.
All these schemes had to be suspended
owing to the outbreak of war. No cottages have been built in that county
under the Labourers Act schemes since
1912. I have no information as to any
adjournment of schemes in the manner
suggested by the hon. Member, but as he
will understand, the council may adjourn
dealing with the representations received
from labourers until a sufficient number
to warrant the making of a scheme has
been received. I agree with the hon.
Member that the housing conditions in
Co. Fermanagh leave much to be desired.
I have no information as to how many
labourers have left the county, but I am
informed that the reduction in the quota
.

WRITTEN ANSWERS.
Temporary Civil Servants.
Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Finance whether in view of his statement
in the House on 6-2-44 that there were
829 persons at present ranking as temporary civil servants in the employment
of the Northern Ireland Government
with over five years' service, and that
about 40 per cent. of these must be regarded as having no claim to established
rating, he can now state with reference
to the remaining 60 per cent.-how many
are ex-Servicemen; why these men have
been retained in Government employment
for so long if inefficient and if not inefficient why have they not been upgraded
to established rank; whether it is a fact
that of this latter class the Imperial Government automatically upgrade to established rank all those of this class who
have satisfactorily completed four years'
service in a temporary capacity, and if so
why has the Government departed from
the step-by-step policy; whether he is
aware that during the past year only five
temporary officers have been upgraded to
established rank in the Ministry of Labour
and none at all in the Assistance Board;
whether he can state the reason for this
discrimination and take immediate action
to instruct departmental chiefs, especially in the two Departments named, to
see that the step-by-step policy is maintained in this matter in the case of the
survivors of the last war who have been
so long in continuous temporary Government employment.
The
MINISTER OF FINANCE
(Major Sinclair): From the general tenor
of the hon. Member's question, I assume
that his concern is for the ex-Service temporary clerks in the Northern Ireland
Civil Service. The total number of ex-
Servicemen in such posts with five years'
service and upwards is 182. All these
temporary clerks have been considered
for established appointments more than
once, but the number of established posts
in any grade of the service must depend
upon, and be limited by, long-term staff
requirements, and therefore a process of
selection becomes necessary.
For the reason given to the hon. Member in my reply to his question of the
29th February last, it has been the policy
of our Government to fill established
appointments on a competitive basis with
efficiency as the main consideration in
determining selection; and it would not
be in accordance with the sympathetic
attitude towards ex-Servicemen, which
the Government has consistently adopted
for more than 20 years past, to dispense
with the services of men merely because in
competition with their fellow ex-Servicemen they failed to secure permanent appointments. It is our policy to retain
these men as long as they are capable of
discharging their duties and as long as
the need for their services continues.
I understand that the Imperial Government practice in the matter of establishing temporary clerks has not been
quite on the same lines as the practice
here, but that it would be an overstatement to say that the grant of established
status on completion of any prescribed
period of service as a temporary clerk in
the Imperial Service is automatic. Indeed
my information is that all establishments
under the conditions laid down by the
Imperial authorities ceased about two
years ago, while in our service establishments are still proceeding. On this part
of the question I would refer the hon.
Member to the observations of my predecessor in answer to a question put to
him on the 10th February, 1942-Official
Report, Vol. XXV, col. 117.
Finally, I would explain that establishment does not rest with departmental
chiefs, but with the Civil Service Commissioners for Northern Ireland, of whom I
am one. The procedure in the case of
serving officers is to call for recommendations from Departments, to arrange for
the interview of all recommended can-

Lump Sum Payments to Teachers.
Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Finance whether he can state approximately when those affected by the Superannuation (Teaching Services) Bill are
likely to receive the payments authorised
by that Bill.
Major SINCLAIR: In reply to the
hon. Member, the teachers' superannuation schemes, authorising the payment of
lump-sum allowances to teacher pensioners
in accordance with the recently announced
concession, have been presented to Parliament, and on approval by Parliament will
require confirmation by Order in Council.
In the case of the public elementary
school teacher-pensioners, it should be
possible to commence the issue of the payments towards the end of this month and
complete them during June. In respect
of other classes of teacher-pensioners,
payments will commence immediately
after the schemes have been approved by
Parliament and confirmed by Order in
Council.

reports of future appointments
suppressed at my instigation. I adhere to

on the 15th February last regarding the

eloquence to which you have been

I cannot emulate her, but I can and do
bring energy and enthusiasm to bear,
which is only equalled by my desire to
serve my day and the rising generation.
In the few weeks at my disposal since I
became Minister of Education, though I
have had the fullest co-operation of a very
willing and efficient staff, I have not been
able to touch more than the fringe of the
problem, and that has been almost exclusively directed towards the framework
of the proposed White Paper and subsequent Education Bill. I must, therefore,
ask you to be to my faults a little blind
while I present this year's Estimates. I
shall not make a lengthy speech, wandering through every detail of our expenditure and administration, but shall deal
only with matters which I think are of
particular importance, and shall do my
best to answer afterwards any questions
that may be put to me on matters arising
out of the Estimates.
We are asking this year for £2,869,633
with which to carry out our activities, an
increase of £87,526 over last year. About
£6,000 of this is attributable to the No. 1
Vote for the staff of the Ministry, and is
due to three factors-war bonus payments
to staff, the appointment of an additional
principal officer in connection with the
service of youth and an increase in the

the total Estimate-about £81,000arises from payment of increased war
bonus to teachers, a very large provision
of grants in respect of meals and milk
schemes, and an increase of about £17,000
in the Estimate for youth welfare. On
the other hand, our estimate for expenditure on air-raid protection has greatly
fallen, as was to be expected, but the net
increase in the total Estimates is, as
previously mentioned, £87,526.
Our schools of all categorieselementary, technical and secondary-continue to function with their usual standard of efficiency in spite of the fact that
their difficulties in the fifth year of the
It is
war have not grown any less.
becoming more and more difficult to find
staff for appointment as substitutes in the
elementary schools, while the technical
and secondary schools have practically
reached the stage when teachers of
mathematics and science are not to be
secured; text books are becoming scarcer,
transport is a problem, and over all is the
natural and proper demand that the
children shall give their own contribution to the general war effort. I am glad
to say that this is being done-salvage

carried out with zest and enthusiasm and,
so far as the Ministry is aware, without
any loss to the content of the education
of the children themselves. Hon. Members will agree with me, I am sure, that
the contribution of the school children in
this respect is very valuable; it teaches
them that they are not isolated individuals but members of a community, that
they have a duty to that community, and
that when they leave school it will still be
their duty to interest themselves in their
fellow-citizens and help them and their
country to the best of their ability.

there are admitted difficulties in the

We must always bear in mind the claims

It will also interest hon. Members to

from less than 13,000 to 17,500. I

above all, what is most gratifying from

children are entering the secondary
school earlier in life and staying on

This increase in numbers has created

Hon. Members who represent Belfast constituencies probably know that in

Our technical schools also have been

on young people, both in day and evening

hardly say that these schools continue to

and other branches of the national effort;

I have done no more than sketch
briefly the work done in our schools, but
there is one matter on which I should
like to speak more fully, the supply of
meals and milk in schools. I think it is
generally known that this service is under
the control of local education authorities
who have the advantage of very generous
grants from the Ministry: we provide,
free of cost, all kitchen and table equipment, we pay 100 per cent. grants for
milk and 90 per cent. for meals, it being
always understood that the child who is
able to pay for milk does so, and for a
meal the cost of the uncooked materials:
It will be seen then that the cost to the
education authority of a meals and milk
scheme is comparatively small. One
would expect where there exists a demand
from the parents of the children for the
provision of meals and milk there would
be no hesitation on the part of the
education authority immediately to take
steps to meet the demand. It is
regrettable that in many areas nothing is
done; the difficulties, and admittedly
there are difficulties in rural areas, are
stressed and enlarged, time is wasted
talking about them when a little practical
work in putting an experimental scheme
into force would be of more value than
countless meetings and debates. Every
education committee which has started a
scheme has found that it works and that
it confers an undoubted advantage on
the children of the schools; there are
other committees which, after two years,
are still debating the matter and trying
to find difficulties rather than solutions.
This is most disappointing; the money is
available, the equipment can be got, the
parents in many cases want the schemes
and still the meals and milk are not
provided. Belfast is supplying 4,000
meals a day and no fewer than 45,000
children in this city are receiving milk;
only last week the Ministry approved of a
scheme for the provision of three kitchens
in various parts of the city which will
have an output of about 6,000 meals
every day. Again in County Down most
welcome progress has been made, and I
would urge those other education committees which have not yet even made a
beginning to reflect and consider seriously
whether they are carrying out their duty
to the children of their area. Many of
them are actually working on the preparation of schemes, and these the
Ministry is helping and advising as best
it can.
We hope that the day is not far
distant when we shall be able to report
that there is no education committee in
Northern Ireland which has not in
active operation a meals and milk scheme.

This is a great increase, but fully
justified; the youth movement is making
very gratifying progress. As hon.
Members are aware, the Youth Welfare
Act was passed by this Parliament in
January of this year, and the Youth.
Committee was established by my predecessor immediately afterwards, with the
hon. Lady as chairman. I am pleased
to be able to inform the House that she
has accepted my invitation to retain this
important position. The Committee
comprises ladies and gentlemen of wide
knowledge and experience of youth welfare in its many forms, and has addressed
itself to its task with great energy and
enthusiasm, as is quite evident from the
many careful minutes and memoranda
they have forwarded to the Ministry. I
think the Committee may fairly claim,
and I would certainly support their
claim, that there is a growing sense of
public responsibility for the welfare of
boys and girls. The movement is spreading rapidly, but on excellent lines which
all must commend; there is an increasing.
number of new youth institutions which
are being organised by the various
churches and other bodies, and there is a
steady expansion of the long-established
organisations such as the Boy Scouts, the
Boys' Brigade, and the Guides. Another
feature which is particularly gratifying
is the realisation that there is a great
need for youth work among girls, and
that this need must be met urgently.
This week, as I hope all hon. Members
know, is Youth Week in Belfast, when
under the auspices of the Standing Conference of Youth Organisations displays
and exhibitions of the many activities in
which youth engages are being given and
when many of the clubs and organisations
are open to the public. The youth movement depends in the final issue on the
support it receives from the public at
large; Youth Week is designed to show
the people what is being done for boys
and girls. I hope that very many people,
among them hon. Members of this House,
will take the opportunity of going to see

citizens in Northern Ireland.
There is at last a feeling of satisfaction
that the youth movement is firmly established; difficulties are being met and overcome, premises are being obtained,
leaders are being trained, thirty new
clubs have been established in the past

about 4,000 boys and girls in the clubs,
and the uniformed organisations cadets,
brigades, scouts, guides, etc.-have
membership of over 32,000. The leaders
of the youth movement have every right
to congratulate themselves

I hope I have not delayed the Committee unduly and that hon. Members will
make allowance for my lack of experience
in the task on which I am engaged, and
permit me a few minutes more in which
to speak on educational reconstruction.
As said in my opening remarks, during
the short time I have been Minister the
greater part of each day has been devoted
to the study of documents on development, to consultation with the indoor
officials and the inspectors of schools and
to discussions and interviews with all
those and they are many-who have a
right to make known their views on what
our future educational system should be.
I have attended conferences of teachers
of all types of schools and profited greatly
from the opinions which were freely expressed there; I have met chairmen of
education committees, and members of a
special liaison committee of the association
of education committees. I have met representative leaders of various denominations
and religions, and last, but by no means
least, have had a most informative discussion with a deputation representing
associations of parents-and here I may
say that I, personally, consider it a most
healthy sign that these parents' associations are being formed and are taking an
active interest in the education of the
child; I will welcome an equal constructive interest by Members of this Committee.
I have been into the schools themselves—
in short, am back in school myself, learning the business and the administration
of education, and while not pretending
that I could pass any examination, I hope
I may say that I am taking my duties
earnestly and zealously, and know infinitely more than when a private Member; I still have a long way to travel, but
am travelling hopefully.
We could not be more actively engaged
on this matter of reconstruction than we
are at present; there is no aspect of our
Estimates-
Ministry of Education

[Lieut.-Colonel Hall-Thompson]
system which we are not examining and
testing, and there is no detail on which

and opinion of those who are able to advise

I have formed the opinion that we can

we conceive to be the best educational

I do not like to make rash promises,
but I hope that that White Paper will be

House rises for the Summer Recess. I

and consultation will take place, out of

Mr. BEATTIE: Allow me to extend
to the right hon. and gallant Gentleman
my appreciation of the able manner in
which he has made his first presentation
of the Estimates for educational purposes
in this Committee. Not by any means
can I come to the conclusion that he is
inexperienced. I think he explained the
Estimates in a way that would do credit
to an experienced representative of the
Cabinet in that honoured position. I do
feel that this is not the time for me to be
too critical of the presentation or of the
money that is being sought owing, of
course, to the whole educational system
at the moment being in the melting pot.
Out of that pot we expect to have a
finished article an educational system
that will give equal opportunity to all.
I am referring to our present educational
system as it has worked and the prospects
of the new system working in a different
direction. In this post-war reconstruction, from the educational standpoint, we
are now tackling the job. I only wish and
hope that other jobs such as housing and
unemployment were tackled likewise and
not allowed to wait until the fatal day
arrives when everything will be found in
chaos and disorder.
The right hon. Gentleman has now
taken over this position, and his presentation of the Estimates has shown the
Committee that he is not going to be
subject to a limitation in the educational
views he is going to seek. He is prepared
to accept views on the reconstruction of
education from the man in the street if
he finds they are going to be useful and
serviceable in the new system. I know to
a certain extent the work that has been
put into this job by the right hon.
Gentleman. I know he has started well.
I know he has gathered the opinions of
different classes of the community that
are likely to bring forth something useful
and something serviceable, something that
will be beneficial, not too heavily laden
on the one side and not too lightly laden
on the other side, but something that will
give equal opportunity to every child in
the community irrespective of creed, class
or calling.
The only thing I do fear is that there
may be a tendency in this reconstruction
for the Minister to harness himself too
closely to the English educational system,
or there may be a tendency for him to
harness himself too closely to the Scottish
educational system. Knowing those two
systems I am inclined to reiterate the
views I hold. I think our system here is
different in many respects from either of
those two systems. I believe we might get
a little from each that could fit in to the
educational life of this part of the world,
and perhaps meet the requirements of the
people here to a greater extent than was
the case in the past.
I may as well be blunt on this point.
In the past there has been a sort of
privilege for one and a sort of semiprivilege for the other. We must all
accept this as being a fact because it is
there laid down. We have two sections
in our educational life in Northern Ireland. We have a Protestant section, the
Estimates-

majority of which have transferred their
schools to the local authorities. We have
a Protestant section which still holds on
to their managerial rights over a very

section of the community which has not
accepted the four-and-two system as it
was the wish of the Minister in 1923.
Those in that section, along with the

handicapped and hampered, and the
children have not had the same equal

that were handed over to the local

Í think that is a difficulty that can be
got over very nicely in Northern Ireland.
It has been a contentious point in the
life of our educational system in this
country. There is no use in having a
new educational system if that same
vicious point is retained in it. It matters
not to me whether children are Catholic
or Protestant. In my view they are
entitled to a school; they are entitled to
have the equipment of that school and to
all appertaining to the working of that
school. That does not go to the extent
of interfering with managerial control,
but both classes in the community should
have the right not only to the school
building but to every requisite necessary
for the education of the child.

Another point I wish to raise is in connection with the youth organisation. I
do not agree with the right hon. Gentleman in his contention that the retention
of the present chairman is in the best
interests of the youth of this country. I
say that no person who is over the age of
70 is a fit and proper person to enter into
a new orientation in the life of the youth
of this Province. I say you have to
modernise not only the Committee, but
you have got to set an example in regard
to the chairmanship of the movement.
If you are going to retain in that position
the present chairman, then I think you
are making a blunder and you are going
to stampede the whole organisation. Out
of the great number of youths who have
jained this organisation last night an
audience of only 150 could be found. I
want this youth organisation to be put
into proper working order. If you are
going to retain the chairman about whom
we hear so much and against whom so
much criticism has been levelled, you are
going to destroy the movement. It is
quite true that she appointed herself. In
my opinion these self-appointed individuals should be removed. These positions
are not sinecures for life.
I would ask the right hon. Gentleman
not to destroy a good movement, one
in regard to which he is going to receive
co-operation from the community, and
one which needs young ideas and young
leaders in order that the best help and
advice may be received. Such a movement requires the head to be in line and
in keeping with the thoughts, desires and
aspirations of the rank and file of it. I
still claim that the present chairman is
not in the grade to which I have referred,
and that a new chairman should be appointed. That is the fault I have to find
with the youth movement. For the sake

the farmers in Northern Ireland have not

summer
months many of them are working from

Children in the country have to walk
three or four miles to school, and even
further. Sometimes they have uppers on
their boots, and sometimes they have no
boots at all. In Belfast some of us have
taken steps to see that the children are
properly shod. They cannot get home
for any food during the day. They take
with them to school a little piece of bread
with a taste of national butter, which
they, have a better opportunity of getting
in the country than they have in the
town. That is all they have to eat during
the day, and when they get home at night
it is almost time to go to bed. Why do not
the local authorities outside Belfast see
that their children are properly fed in the
same way that the Education Committee
of the Belfast Corporation has done. In
Belfast a child can get a good two course
dinner for 3d. The reason is that the
education authorities outside Belfast are
composed of farmers who, like Scotsmen,
are very near. The members of these
education committees must all be Scotsmen or the descendants of Scotsmen, because they will not spend money on these
necessary things.
What has the Minister of Education
done in the matter of looking after the
health of the school children? We are
as far back as we were twenty years ago.
Some fifteen years ago in this House I
asked the Minister of Education to install
mass radiology to detect disease in the
children in its early stages. Thousands
of children in public elementary schools
are to-day suffering from all sorts of
internal diseases, and especially tuberculosis. The Member for the University
(Dr. Lyle) has drawn attention to the
terrible state of the public health services
throughout Northern Ireland, and I
suggest that the Ministry of Education
is not doing a fraction of what it ought
to do in the matter of looking after the
health of the school children. The conditions in many schools are deplorable.
There is no sanitary system, no water
supply, and no food provided during the
day, not even a glass of milk. That is a
crying scandal. The school children of
Northern Ireland are entitled to a proper
water supply, and a proper sanitary
system, and they should be properly
clothed and shod, but unfortunately there
are none of these things provided for a
great many of the school children of this
Province.
The local authorities, outside Belfast,
who are responsible for these things refuse
to put into force the Act enabling them
to provide them which was passed by this
House. The Member for South Derry (Mrs.
Parker) has devoted great attention and
thought to this question, and she fought
very hard to get the children attending
schools in County Derry provided with
meals during school hours, but I know
what she was up against. I would have
no hesitation in exterminating the people
who refuse to put this Act into operation
by giving them a dose of Rodine in their
drink, or on a bit of bread well buttered,
because they are holding back a big
advance in our educational services. We
want the Minister of Education to be a
dictator in this matter, and where a local
education authority which has power to
feed and clothe the children and provide
them with proper health services refuses
to do so, the Minister should not have
the slightest hesitation in doing with that
body what the Government did with the
Belfast Corporation and the Poor-law
Guardians.
The Minister will admit that a great
many education authorities throughout
Northern Ireland are doing absolutely
nothing in this matter. On a previous
occasion in this House I referred to an
old school not a thousand miles from
the boundaries of Belfast that was a disgrace to civilisation. All the windows on
the ground floor were boarded up, and
when attention was drawn to the matter
they were compelled to put in glass, but
the rats ate the putty off the windows.
That is the kind of schools we have, and
we sit here like a lot of fools blethering
about our advance in education. We are
not advancing as fast as we should do. I
do not know how the Prime Minister can
face his constituents while he allows the
stinking state of affairs that exists and is
a disgrace to civilisation to continue. In
a way the people themselves are to blame.

Speaking the other night the Prime
Minister and the Minister of Labour
blethered about the Border after the war.
The Border is as safe as the rock of
Gibraltar. Hitler tried to exterminate
Gibraltar but failed, and Ulster is just as
safe. Under the Act of 1920 the Border
cannot be touched.
The CHAIRMAN: We are dealing
with the Education Estimates.

The time has come when the Ministry

cannot see any reason why the smallest

issued and legislation ensues from it the

Under the heading of elementary
education I see that the total expenditure

higher education the figure is practically
one-fifth of that for elementary education,
being £321,000 odd, leaving out what is
required for technical instruction.
ceeding to the Estimate for Queen's

Northern Ireland people pride themselves on the fact that they are Britishers,

but although Great Britain has already
decided what part religious instruction

Northern Ireland as to whether they are

Ireland the same facilities for religious

7-30. They get to Omagh at least an

place for them to go in Omagh. They
wander about until the school opens at
perhaps 10 o'clock. These children spend
the most of five hours in school. Then
they go and wait for the train to take
'them back to Fintona Junction and get
the tram from Fintona Junction down to
Fintona town. There they have to get
their bicycles or walk two, three or perhaps four miles before they get home.
They do not reach home, some of them,
until after six o'clock in the evening.
These children have been out all day,
twelve hours, and then they come home
and have a great deal of home work to
do. I should like the Minister of Education to visualise for himself the condition
these children are in to do the great deal
of home work they are expected to do.
What time have they for recreation or
for rest? I think at the present timethe Minister may not know it- -a great
deal more stress is being put on the
prestige of the schools in Northern Ireland in order to see which can get
most exhibitions or most school distinctions, or which can get the best results
from the intermediate or other examinations, and that, in my opinion, is being
got at the expense of the health, welfare
and well-being of the children. I think
the Minister of Education ought to take
some steps to see that these children of
the tender years of childhood are not deprived of the recreation and rest and
refreshment that they ought to receive.
I think the Minister ought to put into
operation the recommendation made some
years ago that there should be no homie
work for children from standard three
downwards, and that home work for other
children ought not to be more than one
hour. In many localities the home work
that has to be done by the children
occupies two or three hours, and the
parents themselves have got to be the
teachers of the children at home. It is
unfair to the parents and more unfair to
the children. I wish more attention was
paid to the fact that the teaching ought
to be done in school, and that any rehearsing that has to be done can very well
Estimates-

[Mr. Elliott]
be done in the home instead of in the
school. It is no good for the parents today to have to send their children to
school to repeat lessons they have taught
them at home. What the parents want
is to send children to school to be taught,
and the parents, I am sure, do not object
to hear the children's lessons when they
come home.
It is unfair that the burden
I
of teaching should be thrown on the
parents, and that the home work allotted.
to the children should be such that it is a
trial to the children and a tax on their
strength and energy to have it done.
hope something will be done to clarify the
position so far as home work is concerned
and allow the children to get their education under hygienic and congenial conditions and not at the expense of
recreation and time that ought to be
spent in leisure and rest.
I should like also just to mention what
the hon. Member for Antrim mentioned,
agriculture. I think the time has come
when in our educational programme agriculture ought to play a far more important part than it does. Agriculture is
our greatest industry in spite of the fact
that we have other great industries, and
our children, particularly in rural areas,
should know the benefits they receive in
being brought up on the land, and being
reared in the countryside, and something
ought to be done by the Minister to make
agriculture a more important part of our
educational programme than it is now.
The children ought to be taught, particularly in the rural areas, that agriculture is not a despised industry, but that
agriculture is an important industry, and
they ought to be taught that it takes men
and women of brains and calibre and
brawn to make good agriculturists.
That is pretty well all I intended to
say on this Estimate. I do not agree
altogether with the hon.. Member for
Antrim that we all pay taxation without
a grudge. I think a great many people
when they come to pay taxation pay it
with a grudge. At any rate I am not
prepared to subscribe to the doctrine that
taxation is always paid without a grudge.
But I do say that money spent on education is not lost money. I think if the
Minister comes forward to this House for
an increased Estimate and if that increase
is going to the benefit of the children of
the nation, if it is going to make the
children happier and better, if it is going
to give better facilities for them to make
good in the world and to make them good
citizens-I for one will not object to the
increase. I hope the right hon. Gentleman's guidance of the Ministry of
Education, which I look on as the most
important Ministry we have, will play an
important part, as it ought to play, in
the life, liberty and progress of Northern
Ireland.
Dr. LYLE: I should like first of all to
congratulate the new Minister of Education on the very full statement he made
to this House, and to wish him a happy
tenure of office. I think there is no
doubt at all that the sanitary conditions
in a great many of our schools or a very
large proportion of our elementary schools
are deplorable, and something should
have been done to remedy it long ago.
That has already been dwelt upon by
previous speakers and I need not say any
more about it.
I should like also to call the attention
of the House to the very unsatisfactory

school-children. You have several
different systems of inspection in Northern Ireland. You have a few whole-time
school medical officers, but the great
majority of the school medical officers are
only part-time officers engaged in private

work as school medical officers and without any efficient supervision of that work
-no one to see that it is properly done.
I think in very many cases that work is
not properly done under present conditions.
Now it may be hoped that in the new
Ministry that is proposed all these things
will be remedied. I personally have not
much hope in that direction that any

mongrel Ministry that has been proposed.
If it had been a Ministry of Health
solely concerned with health as was recommended in the report of the Select
Committee there would be every hope
that these and many other deficiencies
would be corrected. But if the Ministry
which I have described as a mongrel
Ministry, a Ministry that will be probably occupied with local government,
roads and bridges, the registration of
motor vehicles and so forth, I am afraid
the school medical service and the medical
service generally in connection with

education will get very little attention
indeed. I hope that the Ministry of

Lieut.-Colonel HALL-THOMPSON: I

The hon. Member for Shankill and

Reference has been made to milk and

The suggestion has been made that the

made compulsory, and that the local

The same thing applies to opportunity for

We hope to put such recommendations before the House as will achieve the

The Member for Carrick referred to

authorities do already supply free books.
Where this is done it is done by the local

whether this system should be extended

The Member for North Tyrone is also
an advocate of hot meals and free milk
for children. I am glad to hear that an

is any part of Tyrone which does not

He, and another speaker also from
Tyrone, referred to the difficulty of
children getting to certain schools, particularly secondary schools, in their area.
This matter was taken up and ultimately
was dealt with by the Transport Tribunal.
They have decided that during the present
difficulties, that is, owing to the war,
they cannot improve the transport
facilities in the area for the present. But,
of course, we are quite hopeful that
immediately the war is over and we again

The Member for Antrim has referred
to the failure of his request to reopen a
school. I assume he means Ballyutoag,
in County Antrim, to which he drew
my attention a few weeks ago. I
immediately took this matter up, and it
is now in the hands of the local authority
to decide whether or not the school shall
be reopened. I shall be very surprised if
they do reopen it, because if every child
in that district went to it it would not
be well attended. In view of the fact
that there is a good bus service to Belfast
and that the children from that district
are attending the very up-to-date school,
Everton, on the Crumlin Road, I think
it very unlikely that the local authority

The same speaker referred to agricultural education. Of course, he is aware
that that matter has already been dealt

of Agriculture, but I can assure him that
