Mr. BEATTIE: This House seems to
be very highly efficient in bringing to a
close the Parliamentary time and the
right of its Members at every possible
opportunity. Last week the House met
on Tuesday for one hour or so; it sat
yesterday, and it sits to-day, and now
it wishes to be relieved from its duties
until next Tuesday. I cannot agree with
that, because there is much in the life
of the people that requires immediate
attention; in fact, the people of this area
feel there is something very seriously
wrong with the Parliamentary practices
here. We on this side cannot escape
from that charge if we sit silent and
allow these things to happen.
There are rumours going about in connection with many urgent matters such
as housing and planning, and what are
the Government going to do in that
respect? There are other questions such
as the rising figures of unemployment.
What are we in this part of the world
going to do? We are going to be left
solely on our own resources to provide
the means to meet the after-the-war
conditions. Those points in themselves
give scope to this Parliament to discuss
ways and means by which an approach
can be made towards the problems
which I have mentioned, and the time
of the House can be allotted for those
discussions in a manner which, I think,
will prove to the outside public at large
that we are really sincere and earnest in
our desire to bring forth that better
world which we hear talked of so much
by politicians on this side of the Channel
and politicians on the other side.
We are not hampered at the moment
by business that I might call governmental. I understand that there is to
be another burden imposed on the people
of Northern Ireland by increasing the
landlords' rights to take away from
property an amount of money greater
than that which they at present receive.
I understand the Cabinet at the moment
are discussing ways and means whereby
they can increase the rents of the homes
of the people. That may be true or it.
may be untrue, but that is in accordance
with a statement I read in the Government organ.
I never find it going very
far wrong so far as the Government are
concerned. It always goes more in the
direction of wrong so far as I am concerned; the Government point of view
is always more correctly expressed.
What better service could we give than
sitting to-morrow and, if necessary, on
Friday, because Friday is a Parliamentary
sitting day, and getting down to the things
that matter to the people outside, that
matter so much in the lives of our million,
and a quarter inhabitants? They matter
so much that the Government have spoken
from platform after platform, and I presume that at an early Orange demonstration they will also throw forth their
platitudes as to what Toryism means to
the working people of Northern Ireland.
Of course, I do not believe they will be
able to put it over on the gullible section
of the community who hitherto have
listened to the far outworn cry of the Tory
party; it will not be so easy to convert
people to that view in the future.
I want to get down to something useful,
and I believe the time of this House can
be applied in that direction. If we have
the will we have the time, but certainly
if there are not the will and the desire to
do something for the benefit of the people
then time does not matter.
In my
opinion apathy has been shown by this
Government, and it is very essential that
the points which I have mentioned, and
which affect the welfare and wellbeing
of the people of this area to an extent
which I believe warrant our doing worth
while, should be considered during a few

extra hours sitting on the Parliamentary
days available to us.

The CHAIRMAN: With the permission of the Committee I propose to allow
the Minister of Labour to go over the
whole field of this Ministry's Estimates.
It is a very wide field. Is that the opinion
of the Committee?
The Committee indicated assent.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Grant): As hon. Members know, the
first step in the establishment of a
Ministry of Labour was the setting up of
employment exchanges. Their business
was not to provide employment-but to
bring employers and workers into touch
with each other. That is still our first
duty and with it I shall begin what I
have to say.
unem-
In April, 1943, the total number of
persons signing our registers as
ployed was 18,116. In October, the demand for farm and other labour had reduced this to 12,600, which is the lowest
unemployment figure on record; and in
April last it had risen again to 16,113or 2,000 less than a year ago.
I must
remind the Committee that these figures
include, not only the wholly unemployed,
but casual workers such as dockers who
may be in and out of employment several
times in a week. They also include people
temporarily stopped-that is, persons who
are still with their firms, but whose work
has been held up for a few days owing to
shortage of material, or for some other
passing reason.
No matter when we take our count,
there must always be some such people
who are, at the moment, out of work, but
are not out of their job. In April last
these two classes accounted for over 2,700
of the 16,000 on our registers. Even of
the remainder, while the numbers may
not alter much from one month-or even
one quarter-to another, the classes of
persons who make it up do alter rapidly.
It is true that there is a small minority
who are not easy to place owing to their
age or infirmities or other causes; but
broadly speaking two-thirds of the people
on our register change over every month.
Estimates-
Ministry of Labour
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Grant]
In fact, last year-although we had a
smaller average register for what I might
call our stock in trade-we placed over
100,000 workers in employment as against
less than 90,000 the year before.
Incidentally, I may mention that amongst
these placings there were 5,214 ex-Service
men, as compared with 3,076 placed during 1942.
I should say just a word about the
scheme for using ordinary labour for harvesting work which was operated by the
Ministry of Agriculture with the help
of my Department. As hon. Members
know, it met with general approval, and
we hope to repeat it successfully in the
coming season.
The employment exchanges of the
Ministry have had a very busy year.
Unemployment has fallen and the
number of payments of benefit is,
therefore, greatly reduced, but the fall
in unemployment brings new problems.
Perhaps, the chief of these is how to
meet
the demands of industry for
workers able to take their place in the
vast organisation that has been built up
in connection with our war effort. The
work is often available in centres far
from the workers' homes; it may be
something entirely different from what
they have done before; and there are
the questions of fitness, both industrial
and physical, wages and transport. In
addition, whenever anybody refuses an
offer of employment or leaves employment without reasonable cause his title
to unemployment benefit must be looked
at carefully. In 1943, 64,260 decisions
on benefit claims had to be given by
our insurance officers, and 10,359 appeals
were heard by Courts of Referees.
All this throws a heavy burden of
work on the staff of our Employment
Exchanges. Then, too, the value of
the employment exchange service is being
more and more appreciated by other
Departments and by the public, and this
means extra work. For years past our
managers have assisted the Ministry of
Finance and the public in the obtaining
of grants of probate on small estates.
During the last couple of years they have
been responsible, on behalf of the Board
of Trade, for the issue of supplementary
clothing coupons to industrial workers on
the application of their employers. And
I have just agreed to undertake, on behalf of the Inland Revenue, the repayment of income-tax to wage earners who
become unemployed. I hope what I have
said will be borne in mind by anyone
who is tempted to think that, because
the number of unemployed is low, the
exchanges must have nothing to do.
At this stage I should like to express
my gratitude to the staff for the willing
and efficient way in which they continue
to discharge these never-ending duties.
At a period in the war we were compelled
for security reasons to disperse certain
of our headquarters staff and records.
This was done at the cost of considerable
difficulty in administration, and I hope
the day is not far distant when the entire
headquarters staff of the Ministry will
again be housed under one roof. The
Assistance Board also are able to facilitate
other Government Departments and the
public by undertaking agency duties for
which their organisation is especially
adapted.
It may not be known that the Board
acts as agent for the Ministry of Pensions
in making payments under the Personal
Injuries to Civilians Scheme, in paying
additional grants to aged pensioner
I widows of men who served in the last
war, and in investigating applications for
war service grants where the normal
dependants' allowances are inadequate or
are not payable. It also acts as agent for
the Service Departments in investigating
claims to service dependants' allowances,
and as agent for the Board of Trade in
the replacement of clothing ration documents which have been lost or destroyed,
and on certain questions of compensation for war damages. In spite of this
very wide range of duties I am glad to
be able to say that the net estimate of the
cost of administration of the Ministry and
of the Board is reduced as compared with
last year.
Indeed, as the Committee will have
noticed, the only Vote in which I am asking for an increase as compared with last
year is that for supplementary pensions,
where the amount required has risen by
about a quarter of a million pounds to a
total of £1,512,000. This increase is in
part consequential on the extension of
the scheme last summer to cover widows
drawing contributory pensions which

The experience which we have had of

The review of certain existing pensions
which was carried through in recent
months brought to light a few remarkable
cases. Elderly farmers whose income
before the war qualified them for an old
age pension were found in some cases to
be making as much as £1,000 a year out
of their holdings.
Mr. BEATTIE: Shame on them for
drawing the pension.
Mr. GRANT: They were, of course,
particularly fortunate in being able to
specialise in a crop which commanded an
exceptional market. The ordinary farmer
is not so fortunate and may be able to
show that he is entitled not only to an old
age pension but, in many cases, to a
supplementary pension also.
Turning to the health services administered by my Department, I refer with
great regret to the death during the year
of his Honour Judge McGonigal. Judge
McGonigal was a member of the Medical
Benefit Council since its beginning in
1930, and followed the late Sir Robert
Johnstone, F.R.C.S., M.P., as chairman
in 1939. Both as a member and as chairman he gave invaluable assistance, and
at all times placed his great abilities and
experience at the service of the Council.
I have been fortunate in obtaining the
services of the Right Hon. Judge Robb,
K.C., to succeed him as chairman of the
Council.
I am glad to say that the state of health
of the community as judged by the number
of claims to benefit shows little sign of
deterioration in spite of the continued
strain of the war. There has been a
slight increase in claims especially amongst
women workers, but, on the other hand,
there has been a marked reduction in the
number of men claiming disability benefit,
that is men whose incapacity has lasted
for more than six months.
The good relations between my Department and the medical profession continued
throughout the year. The capitation rate
Turning to another branch of my
Ministry, the Inspection Division, we find
a background of steady day-to-day work
similar to that I have already mentioned
on the unemployment and health sideswork which is absolutely necessary, but
little known, except by those actually in
contact with it. Thus, last year, my
inspectors had to pay nearly 19,000 visits
under the various Insurance Acts and
more than 15,000 visits about claims to
pension, in addition to inspections under
the Trade Board Acts and the Factory
Acts. They have devoted much attention
towards promoting the welfare of workers.
They have encouraged the establishment
of accident prevention committees, and
the employment of persons skilled in welfare supervision.
In this connection may I refer to the
three-day conference organised by the
Industrial Welfare Society in co-operation
with my Department and held in Belfast
last October. This led to the emergency
training course on industrial welfare and
personnel management that my Department arranged with the help of Queen's
University. It was intended mainly to
assist those already in industry who had
to deal with welfare and management
problems, but it proved more widely attractive than we expected. We planned
for about 50 people, but we accepted 141,
when we had to refuse further applicants
because we had reached the limit of the
accommodation available.
The course included not only lectures
by experts on all branches of the subject
and discussions and tutorial classes, but
also visits to factories, employment exchanges, school-meal centres, welfare
societies and clinics, and other places
where students could see the actual work
in progress about which they had heard
in the lectures. It ran from January to
April last, so that it is rather too soon
to speak of its results; but we know that
it was much appreciated by all who attended.
I cannot pass from this topic without
saying that I feel that the Government

The scheme introduced in 1941 by my

for lunch-time concerts for war-workers

enjoyed, but it is also realised that they

their value was formerly doubted.
time conditions make it difficult to do

Let me refer now to the Industrial
Relations Branch. I need not assure the
House that my Department has faithfully
endeavoured to keep the needs of the war
effort constantly in view. In this respect,
by the proper use and distribution of
skilled labour through the activities of
the labour supply inspectors, valuable
results have been achieved. The total
numbers employed on engineering and
aircraft work, in spite of programme
changes, have been steadily increasing,
and the necessary skilled labour has also
been found for a number of new undertakings of vital importance. We have, I
am glad to say, been able, for the most
part, to secure the requisite transfers and
redistribution of labour without resort to
the powers of direction under the Defence
Regulations, and I am confident that
future requirements can be dealt with
along the same satisfactory lines.
an
The Ministry has also continued to
give men from Northern Ireland
opportunity of training for munitions
work at the Government training centres
in Great Britain, and more than 2,000
Northern Ireland men have been placed
in war industries since the inception of
this scheme. Training of a corresponding
type has also been carried on in technical
schools in Northern Ireland where the
necessity arose, and we have participated
in a training scheme for boys for the
Merchant Navy Reserve Pool.
During the year the National Arbitration Tribunal (Northern Ireland) gave
awards in 124 trade disputes, and I
should like again to pay tribute to the
services that have been rendered to the
Ministry and to the community generally
by the Tribunal. The use and establishment of joint machinery of negotiation
for the settlement of disputes continues
to be encouraged. With the assistance of
the Ministry a Joint Industrial Council
for the retail drapery, outfitting and footwear trades in Belfast was set up at the
beginning of this year and the Northern
Ireland Conciliation Board for the cinematograph and theatrical trades has been
re-established.
Variations in the wages of workers in
12 of the 18 Trade Board trades were
made by the Boards concerned and subsequently confirmed. It is noteworthy
that holidays with pay are now compulsory
in 17 of these trades. In certain other
trades, such as the building trade, voluntary schemes for this purpose are, I am
glad to say, being established; and, in
addition, schemes introducing holidays
with pay came into operation in nine cases
by awards of the National Arbitration
Tribunal.

I trust I have not been unduly long
over this description of the Ministry's
work during the past year. If so, my

The assurance given to this House about
surplus labour being sent across the
Channel was that no boy or girl under
the age of 18 years would be compelled
to go.
I want to tell the Committee that
that promise has been broken, bringing
the Government into ill-repute, as the
public cannot depend on the word of a
Government representative. The right
hon. Gentleman's predecessor stood at this
Box and promised me that no person under
the age of 18 would be sent across the
water. We now find that a number of
those boys are stranded in London. I will
refer to that matter later on in
my speech.
How are we to stand before our constituents? As far as I am concerned I find
that the truth always brings its own reward. My constituents both east and
west know the attitude I took up in regard
to the shipment of Belfast and Northern
Ireland workers across the Channel.
The right hon. Gentleman did not go
out on to the Dublin-Belfast road and
order the Dublin Fire Brigade home. He
did not refuse them permission to be in
the Six-County area. Oh, no. The
Minister did not refuse the 4,000 or 5,000
skilled workers permission to come across,
and he did not refuse to allow many other
classes of industrial workers to come here.
What is a man but his word? The word
of a man is his bond. A representative
of the Ministry of Labour went down to
Eire and made a definite promise through
the various trade unions. Now what do
we find? Every letter and every word
of that promise have been broken,
trampled upon and dishonoured by the
right hon. Gentleman. Is there no
obligation on the Minister to uphold the
prestige of his predecessor?
In my
opinion there is.
The Minister may tell me that he cannot renew a residence permit. That is
quite true. I presume I have received
more replies from the Home Office in regard to residence permits than any other
hon. Member of this House.
In every
reply sent out by the Home Office the
responsibility for refusal was placed on
the right hon. Gentleman. That responsibility is placed on him owing to its
being stated that there is labour available
for the trade, calling or position which the
person applying for a residence permit
is engaged in. The application is refused
on those grounds. Let me tell the right
hon. Gentleman some of them.
The first is the catering trade. We
have not sufficient suitable labour available in Northern Ireland to keep that
trade moving in the way it is desired.
Repeated applications have been made by
employees engaged in that trade but they
have been disallowed on the ground that
the right hon. Gentleman says there is
labour available. That point has been
challenged. They have been asked to
send suitable labour to the jobs vacated
by the non-residents of Northern Ireland.
Ninety per cent. of those sent never did
a day's work at that particular trade,
and they are not suitable.
Then take the nursing profession. It
has been depleted owing to the calls of
war. The supply of private nurses in
Northern Ireland is very low at the
present time. I have had experience in
regard to this matter. I had to go north,
south, east and west to try to get accommodated through the medical profession.
It was a very trying time. People lying
ill could not find a local nurse who was
prepared to look after them. As a result
several fully trained nurses came from
Dublin and started up as private nurses,
but when they applied for a renewal of
their permits their applications were
refused.

was in regard to domestic servants. Can
any hon. Member in this House that

now

I want to make it perfectly clear.
Member for Pottinger said that in his

want to make that clear in the Committee
for I have nothing to do, good, bad, or indifferent with the granting of permits to

hon. Members cannot ask me to allow any

When I have done that, that is all I have
to do with the permit question. Whether
a permit is granted or is turned down is
not my responsibility and I am not going
to accept any suggestion that I have such
a responsibility. The hon. Member says
he gets letters from a certain Ministry
blaming the Ministry of Labour because
certain workers did not get permits.

He then talked about the catering

was a time not very long ago when
Guinness was in short supply. Everybody
knows what Guinness is, though everybody does not know what it tastes like.
This short supply of Guinness was worrying a good many people in Northern Ireland. It never worried me at any time.
I was approached by the representatives
of these barmen, and they said, "We are
going to have so many barmen out of

you do anything to help them." I told

of Ireland barmen, people who were
normally living in the North of Ireland,
if I could do anything to find alternative
employment for them I would put the

disposal to try to find work for these
people.
On the deputation there were people
from Eire, and I said that as far as the
barmen from Eire were concerned, I was
not interested in them; I was only interested in the people from Northern Ireland. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
That is my position. All this shortage
of Guinness did not come about as

Then the Member for Pottinger raised
the question of Eire workers in Northern Ireland. There is only one thing
I want to make clear. Though as an
individual I have nothing to do with the
matter, as a Member of the Government
I aceept my share of the responsibility.
When these men were brought from Eire
to Northern Ireland they were brought
to assist in the war effort. Everyone
knows that this is a mechanical war, an
engineers' war, and to get the machinery
going we had to have experts
good craftsmen in the engineering and
electrical industries. There was a shortage of these craftsmen in Northern
Ireland. We had not got them. The
machines were there, but we had not got
the men. We could get more of our
unemployed people into production by
bringing in these men from the Free
State. Therefore the Government brought
in these people in the national interest.
They had no axe to grind except to help
the war effort. Then they had to make
an allowance of 3s 6d per night to these
workers.
I want to say that since I became
Minister of Labour I have not agreed
with this allowance of 24s 6d per week
that is paid to these people. In saying
that I am not speaking for the Government but for myself. I do not agree with
bringing men from Dublin or any other
part of Eire, or from England to Belfast,
placing them alongside Belfast workmen,
and saying to the imported worker, "You
are to get 24s 6d a week more than
the Belfast workman." Since I became
Minister of Labour I have refused to
sanction this allowance. If this House
decides otherwise I will have nothing
móre to do with it.
.
The Member for Pottinger also raised
the question of the Newry men who are
stranded in London. The information
the hon. Member can get about everything is amazing. He knows there is
going to be a huge demonstration in
Hyde Park on Sunday to deal with this.
matter. That may be the reason he has
hurried away from the House this afternoon.
He may be going to attend that
meeting. He made an attack on
my
Ministry as if we were doing nothing
about this question. He did not even
have the courtesy to ask me if we had
done anything. It was only through the
Press that we heard of this, but im-.
mediately we read about it we got in
touch with the Ministry of Labour on the
other side and almost implored them
to get these men suitable work until
security considerations permitted them to
return to Northern Ireland. Could any
Government Department or any man do
more than that? Immediately we got
word of the situation we took steps to
grapple with it.
The hon. Member also raised the question of farmers with £1,000 a year getting
the old age pension. The position
simply was this. These men were
normally entitled to the old age pension,
and if they had not been entitled to it
they never would have got it. They were
principally growing apples, and owing to
the war and the scarcity and high price
of apples their financial circumstances
had changed. When my Ministry was
checking up on supplementary pensions
they discovered this, and they notified
those concerned that they owed the Ministry so much money. As soon as they
were told that they paid back the money
to which they were not entitled owing to
their changed circumstances. The hon.
Member apparently thinks that in addition to being made to repay the money
these farmers should have been prosecuted
and put in gaol. If we had done that
the Member for Antrim would have raised
the matter in this House. We do not
prosecute anybody so long as they do not
flagrantly disobey the law and do not refuse to pay back any sum they have been
overpaid.
Mr. NIXON: There is nothing wrong
with that policy.
Mr. GRANT: The Member for
Pottinger also raised the question of the
recent strike in Belfast. I do not think

I want to challenge his statement that I
failed in my duty. I can stand at this
Box and honestly say, without being misunderstood, that I do not believe there
was any man in Northern Ireland who
could have done any more than I did

SPECIAL CONSTABULARY.
3. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state if the
Special Constabulary in and around
Belfast are performing similar duties to
those performed by the R.U.C.; whether
the Special Constabulary are liable to be
disbanded at any time; what is the total
pay and allowances of the Special Constabulary as compared with the R.U.C.;
and whether owing to the fact that the
prospects of the Special Constabulary are
nil, the Government will grant the
members of this Force the same pay and
allowances as the R.U.C.
Mr. LOWRY: In so far as their training permits, members of the Ulster
Special Constabulary mobilised for fulltime duty in and around Belfast are performing duties similar to those performed
by the R.U.C. The whole group of
mobilised special constables, including
those in Belfast, are employed on a
temporary basis and in this respect they
are in the same position as other groups
in the community which owe their
existence to the situation arising out of
the present emergency. I may say, however, that there is no intention at present
of demobilising the group or of disbanding the Force to which they belong.
The total pay and allowances of a
mobilised special constable in the city is
80s per week on appointment with a
further 5s per week after six months'
service. In addition, he is entitled to a
post-war credit of 3s 6d per week and
further increases under the heading of
"Service pay" will shortly be announced.
The corresponding figure for a constable
of the R.U.C. ranges from 84s week
per
on first appointment to 117s per week
after 22 years' service. In addition, an
R.U.C. constable not provided with free
quarters may qualify for rent allowance
up to a maximum of 14s 6d per week.
The pay element in R.U.C. emoluments
is subject to a deduction for pension, at
present fixed at 5 per cent. The above
figures take no account of allowances
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Lowry]
which are in the nature of a recoupment
of out-of-pocket expenses or which are
paid in respect of special duties in these
matters the mobilised special constable
and the regular policeman are in general
on the same footing.
I do not consider that the fact that
special constables are employed on a
temporary basis is any justification for
granting them the pay and allowances of
the R.U.C. The Northern Ireland special
constable in the matter of emoluments is
in at least as favourable a position as his
counterpart in Great Britain.
Mr. NIXON: Is it not a fact that the
mobilised Special Constabulary have performed their duties on the whole satisfactorily? Is it not a further fact that
at the present time the right hon. Gentleman is going outside the Special Constabulary to recruit men for the Royal Ulster
Constabulary contrary to what is being
done in Great Britain, and in that respect is competing with the Army for
man-power in a way that is calculated to
discourage recruiting at home?
Mr. LOWRY: With the first part of
the supplementary question I agree,
namely, that the Special Constabulary are
performing their duties in a most excellent
manner.
Mr. NIXON: Hear, hear.
Mr. LOWRY: With regard to the rest
of the question, which consists of a number of assertions, if it were put into the
form of a question by the hon. Member
I should be very glad to deal with it in
full.
Mr. NIXON: That is fair enough, but
is it not a fact that the prospects of these
men are being diminished by the action
of authorities at the present time in recruiting for the Royal Ulster Constabulary from outside sources contrary to
anything that is allowed in Great Britain,
or in America for that matter?
Mr. LOWRY: As regards recruitment,
a good many of the Special Constabulary
are above the age, and some have the
further disqualification of being married,
although now and again we do take in
married men in exceptional circumstances.
There is a great distinction between the
two Forces. A regular policeman joins
the Force and he cannot leave it at will,
but a special constable, if he wishes to
better himself, is not frozen in the Force.
As I have said, compared with their
counterpart in England the case of the
Special Constabulary here is as good; in
fact, in certain respects in regard to pay
per week it is better.
Mr. NIXON: With regard to the
Minister's comparison with England, is it
not a fact that there is no recruiting for
the regular Police Force in England at the
present time, and also with regard to the
Minister's statement about marriage being
a disqualification, is it not the policy at
present, owing to our falling population,
to encourage marriage? Is that not the
policy that we have here?
Mr. SPEAKER: The hon. Member
cannot introduce a question of policy.
MOTOR TRANSPORT DEPOTS.
4. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state if any
allowance is paid to storekeepers and
assistant storekeepers in police M.T.
depots in Belfast, the number of men so
employed, the number drawing allowances and the amount paid to each man;
whether some of the men acting as storekeepers are being paid drivers' allowances
although they are never employed on
driving, and what is the amount paid to
drivers.
Mr. LOWRY: Head or other constables,
qualified as motor transport storemen or
assistant storemen, and allocated by the
Inspector-General to such duties, are entitled to an allowance at the rate of 1s per
day. This allowance is paid to storemen
and assistant storemen, because they have
definite store accounting responsibilities.
It is not payable to other members of the
staff who may be called on during rush
periods to assist the storemen.
The corresponding allowance for motor
transport drivers similarly qualified and
allocated is 6d per day.
The number of men employed as storemen or assistant storemen in the police
motor transport depots in Belfast is two,
and the allowance paid to each is 1s per
day. Neither of these men is paid driver's
allowance, and neither is a qualified
driver.

Repair of Blitzed Premises.
8. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Finance whether he can state the amount
spent by the Belfast Corporation repairing the blitzed shop and dwelling-house,
172 Cliftonville Road; whether the hairdressing saloon was left waterproof;
whether the proprietor spent money erecting a glass roof to do what the Corporation engineers failed to do; whether when
the owner, Mrs. Herron, had succeeded
in making the place waterproof the Corporation under the direction of the
Administrators prosecuted her for doing
so and got a Court Order to compel her
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Nixon]
to remove the protection; whether this
lady has four children in His Majesty's
Forces, and whether he will take steps to
stop this persecution.
Mr. LOWRY: I have been asked by
my right hon. Friend to reply.
I am informed by the Belfast Corporation that the premises, 172 Cliftonville
Road, consist of a dwelling-house with a
shop facing Cliftonville Road and a hairdressing establishment in Elimgrove
Street at the rear of the above house,
formerly forming the yard or open space
to the said house. These premises were
damaged by enemy action, and the house
portion of the premises has been repaired
by the Corporation, but the powers contained in the Housing (Emergency
Powers) Act (N.I.), 1939, do not give the
Corporation power to repair the business
portion of the premises. In consequence
no repairs were carried out to the roof of
the hairdressing establishment, the responsibility for such repairs resting with
the owner, and Mrs. Herron was so informed by the Corporation's District.
Officer on 27th June, 1941. The Corporation are not required to keep separate
costs for the repair of individual houses,
and therefore I am unable to state the
amount actually spent on the repair of
the house.
The hairdressing saloon was erected in
1923, the roof of which formed the yard
space required under the Local Acts for
the dwelling-house. On 25th May, 1943,
the Corporation's Building Inspector
observed that an additional building was
in course of erection on the roof thereby
contravening the Local Acts in reducing
the yard space required. A notice was
served on Mrs. Herron on 25th May,
1943, and a plan was lodged by her on
7th June, 1943. This plan was
disapproved by the City Surveyor on 11th
June, 1943, but notwithstanding this the
building was completed, it is understood
on Mrs. Herron's directions. A further
notice to remove the building was served
on 22nd February, 1944, and on failure
to comply with this a summons was taken
out for hearing in court on 25th April,
1944. The case was adjourned at the
request of Mrs. Herron's solicitor,
that he might have an opportunity of
discussing the matter with the City
Surveyor. This discussion took place and
SO
the position was clearly explained. The
case came before the court again on 2nd
May and was adjourned for a further
week. The case was heard on the 9th
May, but the defendant did not put in
an appearance, and it was again adjourned
for seven days, the Corporation's solicitor
being requested to write to Mrs. Herron
and inform her that if the building was
not removed within seven days a continuing daily penalty would be imposed.
This communication was sent, but no
attempt had been made to remove the
structure at the 16th May when the case
was again heard. The defendant again
did not appear.
A fine of £5 and costs
and a continuing penalty of 2s per day
was imposed.
I am informed by the City Surveyor
that Mrs. Herron's suggestion that the
only way to prevent the roof of the
hair-dressing saloon from leaking was to
put a glass roof over it is quite incorrect,
for in his opinion the concrete roof could
be made watertight without the building
being erected over it. The matter is entirely one for the City Surveyor, and
neither my Ministry nor the Administrators have any jurisdiction.
Mr. NIXON: With regard to the
Minister's statement, which he has read

The MINISTER OF FINANCE

Britain. The powers of the

Northern Ireland Labourers in London.
7. Mr. BROWN asked the Prime
Minister whether he can state if he took
any steps in connection with the plight
of the eighty builders' labourers from
Northern Ireland stranded in London;
and, if so, with what result; and whether
he can state the present position of affairs
in this matter.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Grant) I have been asked by my right
hon. Friend to reply.
:
Immediately my Ministry learned from
Press reports about these men, we got into
communication with the Ministry of
Labour and National Service in London.
The officers of that Ministry got into
touch with the men, but had some difficulty in finding acceptable work for them,
because the majority objected to separating into smaller parties that could easily
be placed in good jobs. Openings have,
however, now been found for nearly all
of them at their own kind of work with a
large firm near London. A few who
wished to go to other districts have been
helped to do so.
Mr. BROWN: May I be allowed to

in London, with which I got into telegraphic communication as soon as I heard

and energetically taking up the men's

THE BUDGET.
Major Maynard Sinclair's Statement.
Major SINCLAIR: Whatever may
have been the significance in peace-time
of our Northern Ireland Budget, I am
sure hon. Members will agree with me
when I say that its introduction to-day
is overshadowed by the great events
which are passing on the Continent of
Europe and elsewhere, almost all over the
world. If, in the course of my statement,
I refer to plans for the financing
of post-war reconstruction, the House
will appreciate that I am not suggesting that the British people are out
of the wood yet. Indeed, while
may plan for the future, and are right in
doing so, we cannot afford to relax in our
main purpose, and the hearts and minds
of all of us must be directed to securing
the early victory of the United Nations,
and with it peace for a distracted world.
we
Without that victory and without that
peace, plans for security, reconstruction
and ordered progress are futile.
Much has been said from these
Benches and elsewhere about Northern
Ireland's share in the prosecution of the
war, and much more will be said when
the embargo, for security reasons, on the
full story has been lifted. But this is a
financial statement, and I propose to confine myself to my own subject this
afternoon.

war savings is a field in which practically
everyone of us can take some share. even
though it may be a small one.
before in our history, has it been given to

some part in, to make some sacrifice for,
the achievement of victory, with its

to the overthrow of Nazism and to the

Since the beginning of the war the
people of Northern Ireland had invested
up to March of this year £91,000,000 in
all forms of War Savings. Of this total
over £15,000,000 represents the proceeds
of the sale of Ulster Savings Certificates
received in this Exchequer and transferred in their entirety to the Imperial
Exchequer. The amount so transferred
during the year under review at
£5,003,000 greatly exceeded all previous
annual amounts, and is a finer tribute to
the untiring and unflagging zeal of our
splendid voluntary workers than anything I could say. It must be a source
of great satisfaction to them to know that
their work, frequently undertaken when

in the factory or in the home, has been
so highly successful. I should perhaps
make it clear that, while I am referring
only to the money which
thus passes
through our Exchequer on its way to the
Treasury, these voluntary workers are
also responsible for a substantial amount
of the money invested by our Northern
Ireland people in British Government
securities, and deposits in the Trustee
Savings Banks and in the Post Office.
As hon. Members are aware, the entire

•
.
A recent speech has drawn attention
once again to our Imperial Contribution,
and, once again, the parrot cry that we
should "keep back" some of this has been
raised. Although I discussed the nature
of our contribution at some length last
year, I think it desirable that I should
refer to it again to-day. In the first
place, it reveals a complete misunderstanding of our financial relations to talk
of keeping anything of this contribution
back, and not paying it over to the
Imperial Exchequer. The contribution
is wholly derived from Reserved Revenues;
that is, taxation imposed and collected
by the Imperial authorities, and paid
direct to them by the taxpayer or, in the
case of Customs and Excise, indirectly by
the consumer.
I feel that I cannot emphasise too
strongly a fact which must be known to
every Member of this House, and I should
have thought also to those who represent
us at Westminster, that this Reserved
Revenue is paid into the Imperial
Exchequer, and not into our own. What
we receive here is that part of it required
to meet, together with our transferred
revenues, the cost of local administration.
The actual amount which we so receive,
called the Residuary Share of Reserved
Taxes, is determined by the Joint
Exchequer Board. It follows from this
that the balance of our Reserved Revenue,
which forms the contribution, never
leaves the Imperial Exchequer.
The Budget-
Major Sinclair's Statement
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Major Sinclair]
The present high rates have been fixed
in order to raise by taxation the
maximum amount of money for war
purposes so that we as a nation may pay
our way to a substantial degree, and keep
our debt burden down to a minimum. We
all know how heavily income tax and the
other taxes on income bear on us, and
just the other day my right hon. Friend,
the Chancellor of the Exchequer, told us
that when we pay 2s 4d for twenty
cigarettes ls 9d represents the duty, and
that in the case of a bottle of whiskey
no less than 18s 41d goes to the National
Exchequer. These amounts and many
others like them go to swell that Imperial
contribution which consists wholly of
moneys raised in this and other ways for
Imperial purposes. Those who talk of
diverting this money for local needs for
the post-war era do not perhaps realise
what harm they are doing to Northern
Ireland.
Mr. NIXON: Wrong.
Major SINCLAIR: Instead of this
kind of suggestion being made, we should
be proud that we are able to make such
a substantial contribution to the common
cause, secure in the knowledge that when
victory is achieved we, as citizens of the
United Kingdom, will share in the
benefits we all hope peace will bring to us.
Having said that, I will remind the
House that I made a passing reference
at the beginning of my speech to the
financing of post-war reconstruction, and
I would now ask hon. Members, who have
followed me so far, to listen carefully to
what I am about to say, as I believe they
will find it of particular interest.
The Government, and indeed this
House itself, have recently given much
consideration to the standard of health
services in our area, and to the allied
problems of water supply and sewerage,
and there is general agreement that these
essential public services in Northern Ireland are inferior to the comparable
services in Great Britain. As a result,
the House has recently passed the
necessary legislation to set up a new
Ministry of Health and Local Government to deal with these questions.
The existence of considerable leeway on
these and other vital services having been
recognised some considerable time ago, a
general understanding had been reached
with my right hon. Friend, the Chancellor
of the Exchequer, whereby means would
be found to ensure equality of standards
with the remainder of the United
Kingdom.
It is clear that the attainment of
parity in this respect will involve capital
expenditure on a large scale, and that
local authorities-being the responsible
bodies concerned-will require to be
given a substantial degree of special
Exchequer assistance in carrying out the
programme if this leeway is to be overtaken while further developments are
provided for concurrently.
As in my view, the time had arrived
when something more definite than the
general understanding, to which I have
referred, should be reached in regard to
the financial aspect of this special postwar problem, I thought it necessary to
make further 'representations to my right
hon. Friend, the Chancellor of the
Exchequer, and I am now in a position
to make the following statement.
There are certain items of capital expenditure, such as emergency accommodation for tuberculosis patients and other
similar services, which can be shown to
be essential in war-time, and which may
be considered to be so urgent as to
justify immediate execution. These will
be reviewed without delay so that representations may be made for the release
of materials, and the requisite finance
provided under our war-time financial
agreement.
However, as the House recognises, the
execution of the main programme of
capital health services must necessarily
await the termination of hostilities. But
steps will be taken now to review our requirements, and to select for priority
execution those items the provision of
which must be accelerated in order to
give effect to the policy of making up the
leeway between our standards and those
of the remainder of the United Kingdom.
This selection will be the subject of special
Exchequer assistance which will be in
addition to any measure of such assistance
to local authorities which may be given
after the war in connection with the
development of health services in parity
with Great Britain.
For instance, the leeway proposals I am
about to submit are not intended to cover

the Northern Ireland counterpart of the
recently announced expenditure on the

in this respect.
Both the selection of leeway items and
the degree of Exchequer assistance to be
given them must be the subject of investigation by the new Ministry of
Health and Local Government. But it
can be said now that the range of health
services under consideration includes
water supplies and sewerage, additional

sanatoria, accommodation for mental defectives, and maternity and child welfare
clinics.
It will also be necessary to institute a
programme of accelerated capital expenditure on certain public, as distinct from
local authority institutions, in order that
deficiencies in our standards may be made
good. Here again it would be premature,
in advance of further investigation of
requirements, to specify exactly the
services to be included in the programme,
but the following may be mentioned:
Modernised prison and criminal lunatic
accommodation, training centres for unemployed, agricultural and central educational institutions, and the completion of
the pre-war programme of R.U.C.
barracks and labour exchanges.
A definite estimate of the capital cost
of these cannot be given until a detailed
examination has been made, and, in the
case of services to be executed by the
local authorities, decisions taken about
the degree of Exchequer assistance, but
a preliminary review suggests that the
amount required from the Northern Ireland Exchequer, related solely to leeway,
will be in the neighbourhood of
£6,000,000.
In view of the non-recurrent nature of
these works, it will be proper for all our
major capital liabilities to be spread over
a term of years and not borne entirely in
the period in which the expenditure is
incurred. Arrangements will therefore
be, made under which the exchequer share
of the cost of these programmes may be
met by borrowing, as and when the funds
are required, and the Budget will be
charged with the annual sums necessary
to meet the interest and sinking fund
charges on the loans raised for these purposes. The currency of these loans, which
are of a special nature, will not be related
to the life of the asset as in the case
of normal Government Loans Fund
advances, but the capital so raised will
be paid off in the shortest time that
proves to be financially practicable..
Mr. Speaker, I should like to record
how grateful I am to my right hon.
Friend, the Chancellor of the Exchequer,
for the understanding way in which he
received my proposals, and for the way
in which they have been met. I should
also like to voice my appreciation of the
work of the officials in this connection,
those of my own Ministry, who in an
endeavour to reach a satisfactory solution
put forward many suggestions, both
ingenious and ingenuous, and those of
H.M. Treasury, who examined our suggestions so carefully and so helpfully in
the middle of their pre-occupations with
matters of moment for the United Kingdom and the world.
I hope the House will receive with
satisfaction the concrete contribution I
have been able to announce to the solution
of those problems which have come to be
known to us all as leeway, and that with
the knowledge that funds will be available
when required, the new Minister of
Health will be able to tackle his huge
task with confidence, determination, and
success.
The House will, no doubt, have noticed
that the important question of housing
has not yet been mentioned. I have
thought it proper to exclude housing
from the leeway arrangement I have outlined, not because I do not recognise its
importance, but because the magnitude
of the problem and the physical necessity
for spreading the building of houses over
a number of years naturally make it a
matter of long-term policy. By this, I
am not to be taken as implying that steps
will not be initiated without delay to
meet the acute shortage of houses in
Northern Ireland, or that the leeway
aspect has been in any way lost sight of,
but I feel that to attempt now to gauge
the probable cost to the Exchequer over
a fairly long period would not be of

I have listened to many Budget

We on this side might not agree with all

you admired his dignity and determination, and he always gave Ulster its place.
When Ulster made a contribution to the

Ulster, and it does not matter who collects

partially manufactured products. The

There is passing to-day, and there has
been passing for many many years from
this country to England a large proportion of our natural wealth, never to
return. Let me illustrate it by one or two
examples. If a man in Manchester buys
500 tons of coal at £2 a ton he pays £1,000
for that coal. But that £1,000 remains
in circulation in Great Britain. The
Welsh miner who won the coal gets his
wages out of it, the transport system in
Great Britain gets its freight charges out
of it, and the money is not lost to England.
If, however, a merchant in Belfast buys
500 tons of coal at £2 a ton, that £1,000
crosses the water never to return. That
is the first drain upon our natural resources, which is not good for either
England or this country. The second
drain is the vast quantity of finished
manufactured articles which we have to
import from England by reason of the
presence of heavy industries there.

recognise the value of the re-insurance

The whole financial relationship between this country and Great Britain
must inevitably be reviewed in the very

and other essential services. The old

-that when we are considering the

as
These remarks that I have made to-day
have been the subject of thought for a
good many years. I have never felt that
this country was in a position to stand
precisely the same rate of indirect taxation as a wealthy country such
England, which sends into this country
vast quantities of finished and semifinished articles for which we have to pay,
and for which we get very little adequate
return. Really, in truth and in fact, we
are in the making-up trade. That is the
plain truth of our economic life. Every
piece of steel which comes for our shipyards is processed in England and is
partially finished. Every bit of flax that
comes into this country is partially
processed, except the negligible portion
which we need for the coarser end of the
trade and which we grow ourselves. I
cannot think of one really considerable
article which we can export in considerable quantities in the absolutely raw state.
Our only primary industry is agriculture.
In nearly every other branch of industry we are making up and finishing
something that has been partially and
very largely finished in Great Britain. I
think that when the financial position

between Great Britain and Northern
Ireland comes to be reviewed we are

Mr. MINFORD: I rise to congratulate the Minister of Finance on the able
presentation of his Budget statement.
Other hon. Members have also congratulated the right hon. Gentleman, but I
think it is time someone congratulated
the men and women of Ulster who have
made possible such a magnificent Imperial
contribution by paying this huge amount
of taxation into the Exchequer. You do
not get this money by any act of statesmanship, but only by long hours of hard
labour on the part of the working people,
who are to be congratulated on their great
effort in making possible the magnificent
Imperial contribution of £35,000,000.
The Minister of Finance referred yesterday, and some of the newspapers also
refer to the so-called parrot cry of those
who want to withhold part of this contribution for improving our health and
housing conditions. I suppose I am one
of the parrots, but my interpretation of
this parrot cry is that we want to be in a
position to build decent houses for our
people to live in, and we want health
services comparable to those in Great
Britain.
We are not by any means a poor
country, and we do not want to beg at
the door of the British Exchequer. We
have invested almost £100,000,000 in war
savings. Last year we gave an Imperial
contribution of £32,000,000, and this year
we are going to give £35,000,000. That
fact alone should be sufficient to do away
with all talk about our being a poor
country and a poor people. Now the
Minister of Finance has announced that
Sir John Anderson is going to give us
back £6,000,000 to start to make up the
leeway in our social services. If the
Minister had told us that six months ago
we would not have said anything about
withholding part of our Imperial contribution, but in my opinion it is this socalled parrot cry that has induced the
British Chancellor to give us this
£6,000,000. It would be scandalous if
we allowed our boys and girls to come
back from the war to live in the hovels
that exist throughout the country. We
want to see built in Ulster houses worthy
of Ulster men and Ulster women.
We have a right to demand that our
health and housing conditions should be
on a par with those in Great Britain.
Some time ago this House set up a Committee of ten Members to investigate the
position of the health services of Northern Ireland, and I am sorry to say that
it was found they were not good, or comparable with those across the water..
Therefore we are entitled to get from the
British Exchequer a grant sufficient to
bring our health services up to the standard of those in Great Britain. We pay
the same amount of income-tax as do
the taxpayers of Great Britain, and we
never grumble. We send our sons to
fight and we are proud to do so, but so
long as I am a Member of this House I
shall keep up the cry for equal treatment
with Great Britain. The right hon.
Gentleman the Member for Bloomfield
said that in England they were spending
£1,200 each on the erection of labourers'
cottages, but in Northern Ireland you can
scarcely get a hinge put on a door.
The time has come when Members of
this House must speak out, and I am
proud to be one of those who raised that
parrot cry to which the Minister has referred, and I shall continue to keep up
that cry until our health, housing, and
other social services are comparable with
those of Great Britain. I do not see why
we should go down on our hands and
knees to any Chancellor of Great Britain
and ask for parity in these essential
matters. We demand parity, and we do
not apologise for it. If you look up the
statistics you will find that the farmers
of Northern Ireland have, individually,
done more in the matter of the production
of foodstuffs than the farmers of England
or Scotland. Throughout the war we
have fed the people of Ulster, as well as
a large part of the Navy, Army and Air
Force, and in addition we have sent
millions of pounds worth of produce to
Great Britain.
The Member for St. Anne's talked
about our natural resources. Our chief
natural resource is agriculture, and therefore the Government should see that the
farmers are helped in every possible way
and not persecuted. In one respect I am
The Budget-
Resumed Debate
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Minford]
disappointed with this Budget, because
the Minister of Finance was not in a
position to forecast a post-war scheme for
Ulster. When this war is over incomes
will be lower and unemployment will become more prevalent, and then we may
be back where we were seven years ago
when we had to raid the Road Fund and
the Land Annuity Fund. This year we
are going to give the Imperial Government £35,000,000, and I am delighted,
because as an Ulsterman there is nothing
I would not give to defeat the Huns and
bring peace and prosperity to the civilised
world. We should remember the letter
that Mr. Churchill sent to the ex-Prime
Minister the Member for Mid Down, in
which he said that this bridgehead of ours
had saved the civilised world. Surely
such loyal people are worthy of being
treated on equal terms with those in
Great Britain. But we have a duty to
our Ulster men and women as well, and
that duty is to give them decent houses,
good health services, and a good education for their children. When we see
tuberculosis rampant throughout the land
and when we look at the condition of some
of our mental hospitals, is it any wonder
that the Imperial Chancellor has to admit
that we have leeway to make up in these
respects.
I congratulate the Minister of Finance
on getting so much done, but I do not
want him to go to the British Chancellor
in a grovelling manner. He should go
to him and demand equal rights, and if
we get parity with Great Britain I for
one will be satisfied. I remember the
time in this House when we had to go
very warily, but I hope those days have
passed for ever. I do not want to see
unemployment figures of 100,000 in Ulster
again. I do not want the unemployment
figures to rise above their present level,
but if they are not to do so the Government will have to treat the basic industry
of Ulster, agriculture, better than they
are doing to-day. They will have to give
some inducement to men and women to
go back to the land, and give them houses
worthy of Ulster men and women to live
in. They will have to guarantee farmers
a reasonable price for their produce in
order that they may be in a position to
pay their workers a fair wage and ensure
for them decent amenities of life.
I am delighted that the Minister has
obtained the admission that we are not
getting equal treatment with Great
Britain. I am also pleased to know that
he has obtained a promise of £6,000,000
to spend on making up some of the leeway
in our essential services, and I hope that
this will prove to be an annual grant
from Great Britain for some years to come.
Ulster men and Ulster women have played
a noble part in this war, and it was the
duty of the British Chancellor to make
this gesture. Now that he has made it
I hope he will keep it up. I have been
told in this House by the Minister of
Finance and by former Ministers that
any suggestion to withhold money from
direct taxation to improve our social and
health services, and to enable our local
authorities to build houses, was out of the
question. Yet this so-called parrot cry
has now borne some fruit. We on the
back benches are just as much concerned
about Ulster as are Ministers on the Front
Bench. I love Ulster and my people love
Ulster, and I repeat that so long as I am
a Member of this House I will do my best
to see that housing, health, education and
hospital services are comparable with those
in Great Britain. I ask for no more, and
I will take no less.
The right hon. Gentleman, the Member
for Mid Down, referred to the progress
made by the Government during the past
twenty-one years, but that progress has
been too slow, and I hope it will be
accelerated in the future. In his speech.
the Minister of Finance said housing
schemes for our people must be left until
after the war. But we can and should
make plans now for obtaining and preparing sites. There is no necessity to wait
until the war is over. Our Imperial contribution in the years following the war
will not be so great as it is now.
In conclusion, I should again like to congratulate the Minister on his statement that
Ulster will be placed on an equality with
Great Britain in the matter of social and
housing services, and so long as he does
that he will have my support. I should
also like to reiterate my congratulations
to the loyal people of Ulster on the
magnificent effort they have made in the
present tremendous struggle.

the coal mining areas of England.
course the same thing applies to coal sent

The money travels up North and to that

As long as we are part of the United
Kingdom I cannot see that we have any

But there is one great advantage about
agriculture, and that is, we do not live
on capital, whereas in England coal and
iron taken out of the earth are, in
fact, capital, which is disappearing.
Agriculture, on the other hand, is
not capital, and will continue indefinitely. The other point about the
taxable capacity is that we here are taxed
as individuals and not as a country
and if we are not earning as much as
they do in Great Britain naturally we pay
less. That applies both to direct and indirect taxation, because if we cannot
afford articles that are taxed as luxuries
we do not buy them. It is quite impossible to make out a case that because
we are not as wealthy a community here
we should be taxed on a lower basis. The

Northern Ireland Labourers in Great

1. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Labour whether his attention has been
called to the statement in a cross-Channel
newspaper that some of the 80 builders'
labourers who recently became stranded
in London had been earning up to £32
per week; whether this statement is correct and if not whether he can state the
highest and lowest weekly wages which
were in fact paid to these builders'
labourers on this particular contract.
THE MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Grant): My attention was not called to
the statement in the cross-Channel newspaper. My Ministry, however, telegraphed
to the Ministry of Labour and National
Service, but I have not yet received information to enable me to answer the
question. As soon as I do so, I shall

Evacuation-Mrs. Elizabeth
Smallwood.
2. Mr. THOMAS BAILIE asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he
can state if it is a fact that a Mrs.
Elizabeth Smallwood, in common with
other mothers of large families left
Belfast in 1941 at the request of the
Ministry; whether she was accepted as an
official evacuee and provided with accommodation in Bangor at the expense of the
Ministry; whether ejectment proceedings
have been taken against her, and a decree
granted to take effect on the 1st June,
1944; whether he will state the grounds
upon which the proceedings were instituted; whether these were based upon the
charge that the woman's husband was
living with her, having transferred to
employment in the district; whether the
woman undertook to pay the rent of the
house, and that in spite of this proposal
she is being left without housing accommodation for a family of eight children,
and whether he considers that upon
humanitarian grounds the ejectment
should be annulled.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Mr. Lowry): The answer to the first and
second parts of the question is in the
affirmative.
With regard to the ejectment proceedings, the position is that the Ministry
has no power to continue to provide
accommodation under the Government
evacuation scheme for a family when the
husband joins the family in the reception areas. In this case, it is clear that
Mrs. Smallwood's husband has been resident for some time in the house provided
for her and her children under the evacuation scheme.
The Ministry was not notified by Mrs.
Smallwood of this fact and when it came
to light the Ministry had no option but
to strike the family off the evacuation
scheme.
It is understood that Mrs. Smallwood's
husband was prepared to rent the premises at his own expense, but that the
agents for the owner would not accept the
Smallwoods as tenants as she required
vacant possession.
In these circumstances, the Ministry
had no option but to cause proceedings
to be instituted for the ejectment of the
family.
Mr. BAILIE: Does the right hon.
Gentleman realise that in this case the
entire family, including eight children,
will be unable to get accommodation and
will have to go to the workhouse? Surely
if the existing statute debars accommodation being given some arrangement can
be made, by regulation or legislation, to
make it possible that families would be
dealt with in a more humanitarian way
than is provided in the present instance?
Mr. LOWRY: It would be quite impossible to introduce legislation to take
effect before 1st June. A stay of execution was placed on the decree until 1st
June. I think that the proposition that
legislation should be introduced and carried through in the meantime for the protection of this particular family is impossible of execution, but if the hon. Member
will see me some time to-day I shall put
him in possession of the full facts of this
case which will put an entirely different

Ministry of Health and Local
Government.
4. Mr. STEVENSON asked the Prime
Minister whether he can state when the
Government propose to establish the
Ministry of Health and Local Government under the Ministries Act.
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir Basil
Brooke): Yes, sir. I am happy to be
able to inform the House that the Government propose to submit, for the approval
of His Grace the Governor in Council, an
Order in Council, fixing the 1st June,
1944, as the appointed day for the establishment of the Ministry of Health and
Local Government, and for the Ministry
of Home Affairs to take over the public
services administered immediately before
that day by the Ministry of Public
Security.
Dr. LYLE: Is it not a fact that the
Select Committee on Health Services
recommended the establishment of a
Ministry of Health concerned solely with
health matters, and dealing with all health
matters, and not a conglomerate Ministry such as it is now proposed to set up?
The PRIME MINISTER: The point
really is that the Ministry of Health in
Great Britain is composed on the same
lines as the Ministry we propose to set
up here. Further, the Minister in charge
will have to be in very close contact with
the various local authorities, and I think
there is no doubt that it is advisable that
he should be responsible for both health
and local government.
Dr. LYLE: Is it not a fact that there
is a good deal of dissatisfaction about the
constitution of the Ministry of Health in
England, and that many Members of the
British Parliament desire to have its
functions more clearly defined and more
closely associated with health alone; and
is this setting up of this conglomerate
Ministry not an attempt on the part of
the Government to sidetrack the recommendations of the Select Committee?

that come under my Ministry. The

of an

over the year. This renovation and reconstruction of scutch mills has been going
on for a very considerable time, and a

expanded in connection with the war
effort it was necessary to bring into operation mills that had been out of use for a

the necessary facilities for dealing with

I do not propose to weary the Committee by going into detailed items in
the Estimates. The headings are pretty
clearly set out in the book of Estimates.
as supplied to hon. Members. There is
really very little difference
in the
Estimates, as compared with those sub-
Estimates-
Ministry of Agriculture'
25 MAY 1944
mitted to the Committee last year. Whilst
that is so, I do wish to point out at the
same time that as a Ministry we have
been laying emphasis on
somewhat
different points of policy. During the
earlier years of war we were compelled
owing to the national necessity to increase
the acreage of plough land year after
year. The quota of plough land had to
be pushed up until it became a burning
question. Serious questions were asked
as to whether we were not pushing it too
high. Last season after I became
Minister we went into the whole question
again, and we came to the decision that
we had pushed the quota for plough land
as high as it was wise to push it, namely
to 45 per cent. of the arable land in the
different holdings.
Since then we have arranged even to
allow a certain reduction on that quota
under certain conditions. We have eased
the situation in County Fermanagh owing
to the unsuitable nature of much of the
soil there for cultivation. In other
cases over the Six Counties we have
made certain concessions as we felt individual cases required it, but, on the
whole, we have tried to maintain the
quota in principle up to the 45 per cent.
I should like just to turn aside for one
second to pay a tribute to the farmers for
the way that they handled the harvest of
1943 over that very extensive area which
we insisted on their ploughing. Hon.
Members will remember that we have had
a sequence of bad harvests; 1941 was bad,
1942 was not any better, and 1943 was a
long and protracted frost. The farmers
certainly did a magnificent job in the
harvest of 1943.
I have referred to the fact that in some
cases we have eased on the matter of the
plough land quota. That does not mean
that the food supply situation is eased
in any degree, nor is it likely to get easier
even after European hostilities have come
to an end. From all the pronouncements
of those who might be expected to be best
qualified to speak on matters of this kind,
the demand for the utmost production
from our fields and farms for a considerable period after the war will still be
there, and will be as insistent as in the
war period. We have therefore set
ourselves to try to induce our farmers to
go in for intensive, or as I should more
correctly describe it, higher farming.
Early in this season I, as Minister,
sent a letter to every farmer in the Six
Counties pointing out that a good deal
more could be done by a more literal and
judicious application of fertilisers.
Whilst we had quite a proportion of
farmers who were using all the fertilisers
we could obtain for them, there were those
who were using them in too niggardly a
fashion, and we appealed to them to take
up all the fertilisers for this year that
we could allocate to them. In that connection it might make the matter more
clear in fact than any other way I could
adopt if I gave hon. Members some figures
as to the actual amount of fertilisers used
this year compared with 1939. In 1939
the total tonnage of fertilisers used by our
farmers was 40,000 tons; for this year
the figure is 185,000 tons. As a matter
of fact, the increase for this year alone
is 40,000 tons; in other words, our farmers
are using as compared with last year as
much more fertilisers as they used
altogether in pre-war years. In addition
to that the crop as a whole was never
better planted. The spring, though cold.
and backward in some ways, has been dry
and the soil has been cultivated in a very
good way, and with this greatly increased
application of fertilisers and the way the
crop has been planted, there is every prospect of, perhaps, the best harvest that
was ever reaped in Northern Ireland.
I might say a word, perhaps, particularly about flax. Hon Members will
realise that so far as the acreages of
individual crops go any figure that I
might submit to the Committee could only
be an estimate at the present juncture.
The actual figures will be available later
on, but it is possible to make a fairly
accurate guess in regard to the acreage
of flax through the amount of seed that
is distributed to the growers, and going
on that basis we are satisfied that the
target of 100,000 acres for flax will be
considerably exceeded-by, I should say,
10,000 acres and possibly more. Indeed,
personally I am satisfied that the acreage
sown to flax this year will put a pretty
severe strain on the labour resources
available to our farmers for handling and
harvesting the crop. I am also satisfied
that the acreage is the very maximum we
can afford, having regard to the food
necessity-the necessity of having ample
fodder and other food crops both
for the human population and for our
livestock.
Estimates-
Ministry of Agriculture
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Rev. Robert Moore]
There is one other product that perhaps I should say a special word about.
I think if I remember aright I did refer
to it on the Supplementary Estimates,
and that is milk. The consumption of
milk by our people since the outbreak of
war has been very great indeed. Pre-war
the figure for liquid milk consumption
was about 15 million gallons and to-day
it is over 30 million gallons. We have
been in the fortunate position that, while
the demand was increasing at this rate,
production was also increasing rapidly,
and whereas in 1939 the production of
milk, that is the total milk sold off farms
in Northern Ireland, amounted to 39
million gallons in the year, for last year
the figure was 542 million gallons, so
that we were comfortably able to meet the
whole domestic consumption demand and
at the same time allow Scotland over 21
million gallons to ease the situation there
in the winter months. The increase in
milk production is a very gratifying feature of our farming economy at the present moment. The feeding stuff situation
has not been easy, but in spite of all
their difficulties our farmers have been
able to increase their output steadily up
to the figure which I have already given
to the Committee. That would seem to
augur well for the livestock side of the
industry recovering very rapidly after the
war.
There is one other matter I should like
to mention to the Committee-agricultural research. We know something
about the tremendous strides that scientific research has been making during the
war. Unfortunately the results of a
great deal of that research have had to
be turned to destructive ends. In my
Ministry the results obtained from this
research are happidly turned to constructive ends. One of the most serious
troubles afflicting the livestock side of our
industry has been that of infectious
sterility. We have in our veterinary
research laboratories been able to discover
the organism which causes this trouble,
and we have been able to trace the
methods by which it is spread and have
devised a simple test for diagnosing the
disease. Experts from other countries
have visited our laboratories to study our
work. In addition to the field trials in
progress here comparable tests are being
undertaken in the English Ministry's
laboratories and by the Welcome Physiological laboratories. We have every hope
that as a result of this work we shall be
in a position in a very short time to deal
on a practical scale with this problem of
infectious sterility.
There is another feature of our research
work which I should like to mentionseed borne diseases in plants. I have in
mind particularly the flax crop. For a
considerable time, even before the war,
I had an idea of my own-I had not anything to go on; it was only a notionthat what farmers had from time to time
attributed to frost and that sort of thing
in connection with young seedling crops
was not really due to frost at all but to
certain diseases that they were not able
to distinguish and did not know anything
about. These diseases under certain conditions kept back the crop and reduced
for the time being its fertility.
research experts in the Ministry of Agriculture were eventually put on to this
whole question. They have been able to
single out and distinguish not only these
different seed borne diseases peculiar to
flax, but they have perfected what is now
called the Ulster method of treatment.
We have been able to see to it that all
the flax seed distributed to farmers in
Northern Ireland, whether it is produced
from our own crops or sent here from
England, is treated in accordance with
our method before being sent out.
The
I am, I know, precluded from mentioning names, but in this connection I should
like to say what a satisfaction it is to
me to know that the importance of the
research work done here is recognised
outside our own Province. One of our

awarded the Doctor of Science Degree of
London University in recognition of a
published contribution to research on

occasion on which London University has

plant diseases.
I should like before sitting down to pay
tribute to the splendid work of the staff
of my Ministry during the year.
Mr. NIXON: You wanted to dismiss
one of them a few years ago.
Rev. ROBERT MOORE: We are all
inclined to resent the ever growing volume

of controls and restrictions that the war

With one exception I believe I am the

farmers whom I have the honour to represent in Mid Tyrone, and also indirectly
throughout Northern Ireland, if I did

.
The great majority of the farmers of

we should have in our midst is a sound

I am indeed shocked, and so will many
other agriculturists in Northern Ireland
be shocked when they read in the daily
Press that there is a reduction in the
agriculture Estimates for 1944-45 from
last year's Estimates of £145,744. I am
of the opinion that the Minister knows
as well as I do that the farmers of Northern Ireland are not getting the consideration they should. As the agriculturists
of the Six Counties took up the burden
placed on them without a frown to do their
part, and more than their share, to help
the Allies in every way so that they should
win the war. The Prime Minister of
Great Britain, the right hon. Winston
Churchill, said blood and tears and lives
sacrified would have to be undertaken to
achieve victory. I may say, without fear
of contradiction, that if the farming community had not risen to the occasion,
working from early morning to late at
night to raise food to feed the Forces at
war and the population of our great industrial centres throughout Great Britain and
Northern Ireland, the war would have
been lost. Northern Ireland's part in
the struggle was helped by the farmers'
sons who joined and volunteered to do
their bit on the battlefields of France,
Africa, Italy and elsewhere. Their
daughters left their homes in many cases
and joined some of the Services connected with the Army to do their bit.
Surely all the sacrifices suffered by the
farming community should in some small
way be appreciated by giving to those

the second front, a fair and reasonable
remuneration for their products. At the

not got a decent price. I have on different occasions brought to the notice of the
Minister of Agriculture the unremunerative prices paid for flax. I have asked the
Minister to make representations to the
Imperial Ministry for an adjustment,

office on the 6th or 7th May, 1943. Consequently there was no provision made
