words, there was no Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of Agriculture.
Later in the financial year there was an
estimate for £600 brought in for the
salary of the Minister of Agriculture. It
was commented on here at the time, and
it was passed. The nature of the comment was, why was there not some provision made for the Minister for approximately 11 months? The excuse that was
put forward for that was that in consequence of the office of Parliamentary
Secretary of the Ministry having ceased
to exist, the Minister was drawing on the
£1,000 voted for the Parliamentary Secretary.
That is most improper and wrong. This
House voted £600 to the Minister for the
financial year ending 31st March, 1944,
and I would venture to state-contradict
me if you can, and if you do you are in
a position to know-that the Minister
drew about £1,400 or £1,500. You cannot juggle with figures like that. If you
do there is no use our being here at all
or considering any Estimates. That is
not saying that if there was a proper
Supplementary Estimate submitted we
would not pass it, because we would. But
you cannot juggle with figures like that.
The Parliamentary Secretaryship is a
different office, and if you can take money
voted to one office to pay someone in
another office then your whole accounting
system is not worth the paper it is written
on, nor is it worth coming here and bringing it up, for if this happens in one
place you do not know where else it is
happening.
There is no use bringing in Estimates if
that is going on. You had a warning
during the last financial year that the
proper way to do it was to bring in a
Supplementary Estimate and give the
Minister for the time he was Minister as
much as any other Minister. There is
not a Member of this House who would
or could object to that, but instead of
doing that you juggle a salary that is
voted for one office on to another office.
You have no authority for that.
The Permanent Secretary of the
Ministry of Finance is retiring, presumably under the age limit. The Comptroller and Auditor-General should have
retired years ago under the age limit, but

Act of Parliament or a Resolution
brought forward in this House to extend

the Government cannot interfere with
him. He can surcharge the Prime

are
give these lads and girls-and the girls

In this country of ours farming is an

There is another point in the speech
of the right hon. Gentleman which I
should like to mention. To me personally
it was very gratifying to hear that the

than last year. My right hon. Friend
will remember that it was hardly one of
my most popular actions when I gave a

I was advised to give so much per stone.
I am not against the arguments used on
that occasion, which were that if you gave
so much per stone you would get betterclass flax. I saw that what was really
wanted was to give confidence to the man
who had never grown flax before, and by
giving him £10 an acre you gave him
confidence to go forward, as he would
know that he would lose nothing. I am
glad to say that scheme has been successful.
I am also glad to hear the slight note
of warning in the Minister's speech
because it must be remembered that we
could overdo this flax business. We want
food, and we want it very badly, and if
our stock is going to take up the position
it should after the war it will only do so
if the animals are well fed. Therefore, we
must be very careful that we do not grow
too much flax. I do not suppose my right.
hon. Friend the Member for Mid Down
(Mr. Andrews) will agree with me about

Estimates-
Ministry of Agriculture
HOUSE OF COMMONS

[Lord Glentoran]
There is another matter which I should
like to raise here. I should like to see
some preparations made for what is to
happen after the war. I am not at all
carried away by the extraordinarily
optimistic picture which is being painted
all over the country about what is going
to happen to farming after the war. I do
not believe in any optimistic picture of
that kind, and I am fortified in belief
my
by reading only last week the Labour
Report on post-war matters.
To my
amazement I found that they were even
greater Tories than I thought they were.
They have not moved an inch from
Cobden. They want cheap imported food
for the people which we would meet by
selling our products to the Dominions;
in other words, that we should sell wireless sets to Hottentots to enable them to
listen to B.B.C. men talking.
I do not believe in that at all. On the
contrary, I am rather afraid that after
the war people will have learned so much
about manufacturing their own goods that
they will not want our goods as much as
they did before. However that may be,
I am satisfied that agriculture will go
through a bad time after the war unless
we make the ship absolutely watertight
now. I know myself that the Ministry
and the Minister have got that in view,
but I should like to see more of it. I
spoke yesterday about houses, about lanes,
and about farmyards. I should like to
see those made right, because farmers will
not have money to fix them after the war.
I think the Ministry-I know they are
pressed at the moment-should set up
some little committee to try to find out
exactly what crops are economical here;
I mean to find out whether wheat is an
economic production, whether oats is an
economic production, whether barley is
an economic production. At the present

after the war which would have a market

In the meantime I would say that our

Our Ministry, considering the war is on,

All over the country I see most extraordinary cases of cross-breeding, and
nothing is so fatal to production as crossbreeding. I know that in England they
are trying to solve this difficulty by means

insemination

Major ROBINSON: Owing to the
long and very eloquent speeches that have
been made on these Estimates, I do not
intend to detain the Committee very long,
but I must say that I view with great
alarm the smug complacency that the
Minister seemed to display when presenting these Estimates. He begins by talking about the land ploughed in connection
with the tillage campaign. There are a
great many parts of this country which
should never be tilled at any time except
in a very dry year, but evidently the
Ministry have not awakened to that fact
yet. I know that down in my part of the
country it is all hilly, heavy ground, and
it is excellent ground for cattle. I maintain that the country ought to rear cattle
on good cattle-rearing limestone soil, and
that the Ministry should not tie themselves up to make every person do the
same thing in every part of the land.
In County Antrim, where I live, if you
get three or four tons of potatoes to the
acre you are doing extra well. In County
Down if you get 16 to 20 tons that pays
the farmer well. There are lots of little
farms where one man has to be employed.
The man who is employed is actually getting more money out of the farm than the
man who owns the farm. Is that doing
the country any good? I do not think so.
The Minister of Agriculture seems to get
great pleasure from the fact that a great
deal of chemical manure is being used.
My experience of chemical manures as a
man who has spent all his life in the
country and is interested in all kinds of
sport is not the same as the Minister's.
In England enormous bags of game
used to be got years ago when people shot
with the muzzle-loading guns against the
breech loaders they have nowadays, and
people generally think that the smaller
bags of these days are on account of so
much chemical
manure being used.
Whether it is actually poisoning the game
like partridges and hares, or whether it
interferes with the fertility of the ground,
on which the Minister of Agriculture
seems to be satisfied, I do not know, but
I am inclined to think that it is a little bit
of both. At any rate all these things are
going down. A short time ago I met a man
who was interested in greyhound racing,
-1329
Ministry of Agriculture 1330

and he used to go out on to a farm and
run his greyhounds after a rabbit or two.
He told me the place used to be filled with
rabbits, but some time ago the man who
owned the place used some chemical
manure and now there was not a rabbit
within four miles of the place.
The Minister prates about the amount
of milk that is being drunk. I can tell
him how much more milk could be drunk.
If a tax were put on it the same as is on
whiskey ten times as much milk would
be drunk as at the present time.
(Laughter.) I should like to say a few
words in regard to cattle breeding. I
have been greatly interested in cattle
breeding all my life. The noble Lord said
a lot of things about cattle, but I was out
at the time, and it would be with regret
that I should repeat anything that he
said. At the same time remarks have
been made with regard to the subsidising
of bulls. I have some views with regard
to cattle and horse breeding. I have not
been altogether unsuccessful as a breeder,
and I am of the opinion that something
ought to be done not only to subsidise
bulls but also cows and mares.
I think everyone will admit that there
never was a good man who had not a
good mother, and I am perfectly certain
that if the nucleus of good breeding
family stock was introduced into the
country it would do good eventually.
After all, we have in Ulster, which I
believe to be the greatest place in the
world for breeding cattle, a great stock
record. A great deal has been done for
Scotland in this respect by propaganda
and advertisement, but if one looks back
into the history of their cattle, particularly the shorthorn breed which they
all boost so much in Scotland, one will
find that a great many of those very fine
animals originally came from Ireland, and
I do not see any reason why Ulster should
not be kept in the forefront and have a
fair crack of the whip.
In the first year of the war I was fortunate to have an animal that was sent
out to the Argentine. He realised the
second highest price of 1,800 guineas, and
that in a bad year. Two years later I
had a bull which was bred off one of my
bulls. It was the first champion, and
was sold at Perth for 1,000 guineas.
After he had gone to the. Argentine he
fetched 4,000 guineas, and I am told that
one of the best bulls of this year is an
own brother of that bull. That could be
done all over the place, and where there
are limestone soils it would be much
better for breeding cattle. That is one
thing Ulster can do successfully. We can
grow potatoes on allotments, but cattle
and horses should really be reared on the
limestone, soil of Ulster, for there we can
produce the type of animal that will be
profitable to ourselves and beneficial to
the world. I only mention that because
the Minister of Agriculture referred to
research and its results.
This cry for milk, milk, milk, is absolutely ruining our cattle trade in the
North of Ireland as far as I can see.
The farmers are calling for Ayrshire and
other milk producing breeds, and they
are crossing them with good native cattle
which should have been built up with
their own kith and kin to establish a proper breed which will flourish and be
profitable in the North of Ireland. Breed
tells in everything, man or beast, and
there can be no doubt about that. If
we establish a proper pedigree stock
throughout the country we will eventually
have a great asset which we can hand
down to our children.
Compliments have been paid to the
staff of the Ministry of Agriculture. The
staff has always been helpful and always
willing in every way to give all the
assistance it possibly can. I feel it is the
policy of the Ministry that is wrong. I
believe a great deal could be done to
assist this country, and I feel that very
little is being done, chiefly because,
the Member for Antrim said, a great
deal of the work of the Ministry is done
on behalf of the Ministry of Food.

Mr. ANDREWS: I wish, in the first

right hon. Friend, the Minister of Agriculture on the very interesting and instructive speech he delivered to-day in
introducing his Estimates. I think every
Member of the House must have been
impressed by his earnestness and his very
evident desire to do everything humanly
possible to help our agriculture. I speak
as a large practical farmer myself, and
also as the representative of probably the
most progressive and energetic agricul
tural community in Northern Ireland. I
feel I am entitled to say that where the
Estimates-
Ministry of Agriculture
25 MAY 1944
farms are of a reasonable size, where they
are really economic holdings, and where
the fertility of the land is really good, the
farmers are reasonably satisfied, speaking
generally. It is true that, as the Minister
knows, a great deal of dissatisfaction
exists owing to the fact that the price
of late crop potatoes was fixed much too
low last year, and I hope the same mistake will not be made on this occasion.
What is making the farmer anxious
at the moment is what is going to happen
when the war is over. I very fully appreciate the difficulties of the Imperial Government in defining post-war agricultural
policy. We do not know what world
conditions are going to be when the war
ends. We do not know how far it will
be possible to restore our import and
export trade, and if it is difficult, as I
believe it is, for the Imperial Government to decide upon its post-war agricultural policy it is even more difficult for
our Department here to do so, because of
the fact that it is inevitably closely linked
up with what takes place in England and
the policy that is adopted there. I feel
that the Department is doing a very
great work in the interests of the farmers
of Northern Ireland, and I believe that,
notwithstanding some of the things that
have been said to-day, that that has been
recognised by our farming community.
The Ministry's land improvement
scheme has been of great advantage.
Again, the research work, both as regards
the diseases of cattle and of plants has
been of very great benefit. The improvement of livestock scheme has also accomplished a great deal, and again agricultural credits have been a help to farmers
who were in financial difficulties.
For
all these reasons I feel I am entitled to
congratulate this Department on the work
that they are doing, and I agree with
those who have said to-day that the staff
are most helpful to our farming community. I have experience myself of the
staff and I feel grateful to them for the
help they have given to me. I am sure
I am not an exception.

The question of the allocation of petrol
is a serious one. Many farmers have
told me that they cannot get petrol to
carry on their agricultural work. The
Transport Board can get all the petrol
it requires. There are no limitations or
restrictions so far as that Board is concerned. Judging by the number of buses
and lorries the Transport Board have on
the road they can get plenty of petrol,
but the farmers cannot get it in order that
they may carry out the most important
work of providing food for the people. I
will not pursue that matter now, but
certainly the whole scheme will have to
be revised, because the position is very
unsatisfactory at the present time.

think the post-war programme for agriculture must include some steps for reducing
the bureaucratic conditions we have in
existence to-day.
Then again I say we are not getting fairplay with Great Britain in the matter of
subsidies. At first blush it might look
that we were. For instance, in oats and
wheat the subsidy payments are the same,
but they work out differently in this way.
The concession granted for wheat are far
more generous than they are in the case
of oats. Wheat is the principal cereal
grown across the Channel, whereas our
principal cereal crop is oats, and in oats
we come off a bad second best indeed.
The whole position will have to be reexamined the whole matter of financial
relations with Great Britain and the whole
position in regard to these subsidies and
everything else, because they do not work
out on a basis of equality.

and the relation of this number to the
total number of houses in the area.
the case of all these areas the percentage

Mr. MIDGLEY: Twelve months
ago I
presented Estimates for the first time. I

were realised to the full. In the intervening year I have been privileged to
learn the romantic and absorbing story
of Civil Defence in all its phases from
those best qualified to impart the
knowledge, namely, the splendid men and
women of Northern Ireland who have remained steadfast and true throughout the
vicissitudes of the war.
I should, in the first place, explain that
the Estimates which I am asking the
Committee to pass consist, first of all, of
a revised Estimate for the Ministry of

of the Ministry only for the first two

the twelve months covered by the original

asked in No. 1 Vote is £7,650.
I should like to pause for a moment to
say that as this is for the two months
during which we had jurisdiction, a person

should be divided by six and the result

exactly one-sixth of the twelve months is
because the expenditure in connection

I am also moving for £718,000 under
Vote 2-that for the Civil Defence
Services and £620,000 under Vote 3, for
the National Fire Service, in their original
form, as they appear in the bound volume
of the Estimates. The revised total for

It is natural and indeed necessary
that I,
as the Minister responsible,
should come to the House before
I leave my present post and should
ask for such sum as is necessary to meet
payments which will be incurred by the
Ministry up to and including to-morrow,
which is the last day of its official
existence. Upon me also rightly devolves
the task of defending the policies upon
which are based the figures contained in
the Civil Defence and National Fire
Service Estimates for the current year.
I do not propose to go through any of
the figures in detail. They are there for
the Committee to see and criticise, and I
shall be happy to answer, to the best of
my knowledge and ability, such questions
as hon. Members may wish to raise. In
general, it will be noted that the expenditure which was forecast for the year
for Civil Defence, as a whole, represents
a reduction of £760,000 as compared with
last year, and is lower by a considerable
sum than similar Estimates for the past
four years.
That, I should like to impress upon hon. Members, is due in very
large measure to the fact that the major
structural works and supplies of necessary
equipment have been provided in past
years. As regards the Estimates as a
whole, we have provided neither for
extravagance nor waste, but neither has
there been any cheeseparing. It has been
the policy of the Ministry to encourage
local authorities to maintain their civil
defence arrangements at the utmost point
of readiness and efficiency. I make no
apology for that policy, and I believe that
few thinking people who have recollections of the past or any imagination about
the immediate future will quarrel with it.
I can assure the Committee that the
money provision which it is being asked
to make is necessary for the maintenance
of those measures which, in the opinion
of the Government, it is prudent and
indeed essential to maintain after giving
full consideration and regard to the existing war position. More than that, I do
not at this stage propose
to say
with
regard to figures though, as I have said,
I shall be very happy to do my best to
simplify any point about which hon.
Members would like to have information.
In times of war, however, people are
compelled to think in terms of service and
efficiency rather than in terms of cost.
They want to know that our Armed
Forces are content, well armed, well led,
and well organised. They want to know
that their equipment is of good quality
and in ample supply, and they want to
know that the rank and file are resolutely
behind their leaders in a determination
to see the war through to final victory.
Those are the tests which the people of
this country apply to their fighting forces,
and equally they should be applied to the
volunteer armies, paid and unpaid, who
by their activities in Civil Defence help
to keep the home front secure.
During the past year people have often
said to me how remarkable it is that the
Civil Defence Services retain their enthusiasm as they do, when so little active
service comes their way, and when the only
variant to stand-by duty is the repetition
and perfection of training which all of
them have undergone again and again.
The answer, I think, is that the Civil
Defence Services are a cross-section of a
people who love peace and who are sternly
determined to secure it for themselves
and their children by bringing this war to
a triumphant end and by teaching
aggressors wherever they may be that
aggression does not pay.
I served for four years in what we used
to call the Great War, and when I came
home from it one of my greatest disappointments was to see the spirit of
comradeship waning under peace conditions. When I became Minister of
Public Security and began to go about
among the part-time civilians in the Civil
Defence Services I found, perhaps a little
to my surprise, but certainly to my very
great pleasure, that they had managed to
recapture a good deal of the spirit of
comradeship which I remembered from
my Army days. It is a great tribute to
the qualities of our Ulster people that all
over the country they should have banded
!

T
Estimates-
Ministry of Public Security
30 MAY 1944
themselves together in these very democratic organisations, and that they should
be working in such harmony, particularly
after a prolonged lull in active operations.
This spirit is, I believe, very largely what
has saved us from extinction in the war,
and will, I trust, help to secure us a
glorious victory. I very sincerely hope
that it may be carried forward into the
peace where it will help in building up
the better world for which all of us are
working.
The National Fire Service has had a
very busy and an interesting year. It is
as yet only two years old and, like all new
organisations, is still in process of settling
down into a smooth and efficient routine.
During the year ending 31st March last
it received no fewer than 1,338 calls.
One-third of these, I much regret to say,
were malicious, but the balance as you
will see works out at an average of twoand-a-half actual fires for every day of
the year. A great many of these fires
were in country districts and I should
like to pay a special tribute to the
efficiency and public spirit of the parttime firemen who give up their work,
their leisure, or their sleep to go to fight
these fires without fee, or reward. They
deserve well of the country and I am
glad to know from local contacts that
their courage, public spirit and goodwill
are greatly appreciated.
I spoke of malicious calls just now.
They are a real crime against the community. In these days when road transport is so bound up with the progress of
the war, or emergencies in connection
therewith, the sender of a malicious call
may be responsible not only for impeding
the carrying on of essential work or
diverting fire-fighting vehicles from where
they would be urgently required, but may
actually be responsible for loss of life
through adding to our already congested
road traffic.
Hon. Members will not expect me to
offer any forecast about the course of the
war, even over the next few months, but
I would like to remind them that ports
are an obvious objective for enemy attack,
particularly when seaborne operations
are in progress. I need not emphasise
the responsibility which we in Northern
Ireland bear in this connection. There is
not a single member of the Civil Defence
services in this country who may not, at
any moment, be involved in an attack on
our ports either in bearing the first brunt
or in bringing help and reinforcement.
I have never attempted to exaggerate
or to terrify our people with dreadful
warnings of what the Germans may be
planning against us. Our people know
well enough without any prompting from
me that no consideration of decency
would deter the present German Government from any outrage against the laws
of humanity. They will shrink from no
act if they think that they can thereby
secure an adequate military advantage,
or even a breathing space, when once the
full force of the Allied war effort breaks
upon them.
It may well be that some unpleasant
or destructive surprise will be used by the
enemy but no poison is without its antidote; and all Hitler's best surprises so
far have been quickly and effectively
countered. The one menace which we
know the Germans hold over our heads,
but which they have not yet chosen to
use, is gas, and the reason that they have
so far refrained from this diabolical
method of warfare is certainly not their
kindness of heart. They know of our
elaborate gas precaution system and they
dread our reprisals on their own country,
but gas precautions are not a thing that
the State or the local authorities can do
more than facilitate. Their completeness
and success depend on the individual
citizen's care and courage.
I want to say to the Committee, and
through it to the Civil Defence services
and the people of Ulster, that great
events are pending. The next few months
are likely, therefore, to be a testing time
of all the patient planning that has gone
in the last four years to build the peaceloving British people into an effective and
united entity which, with our Allies, can
smash Hitlerism for ever. Just at the
moment the atmosphere resembles that of
1940 between the invasion of Norway and
the blitzkrieg in the Low Countries and
France. There is the same feeling of
nervous tension and realisation that great
events are imminent; this time, however,
it is not we but the Germans who are
wondering where the blows will fall. On
our side there is the realisation that we
and our Allies are about to make a
supreme effort to end the war in a succession of direct hammer blows; and that
all our energies must be directed to sustaining the great offensive when the day
comes.
Ministry of Public Security 1354
Estimates-
HOUSE OF COMMONS
•
[Mr. Midgley]
This is, I suppose, my swan song as
Minister of Public Security and also that
of the Ministry. As one who came on
the scene at a fairly late hour in its
history, I will not, I hope, be regarded as
egotistical if I pay some tribute to its work
during its comparatively short life of less
than four years.
Hon. Members will recall that it was set up under the charge
of my right hon. Friend, the Attorney-
General, in the dark days of Dunkirk.
Invasion was then the cry, and within a
very short time the Ministry had promoted the organisation of the Local
Defence Volunteers, who afterwards
became the Ulster Home Guard. The
Ministry and the police authorities can
say with pardonable pride that they had
thirty thousand men reasonably armed,
equipped and undergoing training even
in advance of many comparable units in
Great Britain.
Very substantial progress had been
made in building up and equipping the
Civil Defence machine, at any rate in the
vulnerable areas, when the heavy raids
came in April and May, 1941. Much, of
course, was still lacking on account of the
appalling supply difficulties which we then
faced and the clamant need for measures
of active as well as passive defence.
Nevertheless, thanks to many days and
nights of anxious planning, the city withstood and soon recovered from blows which
had they come even a few months earlier
might well have been mortal. The people
were fed.
Public services were restored.
Bomb damage was cleared. Houses were
repaired. Vital factories were rapidly
brought into full production. Faults
there were. Deficiencies there were. Air
attack will always teach new and grimmer
lessons. But we must not let the natural
impulse to criticise what may have been
defective during those difficult days blind
us to the magnitude of the task, and all
that was achieved in the all too short
period of intensive preparation which was
granted to us.
Coincident with the handling of postraid problems the air raid shelter provision throughout Northern Ireland was
surveyed and dealt with, and the Civil
Defence machine as a whole-its organisation, equipment and training-was overhauled and improved.
In April, 1942, the Ministry undertook
the establishment of the National Fire
Service, with the goodwill and, support
both of this House and of the local
authorities. To-day preparations to meet
enemy attack are virtually completed in
so far as they can be planned in advance.
The machine is in good order, and I feel
that I can hand it over with confidence
to the care of the Ministry of Home
Affairs. I think I can claim that whatever its faults it made fewer enemies in
the four years of its life than was to be
expected from the speed and vigour with
which its work was pressed, and I trust
that everyone in the local authorities and
in Civil Defence who had dealings with
my Ministry will find the same spirit of
helpfulness in the Department's new role
as a branch of the Ministry of Home
Affairs.
Euclid says that no object can be bigger
than the sum of its parts, but then he
was, after all, a pure formalist.
At any
rate, I am convinced that the staff of my
Ministry are an exception to Euclid's rule.
They brought to their work a spirit which
built them into a team, and as a team the
sum total of their work was of much
greater value to the country than they
could have been expected to contribute
as individuals. But not only did they
themselves work as a team. They had
the attribute in an extremely high degree
of working amicably with those local
authorities and members of the Civil
Defence Services with whom their work
brought them into contact.
This did not happen by accident. It
was the fruit of good leadership and willing co-operation by every member of the
staff. If I have spoken highly of them,
it is no more than I think they deserve.
I know that the high regard in which I
hold them is shared by my two predecessors, my right hon. Friends the
Attorney-General and the Minister of
Labour, and also by very many people
outside this House who have learnt to
know and appreciate their real worth.
My predecessors guided and organised the
work in a way most satisfactory to the
country, as a whole, and I have done my
best to follow their example.
It would be invidious to single out
names from amongst the thousands of
splendid men and women throughout
Ulster who enlisted in the Civil Defence
Services, but I feel that a special expression of appreciation is due to the Civil
Defence authority in each area, more
Estimates-
Ministry of Public Security
30 MAY 1944
especially in the most vulnerable of all,
namely, Belfast. Words are inadequate
to express all that the citizens owe to the
unselfish, unpaid services of these gentlemen. By their magnificent contribution
to our cause, their sacrifice of home life
and their private businesses, but, above
all, by their unswerving devotion to the
highest standards of community service
they deserve and are here accordedthe grateful thanks of our country.
I have valued my year of office as
Minister of Public Security. It has
given me an insight into the finest
qualities of our people, and I look forward with confidence to the day when the
goodwill and public spirit that they have
shown so generously and so spontaneously
under the stress of war shall be turned to
the paths of peace and to the setting up
of a new and finer civilisation in this
Ulster of which we are so proud. I beg
to move.

It is not necessary for me to go any

across the water it has been made out on

could not be any explanation given in
regard to this matter that would be
acceptable. I do not know whether the
right hon. Gentleman or the Minister of
Finance noticed it or not. We heard a
great harangue about policy. So far as
I can see the principal policy is to spend
as much as possible while the going is
good.
The Minister mentioned shelters. I
would not mention them if he had not
done so. He also mentioned experts.
Practically every shelter built in the city
of Belfast had to be taken down inside
a year or a year and a half of its being
erected. There was a terrible accident or
tragedy in Percy Street. A shelter fell
there and killed over 60 people. As the
right hon. Gentleman said on a previous
Ministry of Public Security 1358

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Nixon]
occasion that was not the fault of the contractor. The shelter was built to specification. There was a thick cement slab
on top of the bricks. The bricks gave
way and the slab came down. The technical staff passed that shelter. After that
tragedy they started building shelters
across the road, and they filled them up
with the muck they took off the street.
This could have been taken out with the
hand. I rang up the ex-Prime Minister
and he came up to see them. The Minister
of Finance also came and saw the condition of them. They did not deny the
position, and they would not deny it even
now.
Then there was a tailor prosecuted for
being a contractor. Who gave him the
contracts? Whose duty was it to watch
the tailor? Is it not a fact that some of
the experts were the real contractor and
put in the tailor's name-of course that
was done with the tailor's consentbecause he was to get something out of it.
I thought the Minister would not have
bothered mentioning shelters. He was
not responsible, because he was not in
office at the time. At that time he was
standing here helping me to expose it, and
he should be here still.
I do not say
that because I begrudge him the position
he now fills.
Then there was the question of the repair of houses. House repairing in the
city of Belfast was the biggest ramp in
the world. The right hon. Gentleman
mentioned the repair of houses. I saw
men going into empty houses ostensiblyfor the purpose of repairing them, and
they sat down and played cards all evening. I also saw them going off the job at
three o'clock in the afternoon. Although
I stand for the working man, I am not
afraid to expose idleness. I reported that
matter to the Minister of Finance What
did he tell me after making inquiries into
the matter? He told us they were
going to get their pay-that was at three
o'clock in the afternoon-and they did
not come back. Once they got into a
house they could not be got out of it.
They did not half repair the houses.
I saw another case in connection with
glazing. I did not report this matter to
the Ministry, but I reported it to the contractor. He waded into them and sacked
them. These men went away to watch a
football match in the park, although they
were paid so much an hour for glazing.
As I have stated, I reported the matter
to the contractor, and he sacked them
right off the reel. That is a sample of
what went on in connection with the repair of houses-squandering money while
our men were fighting. We heard something about what is going to be done for
our fighting men when they return. I
know men who were at Dunkirk who could
not get a house in the city of Belfast.
They could hardly get a job much less
a house. In case I should be misunderstood, I should like to say that the Minister of Labour is very good in regard to
ex-soldiers.
These Estimates are things we can go
over and over again. I am sorry they
have been presented in such a form and
at the last minute. Whoever did that
has no respect for Parliament at all; it
is treated with contempt. I say that
document was not necessary, and even
if it had been necessary there was no
reason why we should not have got it a
week ago.
The document does not convey anything. There is no information
in it which anyone could make anything
out of. I hope that this criticism will
help the Minister in his new position. I
hope that in future he will have a look at
the Estimates before they are submitted
to the House, and I also hope he will not
start appointing too many staff officers
and other high officials, because
Servicemen, who at the moment are winning battles and are being paid only a
few shillings per week, will be coming
back. Something should be left for them.
We heard something about petrol. Is
it not a fact, and was it not admitted
here, that one of the officers took a service
car in order to convey himself, his wife
and family to Portrush? That did not
happen in the Minister's time. When I
raised the matter here the bogus excuse
Iwas made that he started off in his own
car and when it broke down he took a
service car.
I asked about the petrol,
and I was told that he used his own
coupons. I said that if he used his own

Major SINCLAIR: There are a few
items in this Vote on which I wish to
comment. In the first part of Sub-head
A provision is made for a contingencies
allowance for the Prime Minister at the
rate of £500 per annum. The actual
sum shown as payable in this year is
almost double this amount, and this is in
accordance with the statement which I
made on the Supplementary Estimate for
this service presented in the spring that
the allowance should be payable from the
date on which the Prime Minister took
up office.
As no allowance was drawn in
the last financial year retrospective provision is made in this year's Estimate.
In the second part of Sub-head A it will
be noted that a full year's provision has
now been made for the expenses allowance
payable to the Honorary Director for Information Services attached to the office
of the Agent for Northern Ireland in
London.
In Sub-head B the sum of £900 shown
opposite the item for travelling includes
a figure of £250, corresponding to the
£250 in italics lower down in the 1943-44
column of this sub-head, for travelling by
officials at the Ulster Office. The real
increase over last year's provision for the
travelling expenses of the Prime Minister
and officials of his Department is therefore £70, and this is explained by the
fact that last year's figure was an underestimate, and necessary visits to London
tend to increase as the end of the war
approaches and discussions on plans for
the post-war period become more frequent.
Finally, in Sub-head E we have a sum
of £1,250 for general expenses in connection with publicity. The Committee
will understand that I cannot say now
how this money and any further sum
which may be found necessary, for which,
of course, sanction will be sought by a
Supplementary Estimate, will be spent,
but I can say that it is the Government's
intention that no effective method will be

a
week. It is over one half of Mr.

Would anyone believe that?
was
Dealing with the record and achievements of the Prime Minister during the

In setting up the Ministry of Health

role in the Corkey crisis. The Prime
Minister clamped down free discussion on
that matter with the help of a coercive
three-line whip a short time ago,
in a
Parliamentary situation without parallel,
a situation of Ministerial animosities,
Ministerial recriminations, and Ministerial
trampling on elementary fair play.
Minister was thrown from office with
harshness and with contumely. Not one
of the Unionist rank and file, the Back
Benchers who are so vociferous in their
speeches and so hesitant in their voting,
had the manhood to stand up and say

wonder the hon. Member for Antrim is
getting restless.
The Government at that time had
become a by-word and a jest. Plain men
were asking one another, "How can you
believe a word which comes from its
mouth?" The public were baffled and
bewildered and perplexed by the contradictory statements on the material facts
surrounding the enforced resignationin plain words, the summary expulsion
from his post of the Minister of Education. The issue raised was not a party
issue. It was an issue of the bona fides
of the spoken word. The Prime Minister has shown a peculiar insensitiveness
to the value of the truth of the spoken
word.
A lofty standard of candour in matters
of fact is justly looked for in men holding Ministerial office. Facts are sacred.
Opinions are free. Men differ and will
differ in opinions. Men ought not to
differ on facts. The Prime Minister in
public view arraigned his colleague for
gross and persistent neglect of his duties.
His colleague complained bitterly that his
honour as a Cabinet Minister was impugned by the Prime Minister. The
Prime Minister in substance declared that
his colleague's word was not to be taken.
The ex-Minister was Dr. Corkey. Who
is he? He is the vice-principal and the
Professor of Christian Ethics of the
Assembly's College, and has much to do
with the training of students for the
ministry of the Presbyterian Church.
His father was a clergyman of that
church. So were six of his brothers.
One so circumstanced as he is was prima
facie unlikely to juggle with facts.
It was in June last, just twelve months
ago, after the mutiny on the lower deck
which overpowered the captain and the
chief officers that Dr. Corkey began to
serve Mammon as a Minister of the
Crown. In his first flush of exultation
on assuming office he boasted that the
Prime Minister would have nobody but
him for the post. The period of wooing
was brief. The first giddy paroxysm soon
subsided and then there came the period
of disillusionment, as happens so often
in the case of hasty, ill-assorted matches.
After a troubled tenure of eight months
the Prime Minister summoned him to a
drum-head court-martial, not for trial,
but for judgment and sentence of dismissal. "Cassio, I love thee, but never
more be officer of mine.'
""
The ex-Minister, Dr. Corkey, says that
the Prime Minister without giving the
slightest warning or any opportunity of
stating his case, requested his resignation on the ground that he had not gone
often enough to the Ministry's temporary
headquarters at Portrush. He got what
the man in the street would call the order
of the boot, the Prussian jack-boot. He
went into the Prime Minister's presence
a Minister. He left degraded to the
ranks, he left a wounded man-
-he says a
wronged man-certainly a heart-sore and
humbled man. What kind of treatment
was that? Was it elementary fair play?
The Prime Minister obviously takes
politics for a cruel trade, and sees in good
nature only a bungler in the business.
His parting with his colleague was not
gracious or graceful. He had not the
grace of the gentleman who
Kicked them downstairs with such a
sweet grace
They might think he was handing

Why did the Prime Minister not hear

Minister said he warned the Minister in

with the headquarters at Portrush. The
Minister denied that statement pointblank. He said the Prime Minister did
nothing of the sort. He said that until

[Mr. Campbell]
On 12th February, the day after the
last eventful interview, and before his
resignation was accepted the Minister in
a letter to the Prime Minister wrote in
strong words of the difficulties and objections he had met with during his tenure
of office. The Prime Minister in no
letter subsequent to that challenged that
averment, and ten days later the Prime
Minister solemnly gave this Parliament
to understand, and to understand from
the plainest words, that he was satisfied
no difficulties had occurred in educational
policy between the two responsible heads
of the Ministry. Was this treating the
public with veracity, with fairness, or
with frankness? Was it cricket? It
gave the lie direct to the ex-Minister.
One or other must be taxable with the
inaccuracy of Ananias. One or other
must not have been morbid about the
truth. Which?
Veracity is everything in parliamentary as in other spheres of public life.
Without it there is no public life worth
having. Without it there is no safety
in public life. The old Roman state
perished when the Roman's word could
no longer be trusted. That was the beginning of the end. The contradictions
to which I have referred were not differences on trivialities, but on matters of
high import. Parliamentary candour is
involved here. There has been, I regret
to say, a lowering of the standard of
parliamentary uprightness and decorum
and from this must ensue a grave weakening of public trust. I do not accuse
the Prime Minister of being untruthful
in the strict sense of the word, but I do
accuse him of a deep disdain for the sterling
value of the spoken word. Humiliation
is a painful sight at any time. If one
wants to see it he need but look at this
Government-at the Front Benchcrouching in sufferance as tenants-at-will
of the noble Lord the Member for Bloomfield, haunted day by day by the fear of
eviction, clinging pitiably and precariously to office and powerless to scrape together more than 11 to 15 votes in a
Division, each of this sergeant's picket
being a place holder. Could any spectacle
of humiliation be more painful?

Minister down. I must protest again
to-day against this proposal to increase
the emoluments of the Prime Minister by
a sum of £500 under the heading of
"Allowance for contingencies of office."
That sum, which will be free of incometax, is the equivalent of £1,000 a year.
I think it is quite wrong that at this time
when Northern Ireland is engaged in a
great war savings campaign, and the
people are being called upon to save, this
proposal should be brought forward to
increase the emoluments of the Prime
Minister. There is a campaign going on
to build up the Prime Minister into a
superman. I am not going to enter into
that to-day. I am making no personal

ment. Therefore I must strongly resist

the opportunity. It is about time we

who thinks we are all rebels took
charge, and he gave orders to the Press
and everyone else. The police should
have been told to remove him. I would
not stand their bullying in other places
for five minutes, and that is not long. I
have proved that more than once.
I was in the City Hall when the Duke
of Windsor visited Belfast as Prince of
Wales. One of these gentlemen came in
to tell us what to do, but he did not go
very far. According to him, we did not
know when to get up or sit down, or when
to do anything, but the least of us knew
more than he did. I was not long in
putting him in his place, and we got on
very well without him. I knew what to
do as a result of my experiences during
the little bit of travelling I had done.

Mr. MINFORD: In my opinion we do

Some of them were surprised to find that

shipbuilding, ropeworks, and other industries. We should have started years
ago spending money on publicity, because
we cannot expect propaganda to be

we were and what we were.
It makes me rather annoyed when I

tractors, and binders were at work. I met
one of these, men who came to see this

someone looking over the half-door of a

You would think Ulster was some place
100 years behind the times. What we

ORAL ANSWERS TO
QUESTIONS.
Agriculture.
LIME SUBSIDY.
1. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he intends to
increase the lime subsidy during the
summer months of the present year as
was done in the summer of 1943, and if
so, whether he intends to make any
announcement on this matter in the near
future; and whether he is aware of the
fact that many farmers are holding off
their lime purchases until this matter has
been decided.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Rev. Robert Moore): I should, perhaps,
explain to the hon. Member that in the
year 1942 the lime subsidy was increased
from 50 per cent. to 75 per cent. of the
cost during the period from 18th May to
31st August inclusive, and that in 1943
the subsidy amounted to 60 per cent.
instead of the normal 50 per cent. during
the period 1st May to 31st August
inclusive.
The object of this additional subsidy
during the summer months was to encourage a steady demand for agricultural
lime so as to keep the lime works in full
production at a time when the demand
usually falls. In recent months, owing
to factors of which the hon. Member is no
doubt aware, the problem has become one
of maintaining supply rather than of encouraging demand.
The lime subsidy is payable from the
Imperial Exchequer and the scheme is
applicable to the United Kingdom as a
whole.
I am informed that it is not proposed
to increase the subsidy this year, and
having regard to the purpose for which
the increase was made in previous years
I do not propose to take exception to this
decision as it affects Northern Ireland.
A Press notice announcing this decision
will be issued at an early date.
SCUTCH MILLS.
2. Mr. JOHN BAILEY asked the
Minister of Agriculture whether he can
state why a permit was not recommended
to Mr. David Cromie, Drumlough, Rathfriland, to enable him to have electricity
installed in his scutch mill; whether he
considers that oil lamps are safer in a
scutch mill than electric light; whether
he refused to recommend the application
of Mr. Joseph Malcomson, Cullion,
Newry, for permission to erect a new
scutch mill on his farm; and whether a
Ministry of Agriculture inspector gave.
every encouragement verbally to both
Messrs. Cromie and Malcomson to proceed with the work and afterwards turned
it down.
Rev. ROBERT MOORE: As the hon.
Member is well aware I have given both
the cases to which he refers careful personal consideration and have conveyed to
him verbally the reason for my Ministry's
decision in each case.
In the case of Mr. Cromie my Ministry
approved of a grant and recommended
the release of the necessary materials for
the restoration of the twelve-stock mill
which was destroyed. Mr. Cromie, however, subsequently wished to increase the
number of stocks to 18. This my
Ministry could not approve. As far as
the installation of electricity in the mill
is concerned it is wrong to suggest, as the
hon. Member does in his question, that
Mr. Cromie's sole object in wishing to
have it installed was for lighting purposes. I agree that electricity is safer
than oil lamps, but the mill is already
lighted by electricity driven from engine

Post-War Employment.
3. Mr. DOWLING asked the Prime
Minister whether the proposals in the
White Paper on post-war employment as
presented by the Minister of Reconstruction (Lord Woolton) will apply to Northern Ireland, and whether it is the intention of the Government to issue a copy
of these proposals to Members of this
House.
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir Basil
Brooke): As the hon. Member will
appreciate, the time which had elapsed
since the issue of the White Paper on
employment policy is brief, and he will
not, therefore, expect me to make a detailed statement at this date.
A study of the White Paper will, however, show that the policy outlined is, in
many respects, one applicable to the
United Kingdom as a whole. In so far
as it falls within the powers of the
Government of Northern Ireland it covers
ground already explored by the Government here, and is therefore welcomed by
my colleagues and myself..
As regards the final part of the hon.
Member's question, I understand that
copies of the White Paper have now been
placed in the Parliamentary Library for
the convenience of hón. Members.
THE WAR.
INVASION OF WESTERN EUROPE.
Messages to General Eisenhower and
General Alexander.
Mr. SPEAKER: I need hardly remind the House that the most critical
moment in our lives has now arrived with
the invasion of France. The Prime
Minister has expressed a wish to make a
statement to the House at the earliest
possible moment. This is not a time for
Rules and Regulations or red tape here,
and I propose to allow the Prime Minister
Invasion of Western Europe 1402
The War-
6 JUNE 1944
to make his statement, and also to allow
any right hon. Member or hon. Member
who wishes to do so to make what remarks
he may think fit.
The PRIME MINISTER: On a day
so momentous as this, when the forces of
the Allied Nations have launched a new
attack against the enemy in Western
Europe and opened what we all hope will
be the final chapter in this War of
Liberation, I am sure that every Member
of this House will deem it fitting that
some reference should be made here and
now to the events that fill our thoughts.
I believe that I truly interpret the
feelings of the House when I ask you, Sir,
to convey to General Eisenhower,
Supreme Commander of the Allied Forces,
an expression of our confidence in his
leadership and in the fighting qualities
of all under his command-(hon. Members: Hear, hear)-together with our
hope and prayer that, at no distant date,
the great enterprise in which the United
Nations are engaged will issue in overwhelming victory.
Behind the Allied Armies are the
people on the home front, all of them
eager to support the fighting men with
all the energy and all the moral and
spiritual resources they possess. At this
moment American, Canadian and British
Forces are making a supreme effort for
victory, and the very least we at home can
do is to support them to the utmost by
redoubling our efforts to supply to them
all the munitions and equipment which
they will need until the day of triumph
dawns. I therefore call upon all managements and workers alike in the factories
turning out supplies of all kinds not to
lose one minute in getting down to their
jobs and sticking to them until complete
and final victory has been won. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)
Mr. NIXON: I have the greatest possible pleasure in supporting everything
the Prime Minister has said, and it is not
necessary to waste any words. I think
we are all behind the war effort. We all
admire the command, and we all admire
our fighting men. With regard to the
Prime Minister's call to those behind to
give all possible moral and other support
I endorse that too. But I would suggest
to the Prime Minister that he would put
the people behind in a position to give
that support. I know the Prime Minister
himself would, but I also know that there
are petty Hitlers persecuting-I can
prove that here and now-the parents of
some of these men that are in the front
line at the present time. I would ask
the Prime Minister to call that off, and,
generally speaking, it comes from the
Ministry of Home Affairs.
Mr. BEATTIE: I think I can give
full endorsement to the appeal of the
right hon. Gentleman, and I can do it
not only as an individual but as a person
who carries the responsibility of the
representation in this House of the
organised workers in Northern Ireland.

The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
COMMERCE (Mr. Maginess): The Estimates which I present for the consideration of the Committee are undisguisedly
those of a war-time and war-making Department. Hon. Members will have
observed the new form in which the
organisation of the Ministry has been cast
to meet war conditions. Prior to 1939
there were two main divisions of the
Ministry-one concerned with the furtherance of our trade and commerce and
with the fisheries services, the other with
the statutory services relating to such
matters as harbours, power and transport, the registration of companies and
friendly societies, and industrial assurance. In the Estimates now before the
Committee it will be seen that, while all
these services remain, the organisation
has been recast so as to assimilate the
numerous war-time functions which the
Ministry is now called upon to discharge.
Instead of two divisions performing the
duties of the pre-war years, we have now
three divisions whose functions relate
almost entirely to Ulster's war effort.
In Division I we have the war-time
control of textile production, priorities,
the allocation and control of building
materials, and the control of civil building. In Division II come the production
of munitions and fighting weapons, the
control of factory and storage premises,
as well as the control of coal and civil
engineering supplies. To Division III
fall consumer rationing, the administration of prices of Goods Acts, the location
of retail businesses, salvage operations,
the erection and equipment of the Ministry of Supply flax processing factories,
and the control of laundry, dyeing and
cleaning services and of footwear repairs.
As hon. Members will see from the Estimates, the list which I have given is not
exhaustive, but it is sufficient to justify
my earlier remark that the Ministry of
Commerce is not merely a war-time but
a war-making Department and that its
activities cover a large part of Ulster's
war effort.
So much for the Ministry's functions
and the organisation which has been devised to cope with them. Hon. Members
will naturally ask "How has the machine
worked and what has it accomplished?"
Let me say that no organisation, however
perfect, can in itself achieve results.
Organisation, not only in the Government Department, but in the factory and
in the workshop, must be as perfect as it
can be made, but, when all is said and
done, organisation is only a means to an
end. On the home front as on the battlefield, the human spirit is the one element
indispensable to victory. The will to
work, to face up to all difficulties and, if
need be, to suffer that from all and at
all times, is what the present hour demands.
The volume of industrial production,
in the service of the war effort of the
United Kingdom, is greater now from
Northern Ireland than it has ever been.
Output can be but inadequately gauged
by the contraction of our unemployment
figures, because so much unregistered
labour and labour formerly on less essential work has come directly into the service of war production.
Our war factories are throbbing with
activity. Factories that last year were
strangers in our midst are now working
towards maximum production.
New
plant is building up output of vital
weapons and equipment and bringing into
employment many of our men and women
who have never done factory work before.
As I speak, important new factories are
going up in three different parts of
Ulster, and in a short time they, too,
will swell the tide of production. Plans
are being made, too, for the utilisation
of additional industrial capacity.
Z
Estimates-
Ministry of Commerce
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Maginess]
The progress to which I have referred
is chiefly in the field of aircraft, aircraft
components and accessories, ships, shells,
shot and vital engineering products. It
is difficult to do justice to the excellent
work being done by workers and managements alike in each section of the
engineering industry. Let me mention
as typical the case of a new establishment
I recently visited, where most of the
women workers had never before worked
in a factory yet they constantly amazed
the management by their quickness and
adaptability. In the first few weeks of
their new employment these girls had
beaten the production average of their
fellow workers in the firm's associated
factory elsewhere. This, I am assured,
is by no means unique.
Turning to the activities of the Production Council, I am glad to have this
opportunity of thanking the employers'
and workers' representatives for the excellent services they have rendered and
are rendering. Of necessity much of
their work never reaches the light of publicity, but without their goodwill and
helpful advice the turning wheels would
soon lose some of their speed. Only those
who know the intricacies of the interdepartmental organisation of war production can appreciate the importance of
smooth team-work where interplay and
co-operation count for so much. This
team-work in the factory also, as exemplified in the joint works production committees, is a thing to be encouraged. I
would like to congratulate those committees on their efforts to improve production and eliminate causes of inefficiency, and to urge those workers and
managements who have not yet embarked
on this experiment to give it a trial.
There are two off-shoots of the production organisation for which the initiative
or the Production Council has been responsible, on which I should like to touch.
One is the development of what we call
the works relations organisation. Northern Ireland, in some ways to its cost perhaps, has never been publicity-minded,
but a war-time development here has been
the growth of this organisation, staffed
by the Ministry of Supply, which sets
out to explain to the factory worker the
part his work plays in the war effort, to
show how his particular job fits in and
how the efficiency with which he or she
carries out the individual task ultimately
helps the soldier, sailor or airman on the
battle front. The works relations organisation provides demonstrations, exhibitions, film shows, talks and displays of
all kinds, and is helping to bring about
that sense of being part of a whole, vitally
linked up with great events and great
efforts; it reduces apathy and makes for
corporate spirit and intelligent interest.
Linked with the job of explaining to the
worker the significance of his work is
that of promoting good relations between
the factory and the public. Everything
that tends towards a sense of unity in
the community and promotes mutual
understanding is a force for good.
The importance of the human factor in
industry is seen in another service we
have developed during the past yearthe provision of nursery accommodation
for young children whose mothers are in
essential work. This scheme is growing
and proving of great value from a
humanitarian and educational standpoint
as well as from the production point of
view. There are at present, besides seven
day nurseries in Belfast, two "residential"
nurseries. where the children of women
on night work may receive expert care.
May I pay a tribute to the excellent work
of the Northern Ireland branch of the
Nursery Schools' Association which has
co-operated with the Ministry in the
running of these centres, and thank them
for the pioneer work they have done in
this field, much of it of a voluntary
nature.
During the year just past the linen
industry has maintained its war-time
level of activity. There has been little
change in the weaving section; practically
all the capacity in the coarse end of the
spinning trade is being fully utilised, and
it has been due to the shortage of suitable
material that the capacity in the fine end
has been only partially occupied.
In the past war years our export trade
has been handicapped by this lack of raw
material, and manufacturers have had to
rely upon their stocks.
By now these
stocks are seriously depleted, and thus the
recent Board of Trade decision to allocate
a certain quantity of raw material to Northern Ireland to enable us to maintain our
connections in the export trade came most
opportunely. Hon. Members will share
the view held by the Ministry that our
valuable export markets are important

Board of Trade in the regional control of

cleaning services and the control of footwear repairs. When the Ministry undertook this control it was realised that in

armed forces stationed in Northern Ireland. This has been achieved and the

demands on two small industries catering
for normal peace-time requirements, has
suffered little disturbance.
The control of footwear repairs is intended mainly to ensure an equitable

that this percentage cannot be supplied.

Thus far I have dealt with the
Ministry's war functions. Let me now
say a few words regarding our post-war
plans. No one doubts the complexity
and variety of the problems which are
Ministry of Commerce 1412

likely to face us in the immediate postwar period, and it is the duty of the
Ministry to concern itself about the kind
of world in which the industry and commerce of Northern Ireland will have to
win its place.
""
First of all, the linen industry. Hon.
Members may already know that the
Minister of Commerce and Production in
January, 1943, appointed a committee of
the trade to examine the problems likely
to engage the attention of the linen
industry after the war, and, here I quote
from the terms of reference "to advise
as to the measures which could best be
taken to ensure the maintenance and
development of the industry in future
years. The Prime Minister has now
received the Committee's Report which
puts forward several major recommendations for the consideration of the Governments both here and at Westminster, and
of the industry as a whole. That Report
has already formed the subject of discussion with the various trade bodies, and
when the reaction of the industry to it
both in Northern Ireland and Scotland
is more definitely ascertained, the recommendations will be considered by the
Prime Minister in consultation with the
various Northern Ireland and Imperial
Ministers concerned. The Report, which
has now been published, will, I am sure,
prove of interest to hon. Members.
Apart from long-term planning it has
been necessary to consider the problems
which will arise in the linen industry during the transitional period when a measure
of control will still be necessary. Many
of us will remember the conditions which
ruled at the end of the last war, when
prices went sky high and then fell with
such calamitous results to many firms in
the industry. I am glad to say that the
industry is determined to take all possible
action to avoid a recurrence of such unhappy events, and plans have been drawn
up to stabilise production and prices during the transitional period. These plans
are at present under consideration but, by
way of experiment, certain recommendations are being put into effect immediately,
and the experience which will thus be
gained should provide a useful guide for
the industry in the post-war period.
At the request of the Prime Minister in
his capacity as Minister of Commerce and
Production, I have had informal conversations during the past year with various
trade associations and representatives of
individual firms, who have freely discussed their plans for the post-war period
and have indicated what they consider are
the problems and difficulties likely to arise.
I am glad to say that so far as our export
trade is concerned the prevailing feeling
seems to be one of optimism-but of
optimism strongly tempered by caution. It
is obvious that many of the factors which
will govern post-war export trade are not
yet assessable, but I am confident that our
traders will face the future with courage
and resource. I do not decry this feeling
of caution; the war-time achievements of
our industrialists and may I particularly
mention the way in which our linen manufacturers turned their attention from, say,
sheer linen Kandkerchiefs to turning out
incendiary bullets or aircraft parts-leave
one in no doubt that enthusiasm, the will
to overcome difficulties, and an intense
patriotism, are still to be found in
generous measure in the character of our
people. I beg to move.

I want to say to the right hon. Gentleman-pardon me, he is not right honourable yet, but I should like to see him

The Prime Minister is the head of the

I was waiting to hear about the post-war

has been achieved. I hope that in Northern Ireland we will never again have
50,000 or 100,000 unemployed. If the

we were before, and to me, at any rate,

When our industries in Northern Ireland are able to absorb our employable
people, then something useful will have

developed in the way in which I believe

We had not sufficient work
at home.. I think that state of affairs

I come now to the question of coal.

I also want to go into another matter
where our national war effort is being
endangered. We have ex-Service men who
have fought in this war up to 1943, and
they are now in the city of Belfast doing
work of national importance. They are
men whom I would call key men, but
they did not come off the Army because
they were key men. They came off the
Army because they were disabled by war
service. This is the case of Mr. Robert
Cairns, of 58 Roseband Street, Belfast,
discharged with a disability pension on
28th May, 1942, after ten years' service.
He is married, and took up residence in
Belfast in April, 1942. He has been
employed on essential war work from the
date of his discharge. He was requested
by the Food Office two months ago to
return his identity card, and a temporary
card was issued. Anyone knows what a
temporary identity card means.
His wife called at the Food Office last

Office official at the Permit Office said
the Food Office got no instruction to
withdraw the identity card. The Food
Office said they were given the authority

After the review of the activities of the Ministry given to the Committee to-day I am satisfied that it can

keen to have prosperity in our midst. I
think the Prime Minister as head of the
Government and as Minister of Commerce,
considering that certain departments are
set up inside his Ministry, must make a
declaration of policy showing the workers
that practical steps are being taken in
regard to present and post-war planning.
Post-war reconstruction has been talked
about on many occasions, but we who live.
in Armagh have to face up to realities.
Once we had a successful linen industry.
To-day we have absolutely no industry.
If the Prime Minister is going to fulfil
his duty he must do something practical.
As I have said, I have asked him questions on many occasions, but there is no
use in having a particular department
telling you of its plans when we find that
in the fifth year of the war County
Armagh has been practically neglected as
far as industry is concerned. What can
the Government offer for those who return
after the war is over? Can the Government give any guarantee that we will have
industry in which these men can get work,
or are we going to see them once again in
hundreds at the labour exchanges? I do
not wish to see that, and I am sure the
Prime Minister does not wish to see it.
He may present his Estimates and give
facts and figures, but we who live in particular areas have to face up to realities.
So must the Government and the Minister concerned.
The people of Armagh want a scheme
of production of some kind. The only
work we can find is, unfortunately, cross-
Channel work. I make a particular
appeal to the Prime Minister to remember us, because we have been neglected
too long. I have approached his Department on many occasions, particularly in
connection with fisheries at Ballycastle,
and I have been received very courteously.
My main concern is the prosperity of the
county in which I live. If the Minister
can give a guarantee or assurance that
County Armagh, Mid and South, will receive its just share then we can say that
the struggle which is taking place to-day
will not have been in vain, and those who
will return will have jobs and a degree of
confidence, and above all, a degree of
security.
The PRIME MINISTER: The debate
has turned on two matters in connection
with my Ministry, namely, coal and
bricks. Other matters were raised which
I shall deal with later. I am satisfied
that, taken by and large, the quality of
the coal delivered here is equal to the
quality of the coal in Great Britain. I
I am sure the hon. Member for Pottinger

house coal than others. Any complaints
that we have made to the Ministry of
Fuel and Power-we have made complaints have been sympathetically dealt
with. I am sure the Committee will
understand how difficult it is at the present time owing to the scarcity of manpower to pick the coal as it comes along
the belts. There is also the great
difficulty occasioned by the great events
which have been heralded to-day.
Harbours are congested, and there is also
difficulty in connection with trains. There
have been complaints. We know that to
find half-a-dozen stones in coal is not a
pleasant thing. The same thing is
happening everywhere, and we are not
getting a hard deal in so far as coal is
concerned.
The hon. Member for Pottinger asked
or rather attacked me on the question of
conceding one thousand tons of coal. I
think that that was a proper attitude for
us to take up, and a proper gesture for
us to make. In point of fact we were in
a more advantageous, position than the
people on the other side in so far as coal
was concerned. I do not believe that any
person in Northern Ireland wants to be
either at an advantage or a disadvantage
as compared with the people in Great
Britain. I do not think that the coal
consumers in this country have suffered
as a result of that action.
Various hon. Members touched on the
matter of electricity. I am not yet in a
position to tell hon. Members the details
of the discussions which are going on
in order to get proper organisation of
generation and supply. The talks are
proceeding successfully. Everyone is
beginning to realise that only by proper
organisation of the production and distribution of power are we going to get the
one essential necessary for our future industries, namely, cheap power. When
we get that matter arranged in a satisfactory manner to all concerned-it is
naturally a very difficult question because
there are all sorts of interests involved—
I feel sure that good will come of it. I
am sure we will arrive at a satisfactory
solution along those lines. In the meantime my hon. and gallant Friend (Lieut.-
Colonel Gordon) can rest assured that
that work is going on and that the matter
is being investigated. The figure of
£287,000 is a varying one as all the
figures are. The £100 is merely a token
figure to keep the matter open.
I come now to the question of bricks.
We have had a great deal of trouble,
caused partly by the tremendous demand
placed on our brick manufacturers and
by the wear and tear of machinery. Not.
all the clay in this country is satisfactory
for brick making. There is a good deal
of gypsum and lime in some of it. The
machinery has been running for five years
without any great repairs being carried
out, and if great care is not taken these
harmful ingredients get mixed up with
the clay. The result is apparent when
the brick is fired and built into the
houses, and a good deal of trouble is
experienced. The Ministry are forming
a committee, or rather they are asking
the members of the building industry if they will be good enough to
form themselves into a committee,
to advise us as to how the brick
situation can best be improved.
are the people who will have to use
the bricks when the building programme
comes along, and I think the Committee
will agree that it is up to them to see
that they get the right type of brick.

Now I come to the points raised by the

this country. At the present time it is

war effort. As far as I have been able
I have endeavoured to get industries to
come here the owners of which are prepared, given certain conditions, to continue on in the post-war period. There
are some purely war-time industries
which will not remain with us after the

hon. Member for Ballynafeigh asked me

The essential thing and this rather
deals with the hon. Member for South
Armagh-for inducing new industries to
come to this country is, of course, an
economic one. No new industry is going
to come here unless it can get good
labour, freedom from industrial troubles,
cheap transport, and cheap power.
If
those are to be had we will have no
difficulty in getting new industries, but
we do unfortunately suffer from the fact
that we have a sea between us and the
main market, which causes a double handling of certain types of goods. The hon.
Member for South Armagh complained
that no new industries had come
Armagh. I think he was talkingthough he did not say so about his own
constituency, because very many new industries have gone to Armagh, and many

to
If you go in certain parts of my own
constituency there are no new industries
other than agricultural, for the reason
that I am not in a position to compel any
industry to go to any part. I have to
ask them to come over and then do the
best I can to accommodate them in places
that suit them. Naturally they do not
want to incur heavier freight rates and
costs than they need, and if there are
places and factories and power and transport available in places nearer the sea
than, say Co. Armagh, it would be very

to go to Armagh. If I tell them they

we have got to create an economic situation here which will induce these industries to come to Northern Ireland. I
think that once that is done most of our
troubles will be over.

I am talking about good bricks made in
Northern Ireland. They give you a very
dry house, because a lot of the dampness
in houses that are properly built with
cavity walls does not come from the outside at all. It is due to the heat inside,
because in the case of houses with cavity
walls dampness could not come from the
outside. The dampness is produced by
the moisture being condensed against the
wall if it does not happen to be papered.
You will see dampness running down a
painted wall in a house with cavity walls,
but that is vapour being condensed against
the wall. It is not dampness coming
through the wall. My information, and
my opinion, is that that is more likely to
happen with these hard bricks than with
the porous bricks they manufacture in
Northern Ireland.
Cement is very hard, and one of the
objections to building houses with concrete is that vapour will be condensed
against the cement, and it is bound to,
unless the wall is papered. I am informed and I have a little judgmentthat the same thing applies to hard bricks,
but not to the bricks we make in Northern

Get on

Another matter I referred to was the

Mr. NIXON: Thank you. It is important or I would not have bothered. Later
on everybody would feel that. I do not

no Minister gets so many deputations as

and I can say this that the poorer they
are the better they are treated. They
come out here with some grievance about
an old-age pension. These are the people
to be good to, because they cannot help
themselves.
The trolleybus takes them right to the
door. They tell the first official they
meet what is troubling them. He takes
them along to the lift and they meet some
officials of the Ministry of Labour, and
if the officials cannot by virtue of the

treat them courteously and kindly beyond
all manner of doubt. Well, now, why

are not for the purpose of accommodating
the Ministers or anyone else but the
public. All I can say, in the absence of

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Wednesday, 7th June, 1944.
The House met at Two of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.

1945. (By Command.)
to
THE WAR.
Telegrams to General Eisenhower and
General Alexander.
Mr. SPEAKER: The House instructed
me yesterday afternoon to send telegrams
General Eisenhower and General
Alexander. These telegrams were sent
off in the course of the afternoon. Copies
of them were handed to the Press at the
same time, and have since appeared in the
papers. I think this House would like
these telegrams quoted in Hansard.
Therefore, I am sure, although right hon.
and hon. Members have already seen
them, they will agree with me that it will
be advisable to read them now. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) The telegrams
go through the medium of the Prime
Minister of Great Britain.
TO GENERAL EISENHOWER:
I am directed by the Members of the
House of Commons of Northern Ireland
to convey to you personally, and to all
Forces under your command, their
heartfelt wishes for the speedy success
of the immense and vital operations in
which you
are at present engaged.
They would like to send a special
message to all ranks from Northern
Ireland under your command, and also
to those from other parts of Ireland
who are fighting with them.
TO GENERAL ALEXANDER':
I am directed by the Members of the
House of Commons of Northern Ireland
to extend to you, and the Forces under
your command, their wholehearted congratulations on your great victory.
They are proud to think that this has
been achieved by an Ulsterman, and
wish you continuous success until the
enemy is annihilated. They express
their pride in the achievements of the
men from Northern Ireland who have
shared in your victory, and also record
their warm appreciation of the gallantry
displayed by the men from other parts
of Ireland.

The CHAIRMAN: I think it is the
