The Committee signified assent.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE
(Major Sinclair): The over-all increase in
the Finance Group of Estimates is
£36,000, but this sum is more than offset
by a decrease of £76,000 in the Public
Works and Buildings Vote giving a net
decrease for the group over last year's
Estimate of about £40,000. The first
Vote on which I wish to comment is
No. 1. The increase on the whole Vote
is mainly attributable to the fact that a
full year's provision is being made for
the increases in war bonus which took
effect towards the middle of last financial
year.
I should like to make one or two observations on the provision for staff under
certain heads of Subhead A. Under the
heading "Headquarters," on page 13 of
Estimates-
Ministry of Finance
7 JUNE 1944
the Estimates, the second officer in my
Ministry is designated as hitherto, a
"Principal Assistant Secretary" whereas
an announcement was made subsequent to
the printing of these Estimates of the
change in title of this officer to that of
a "secretary." As hon. Members are
aware, this post has always been remunerated on the same scale as that applicable to Permanent Secretaries in other
Ministries, and it was felt that the 'position should be regularised by designating
this officer as a secretary instead of as an
assistant secretary. The change in title
has been followed by a clear definition
of the functions of the two officers holding
the rank of secretary in the Ministry,
and for the information of the members
of the Public Accounts Committee, who
are naturally particularly interested, I
may say that the officer now to be called
"second secretary" will continue to be
the accounting officer of the Ministry.
The Works Division shown at Part (5)
of Subhead A is alone responsible for a
considerable amount of the increase
-- amounting to £7,000, and this not only
on account of war bonus, but to a regrading of part of the technical staff and to
the employment of a a few extra staff
units, chiefly in the Civil Engineers
Section. Though the appropriations in
aid from Imperial Departments for our
agency work on Works Services on their
behalf, as detailed in Sub-head L, are less
than for the previous year, it must not
be assumed that the Works Division is
handling any less work. On the contrary
notwithstanding the fact also that the
programme for new Transferred Works
Services, as set out in Sub-head A of the
Vote, shows a substantial decrease, the
division is as busily occupied as ever,
mainly on work for Imperial Departments.
The reason why the amount of agency
fees is not greater is that the amount
shown in the Vote as a receipt in any
year does not necessarily reflect the work
performed in that year, the method of
calculation being to take a percentage
on the cost of the works, and this may
be brought to account at any time, not
necessarily in the year in which the
charge for the staff engaged occurs.
Owing to the continued freedom from
air attack which we have enjoyed in
Ulster, hon. Members might have expected
that the portion of Sub-head A which
deals with the War Damage Commission
and Board of Trade (War Damage)
Agencies would now show a reduction.
Work is actually on the decrease, but any
saving on this account is not entirely revealed here, because the work of making
payments which was formerly dealt with
by the Ministry's Accounts Branch at
Stormont is now dealt with in the War
Damage Commission Offices with the consequent employment of additional staff
formerly borne on another sub-head.
In Sub-head H there is a big addition
to the staff employed on Ulster Savings
Certificates Administration owing to the
increase in work on account of new certificates issued, and also to the consequential
growth of work involved on repayments.
The agency fee shown in Sub-head L.is
calculated not directly on the actual cost
of staff, but on the number of certificates
issued. I have pleasure in informing the
Committee that quite recently the Belfast
War Savings Council recouped the Ministry in full for all expenses which the
Ministry met in the first instance in connection with the different special war
savings weeks, culminating in the recent
successful Salute the Soldier week. This
recoupment takes the form of a free gift
to the Exchequer, and was made possible.
by the committee's energetic programme,
which included many side-shows and the
sale of special badges. The increase in the
staff employed on National Registration
work is covered by a corresponding addition to the agency fee.
War bonus and normal increments
account for the greater part of the increase in the provision required for Vote
2-Valuation and Surveys-but a part is
also attributable to a full year's provision being required for the additional
staff to which I referred in presenting the
Supplementary Estimate for this service
last March.
The decrease in Vote 4 (Public Works
and Buildings) is in the main due to the
virtual completion of the accommodation
required for the National Fire Service.
It was anticipated that all the work on
emergency water supplies would have been
completed during the course of last year,
but some work had to be held over owing
to difficulties in obtaining sites for a
number of water tanks, and to late
deliveries of a few pumps. The new
Drawing Office in the Law Courts is now
complete, and the £1,800 provided for this.
year covers expenditure not met in the
year just ended. As I announced at the
time of the Supplementary Estimates last
Ministry of Finance 1452
Estimates-
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Major Sinclair]
March, a considerable sum is required for
adaptations and repairs to the building
purchased as a Remand Home and Reformatory for Girls. Provision is accordingly made for this purpose.
The Committee is already aware of the
erection of buildings at Stranmillis for
the war-time housing of the Ministry of
Education, and, later, for purposes connected with the Training College. I have
already informed the House that it is
anticipated that this accommodation will
be ready in July next, but owing to unforeseen changes in Service requirements
for hospital accommodation there, it has
been possible to move the bulk of the
Ministry of Education already.
Owing to the increased numbers of
inmates in Belfast Prison, the existing
recreation room is now inadequate, and,
accordingly, the erection of further
accommodation for this purpose has been
authorised. The new accommodation will
take the form of a brick building linked
with the present room.
Finaly, it is proposed to replace the
Ulster Special Constabulary Drill Hall at
Dunmore Park which was destroyed by
enemy action in 1941. Difficulties in
obtaining sites have caused considerable
delay in this matter, but approval has
now been obtained for the use of the
original site. The proposal is to use
Nissen hutting if obtainable.
Under Sub-head B the only point to
which I wish to draw attention is the provision of £2,500 for furniture and fittings
for Air Raid Precautions. This is for
the maintenance of black-out curtains,
and so on, for which, unfortunately, the
need still exists.
Under Sub-head F the amount required
for drainage plant is a carry-over from
last year, our requirements for plant of
this kind having been satisfied.
In the Vote for Stationery and Printing: Sub-head B-Stationery Office Publications-shows an increased sum for the
printing of our own Northern Ireland
official publications and, apart from the
rise in printing costs generally, this is to
cover the printing of the report and
minutes of evidence of the Select Committee on Health Services.
Sub-head D similarly shows an increase for printing and binding, and
included in it is £750 for the Ulster
Bridgehead leaflet.
The next Vote is No. 10-Miscellaneous
Expenses. Under Sub-head A-Statute
Law Committee-it will be noted that the
fee payable to the Editor of the Statute
Law Committee for Northern Ireland has
been increased by £50. Though local
legislation has tended to decrease since
the war, the Editor's work is now considerably greater on account of the very
large number of Statutory Rules and
Orders issued under Imperial Legislation,
which are, in many instances, applicable
to Northern Ireland, and have to be listed.
by the Editor as such. Moreover, Orders
made by Northern Ireland Departments
in the exercise of delegated powers have
to be published in
Volumes of
Statutory Rules and Orders.

£200. This reduction takes account of

Observatory is now engaged on war
service, and, as he is not being replaced,
the expenses of the Observatory have been
temporarily curtailed.

Sir
normal custom in the present case.
Wilfred Spender has been associated with
our Service from its inception 23 years
ago, during 19 of which he was head of
the Service. I should like to record my
appreciation of the help and consideration
I have received from him at all times,

rendered to Ulster. I beg to move.

The Estimate with which we are dealing is the most important one that comes
before this House. The right hon.
Gentleman is controller of the finances of

He is inclined to ease up in regard

The weakness of the right hon. Gentleman

Next there is the Valuation Act. I
see that we are still keeping it going, and
I want to refer to it. We have a staff
there, and it is what we would call a wartime staff. I was on the Revaluation
Committee, and I must say that the staff
did their work when they got down to the
normal way of working. I want to ask
the right hon. Gentleman whether there
is any possibility of bringing the valuation of this part of the world back to the
normal position. Have his thoughts ever
turned in that direction? At the moment
we are overvalued. At one time I was
told from the other side of the House by
a former Minister of Finance, the late
Mr. Pollock, that it was a friend and
colleague of mine, Mr. Philip Snowden,
who had made this demand on Mr.
Pollock.
I am going to tell you-and I have
said it elsewhere-that we were always
valued with England, Scotland and Wales
on the basis of 45-55, but to-day we are
valued on an equality with England.
That basis of equality is certainly hitting
our industries very hard, and sometimes
I think that at periods it is responsible
for unemployment. We cannot pay more
than we have at our command, and if we
try to keep ourselves on the same rich
pedestal as Great Britain, then we are
going to impoverish ourselves in future
years. That is what has been happening
since this new valuation of Northern Ireland came into operation.
I agreed then, and I still agree that
there were anomalies, and that there was
justification for raising certain valuations,
but to have a general increase over the
area and over all dwellings was unfair
and unjust to this part of the country.
I hope the right hon. Gentleman will set
his mind on something being done in
regard to valuation, because derating will
have to go. Derating is not going to be
a sop for all time. We in the City have
got to pay towards derating, and if this
war is being fought for anything it is
being fought for justice for all and
privilege for none. I say now that derating will not always be continued, and
it is regrettable to see derating applied
to certain industries where big dividends
are being paid and not applied to people
who cannot pay their rent. We are not
going to have that sort of injustice in
the future. That brings me again to the
point mentioned by the hon. Member for
Woodvale, that the gulf has got to be
bridged, no matter how it is done.

Dr. LYLE: I do not intend to detain
the Committee very long, but there is one
matter about which I should like to make
a few remarks. I refer to the office of
the Registrar-General and Statistician.
The registration of deaths in Northern
Ireland is in an appalling condition in
the rural districts, and the vital statistics
that are published by the Registrar-
General are in consequence usually
fallacious. The tuberculosis death rate
as published by him is much lower than
the actual death rate from tuberculosis.
The same thing applies to other diseases
-cancer, for instance. Many cases of
cancer are registered as dying from other
diseases. This is due to the fact that in
the rural districts the Registration Office
is open on only two days of the week for
two hours each day, and I do not think
I exaggerate when I say that the majority
of people who die are buried before their
deaths are registered. In some cases it
is weeks afterwards that the death is
registered.
A very large proportion of these
deaths are registered without any medical
certificate showing the cause of death.
This is done at times even in cases where
there has been a medical attendant, but
there are many cases where there has
been no medical attendant, but there
should have been. Old people who have
perhaps got troublesome to those who had
to maintain them, and whose lives there
was no great anxiety to prolong, have
been allowed to die without medical
attendance, and without the proper
nursing or attendance they should have
had. Those deaths are registered by someone who was present at the death or was
present in the same house, and they are
registered as "Cause unknown. No
medical attendant." Some years ago the
Registrar-General issued a circular to
registrars of deaths asking them to avoid
that entry and to obtain, so far as they
could, information from the person
registering the death as to the possible
cause of death, and to put down a definite
cause of death. I, as a registrar of deaths
at the time, absolutely refused to do that,
because it was dishonest and inaccurate.
Of course, it made the registration
statistics tidy. There were not so many
shown as having died without any ascertainable cause.
But there is a more serious side to this
than the mere inaccuracy of vital
statistics. There are a good many cases of
undetected crime in Northern Ireland due
to this laxity in registration, and a few
cases, not many, I hope, of actual
murder. But there are a great many
cases where elderly people have been
allowed to die whose lives could have been
prolonged had they received proper
medical attention. I hold that every case
of death in which there is not a medical
certificate forthcoming should be the subject of a coroner's inquest.

accustomed to bamboozling a jury, and

I do not doubt at all that many a

I do not understand what he means by

But I should think it is nothing as

A few cases of manslaughter, or one or
two murders, are not of any importance or
significance to the Minister of Home
Affairs. That shows the difference
between the medical and the legal point of
view. The medical point of view is that
every life should be prolonged by every
possible means, and the legal point of
view, as exemplified by the words of the
Minister of Home Affairs, is that a few
of these deaths do not matter. Perhaps
the difference between our points of view
might be due to the fact that deaths are
profitable to the legal profession. Probate
has to be taken out, and estates have to
be administered. But they are not profitable to the medical profession, because
Al
Estimates-
Ministry of Finance
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Dr. Lyle]
when a patient dies the doctor gets no
more fees. The Minister went on to say:
On this matter of registration and
the compilation of vital statistics and
holding inquests, these are all matters
of mere machinery and can be set right
any time.
My experience has been that a thing
that can be done at any time is never
done. Any time is no time, and it is high
time there should be some reform in the
Registrar-General's Department of the
Ministry of Finance. No scientific statistician would accept this registration of
deaths as the basis for statistics. Of
course, I know that a good deal of what
is wrong in this Department is due to the
fact that there is no scientific statistician
and no medical man in that Department
dealing with the life and death of the
people of this country. The registrar's
office in Belfast and in the larger towns is
open day and daily, and the same difficulty does not there arise as arises in the
rural districts, but the same thing should
apply to the rural districts. Those offices
should be open every day.
That comes down to the question of
remuneration. The remuneration of the
local registrar of births and deaths in the
country districts at the present time
amounts to about £20 a year, and out of
that he has to supply an office and provide
his own deputy and assistant registrar.
I submit that that is ridiculous, and that
these registrars should be paid a decent
salary in addition to the individual fees
they receive for each registration. Many
years ago a deputation was received by the
Registrar-General, and he then promised
that he would use his influence with the
Ministry of Finance to get the fees increased. But there should be not only an
increase in the fees, but a reasonable
salary and an allowance for his office.
There should also be a salary for the
deputy and the assistant registrar. and
until that is done the registration of deaths
in Northern Ireland will never be on a
satisfactory basis.

Questions were also raised by the hon.
Member for Pottinger about the water
supply of Northern Ireland. I was rather
disappointed at the right hon. Gentleman
who represents Mid Down and who made
the statement that the local authorities
would not act. I have sat in this House
16 years, and I have demanded from
previous Governments that they should
take action in regard to the housing situation in rural areas and the water supply.
I was always told the local authorities
were democratically elected. I do not
think these local authorities are democratically elected, because there are no
elections and there is co-option. But
whether they are elected or not we cannot
get rid of our responsibility for housing
conditions. If the local authorities refuse
to progress it is the duty of this House
to ask them to stand aside. Why should
Members of Parliament come here and
sit if the local authorities do nothing?
I think Members of Parliament are on
the highest rung of the ladder for
justice, and if these local authorities will
not act and keep these hovels of houses
with no water supplies and bad health
what is the good of Members coming here
at all? I hope the Minister of Health
will take action and compel the authorities to act. In my district and all other
districts the same thing could apply. What
is the good of a Member at election time
giving pledges to see that the people get
decent homes and decent services if when
we come here we are to be told these
things are the responsibility of the local
authorities? I say the Government of the
country is responsible to the people for
all these services. If they find these local
services are not being carried out let
them take steps to do it. I say without
fear of contradiction that we are the body
responsible to the people of Northern Ireland for all this.
I raised the question of holding back
part of the large contribution and was
told it was a parrot cry. This £6,000,000
that was allocated I am told is only the
amount we can borrow. The hon.
Member for Pottinger, who is now in
the Chair, told us that we were paying
that contribution into a fund which paid
for water supplies over there. If it is
true that our £35,000,000 goes into a
pool in Great Britain in order to enable
Scotland and England and Wales to get
their water supplies and other needs
surely we have a perfect right to say to
Whitehall or Westminster that we want
to put our own house in order. All we
demand is parity with Great Britain, and
I think no person can deny us that. We
are playing a very important part in this
war. We have given practically all we
can give. Our families have given their
blood. The Minister of Finance will be
fortified in the knowledge that he has
behind him the entire House of Commons
when he puts the case for parity with
Great Britain.

Major SINCLAIR: This debate has
ranged over a great number of subjects,
some of which have been new and some
of which have been hardy annuals, and
it is very difficult for me to know just
where to begin in replying to the various
remarks made by hon. Members. I propose to refer first of all to the speech by
the hon. Member for the University (Dr.
Lyle), reinforced by the right hon. Member for Mid Down, in regard to the registration of deaths. I should say that this
registration has shown a steady improvement over this last number of years, but
I will not deny that there is room for
further improvement, and so I propose to
discuss the whole question with the new
Minister of Health and Local Government at the earliest possible opportunity.
I listened with great interest to the statement made by the hon. Member for the
University, and no one can deny, if the
facts are as he stated, and I am sure they
are, that the situation is far from satisfactory.
Another point, which was rather less
important, was raised by the Member for
Antrim, who asked about the forage
allowance. This is a survival of the old
Dublin Castle travelling allowance and
dates back to the time when horses had
to be used. There are now only two
resident magistrates left whose terms of
appointment entitle them to draw that
allowance. When they cease to hold their
appointments the expenses allowance will
be drawn in the ordinary way and the
term "forage allowance" will disappear
altogether.

course, they relate to the actual holders

I am sure it was, but I think if the hon.

Both the Member for Carrick and the

and lands both on behalf of our own

to the question of

The Comptroller and Auditor-General's

sure the Member for Woodvale does not

Member for Mid Down is perfectly right

I did not quite follow the Member for
Pottinger when he referred to the fact
that our thirty-five millions which we are
paying as an Imperial Contribution, was
going to provide water supplies in
Scotland. Perhaps he would elaborate
that a little further in private conversation with me later. He did say in referring to valuation that we here could not
expect to keep on as rich a level as Great
Britain. That is the whole idea of this
leeway programme. The whole idea behind everything we are doing is to get
this country on as rich a level as Great
Britain. My whole object as Minister is
to make sure the money is available for
that very purpose.

Home Affairs.
FEMALE OFFENDERS.
1. Mr. THOMAS CAMPBELL asked
the Minister of Home Affairs whether he
can state the number of police prosecutions in Belfast since the beginning of the
war of women under 21 years of age for
offences of drunkenness, disorderly conduct, offences against public morals, theft,
or other dishonesty; the corresponding
figures for the five years before the war;
the relative figures for the rest of Northern Ireland for the same two periods; the
number of such women committed to
Armagh Jail since the beginning of the
war and in the five years before the war;
the names of the recognised reformatory
and remand homes in Northern Ireland
for such women; the age at which they
can be committed to those homes, and the
age beyond which they cannot be detained; the number committed to those
homes since the beginning of the war and
in the five years before the war; whether
any reformatory or remand home is provided in Northern Ireland for Roman
Catholic girls or girls of other denominations convicted of the offences referred to;
and whether the Government has any plan
for the provision of such home or homes
as a matter of urgent public importance.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Mr. Lowry): With the permission of the
hon. and learned Member I propose circulating the statistical details, as these are
somewhat lengthy.
The only reformatory school in Northern Ireland (which is also available for
remand cases) is St. Joseph's Reformatory for Roman Catholic Girls; girls and
young persons can be committed to
reformatory schools between the ages of
12 and 16-the period of detention being
not less than three years and not more
than five years. The maximum age for
detention in a reformatory school is 19
years.
Up to 1st April, 1943, Shamrock Lodge
Reformatory School was available for the
reception of Protestant girls and, as stated
above, a reformatory school and remand
home is still available for Roman Catholic.
girls.
The Government has recently purchased
premises for use as a remand home (which
will also be available as a reformatory
school for Protestant girls) and tenders
for the adaptation of the premises will
shortly be invited. I realise that the provision of this home is a matter of urgent
public importance, and I am making every
endeavour to have the premises available
for occupation without delay.
Mr.
CAMPBELL : Is the Minister
aware of the vast amount of good that is
being done in England and elsewhere by
these reformatory and remand homes
dealing with youthful female offenders,
and does he not consider that it would
be a decided advantage in this area to
provide as far as possible similar accommodation for all denominations in the
area?
Mr. LOWRY: I am trying to have the
first step for the provision of such a home
taken as quickly as possible, but it is not
very easy at the present time.
The details referred to are as follows:-

CHARGES AGAINST GIRLS.
2. Mr. THOMAS CAMPBELL asked
the Minister of Home Affairs whether
the Ministry have under consideration the
observations made from time to time
recently by magistrates in the summary
courts on the numbers of girls of from
14 to 17 years of age, apparently beyond
control, appearing in the dock; whether
the Ministry realise the danger amid the
prevailing laxity of morals, of their
lapsing into evil ways, and whether
the Ministry have in contemplation any
remedial measures.
Mr. LOWRY: The Government is fully
aware of the dangers referred to by the
hon. and learned Member, and as was
foreshadowed in the King's Speech it is
proposed to introduce legislation at the
earliest possible date to amend the law
SO as to strengthen the hands of the
administration in dealing with children
and young persons generally.
I am hopeful that the recent appointment of trained police women in Belfast
city will have a good effect in dealing with
this difficult social problem.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Has the Minister
information sufficient to enable him to
say whether or not offenders of this class
are coming into the courts with a marked
increase in numbers and frequency in
recent months and years? Has his attention been drawn to a case at Rostrevor
last week when six young girls were sentenced each to three months' imprisonment for having been found wandering
and lodging in the open air?
Mr. LOWRY: The statistics which I
am circulating, and which will also be
furnished to the hon. and learned Gentleman, bear out the suggestion that he
makes. I am aware of the particular case
he mentioned, but it is very difficult to see
what can be done.
Mr. BEATTIE: I should like to ask
the right hon. Gentleman if he can state
whether in his opinion there is or is not a
laxity of morals in the Six Counties.

Where they can form a committee of

are taken by those people to preserve the

age

The MINISTER OF EDUCATION

Labour for the Harvest.
5. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he can state what
plans he has made concerning the saving
of crops on similar lines as last year
when he sent industrial workers in squads
to do this work, and whether he will
consult with the Minister of Labour to
reserve sufficient numbers of workers in
all exchange areas in Northern Ireland
to carry out this work.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Rev. Robert Moore): I am glad to be
able to inform the hon. Member that
my Ministry has arranged to provide.
assistance in the saving of the harvest
this year, and the plans are similar to
those which operated in 1943. Consultations have taken place between my
Ministry and the Ministry of Labour,
and I can assure the House that where
necessary all available labour will be
diverted to the essential work of saving
crops in Northern Ireland.
A Permanent Secretary's Pension.
6. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister of
Finance whether he can state if it is a fact
that Mr. W. Iliff, who was Secretary to
the Ministry of Public Security until he
was seconded, on or about December,
1941, for service abroad, has been granted
a pension, and what is the amount of the
pension granted; whether it is a fact that
this pension has been incorrectly allowed,
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Beattie]
as this officer ceased employment in the
Civil Service of Northern Ireland at his
own request, and that the post which he
held was immediately filled by the promotion of another officer to the rank of
Secretary to the Ministry.
OF FINANCE
The MINISTER
(Major Sinclair): Mr. Iliff, formerly
Permanent Secretary to the Ministry of
Public Security, was seconded in December, 1941, for duty with the Imperial
Government as Financial Adviser to the
British Minister in Iran. Under this
arrangement the salary of his post here
continued to be paid to him and recovered,
with the usual addition of 15 per cent. in
respect of pension liability, from the
Treasury; and an acting secretary was
appointed to carry on his duties during
his absence.
Mr. Iliff rendered distinguished service
in Iran, and upon the conclusion of his
term of office there the Treasury
approached my Ministry with the object
of securing his further services for an
extended period as Financial Adviser to
the Governor of Burma. It was felt that
everything possible should be done to
facilitate the Imperial Government, but
that, on the other hand, the secondment of
a Permanent Secretary for several years
would inevitably give rise to many difficulties here. The matter was, therefore,
fully discussed between myself and the
other Minister concerned, and as a result
it was decided that in the public interest
Mr. Iliff ought to be retired from our
Service with a view to enabling the
Imperial Government to use his services
in the manner proposed, without creating
complications in our own Service. This
has since been done under the authority
of Section 6 of the Superannuation Act,
1909, the superannuation allowances
awarded to Mr. Iliff comprising a pension
of £496 per annum (part of which varies
in accordance with movements in the cost
of living figure) and a lump sum of
£1,434.
Mr. NIXON: On what grounds does
he do the like of that at all? Has the
Minister done anything else since he took
up office except pay out money and raise
the salaries of people who have already too
much? When was Public Security
abolished? You could not do that unless
it was abolished. It never was abolished.
Lord GLENTORAN: Might I ask the

British Civil Service?
Mr. BEATTIE: We all appreciate the

all other, civil servants in Public Security

abolition of that Ministry?

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
SUPPLY
Estimates 1944-45.
Considered in Committee.
[Sir ROBERT LYNN in the Chair.]
CLASS IX. No. 1.
Ministry of Health and Local
Government.
Motion made and Question proposed,
"That a sum not exceeding £64,710 be
granted to His Majesty to defray the
charge that will come in course of payment during the year ending 31st March,
1945, to pay the salaries and expenses of
the Ministry of Health and Local Government."
Mr. GRANT: I have the honour to
present to the Committee the first Estimates for the Ministry of Health and
Local Government. The Estimates are
three in number. First of all, that for
the Ministry itself; secondly, an Estimate.
of grants to local authorities, and thirdly,
a vote for certain emergency services arising out of the war.
The total amounts are-for the No. 1
Vote, £64,710; for the No. 2 Vote,
£1,790,830; and for the No. 3 Vote,
£210,950; the grand total being
£2,066,490. In the case of the No. 1
Vote, as the Ministry was not established
until the 1st June, provision is made on
the basis of ten months' expenditure only,
instead of for the full year.
At this point I would draw the attention of hon. Members to an error in the
printed copy of the New and Revised
Estimates. On page 10, near the bottom
Belfast Board of Guardians in respect of
the salary of an officer. This salary is
only for ten months. It should be £1,000
instead of £1,100. For the Belfast
County Borough Council Tuberculosis
Committee in respect of an officer
appointed as commissioner the figure in
the Estimate is £400, and it should be
only £340. I just wanted to point out
these mistakes to Members of the Committee.
The other two Estimates cover the
whole year, and my Ministry will account
for them in full, although the Vote on
Account for these services has been used
during the months of April and May by
the Ministry of Home Affairs.
With the permission of the Committee
I shall deal with the three Estimates as
a whole. Hon. Members will appreciate
that I am faced with some difficulty in
presenting these Estimates in that they
have necessarily been prepared as a
matter of urgency, and that after a period
of office which can be numbered in days
I was not in a position to forecast with
any degree of completeness or accuracy
the developments which might ensue during the present financial year. All that
it has been possible to do in the short
period available has been to sort out as
between the new Ministry and
and the
Ministry of Home Affairs the services
which now come under my direction and
to present the Estimates as revised on this
basis for your approval so that the necessary finance may be available to enable
my Department to meet its immediate and
necessary expenses for existing services.
I would therefore like to make it quite
clear that I can give no guarantee that I
shall not be coming back to the Committee at a later stage in the year for
supplementary provision and indeed it
is almost inevitable that I shall have to
do so.
Dissatisfaction has been expressed in
some quarters with the fact that all the
services which could reasonably be regarded as health services have not immediately been transferred to the new
Ministry. That is a point of view with
which I myself and, I may say, the
Government, have a certain amount of
sympathy. I should, however, like hon.
Members to realise that the setting up of
a new Department to deal with these
matters is by no means a simple business
and it cannot be achieved by a stroke of
the pen. The law on public health and
local government is complex and in order
to achieve the transfer of the various
services satisfactorily very careful research
is needed. The Government therefore
decided to proceed by first of all transferring to the new Ministry such of the
services administered by the Ministry of
Home Affairs as should obviously come
under my jurisdiction and aimed at getting the new Ministry established with
the least possible disturbance to existing
services.

I
Another criticism has been that the
activities of the new Ministry should
have been confined entirely to health services and should not have included ancillary services such as local government and
housing. I would, however, remind hon.
Members that the administration of health
matters is largely in the hands of the
local authorities of the Province. The
Government came to the conclusion, after
very careful consideration of this problem,
that unless the local government administration of Northern Ireland were under
the supervision of the new Ministry, its
activities on the subject of public health
might well be hampered from the outset
and it was felt reasonable and logical that
the major portion of the field of local
government activities should be under my
control.
One of my first tasks will be, of course,
to deal with the recommendations made
by the Select Committee of the House on
the health services. These recommendations do, as the Committee know, raise
very important issues, and I am sure hon.
Members will not expect me at this stage
to make any pronouncement of Government policy on them. A considerable
amount of consultation and discussion
must take place if some of the major
changes which the Committee recommended are to be made without losing
ground instead of gaining it.
I should like here to say a few words
on one aspect of the problem which arises
in connection with local authorities.
Certain of the reforms, suggested would
involve taking away from the existing
powers of some local bodies. But let me
say quite clearly at the outset that if
as a result of my decisions, changes of
this sort are made, they will be made in
the interests of the country as a whole
and in the best interests of the persons
served by the existing local authorities,
and not because I favour one class of local
authority as against another, or wish to
concentrate control in Stormont instead
of in the local areas.
I am a firm believer in the policy of
building up strong local authorities and
entrusting them with the tasks for which
local government is suitable. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) No Government
will give of its best unless it is constantly
subjected to constructive criticism, and 'I
know of no better quarter from which
such criticism can come than from strong
and efficient local bodies carrying out
tasks for which they are suited and well
equipped.
The field of local government work
must be surveyed, and where local
authorities have in the past been saddled
with responsibilities for which they are
neither well suited nor properly equipped
alternative arrangements must be made.
We shall have to establish other bodies
to do the work; or we shall have to add
powers to existing local authorities to
place them in a position to fulfil their
responsibilities.
When I come to deal with these matters
I shall want the goodwill and assistance
of members of the Committee and of the
local authorities, and I am confident that
with mutual trust on both sides the
necessary improvements can be made without friction, to the advantage of both the
Government and the local authorities
themselves.
.
One of the most outstanding health
problems-and I say health problems
deliberately-is the provision of adequate
and decent housing for our people. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) The housing
situation generally throughout Northern
Ireland is regrettable, and it will take a
very long period to put it right even
when materials become available in full
Health and Local Government 1506
Estimates-
20 JUNE 1944
measure.
We are behind Great Britain
in our present housing standards and in
the extent to which new building and
slum clearance was carried out between
the wars. There is much leeway to make
up and I can promise no miracles to
anyone.
There is no use in my telling Members
of the Committee or the people of Northern Ireland that any substantial
improvement in the situation can be
achieved in present circumstances. All
that can be done will be done, but we
have to face the fact that at the moment
all the energies of the Kingdom and
Empire must be directed to the defeat
of our enemies in the shortest possible
time, and we shall have to put up with
the lack of facilities for attacking our
own domestic problems. Some little easement has already been promised in the
shape of the 1,500 new houses which have
been allocated to certain areas by my
right hon. Friend, the Minister of Home
Affairs. I am hopeful that we may be
able to arrange for further limited
supplies as soon as substantial progress
has been made with
with those already
allocated, but I am holding out no
promise that I can achieve anything but
a mere palliation of the present conditions until the war emergency has passed.
to
I share the disappointment which is no
doubt present in the minds of Members
of the Committee at the apparent lack
of progress with the building of the 750
houses which have been allocated
Belfast. As soon as I was appointed
Minister of Health and Local Government I made it my business to interview
the chairman of the Housing Committee
and the town clerk and to impress upon
them the urgent necessity of allowing
nothing to hinder progress with the building of these houses. They were good
enough to assure me that so far as
Government Departments were concerned
they had had every assistance and that
there was at the moment nothing additional which the Government could do to
help them in their task. I am watching
the position closely and will endeavour
to ensure that not a moment's unnecessary delay will take place so far as
my Department is concerned, but I
would warn the Committee that there are
some preliminary steps yet to be taken
by the Council before actual building
operations can take place.
The local authorities are, of course, in
great difficulties on this matter. The
number of houses available is not nearly
sufficient to accommodate all those who
are wanting houses, and it is not possible
to build upon anything like the scale
required. The Act recently passed giving
powers to local authorities to requisition
empty houses for the accommodation of
people wanting homes may, however,
help to some little extent in providing
more accommodation.
We have heard a good deal about
planning and this is one of my Ministry's
responsibilities. My first reaction to
planning is probably the same as that of
the man in the street who thinks that
planning means nothing but town
planning, and who associates it with
slogans about the beauty of the countryside and the ugliness of the town. In the
first place planning does not mean town
planning alone; it means planning for
the country as a whole. At its worst it
can become a spare-time amusement for
people who think themselves superior to
their fellows. At its best it is a
thoroughly practical man's approach to
the needs of our country.
The idea behind planning is to see that
our people are decently housed, convenient to their
their work,
work, with shops,
cinemas, playing fields, etc. It is not
merely the inactive business of saying to
the individual, "You must not build a
house there because it will spoil the
view." but it does mean saying to people,
"Build your houses where we can provide
water, sewerage, electricity and gas, and
where you can get to your work without
heart-breaking delays." Well-planned
roads will carry traffic instead of blocking
it, and will be designed so that children
living in the houses adjoining the roads
are not exposed to the dangers of passing
vehicles as they have been in the past.
There are just three things I want to
say about planning at this stage. First,
we must plan so that our post-war programme of housing and re-housing falls
into an ordered scheme. Second, the replanning of our present towns and cities
must be encouraged so that they too may
become healthier and happier places in
which people can live and work. There
are enormous difficulties in the way of
this, but I hope that they may be overcome by the enthusiasm and goodwill of
all concerned. Planning is, I think,
Health and Local Government 1508

[Mr. Grant]
infectious, and when once people see
what can be done they will, I am sure,
be encouraged to correct the mistakes of
the past as well as to legislate for the
future.
My third point, and I want to emphasise
it, is this, that planning must not be
allowed to delay the programme of housing and re-housing, which is necessary
and which I intend to press forward as

that it does not hinder, it.
are
And this brings me to a final point
about planning. Now is the time for
local authorities to get on with their
planning, when materials for building
cannot be obtained, and when a good many
of their constructive activities
hampered by the war situation. When
the war is won and materials begin to
come forward in steady supply the urgent
needs for housing and other works will
be so great that local authorities will be
swamped with the demand, and people
simply will not put up with delay in getting ahead with actual building while the
planners are trying to make up their
minds.
It is no excuse for local authorities to
say that they cannot plan before they
know what financial assistance they are
going to get from the Government. So
long as they are told before they put their
plans into execution they will have no
reasonable complaint, and believe me this
question of finance is not going to be an
easy one to solve.
I do not propose to go through these
Estimates in detail. I have had only a
few days to think out some of the difficulties which I am going to encounter in this
job and the ways in which I hope to get
round those difficulties, but there are, I
am sure, many hon. Members who have a
good deal to say on the future tasks of my

Here I should like to refer to my staff.
While at the moment it is not possible

I do want to say that the staff I have

do everything they possibly can to bring

so essential for the welfare of our community.
We are coming to a period of immense
development in the services which we shall
be expected to provide for the health and`
well-being of our people, and we shall
enter that period knowing that we are
substantially in arrears with much that
might have been done before, but cannot
be done during the war.
Without the co-operation of Parliament and people the task will be im-
Without their sympathy and
possible.
understanding of the magnitude of the

But there is no need for us to be

loud-voiced people who only make speeches
for the newspapers and Hansard, and
have very little interest in the welfare of
the community, for they could not stop
here to hear the Minister's reply.
Then the Member for Pottinger very
unfairly said that he saw by Hansardhe must see things in Hansard that
nobody else can
can see nothing but increases in salaries for officials in the new
Ministry. The real truth of the matter
is that there is only one official in my
Ministry and I am very proud that he
is in it has got an increase of salary,
because he came in on promotion. He is
an officer who was in my previous Ministry, for whom I have the highest regard,
and I wanted him in my Ministry because
I thought he would do a good job of
work. He got promotion, and he is the
only man on the whole staff that got an
increase. Others got the usual increments that every civil servant gets. That
is very unfair criticism. It does not do
How that is to help the
any good.
future health of the community is beyond
me.
Then the hon. Member went on to talk
about the restoration of the Belfast
Health and Local Government 1546
Estimates-
20 JUNE 1944
Corporation's powers. Other Members
also raised this question and I want to
deal with it generally. There is not any
Member of the Committee more anxious
to see the Corporation's powers restored
than I am. I mean that when I
say it because I am a citizen of Belfast.
I am proud of being a native of the city.
I want to see a properly constituted local
authority presiding over the destinies of
the city of Belfast. I hope that while I
am in this position I will be able to see
it. I will certainly do all I can for the
restoration of the Corporation's powers.
He then went on to talk about the
restoration of the powers of the Water
Board to the Corporation. I had already
pointed out, in reply to a question this
afternoon, that I have no power to deal
with the Water Board, which is a
separate, constituted body. I want to
say that I am not a bit anxious to have
any powers over the Water Board. If I
had I certainly would not transfer them
to the Belfast Corporation, because from
my knowledge of it the Water Board is
a body that is working very efficiently
and in the best interests of the citizens,
not only of Belfast, but of Northern
Ireland. I hope to have the sympathetic
and whole-hearted co-operation of the
Belfast Water Commissioners in any
water schemes I undertake in the future
-and I believe I will.
The hon. and gallant Member for East
Down raised a question which I expected
him to raise the question of sanatorium
treatment. He also made suggestions
about temporary measures. I want to
tell the hon. and gallant Member and all
other Members that this is one question
I am devoting my undivided attention to
at the moment. Anything I can do to
bring about even a temporary measure of
relief to the victims of this terrible
Scourge will not only be my duty, but
the greatest pleasure in my life to perform. That is the only undertaking I
can give at the moment.
The Member for Queen's University
(Mr. Stevenson) raised, the question of
tuberculosis, child welfare and mental
hospitals. Every Member who raised
any question to-day said that was the
first thing I must do. I want Members
to realise that I am only one person,
and cannot do all these things at once.
Things that are done in a hurry are never
done well. I would remind Members who
were members of the Select Committee
on Health Services that they sat for over
a year. It took them a year to bring
in the Report, and they are all experts.
I am only head of a mongrel Ministry,
and yet they want me to do this in a fortnight. It would take me three weeks
or a month to do this. (Laughter.) All
I can say is they will have to be patient
with me. They have promised their help.
Some of the promises that have been
made were peculiar. They have to give
me a chance on this thing. I am not
despondent about it and I am going to
get down to every question. The Member
for South Armagh remarked-one of the
few sensible things he has ever said that
we would have to work together on this
question. That is the spirit in which we
will have to go into it.
The Member for North Down raised a
question about advisory committees. No
Minister in Northern Ireland gets more
advice than I do. Everybody advises me
what to do, how to do it and when to
do it. I hardly ever take anybody's
advice. I would never be out of trouble
if I did so. (Laughter.) I even attended
a meeting the other day of people who
wanted to advise me. They asked me to
come and see them. I went, and was not
there ten minutes until they were
quarrelling. One half wanted one thing
and the other half another thing, and
yet both wanted me to take their advice.
I said to them, "Gentlemen, when you
have made up your mind what you want
me to do ask me to come back and I will
come and discuss this matter." It is an
easy thing to advise people. This country
is full of advisers. I want fewer advisers
and more helpers.
As to the question of training sanitary
inspectors, this is a matter I fully appreciate, but after all I have to set out a
programme. I am going to work, but
first things must come first. I am afraid
this question of sanitary training will
have to take a back seat until I press
forward with things that are more important in the interests of the community.
Then the Member for North Down,
referring to the Act passed some time
ago in connection with taking over empty
houses or shops to provide accommodation for people, said it was valueless and
there were no empty houses. I am amazed
at that, because he ought to know.
is in the business. Occasionally I see
notices in the papers showing he has houses

a
to sell and promising possession. I know

The hon. Member for North Down
raised a matter that happened in connection with the City Administrators. It
seems very strange that it takes a man
from Bangor to tell us what is happening
in the Belfast Corporation. There was a

I want to say is that my Estimate speech
was not of the usual type. When a
Minister is making his speech he usually
gives an account of his stewardship
during the year and says what he hopes
to do in the future. I could not give

it was not then in existence. I am not

any
Minister; I am going to have enough of

The hon. Member for Pottinger raised
a question which was very fully answered
by the hon. and gallant Member for East
Down-huts for refugees coming from
Normandy. The hon. Member for
Pottinger stated that I had made preparations for the reception of these
refugees and that it was splashed all over
the English newspapers. Splashing things
in newspapers is not a weakness of mine.
I find it gets one into trouble. The only
point I wish to make about the people
coming from Normandy is that the
British Government have a scheme in connection with the matter, and when it is
found necessary, owing to service requirements, to bring refugees from the
Continent to Great Britain they will have
to find accommodation for them. We are
part and parcel of Great Britain; we
claim equal citizenship with the United
Kingdom, and if the British Government
ask us to house these people in huts
which they have already provided—they
were not provided by the Northern
Government in the case of raids by
the enemy-the huts are not being
used and we hope they will never
be used for that purpose-I am going to
find the accommodation for these people,
and I will take full responsibility for
doing so. The House can turn me down
on that question if it wishes, but I do not
think it will. When we contemplate the
plight of some of the people in the
occupied countries we should realise that
we have a great deal to be thankful for.
We should remember that we are our
brother's keeper, and we should be prepared to offer these people food and
shelter so long as we have the accommodation at our disposal.
The hon. Member for Antrim in his
jocular way said he was terribly disappointed that my speech was the best
the Government could do in regard to this
question of health. I am sure he never
heard my speech at all.
Mr. MINFORD: I listened most
attentively.
Mr. GRANT: Probably I should say
that he was not listening to the speech.
He might have heard the sound of my
voice, but did not take in anything I was
saying. I know that the hon. Memberhe is a great friend of mine and I hold
him in the highest esteem-is going to
give me great help in connection with the
new Ministry. He is so popular that hon.
Members from all parts of the House are

time to listen to Ministers when they are
making their statements. I would suggest to the hon. Member that he should
read my speech. If he does so he will
find that there is a great deal of meat in
it. It is probably not cooked, but we are
getting it ready.
As I stated previously, I am only a
fortnight and three days in my present
position. I am entitled to be allowed to
be in it a little longer in order to see if I
can fulfil the promises I made in my

The hon. Member for Mid Armagh is

Mr. AGNEW: Central Armagh.
Mr. GRANT: I am sorry that the hon.

the only answer I can give to the hon.

The hon. Member for Carrick raised a

want to thank him very much. Nobody

Mr. MINFORD: I want the Minister

Stevenson)-were anxious to see the programme carried through. I want the
Minister to tell us what his programme is.
We want a programme. We do not want
what has happened during the past 80
years perpetuated; we want to see the
people of Ulster enjoying good health.
In order that they may do so sweeping
changes will have to be made.
Four years
ago I mentioned that a Ministry of Health
should be established. It was through my

Minister should give the Committee some

Members of Parliament are human beings

Britain. I want to say that I am not

I warn the. Minister I do expect a programme. He said he was not prepared
to allocate medical men to his Ministry.
Surely the time is ripe when the eminent

be given an opportunity of advising him.
We want the best men in his Ministry.
I want to assure the Minister that I am
here to help him, and I am as anxious as
any member of the Government to see the

good citizens. I listened to the Minister's

Mr. GRANT: I want to point out to
the hon. Member for Antrim that, as I

Now he wants me in a fortnight to outline the policy of carrying out the recommendations in that Report.
Mr. MINFORD: Oh, no.
Mr. GRANT: That would be an insult
to the members of the Committee. When
I outline that policy it will be a policy.
that I can stand over. It will be a policy

The MINISTER OF EDUCATION
(Lieut.-Colonel Hall-Thompson): Before
presentation of the White Paper to
Parliament certain legal difficulties had
to be considered, and these are at present
being examined. The settlement of these
difficulties will take rather
more time
than was anticipated. I regret, therefore, that it will not be possible to present
the White Paper before the recess as I
had originally hoped.
Mr. NIXON: Would it be in order to
ask in view of the fact that the Minister
is very properly having a discussion with
the various bodies in Northern Ireland
regarding the White Paper, would the
Minister have an informal discussion with
the Members in this House before he
introduces the White Paper?
Lieut.-Colonel HALL-THOMPSON :
That is the manner in which there will
be an informal discussion. The White
Paper will be introduced with the express
object of giving this House a full opportunity of expressing its views. The White
Paper is not binding upon the Government. It is the Bill which it precedes
which will have the ultimate binding
effect.
Mr. NIXON: With regard to the
Minister's statement that the Paper will
be discussed across the Table, that is not

that an informal discussion constitutes a

official?
Mr. MINFORD: Does the Minister
not think that after all the back benchers

we are the people that represent these

Ministry of Home Affairs.
Motion made and Question proposed,
"That a sum not exceeding £108,951 be
granted to His Majesty to defray the
charges which will come in course of payment during the year ending 31st March,
1945, for the salaries and expenses of the
Ministry of Home Affairs.""
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Mr. Lowry): If it is agreeable to the
Committee I will deal generally with
these Votes, Class II, Nos. 1 to 7.
The CHAIRMAN: I will have to ask
the Committee is it agreed.
Mr. NIXON: No. Nothing personal,
but these Estimates want absolute investigation which will take three months
to carry out.
The CHAIRMAN: Then we will take
them Vote by Vote.
Mr. LOWRY: The first one is for
£108,951, which covers the salaries and
allowances of the Ministry of Home
Affairs staff, and falls naturally into three
divisions. The first covers a period of
12 months for the functions not transferred. The second covers two months
for those transferred to the Ministry of
Health and Local Government. The
amount shown is the advance of salary
Estimates-
Ministry of Home Affairs
21 JUNE 1944
paid during the two months of April and
May. The third covers a period of ten
months for those taken over on the
abolition of the Ministry of Public
Security. In this connection I would like
to make
some reference of a personal
nature to the transfer of staff between
the two Ministries. I think it is a high
tribute to our Civil Service that there
was a strong inclination, both on the part
of my right hon. Friend and myself, to
keep with us the officers with whom we
had been working to the greatest possible
extent. This was in no sense due to any
doubts as to the capabilities of the officers
who had in the past been dealing with
the work that was coming to us, but was
the natural result of the satisfaction we
had had from our own men.
That, as I say, was our inclination,
but we of course realised that the work
transferred was in many respects of a
highly technical character and that it
was essential that each of the Ministries
should have in it a substantial foundation
of men who were familiar with the technique of the work of which it would be
in charge. To those former officers of the
Ministry of Home Affairs who have now
gone to the new Ministry of Health I
desire to express my thanks for the
assistance they have been to me in the
past and my confidence that my right
hon. Friend will find them of equal
assistance to him in the future.
To those officers who are coming to the
Ministry of Home Affairs I extend a
very cordial welcome, together with an
assurance that I feel my Ministry is fortunate in having their expert knowledge
and experience at its disposal. To certain
other officers at present with my Ministry
but whose ultimate destination is as yet
uncertain I wish very happy landings.
This first Vote as a whole shows an
increase of £3,900 and this figure is not
of much value as comparable with the
1943-44 figure, for the cost of the staff
taken over from the Ministry of Public
Security is not shown on this Vote, as it
has already been shown in the Ministry
of Public Security revised Estimates presented last month. In addition a full
year's costs of the local government
evacuation division 1943-44 are shown
compared with the two months' provision
for the current year. In Headquarters
division provision is made for an assistant
secretary for two months and for a secretary for a full year. In the Home Office.
division provision is made for a medical
inspector and a pharmaceutical inspector
which accounts for most of the increased
cost. In the Roads and Transport division the engineering staff is similarly
shown. They also perform duties on behalf of the Ministry of Health and Local
Government such as water supply. In
the petroleum office agency additional
staff are required to reinforce it and will
be engaged in investigation duties. A
reduction is shown in the receipts appropriated in aid representing a reduction
in the cost of evacuation. I beg to move.
Mr. NIXON: Perhaps we will take
the things that are most important in our
way of looking at them first. Of course
the Estimates will be a bit difficult from
no particular person's fault on account of
the way they have been divided and subdivided. We hear a lot of talk about
constructive criticism. Constructive criticism is advice to the Government to
rule this country in the interests of the
majority of the public. I reckon that
that is constructive criticism. The Prime
Minister, through no fault of his own,
is rather unfortunate, because he is being
pulled down all the time. One of the
first things a Government should do is to
face their responsibility, whatever that
responsibility is, without trying to shift
it across to Great Britain. I do not think
that I have said anything out of the way.
The CHAIRMAN: The hon. Gentleman is on the verge.
Mr. NIXON: I would not say so. I
am reflecting on the Government trying
to shift the responsibility to Great
Britain by pretending to the House and

that remark. Perhaps the correction
from the Chair made me make it plain.
It was plain enough to me. Everything
is plain to the man talking, but may not
be so plain to the people listening. That
is one thing that has always been persisted in here. Another thing: I know
the Minister of Home Affairs is a firstclass lawyer-he is at the head of his profession-but he certainly is not a firstclass Minister.

Member's attention to the fact that in

Estimates-
Ministry of Home Affairs
HOUSE OF COMMONS

[Mr. Elliott]
As regards the question of petrol
supplies for Members of this House, something ought to be done by the Government in the way of laying down exactly
what a Member of Parliament gets his
petrol allowance for and what he does
not get it for. I think it should no longer
be left in the hands of any subordinate
official of this House to tell any Member
what he gets his petrol supplies for and
what he does not get them for. He ought
not to be in the position of a dictator.
A Member of Parliament ought not to
be in the position that he has to ask the
Clerk-Assistant, "Can I go here or go
there?" You must be guided apparently
by the Clerk-Assistant as to where you
can go.
Take a case that happened not very
long ago.
The Clerk-Assistant of this
House stated in a public court that I,
as a Member of Parliament, could travel
to Castledawson, which is outside my constituency, and that I could travel anywhere outside my constituency if I were
asked to do so in my capacity as a
Member of Parliament, but that I could
not go to a certain congregation in County
Antrim because my brother happened to
be the minister of the church there. That
was laid down by the Clerk-Assistant of
this House. Apparently nobody has any
right to say anything against that. It is
about time the Members of this House
were masters of their own house. They
ought to ask the Government to lay down
orders as to what a Member of Parliament
can do and not leave it to a subordinate
official of the House. We have certain
rights in this House, and we are not
going to have them taken away from us
by a subordinate official of the House.
No Member of this House wants to do
anything that is wrong. I do not want
to do anything that is wrong, but I am
not going to take my orders from a
subordinate official of this House. He
should not be able to tell me what I can
do and what I cannot do in so far as my
petrol allowance is concerned.
It is a strange thing that the only
people who can travel to a court of justice
in Northern Ireland to-day and use petrol
in doing so are, first of all, the magistrate who adjudicates; secondly, the
district inspector who prosecutes, and,
thirdly, the officials who attend from the
petroleum office and this House of Parliament to give evidence. At Toomebridge
Petty Sessions a few days ago a number
of Presbyterian clergymen were prosecuted for wasting petrol. In order to
prove the offence three officials from the
petroleum office came down the whole way
from Belfast in a motor-car. They were
to give evidence in regard to the misuse
or waste of petrol. Bus facilities were
available, railway facilities were available, yet these men who came down to
give evidence arrived in their motor-car.
They wasted far more petrol travelling
down to Toomebridge than many of the
defendants would have wasted, but the
latter had to travel to the court by bus.
These people can get petrol whenever they
want it. They can get petrol in order
to prosecute other people for misuse of
petrol.
I was told by the Clerk-Assistant of
this House that in order to save petrol I
should have travelled 56 instead of 26
miles. He laid down the law to me and
told me that in order for me to get to a
congregation in County Antrim I should
have taken my own car to Cookstown,
and then taken a taxi from there to
Duneane. That would have meant travelling a distance of 56 miles. Because I
did not do that I was prosecuted, and
the Clerk-Assistant of this House gave
evidence that I wasted petrol because I
did not travel 56 miles instead of 26. It
is time something was done. If there is
no petrol available for Presbyterian
ministers to travel to conduct their services surely there should not be petrol
available for officials of the petroleum
office to enable them to travel by car to
prosecute such people. It is altogether
wrong. I hope the time is not far distant
when the Minister of Home Affairs will
take this matter up and see to it that
what is sauce for the goose is also sauce
for the gander. The people who are so
particular about the misuse of petrol
should travel to the court in the same way
as the defendants have to travel-by bus.
I asked the Clerk-Assistant of this
House about travelling to Castledawson.
He said, "Yes, certainly you can go to
Castledawson. Go to Castledawson, go
anywhere, but do not go near the congregation of which your brother happens
to be minister." I do not like to bring
the personal element into this, but I
think this matter should be made public.
A man is penalised because he happens to
have a brother who is a Presbyterian

minister. That is why I was penalised. I
put the case before a very eminent lawyer.

Royal Ulster Constabulary.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That a sum not exceeding £658,492 be
granted to His Majesty to complete the
sum necessary to defray the charge which
will come in course of payment during the
year ending 31st March, 1945, for the
salaries and expenses of the Royal Ulster
Constabulary, including police women."
-(Note-£325,000 has been voted on
account.)
Mr. LOWRY: This is a reduction of
about £10,000 as compared with last year.
The decrease arises in the provision of
clothing, arms, ammunition and transport. In the interests of economy the
frequency of issue of certain items of
uniform has been reduced, and this,
together with the fact that last year's
estimate for clothing contained provision
for arrears of payment unavoidably
carried forward from previous years'
contracts, against which no corresponding
provision has been found necessary in the
current estimate, accounts for the redution of £15,000 in the clothing sub-head.
The amount provided last year for arms
and ammunition was abnormal in that it
included provision for the cost of a new
type of more efficient weapon for the
force. No corresponding provision is made
in the current year. The reduction here
is £4,500.
The reduction of £6,000 under the head
of transport is due in the main to provision being made for the purchase of
a smaller number of replacement cars.
These savings, totalling about £26,000,
are offset by an increase of £16,000 in the
amount required for pay, allowances,
pensions and gratuities. Pay shows an

Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.

Home Affairs.
RESIDENCE PERMIT-
BENJAMIN MCKANE, URNEY.
1. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state if
Benjamin McKane, Inniscalan, Urney,
Strabane, has been refused a residence
permit, was prosecuted and ordered to
leave Northern Ireland; whether this man
is married to a County Tyrone woman
and has a family some of them born in
Northern Ireland; and whether he can
state on what grounds he is using his
position to separate this man from his
wife and family.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Mr. Lowry): The reply to the first part
of the question is in the affirmative.
According to our records, this man's
wife was born in County Tyrone, but
they both came to Northern Ireland from
Scotland in 1941.
I am not using my position to separate
any man from his wife, but I cannot
concede the implication that marriage
should be a method of defeating the
object of the Residence Permit Order.
Benjamin McKane is a joiner by
occupation, and I am informed by my
right hon. Friend, the Minister of
Labour, that there is a substantial
number of Northern Ireland joiners unemployed at the present time.
Mr. NIXON: With regard to the
Minister's statement that the wife came
from Scotland, does the fact that a person is born in Northern Ireland and goes
to Scotland to look for work disqualify
that person from living in Northern
Ireland?
Mr. LOWRY; No, sir.
Mr. NIXON: Then if it does not disqualify such a person, why does the
Minister take it upon himself to put her
out of Northern Ireland?
Mr. LOWRY: From my answer to the
main question, the hon. Member will see
that this depends upon whether there is
work for this man or not. Primarily in
regard to people resident in Northern Ireland who have been out of work the
Ministry of Labour take the view, and I
think correctly, that those people should
be placed in employment first.
Mr. NIXON: While agreeing with the
latter part of the right hon. Gentleman's
statement, I would point out that this
was born in Northern Ireland,
and because she went to Scotland the
right hon. Gentleman takes it upon
himself to throw her out of the country.
woman
POLICE QUESTIONING OF
BELFAST WOMEN.
2. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state on
whose instructions Miss S. White, 78
Andersonstown Park, Belfast, together
with her sister, Kathleen (aged 16), May,
and Mrs. M'Kee were arrested and taken
to Chichester Street Police Station on
12th June, 1944; whether it is a fact
that finger prints and photographs of
these persons were taken and that they
were interrogated by members of the
R.U.C. for four hours; whether on arrest
any charge was preferred against them;
whether it is a common practice of the
police to make raids on this home; and
whether he will ensure that such tactics
will cease and so put an end to this worry
and inconvenience caused to these people.
Mr. LOWRY: The police have general
authority to enforce the provisions of the
Civil Authorities (Special Powers) Acts,
1922 to 1943, and the Regulations made
thereunder.
The persons named were detained by
the police for interrogation and their
finger prints and photographs were taken.
No charges were preferred against the
White sisters who were detained for about
2 hours, or against Mrs. McKee who
was detained for less than an hour.
The White residence has been searched
on a number of occasions and Mrs.
McKee's house was searched on one occasion.
I deplore the necessity for investigations of this sort, but the continued exist-

Orders made under Defence Regulations.
5. Mr. JOHN BAILEY asked the
Prime Minister whether he can state how
many Orders or Regulations have been
issued under the Defence of the Realm
Act since the outbreak of war; under
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
27 JUNE 1944

what system they are issued; whether
Members of Parliament receive a copy of
them; and whether he would take into

The PRIME MINISTER (Sir Basil
Brooke): This is a highly technical
subject and necessitates a lengthy and
comprehensive reply. I propose, therefore, with the hon. Member's permission,
to circulate it in the Official Debates.
Briefly, the position is that Defence
Regulations made under the Emergency
Powers (Defence) Act, 1939, must be laid
before the Imperial Parliament and are
subject to annulment by His Majesty on
an address presented to him by either
House.

certain laws?
The PRIME MINISTER: As I suggested, the reply is a very lengthy one,
and I suggest that hon. Members should
peruse that reply first and then put down
another question on the point raised by
the hon. Member.

when this House is going to lose what
power it has in regard to these matters.
Mr. SPEAKER: I have been asked a
question by the hon. Member for Antrim.
All I can do is to make arrangements in
my Department to see that such Orders
as are issued are forwarded to hon. Members who wish those Orders sent to them.
I do not know that that applies to these
particular Orders laid before the British
House of Commons. I may be wrong,
but I do not think it does.
Mr. MINFORD: Would it not be
wiser that these Rules and Regulations
should be discussed before becoming law?
A Motion should be put down in order
to enable that to be done.
The PRIME MINISTER: As I stated,
the Defence of the Realm Regulations and
Orders are laid on the Table of the
Imperial House. I do not know whether
it would be right that they should be laid
on the Table of this House. There are
certain Orders made by virtue of powers
conferred upon agencies here, and if, after
perusing my reply, the hon. Member will
put down another question the Government will consider whether Orders strictly
limited to Northern Ireland should be
considered in the same way as at Westminster.
The following is the reply referred to:
The hon. Member, no doubt, has in
mind the Act under which Regulations
and orders are issued for "the public
safety, the defence of the Realm, the
maintenance of public order, and the efficient prosecution of any war in which His
Majesty may be engaged, and for maintaining supplies and services essential to
the life of the community." That Act is
the Emergency Powers (Defence) Act,
1939, which was passed by the Imperial
Parliament immediately before the outbreak of war. It empowers His Majesty
in Council to make Defence Regulations,
and these unless the contrary intention
appears therein-apply throughout the
United Kingdom, including Northern
Ireland. It also provides that Defence
Regulations may contain provisions for
empowering such authorities as may be
specified in the Regulations to make
orders, rules and by-laws for any of the
purposes for which such Regulations are
authorised to be made. As regards
Northern Ireland, several competent
authorities have been empowered by the
Defence Regulations to make such orders,
etc. These are, for the most part,
Imperial authorities, such as a Secretary
of State, the Admiralty or the Board of
Trade, but in a few cases some department of the Government of Northern
Ireland has been designated for the performance of particular functions. Many
of the Defence Regulations enable the
Imperial authority concerned to delegate
its powers. In particular, the Secretary
of State for the Home Department is expressly empowered to delegate his powers
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[The Prime Minister]
to a department of the Northern Ireland
Government in cases in which his powers
are, under the Regulations, exercisable in
Northern Ireland. Numerous delegations
of this kind are in force.
The Defence (General) Regulations are
more than 340 in number, and from time
to time they are reprinted by His
Majesty's Stationery Office in their revised form in a single volume; the latest
of these is the 15th edition, and it contains the Regulations as in force on 24th
March of the present year. A similar
volume containing Miscellaneous Defence
Regulations is produced and published
from time to time, the latest edition bringing those Regulations up to the 10th
August, 1943. It would not be possible,
without prolonged research, to state
definitely the number of subordinate
orders issued as respects Northern
Ireland since the outbreak of war in pursuance of powers conferred by the Defence
Regulations, whether issued by Imperial
authorities Northern Ireland departments directly under the Regulations or
under delegations given by an Imperial
authority. It may be said, shortly, that
powers are exercisable by specified Northern Ireland departments for various purposes under those Defence Regulations,
which have for their object the maintenance of supplies and services essential to
the life of the community.
or
All Imperial authorities having powers
under the Emergency Powers (Defence)
Act as respects Northern Ireland are responsible to the Imperial Parliament for
the exercise of those powers, whether
exercised directly or by delegation to some
Northern Ireland department. As regards the raising of emergency matters
in this House, I would refer the hon.
Member to the ruling which Mr. Speaker
gave on 8th November, 1939, in which he
pointed out that, generally speaking, it
would be through Members of the
Imperial House of Commons representing Northern Ireland that Northern
Ireland questions on Imperial and reserved matters should be brought before
the Imperial House or the Imperial
authorities, and that any steps in this
House could not go beyond the putting
down of questions asking for information,
or Motions asking for representations to
be made to the Imperial Government.
Defence Regulations must be laid before
the Imperial Parliament, and they are
subject to annulment by His Majesty on
an address presented to him by either
House. This provision applies only to
Defence Regulations and does not apply
to orders, rules and bylaws made by competent authorities under powers conferred
by Defence Regulations.
The hon. Member, in referring to the
system at present in force in the Imperial
Parliament, probably has in mind the
Committee set up by the Imperial House
of Commons on the 21st June to scutinise
regulations and orders which, according
to the Act under which they are made,
either-
(a) cannot be effective unless approved
by an "affirmative" resolution of
either House, or
(b) can be annulled within a specified
period upon an address to the
Crown or a "negative" resolution
of either House.
This arrangement will apply to Defence
Regulations, because of the annulment
provisions contained in the Emergency
Powers (Defence) Act, and, therefore, to
such of these Regulations as are in force
in Northern Ireland. It does not apply
to "subordinate" orders, etc., made
under powers conferred by the Defence
Regulations.
The Defence (General) Regulations
contain a provision under which orders
made by departments of the Government
of Northern Ireland, in the exercise of
powers given to them for the purpose of
any of the Regulations, are published by
His Majesty's Stationery Office in Belfast
in the series of Statutory Rules and
Orders of Northern Ireland, and such
orders are thus on sale locally.
