LOCAL GOVERNMENT (FINANCE)
BILL.
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF HEALTH AND
LOCAL GOVERNMENT (Mr. Grant):
This Bill is being introduced to enable
my Ministry to pay derating grants to
local authorities on a new basis. Hon.
Members will recollect that under the
Act of 1929 occupiers of agricultural land
were given complete exemption from pay-
Local Government Bill-
Second Reading
27 JUNE 1944

ment of rates, and occupiers of industrial
premises were given relief in respect of 75
per cent, of their rates. As a result of
these exemptions the revenue of local.
authorities was reduced and the Government accordingly made special grants to
local authortiies towards making up the
deficiency.
So far as urban authorities were concerned the Act of 1929 empowered the
Ministry to make good the whole amount
of the deficiency, but in 1936 this position
was modified by the introduction of a
maximum sum which could be paid in
any particular case. The present Bill
removes the maximum and restores the
1929 position. That is to say, urban
authorities will receive grants sufficient
to make good the actual loss of revenue
due to derating legislation.
Local authorities, other than urban
authorities, receive grants on a different
basis. Under existing practice each local
authority receives-
(1) a standard
standard grant calculated in
accordance with the provisions of
the Act of 1936;
(2) a supplemental grant representing
the local authority's share of a sum
calculated as set out in the Act of
1936;
(3) an extra-statutory grant paid in
addition to the above-mentioned
grants.
The Bill provides for the consolidation
of these three grants on the basis of the
amounts actually paid to each local
authority in respect of the year 1942-43,
the latest year for which audited accounts
of local authorities are available. The
total consolidated grant will be £871,542.
As an
addition to the consolidated
grant, a variable grant will be paid in
respect of each year
to the rural authorities. The total amount of the variable
grant is restricted, under the Bill, to 65
per cent. of the excess of expenditure by
all the local authorities concerned in the
grant year as compared with the basic
year-1942-43. The figure of 65 per
cent. has been calculated with reference
to the proportion of derated hereditaments in the areas in question. It is intended that the grant so calculated,
together with the consolidated grant, will
be sufficient to recoup to the rural authorities taken as a whole the total loss in
rate income attributable to derating.
I have made provision in the current
year's Estimates for £134,000 in respect
of the new additional grant, but the
amount will, of course, rise or fall from
year to year according as the expenditure
of the local authorities rises or falls. The
principle contained in the Act of 1936,
which restricted the amount of grants to
a maximum, has thus been completely
abandoned. The imposition of a ceiling
on derating grants undoubtedly tended to
retard the development of local services,
and its abolition will, I am sure, be
welcomed both by the local authorities
and the House. I beg to move.
Question proposed, "That the Bill be
now read a Second time."

PLANNING ACTS AMENDMENT
BILL.
Order for Second Reading read.
Mr. GRANT: This is a short Bill
designed to clear up some small difficulties which have arisen in the administration of the Planning Acts.
The reasons for the Bill are as follows.
First, the Planning and Housing Act of
1931, which is the principal Planning
Act, provided that the planning authorities should be the councils of the county
boroughs, boroughs and urban districts,
and in rural areas the county councils.
In the latter case, however, provision was
made whereby the county council could
delegate its powers to a rural district
council where the rural district council
Planning Acts Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Grant]
wished to become the planning authority
for its area. In many cases such transfer
of powers took place. Secondly, the
Planning (Interim Development) Act of
1944 brought the whole of Northern Ireland under planning control and made.
it the duty of every planning authority to
prepare a scheme for its area, and so
made possible the co-ordinated planning
of the Province. In order to achieve
voluntary co-ordination, and also to
enable planning schemes to be prepared
as smoothly as possible and in the most.
economical way, it is desirable that planning areas should be as large as is practicable.
Accordingly, discussions have been
taking place between the various local
authorities involved, and as a result
certain rural district councils wish to retransfer some of their powers to the
county council, and the county council is
prepared to take these powers back. It
was found, however, that, as the Acts
stand at present, there is no power
whereby this can be done.
Further, certain urban districts which
are small, with limited financial resources,
consider that it would be more economical
for them to have their planning schemes
prepared as part of a county scheme.
Again, however, there is no means whereby such urban councils, if they so desire,
can hand over some of their planning
powers to the county council.
The main object of the Bill is, therefore,
to enable any rural or urban council to
transfer whatever powers it so desires to
the county council, subject to the county
council on its side being willing to take
the powers over. This object is dealt with
in Clause 1 of the Bill.
In passing I wish to mention that on
the Committee stage of the Bill I am proposing to move an Amendment to the last
paragraph of sub-clause (3) of this Clause,
which will allow the arrangements regarding the sharing of expenses to be
somewhat more flexible than the present
wording of the paragraph would permit.
I hope hon. Members will realise that
by bringing in this Amendment on the
Committee stage I am accepting responsibility for the fact that it was left out in
the drafting of the Bill. When the
matter was discovered I thought it better
to confess to the House that this matter
had been overlooked. I want to move
the Amendment on the Committee stage
in order to put the matter right.
In Clause 2 power is given to a joint
committee to co-opt members of a rural
or urban council. This is a necessary
provision following on Clause 1 of the Bill,
as under the principal Act only those
local authorities with planning powers
may be represented on a joint committee.
Now there may be authorities who wish to
surrender all their planning powers, provided they secure representation on a
joint committee. It may also be desirable to give direct representation to
certain rural authorities which never
became planning authorities. This would
make it possible to form a joint committee consisting of representatives of a
county council and of urban and rural
district councils.
Clause 3 deals with the further point
that, where transfer of planning powers
takes place, the planning resolution passed
by the original authority, and the effects
of such a resolution, are transferred to the
new planning authority. It might be
inferred from the Acts as they stand that
this would take place automatically, but
it is essential to place the matter beyond
doubt.
Clause 4 of the Bill deals with an
anomaly which has arisen. Under the
Act of 1931 planning authorities were required to keep a register showing the
ownership of land in their areas. The
1944 Act, however, did not require those
local authorities who then became planning authorities to do so. The result is
that some planning authorities have to
keep registers, and others have not. This
Clause, by repealing Section 12 of the
1931 Act, does away with the necessity
for the former authorities to keep, a
register, and puts all planning authorities on the same footing in this respect.
As local authorities have been working
very harmoniously together in regard to
these matters, and have already made
provisional arrangements on the understanding that enabling legislation would
be introduced in Parliament, I strongly
commend this Bill to the House. I beg
to move.

My first reaction to planning is probably the same as that of the man in the
street who thinks that planning means
nothing but town planning, and who
associates it with slogans about the
beauty of the countryside and the ugliness of the town. In the first place
planning does not mean town planning
alone; it means planning for the country
as a whole. At its worst it can become
a spare-time amusement for people who
think themselves superior to their
fellows. At its best it is a thoroughly
practical man's approach to the needs
of our country.-(Official Report, 20th
June, 1944; Vol. XXVII., col. 1506.)
In this great matter planning is
essential, and we feel that this Bill, to
which we are asking you to give your
approval, will clear up what we have
already found to be wrong, and will help
towards that time when there will be
houses for all the people who need them.

The MINISTER OF
(Major Sinclair): This Resolution enables
the payment out of moneys provided by
Parliament, of the sums required under
the provisions of the Local Government
(Finance) Bill which received its Second
Reading yesterday. The purposes for
which this additional money is required
have already been fully explained

I feel that there is very little
which I need add to-day. As hon.
Members will have observed from the
Estimates, the increase in derating grants
in the current financial year is put at
£171,000, and that of this amount no
less than £134,000 is accounted for by
the new additional grants to be paid to
rural authorities. What further sums
may be required from the Exchequer in
future will, of course, depend on the expenditure of the local authorities themselves, but the advance in locally administered services in the post-war years will,
or should, be such that I anticipate that
there will be further substantial increases
under this head. I beg to move.

There was a misprint in the Amendment as shown on the Order Paper. I
therefore arranged for the circulation of
a revised Amendment to Members, and it
is the Amendment in its revised form
which I am moving. Opportunity has
been taken to substitute a complete new
sub-section for sub-section (4) of Section
16 of the Act of 1931 in preference to
the method suggested in the original
Amendment, thus avoiding, to a certain
degree, a rather complicated piece of
legislation by reference.
The object of this Amendment is to
clarify the question of how expenses incurred by the county council under the
Planning Acts are to be defrayed. The
present wording of the Bill says that the
expenses shall be defrayed either as a
county-at-large charge or as a charge
upon the urban district. While some
small urbans may wish to get their schemes
prepared as part of the county scheme,
the boroughs and certain other urban
districts will be preparing their own
schemes and will be meeting their own
expenses.
The Amendment is designed
to ensure that the boroughs and the
urban districts which prepare their
own schemes shall not bear any part of
the county expenses. Again, it might, in
a number of instances, be desirable for
the county council to split certain
planning expenses in varying proportions
over various districts or between urban
districts and rural districts. The Amendment will allow this to be done.
Yesterday the hon. Member for Woodvale said that the idea behind this
Amendment was to make it more elastic,
so that there could be more charges made.
It has just the opposite effect. May I use
an illustration? Take the case of Bangor,
in County Down. That borough may like
to have a planning scheme of their own
independent of the county, and as the
original wording in the Bill stands they
may be liable for part of the county
charges for planning although they are a
This
planning authority on their own.
Amendment is to make it quite clear that
there will be no charge on any borough or
urban council carrying out their own
scheme. I beg to move.

Mr. AGNEW: When discussing the
Appropriation Bill we can deal with
many of the problems facing the Government and also the expenditure involved.
For any laxity on the part of the Government in dealing with such matters the
Prime Minister must accept a certain
amount of responsibility. The right hon.
Gentleman is the head of the Government. He has declared a policy for
Northern Ireland, but when speaking to
other parts of the Empire it is only right
that he should confine himself to the
facts as he finds them in Northern Ireland. Not only is the right hon. Gentleman Prime Minister, but he is also
Minister of Commerce and Production.
By virtue of the fact that he is Minister
of Commerce and Production, hon. Members of this House who belong to the
working class movement look to him to
do something practical for the people of
Northern Ireland. There is no use in
making promises if they are not fulfilled.
In so far as the spending of money is
concerned we must ask the Prime Minister
and his Government to do so in a proper
way. It should be looked at from
the point of view. of how much
happiness, security and prosperity can
be achieved.
As I look at the various services on
which money is being spent, I am amazed
to find that we spend far more on the
maintenance of a strong Police Force,
including Special Constabulary, than we
do in combating tuberculosis, in connection with maternity and child welfare
schemes, and on the blind. When one
looks at it from that angle one feels very
keenly about it. We are told by the
people whom we meet that there is something wrong with the Government of
Northern Ireland. After 22 years in
office the Unionist Government has
neglected the Province, with the exception of the city of Belfast and other areas.
I am not going to exaggerate the position.
On many occasions I have appealed to the
head of the Government to do something
for us. Mid Armagh is represented by
the Chief Whip. He is competent to
answer questions for the Minister of
Home Affairs. When he is fit to do that
I should like to know if he has found a
solution for the position existing in his
own constituency.
Let us take the city of Armagh as an
example. There are a spinning mill and
a weaving factory lying idle. There is
no excuse for that. If the Government
had done the right thing in the years
that are past, and had been candid about
the fact that we were a distressed area,
we should have had better results. In
one of our local newspapers it is announced that nine firms in Scotland are
planning to spend £10,000,000 on industry. Scotland has not got a Government of its own; it is controlled from
Westminster. After 22 years in office
the Northern Government has not told
us, despite all their post-war planning,
what amount of money they intend to
spend in an endeavour to encourage new
industries in the Province. Armagh is
only one example. South Armagh is another. The industries in that area are
falling into decay. The Prime Minister,
as head of the Government and also as
Minister of Commerce and Production,
has a lot to answer for. He should tell
us what he intends to do. He has made
many promises. I would ask the right
hon. Gentleman to turn his gaze to South
Armagh and the city of Armagh when he
is planning for prosperity, as I believe he
must. I do not know how the Prime
Minister will face up to realities when he
has to adopt a Bill in this House calling
for work for all the people in Northern
Ireland. A Bill on similar lines is being
promoted in the British House of
Commons. I do not know what argument
he will put forward then.

It is a sad feature of our administration
that so much money is being spent on

We are told that so much money is to be
spent on the Ulster House in London. I

to Northern Ireland. We have the people,

to work, but the Northern Government
was not in a position to offer it.
We never want to have such a state of

But nothing was done. All I can see in

just as loyal as they would like them to
All men in Northern Ireland are not

aerodrome, or at a supply base, about

As the hon. Member for South Armagh
stated, we are spending a great deal of
money on special police. It is far better
to maintain peace when we have it, and
the only way we can do that is by keeping
a strong force of regular and special police
as well as the Home Guard. Surely
when there is any safety work or any
security work to be done, there should be
no question about the loyalty of the, men
carrying it out. Men who have taken
an oath of allegiance to the King, men
who wear the King's uniform as special
constables or as members of the Home
Guard should be appointed as Security
Police at aerodromes and supply bases.
Tribute after tribute has been paid by
Government after Government, Prime
Minister after Prime. Minister, and by
Members of Parliament to the members
of our Home Guard and Special Constabulary, but when it comes to a question of protecting supply bases and aerodromes these. men, who have given good
service to the Government, are overlooked
and men are placed in charge of such
places who, in many cases, are not loyal.
Men who stood at the corner and watched
these men going to their drill night after
night are put into positions of trust and
responsibility.
I hope the Minister responsible will
see to it that no men are placed in such
a position as I have described except
members of the Special Constabulary,
Home Guard or others in whom the
Government have every confidence. Only
men in whom the public have confidence
should be so employed. Looking back
over the years, we know well enough what
happened when there was a traitor in the
camp. I want to warn the Government
about this matter. If something serious
happens at one of these aerodromes or
supply bases it will be the fault not of
the local loyalists but of the Minister and
the others responsible for putting into
such positions men who have no right to
be put into them. I may be a voice crying in the wilderness so far as this matter
is concerned, but I will continue to draw

and the loyal people are satisfied that
these places are guarded by men in whom

I should also like to say a word about
the R.U.C. I think it is a force of
which we have every reason to be proud.
As a whole they have carried out their

for the rank and file, but I feel that so
long as the present system of pitchforking
men into positions in the force is continued so long will there be dissatisfaction
amongst the rank and file. Promotions
in the R.U.C. ought to be made on merit

the R.U.C. should, if he has the ability,
be able to climb to the top of the tree
in the same way as any citizen in the
United States of America has an opportunity, if he has the ability, of getting
into the presidential chair at some time

of the force that appointments should be
made over the heads of men who have
given good service in the force. I hope
this matter will be taken in hand, and
that all ranks in the force will get an
opportunity of promotion.
The hon. Member for Woodvale mentioned the other day the fact that
gratuities or advances were being given to
the heads of the R.U.C.
When any
financial benefit is to be conferred on the

The advance should not be confined to

it will be one to which we will be able
to give our benediction and our blessing?
I want to tell the right hon. Gentleman
that if the White Paper does not give the

I want to say something about holidays.
Holidays very often in the country are

People in the country want their children at home during the potato gathering.
I know many schools where the managers

parents. Surely something could be
done to bring these two things into line

was seconded in December, 1941, for

Mr. Iliff rendered distinguished

The question of the promotion in the
Royal Ulster Constabulary was raised by
the hon. Member for South Tyrone.
There is the matter of appointing cadets.
I know that cadets were appointed in the
Royal Irish Constabulary. Half the
vacancies for officers went to cadets, who
also had to pass a competitive examination held by the Civil Service. It was a
Civil Service examination. The entrants
were known only by numbers. Of course
they had to be duly recommended and so
forth, but whoever got the first place in
the examination got the first cadetship.
Every other vacancy went-one to a cadet
and one to the rank and file. But there
was a very different system in promoting
the rank and file to what there is now.
They were all promoted on examination
held by people competent to hold examinations, and not after an interview. Supposing that our prospects depended on our
appearance, I would not be in it and
neither would the Minister of Home
Affairs; he is not good looking either.
(Laughter.) The Minister of Finance
would get on well; he is very handsome
looking. (Laughter.) That is what it
amounts to. Then, of course, people say
there is more than that. They say that
before they are summoned to these interviews the promotion is made, and it
certainly looks very suspicious.
All promotion should be from the ranks.
In Australia all promotions are from the
ranks. Furthermore, if a man thinks he
does not get fair play he can go to a
tribunal, which will re-hear his claim and
which has often reduced the man the
Commissioner promoted, and promoted
the man who appealed on the ground that
he was best entitled to it. The rank and
file here are a most efficient force.
Nobody could say anything else about
them. In all the years I have known

man, and that was not very much either.
That is about the best testimonial they

Would it please any Minister if he were

We should try to take some steps to have

There should be some way of making them

When they are young is the time to reform them, not when they are old
criminals. I feel for these boys, because

which I think will convince him. These
are things we should take note of, because
in view of the sacrifices made by Ulstermen in this war, any persons who do not
belong to Ulster, and who probably do
not agree with Ulster, should not have
these jobs given to them.
Now I come to the question of tourist
traffic. I wonder if the Ministry of Commerce really gives the Ulster Tourist
Development Association the financial
support they are entitled to. I listened
last night to the Brains Trust, and one
of the questions put to them was whether
England would develop the tourist industry after the war in order to bring
people to England to buy goods from
Great Britain. After the war we will be
confronted with the very big problem of
getting back our export trade. We have
a London office, but in my opinion it is a
very poor one so far as the building
itself is concerned. We ought to spend a
great deal more money on letting people
who go to London know that Ulster is a
place of some importance. Instead of
doing that we spend only a few thousand
pounds. I understand we have a very
good man in charge of the office, but I
do not think we have premises that will
attract people. They are away down a
side street, and we should have an office
that is more conspicuous and attractive.
At present people wonder where Ulster
is and who are the people of Ulster. If
necessary we will vote the Government
the money to make Ulster House a
building worthy of the Province and its
people.

When I spoke about the Security
Police I did not want to imply that the
heads of this Force are disloyal, but we
have in Ulster to-day men who are able
to fill those positions. If these people
from Eire want to help Great Britain in
her difficulties there are other places they
can go to. They can get uniform in
other capacities, but while we have
ex-Service men of this war who are signing on at the employment exchanges
they should be given these jobs, because
they are worthy of them. When our
troops landed in Normandy Mr. Bevin
said that when they returned they would
come back to employment. He made
them that promise, and I believe he will
keep it. I wonder if we can make that
promise to our boys. That is why I mentioned this subject of the Security Police.
It is our bounden duty to these lads who
have fought and bled for us to see that
they will not have to stand in queues at
any labour exchange when they return
from the war. We should place them in
employment that will suit their physical
condition.
It will be a blot on Ulster if we allow
these lads to hang about the stage door.
A man who was discharged from the
Army told me that when they went to
sign on at a labour exchange they were
treated like cattle. I understand it took
two days for some of these men to sign
on; they had to go through so much
procedure. I do not know whether that
is true or not, but I think these boys
should get every consideration. No treatment could be too good for those who have
fought in the different theatres of war.
Yet there are ex-Service men going about
and living on the dole, while men from
Eire are in charge of the Security Police
in Northern Ireland. That state
affairs should be remedied at once.
of
I come now to my final subject, which
is housing. I have spoken very strongly
on this question, because I know the conditions in the country probably better
than any man on the Front Bench, as I
live in a rural district. I hope the
Minister of Health and Local Government will put some time limit on the deliberations of the Planning Commission
so that we can get on with the building
of houses for our people. It was to me
a very sad thing when I visited an ex-
Service man of this war to find his wife
and children living in a cowshed. Surely
we could utilise some of these Army huts
and tents to house people who have no
homes. When a man has to leave his
house because it is wanted for a farm
worker, where is he to go? At the present time I have four men who have
orders to leave their houses. They must
go, and they have asked me if I could
get them some shelter in these Army huts
or tents.
I have in my constituency an old-age
pensioner who has been drawing a pension
for five years, and because his son-in-law
could not get a house after being evicted
he brought the son-in-law to live with
him and his wife. Because he did so the
Ministry of Labour cut down the man's
pension, with the result that he had to
go out and do a few hours work to eke
out a living. That is most unjust and
unfair. These are some of the anomalies
which, I think, this House should adjust.
We shall probably be told that we must
follow step by step with England in these
matters, but that is not right. The
Minister should use his own discretion
and powers. There are many more things
I could refer to, but time is going on.
I only want to say this in conclusion.
The Government may rest assured that,
although we back benchers criticise, we
do so with the one object of assisting
them. They may think at times that it
is destructive criticism, but I want to
assure the Government that the back
benchers are at all times willing to assist
them in every way they can. When we
do criticise we do it because we feel it is
our duty to bring these things to the
notice of the Government. But we
never do it in any way of malice to
injure the Government.
I think the Government here would be
a good Government because. of this criticism. I think they are a good Government. As far as I am concerned, it is
my intention to help them in every way
possible when they are doing what is
right. There are a lot of complaints
that I receive, and I lay before them
suggestions. After that I leave it to
other Members of the House, and I find
their suggestions are very similar. I
think the Government should come to the
back benchers for advice, and I think it
is their duty to respond to it. I must
say the Prime Minister has always

think if all schools could boast of the

I quite agree that our prison is not a
modern one. That is one of the things
everyone, would like to see right, but it
would cost almost £300,000. The last
prison built in the British Isles was at
Edinburgh long before the war, and is a

require, but it cost £292,000. To replace
Belfast Prison would cost at least
£300,000. I think the hon. Member for
Antrim would be the first man to suggest
that £300,000 would be much better spent
on housing the people who have never
got into such an institution as the prison.
It is not practicable now, and I do not
know when it will be practicable. It is a
thing, of course, that will have to be done
at the proper and appropriate time, and
in proper priority.
There is just one other matter I wish
to deal with. The hon. Member for
South Tyrone alluded to what he styled
the Security Police. I think what was
really alluded to was watchmen employed
by our American Allies. I need not tell
the House that neither I nor the Government as a whole have the slightest control
over whoever shall be employed in that
capacity. It is true that we may be asked
as to the reliability of such-and-such a
person and a report may be given, but
the person who employs that person is by
no means bound to follow the advice that
may be given. The person who gives the
employment and makes the appointment
has the final say. I think that is a
natural enough state of affairs.

The hon. Member spoke about destroying all cows that had tuberculosis. I am
sorry to say that the incidence of tuberculosis is quite enormous, but if you
attempted to do away with all cows so
affected there would be no milk for the
people at all. You are faced with the
fact that one has to take milk from cows
that are suffering from tuberculosis-not
outward tuberculosis but tuberculosis in
the system. The remedy for all that is
clean byres, good stock and plenty of
open air.
There is only one point. Do
not build little groups of houses at one
point. Spread them all over the country
and get a general improvement. When
you get that you will have done a lot of
good.
Mr. THOMPSON: I just wanted to

We
know that the municipalities are at the

Several builders have mentioned to me

the pocket of the builder. I think it

rent. If builders are ready to go forward will the Government be prepared to
allow them to get on with the job? My
greatest difficulty in connection with the

baths. There may be some difficulty in
getting baths for a large number of

made for them to be installed later. The

into position when they become available.
I make no apology for talking about
this matter again. If the matter were
tackled and private enterprise allowed to
come in, the type of house I erected could
be built at the present time. The
material is available in Northern Ireland.
Can some steps not be taken to get into

We have heard a great deal to-day
about the farmers. I want to make a

I want to say a word to the new

have not the same facilities for our young

should like to give one example. When
a cripple in England reaches the age of
16 a grant is given in order that he or
she may be trained. No such grant is
given here until they reach the age of 18.
After they leave school they are allowed
to roam about the streets for two years.
They are then brought in under our care.
I want the age at which cripples here can
be trained to be reduced to 16, the same
as it is in England. They should be
taken care of at an earlier age than at
present. I hope the Minister will give
that matter sympathetic consideration. I
understand a Bill is to be introduced,
and I hope provision will be made to take
care of them from the age of 16.
The hon. Member for Woodvale raised

have not to do committee work, but if they

Here our reporters have to do the Senate

Then if the House of Commons in

The hon. Member for South Armagh,
at the outset of his speech, referred to the
fact that we were spending more on the
police than on our health services. He
omitted to point out that the police is a
centralised force, and that the whole cost
of the police appears in our Estimates,
whereas the health services are the responsibility of the local authorities, and
the only amounts appearing in our
Estimates are the grants we make. In
most cases these grants are limited by the
amounts spent by the local authorities
themselves, as the grants are related to
the total expenditure.
The hon. Member for South Armagh
went on to refer to post-war industry,
and drew our attention to a statement
which appeared recently in the Press,
that nine firms in Scotland proposed' to
spend £10,000,000. I think that was a
very interesting statement to come from
the hon. Member who professes to be a
Labour Member, because it is, to my
mind, a very good advertisement for the
necessity of private enterprise both now
and after the war. These nine firms are
going to spend that money of their own
volition and not by means of any Government grant or Government control. The
same Member referred to the Ulster Office
in London, and that was also referred to
by the hon. Member for Antrim. They
referred to it from slightly different
angles. The hon. Member for Antrim
seemed to suggest that the Ulster Office was
not doing any effective work. I am sure
the Prime Minister will bear me out in
saying that the Ulster Office has been of
the greatest help to him in attracting industries here. Although at present they
are war industries we hope many of them
will stay here after the war.
The hon. Member for Antrim criticised
the Ulster Office because the building was
not adequate for the purpose. It will
probably interest him to know that the
lease of that place is about to run out,
and that at the present time we are looking to see if we can find some more commodious and more suitable place. I must
take exception to the hon. Member's impression that Cockspur Street is just
back street in London. The hon. Member for Ballynafeigh referred to the question of the payment for cripples. I am
sure my right hon. Friend, the Minister
of Labour, will look into the question, and
if in fact our cripples here are not treated
on the same basis as those in Great
Britain, the situation I am satisfied will
be put right with the least possible delay.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) The hon.
Member for South Tyrone told us a
harrowing story about a child, 16 years of

11 o'clock doing her home work. The
hon. Member probably overlooked the fact

Ministry of Education there are no regulations for home work for children attending secondary schools. As I said before,

Labour.
APPEALS TRIBUNAL IN COUNTY
ARMAGH.
1. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Labour whether he will consider the question of restoring the Appeals Tribunal
under the Assistance Board to Armagh in
view of the inconvenience caused by the
present arrangements to pensioners and
others; whether he will go into this whole
question with the Assistance Board as it
affects Lurgan as well as Armagh, as the
Portadown Area Office is the centre; and
whether he will inquire into travelling
facilities for claimants from Middletown
and Markethill.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Midgley): In reply to the first and second
parts of the hon. Member's question I
am informed by the Assistance Board that
the position as regards appeals from the
three areas mentioned has not materially
altered since his previous questions on the
subject on 16th February, 1943, and 12th
October, 1943, and I would refer him to
the answers then given by my predecessor.
The matter is kept under constant
review and alternative arrangements can
be made if the number of appeals
increases sufficiently to warrant it.
As regards travelling facilities from the
two places referred to in the question, I
must point out that the curtailment of
transport affects all classes of the community at present and that during the
last three months only three appeals have
been received from each of these two
places. Cases from such districts are
arranged to be heard at such hours as
allow the appellants to return to their
homes the same evening.
Mr. AGNEW: Arising out of the
reply, will the right hon. Gentleman be
good enough to make inquiries as to the
transport facilities between Armagh, and
Markethill, and Middletown?
Mr. MIDGLEY: I have already done
so. I have the schedule of the times, and
I have been informed by the Board that
they endeavour to arrange it so that cases
from those districts will be held in time
for each applicant to get the bus when
he returns to Armagh.
Mr. AGNEW: Is it not a fact that
the Appeals Tribunal does not start until
2-30 p.m. in Portadown?
Mr. ELLIOTT: May I ask whether it
is not a fact that the only complaint the
Ministry of Labour have ever received
about the change of these courts from
Portadown elsewhere has been made by
the hon. Member for South Armagh?

Mr. AGNEW: Is it not a fact that the
Minister received a very strong protest
recently from Lurgan?
Mr. MIDGLEY: That does not arise.
With regard to the other place which does
arise on this question, I think it is only
right to mention that in three months
there have been only three appeals and
that those three appeals have been from
the one person.

workers (all grades) in view of the inadequate wages paid to such workers by

could be established joint representations
would need to be submitted to this
Ministry. I should, however, point out
that wages claims on behalf of county
council road workers employed by four of

The MINISTER OF HEALTH AND

Member that the facts, in the main, are

any
without sanitary accommodation of some

Dungannon Rural Cottage Rents.
4. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Health and Local Government whether
he will direct an inquiry into the recent
increases of rents of labourers' cottages by
Dungannon Rural District Council to
ascertain whether such increases are justified and reasonable.
The following question also stood on the
Order Paper in the name of Mr. Beattie:
5. To ask the Minister of Health and
Local Government whether he is aware
that no inquiry was made by Dungannon
Rural District Council as to the financial
position of tenants, or as to their ability
to pay increases of rent, before such increases were imposed, and whether this is
in accordance with his directions to the
council.
Mr. GRANT: With the hon. Member's
permission I should like to deal in a
single answer with the two questions
which he has asked about a recent increase
of rents of labourers' cottages in the
Dungannon rural district.
I should explain that these increases
were authorised by the Ministry of Home
Affairs before the setting up of my De- .
partment, and it will perhaps be convenient to the House if I indicate the
policy which I propose to adopt in dealing
with matters of this kind.
Before I am prepared to authorise any
rural council to increase the rents of its
labourers' cottages I shall require to be
satisfied first of all that tenants generally
in the area can afford the increased rents
and that individual cases of hardship will
be sympathetically considered by the
council; secondly, I shall require to be
satisfied that the continuance of the existing rents is unfair to the ratepayers in
the area, and, thirdly, I shall expect any
house which has been the subject of an
increased rent to be put and kept in a
reasonable state of repair.
In the light of these considerations I
have looked into the application put forward by the Dungannon Rural District
Council and am satisfied, from the information at my disposal, that the increases
authorised in that case were reasonable.
If the hon. Member is aware of any case
of real hardship I shall ask the council
to investigate it.
Mr.
BEATTIE: May I ask the
Minister if he would think it worth his
while to set up a rents tribunal for the

CLOSED MILLS.
7. Mr. AGNEW asked the Prime
Minister whether he can state the number
of mills and factories, usually engaged in
textiles, now closed in Armagh and
Keady; whether he can hold out any hope
of their reopening under his post-war
planning schemes; and whether his
Advisory Committee will soon give a report of their plans on textiles in the
post-war period.
Mr. MAGINESS: I have been asked
by my right hon. Friend to reply.
So far as I have been able to ascertain
the information requested by the hon.
Member is that during the past 10 years
two spinning mills have been closed in the
districts named. In one of these mills
other textile work is now being carried
on. No weaving factories in the district
have been closed during this period,
though one was destroyed by fire. The
owners have, however, reopened some
distance away.
With regard to the reopening of the
spinning mills, I cannot say more than that
my right hon. Friend is endeavouring in
conjunction with the representatives of
the linen industry to provide the fullest
possible scope for the maximum production in the liner industry of Northern
Ireland after the war.
The report to which the hon. Member

other
9. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he will investigate
the conditions prevailing at Downpatrick
grading station in order that better facilities will be given to the farming community; whether sufficient pens are
available; whether complaints have been
received from the Democratic Farmers'
Federation as to the checking of weights;
whether farmers have been refused admission to the station; and whether police are
on duty at this station.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Rev. Robert Moore): The Ministry has
purchased fat stock at Downpatrick since
1940 and the facilities for doing so have
proved satisfactory. Complaints of a
general nature have been made recently
by a newly-formed body called the
Democratic Farmers' Federation of whose
activities or right to speak on behalf of
farmers I know nothing. The Ministry's
attitude with regard to all purchasing
centres is that if farmers want refinements
introduced above the standard ordinarily
considered necessary by my Ministry, they
must arrange for these refinements to be
carried out by the owners of the purchasing centres. My Ministry is not responsible for the provision of purchasing
centres, but merely uses those in existence
and has only asked the owners to carry
out improvements considered essential for
the better working of centres in the
interests of farmers as well as the
Ministry.
Mr. AGNEW: Arising out of that
reply is the Minister prepared to listen to
complaints from all legitimate organisations?
Rev. ROBERT MOORE: I always
have done so.
Mr. ELLIOTT: May I ask whether
the hon. Member for South Armagh is
speaking for the Democratic Farmers'
Federation?
Mr. AGNEW: I am speaking for
South Tyrone.

answer is he prepared to recognise all

has now been established and is here to
stay, and whether he is aware that it is
prepared to play its part in the organised
state of society after the war, and in view
of that will he now say he is prepared to
receive that Federation on the same basis
as the Ulster Farmers' Union?

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
PENSIONS (INCREASE) BILL.
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE
(Major Sinclair): The provisions of the
1737 Pensions (Increase) Bill-

25 JULY 1944
Second Reading

Bill which I now submit to the House
follow in the main those of the Pensions
(Increase) Act which was recently passed.
by the Imperial Parliament.
The Bill proposes, with effect from the
1st January last, to increase within
certain limits pensions which have been
already granted, which may be
or
awarded up to the end of next year, to
State pensioners and pensioned servants
of local authorities. The memorandum
which prefaces the Bill will, I hope, have
assisted hon. Members to grasp the main
features of the Measure, but it is
necessary to say something of
of the
principles on which its provisions are
based.
The Bill provides for two schemes,
identical with those contained in the
Imperial Act. The first is intended to
cover pensioners of slender means whose
resources have been strained through the
rise in prices brought about by war-time
conditions. These persons cannot claim
as of right that their pensions should be
increased, but the Government and the
local authorities of the Province, whose
views were sought in the matter, think
that there is a moral obligation to hold
out a helping hand to those who, after
retirement from the service of the public,
find that their small incomes, measured
by pre-war standards, have shrunk, and
that their circumstances are such as to
make it difficult for them to redress the
balance by any effort of their own.
The purpose of the scheme is thus to
alleviate hardship, and it is with that
purpose in mind that the scale of increases set out in the Second Schedule to
the Bill has been framed. Married
pensioners, or pensioners with a dependant, will be eligible for an increase of
30 per cent. on pensions up to £100 per
annum, 25 per cent. on pensions between
£100 and £200, and 20 per cent. on
pensions over £200. For other pensioners
a pension not exceeding £75 will qualify
for an increase of 30 per cent., a pension
between £75 and £150 for an increase of
25 per cent., and a pension over £150 for
one of 20 per cent. These increases will
be subject to an over-riding income limit
which has been fixed at £300 a year if
the pensioner is married or has at least.
one dependant, and at £225 a year in
other cases; though in the assessment of
means the first, £52 a year of any income
other than the pension or pensions on
which increases under the Bill are calculated will be disregarded.
The other qualifying conditions are set
out in Clause 1. In general, a pensioner
must either have attained the age of 60
or have been retired on health grounds,
or have become unable through infirmity
to engage in any regular full-time employment, or if a woman, be supporting
at least one dependant. A widow receiving a pension in respect of her
husband's services will be eligible for an
increase if she has reached the age of 40,
or has a dependant, or is disabled by
physical or mental infirmity.
Considerations of another kind than
those which underlie the first scheme
apply to the second, which covers those
civil servants who have gone out on pension since February, 1922. From that
time
up to 1934 the pensions of these
persons contained a
variable element
which rose and fell within the upper limit
of the cost-of-living figure ruling at the
time of their superannuation. In 1934,
however, pensions as well as salaries were
stabilised at a cost-of-living figure of 155,
and pensions have been paid on that
basis since, though the present cost-ofliving figure stands at 200.
For the large majority of serving officers
the war-time increase in the cost of living has been recognised by the award of
bonuses of varying amount, the first being
given in 1940; and the few pensioners
who have retired from our service since
that date are now participating in those
awards as a result of the recent decision
that bonus is to be regarded, with retrospective effect, as a pensionable emolument. Owing, however, to the statutory
requirement that pensions shall be calculated on the average pay of the three
years immediately before retirement, the
concession to which I have just referred
has had a very small financial effect; and
there remain the earlier pensioners for
whom nothing has as yet been done.
When pay and pensions were stabilised,
there was no anticipation that a universal
war would within a few years completely
upset economic conditions; and as there
have been adjustments on that account in
the pay of civil servants in post, there is
a strong case, on equitable if not on legal
grounds, for making adjustments in the
pensions of civil servants who have retired.
There is, moreover, a further point: this
Pensions (Increase) Bill- HOUSE OF COMMONS
Second Reading
[Major Sinclair]
is, that the benefits of the Imperial Act
are accorded to existing Irish officers,
many of whom, as the House knows, came.
into the service of Northern Ireland when
our Government was set up. The pensions of these officers, as they retire, are
paid out of Imperial funds, in accordance
with the special provisions of the Government of Ireland Act, 1920, and hon.
Members will, I am sure, readily agree
that it would be at least illogical if we
did not provide for similar benefits for
those of our officers who entered the service since the establishment of the Northern Ireland Government and have been
working side by side with the existing
Irish officers. This is particularly so
since the pensions in both cases are ultimately a charge on Northern Ireland
funds.
It is accordingly proposed to increase
Civil Service pensions up to £400 a year
by 10 per cent.; those between £400 and
£600 a year by 7 per cent.; and those
over £600 a year by such an amount as
will bring the pension up to £645. There
is to be no increase for pensions in excess
of £645, this upper limit having been
fixed broadly in relation to the limit at
which the war bonus for serving officers
ceases to be payable.
Pensioners qualifying for the benefits
of this scheme who would be eligible for
an increase under the scheme proposed in
Clause 1 will, of course, be dealt with
under whichever scheme is the more
favourable to them.
Two further provisions which have a
limiting effect on both schemes alike remain to be noticed. The first of these is
contained in Clause 3 (2) and is designed
to ensure that there shall be no inequality
of treatment as between one pensioner
and another by reason of the fact that
some may have already received increases
in their pensions because their pensionable emoluments included a war bonus or
any similar allowance in recognition of
the rise in prices due to the present war.
Such additions to pension will, therefore,
be taken into account in arriving at the
amount of increases allowable under the
Bill; but no account will be taken for this
purpose of any increases given under the
earlier Pensions (Increase) Acts.
The second limitation arises from the
aggregation of pensions in the relatively
few cases where more than one is enjoyed
by the same person, the object being to
ensure that for the purpose of the ceiling
and of determining the percentage increase such a person will not be treated
more favourably because he has two pensions than he would be if he had only one
of the same amount. The relevant provisions are to be found in Clause 6 and
paragraph 7 of the Second Schedule, and
may be illustrated by a simple example
under Clause 1. I will take the case of
an ex-policeman who enjoys a pension
from Imperial Funds in respect of service
in the Royal Irish Constabulary and one
from Northern Ireland Funds for subsequent service in the Royal Ulster Constabulary. Let us suppose that he is a
married man with no other resources, and
that the first pension amounts to £140 a
year and the second to £80 a year. If.
these pensions were dealt with separately,
he would be given an increase of 25 per
cent. on the first and 30 per cent. on the
second, amounting to £35 and £24 respectively, or £59 in all. When, however,
the pensions are aggregated, they attract
an increase of 20 per cent. only, representing a total increase of £45, of which
only £10, being the over-plus on the
Imperial award, falls to be paid from
Northern Ireland Funds. For similar
reasons, paragraphs 6 and 9 of the Second
Schedule provide for aggregation in cases
where a husband and wife, or a widow and
dependant, are each in receipt of a pension.
It will be noted, however, from paragraph
8 of that Schedule that the principle of
aggregation will not apply to pensions
awarded on account of death or disablement attributable to service in H.M.
Forces. The other provisions of the Bill
deal with matters of administrative detail.
I beg to move.
Question proposed: "That the Bill be
now read a Second time."

when this most vicious test was to be

lump sum to Northern Ireland teachers

Gentleman. Those two types of men
have to live. Because one happens to

less than they cost the higher paid official.
Let the Minister mete out justice to all
and make the increase a uniform one. It
will require every penny he can give to
enable these people to meet the increased
cost of living.
Those civil servants who retired since
1922 that is within the life of this Government—but who did not give full service to this Government-part of it was
given to the Imperial Government-and

without any means test being applied.
Their pensions are to be increased according to the rise in the cost of living. It
would appear that the cost-of-living figure

up to £600 a year receive such preferential treatment? There is the whole matter
in a nutshell.
A similar Bill has been passed in Great
Britain, and the democratic representatives were in agreement in regard to one
fundamental principle that there should
not be any preferential treatment, and
that the lower paid pensioners should
have a higher increase in order that they
might be able to live in the decency and
comfort to which they are entitled. By
bringing in this preferential treatment
Clause the Minister wants to keep in
step with Great Britain. All things

all things are not equal. Just recently

to the teachers in Great Britain under
the terms of the lump sum agreement.
Teachers here only receive 50 per cent.
of their service prior to 1922, whilst those
in Britain receive 100 per cent. That

If

Major SINCLAIR (by permission of
the House): Several hon. Members have
taken part in the debate on this Bill,
but in practically every case they have
covered more or less the same ground.
I propose to reply to them in globo
rather than to go through each hon.
Member's speech in detail. In the first
place, I would like. to point out to the
House that this Bill deals with pensions
as they are, and has nothing to do with
any change in the basic rates of pensions.
It is a question of increasing pensions
that are now being paid, and the Bill has
nothing whatever to do with rates of
pensions, and still less with teachers'
salaries, to which one hon. Member for
the University referred. While I have
taken a note, of what hon. Members have
said, I want to put the Bill in its proper
perspective.
The object of the Bill is the removal of
hardship. It is not intended to be a Bill
to increase pensions as such; it is merely
to remove hardships. The Member for
the University (Dr. Lyle) remarked that
these pensions were in fact deferred payments for services rendered, and as such
they did not take into account the private income of the individual concerned.
But neither did they take any account
whatever of what the cost of living might
be at a future date. The Government
consider that there is no legal obligation
on them, or on local authorities, to increase pensions because the cost of living
has risen, but they do feel there is a
moral obligation on them to meet and to
alleviate if they can cases of real and
severe hardship.
Several hon. Members spoke about this
question of the means test. I entirely
agree with those who said that in the
ordinary way it was iniquitous that a
man who has saved to make provision
for his old age should be penalised, but
in this connection again I want to refer
to the object of this Bill, the relief of
hardship, and it is for that reason that
these pensions are based on the total
income of the recipient. As I have
already said, the maximum pension
eligible for increase in the case of a
married man with at least one dependant is £300 per annum, but under the
Bill the first £52 of his income is being
ignored, so that the maximum amount
which will qualify for an increase in
pension must not exceed £352. In the
case of an unmarried man the figure is
£225, to which we add £52, giving a
total maximum pension of £277. It is
only for that reason that there is any suggestion of finding out the maximum
income of the recipient-simply because
it is a case of relieving hardship.
The hon. Member for the University
asked whether poor law
(Dr. Lyle) asked
medical officers would be covered by this
Bill, and I am glad to give him an assurance that they will.
Dr. LYLE: Thank you.
Major SINCLAIR: Reference was
made to the fact that the second part
of the Bill dealing with civil servants
carries these proposals through on a somewhat different basis. As I said at the
beginning, the pensions for ordinary
classes of pensioners are not in any way
based on the cost of living. At one time
Civil Service pensions were put into a
somewhat different category, because they
were not in effect based on the then cost
of living. The reason why there is a
different method of treatment now is for
the purpose of removing what has been
a grievance. Civil servants retired at a
certain date with their pensions stabilised
at that date's cost of living were losing
on the transaction now when the cost of
living has risen. If we were going to
restore that cut in full it would be a
considerably higher percentage increase
than is proposed.
Following out the general principle of
the Bill the percentage increase of Civil
Service pensions varies. As the pension
rises the percentage increase becomes
smaller. That is exactly the same as in
Part One of the Bill, in which the percentage increase rises as the income
Drainage Act, 1942

Drainage Act, 1942

becomes smaller. That is the general

The idea in the first place was to look

The basis of the increase is the percentage increase in the cost of living since
the beginning of the present war.

Mr. LOWRY: I beg to move,
That the Order made by the Minister
of Home Affairs on the 3rd day of July,
1944, with the consent of the Minister of
Finance, under sub-section (3) of section
two of the Drainage Act (Northern
Ireland), 1942, postponing the date prescribed under the said sub-section beyond
which grants towards any expenditure incurred by a county council shall not be
made, be hereby confirmed.
This Motion is necessary under Section
2, sub-section (3) of the Drainage Act,
1942. For the convenience of hon.
Members I shall read the sub-section in
question :
Grants shall be made under this
section towards any expenditure incurred by a county council after the
prescribed date which, subject as hereinafter provided, shall be the thirtyfirst day of October, nineteen hundred
and forty four:
Provided that the prescribed date
may be postponed for not more than
two successive periods of one year each
by orders made by the Minister of
Home Affairs with the consent of the
Minister of Finance and confirmed by
a Resolution of each House of Parliament.
Pursuant to that, I made an Order with
the consent of the Minister of Finance
extending the period for one year in the
following circumstances. Under this Act
up to the present twelve schemes have
been completed or are in process of completion, involving the reclamation of
8,420 acres for food cultivation. The
cost of these schemes to date is £144,963,
and the amount of State grant earned is
£106,649. In addition to these schemes,
preliminary steps have been taken for the
inauguration of ten further schemes.
Owing to the limited engineering staff
and a restricted amount of mechanical
equipment, it would be physically impossible to complete all these schemes
before the 31st October next, the last day
on which expenditure on schemes can
qualify for State grant. Consequently,
under these circumstances it is necessary
to have this Order confirmed by a Resolution of both Houses. I am perfectly
confident in the circumstances, and considering the object of the grant, that the
confirmation of the Order will commend
itself to every Member of the House.

fighting to have that standard maintained
when the war is over. I wish to supplement what I have said by stating that in
regard to this extension for one year an
appeal has been made by the hon. Member
for another year's extension. In my
opinion this piecemeal legislation of
palliatives will never bring stability to
any industry. The farming community
will have to be made aware of the conditions under which they live. They do not
enter into this industry for a year or two.
When they do enter it the prospects are
that they spend their lives in the industry.
The greater part of their lives has been
fighting and asking the Government to
give them help towards building up an
industry which the country cannot do
without.
I am prepared to support the hon.
Member if he would appeal for the
placing on the Statute Book as a permanent fixture of a Bill giving the farming
industry the right to be protected by the
Government financially and otherwise. If
anything taught us the necessity for keeping intact that industry it is the war.
This industry should, in my opinion,
have first priority. It is the key industry
in the life of the nation. These petty
appeals and expressions of thanks for
kindness of right hon. Gentlemen should
not be made. I am not a farmer or the
son of a farmer.

Mr. MINFORD: I thought you were.
in
Mr .BEATTIE: Perhaps in the distant past I had some ancestor who was
engaged in farming in County Antrim,
the home of the United Irishmen. I
think the town of Antrim was the most
rebellious town in Antrim. I do not like
these little extensions. I say it is necessary and important that the land should
be drained and properly equipped
every direction for the benefit of the
crops it produces. We cannot do without
farming. We cannot have the crops
spoiled by flooding. I sat on a Drainage
Committee set up by this House, which
dealt with the whole question of the
drainage of agricultural land. The report
of that Committee should be taken as a
text book and a scheme, devised whereby
the Government would place on
Statute Book something that would prove
beneficial and helpful by keeping the land
preserved from flooding. I support the
Member for Antrim, but not in his expression of thanks. Thanks should not
be returned to the Government for anything they are doing for the farmers.
Anything they are doing they are compelled to do by public opinion. It is not.
because of kindness, generosity, foresight
or charitable disposition that this extension is brought in by the Government.
It is because the Government are driven
to it.
the
Mr. McGURK: I was very glad to hear

behalf of the farmers. It came as a surprise to me. I agree with the policy he

Mr. LOWRY (by permission of the
House) I should like to correct one or
two misapprehensions. The Act of 1942
was passed to carry out one of the recommendations of the last Drainage Committee that sat, and the first section of
that Act shows clearly that it is an
emergency provision to increase the land
available for cultivation during the
present emergency. It in no way takes
away from the power of county councils
under the previous Drainage Acts. It is
only a supplemental provision, and the
reason is a perfectly obvious one-in
order to encourage people to do this work
during the emergency. The provision
in no way takes away from existing
powers. It is an emergency Measure. It
is not introduced because the Government is driven by public opinion to do it.
It is simply carrying out the provision in
the Act of 1942.

Ballycastle Fishermen.
7. Mr. AGNEW
are
asked the Prime
Minister whether he is aware of the indignation amongst Ballycastle fishermen
regarding the present system in operation;
whether he can explain why fish were
dumped into the sea recently; whether
any representative of his Department was
present when these fish were dumped;
what class of fish were dumped; and
whether he will set up an inquiry into the
fishing conditions at Ballycastle to ensure
that this industry is maintained and a
market found and thereby stop this dumping.
Mr. MIDGLEY: The same conditions
apply to this reply as to the last. The
system to which the hon. Member refers
is presumably the arrangement made by
the Ministry of Food and known as the
Allocation Scheme, whereunder fish
landed at a particular port must be distributed in specified proportions amongst
the normal pre-war wholesale buyers at
that port on all occasions when the price
of the fish reaches the maximum
scribed by the Price Control Order. This
system operates throughout the whole of
the United Kingdom and I am not aware
that it has caused any indignation
amongst Ballycastle fishermen in particular.
pre-
As regards the dumping of fish at
Ballycastle I understand, as I have already
informed the hon. Member in reply to a
written inquiry on the point, that on a
recent occasion the local buyers declined
to accept a quantity of dog-fish owing to
the inability of their London customers
to dispose of the fish at that particular
time. Dog-fish have always been unsaleable within Northern Ireland itself, and
although one of the fishermen concerned
on the occasion in question did, in fact,
attempt to dispose of his catch locally the
other fishermen similarly situated decided
to dump their catch. No officer of the
Ministry of Commerce was present at the
time.
My Ministry is keeping in close touch
with the situation, but it is obvious that
no inquiry such as the hon. Member suggests would be able either to restore the
London market for this class of fish or
create a local market for a class of fish
which the producers have hitherto not
been able to sell for local consumption.

VENEREAL DISEASE IN ARMAGH
JAIL.
9. Dr. LYLE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs what is the percentage of
the prisoners in Armagh Jail last year
who were suffering from venereal diseases;
was adequate treatment given; were those
affected isolated from the other prisoners,
and, if not, what steps were taken to
prevent the infection to unaffected persons.
Major SINCLAIR: In the unavoidable
absence of my right hon. Friend, I have
been asked to read replies to the questions
addressed to him. Two point five per
cent. of the 476 prisoners committed to
Armagh Jail last year were suffering from
venereal disease, and all of the 12
prisoners concerned received adequate
treatment from the prison medical officer.
In one particularly bad case the prisoner
was transferred to an outside hospital for
treatment. On the discharge of the
prisoners a note of the treatment carried
out is given to the prisoner for the infor-
Imation of her own doctor or V.D. clinic.
The prison rule for dealing with infectious diseases is as follows:-
"The Medical Officer shall give
directions in writing for separating
from the other prisoners any prisoner
suffering from any infectious, contagious or mental disease or suspected
thereof and shall immediately take
such steps as may be necessary to prevent the spread of any contagious or
infectious disease."
This rule is strictly observed in all prisons
in Northern Ireland, and separate baths
and clothing are kept for affected cases.
Dr. LYLE: Are the utensils used for
feeding the affected persons kept separate
from those that are used by other
prisoners not affected?
ALLEGED MALTREATMENT IN
BELFAST PRISON.
10. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he will investigate conditions prevailing in H.M.
Prison, Belfast; whether it is a fact that
on certain dates between October, 1943,
and June, 1944, the following prisoners
were man-handled by prison officers:
James Steele, Samuel Holden, and Daniel
Rooney-and whether he is prepared to set
up a Commission to inquire into these
allegations so that those who have complaints of maltreatment may be heard.
Major SINCLAIR: I am quite satisfied
that the conditions prevailing in H.M.
Prison, Belfast, do not call for any
special investigation. There is no foundation whatever for the allegation that
prisoners were man-handled by prison
officers during the past nine months.
Prisoners must conform to the prison
regulations and any breaches of these
regulations must be punished.
During the period referred to, the
prisoners named were guilty of breaches
of the regulations as follows:-
Steele-Refusing to wear prison clothing and to be searched;
Holden-Idling at work;
Rooney-Assaulting another prisoner
during association;
and for these breaches the prisoners were
suitably punished.
There is a Board of Visitors for the
convict wing of the prison, and all convicts have the right of appearing before
this Board which meets each month, if
they wish to have any complaints investigated. In view of this I am not prepared
to set up
a special Commission
suggested.

does not exceed such limit as may be

1938, the National School Teachers

Act as applied by an Order in Council,

Major SINCLAIR: In moving this
Resolution I wish to take the opportunity
of telling hon. Members the probable
financial effect of the provisions of the
Pensions (Increase) Bill which is at present before the House. The Resolution,
of course, deals only with those pensions
which are payable out of the Exchequer,
and it is estimated that the extra cost to
be borne on public funds will be about
£62,450 per annum. Of this £62,450,
teachers' pensions are responsible for by
far the greater part, their share being
£54,000, while increases in police pensions
will account for £6,000, and Civil Service
pensions £2,000. This estimate does not,
however, include the cost of fire brigade
pensions, which are normally payable by
local authorities but are payable directly
from the Exchequer while the Fire
Services (Emergency Provisions) Act
(N.I.), 1942, remains in force.
Though, as I have said, the Resolution
is only concerned with those pensions
payable from the Exchequer, it may not
be out of place if I indicate the probable
cost to be borne by local authorities under
the Bill. In their case, it is estimated
that the total increases in pensions will
not exceed £21,000 in all, including
£1,500 for fire brigade pensions. In the
case of Belfast and Londonderry this will
mean an extra ld on the rates, and elsewhere it is thought that an extra d will
be sufficient. I beg to move.
Question put, and agreed to.
Resolution reported and agreed to.

Major SINCLAIR: In reply to the

I explained why a means test was introduced. It is not a means test in the proper

hon. Member has described it, does not
take into account the income of members

The following question stood on the
the

whether he can state if the English

education authorities in England and

heating and cleaning the elementary
voluntary schools under managerial
control, and will also defray the indoor

of outdoor repairs will henceforth be
borne by the British Exchequer ;
whether in Northern Ireland no public
help is available for the repairs of
managerial voluntary schools, and
whether only one half of the cost of
lighting, heating and cleaning such

Bill"
should now be "Education Act?''
When the questions were handed in the
It
Bill was in progress across the water.
is now an Act of Parliament.
Lieut.-Colonel HALL-THOMPSON:
The answer to this question is extremely
long, and I propose to circulate it in the
Official Report. The hon. and learned
Member has kindly consented.
The following is the reply:
Under legislation prior to the new Act
there were two classes of public
elementary schools in England and

Wales-
(i) schools provided by the local
education authority;
(ii) schools not provided by the local
education authority.
Schools of this second class were
usually referred to as non-provided
schools and would be called voluntary
schools in Northern Ireland. Every nonprovided school (or group of non-provided schools) was under the management
of a school committee, two-thirds of
whose members were appointed in accordance with the trust deeds of the school
or schools and one-third by the education
authority. There is, therefore, no such
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
10 AUGUST 1944

1.
thing in England and Wales
as a
voluntary school under the management
of an individual manager; every voluntary
school was managed by what in Northern
Ireland would be called a four-and-two
committee.
Under the provisions of the new Act
public elementary schools will cease to
exist and be replaced by primary schools
for the younger pupils and secondary
schools for the older ones. The old
terminology of provided and non-provided is also abolished. In future there
will be two main classes of both primary
and secondary schools-
(i) "County" schools (i.e. provided
schools).
(ii) "Voluntary" schools (i.e. nonprovided schools). In the Bill as
originally drafted these schools were
named "auxiliary" schools, but in
its passage through Parliament the
designation was altered by amendment to "voluntary" schools.
"Voluntary" schools will be further
sub-divided into three categories—
(a) Aided Schools: One-third of whose
management committee or body of
governors will be appointed by the
education authority and two-thirds
(the foundation managers or
governors) in accordance with the
trust deed of the school concerned.
In these schools the appointment of
teachers will remain with the body of
managers or governors. The full cost of
lighting, heating and cleansing, of indoor
repairs and of the upkeep of the playgrounds will be borne by the local education authority; half of the cost of outdoor
repairs to the school buildings will be
borne by the Exchequer and half by the
managers.
(b) Controlled Schools: Two-thirds of
whose management committee or
board of governors will be ap
pointed by the education authority
and one-thrd (the foundation
managers or governors) in accordance with the trust deed of the
school concerned.
The appointment of teachers in these
schools will pass to the education authority
save in so far as in schools with more
than two teachers one-fifth of the staff
may be "reserved" teachers specifically
appointed after consultation with the
foundation managers for the purpose of
giving religious instruction in accordance
with the trust deeds of the school. Full
financial responsibility for the indoor and
outdoor upkeep of these schools and their
playgrounds will pass to the education
authority.
(c) Special Agreement Schools:
A
to
small class of schools in the case of
which an application was made
under the Education Act, 1936,
the local education authority for a
grant (50 per cent. to 75 per cent.)
of the cost of alterations and buildings necessary for senior pupils.
This category need not be considered in detail as it has been
created to meet a special difficulty
arising out of the 1936 Act for
which there will be no parallel in
Northern Ireland.
In Northern Ireland, if a public elementary school is vested in the Ministry, it is
kept in repair at the expense of the
Exchequer. If it is not so vested it must
it must be kept in repair at the expense
of the manager, unless it is placed under
a four-and-two committee. Only one-half
of the cost of lighting, heating and cleaning a public elementary school can be met
from public funds (i.e., by the local
education authority) and this percentage
remains the same whether or not the
school is managed by a four-and-two committee.

GRANT FOR ALTERATIONS AND

4. Mr. THOMAS CAMPBELL asked
the Minister of Education whether he can
state if it is a fact that the Education
Bill in England provides that the
managers of elementary voluntary schools
will for the first time receive from the
English Ministry of Education a grant of
50 per cent. towards the cost of any alterations or improvements which may be
required to the schools; whether this grant
will apply also to substituted schools
where a school has been transferred to a
new site from specified causes; and
whether the Bill provides that the
Minister can authorise local authorities
to provide temporary additional accommodation for the children in such schools
if alterations are difficult through war
conditions and that the entire cost is to
be met from public funds so long as the
temporary period lasts.
Lieut.-Colonel
HALL-THOMPSON:
The hon. and learned Member is referred
to the reply given to question No. 2. The
English Act provides that aided schools
will receive a grant of 50 per cent. of
the cost of new buildings and alterations
from the Exchequer. No similar grants
were available under previous legislation
for non-provided public elementary
schools. Under certain conditions an
aided school may be transferred to a new
site and the 50 per cent. grant will be
available for the re-erection of the school
on the new site, or alternatively the grant
may be made available for the erection
of a new aided school to replace one or
more existing aided schools. The full cost
of erecting a new controlled school will
be borne by the education authority so
that the question of an Exchequer grant
to the body of managers or governors will
not arise in the case of these schools.
A general duty is placed upon local
education authorities to provide education
for all children in their area, but I cannot find any express provision in the Act
under which they can be authorised by
the Minister to provide, at a cost entirely
met from public funds, temporary additional accommodation for children in
voluntary schools where alterations are
difficult because of war conditions.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Do the Catholic
elementary pupils in England form only
about 6 per cent. of the elementary pupils
there, and do the Catholic elementary
pupils in our area form 37.77 per cent.
of the elementary pupils here.

right hon. Gentleman's reply, may I ask

payable for the lighting and heating of
schools in Northern Ireland under Roman
Catholic management are obtainable on
the very same conditions as apply to
schools under Protestant management.
Lieut.-Colonel HALL-THOMPSON:
The answer is in the affirmative.
