ORAL ANSWER TO
QUESTION.
Internees in Belfast Prison.
Mr. THOMAS CAMPBELL (by
private notice) asked the Minister of
Home Affairs if conditions affecting internees in Belfast Prison have become
more rigid during the last fortnight; if
the food rations of a number have been
sharply cut; if they have been denied
cigarettes from relatives; and if thirty of
them are without clothing coupons and
have only very far worn-out clothes.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Mr. Lowry): The internees in Belfast
Prison have recently refused to clean or
sweep the dining-hall wards, and exercise
yards as they are obliged to do under the
Regulations. Accordingly, in accordance
with these Regulations, certain privileges
-in fact the majority of their privileges,
as, for example, the receipt of cigarettes
from their relatives-have been suspended, and I may inform the hon. and
learned Member that this suspension will
be continued until such time as the internees behave as the Regulations call
upon them to behave.
This punishment does not include any
reduction whatever of the ordinary
dietary prepared for internees, and the
dietary for this class of person in Belfast
Prison is in no way inferior to that which
they received while in Londonderry
Prison. The two dietaries are, in fact,
almost identical.
In regard to clothing coupons, the internees receive the full number of clothing coupons to which they are entitled.
Some of these persons are holders of temporary identity cards, and, as the hon.
and learned Member is no doubt aware,
holders of temporary identity cards receive their clothing coupons in a different
manner from persons who have permanent
Oral Answer
•
19 SEPTEMBER 1944
Housing Policy

-
identity cards, and this may result in the
holders of temporary identity cardswhether in prison or not finding
difficulty from time to time in providing
themselves with suitable clothing. In the
case of internees, if their clothing is for
this or any other reason inadequate, they
are provided with prison clothing of the
type and colour provided for prisoners
awaiting trial.
Mr. CAMPBELL: May I ask was the
refusal to which he refers, the cessation
of work in certain departments, in the
nature of a protest against the humiliation which it was felt was being put on
these men with temporary cards whose
relatives in the absence of those cards
cannot replace tattered clothes and the
Government will not replace them?
Mr. LOWRY: No, sir. That was not
the reason. The reason for the disobedience of the Regulations was this.
In the first instance a person styling himself commandant wanted to interview the
governor on behalf of the rest of the
internees. That is a system that could
not be recognised, but any separate internee can make his own complaint and
will be interviewed. As a matter of fact
137 were interviewed.
Mr CAMPBELL: May I ask the Prime
Minister if all visits to internees by
relatives have been forbidden and does he
know that the time has arrived in the case
of men suffering five years' internment
without trial when their release should be
ordered.
Mr LOWRY: As I have indicated
already in my answer the bulk of the
privileges for all I know at the moment,
all of them-have been suspended, which
would include receipt of letters, visits
from relatives, cigarettes and matters of
that sort, and as I have indicated that
system will be continued until they conform to the prison Regulations
Mr. CAMPBELL: The right hon.
Gentleman does not want these men to
wear criminal dress?
Mr. LOWRY: I do not expect them to
wear criminal dress, but adequate clothing will be provided, clothing given to
prisoners awaiting trial. If they prefer
to remain without any clothes that is
their own business.
Mr. AGNEW: Is it a fact that the
majority of these men are untried
prisoners, and that no charge has been
made against them?
Mr. LOWRY: These men are interned.
They are untried.
Mr. AGNEW: That is what I wanted
to know. That is justice?

Mr. NIXON: The war news is good
since we met before. That is one thing
we are all proud of. I also got pneu-

monia over me since I was here before.
If I am to show that I am recovered I may
as well set about doing so now.
I gave
the Minister of No-housing and Poor
Health notice this morning that I would
raise the question on the Adjournment.
Although I like him, strictly speaking, I
should not have given notice, because he
gathered about 60 people, I think, in the
Labour Exchange on about the 25th
August, 1944, and he made a statement
on his housing policy to them, a statement that he might very well have made
to this House. I think this is the first
place to make any statement on important policy. But I presume the
Minister took it for granted that whatever he would say would get the support
of the House.
Well, if we are to judge his policy by
his actions he will not get very far. I
think it is a ten-years policy. He intends to stay in a long time evidently.
Now the housing estate that has been
purchased is up beside me, and I pass
it every day and every time I have been
talking to you here I have told you they
were surveying, and they are still surveying. I had a look at it yesterday and
instead of surveying there were four of
them walking like this. The public will
have to pay for all this. Making all due
allowances for the shortage of material,
it is a remarkable fact that the hon.
Member for Ballynafeigh (Mr. Thompson)
after almost begging for permission to
build obtained it, and in about a month
or six weeks he had without any subsidy
built two houses similar to those that are
going to be erected.
I know that if the right hon. Gentleman
goes on the way he is going there will
never be anything done. There are huts
belonging to the Government in which
these unfortunate people who are without
houses could be accommodated, but they
will not get them. The Government
prefer to keep those huts idle. When
the refugees from Gibraltar came along
they could get into the huts. I saw a
beautiful photograph of the Minister with
them in the huts, but I do not think they
are very thankful to him when all is said
and done, even though he got his photograph taken with them. No constituency
in Northern Ireland suffered more war
damage than the constituency represented
by the right hon. Gentleman. I do not
want to press the Government to build
houses with timber when they cannot get
it, I am not such a fool as to take advantage of the present situation to do
that but I know there is any amount of
accommodation that can be made available for those people who have the first
claim on it.
There have been numbers of military
huts vacated which, I am glad to say,
will never again be occupied by the
military. There will never be the occasion
to occupy them. There are hundreds and
hundreds of them, yet you will get a
whole family in one room in a small house
in Belfast. All we get are long speeches
and reports from various committees. I
could not tell how many committees are
reporting on housing, but a lot of them
forget altogether about finance. I myself
went to a meeting at which a few clergymen gave lectures on housing. They were
more concerned with big parks, and they
never told the people that those parks
would cost money and that it would come
out of their pockets, because all municipal
expenditure is put on the rates and added
to the rents of the people in workingclass houses. That is one thing a lot of
the advisers seem to forget, good, bad,
and indifferent.
The Minister may be pleased with his
ten years' plan. Some parts of it please
everybody, and some parts do not. A.
great many people do not understand the
Trust operating on money provided by
Parliament and by the municipal authorities. I think that but for the fact that
the Minister did not like to use the
expression he would have called it a
Board, something like the Electricity
Board, or-
Mr. AGNEW: The Pigs Board.
Mr. NIXON- -some of those other
Boards. He told us that the members of
the Trust would receive no payment. We
might have had more confidence in his
word in that respect if he had not told
us in this House that the Commander of
the National Fire Service would receive
no payment. That was the first story the
right hon. Gentleman told us; the next
story he told us was that the Commander was getting £800, and then he
told us that he had been persuaded to
take £1,000. I do not know how much
he has now. I have my own opinion
about whether the Trust will be paid or

not. I am quite certain they will have

There is another thing I wish to say to

That Bill will automatically expire in

There has been enough damage done.
Get on with the war until Parliament

that nothing contentious would be

All I can say is that I do not want

because you happen to know them.

never built a house in my life, and I

If you are only going on holiday,

Mr. GRANT: I will try to get a satisfactory

Mr. AGNEW: I have one down.
Mr. GRANT: If there is a question
put down for the next day it is hardly
fair to raise the matter now. However,
we will pass that. The Member for Woodvale raised a very important point. He
is perfectly right in stating that I
discussed this question of housing policy
with people outside the House before I
discussed it with Members of the House.
I want to accept responsibility for that.
In ordinary circumstances I would not do
anything of the sort, but during the last
four or five meetings of the House,
Members on both sides of the House
repeatedly urged me I do not require
any pressure-to do something about this
alarming situation at the earliest possible
opportunity. It is an alarming situation,
and nobody realises it more than I do.
There is no one working harder than I
am to arrive at some solution of the
problem. I believe I have the sympathy
of Members on all sides in my effort to
try to get something done about this allimportant question, but I have largely
to depend for co-operation in connection
with housing in Northern Ireland on the
representatives of the local authorities.
The local authorities have a responsibility as well as the Government for
providing housing accommodation. I
thought I would take a chance and call
these people together and explain the
ideas I had in my mind on this question
and ask for their co-operation. I want to
remind hon. Members that when other
Ministers introduced legislation into the
House almost the first question they were
asked by Members was, "Have you ever
consulted the people who are concerned
with this legislation?" The Minister of
Agriculture has been time and again
criticised by Members for not taking the
farmers into his confidence when introducing legislation. With all that
experience behind me I thought I was
safe in this particular case in asking the
local authorities to work in co-operation
with me on this all-important question
and see if I could secure their sympathy.
The Member for Woodvale says rightly
that we have been reading reports and
making speeches and nothing has been
done. It is because I am tired of speeches,
which do not bring us any nearer to

securing the object we have in view,

Mr. GRANT: I never said that. What

statements made in connection with

question of selling houses would introduce
bad workmanship.. The statement I
made in that connection was with reference to the lump sum subsidy. In spite
of all outside interference and antagonism I am trying to formulate proposals
which I will put before the House at the
earliest possible opportunity. I want to
get something into operation immediately
that will provide if not permanent accommodation certainly temporary accommodation for our people.
I wonder if hon. Members who criticise
me much on this particular subject have
the same painful experience as I have in
meeting women with children at their feet
who come to Stormont or to where I live
crying that they cannot get homes of any
sort. There are women with seven or
eight children huddled in one room. If
they had that experience I think they
would be less lavish in their criticism and
would come along and say, "Anything
we can do to help you we will do it."
There are a lot of people doing that. They
are serious and their intentions are good.
Other people are wishing me well and are
then going out to do all the harm they
can to prevent my getting ahead with the
scheme I am determined to put before
the House which will have to accept the
responsibility of turning down my proposals.

by reason of the fact that it has not been
primarily taken into confidence by the
Minister in regard to such an important
step as the creation of a Housing Trust.
To my mind the creation of a Housing
Trust is something that formulates a very
important measure of public policy. I
am speaking as an individual Member of
Parliament, but in my judgment the
Minister had no right-I speak quite
deliberately when I say this-to intimate
to the outside public the formation of
a Trust of this kind without, in the first
instance, having put such a proposal
before this House.

ORAL ANSWERS TO
QUESTIONS.
County Armagh Assistant Planning
Officer.
1. Mr. JOHNSTON asked the Minister
of Health and Local Government whether
he can give an explanation of the action
of his Ministry in appointing Mr. D. J.
MacRandal as its Assistant Architect one
month after the appointment of that
officer had been sanctioned by his Ministry
as Assistant Planning Officer to the
Armagh County Council, and will he take
steps to prevent such an occurrence in the
future and avoid disagreement with local
authorities in engaging officials without
their consent or knowledge.
The MINISTER OF HEALTH AND
LOCAL GOVERNMENT (Mr. Grant):
Mr. MacRandal applied for a post on the
Ministry's staff in response to a public
advertisement inserted by the Ministry of
Finance and was summoned for an interview, together with other applicants, being
subsequently offered the position of temporary Assistant Architect in the employ
of my Ministry.
There are two things I should like to
make clear; the first is that it is not the
practice to take into Government employment persons employed by local authorities
without prior consultation with the authority in question, and in Mr. MacRandal's
case the Ministry's senior architect in the
.
course of a visit to Armagh discussed the
whole question with the secretary of the
County Council and left with the understanding that the Ministry would proceed
with the appointment.
The second point is that Mr. MacRandal
had not, in fact, started work with the
County Council.
I very much regret that there should
have been any difficulty about this case,
particularly as it seems to have arisen
largely from a misunderstanding between
an official of my Department and the
secretary of the County Council; I should
also like to assure the hon. Member that
there was no desire on the part of my
Ministry to treat the Council discourteously in the matter, and I shall take
steps to prevent similar misunderstandings
arising in the future.
Mr. JOHNSTON: May I suggest that
the Minister should circulate a copy of the
Tenth Commandment? (Laughter.)
Evacuation Service, Staff.
2. Mr. McGURK asked the Minister of
Health and Local Government whether he
can state the position of the staff engaged
in the Evacuation Service and acting as
temporary Civil Servants; what provision
has been made for them or if their services
will be required when the Evacuation
Scheme ends; and whether he will issue
instructions to the staff engaged in this
very essential service as to the future.
Mr. GRANT: The staff mentioned by
the hon. Member are in the same position
as other temporary staff in the Government
service. They are liable to be discharged
when the need for their services ceases;
but they would then be considered for
alternative service in Government employment if it were available.
I am sorry that I cannot say to what
extent such employment will be available
to Evacuation Staff whose appointments
are terminated, nor can I forecast the staff
likely to be required when the official
scheme for evacuation ceases.
.
All the staff in question know that
their appointments are on a purely temporary basis, and I cannot see that there is
anything at present which I can tell them
about their prospects of future employment in the Government service.
Mr. NIXON: Arising out of the
Minister's statement about finding other

The Assistance Board.
3. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Labour whether he can state the names
of the Chairman and Members of the
Assistance Board, the annual salaries
and allowances, inclusive, paid to each,
the number of meetings which each
attended in respect to the business of

ended the 31st March, 1944.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.

Gordon, and the Members are Mrs. M.
R. Collis, Mr. R. H. Coulter, Mr. R.
V. Williams, and Captain Sir James
Wilton, M.C. The salary of the Chairman is £600 per annum, and the
Members receive salaries of £350 per
annum.
Twelve formal monthly meetings of the
Board were held during the financial year
ended on the 31st March, 1944. Mr.
Coulter was present at all twelve meetings, Mrs. Collis at eleven, Mr. Williams
and Sir James Wilton at ten, and the
Chairman, who was not appointed until
the 1st July, 1943, at nine meetings.
Apart from the formal monthly meetings of the Board, the Chairman and
Members were frequently in attendance
at its offices for discussion and consultation.

Cabinet Minister every time he attends?
Mr. BEATTIE: Does the Minister
think it in keeping with the position in
Northern Ireland and the position of
the Assistance Administration to pay

5. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Labour whether he can state the names
of the umpire and deputy umpires and
the functions they perform; also the total
salaries and allowances, inclusive, paid to
each.
Mr. MIDGLEY: The umpire under
the Unemployment Insurance Acts, the
Widows', Orphans' and Old Age Contributory Pension Acts, and the Old Age
Pension Acts is Major W. Johnson,
barrister-at-law, who is at present serving with His Majesty's Forces. Mr. L.
E. Curran, K.C., and Mr. H. A.
McVeigh, barrister-at-law, are deputy
umpires under the Unemployment Insurance Acts and the Old Age Pension Acts,
and Mr. McVeigh also holds the office of
deputy umpire under
under the Widows',
Orphans' and Old Age Contributory
Pension Acts. These Acts constitute the
umpire and his deputies as the final
authorities for the determination of
claims to unemployment benefit, pensions
and admission to Special Voluntary Insurance, and of certain questions related
thereto.
The umpire and the deputy umpires
are paid on a fee basis, but while on
military service the umpire receives an
allowance of £250 per annum. The fees
paid to Mr. Curran and Mr. McVeigh
for their services as deputy umpires during the financial year ended 31st March,
1944, amounted to £303 13s 2d and

speaking, the fees paid to the Umpire
and Deputy Umpires are three guineas
per session of approximately three hours'
duration, with an additional two guineas
where the session is held outside Belfast.
In cases decided otherwise than in a

Larne and Stranraer Goods Traffic.
7. Major ROBINSON asked the Prime
Minister whether he is aware of the hardships and the loss of trade which many
traders in County Antrim district are at
present experiencing owing to the fact that
all carriage of goods has been stopped on
Larne and Stranraer route; whether he
will use his influence to have this traffic
restored at earliest possible moment, and
can he state when this is likely to be fully
restored.
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir Basil
Brooke): I am aware that the suspension
of the goods service on this route has given
rise to some inconvenience which is not
confined to traders in County Antrim,
but the temporary diversion of traffic to
other ports in Great Britain provides
reasonably adequate alternative facilities
in the circumstances.
I am confident that the Ministry of
War Transport will restore the Larne-
Stranraer goods service at the earliest date
consistent with military requirements.
Major ROBINSON: Does it not seem
that there is a very great likelihood of a
great amount of business which used to
be transacted through Larne being lost at
some future date as it has to go by a circuitous route and people who had been
dealing with Larne business houses are
now transferring their business to Belfast
and Londonderry?
Mr.
THOMPSON: Is the Prime
Minister aware that the Ministry of Food
sent a boat regularly to Stranraer with
milk, and will he take steps to see that
the traders of Larne are permitted to use
that steamer for the purpose of sending
their own goods? That would help things.
The PRIME MINISTER: I shall certainly look into the suggestion put forward by the hon. Gentleman. I sympathise
with the traders of Larne and am taking
the matter up personally. I am hopeful
that the result may be satisfactory.

Londonderry Prison-Temporary
Warders.
8. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state the
number of ex-Service men recently paid off
from their positions as Temporary
Warders in Londonderry Prison and the
service of those men as Prison Warders.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Mr. Lowry): Four ex-Service men of the
last war (two of whom also had service in
the present war) were recently paid off
when the establishment at Londonderry
Prison was reduced owing to the transfer
of internees to Belfast Prison and the reopening of Londonderry Prison as a local
prison.
These men were recruited for guard
duty, a duty which has now been abolished. Two of the men had 18 months'
service and the others had 9 months and
7 months respectively.
Men employed on guard duties are not
always suitable for duty as prison officers,
and in selecting the men to be retained for
the latter duty the most suitable and
efficient men were retained.
Mr. NIXON: Arising out of the
Minister's answer, in practice will the
Government give any effect whatever to
all the promises they have made to ex-
Service men since the war started?
Mr. LOWRY: In this particular case
in which the services of 33 warders were
dispensed with, only four were ex-Service
men, 29 were not ex-Service men. Ex-
Service men have been retained in the
same proportion. The proportion of dismissals was seven to one. Two of these
ex-Service men were not of sufficient
height even to be prison officers although
they could efficiently and usefully carry
arms, and use them if necessary.
Mr. NIXON: Would the Minister be
surprised to know-I am not giving my
own opinion-that something like twelve
or thirteen were paid off?
Mr. LOWRY: That is not so.
Mr. NIXON: Well, I do not know.

CLOTHING.
11. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state the
number of suits of uniform issued to the
mobilised Special Constabulary during
the past three years.
Mr. LOWRY: Some 4,144 frocks,
4,415 pairs of trousers, and 1,416 greatcoats were issued to the mobilised members of the Special Constabulary during
the three years ending 15th September
last.
Mr. NIXON: Would the Minister say
what was issued to the men individually,
and does he know that some of the men,
so far as uniform is concerned, are practically naked; and does he think that
4,000 suits of uniform for, I think, three
or four thousand men- -I do not know the
exact number-are anything like enough?
Mr. LOWRY: I cannot give the exact
number of men, but I think it to be in or
about 1,000. The position is that each
part-time member of the "B" Special
Constabulary is in possession of a suit,
that is a frock, a trousers, and a greatcoat. When he is mobilised for full-time
duty he receives an additional suit and
greatcoat. After six months' mobilised
service he is issued with a further suit,
so that after completing eighteen months'
mobilised service he receives a replacement issue of a suit. Accordingly, when
a man has been mobilised six months he
is in possession of three suits and two
greatcoats, and with reasonable care I
do not think he would be naked.
Mr. NIXON: That is right.
Loans to Local Authorities.
12. Mr. THOMPSON asked the
Minister of Finance whether, in view of
the cheap money policy enunciated by
the Chancellor of the Exchequer and the
necessity for capital expenditure on an
extensive scale by local authorities on
housing and public health purposes in the
post-war period, he will take steps to
ensure that loans will be available at low
rates of interest to local authorities in
Northern Ireland; and whether the policy
announced by the Chancellor, which will
preclude long-term borrowing by local
authorities in the form of stock issues
to the public, will have its counterpart
here.
The MINISTER OF EDUCATION
(Lieut.-Colonel Hall-Thompson): On
behalf of my right hon. Friend and with
the consent of the hon. Member, I am
answering this question.
I am fully alive to the necessity for a
cheap money policy in the post-war
period, and am happy to be able to
announce that not only will the resources
of the Government Loans Fund continue
to be available to local authorities, but
that the basic rate of interest on local
loans issued by the Ministry of Finance as
from 2nd October, 1944, has been fixed at
31 per cent., which is the rate current
for advances from the Imperial Local
Loans Fund to local authorities in Great
Britain.
As regards the latter part of the
question, the restriction on issues of stock
by local authorities will apply in
Northern Ireland, and long term borrowings by these local authorities will be
confined to Government sources.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.

BELFAST COUNTY BOROUGH
ADMINISTRATION (AMEND-
MENT) BILL.
Order for Second Reading read.
Mr. GRANT: Hon. Members have
already had with the Bill an explanatory
memorandum setting out in some detail
the proposals of this measure. I do not,
therefore, intend to take up the time of
the House by going through the various
clauses of the Bill, but I should like to
refer to the circumstances which have led
to its introduction and the reasons why
the Government feels justified in asking
the House to pass it.
Hon. Members will remember that, following upon certain events in connection
with the Belfast Borough Council, and, in
particular, arising out of an inquiry held
into the activities of the Tuberculosis Committee, a great deal of disquietude was
aroused in the public mind and within
the City Council itself as to the inadequacy
of the arrangements for the management
of the municipal affairs of the City of
Belfast. My right hon. Friend the
Minister of Home Affairs had lengthy
discussions and negotiations with a committee of the City Council specially
appointed to consider the whole situation,
and, after much debate the Belfast County
Borough Administration Act was passed
in 1942. That Act provided for entrusting to three Administrators, to be appointed by the Government, certain of the
powers hitherto exercised by the Council.
The powers in question were in the main
those concerned with finance, including
the levying of rates and the raising of
loans; the appointment of officers; the
purchase of land and the making of contracts. As originally introduced, the Bill
envisaged the continuation of these ar-
1819 Belfast Administration Bill- HOUSE OF COMMONS

Second Reading
[Mr. Grant]
rangements on a permanent basis, or, at
any rate, until Parliament should otherwise determine.
During its passage through this House,
however, the Bill was amended so as to
provide that the jurisdiction of the
Administrators should run only for a
period. That period would, in default of
further legislation by Parliament, terminate on the 31st March, 1946. I have
seen it suggested that as the term of office
of the Administrators will not come to an
end for more than a year it is premature
to embark upon this legislation. It is
true that the existing Administrators are
performing their functions with very
great efficiency and, I understand, to the
satisfaction of all concerned. Indeed I
think it would only be right for me to say
that both the Government and the city
owe a deep debt of gratitude for the unselfish service which has been given by the
three gentlemen concerned-two of them
in an entirely unpaid capacity-in this
most onerous and difficult position.
But while, as I have said, the existing
arrangement is working as smoothly as
could be expected, it is inevitable that the
uncertainty which at present exists with
regard to the arrangements for the future
government of the city is tending to
impede the current work of municipal
business, and the perfection of plans and
machinery for the even larger tasks that
lie ahead. I have already told the House
that it is my policy and my desire to build
up in Northern Ireland a strong local
government machine. I am satisfied that
so far as the city of Belfast is concerned
the present position of uncertainty is not
in the interests of the city. I feel that the
sooner it is brought to an end and everyone knows where he stands the sooner
can I reasonably look to the establishment
in the city of strong, effective and efficient
local government.
The issue which we have to face is
whether the powers of the City Council
should be restored in full exactly as they
existed prior to the passing of the Act of
1942; whether the Act of 1942 should be
extended for a term so as to continue the
jurisdiction of the Administrators in its
present form; or whether some alternative
arrangement should be made. This Bill
represents the united answer of the Government and the Belfast Corporation to
that issue.
In effect the Bill proposes to restore to
the Council on the 1st January next full
powers to direct the policy upon which
the city's affairs are to be managed. But
it places the responsibility for the execution of certain matters arising out of
policies decided by the Council, not upon.
the members of the Council themselves,
but on two of the city officials-the Town
Clerk and the Town Solicitor who are, of
course, the Council's paid officers. These
two officers would jointly be responsible
for purchasing the necessary supplies, the
acquisition and disposal of land, and the
placing of contracts.
It is fully appreciated that this is a
new principle to be imported into the
machinery of local government, but
because it is new it is not necessarily
objectionable. It is a principle, I may
say, which has worked with extreme satisfaction in the machinery of central
government for a very long time. In
central government the Cabinet as a
whole, and individual Ministers in their
departments, prescribe the policy which
is to be followed. The responsibility for
executing that policy and accounting to
the Public Accounts Committee for the
amounts voted by Parliament for the service of the various departments rests, not
upon the Minister himself directly, but
upon the permanent head of his executive
staff.
This principle, therefore, of entrusting
the responsibility for the execution of
policies already decided by the Council
to certain of the Council's paid officers
is one which, though new in the realm of
local government, has ample precedent.
I would not like to say that it is one
which is suitable for application to all
local government bodies, but I feel that
in the case of an extremely large city such
as Belfast, having regard to the growing
complexity of municipal business, it is
well worth adopting. Outside the introduction of this principle the Bill contains
various clauses which, in the main, deal
with the position as regards appointment,
security of tenure and superannuation of
certain officers of the Corporation.
Mr. NIXON: Yes, certain ones.
Mr. GRANT: In deciding to place
upon the city officers greater responsibility for certain actions taken on behalf
of the Council, the Government must
obviously satisfy itself that the officers

Belfast Administration Bill-
3 OCTOBER 1944

troversial legislation to be brought into
this House. I respectfully submit that
the Bill which is before us to-day and
introduced by the Minister of Health and
Local Government is infinitely a far more
controversial Bill than the previous two
Bills which were withdrawn on the grounds
stated by the Prime Minister.
This Bill constitutes, in my opinion, a
definite attack upon democratic government, and for that reason it should be
strongly resisted by every Member no
matter on what side he sits.
Local government administration is, in my opinion,
and I trust in the opinion of every Member
in this building, the backbone of the
administration of the country, and we
cannot afford lightly to look upon a Bill
which in its very essence and true implication is a direct assault upon local government. The Bill refers primarily to the
Belfast Corporation, but I do not think
that we should for one moment forget
that the measure in its true application
applies to every portion of local government in this country.
In a circular sent by the Belfast Corporation to the Members of this House,
including myself, and also, I understand,
to the Members of the Senate, it was
stated that the functions of the Belfast
Corporation were being restored to the
members of that body with the exception
of certain minor matters which were being
put into the hands of the Town Clerk and
Town Solicitor. What are the minor
matters that are thus referred to? We
find that No. 1 is the vitally important
matter of the purchase of goods and supplies, including supplies required by the
gas, electricity and transport undertakings. These minor matters also include, as the hon. Member for Woodvale
pointed out, the acquisition and disposal
of land, including the purchase of land
otherwise than by agreement, and the
making of contracts for the carrying out
of works required by the Council. I
heard the Minister of Labour give a rather
enthusiastic "Hear, hear," to that proposal. I suggest to him that so far as
the fixing of contracts is concerned, and
despite all the abuses that have taken
place in the past, you are on infinitely
safer ground if the placing of these contracts and the acquisition of lands is in
the hands of 60 men rather than in the
hands of two men. I suggest that the
danger of abuse and corruption is infinitely greater where the fixing of contracts and the acquisition of land is in
the hands of two men than where it is in
the hands of 60 members of the Corporation. I cannot for one moment agree
that we are within the bounds of safety
so far as local government is concerned if
we delegate these all-important powers
into the hands of two individuals.
I am not saying one word against these
men individually, but I am impressed by
the fact, as every Member must be, that
you cannot always guarantee the integrity
of those who hold these offices. The hon.
Member for Woodvale has instanced
cases where corruption and malpractices
have taken place on the part of two
officials in the employment of the Belfast
Corporation.
What undertaking have
I
we here to-day or what knowledge have

sincerely trust not, but there is no guarantee that the conditions to which the hon.

In my humble judgment there is only
one solution of the problem of the

The solution of that problem does not lie
in the dishonest method of turning a

Bill, into a permanent position. I sug
gest that the Members of this House, who

That was only a temporary expedient
The Bill was assented to by the majority

is the proposal in the Bill which is before
the House to-day? It is now to be turned

by the Belfast Corporation and an ultimate veto by the Ministry.
No matter what the Minister of Health
and Local Government may have said

I am referring to the. people of Belfast.
If he does so, I think he will find that the

their opinion, and that that opinion

known medium-a municipal election.

two officials? I suggest the only proper

May I also quote a statement by the
Minister at that time, the right hon.
Member for Victoria. He said:

Order for Second Reading read.
The
ATTORNEY-GENERAL (Mr.
MacDermott): I beg to move, "That
this Bill be now read a Second time."
The Bill is in the usual annual form. It
provides for the continuance of the
Expiring Laws Bill-
Second Reading
4 OCTOBER 1944
operation of certain measures for another
year ending 31st December, 1945. The
measures it proposes to continue are set
out in the Schedule to the Bill. In the
first part of the Schedule is contained the
only Imperial measure to which the Bill
relates. It is the Harbours, Docks and
Piers (Temporary Increase of Charges)
Act, 1920. One or two harbour authorities in Northern Ireland still regulate
their charges under that Act. The present is a very inopportune time to fix a
new rate structure, and the Act is therefore proposed to be continued in order to
enable the authorities concerned to levy
their legal charges.
The second part of the Schedule contains the enactments of this Parliament
which it is proposed to continue. The
first in the Schedule is the Local Government (Emergency Powers) Act, 1921,
which has been continued since that date.
It provides for the steps to be taken in
the event of a local authority failing or
refusing to carry out its Statutory duties.
The other four Statutes are Statutes of a
temporary nature passed to meet certain
war conditions. It is proposed to continue them, as well as the Statutes in the
earlier part of the Schedule, it being
hoped that by this time next year the
emergency situation will have been relaxed to an extent that will enable this
part of the Schedule to be curtailed.
Question proposed, "That the Bill be
now read a Second time."

The ATTORNEY-GENERAL: With
the permission of the House I should like
to correct a misapprehension which the
hon. Member for Shankill is obviously
under in respect of the Housing (Temporary Accommodation) Act of 1942. It
is rather surprising that as a member of
a local authority the hon. Member should
not realise the very limited nature of that
measure. It does not, as he says,
power builders to ignore the by-laws.
What it does the two
emergency
measures is to give power to the local
authority, subject to the approval of the
Ministry, to relax certain building bylaws for the purpose of enabling temporary accommodation to be made for the
people. The provisions are not such as
to entail unsanitary conditions, and when
the hon. Member says as a result of this
measure unsanitary and unwholesome
buildings are being built, I challenge him
to point to one single building erected
under the authority of this enactment in
his own area in Belfast which is either
unsanitary or unfit for human habitation.
The whole object of the measure is to
prevent by-laws, which are, for the purpose of ensuring modern building con-
Expiring Laws Bill
Adjournment
4 OCTOBER 1944
ditions being respected, getting into the
way of temporary accommodation which
the emergencies of war or enemy action
have thrust upon us, if it is necessary to
resort to temporary buildings for the
purpose of meeting for a limited time the
present housing shortage. It is obviousit must be obvious to the hon. Member,
as a member of a local authority-that
peace-time building by-laws may here and
there require some modification. This
Bill, if continued, will enable. the Corporation of Belfast and other local
authorities, if need be and subject to the
supervision of the Ministry, to grant
certain modifications of those by-laws
simply to enable housing conditions to be
improved and more. persons to be housed.
The hon. Member is labouring under a
misapprehension altogether if he thinks
anything can be done under this Bill, by
the local authorities or individuals, to
erect unsanitary houses or houses with
conditions that do not make for health.
It is an emergency measure, and unfortunately, the conditions in
in which it
originated are still in existence, which
makes it undesirable that the power
should be taken away at this stage.

whether he arranged for Mr. Robinson to
take part and had a conversation with
him on the subject of the inquiry before
it was held.
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir Basil
Brooke) Yes, sir. Mr. Robinson, who
has very wide experience in business and
considerable knowledge of civic administration attended those discussions at my
invitation in his private capacity. I am
satisfied that his presence and the advice
given by him were of material value
during the course of the deliberations.
With regard to the second part of the
hon. Member's question, the discussions
were informal and of an exploratory
nature, and the results were
communicated to the Belfast Corporation through
the Electricity Committee. Parliament
will, of course, have the fullest opportunity of considering the Government's
proposals when the matter comes before
the House at a later date.
If the suggestion in the last part of
the question is that I discussed policy
with Mr. Robinson, the answer is in the
negative.
Mr. NIXON: Is it usual for the
Government to set up an inquiry and for
the Prime Minister to invite a gentleman
to attend that inquiry and take part in it
in his private capacity, and at the same
time keep the information of what is
going on secret from the Belfast Corporation and Members of Parliament?
Mr. SPEAKER: The hon. Member
knows that this is a supplementary question, and therefore it must be a short
question of fact.
Mr. NIXON: I was endeavouring to
frame a question to cover the answer by
the Minister. Is it usual to invite a
gentleman to a private inquiry in his
private capacity and let him have access
to information that neither Parliament
nor the public bodies concerned can get?
The PRIME MINISTER: I think the
Minister is perfectly entitled to ask anybody he thinks fit, if he thinks he will
assist him in solving the problem he has
in mind.
Mr. NIXON: With regard to the
Prime Minister's statement that the
Minister has the right to invite anyone
he thinks fit if that person is prepared to
assist him, on this question the Prime
Minister must have known beforehand
that Mr. Robinson was prepared to assist
him to get control of the electricity of
Northern Ireland before he invited
him-
The PRIME MINISTER: No, sir.
Mr. NIXON: That is what you said.

.

Housing.
BELFAST CORPORATION HOUSES.
12. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Health and Local Government whether he
can state if the houses built by the Belfast
Corporation since 1918 are paying their
way, and if not, what is the annual
deficit, and what means are being adopted
to make good the deficit, if any; and how
the rents of the Belfast Corporation
houses compare with the rents of houses
built by private enterprise.
The MINISTER OF HEALTH AND
LOCAL GOVERNMENT (Mr. Grant):
There has been a financial loss in respect
of the houses erected by the Belfast Corporation under the Housing Acts since
the end of the last war. It would take
considerable time to have figures taken
out to show the total loss for the whole
period. The actual loss for the year ended
31st March, 1943, amounted to just over
£11,000.
The excess of expenditure on the houses
over the income derived from them can be
reduced either by raising the rents or by
spending less money on maintenance and
repairs. The former course is prohibited.
by the Rent Restrictions Acts, and I am
certainly not going to advocate the second
alternative.
I regret that I am not in a position to
make a general comparison between the
rents of Belfast Corporation houses and
those built by private enterprise.
Mr. NIXON: If the Minister is not
in a position to make that comparison
how does he hold that he is qualified to
be the head of a Department charged with
building 100,000 houses?

13. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Health and Local Government whether

houses.
Mr. GRANT: Within the last
eighteen months three applications from
rural councils in County Tyrone for
increases in the rents of labourers'
cottages have been dealt with.
In two of these cases increases in rents
were approved subject to the cottages
being put in a satisfactory state of
repair.
In the third case, a few of the cottages
were in new condition and increased
rents were authorised. The remainder
are still
under consideration, and no
increases in rent will be sanctioned unless
adequate repairs are carried out.
The Rent Restrictions Acts do not
apply to houses built under the Labourers
(Ireland) Acts.
Mr. NIXON: Could the Minister
tell us how it is that whether the rent
is economic or otherwise in regard to
houses privately owned it cannot be increased, and how is it that large public
bodies can increase rents while private
owners cannot ?

lengthy I
with the hon. Mempropose,
ber's consent, to circulate it in the

The following is the. reply referred
to:-
No war-time houses allocated by the
Ministry to local authorities have yet
been built. The present position in
respect of each of the authorities which
have received main allocations is as
follows:
Belfast Comments on a sketch plan
showing the proposed layout of some
650 houses on a site at the West
Circular Road have been forwarded by
the Ministry to the Corporation with
suggestions for minor amendments.
Preliminary drawings of the house
types, and other requisite documents in
respect of 86 houses fronting on the
West Circular Road, sent to the Ministry on the 2nd instant, have been considered and the Ministry's comments
have now been forwarded to the Corporation. Detailed working drawings
have still to be prepared and approved
before tenders can be invited. The
Belfast Corporation estimate that construction of these houses will commence
in January, 1945.
Londonderry: The allocation of 250
houses which was offered to Londonderry on the 26th May last was
accepted by the Corporation on the 6th
June. I visited Londonderry on the
30th June and urged the Corporation
to do all in its power to expedite the
selection and layout of sites. Little
progress having been made, officers of
my Department journeyed to Londonderry towards the end of August and
made certain concrete suggestions to
the Corporation's representatives with
a view to expediting matters; the Department's suggestions were embodied
in an official letter dated 31st August
last, and the Corporation was requested
to give the matter urgent and serious
consideration. I am afraid that I can
give no indication as to when it is
likely that building will commence.
Lisburn: Good progress has been
made by the Council towards the pro-

[Mr. Grant]
A
vision of the 100 houses allocated.
suitable site has been acquired and
approved. Excellent layout and house

Newry: The Council has

Armagh: This Council has experienced considerable difficulty over

and negotiations are still proceeding in

has gone ahead with the drawing up of

Newtownards: A site has been

and I am afraid I am not able to say
when the Council will be in a position
to commence building operations.
As regards the steps which the Government have taken, or propose to take, with
a
view to expediting the erection of
these war-time houses, it will, no doubt,
be appreciated that apart from such assistance and advice as my Department may
be in a position and, I may say, very
willing to offer, there is not a great deal
which I can do to expedite the completion
of the building works. The early execution of the latter depends to a large extent
upon the drive and energy displayed by
the local authorities concerned. I can do
no more than to give all the assistance in
my power, where such is needed, and exhort those who lag behind to greater
efforts. This I have done and will continue to do.
I should like to make it clear that the
initiation of schemes for the building of
houses, particularly in war time, is one
of great difficulty and complexity. For
instance, the highly energetic and competent local authorities in Lisburn and
Newry, though they have had no site difficulties to contend with, have been fully
engaged since May in the preparation of
their plans, etc., and have not yet been
able to start actual building.
At the same time, however, I am not
satisfied with the rate of progress, particularly in Belfast, where the preliminaries of the scheme have been prolonged
for almost a year; but I want hon. Members to realise that even with complete
efficiency the work which must precede the
erection of houses takes longer than any
of us like to contemplate.

DUMP AT RIVERSDALE,
COLERAINE.
17. Dr. LYLE asked the Minister of
Health and Local Government whether
he can state if it is a fact that the Coleraine Borough Council, in face of several
condemnatory reports from their medical
officer of health, continue to use a dump
at Riversdale which, according to these
reports, contains uncovered masses of
decaying animal and vegetable matter,
causing a most objectionable smell and
attracting flies and other pests; whether
the medical officer of health recommended
that the dump be adequately covered and
no longer used, as it is too close to
dwelling-houses and a danger to health;
whether this matter has been brought to
the notice of his Ministry and previously
to that of the Ministry of Home Affairs;
and whether he will take the necessary
steps to compel the Coleraine Borough
Council to abate this nuisance.
Mr. GRANT: The dumping-ground of
the Coleraine Borough Council, situated
at Riversdale, Coleraine, has been the
subject of reports by the medical officer
of health, who recommended to the Coleraine Borough Council that the dump be
adequately covered and no longer used.
The question has been under consideration both by the Ministry of Home Affairs
and by my Ministry, and one of my
medical officers has, within recent months,
carried out numerous inspections of the
dump. My Ministry did make strong
Oral Answers
Ways and Means
10 OCTOBER 1944

representations to the Borough Council as
to its unsatisfactory condition, and suggested to the Council that consideration
should be given to the question of securing an alternative dumping site outside
the borough area.
As a result of these representations the
Council took steps at Riversdale to cover
with earth the offensive parts of the
dumping-ground, to have the animal
matter dumped elsewhere and to permit
only the dumping of domestic and
innocuous refuse on this site. In
addition, the Council have employed a
man to supervise the dump.
My medical officer, following his visit
to the dumping-ground on the 25th
September, reported that the improvements effected by the Council were being
maintained and that there was then no
offensive odour. He advised the Council's
surveyor to permit dumping at only the
farthest point from the dwelling-houses.
My medical officers will continue to
visit the site, and if present arrangements
do not prove effective I shall take such
action as is within my power to have the
matter remedied.
Dr. LYLE: Arising out of the reply
of the right hon. Gentleman, is he aware

health and his own inspector are carried

which were carried out. He is satisfied

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Ways and Means.
Considered in Committee.
[Sir ROBERT LYNN in the Chair.]
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That it is expedient to amend the law
Ways and Means-
Committee
HOUSE OF Cоммолз
relating to death duties by making retrospective provision as respects those duties
where persons or property are
or is
affected by the law relating to trading
with the enemy, and otherwise to amend
the law relating to death duties, stamp
duty, entertainments duty and certain
excise licences, and to make further provision in connection with finance."
Major SINCLAIR: Hon. Members
will have observed from the explanatory
memorandum which has been circulated
that the proposals to which this Resolution refers are of a somewhat technical
nature. Their main object is to bring
our legislation into line with that obtaining in Great Britain, and while no doubt
they are of considerable importance to
the limited interests concerned, their
impact on our revenue is not likely to be
of any great moment.
Taking the proposals in the order in
which they appear in the explanatory
memorandum, I should like to elaborate
the reasons for the projected changes.
In Great Britain the position arose
that where property was held temporarily
by the custodian of enemy property it
could not be made assessable during that
time for income-tax or surtax, and, when
the owner died, for death duties. Also
-which is perhaps of equal importancerepayments of income-tax in respect of the
property could not be effected.
In the
Finance Act of 1944 the Imperial Government took steps to make the custodian
accountable for such taxes (and repayments) to the extent that the funds, or
proceeds of the property, at his disposal
permitted, and, while provision for the
whole of the United Kingdom was made
in so far as the reserved taxes were concerned, it was left to the Parliament of
Northern Ireland to legislate in respect.
of death duties. As enemy property is a
reserved matter, power was given for this
Parliament to pass, if it thought fit, corresponding legislation to that embodied in
the Finance Act, 1944.
In 1937 the Imperial Finance Act
extended the scope of the exemption
from death duties already granted in
respect of properties passing to the
National Trust. Similar steps were
not taken here at the time, as it was
thought that the cases for which the
Imperial legislation provided were of
such rare occurrence as not to justify
Reprelegislation in Northern Ireland.
sentations have, however, been made to
me that the absence of this increased
scope of exemption afforded in Great
Britain militates against possible
bequests to the Trust in Northern Ireland, and we now accordingly propose
to follow the terms of Section 31 of the
Finance Act, 1937. Under the Finance
Act (Northern Ireland), 1936, the
Ministry of Finance has already a discretionary power to remit death duties where
property is bequeathed to the National
Trust so as to be indefeasibly vested in
the Trust and to be held by the Trust
inalienably for the public benefit. Under
the new proposals, not only will this power
of discretion become mandatory upon the
Ministry, but the property will be transferable to the Trust under conditions
which will give the owner, or his wife or
child, a life interest in all or part of
the property comprised in the gift. An
illustration may help here. An owner
may leave on his death his property to
the National Trust, subject to his son
being allowed to occupy it and enjoy its
income during his lifetime. The son,
on inheriting the life interest, will pay
death duties upon the whole capital
value of the estate, but when the Trust
ultimately inherits upon the son's death,
the property will pass to the Trust without payment of any duties. Provision
will also be made for cases where the life
interest is only in respect of a part of
the estate which is bequeathed to the
Trust and in such instances the
inheritor of the life interest will only
pay his due proportion of duties leviable on the estate as a whole.
As regards succession or legacy duty
payable by an illegitimate child or his
heirs, we are again following the action
already taken by the Imperial Government in Section 43 of the Finance Act,
1944, under which the rates of duty payable are brought into line with those
applicable in the case of a legitimate child.
Coming now to the question of Stamp
Duty on securities which have been
changed from a bearer form to a registered form, it is arguable that the present
position, whereby duty has been paid at
the time of issue in its original form and
is again payable on any transfer or sale
subsequent to its change to registered
form means that, in fact, duty is being
paid twice. It has, accordingly, been
Ways and Means

thought more equitable that the first
transfer made following a change in form
which has taken place since 2nd September, 1939, should be free from Stamp
Duty. The two other changes in Stamp
Duty, which follow the Finance Act, 1944,
do not, I think, call for any special
comment.
Since the increase in the rates of
Entertainments Duty imposed by the
Finance Act (Northern Ireland), 1943, it
has been discovered that in some cases the
rate of duty payable on a season ticket,
or other similar lump sum payment for
admission to a number of entertainments,
was greater than if the duty were paid
piece-meal "
on separate payments for
admission to each entertainment. This
anomaly will, accordingly, be removed by
providing that the duty payable on the
season ticket will not exceed the total of
the individual payments.
""
Where the business carried on in
licensed premises has been suspended
owing to war circumstances, my Ministry
may issue, under our Finance Act of 1942,
a certificate to that effect, and thereby
the licensing certificate attached to the
premises is kept alive. If the war circumstances included damage to the premises
by enemy action, the certificate reads
accordingly, and the Act further provided
that in such cases the provision of the
Licensing Acts as to "avoidance of
licences by reason of disqualification of
premises" should not have effect. On the
other hand, the licence could not be restored until the Licensing Court had been
satisfied that the premises had been
properly reconstructed. Where the war
circumstances, however, did not include
damage to the premises, the premises were
still subject to the before-mentioned provision of the Licensing Acts and were,
therefore, open to disqualification for
structural reasons. It is desirable, therefore, both in the interests of the license
holder and of the licensing court, that
where war damage has occurred subseqquent to the issue of a certificate of discontinuance, an amending certificate
should be issued so as to bring the premises
within the scope of the provisions of the
1942 Act relating to war damaged
premises. I beg to move.

INCREASE IN RENTS OF
LABOURERS' COTTAGES.
Mr. BEATTIE: I placed this Motion
on the Order Paper for the purpose of
drawing the attention of the Minister to
the position which has been communicated
to me in reference to an injustice imposed
upon a certain class of the community
with his consent. The Motion reads as
follows:
That in the opinion of this House a
public inquiry should be held by the
Minister of Health and Local Government into the actions of Rural District
Councils and other Public Bodies in increasing rents of labourers' cottages
under their control to ascertain if such
increases are just and reasonable.
From the information we have received
we feel that an inquiry should be held
into the grievance existing in this area
in regard to labourers' cottages. It is
very curious that none of the rents of
cottages except those built under scheme
No. 7 has been increased. The cottages
built under No. 7 scheme were tenanted
in 1939 and 1940. That is not a very
long time ago. At that period the rent
chargeable for those cottages was fixed on
the basis of the ability of the tenant to
pay. If in the year 1940 the rent was
based on the ability of the tenant to pay,
why has the local authority now got
power from the Ministry to increase it?
Surely some economic change must take
place in the life of the tenants in the area
Increase in Rents-
Labourers' Cottages
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Beattie]
before the Minister would be justified in
giving that authority to the Rural
Council.
In 1939 and 1940 the wages of the
people who occupied those cottages was
about 24s per week. They have not received any increase in the basic rate, but
an increase has been given to them on the
basis of the cost of living. That increase
brings the amount they receive up to 53s
per week. There is nothing in that increase to change the economic position of
the tenants of those cottages owing to the
system of purchasing and the small
amount they purchase. The general increase in the cost of living is based upon
purchasing in bulk. Those who buy in
pennyworths or shillingworths have a
higher percentage to pay than the people
who purchase larger quantities.
When the Council made a demand upon
the people living in the cottages for an
increase of rent they knew that no change
had taken place in the circumstances of
the tenants from 1940 up to the time the
demand was made. The cottagers held a
protest meeting. Might I say that three
protest meetings were held and they asked
the authorities to hold an inquiry into
the circumstances of those tenants on the
basis of their ability to pay.
The councillors said they cared not about the cottagers, or the tenants as we will call them.
They said, "We are going to increase
your rent, and irrespective of whether
hardship is there or not we are going to
increase your rent.' Why did they say
that? Because they had the Minister's
authority to increase those rents.
""
I am going to ask the Minister to-day
to justify his authority being given to
allow those councillors to make an increase
in rent without a change having taken
place for the betterment of the tenants.
That is all I am asking him to do, but I
am also asking, through this Motion,
what the tenants have asked the Council
to do; to hold an inquiry to find out if
the tenants are able to pay the increase,
and whether, if that increase was imposed,
hardship would result. It does seem to
me very curious-and might I say it is
not by any means modern and might be
ancient to suggest for a moment that
the owners of property are the best people
to decide whether the increase of rent
should take place, and whether hardship
would be imposed as a result of that. The
owners of this property were actually
permitted to make the increase without
inquiring whether hardship would be
imposed, although sometime ago I got an
assurance-not from the present Minister
that an inquiry would be made into
every tenant's position, and where hardship could be proved no increase would
take place.
But this local rural council have
actually applied a general increase of rent
on all cottages built under Scheme 7, and
those cottages have only been occupied
from 1939-1940 onwards. I suggest that
those tenants had as much right to claim
the protection of the Rent Restrictions
Act as any other tenant in the land, and
I claim the right to say that when a basic
rent was fixed in 1940, that should not be
changed, at least during the period of the
war. I want the Minister to understand
clearly that the new Rent Act does not
exempt labourers' cottages. It does not
exempt many classes of dwellings that
were exempt before, and he has ignored
all the protection given to the labourers.
I think he has been misguided and misled
in respect of those cottages under Scheme
Now I want to make this statement,
and I have it here in writing from those
who know. It says here:
7.
During the debate on this matter in
Stormont some time ago, Mr. Elliott
the Member for South Tyrone, who is not

stated these cottages showed a decided

No. 7 Scheme, as no work has been

They were not even painted, nor were

Increase in Rents-
Labourers' Cottages
10 OCTOBER 1944

The cottages under the No. 7 scheme
are lacking in every amenity that goes to
make up a dwelling, and the increases
in rent cannot be based on the other
cottages which have water at their doors
and also other facilities. These cottages
have not. They have not been touched
by the Council either inside or outside
since the date of occupation. The Council
themselves fixed the rent in 1940 at the
figure which the tenants were able to pay,
and if no expenditure has taken place on
the cottages since their occupation, what
justification can be shown for an increase
at the present moment?
I want to say that in the erection of
those houses the range that is usual in
country houses was installed. Due to
scarcity of coal the tenants suggested to
the Council that it would be in the
national interests, and it would help to
tide over the serious period owing to the
shortage of coal, if they would put grates
in the cottages instead of ranges. The
cottagers stated that if the Council put
in grates and took the ranges away they
could burn turf, which was a very good
suggestion and one likely to appeal to a
patriotic-minded individual. But the
Council did not give any facilities in that
direction. They kept the ranges in the
cottages. I want to make it very clear
that these tenants are not asking for
anything unreasonable. They are only
asking for a fair deal. If their position
had been bettered by the war they would
not object to paying any increase of rent,
but they do say-and rightly say that
their position has not been bettered. If
anything their position has been worsened,
and why should they be the victims of a
vicious system such as has been put into
operation by this Council through the
power of the Minister being granted to
them.
I call upon this House to support this
Motion. I do not want to develop this
matter. I do not want to be accused of
making political propaganda out of the
miseries of those poor people, who are
suffering at the moment through paying
more than they are able to pay, for every
penny more they have to pay under these
increases is taken out of the stomachs of
their families. I ask for a fair deal in
this respect, and I ask the House to
accept the Motion in the spirit in which
it is presented, and to set up an inquiry
for the purpose of deciding hardship and
whether an increase is justified, or whether
increases have to be withdrawn where they
have been enforced. I beg to move.

I have already referred to the fact that
the Rent Restrictions Acts do not apply
to these cottages. In each case in which
an application is received from a rural
district council for sanction to increase
the rents the Ministry makes arrangements to have the cottages examined by a
housing inspector, so that he can report
on their condition. If the inspector reports that the cottages are in a reasonable
state of repair the finances of the
Labourers' Cottages Scheme in the district.
are examined, and if the scheme is being
carried on at a loss to the rates sanction
is given to a reasonable increase in rent,
but the increase is limited to a sum that
will ensure the council do not make a
profit on the scheme. If the inspector
reports, however, that the cottages are
not in a reasonable state of repair
sanction to an increase in rent is withheld unless the necessary repairs
carried out. In all sanctions a proviso
is made to the effect that the increase
must not apply if in any case hardship
would be involved.

in different parts of the country; but they
are very few, and should not be quoted
as a reason why the rents should be increased to 5s or 6s a week, as they have
been in the Dungannon area.
I believe that the Minister would be
well advised for his own sake, as well as
for that of the Government, to send down
an inspector and hold an inquiry in the
other areas, so that no blame could be
attached to the Government. If the
inspectors had not gone to Cookstown they would have increased the
rents by is 6d, and the cottages would
have been in a deplorable state. The
contractors will not even take the contract
at the amount allowed by the engineer of
the Cookstown Rural Council for the repair of those cottages. Taking everything
into consideration, the increased income
of the farm labourers is not as much as it
is supposed to be when he pays for everything. He has to pay the money out in
other ways, and surely to goodness the
time has come when the ratepayers in the
rural districts should consider the poor
farm labourer.
Question put, That in the opinion of
this House a public inquiry should be
held by the Minister of Health and
Local Government on the actions of
rural district councils and other public
bodies in increasing rents of labourers'
cottages under their control to ascertain
if such increases are just and reasonable.
The House divided: Ayes, 3; Noes,
22.

Written Answers
Written Answers
17 OCTOBER 1944
Scavenging is carried out by contract
and two contractors perform this work
for the Corporation.
.
A large number of cases of diphtheria
and a considerable number of scarlet
fever occurred in the city of Londonderry
during the year 1943.
The majority of diphtheria cases were
of a mild type. No deaths occurred
amongst those who had been immunised,
and comparatively few such persons contracted diphtheria. I have ascertained
that the outbreak of diphtheria was
general throughout the city and was not
confined to those districts where overcrowding exists.
In recent weeks cases of scarlet fever
have been as numerous as cases of
diphtheria. The numbers notified are,
however, much less than the numbers
reported in the corresponding periods of
last year. The diphtheria cases have
been of a mild type.
There have been nine cases of typhoid
fever during the present year, but not
one of the persons affected contracted the
disease in Londonderry.
While it would be assuming too much
to say that the outbreaks of the diseases
to which I have referred were caused by
laxity on the part of the Londonderry
Corporation in the discharge of their
duties, it cannot be denied that the
standard of the public health services in
the city leaves much to be desired. On
the other hand, it will be appreciated
that by reason of existing restrictions on
the undertaking of new works, it is
difficult, if not impossible, for local
authorities to embark immediately on
major improvements, and the Londonderry Corporation has necessarily to
defer certain improvements until after
the war.
Houses in Rural Districts.

erected across the Channel while none

Mr. GRANT: According to information given in the Imperial House of

The present serious housing deficiencies

the basis of a long-term building programme.
I hope to introduce a Bill shortly
which will give hon. Members an opportunity of a full debate on housing both
in urban and rural areas.

New Industries.

Major SINCLAIR: A reduction of onequarter per cent. in the rate of interest

'finance," presented accordingly and read

UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE
(INCREASE OF BENEFIT)
BILL.
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Midgley): It is a great pleasure to me
that the first Bill I have the honour of
presenting to the Parliament of Northern
Ireland should be one to raise the rates
of unemployment benefit. Not that I
imagine that any person, or indeed any
party, has a monopoly of sympathy on the
subject; in fact, I doubt if there is any
matter, except the vigorous prosecution
of the war, on which there is so little
difference of opinion amongst Members of
this House. Any criticisms directed
against previous measures of this kind
have not been that the Government should
not give so much, but that it ought to give
more; and I am sure that everyone here
is glad that more can now be given. But
the privilege of doing something to help
the worker who cannot get work, if I may
say so, is particularly welcome to me,
because unlike most Members who were
brought up in easier circumstances, I have
had bitter personal experience of the
tragedy of poverty to the poor.
Hon. Members will perhaps forgive
this personal reference when I tell them
that I do not intend to make a long
speech on the Bill. The wording of the
various clauses has to be rather technical,
because they are amendments of various
sections in the principal Unemployment
Insurance Act of 1936, which itself was
amended in 1940; but the total effect is
shown in the table at the end of the
explanatory memorandum, which has
been circulated to Members.
There are many classes of insured persons for whom the Unemployment
Insurance. Acts specify rates of benefit;
and each class is to get an increase under
the Bill. I shall not go through these
classes one by one; the details are set
out in the table of comparison I have
1937 Unemployment Insurance Bill- 17 OCTOBER 1944

Second Reading
just referred to. I will only mention a
few examples to show the general effect.
An adult man without dependants gets
an increase of four shillings-instead of
20s he is to have 24s. The allowance for
an adult dependant is raised substantially
-from 10s to 16s; consequently the rate
for man and wife goes from 30s to 40s.
The allowances for children go up by
a shilling. To take, now, a comprehensive example; the rate for a man, wife
and two children will rise from 38s to 50s.
If there are four children, the old rate
is 44s, and the new rate will be 58s.
On the women's side, the Bill introduces a new principle. If an insured
woman is unmarried or a widow, or if she
maintains an incapacitated husband, or
lives apart from her husband and cannot
get support from him, the benefit which
she draws in her own right when unemployed is increased by four shillingsfrom 18s to 22s. In addition, of course,
she may be entitled to an allowance for
dependent children or dependent husband. If, however, a woman is married,
and not in the special circumstances.
mentioned, her benefit rate will change
from 18s to 20s only.
it is hardly necessary for me to point

need than the woman living independently. And the House will remember,
from the numerous special provisions

different rates of benefit for married and

this Bill.
These changes are for the general
scheme. Under the agricultural scheme
the increases are very nearly the same.
Instead of women being given either 2s
or 4s extra according to marital status,
they get 3s all round; and the increase
in the adult dependant's allowance is 58
instead of 6s. Since agricultural benefits
are on a lower scale than benefits under
the general scheme, the increases will
make a large proportionate difference to
the agricultural worker than to others.
So much for the actual proposals. The
House would like, perhaps, to know
something of their background; no doubt
some hon. Members are asking: "How
does the Bill stand in relation to the
new British plans for comprehensive
social insurance?" I am glad to say
that in the more important cases the. Bill
implements at once the White Paper proposals, and this without requiring any
additional contributions.

For an adult single man, and for a
married man without children, or with
one or two children, the new general
scheme rates are exactly as suggested in
the White Paper. So is the rate of 20s
for a married woman living with her
husband and drawing benefit in her own
right. The White Paper, of course,
gives the payment in respect of the first
child in the form of the universal
children's allowances, not unemployment
benefit, but this difference is merely
formal.
I need hardly inform the House that
the changes proposed in this Bill are
identical with those in the British Bill,
and that there are very good reasons,
arising from our constitutional and
financial position, why we ought not to
give less than the increases in benefit
adopted in Great Britain, and cannot
afford to give more.

one can say is, on the one hand, that the

[MONEY].
Considered in Committee under Standing Order No. 65.
[Sir ROBERT LYNN in the Chair]
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That, for the purposes of any Act of
the present session to increase the rates of
benefit payable under the Unemployment
Insurance Acts (Northern Ireland), 1936
to 1940, it is expedient to authorise the
payment out of moneys provided by
Parliament of any such increase in the
sums so payable by virtue of section
fifty-eight of the Unemployment Insurance Act (Northern Ireland), 1936,1
as amended by any subsequent enactment,
Order in Council, or regulation, as is
attributable to the passing of the
said Act of the present session.'
(Governor's recommendation signified-
Major Sinclair.)
"
FINANCE
The MINISTER OF
(Major Sinclair): Though our Unemployment Fund is to-day in a
healthier position than it has ever
been, its invested surplus approaching a figure of £7,000,000, the
fact that the level of employment in
Great Britain is higher than in Northern
Ireland means that payments continue
to be made to the Fund from our
Exchequer under Section 58 of the
Unemployment Insurance Act, 1936, to
maintain our Fund here in relative
parity with the Great Britain Fund.
The original estimate for the year for
the parity payment was a sum of
£671,000 and it is possible that the higher
rates of benefit proposed under the Bill,
which was given a Second Reading on
Tuesday last, may result in an additional
call upon the Exchequer for a payment
to the Fund under this head. In other
words, in so far as a higher percentage
of unemployment in Northern Ireland
may result in a relatively greater drain
on our Fund than that in Great Britain,
the difference will be made up by a
further contribution from our own
• Exchequer.
This was the point raised by the hon.
Member for Ballynafeigh (Mr. Thompson) on the Second Reading, and I am
able to give the definite assurance that
in no circumstances will this proposed
increase in benefit payments involve an
increase in the contributions of employees
and employers to the Unemployment
Fund over those in operation in Great
Britain. It is not possible, however, to
indicate with any degree of precision the
extent of this possible Exchequer payment until later in the financial year,
though a preliminary estimate places the
figure at £126,000.
Hon. Members will doubtless have
noted that though in a few instances the
new rates of benefit attain to the level of
those set out in the Imperial Government's
White Paper on social insurance, still
further increases will fall to be made if
those proposals become law. Just what
effect these social insurance proposals will
ultimately have upon our Exchequer I
cannot, of course, say now, but they
naturally bring to mind that valuable and
all-important safeguard of our people's
social security, that is, the Unemployment
Reinsurance Agreement of 1936. That
Agreement, as is well known, is for the
time being in abeyance, partly for the
very good reason that the unemployment
position in Northern Ireland is at present
such that no inter-Exchequer payments
would arise under the terms of the Agreement, and partly because in any case our
war-time financial arrangements make
such payments unnecessary at the present
time. I can assure hon. Members, however, that the principle underlying the
1936 Agreement has been jealously preserved and though the sweeping changes
1949 Unemployment [Money]—

19 OCTOBER 1944
Committee
which will in all probability be made in
our social insurance legislation will prevent the revival of the Agreement in
exactly its old form, the question of a
suitable and more comprehensive successor
is at present under discussion. While it
would be premature to enter upon details
at present it is my confident expectation
that the outcome of the pending examination of the whole problem will prove satisfactory.
Perhaps I may add a comment on
another point raised by the hon. Member
for Ballynafeigh. He sought from the
Government an assurance that the question of the change over from war to peace
production in our factories is being vigorously tackled. This I can readily give,
for not only is the Prime Minister giving
unremitting attention to the transition
problems of existing industry, but I know
that he is constantly planning and negotiating for the development of further
undertakings within Ulster to absorb our
admittedly efficient labour reserve and to
diversify our industrial structure.
In
the course of this campaign, as hon.
Members will be aware, he has succeeded
in arranging for the erection under the
auspices of Imperial Government Departments of several modern factories in
Northern Ireland.
This development in itself should make
a useful contribution to the solution of
the problem of rising unemployment with
which we shall undoubtedly be faced as
war contracts tend to diminish. I should,
however, like to remind hon. Members
that while the Government can and will
do its utmost to facilitate expansion of
industry, in the final result the success of
such a policy will be dependent in no
small measure on the recognition by all
members of the community of the need
for a sustained effort. The magnificent
response by workers and management alike
during the war years encourages me in
the confident anticipation that this desirable end can be attained. I beg to move.
