Home Affairs.
ROAD BOARD WAITING
ROOMS.
1. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Home Affairs and Security whether he
has received any representations about
the absence of waiting room and lavatory
accommodation in the several towns and
villages of Northern Ireland at present
served by the Northern Ireland Road
Transport Board; whether, in view of the
fact that railway companies are
are by
statute compelled to provide such accommodation, he will take immediate steps
to see that similar accommodation is provided by the Northern Ireland Road
Transport Board.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Mr. Lowry): The answer to the first
part of the question is in the negative.
The provision of waiting rooms and
lavatory accommodation for the travelling public would appear to be covered by
those Sections of the Road and Railway
Transport Act of 1935 which require the
Railway Companies and the Northern
Ireland Road Transport Board to provide
reasonable facilities in connection with the
operation of their undertakings. The
procedure to be followed in order to obtain
any new or improved facilities, as the
hon. Member is aware, has been laid
down in the Act.
The Board has provided the facilities
referred to in many towns, but I am sure
the hon. Member will appreciate that it
is a matter for consideration whether or
not it would be held reasonable to expect
the Board to provide these facilities in
every town and village in Northern Ireland served by the Board.
The position of railway companies who
have fewer stopping places and whose
trains do not use the public roads, is, as
I am sure the hon. Member will agree,
somewhat different.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Arising out of the
right hon. Gentleman's reply, may I ask
whether it is a fact that the only shelter
from wind and weather that these bus
passengers have is what they can get from
a lamp post or telegraph pole?
RESIDENCE PERMITS.
2. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he can state if
it is a fact that residents in Northern
Ireland who have gone to Great Britain
to do war work require to get a residence
permit before they can again take up
residence in Northern Ireland.
Mr. LOWRY: The Residence in Northern Ireland (Restriction) Order, 1942,
applies to all persons over the age of 14
years, except those specially provided for
in the Order, who were not resident in
Northern Ireland immediately before the
1st January, 1940.
Persons who were not resident on the
date mentioned and who later returned
to Northern Ireland must comply with
the terms of the Order and obtain residence permits. Special consideration is,
however, given to these cases.

it is the intention of the Government to
do anything to protect the farming community from the ravages of gipsies and
other travelling merchants, and whether
he is aware of the fact that, although
the farming community have made many
protests about this annoyance, their protests so far have achieved nothing and
the annoyance continues.
Mr. LOWRY: The police are doing
and will continue to do everything in
their power to exercise control over

way

card under the national registration
scheme 48 hours are given for its production. I will take steps to see that that is

6. Dr. LYLE asked the Minister of
Health and Local Government whether
he can state if it is a fact that a Mr.
Watson on 12th November, 1937, and
on several subsequent occasions asked

was refused, an enquiry into the
circumstances connected with the death
and burial of his son-in-law, Wilfred
Shelley Pearce in connection with
which there were suspicious circumstances in Ballymoney Fever Hospital
on 30th August, 1935; whether the
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Dr. Lyle]
deceased was hurriedly buried, at the
instance of the management of the
Northern Counties Hotel,
Hotel, Portrush,
four or five hours after death, and
without the consent of his next-of-kin,
although the nurse in charge of the
deceased had been notified by telephone
that the father-in-law of the deceased
was crossing from England and would
be in Ballymoney in the forenoon of
the day following the death and would
make the funeral arrangements; and
whether he will now hold an enquiry
into all the circumstances connected
with this death.
The MINISTER of HEALTH and
LOCAL GOVERNMENT (Mr Grant);
The facts of this case are, so far as I
have been able to ascertain, as stated
in the first two parts of the hon. Member's question, though the Ministry of
Home Affairs did not consider the circumstance suspicious or at any rate
sufficiently so to warrant special inquiry.
Mr. Watson could have had recourse
to law had he considered that his son-inlaw had suffered from neglect by either
the medical practitioners or the Hospital
authorities involved.
I do not consider that any useful
purpose would be served by reopening
the question of a departmental inquiry
so long after the event.
Dr. LYLE: Is it not a fact that this
death was not registered until several
days after the burial took place and that
when it was registered it was registered
under a false name, the Christian name
being wrongly given; and does the Ministry not consider that, as this man was
hurried into his grave four or five hours
after he died or was supposed to have
died, there were sufficient grounds to hold
an inquiry?
Mr. GRANT: If the facts are as stated
by the hon. Member I think the proper
time to have had an inquiry was immediately after the death, not seven years
afterwards.

Minister's statement that an inquiry
would serve no useful purpose, would it
not be a useful purpose if that inquiry
brought out certain facts which would be

whoever he may be, in dealing with cases
of this kind; and is it not a fact that
there were several cases of complaint
about that time, one from Downpatrick
Mental Hospital where a girl lost her life
and the father was not satisfied, and
another from Purdysburn Mental Hospital
where a girl was burned to death and
there was practically no inquiry, but only

of
8. Mr. LYONS asked the Minister of

children were brought into line with those

in Great Britain, whereby

Mr. GRANT: The answer is in the
negative.
The immunity from smallpox which
Northern Ireland has enjoyed for many
years has, in the main, been due to the
enforcement of the law requiring children
to be vaccinated, and I am not prepared
to take any step which would expose the
community to the risk
the risk of smallpox
through having a large proportion of the
population unvaccinated, nor am I prepared to encourage any action which
would tend to do so even to the slightest
degree.
I am advised that there is no question
in the mind of the medical profession
that vaccination protects from smallpox,
and that no person who has had actual
experience in dealing with the disease
will dispute the protection which vaccination and revaccination afford.
I am
not aware of any definite
evidence that vaccination injuriously
affects young children or causes them unnecessary suffering.
I am publishing in the Report a statement showing the number of cases of
smallpox and deaths therefrom reported
as occurring in England and Wales, in
Scotland and in Northern Ireland since
the year 1921, and I am satisfied that
even a casual examination of the statement
will convince the hon. Member that it
would be a great and needless risk to
bring the vaccination law of Northern
Ireland into line with that of Great
Britain in the manner suggested.

PARLIAMENT (ELECTIONS AND
MEETING) BILL.
Order for Second Reading read.
Mr. LOWRY: This Bill is closely connected with two measures enacted by the
Parliament at Westminster, the Parliament (Elections and Meetings) Act, 1943,
and the Parliamentary Election (Wartime Regulations) Act, 1944.
Under the Representation of the People
Act, Northern Ireland of 1928, the register to be used for elections of members
to this House is to be the register
"containing the names of
persons
entitled for the time being to vote as
parliamentary electors at elections of
members to serve in the Parliament of the
United Kingdom"; subject, of course, to
certain differences established by enactments of this House.
The current Westminster register, and,
consequently, the current register for
Stormont elections, is that prepared in
1939, but even this out-of-date register
will disappear on the day appointed
under the 1943 English Act for the coming into effect of the new procedure. This
will be, at latest, within the next few
weeks. There will then be no register in
existence on which our elections could be
held since, for the present, a register will
be published in England only when required, and in the case of a by-election,
only for the constituency affected.
Steps must, therefore, be taken to
consider what we must do here to provide
machinery for the creation of a register
for use for Stormont elections.
new
A fairly comprehensive memorandum
has been printed as an introduction to the
Bill and is accordingly in the hands of
Members. My review can, therefore, be
brief and in the nature of a summary.
The essential links with the
Imperial system will be found in Sections
5, 8 and 10, which, subject to the appropriate Northern Ireland modifications,
identify the persons entitled to be registered for Northern Ireland Parliamentary
elections with those entitled to be registered for Westminster constituencies in
Northern Ireland in the "Civilian Residence,' "Service Voters," and "War
Workers Abroad" sections of the register.
""
Sections 6, 7 and 9, reproduce for
Northern Ireland the provision made in
the 1943 English Act, as amended by the
1944 Act, for business premises electors,
civilian absent voters, and voting by
Service electors. Section 11 provides for
the making of regulations governing
the machinery of registration, and
specifically permits the application of the
corresponding regulations made under the
United Kingdom Acts. Section 12 provides for the execution of duties in regard
to the register by registration officers and
overseers. Section 23 provides for the
position on the expiry of the United
Kingdom 1944 Act, and brings the Northern Ireland provisions into line with those
which will then apply for the United
Kingdom. So much for the register.
Section 1 gives statutory basis to the
register to be compiled as required.
Sections 2 and 3 reproduce the United
Kingdom alterations of election timetables and the procedure regarding the
dissolution of Parliament consequential
upon the new system.
The general effect of all this is that an
index of prospective electors will be continuously maintained and kept up to date
by registration officers, this index serving
both Westminster and Stormont franchise.
When a general election is imminent, for
either Parliament, the Proclamation will,
if considered desirable, require the dissolution at a future date. The election
will, however, be regarded as having been
initiated on the date of the Proclamation.
The index will be frozen as
on the
"qualifying_date" for the present the
last day of the month next before that in
which the Proclamation is made-and
from the index so frozen a register will be
published, 36 days being allowed for this.
purpose. Approaching the publication
date, Parliament will dissolve, and the
election procedure will proceed, the commencing date of the usual time-table being
the date of publication of the register, not,
as heretofore, the date of dissolution.
When the election is over the register will
lapse, the index carrying on as the basis
for further registers.
At a later stage, when facilities become
available, a basic register will be published, and kept up to date by supplementary lists. This will shorten the
interval needed between the initiation of
the election and the poll.
Part II of the Bill, as hon. Members
will see from the printed memorandum,
is mainly concerned with the clarification
Parliament Bill-

of the law on the direction and conveyance
of writs for the election of members of
the Northern Ireland House of Commons,
a matter which in the past has largely
been guided by custom. I beg to move.

now read a Second time.

Home Affairs.
PAYMENT OF R.U.C. PENSIONS.
2. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state if
arrangments will be made to issue pension
vouchers to ex-members of the R.U.C.
who are in receipt of pensions annually
instead of monthly, and thus bring the
R.U.C. pensioners into line with R.I.C.
pensioners in so far as payments of their
pensions are concerned.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Mr. Lowry): In the case of both R.I.C.
and R.U.C. pensioners the pension is
payable monthly in advance. There is
some slight difference in the procedure
in regard to the payment of these pensioners, but such difference does not result in any more favourable treatment
being accorded to the one class rather
than to the other, and I see no good
reason for making any change in the
method of payment of R.U.C. pensioners.
Mr. NIXON: With regard to the
Minister's reply, as a matter of fact do
not the R.I.C. pensioners get twelve
vouchers in one envelope, which occupies
one clerk for half an hour, whilst the
R.U.C. get twelve vouchers, one every
month, which means that a clerk is occupied every month sending the latter that
the more important authority sends in
one envelope? If they can do it that way
why not for the convenience of the staff
and the convenience of the men, some of
whom are aged, follow the procedure
adopted by the R.I.C. authorities?
Mr. JOWRY: It is correct to say that
the R.I C. pensioners get twelve vouchers
at the beginning of the year and the
R.U.C. get a paying order on the second
day of every month. Personally if I
were a pensioner I would rather get a
paying order like that because I might
mislay any of the other eleven. I think
it is much more convenient.
Mr. NIXON: With regard to the
Minister's statement that he would
rather get a paying order on the second
of every month does the Minister know
that the pensioners prefer to get them
the same as the R.I.C., and does he know
they do not always arrive on the second
day of the month and the man who is a
pensioner of both Forces goes down on the
first of the month and has to go down
again on the second or third of the
month?
Mr. LOWRY: The man who draws
two pensions should make the one
journey do. He could wait until the
second comes.
Mr. NIXON: If the Minister were
living on a small income he would be glad
to get the R.I.C. pension on the first of
the month and would not wait until the
second. These men, not being so favourably situated as the Minister, prefer to be
paid the same as the R.I.C. on the first
of the month. I do not think the
Minister or anyone else can see any objection to it.

Fishing Industry.
BOX POOL.
5. Mr. BROWN asked the Prime
Minister whether he can state by whom
the Box Pool of Northern Ireland
for the fishing industry was set
up; the
names of its chief officials
and
the salaries they receive; the
number of officials employed; the income
and expenditure for the past twelve
months and the total income since its inception; how this income and expenditure
is made up; by whom the income was
subscribed; and whether the question of
its abolition has been or will be considered.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF
THE MINISTRY OF
COMMERCE (Mr. Maginess): I have
been asked by my right hon. Friend to
reply.
I am informed that the Northern Ireland Box Pool was formed by local fish
merchants at the request, and with the
assistance of the Ministry of Food, in
order to economise in the use of timber
and other ancillary materials. The Pool,
which is an non-profit earning concern,
is operated by a Management Committee
comprising six representatives of the
Northern Ireland Fish Merchants, all of
whom are acting in an honorary capacity.
The paid staff consists of a secretary,
three port managers, two lady clerks, and
a washing, repairing and servicing staff
of eight workmen. I understand that
the Ministry of Food does not require
particulars in regard to the personnel,
salaries, or income and expenditure to be
furnished to it, and that such particulars
are not, in fact, recorded by that Ministry. I am, therefore, not in a position
to furnish the information under these
heads for which the hon. Member asks.
Mr. BROWN: If the Parliamentary
Secretary is not prepared to recommend
the abolition of this pool, which I think
he should, is the Ministry prepared to
consider the question of giving the fishermen representation on the pool as well
as the interest represented at present?
REOPENING OF GLASGOW
MARKET.
6. Mr. BROWN asked the Prime
Minister whether he can state if the reopening of the Glasgow market for Northern Ireland fish extends to fishermen
or only to merchants and dealers, and
whether in the event of fishermen being
excluded from the concession he will
take the necessary steps or make the
necessary representations in the appropriate quarters to have restored to the
fishermen the right they formerly enjoyed of direct access to the Glasgow
market.
Mr. MAGINESS: I have been asked
by my right hon. Friend to reply.
With a view to relieving the difficult
shipping position my Ministry recently
approached the Ministry of Food in regard to the possibility of allowing surplus
supplies of Northern Ireland white fish
to be marketed in Glasgow. As the hon.
Member is aware, the Ministry of Food
accepted that suggestion, and shipments
are now being made direct to Ayr and
Glasgow. This concession, however, does.
not affect the Order made by the Ministry of Food requiring all white fish
landed at fishing ports both in Great
Britain and in Northern Ireland to be
sold by auction at the port of landing,
nor the Ministry of Food's Allocation
Scheme which provides for the allocation
of the landings amongst the normal
buyers at each port on all occasions
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
26 OCTOBER 1944

when the fish realises the maximum
control price at the auction. As the
hon. Member will, therefore, appreciate,
shipments to the Glasgow market may
only be made by merchants.
In regard to the second part of the
question, I would point out that so long
as shipping space remains as restricted
as at present, no advantage would be
gained by allowing the fishermen to export the fish on their own account, since
the shipments made by the merchants
would occupy the whole of the shipping
space available on all occasions when the
landings were heavy, and, I understand,
it is only on such occasions that the
fishermen are not assured of receiving the
maximum price at the auction. For this
reason I regret that I cannot make the
representations suggested by the hon.
Member.

fish direct to the Glasgow market as

Mr. MAGINESS: It is not necessary

know what the situation is.
Mr. BROWN: If the Parliamentary
Secretary knows what the situation is
will he tell us what he is going to do to

Hospital Accommodation.
PROVISION FOR TUBERCULOSIS
PATIENTS.
Mr. THOMPSON (by private notice)
asked the Minister of Health and Local
Government whether he can give the
House any information regarding the
provision of sanatorium accommodation
for tuberculosis patients.
Mr. GRANT: I am very grateful to
the hon. Member for Ballynafeigh for
giving me the opportunity of making this
statement.
When I became Minister of Health
one of the matters which came most.
forcibly to my attention was the situation
regarding sanatorium
for tuberculosis patients.
accommodation
Both the main sanatoria of the province the one at Whiteabbey and the
one at Forster Green-had long waiting
lists of patients for admission and I felt
that unless something were done to provide additional accommodation matters
would be desperate.
Various schemes for providing small
amounts of additional accommodation
at institutions throughout Northern Ireland were examined.
Some proved feasible; against some
there were insuperable objections, but
in the main it was extremely difficult to
find suitable accommodation for tuberculosis patients at places where skilled
treatment would be available for them as
well as merely a bed in which they could
be housed.
Meanwhile the Ministry was also faced
with the need for securing additional
emergency hospital accommodation for
general cases.
Whilst various smaller projects were
being investigated, and steps had actually
been taken to put some of them into
operation, the war began to take a very
favourable turn.
the
This seemed to me to open up
possibility of securing some existing
military hospital accommodation of a
size which would be sufficient not merely
to deal with general emergency hospital
needs but which would also enable me to
meet the need of beds for tuberculosis
patients in a comprehensive way.
Negotiations with the military authorities were undertaken through the Department of my right hon. Friend the Minister of Finance, and I am happy to say
that the War Office has now approved in
principle an arrangement whereby my
Ministry will shortly take over as an
emergency hospital the excellent military
hospital accommodation in the premises
of the Industrial School at Balmoral and
in the Musgrave Park.
There will be room for upwards of a
thousand hospital beds and the buildings
are such that emergency hospital accommodation can be provided there both for
general hospital patients as well as for
tuberculosis and other special types of
cases in separate buildings under conditions which I am assured are ideal for
the purpose.
It is proposed in the first place to use
a portion of this hospital to replace
certain emergency hospital accommodation which has hitherto been made
available at the Purdysburn Mental
Hospital.
The freeing of the accommodation at
Purdysburn will in itself be extremely
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
26 OCTOBER 1944
valuable as it will enable many patients
who should ordinarily have been treated
at Purdysburn to be returned there from
the county mental hospitals to which they
have been boarded out, and will save a
good deal of expense and inconvenience.
This, in its turn, will ease the problem
of accommodation at mental hospitals in
the counties.
A substantial proportion of the Musgrave Park accommodation will be
allocated for the reception of patients
throughout Northern Ireland awaiting
tuberculosis sanatorium treatment.
The need is particularly urgent in the
case of the city of Belfast and the
counties of Antrim and Down, and hon.
Members will, I am sure, agree with me
that the emergency accommodation being
situated as it is, is eminently suitable for
this purpose.
"
Expert medical staffs are convenient
and full facilities for treatment will be
available.
Certain details regarding finance and
equipment yet remain to be settled with
the War Office, but my Department will
shortly be communicating with the responsible local authorities. as to the
financial and other arrangements, and
the new accommodation will be staffed
and organised with the utmost speed.
The portion of the premises which will
be available for tuberculosis patients will
provide ample accommodation to deal
with numbers well in excess of the present waiting lists throughout the country.
I hope, therefore, that within a very
short time I shall be in the happy position
of being able to say that there is not a
single T.B. patient willing and anxious
to accept sanatorium treatment for whom
a bed is not available.
Hon. Members will, of course, appreciate that this must be regarded purely
as a temporary settlement of this problem.
My Ministry will hold the premises
under the requisitioning powers granted
by the Defence Regulations, and the
Belfast Corporation will, I am sure, be
anxious to resume occupation of these
premises for their peace-time use as soon
as they can be made free for them.
Nevertheless the scheme will give us a
breathing space to enable the whole question of permanent sanatorium accommodation to be carefully worked out and
undertaken without any necessity for
panic measures.
Before I conclude I should also like
to let hon. Members know that all preliminary arangements have now been
made by my Ministry in collaboration
with the Commissioners acting for the
Tuberculosis Committee of the Belfast
Corporation for the setting up in Belfast
of a system of miniature mass-radiography. This is the most up-to-date
method for early detection of tuberculosis conditions.
The necessary scientific equipment has
been obtained, a medical director for the
new service has been chosen- -a North of
Ireland man, a graduate of Queen's
University, with extensive experience in
the organisation of a similar scheme in
one of the English counties-and at no
distant date the scheme will be put into
operation. There is, of course, a good
deal of training of locally recruited personnel and detailed work to be put in
before the mass-radiography unit can
actually start.
I feel that in very difficult circumstances I can reasonably say that excellent
progress has been made in dealing with
this very urgent problem.
Sanatorium accommodation, expert
medical treatment, and the inception of
the most modern method for early detection of the disease will, at any rate,
lay the foundations for an offensive.
against tuberculosis.

to my question. I feel sure it will be

Minister to tell us whether it is the

regards the Supplementary Estimate it
is not proposed to proceed with Class
II, No. 4, for the present.

was to ask the Minister of Home Affairs
if he proposed to take any steps to implement the promise which he gave in this
Personation at Elections
Personation at Elections
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Nixon]
House very emphatically to take measures
to stop personation for all time. Personation is a scandal that no respectable
man could stand over, and I have heard
nobody inside or outside this House defending or attempting to defend it. Any
little political advantage that may be
gained from personation is no use. It is
only temporary. It is no good at all in
the end. I know it is very demoralising
to young people. At the by-election
there were two young girls who were
brought to personate by older people.
They were arrested and sentenced to three
months' imprisonment. I signed a
memorial with others to get them out,
and the Minister very decently liberated
them, but that cannot go on for ever.
As a matter of fact, the girls were working against the side I was for. That
would not make any difference to me. I
do not want to see young people being
sent to prison and disgraced for all time.
This is an awful scandal in Northern
Ireland. If it would be any help to the
Minister, I suggest that the only way to
stop it is to make all voters use their
identity cards, which the presiding officers
could stamp. The only person fit to be
in charge of a polling station that I know
of is a civil servant, because the persons
appointed for one day are
very often
politicians and partisans, very often of
a bad type. Sometimes they do not know
their job and deliberately favour one
side. If a candidate gets in he lets it go,
and if a candidate is defeated and is
disgusted he lets it go. Parliament is
what we are fighting this for the right
to elect whom we wish, and to abide by
the decisions of Parliament whether you
like the decisions or not. Many a time
I am in the minority, but in any case
I respect the decision of the House. The
foundation of the whole thing is elections.
There is no use in people talking about
juvenile delinquency when young people
and old people, too, are able to steal
other people's votes and make Parliamentary elections a farce.
I am not condemning any particular
political party at all. I am not going to
do that. I do not want any political
party to be allowed to personate.
A
terrible burden is thrown on a candidate
having to pay people to watch for personation. Maybe some are taking payment from both sides as often happens.
I have known it to happen over and over
again.
It should be made impossible
and then there would be no trouble about
it, but it will never be right as long as
the presiding officers, and particularly the
man in charge of the booth, are picked
up here and there. The person in charge
should be qualified to act as presiding
officer, and I think everybody would
have confidence in the Civil Service. If
civil servants were in charge having the
assistance of the police there would not
be any trouble at all. When the election
would be over you would know you got in
by the votes of the majority. Many a
person has gone about believing till his
death and rightly so that he was
defeated by personation.
Personation has been wholesale. It
was at that by-election I referred to. I
know as much about watching as any
man here and I could not stop it.. I gave
an agent's book to a friend of mine. The
book shows who voted. He looked
through the book and saw how many
voters residing within the few streets
where he lived had been personated. He
could tell me there were about 22. Some
of them were dead. The rest were out of
the country. Some people think it is a
joke, but it is not a joke.
demoralise young people by making them
have no respect for the law then you ruin
everything, and in the end you would not
know who got in and who did not get in.
The Minister has expressed himself in
sympathy with what I have suggested, so
has everybody I have heard speaking
publicly on the matter, and I hope, and
I am sure everyone hopes, that he will
get a favourable reply from the Minister
now.

2. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Health and Local Government whether
he can state if it is a fact that he sent a
letter to local authorities urging such
authorities when making appointments

statement to the effect be embodied in the

when appointing the Chairman of the

National Fire Service,
The MINISTER OF HEALTH AND
LOCAL GOVERNMENT (Mr. Grant):
The answer to the first part of the question is in the affirmative.
With regard to the remainder, these
are matters which do not concern my
Department.
Mr. NIXON: With regard to the latter
part of the Minister's answer to the effect
that these matters do not concern his
Department, is the Minister not the individual who made the two appointments

responsible.

ARMAGH URBAN AND RURAL
WATER SUPPLY.
4. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Health and Local Government whether he
can state what is the position of the water
supply in Armagh urban district in view
of the recent inquiry held by his Department; whether a scheme will soon be instituted in view of the fact that Armagh's
water supply position is acute; and
whether he can state the cause of the
delay in having a scheme brought forward.
Mr. GRANT: My Ministry recently
sanctioned the borrowing of £5,000 by
the Armagh Urban District Council for
the purpose of carrying out certain works
in connection with the provision of an
emergency water supply for the urban
district. The necessary pipes have already
been delivered in Armagh.
5. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Health and Local Government whether
he has read Medical Inspector Weir's report concerning conditions prevailing in
Armagh rural district, and if so, whether
he will urge this Council to take steps to
ensure better sanitation and a better
water supply in this area.
Mr. GRANT: The answer to the first
part of the question is in the affirmative.
On the 6th instant my Ministry addressed
a letter to the Armagh Rural District
Council requesting them to take appropriate action to have remedied the various
matters to which the medical officer drew
attention in his report. The Ministry's
letter was considered at a meeting of the
Rural District Council on the 10th instant, and instructions were given to the
Council's medical officer of health and
their engineer to investigate the matters
in question and submit detailed reports
to the Council at an early date.

the

HOUSE OF COMMONS

Health Services.
NON-PULMONARY TUBERCULOSIS
3. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Health and Local Government whether
he can state the main reasons which contribute to non-pulmonary T.B., the ages
at which people are most susceptible to
the disease; what leads to death in some
cases; what permanent disabilities, if
any, are liable to develop among persons
who contract the disease, but do not
actually die of it; and generally such other
information as might be calculated to
assist the public in guarding against infection.
Mr. GRANT: It would be quite impossible for me to deal adequately with the
hon. Member's inquiry by means of question and answer. He will, however, find
full information on the subject in an extremely valuable report of the Medical
Research Council on tuberculosis in wartime-printed by His Majesty's Stationery
Office in 1942.
I appreciate the hon. Member's point
about assisting the public to avoid infection. My Department has already made
suggestions to some of the local authorities on the question of propaganda and
health education generally; and I shall
also seek the advice of the new Health
Advisory Council on this subject.
Mr. NIXON: With regard to the
Minister's refusal to answer the question
on the ground that the answer would be
too lengthy, did he not on the last day
we met, in reply to a question by the hon.
Member for Ballynafeigh, make a longer
answer than would be necessary to deal
with this question in which the public are
very much interested?
TYPHOID FEVER AT LISBELLAW
7. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister
of Health and Local Government
whether he can state the number of
deaths (male or female) from typhoid
in Lisbellaw, Co. Fermanagh, within
recent weeks; whether conditions relating to the water supply and sanitation
are satisfactory; and whether the local
authority responsible is carrying out its
duties under the Public Health Acts.
Mr. GRANT: Two women died in
consequence of the recent outbreak of
typhoid.
Conditions relating to water supply and
sanitation are generally satisfactory and
I have no reason to believe that the local
authority is not carrying out its duties
under the Public Health Acts.
The infection was milk borne and was
not due to the public water supply.
Mr. AGNEW:
Arising out of the
reply, would the Minister kindly investigate the conditions prevailing in Lisbellaw in order to find out the facts as
to what caused this disease?

DRAINAGE SCHEME.
19. Mrs. PARKER asked the Minister
of Finance whether he can state the reason
for the delay in the preparation of the
major drainage scheme of the Moyola
River requested by the Londonderry
County Council three years ago.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Mr. Lowry): I have been asked by my
right hon. Friend to reply.
In September, 1942, the Londonderry
County Council applied for the services
of the engineers of the Ministry of
Finance to prepare an emergency drainage
scheme under the provisions of the
Drainage Act (Northern Ireland), 1942,
in respect of this river.
On the assumption that the scheme was designed to increase the acreage of cultivable land during the present emergency my Ministry
recommended the Ministry of Finance to
accede to the request and the director of
works was duly appointed. Owing to
the large number of schemes submitted
by other county councils and the paucity
of technical staff, it was necessary to draw
up a schedule for the priority of schemes
and to carry out the easiest schemes first.
The director of works, after a preliminary
inspection, was satisfied that the proposed
scheme would be a difficult one, and
accordingly proceeded to carry out schemes
of an easier nature.
He is now, however, collecting the
necessary technical data to enable the
Londonderry County Council to formulate a scheme as soon as practicable.
Mrs. PARKER: May I ask the Minister whether he considers it to be a correct
action to take to give priority to the easier
schemes rather than to the most urgent,
and is he aware of the utter devastation
which has been caused at various periods
for a number of years through flooding?
Mr. LOWRY: The sole reason was that
the director of works selected those
schemes which would give the biggest
possible area of cultivable land and which
would make the best return, because as
the hon. Lady will remember, the object
of the 1942 Act was to increase produce.
No doubt it would have been very useful
to those people to whom she refers but, the
test being as I have stated, it was, I
respectfully submit, the natural and
proper thing for the director of works to
do to pick out the schemes that would
give the best possible and quickest returns.

Henderson & Eadie, Ltd., at Lisbellaw

Number of Civil Servants.
18. Lieut.-Colonel GORDON asked the
Minister of Finance whether he can state
how many civil servants of all grades are
now in Government employment, how
many of these are holding temporary
appointments; and whether before bringing forward a proposal for building more
accommodation he will consider making
reductions in the Service.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Major
SINCLAIR): The total number of persons at present in the employment of
Departments of the Government of Northern Ireland is 7,314, of whom 2,084 are
established civil servants, and 5,230 are
temporary and unestablished employees.
In addition there are 260 established and
69 temporary employees serving with the
Forces or on loan to Imperial Governmnt
Departments.
With regard to the second part of the
question, I can assure the hon. and
gallant Member that the possibility of
effecting economies in the staffing of our
Departments is constantly engaging the
attention of my Ministry. The hon.
and gallant Member realises, I know,
that a large proportion of the staffs at
present employed are engaged on services,
mostly arising out of the war, which have
been undertaken by Northern Ireland
Departments as agents for Departments
of the Imperial Government. It follows,
naturally, that the trend of the staff
numbers must depend to a large extent
on decisions of the Imperial Government
regarding future policy, as well as on
legislative developments in our own
Parliament. Thus it happens that while
on the one hand we are retrenching staff
in certain branches of the Service, on the
other we are faced with some increases,
as, for example, in the new Ministry of
Health and Local Government. The
implementation of whatever decisions may
be taken by our Parliament to provide a
system of Social Security will presumably
also entail the employment of additional
staff. The proposals which the Government have had under consideration for
the building of further office accommodation have not left out of account
prospective decreases in the present staff
numbers. They have originated from the
Government's desire on the one hand to
release for use for their normal purposes
buildings which were taken over during
earlier stages of the war, to be used as
Government offices; and on the other
hand to re-concentrate, in the interests
Oral Answers

of economy and efficiency, the staffs of
Departments of which certain branches
were, as an emergency measure, detached
from their Headquarters within the past

The problem with which my Ministry
was confronted was to plan for the early
release of buildings in Belfast such as
the McArthur Hall, which is part of the
Methodist College; the Richmond Lodge
School; the Assembly College of the
Presbyterian Church; the University
premises in Elmwood Avenue; Hampton

The hon. and gallant Gentleman will

CLASS V. No. 2.
Educational Services.
Motion made and Question proposed,
"That a supplementary sum not exceeding
£38,460 be granted to His Majesty for
the service of the year ending 31st March,
1945, to provide for Educational
Services."
The MINISTER OF EDUCATION
(Lieut.-Colonel Hall-Thompson): The
additional sum required in this Estimate
for Educational Services amounts
£38,460. It is made up under two
headings, increased payments to certain.
to
public elementary school-teachers, and
the cost of administering industrial and
other nursery centres. With regard to
the first, there are in our elementary
schools a number of teachers who have not
been trained for their profession in training colleges, and for that reason most of
them are paid salary on reduced scales as
compared with trained teachers. There
is also a class of teacher known as junior
assistant mistresses who are employed in
small schools where the attendance of
pupils is not sufficiently large to justify
the appointment of a full assistant.
These also, whether trained or untrained,
are paid at lower rates than the assistant
teachers. Our untrained teachers correspond to what are known in England as
"uncertificated" teachers.
The Ministry of Education in England,
on the recommendation of the Burnham
Committee, recently decided to increase
the salary scales of the uncertificated
teachers by 25 per cent. The reasons
which actuated the Ministry in granting
this increase apply with equal force in
Northern Ireland, and, I propose, therefore, to make a similar concession here.
It will not be applied to all untrained
teachers, some of whom are already paid
on the same basis as trained teachers,
but, in general, will have the effect of
giving the teachers who are in receipt of
salary in the lower scales the same
benefits as have been granted in England.
It will also be extended to all junior
assistant mistresses. The arrangement
both in England and in Northern Ireland is of a temporary nature and will be
reviewed at the end of the present
financial year.
Turning to the second heading-Industrial and other Nursery Centreshon. Members will recollect that last
year a number of nursery centres for the
children of mothers engaged in industry
were established in the city of Belfast.
They were originally administered by the
Ministry of Commerce, but the view has
been taken that, having regard to their
close similarity to nursery schools, they
should more appropriately come under
the control of the Ministry of Education.
In addition to these industrial centres
there were es' ablished, in several of the
provincial towns, nursery centres for
evacuated children. These evacuation
centres were administered by the Ministry of Health and Local Government on
2039 Supplementary Estimates- HOUSE OF COMMONS

Educational Services
.
[Lieut-Colonel Hall-Thompson]
behalf of the Imperial Ministry of.
Health. Owing to the return of evacuees
to Belfast, however, they have ceased to
fulfil their original function, but many
are still in operation and caring for the
children of mothers who are working.
These also are being taken over by the
Ministry of Education.
Nursery schools may be expected to
play a much larger part in our future
educational system than in the past, and
these centres, which have been created
as an emergency war-time measure will,
I hope, form a nucleus for a new system
of nursery schools. Parliament has
already made provision, in the Ministry
of Commerce vote, for the cost of the industrial centres during the present
financial year, but that vote will now
show a saving of the total sum granted.
The cost of the centres which previously
formed part of the evacuation service has
hitherto been met by the Imperial
Ministry of Health, but will now become
a charge on the Northern Ireland
Exchequer. I beg to move.
un-
Mr. BEATTIE: I do not want to be
critical of the right hon. Gentleman in the
presentation of this Supplementary Estimate, but I want to try to get some
information in regard to the likelihood
of an all-round improvement in the salary
position of teachers. It is quite true that
you are now giving a 25 per cent. increase
to junior assistant mistresses and
trained assistant teachers. These are a
very deserving class of teacher in Northern Ireland. They were very poorly paid
and they have had to go a long, long time
before they were given any recognition,
although the cost of everything was
mounting up. Now we have got the
Burnham Committee in Great Britain,
and the authorities over there have
decided to give a 25 per cent. increase to
uncertificated teachers. You are following in that direction only to a point, and
the reason you are not going beyond that
point is because if you gave all round a
25 per cent. increase to the junior
assistant mistresses and the untrained
teachers you would be paying some of
them more than you would be paying the
trained teachers.
The only conclusion I can come to in
regard to that is that the trained teachers'
basic amount is too low. Why not extend
the 25 per cent. for the junior assistant
mistresses and the untrained assistants to
the trained teachers, adding 25 per cent.
on to the £145 per year, which is the
salary of those who go through a course of
training? I think you are stopping just
too quickly at the point where you have
stopped, because these untrained junior
assistant mistresses in the second grade
are not going to receive it. Any of those
teachers who have attained to the point
of highly efficient or good service are going
to be kept firm at that point. No improvements are going to be made, not
because they are not entitled to receive
an improvement, but because you have
too low a basic starting rate for trained
teachers, and to give an untrained teacher
a higher salary than a trained teacher
would bring you into serious difficulty
with the trained element.
I know the right hon. Gentleman has
a great desire to do the right thing, and
I want to say to him that I think he is
putting all the time he has at his disposal
into this question of reorganisation. I
know there is a soft spot in his heart for
the teaching profession. Can he give me
an assurance that although this is only
a temporary thing all teachers' salaries
will go into the melting pot, and that in
the White Paper a recommendation will
be made for a review of the salaries of
the teaching staff, because you are not
going to get good teachers if you do not
give them some encouragement to come
along? You do not pick up a teacher
here and there every day. A teacher
must have certain natural qualifications.
You can get plenty of untrained teachers,
but we do not want untrained teachers
for the children; we want to get the best
material it is humanly possible to get for
the training of the children.
Mr. NIXON: That is what you are
providing for.
Mr. BEATTIE: We are providing for
untrained teachers, because they are in
the service, and we do not want to put
them out of the service. Junior assistant
mistresses are a necessary evil. We would
not have them in now, but they are there.
They have done great service to education
in this country, although they were never
trained and have not got the qualifications we would like teachers to have.
Therefore, for the service which they have
rendered, and are continuing to render,
I am prepared, knowing that they have a
very small salary, to give my support to
an increase. In my opinion 25 per cent.

Mr. NIXON: The Minister, towards

I am glad to see something being done

will be able to enlighten us as to the probable number of untrained teachers in
Northern Ireland, because I understood
that the Ministry's regulations did not
allow untrained teachers to be appointed.
Of course if, as the hon. Member for
Pottinger said, they are there it is quite.
right to retain them and to treat them
properly while they are there. I know
that when I was on an education committee we were not allowed to consider an
untrained teacher, and very properly so,

Regarding the junior assistant mistresses, I endorse the treating of those
we have in a proper manner, but I would
suggest that all children, whether they
are in a backward school or not, should
be trained by certified teachers. I am
not complaining about the teachers who
are there, but take any other profession,
the medical profession or the solicitors'
profession, or take the trade unions. Will
a man get into a union in connection with
any trade unless he has served his time,
has passed his examinations and has a
certificate? I mean no disrespect to the
teachers who are untrained, but it must
be very embarrassing for an untrained
teacher to be in a school with a trained
teacher very much her junior. But that
is not her fault, it is the fault of circumstances. I should like to know from the
Minister how many of those two classes
are in Northern Ireland, and how many
have been appointed and recognised since
the Northern Government came into
office. That is as far as we can go in
holding the present administration responsible.
Mr. HENDERSON: I want to congratulate the right hon. Gentleman on
the way in which he has placed this

CLASS VI. No. 2.
Agricultural Services.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a supplementary sum not exceeding £75,525 be granted to His
Majesty for the service of the year ending
31st March, 1945, to defray the expenses
of the Ministry of Agriculture in respect
of agricultural education and research,
improvement of livestock, agricultural development and credit, afforestation and
diseases of animals, including sundry
grants-in-aid."
Rev. ROBERT MOORE: The total
amount of this Vote is shown as £75,525,
which is accounted for mainly by two
items. The first item is the sum of
£50,000. This is an additional provision
to meet the cost of the schemes for the
improvement of agricultural holdings, and
the second main item, amounting to
£22,000, is for the purchase of additional
areas for afforestation purposes.
Supplementary Estimates- HOUSE OF COMMONS
Agricultural Services
[Rev. Robert Moore]
I shall take first the items relating to
the improvement of agricultural holdings.
In this connection the largest amount is
accounted for in the sub-head for drainage, which includes field drainage, the
making of hill drains and of open drains,
and the cleaning of other water courses.
More than half the amount spent on land
improvement is accounted for under this
heading. Then, again, there was
marked increase in the number of schemes
for the improvement of farm roads
a
Another sub-head that accounts for a
good deal of the expenditure asked for
in, or represented by, this Vote is in connection with the construction or reconstruction of flax dams. Hon. Members
by this time, I think, are aware of the
record acreage of flax that was grown in
1943, and it was necessary if this was to
be retted that new dams should be constructed and old dams reconstructed. For
the two financial years just ended the
total number of dams either made de novo
or reconstructed amounted to something
like 12,000.
There has also been a considerable increase in the number of grants for providing water to agricultural land and
certain farm buildings, such as cowsheds
and farm dairies.
Perhaps this would be an opportune
point for me to announce to the Committee a further development in the land
improvement scheme. My right hon.
Friend the Minister of Finance and I
have had under consideration the application to Northern Ireland of the provisions
of a recent Act passed at Westminster
dealing with the supply of water for
domestic purposes to farm houses and to
farm labourers' cottages. Accordingly,
it has been decided that the present
arrangements for the supply of water to
agricultural land under the land improvement scheme shall be extended so that in
areas where a mains supply is not likely
to be available within a reasonable period
the supply may be brought to the farm
houses and agricultural cottages on the
farms. This addition to the land
improvement scheme will come into operation at once, the Government meeting up
to 50 per cent. of the cost of labour and
materials, with this proviso that there
will be no grant available for internal
fittings where the water is being taken
into the house.
To come to the other main item, the
additional sum of £22,000 is required for
the purpose of five new areas for afforestation purposes.
Two of these areas are
situated in Co. Tyrone and three in Co.
Londonderry. When the main Estimates
were introduced the sum asked for under
this heading was £6,000, as in previous
years. It has been, and is, the policy
of my Ministry to purchase new areas for
afforestation as these can be secured, and
it just happens that since the main Estimates were introduced and passed, certain
suitable holdings from an afforestation
point of view have come into the market.
It is for the purpose of these that the
£22,000 is required.
I need not remind hon. Members of the
scarcity that has existed in regard to
imported timber right throughout the
emergency period, and it is difficult to
know how we should have got through it
had it not been that a rather long-sighted
policy had been pursued over quite a
number of years before the outbreak of
war and as a consequence we have been
able to secure supplies of home-grown
timber both from Government-owned
forests and plantations in private hands.
The aim of the Ministry is to go on
planting at least 1,000 acres per annum,
and it may be of interest if I just mention in closing that at present the full
extent of afforested land, or land to be
afforested, in possession of the Government is round about 32,000 acres. The
other items of the Estimate are selfexplanatory. I beg to move.

There have been floods at various intervals. There were bad floods in 1935,

When the first flood which did so much

Home Guard-
Prime Minister's Tribute
HOUSE OF COMMONS
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Wednesday, 1st November, 1944.
The House met at Two of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
HOME GUARD.
PRIME MINISTER'S TRIBUTE.
Lieut.-Colonel PANTER (by private
notice) asked the Minister of Home
Affairs whether arrangements have been
made for "standing down" the Ulster
Home Guard.
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir Basil
Brooke): At the request of my right hon.
Friend I propose to reply to the hon. and
gallant Member's question. It has been
decided to "stand down" the Ulster
Home Guard as from to-day, and instructions have been issued to the
members of the Force accordingly.
Arrangements are being made, as
Great Britain, for holding farewell
parades. This does not mean that the
Home Guard is being disbanded. The
Force will remain in being until the disbandment of the Home Guard in Great
Britain has taken place.
in
Hon. Members, I am sure, will agree
that this is an appropriate moment to
place on record the deep sense of gratitude which this House, and indeed the
whole community, feels for the valuable
services of the Ulster Home Guard since
its formation four and a half years ago.
At that time the United Kingdom was in
peril of invasion, and with the lapse of
time it may now be difficult for us to
realise how grave the danger was.
The
Germans seemed to be carrying all before
them, and the British Forces were fighting with their backs to the wall. It was
obvious that for the safety of the homeland a second line of defence, a great
"citizen army," must be created immediately. The men of Ulster responded
swiftly and nobly to the call. They knew
that they might be called upon at any
moment to face a powerful and ruthless
foe and to save their homes from destruction and their families from
slaughter. No words can exaggerate the
importance of the role they filled in the
scheme of national defence or the
patriotism and devotion with which they
carried out their duties. All of them
were volunteers, and they gave the State
invaluable service, often in the midst of
pressing civilian duties which they never
allowed to stand between them and their
responsibilities as members of the Home
Guard. They had the advantage of being
trained by first-class military instructors,
and by their unfailing keenness and
diligence they quickly attained a very
high level of efficiency. If the need for
hurling back ån invader had arisen the
Ulster Home Guard would have proved
its fighting power and acquitted itself
with a bravery and skill worthy in every
way of British military traditions. At
all times the spirit of the Home Guard
has been exemplary, and all ranks have
earned the admiration and praise of the
authorities and all their fellow-citizens.
Victory, if not yet within our grasp, is
drawing perceptibly nearer. The decision
to "stand down" the Home Guard is one
of many portents of the coming triumph,
to which they have made their own distinctive contribution. The thanks we
now express to all ranks of the Home
Guard will be renewed, with unstinted
fervour, when our war heroes return from
distant theatres of conflict and when once
more the battle flag is furled. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)

and sat in the gallery when there was a
discussion about the Home Guard. How
they knew there was going to be a discussion about the Home Guard I do not
know, but they were there to see how it
I would be received in this House. I got
up in my place and advocated and supported it. I went the length of saying
that if the Government wanted them they
could get 200,000 men.

DUKE AND DUCHESS OF
ABERCORN.
big
Message of Greeting and Congratulation.
The PRIME MINISTER: With your
indulgence, Mr. Speaker, and the indulgence of the House, I think what I have
to say will be agreed on by all sides of
the House. We are all delighted to
see that their Graces the Duke and
Duchess of Abercorn are celebrating today their golden wedding, and I think it
is right for me to express the feeling of
the Government on an occasion such as
this. It is, I admit, a domestic occasion,
not a public occasion, but at the same
time we cannot forget that his Grace was
the first Governor of this part of the
British Empire. Ever since he accepted
this distinguished post he has interested
himself in everything that pertains to
this country. His advice has always
been of the soundest, and has always
been available to any person who endeavoured to obtain it.
It would be wrong for me to omit her
Grace in my remarks, because those of us
who have been fortunate to have good
wives realise the tremendous help they
can be, and we all know that her Grace's
activities, not only in charitable work
but in the work of the Province, have

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
HOUSING (No. 2) BILL.
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF HEALTH AND
LOCAL GOVERNMENT (Mr. Grant):
This is the first time since I became
Minister of Health that I have had the
opportunity of presenting a major Bill to
the House. I think that hon. Members
realise that I have not been idle, and they
have been very patient with me in giving
me an interval to decide how and in what
order I should tackle the many problems
that lie ahead.
To-day it is in respect of housing that
I want to put proposals before Parlia-
Housing (No. 2) Bill-
Second Reading
1 NOVEMBER 1944
e
ment.
Those proposals must be looked
at against the tragic background of our
present housing position. I am not going
to throw stones at the people who allowed
our housing to get into the state in which
it is to-day, but neither am I going to
hand out any bouquets. It is not a
matter on which one can blame the Govrnment or the local authorities, or even
private enterprise; it reflects an absence
in our country of public feeling about
housing conditions which had long since
begun to arouse the public conscience
throughout the rest of the Kingdom.
I am very glad now to see evidence of
growing interest in modern housing requirements, as instanced by the setting
up of organisations like the Women's
Housing Advisory Council. Such organisations will build up an informed public
opinion about housing. There is no doubt
that between the wars the people of
Northern Ireland did not feel as strongly
as they should have done about the housing conditions under which so many of
them were living. Financial stringency
had something to do with the lack of progress, and so had the lower general standards under which our people were living
at that time.
Between the wars we heard a good deal
of talk about "rubber stamp" legislation
and the step-by-step policy. I think we
are only beginning to realise how much
Northern Ireland owes to men like my
right hon. Friend the Member for Mid-
Down, who, whatever the difficulties and
whatever the financial stringency, insisted
that Ulster workers should enjoy the same
social services as their fellow-citizens in
Great Britain. The determination was
his own, but the inspiration for it came
from a firm conviction among the electorate that they should keep to British
standards. I can only regret that the
public conscience on housing was so much
less alert.
There is this to be said for public apathy
in the past, however, and it is that the
facts were not readily accessible. Now
there is no excuse. The Planning Advisory Board has recently published an
admirable report on housing, which sets
out in the clearest possible terms the
deplorable state in which we find ourselves. I am very grateful to the Board's
Committee on housing and the country
owes them a debt of gratitude for focusing public interest upon our housing
needs.
The Report tells us that in 1918 our
housing was at a lower standard than in
Great Britain, and that even in Scotland,
where the standards were very much
lower than in England and Wales, the
position was no worse than in Northern
Ireland. The Report goes on to show
that between the wars the combined efforts
of the State, the local authority and
private enterprise built no more than
half our population proportion of the
houses built across the water. Thus
while in 1939 the housing problem in
Great Britain was well on the way to
solution, here we had dropped relatively
further and further behind. The Housing Report estimates our immediate need
of houses at 100,000, and I was taken to
task in some quarters for mentioning a
figure of such magnitude. I want to say
definitely that this figure of 100,000 is an
understatement. It represents a building
programme which will tax all our
resources for many years, but even when
it is carried out there will still be further
work. There will be the replacement of the
existing houses which have deteriorated
in the interval, the replacement of the
57,000 houses with defective light and
ventilation, and the provision of houses
to cope with the 9,000 marriages which
take place each year in Northern Ireland.
Hon. Members themselves have a fair
enough idea of the number of young
married couples who are at present living
with their "in-laws." While I appremany
ciate the fact that there are
admirable "in-laws," I am quite sure the
House will agree with me in saying that
in starting married life young people
should have homes of their own. The
figure of our real needs, therefore, if our
housing is to be brought up to and maintained on modern lines, is very much in
excess of the 100,000 figure I have already
mentioned.

see
more
Just as our ultimate, aim is to provide
new houses up to our quota of the
numbers which have been built and will
be built across the water, so I want to
the adoption of standards
nearly approximate to those in Great
Britain for the actual houses as they are
built. Between the wars far too many
of our houses were undersized and without proper amenities. The Housing
Report makes certain general recommendations about room sizes and, I
should like to say that, generally speaking, I agree with their recommendations
Housing (No. 2) Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS

[Mr. Grant]
and will see that they form part of our
new housing code.
For the future, the standard I will set
for housing in Northern Ireland is that it
shall, as speedily as possible, be brought
up to the British level. The present
standards fixed represent an immense
advance on anything hitherto applicable
in Northern Ireland, and the next thing
is to get a good number of houses built
up to those standards. The need, therefore, is for many new houses and for
houses generally of a much better
standard than we have been accustomed
to provide for our people in the past.
The need represents a task greater in
some areas than in others, but nevertheless a really large task everywhere.
On whom then is the task to fall? The
Government cannot absolve itself from
responsibility. It has its job to do; it
must do what it can to see that materials
and labour and money are available in
the greatest possible degree. The Government must see to it that adequate
priority is given to the need for new
houses in relation to the need for the
repair of old ones, the building of new
factories, public works, and so forth. In
itself this will be no small task. The
whole question of allocating materials and
labour to the jobs where they will do most
good to the community is one which has
been exercising the Cabinet as a whole
for some time past.
Before I leave this question I should
like to give the House some idea of the
problems involved. Clearly the resources
of the building industry are going to be
heavily taxed in the next few years. It is
not feasible to devote the whole output of
the industry to new housing. There, will be
heavy arrears of repair and maintenance
to existing buildings all over Ulster. New
buildings for industry and commerce will
have to be provided, for there is no use
providing good houses if the people have
no work, and no means of earning their
living.
Naturally we are looking to an expansion of the building industry to meet
the enormous demand with which it will
have to cope.
But hon. Members will
have no difficulty in realising that it requires constant effort on the part, not
merely of one department, but of several,
to see that building capacity is used to
the best advantage, that there are no unnecessary periods of idleness in the building trade, and that our own industrial
resources are used to the fullest possible
extent for the production of materials and
fitments necessary to provide for a large
building programme. Machinery has
already been framed to deal with this
aspect of the matter.
Then, so far as house building is concerned, there are the actual selection of
the sites, the making of plans, the placing
of contracts, the letting of the houses and
their management and repair. All this
part of the work has in the past, except
in so far as it has been done by private
enterprise and the speculative builder,
been the responsibility of the local
authorities. Upon them, at any rate in
the case of the municipal authorities,
there has been laid a specific and direct
responsibility since 1919 for providing
such housing as was necessary for the
working classes in their areas.
But local authorities are limited in
their resources, financial and otherwise.
In my opinion, and I am sure the House
will agree with me, it is quite impossible
to expect local authorities to bear the
financial burdens, or indeed to provide
the essential working machine to cope with
a building programme which in the postwar period would amount to nearly thirty
times the number of houses which were
built by all the local authorities between
the two wars.
They will, however, have to bear a
reasonable share of the work. And one of
the first questions which the local authorities will ask is, what is it going to cost
the rates? That, unfortunately, is a
question which frankly I am unable to
answer. It depends upon a number of
factors of varying importance. Among
them I may mention the amount of
Government subsidy which is to be paid.
On this question the Bill provides an
answer, at any rate in principle.
Another factor is the rate of interest at
which housing can be financed. In regard
to this point, my right hon. Friend, the
Minister of Finance, made an announcement a few weeks ago in this House which
did not at the time bring him the congratulations its importance merited. In
the past the efforts of our local authorities to provide houses at a reasonable rent
were seriously crippled by the fact that
they had to borrow money at a higher
Housing (No. 2) Bill-
Second Reading
1 NOVEMBER 1944

rate of interest than would have been
the case with similar authorities in Great
Britain. The Minister of Finance, however, has now been able to arrange that
housing loans here shall be made at the
same rate as in Great Britain. This rate
is at present 31 per cent.- -a very subtantial reduction from any that has
hitherto applied in connection with this
service. I am grateful to my right hon.
Friend, and I am sure the local authorities will share my gratitude.
As I have already told the House, we
look to securing the same standards in
the housing of our people as those which
hold in Great Britain. We must also be
prepared to pay our proportion of the
cost from the Exchequer and from the
rates. I have included, therefore, in this
Bill provisions regarding finance of
houses built by local authorities which
will bring the law on the subject here into
line with that which obtains in Scotland,
where conditions are, to a large extent,
comparable with our own.
This means importing for the first time
the principle that each local authority
shall contribute annually for a period of
40 years a specified sum in respect of each
house built by it. On condition that this
is done the State will, for its part, pay to
the local authority an annual contribution for the same period in respect of the
house. The sums are £5 per annum and
£13 per annum respectively for a fiveapartment house, with proportionately
smaller sums in respect of smaller houses.
I am satisfied that the payment of an
annual subsidy is much to be preferred to
the type of lump sum subsidy which was
paid towards previous housing schemes.
I think it is a good thing in principle to
require local authorities to make a specified contribution from the rates rather
than to leave the local authorities' contribution to depend entirely on the amount
of loss or profit which arises.
The subsidies provided in the Bill must,
however, be regarded as token amounts
only in present circumstances.
The
amounts represent what was considered
necessary in pre-war conditions. On present building costs they are undoubtedly
inadequate. The trouble is that no one
is in a position to judge now what will be
an adequate amount of annual subsidy to
enable houses built in the post-war years
to be let at rents which tenants can
afford to pay.
This will depend, first of
all, upon the cost of building the houses,
•
and secondly, upon the general cost of
living and the level of wages. The total
subsidy payable in respect of each house
will have to be adjusted from time to
time so as to bring these factors into relation, and it seems to me that it is likely
to fluctuate very severely in the few years
immediately following the end of the war.
When I was speaking to the local
authorities on this matter I promised
them that whatever arrangements were
made to meet the situation would be
applied with retrospective effect to all
houses built under this Bill. I asked
local authorities to trust the Government
to see that they got a fair deal with
regard to the excess cost of building
houses and to push ahead with their plans.
I am happy to say that the local authorities met me very fairly on this point.
They appreciate the difficulty as well as
anybody, and I think they realise that
they have everything to gain and nothing
to lose by a settlement of the financial
question as a matter of actual experience
rather than as a speculation. Believe me,
if a final subsidy were settled in this Bill
it would be purely a speculation.
That is the reason for the reference in
the Bill to October, 1947, as the closing
date for financial assistance. A good
many people have mentioned this date to
me and stated that it was funny to be
talking about a long-term plan for housing while the Bill to give effect to that
plan seemed designed to cut off supplies of
money in two years. But, as I say, that
stop date in the Bill does not mean a
break in the building programme; it is
merely a concrete expression of the
promise I have given to local authorities.
that the finance of their building schemes
will be reviewed, and reviewed retrospectively, as soon as a better estimate can be
formed about post-war costs of building.
It is, unfortunately, true that the effect
of the subsidies paid in the period following upon the last war seems to have been
to maintain the cost of building at an
artificial level. As the subsidy was increased so did the cost of building rise:
when the subsidy fell the cost of building
fell. The Imperial Government have
been perfectly frank on the question and
they have refused to commit themselves to
any subsidy in excess of the pre-war
figures until some experience has been
gained of post-war building costs.
It is certainly clear that so long as we
have building costs increased over pre-

ultimate sums will be decided in relation

So much for the finance of house
building undertaken by local authorities.
The other factor which will affect the
issue, so far as the rates are concerned, is
the number of houses which each local
authority will be asked to build. This in
its turn depends upon other agencies engaged in the building of houses, and the
extent to which they will operate. There
is, first of all, of course, private enterprise and the speculative builder. At the
moment, and so long as materials are in
short supply and the output of new houses
is severely restricted, a very substantial
proportion of the new houses which are
to be, built must be built for public bodies
on whom there is a definite obligation and
who will hold the houses in their ownership and let them to tenants at rents
which the working classes can afford to
pay.
So soon as the immediate famine of
houses to rent begins to disappear, so
soon will private enterprise come fully
into the picture and be able to play its
full share in providing new houses.
Private enterprise will obviously engage
in the building of new houses only if the
investment of private money in house property is made a profitable transaction. I
am not saying a hard thing in making that
statement. I am merely drawing attention
to what is human nature and ordinary
intelligence. With building costs so high
as they are at present, private enterprise
could not be expected, without a fairly
substantial subsidy from Government
funds, to engage in the building of houses
to be let at rents within the means of the
people who need them most. There would
be no difficulty in meeting the housing
shortage if building costs were such that
private enterprise could embark on a
building programme which would give
them a reasonable return for their capital.
Unfortunately, that situation is not at
present in sight.
The difficulty is to decide to what
extent and in what conditions it is right
and proper for the State, that is the
taxpayer, to give a subsidy on housebuilding by private enterprise.
The
Government in Great Britain has already
announced that it accepts in principle
the payment of State subsidy towards the
building of houses by private enterprise.
No legislation has, however, yet been
introduced on the subject, and the details
obviously need careful working out. But
I can give the House this assurance that
so soon as satisfactory proposals for the
payment of subsidy for private enterprise building have been devised by the
Imperial Government I shall without
delay come before the House with proposals which will give private enterprise
in Northern Ireland just as favourable
terms as in any other part of the Kingdom.

So far as actual building is concerned,
there is going to be no interference with
private enterprise. Houses are erected
by builders and by the building industry,
whether they are built for the State, the
local authority, or the private owner. I
give the House a definite assurance that
as soon as supplies permit the full capacity
of Northern Ireland's building industry
will be put into building works among
which housing must take highest place
in urgency and importance. In the
actual building of houses, private enterprise can, and must, play its full part.
Meanwhile, however, I am satisfied
that there is a place for a different kind
of public authority to help to meet the
immediate situation. I refer to the
Northern Ireland Housing Trust which
it is proposed to establish under the Bill,
There is an urgent and desperate need
for houses to rent (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear)-a need far in excess of what
the local authorities could reasonably be
expected to meet, at any rate within the
next few years. Building facilities and
Housing (No. 2) Bill-
