1 NOVEMBER 1944

materials are likely to be in a very great
demand, and it will be necessary to experiment in new methods of construction;
to perfect building organisation, and to
short-circuit some of the formalities in
connection with public building, in a
way which local authorities cannot reasonably be asked to do.
The Housing Trust which I propose to
establish will be working in close contact
with my Ministry. It will be able to
experiment and engage in building by
new methods, and thus be able to develop
experience in meeting many of the
difficult questions which are bound to
arise. Such experience will be of inestimable value to my Department and
to the local authorities, to whom it will
be freely made available. There has, I
think, been a certain amount of misconception about the place of the Housing Trust in the scheme of things. Let
me say first of all that it is in no sense
intended to supersede local authorities.
It is intended to supplement the activities
of the local authorities.
Though I do not wish to go into detail,
hon. Members may like to know in general
terms what is in my mind about the way
the Housing Trust will operate. In
selecting members for the Trust I shall
make it my business to see that I get
people with drive, energy, and a genuine
interest in the work of providing houses.
Other things being equal, I do not intend
to tap existing sources for this job.
Obviously a man whose hands are already
full with work on behalf of the community cannot usefully undertake further
major responsibilities such as membership
of the Trust will involve. I hope, when
the time comes, that I shall be able to
put forward names which will commend
universal acceptance.
I have laid a good deal of emphasis at
one time or another upon the necessity
for a good standard of house management, and I am afraid that an impression has got abroad that the Trust will
be operating as busybodies, prying into
the homes of the people and teaching
them how to cook. The science of house
management-for it is a science- bears
no relation at all to fancies of this kind.
I want to tell the House that wherever
skilled management has been undertaken
in Great Britain it has added greatly to
the happiness of the tenants and to the
efficient running of the housing estates
concerned. One way in which the
difference between proper management
and the methods which the ordinary
private owner adopts is to be seen in the
selection of tenants. The private owner,
through his agent, in selecting a tenant
for a house may take the man with the
biggest income and the smallest family.
This is elementary common-sense on his
part, since it safeguards the rent on the
one hand and minimises the damage to
the house on the other, but proper
management can look at these questions
in the light of the real needs of the
respective applicants, and will do so without regard to considerations which must
guide the private owner. The science of
management in Northern Ireland is still
in its infancy, but there is a great
future for it, and I hope to see it spreading to all housing estates, whether
privately owned or not.
The operations of the Housing Trust
will be financed in full by the Government. The cost will be borne on the
Estimates of my Department and will,
therefore, come up for review every year.
I have heard it said that since the houses
to be built by the Housing Trust will not
cost the ratepayers anything local authorities will be inclined to sit back and do
nothing, leaving it to the Trust to come
in and build the necessary houses in their
area at Government expense. I want to
make it clear at this stage that it is the
statutory duty of every local authority in
Northern Ireland to provide houses to
meet the needs of its working people. The
duty is clearly laid down in the case of
urban authorities in the Housing Act of
1919, and in the case of rural authorities
in an Act passed in 1906.
The fact that these requirements have
in the past been more honoured in the
breach than in the observance does not
mean that they should not be revived to
meet our present needs. The powers which
I have under those Acts entitle me to do
the work on behalf of local authorities
who do not carry out their obligations,
and to charge the costs so incurred to the
I shall see that no local authority
which neglects to do its duty in the
matter of housing is allowed to make a
financial profit out of its neglect. This
means that I must give each local authority a clear direction as to what the
Ministry regards as its duty in the provision of housing.
Housing (No. 2) Bill-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Grant]
I propose to go into this whole matter
shortly with the local authorities themselves, with a view to deciding with them
what their total programme for building
ought to be. Naturally local authorities
are not anxious to mortgage the rates to
an extent which would make them financially bankrupt and believe me I have
no desire to encourage them to do so. As
I have said, the need for houses is so
great that it is far beyond the resources
of our local authorities to meet the need
in full.
At the same time local authorities must take a share in meeting the need
and it is this share which will have to be
very carefully worked out in collaboration
with the authorities themselves and with
full regard to the financial demands which
the provision of housing as well as of the
other public services is going to make
upon the local authorities in the post-war
period.
The amount of building which the
Trust will undertake will be calculated
upon a formula to be agreed upon with
the Treasury. The formula will take into
account the position in those areas where
the need for houses is greatest, and is
beyond the resources of the local authority
to meet within reasonable period.
a
I have heard that there may be objections
to my proposals for a Housing Trust, and
to anyone who has, doubts about the
Government's wisdom in pressing on with
this proposal I should like to address a
few words. It seems to me that objectors to the Trust may be divided into two
general categories-those who are afraid
that the Trust will not do enough to help
in meeting our need of houses, and those
who, for one reason or another, fear that
it will do too much. I think I owe it to
the House to try to put these two points
in their proper perspective.
For the first class I have a great deal
of sympathy, and all I can say to them
is that I will try to pick such a Trust as
will give a speedy and efficient service in
the provision of houses. I can assure the
House that I will help and support the
Trust in every way in carrying out any
programme which is allotted to it within
the limits of the powers conferred by this
Bill and of the supply position from time
to time. Those who fear that the Trust
is going to do too much are moved by
a variety of motives. There are the
people who see in the Trust an incursion
of the State into a field hitherto reserved
for local authorities and private enterprise, and who suggest that the money
which might be given to the Trust should
be diverted to the local authorities so as
to enable them to erect at 100 per cent.
Government expense the homes which
might otherwise be built by the Trust.
I am sure that there will be some local
authorities who, by reason of their requirements, may well be able to handle
their housing problem without it being
necessary for the Trust to come to their
aid. On the other hand I am equally
sure, from my knowledge of the situation and the detailed surveys that have
been made, that there are other areas in
which the need is so great that the local
authorities should welcome the assistance
of the Trust, not only from the point of
view of finance, but also because their
local government machine, however
efficient it may be, would simply not be
capable of coping with the amount of
work involved. In Londonderry a penny
rate produces £850. Even if housing
could be financed at no greater expense
to a local authority than £5 per house per
annum it would cost Londonderry a 1s 10d
rate to provide the 3,800 houses which are
needed there to-day. This figure of
3,800, as I have already explained in
general terms, is a minimum which must
be substantially increased over any longterm view. In Newtownards the 782
houses that are needed would involve the
payment of a 2s Od rate. Taking a
smaller town-Limavady-the figures are
320 houses and a 2s 6d rate. I could
give example after example showing the
same thing. I think it is fair to say from
my consultations with the local authorities that those who most keenly appreciate the housing needs of their areas
welcome the advent of the Trust, and will
co-operate in every way with it.
The Trust will have plenty to do in
providing houses where the demand is
entirely beyond the local authorities'
power to meet without entering upon
areas which are being competently
handled by the local authorities concerned.
I do wish, therefore, that hon. Members
and all local authorities would regard the
Trust not as a fifth wheel on the coach,
but rather as a third horse to help the
wagon up the hill. Some people have
formed the impression that the Trust and
the local authorities are going to work on
formula of mathematical rigidity

until the
under which the Trust waits
local authority has put up a batch of

and carried out with the help and goodwill of the local authorities concerned.
The Bill provides that houses built by
local authorities and the Trust shall be
exempt from the Rent Restrictions Acts.
Mr. BEATTIE: Why is that?
Mr. GRANT: The main reason for
those Acts is, of course, to prevent
tenants being charged exorbitant rents in
a time of scarcity of housing accommodation. That object, in the case of
houses built by the local authority and the
Trust will be adequately secured, by reason
of the fact that the rents to be charged
will be subject to the approval of my
Ministry. I shall have to answer in this
House for the actions of local authorities
and the Trust on this point. But the
Rent Restrictions Acts have an indirect
result, and it is this, that it is exceedingly
difficult to secure possession of a house
from a tenant so long as he pays his rent,
no matter how unsuitable the house. may
be for the conditions of his family.
Under the new provisions, local
authorities and the Trust will be able to
manage their property so that no tenant
is living in overcrowded conditions, and
also so that no house. is under-occupied
by reason of there being a small family
living in one of the larger houses. The
public housing authorities will be able,
when a tenant's family has increased to
the stage where the house in which he is
living is overcrowded, to move the family
to one of the larger houses in its ownership. Correspondingly, when a large
family has shrunk, by some of the members getting married or obtaining work
elsewhere, the tenant will be encouraged
to move to a house which is more suitable
to the number of his family. I know
that people become attached to the house
in which they have lived, but it is, in
my opinion, in the present grave emergency-which I should warn people. is
likely to continue for some timeabsolutely necessary to make the most
economic use possible of our housing
accommodation.
I do not see why the taxpayer and the
ratepayer should have to spend considerable sums on housing only to see on the
one hand a five-roomed house occupied by
a middle-aged father and mother whose
children have set up homes of their own,
or on the other a three-roomed house
overcrowded with a father and mother
and several small children. I am going
to encourage local authorities and the
Trust to manage their property to the
best advantage, and I consider that if
this is to be done I must exempt the
houses from the operation of the Rent
Restrictions Acts. As I have said, the
fact that I must answer to Parliament
for the level of rents charged is, I think,
a sufficient safeguard.
Mr. BEATTIE: The labourers' cottages
will not be safeguarded.
Mr. GRANT: I should like, if I may,
to put this question of the Rent Restrictions Acts into its proper background. I
find that all houses owned by local authorities in Great Britain-nearly a million
and a half of them-and half the houses
owned by local authorities here do not
fall within the scope of the Rent Restrictions Acts. In all the United Kingdom
the only local authority houses subject to
the Acts are three thousand odd in this
country. I suggest that the houses built
here in future should be managed on the
same terms as 99 per cent. of similar
homes in all parts of the United Kingdom. I should like to say a word about
the rural areas.
Mr. AGNEW: Hear, hear.
Mr. GRANT: Up to the present rural
district councils have been enabled to
carry out housing operations only under
the provisions of the Labourers (Ireland)
Acts, which were designed to provide
houses for farm labourers.
There are
many areas within rural districts where
there is an industrial population which
requires houses just as much as the industrial population in the towns. I think
the time has come when the rather artificial distinction between the working
classes in industry and the working
classes in agriculture should be removed.
This is not the time for a complete
statement of my housing policy in regard
to rural areas, but there are just one or
two things that I would like to say this
afternoon. It seems to me that the old
Housing (No. 2) Bill-
HOUSE OF COMMONS
Second Reading
[Mr. Grant]
Labourers' Code
was framed on the
assumption that in rural Ulster there
would always be a class of people very
badly paid, living in sub-standard houses
without any of the comforts which a town
dweller expects as a matter of right, and
compensated for these terrible economic
conditions only by an abundance of fresh
air, potatoes and buttermilk. The war
has brought that era to an end and I hope
brought it to an end for ever. Now the
rural worker is regarded as a skilled
craftsman with a reasonable living wage
and with the right to some, at least, of
the amenities of town life.
If houses in the country can be grouped
together to form the nucleus of little
villagers, then modern conveniences can
be supplied at reasonable cost. The man
of the house may have to ride to his work
instead of living on the actual farm where
he is employed, but his wife can do her
shopping without a five-mile 'bus ride,
and the children will be within a reasonable distance of their school. I recognise
that this will mean a change in the traditional way of life in rural Ulster, but I
am sure that it is a change which must
come if the drift from the land is to be
averted, and if we are to rely in future
upon a prosperous and contented agriculture as the backbone of our country's
prosperity. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
It is proposed, therefore, in the Bill
that the Labourers (Ireland) Acts should
cease to operate as regards new houses in
rural areas, and that the Housing of the
Working Classes Acts should in future
apply to rural districts as well as to
municipalities. This question has been
discussed with a representative deputation from the Association of Rural
District Councils, and I believe they are
in favour of the change and consider that
it will lead to simplification of procedure
and assist them in providing houses where
they are needed. The association assure
me that they will have no difficulty in
meeting the special needs of rural workers
under the new system.
In view of what I have said earlier
about the uncertainty of the measure of
Government assistance to housing in the
post-war period, it would be useless for
me to embark on a comparison of the
terms available under the Housing of the
Working Classes Acts as compared with
the Labourers (Ireland) Acts. As I have
said, there is every argument in favour
of treating urban and rural alike so far
as legal procedure is concerned. But
that is not to say that the financial
problems of the rural districts may not
need special treatment when the position.
is clarified. Provision is contained in the
Bill for exempting houses built by local
authorities and the Trust from local bylaws. This is not put in in order to
enable these bodies to build sub-standard
houses, but because there are many areas
in which there are restrictive by-laws,
which, if strictly enforced, would hamper
the adoption of modern technique and
experimental methods.

which
professional organisations

long ago as 1890 local authorities were

As
The modern tendency in housing is to
provide a substantial amount of built-in
furniture in the actual structure of each
house. I am most anxious to foster this
tendency. It is of the greatest assistance
to people setting up home for the first time,
or to people whose work is such that they
have to move house at shorter intervals
than is normal. If the Housing Trust is
not given this power its work in the provision of modern homes will be cramped.
I have finished my description of the Bill.
The time has come for the House to discuss and then to decide upon these proposals. No one would be happier than
myself to see the usual laws of supply and
demand in operation and houses springing up everywhere in response to the
working of the profit motive. But hon.
Members know that this not the position,

and that without a very substantial

can be laid of houses which ordinary
people can afford to rent.
In this Bill we have, for the local
authorities and the Trust, secured a substantial measure of such aid. It is equal
to that obtaining in Scotland, and is in
excess of the amount granted in England
and Wales. I have already promised that
I shall come back to the House with
definite proposals as soon as I have been
able to arrange, in concert with the Imperial authorities concerned, the conditions under which private ownership
can be encouraged to play its part in
post-war housing. I trust, therefore,
that hon. Members will not ask me to
delay the passage of this valuable contribution to our housing needs until that
further step can be carried through.
Here, then, is the Bill. It will secure
the provision of houses where the need is
greatest. For the first time it provides
for annual payments by the State instead
of a lump sum subsidy.
Annual payments, coupled with the provisions about
a housing revenue account and a house
repair account, will mean that the State
throughout the lifetime of the houses
built under the Bill can ensure that they
are kept in good repair and condition.
In this I hope it will in future be known
as a tenant's charter. The Bill does no
more than lay a sound foundation upon
which we can build. Housing is a human
problem, and it is as a contribution to the
human needs of our people that I ask the
House to support this Bill. I beg to
move. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)

Mr. ANDREWS: I feel absolutely
confident that every Member of this
honourable House desires that an adequate number of houses shall be built
as quickly as possible in order to provide
comfortable, homes for our working people
in town or country, and in holding these
views we are representing the opinions of
those whom we have been honoured to
represent in this House.. It is, therefore, only a question of ways and means.
I would desire to say a few words at the
beginning of my remarks as regards what
has produced the present regrettable
shortage. Hon. Members may not be
aware of the fact that between 1923 and
1936, this Parliament of ours passed no
fewer than twelve Acts for the purpose
of encouraging houses to be built in
Northern Ireland, and also that between
1919 and 1939, 50,000 houses were built
in Northern Ireland. What has caused
the shortage is simply this: First of all,
to be. frank, it was enemy action, and in
the second place some of our local
authorities did not respond to the appeals
that were made to them and the
advantages which were offered them to
influence them to build the requisite
number of houses in their own areas.
Then again, no houses worth the name
have been built since the war, because the
materials were not available. I was very
much relieved to-day to hear my right
hon. Friend the Minister of Health and
Local Government say, as regards private
enterprise, that when the British Governmade up their minds what they were going
to do in the way of subsidising private
enterprise to the necessary extent, he
would introduce a measure in this House
to make sure, that the same standard of
help would be given to private enterprise
in Northern Ireland. Now that clears
the air, and I am sure it is a great relief
to many of us to hear that very definite
statement.
As regards Part I of the Bill, I do not
feel it necessary to say anything to-day.
I may have a few words to say in connection with some of its provisions in the
Committee stage, but I do feel obliged to
make a very definite statement as regards
Part II. May I say, as a foreword to my
remarks in this connection, that I am
convinced beyond measure that my right
hon. Friend earnestly desires to do everything humanly possible to provide an
adequate supply of houses for our working
classes. As I have said, it is only a
question of ways and means. Part II of

the best way to deal with the matter, and
for this reason. I feel that it really
means nationalisation of housing, so far
as the Trust is concerned. It is the thin
edge of the wedge, and I feel also that
it would be a deterrent I do not want
to overstate the case-to local authorities
for this reason.

There is another thing that makes one
suspicious about the whole thing. Name
one Board set up by this Government
that was a success? Take the Pigs
Board. The Prime Minister had to sack

appointed one of them Minister of
Agriculture. If a man could not look
after pigs, why was he put in charge of
horses, cattle, sheep, pigs, hens and
ducks?
Take the Transport Board. Had
it not been for the war, it would be
bankrupt. At a Rotary Club luncheon,
the manager of one of the railway companies admitted that if there is not
co-ordination between the roads and
railways after the war, the railways will
have to close down. The Government
have set up duck boards, hen boards, and
many other boards. This Bill does not
hold out one ray of hope for the people
of Northern Ireland.

The PRIME MINISTER (Sir Basil
Brooke): As the hon. Member was informed in reply to a similar question on
27th June last, the location of new industry in any particular area is determined ultimately by the directors of the
firms concerned, and there can thus be no
question of the Government "granting"
industries to any area. The hon. Member may rest assured, however, that it is
the policy of the Government to assist in
securing the widest possible spread and
the greatest possible diversification of
industry over the Province, and that the
prospects of development within the
County of Armagh are not being, and will

With regard to the second part of the
question, the hon. Member will appreciate that the post-war employment policy
of Northern Ireland cannot be formulated
independently of, or without reference to
the general policy of the United Kingdom,
which in its turn must be influenced by
general world conditions. This matter
has been dealt with comprehensively in
the White Paper on Employment Policy
issued by the Minister for Reconstruction, and my Ministry do not contemplate any separate pronouncement at this
stage.

HOUSING (No. 2) BILL.
Resumed Debate on Second Reading.
Order read for resuming adjourned
debate on Amendment to Question (1st
November), "That the Bill be now read
a Second time."
Which Amendment was to leave out all
the words after "that" and insert the
words
"this House, while in agreement with
the urgent need for adequate housing
accommodation in Northern Ireland, is
convinced that the proposals contained
in this Bill will not achieve that purpose, and therefore rejects the Bill.".
(Mr. Nixon.)
Question again proposed, "That the
words proposed to be left out stand part
of the Question."
Mr. THOMPSON: When the Minister of Health and Local Government first
made public his intended proposals of
creating a Housing Trust, the impression
I formed was that his intentions were to
gather around him a number of experienced men who had a knowledge of the
building trade to assist him in speeding
up the building of houses. I thought this
an excellent idea, but when the Bill now
before the House was received by me, and
when I had an opportunity of examining
it, I came to the conclusion that much of
it is unnecessary, and that instead of
speeding up the building of houses it will
create an elaborate machine that will
defeat its purpose.
I know the Minister of Health is as
anxious as I am to see houses constructed
as quickly as possible, but frankly, I cannot see that this Housing Trust in its
present form will help him in his efforts.
We have already in existence machinery
for carrying out some of the things the
Bill asks for, so that I fear we are going
to create an unnecessary, expensive department. I hope the Minister will make a
statement that he will be willing to accept
amendments put forward in the Committee stage to meet the wishes of the
Members. Will the Minister give us an
assurance that he will include in the Bill
a Clause giving any authorised builder or
builders the same facilities as are being
granted to local authorities. If he meets
the wishes of the House in this direction
I for one will not oppose the Bill. Personally, I should prefer to see a lump sum
subsidy given to private builders as has
already been granted to local authorities.
I submit that we should immediately
make contact with London. Might I
suggest respectfully to the Prime
Minister and the Minister of Finance that
they should immediately proceed to
London and put the whole case of Ulster
before the Chancellor of the Exchequer,
telling him that we have got the bricks,
the cement, the labour, and all the requirements for the building of houses now
and that we want a lump sum subsidy to
enable us to start? If they do that I
believe the appeal will meet with the
approval of the Minister on the other
side. Many of our builders at the present time are idle, and I would like the
Minister before, the Bill reaches the
Committee stage to give the House an
assurance that he will proceed to London
and try to get there an immediate subsidy
such as I have suggested.
If a subsidy of £390 were given for the
next 12 months for the erection of 1,000
houses by reputed builders to rent, not
for sale, in addition to those already
allocated to local authorities, this would
give us inside the next 12 months 1,750
houses in Belfast alone. These houses can be
completed before December, 1945, several
of them should be completed and ready
for occupation in late spring. I have not
the slightest doubt this can be accomplished as I will endeavour to show the
House in a moment or two. At the end
of six months or about July next, the
whole matter should be reviewed by the
Government and local authorities as the
situation will alter very quickly from
month to month next year. The labour
situation will change, the cost of
materials, the supply will change, and
other factors, unforeseen at present, will
call for a review of the position as it will
then stand.
Let us take the most direct and attractive way of providing houses now. A
straight subsidy will allow the Government to see at once their commitment for
the next twelve months. It will allow
local authorities to see exactly where they
stand. They should make a contribution
in addition to the £390. It will enable
the ratepayer to see his position clearly
and it will provide at least 1,750 houses
during the next twelve months. I think
the local authorities should be delighted

HOUSE OF COMMONS

to give this subsidy and I believe that the

Government. I have here, to-day, plans

The ground has been

years

authorities may expect to receive for
,post-war housing schemes. I am unable to give the exact percentage, but
this much I will say here and now, SO
far as one could reasonably judge, one
could, I think, safely hope that any
subsidy would not be less than the
subsidy already arranged to be given
to the city of Belfast for its small wartime programme, and I hope it will be
more.
Speaking of the preliminary work of

Now, I think, an offer of 15 or 20
per cent. paid on account ought to

These quotations are interesting by way

"
Here we are presented with a Bill
which is at almost complete variance
with the implied promises of the former
Minister in charge of housing. Not only
are local authorities to be controlled and
bound under a dictatorial bureaucracy
of the worst kind, but the promises of
the former Minister are to be cast upon
the scrap heap. This assuredly is a
sample of the so-called efficiency of
centralised government. Despite the
assurances given to this House from time
to time the fact clearly emerges that the
Government has no stable policy in regard to
housing. It possesses a weather-vane policy
which changes according to the changing
caprices of its changing Ministers. And
this is the way in which the housing
problem of this country is to be settled.
I have made these preliminary remarks
because I wish it to be clearly demonstrated that it is not the fault of the
body of this House that delay should have
taken place, or unnecessary division
created in proceeding to the job of
tackling the housing problem in this
country. The Housing Act passed this
year, which gave statutory power to the
Belfast Corporation, gives equal power to
every local authority to proceed with a
housing scheme on the basis of the same
lump-sum subsidy. When that Bill was
going through the House, the Minister
was asked to give within its scope the
same powers to rural authorities as to
urban authorities. He replied:
I think it would be a pity to start
up a new method of housing and a new
procedure in the rural districts.
Therefore, this is not an omission, but
is done with a great deal of deliberation.
Now, however, the policy has changed
and rural councils are included in the new
proposals. The salient point I wish to
make is that, apart from the formation
of a Housing Trust there is not the
slightest need for the present Bill. This
is a tragic Bill, tragic because it introduces controversy upon a subject
where we all desire unanimity and agreement, tragic because it is a Bill which
contains within itself the seeds of its own
destruction.
I suggest to the Minister this afternoon
that he would be in a much stronger position in regard to this Bill if he had acceded
to the overtures that were made to him.
He has made the complaint in this House
and outside it that no suggestions had been
offered to him. I suggest that he has not
made it possible for any suggestions to be
made. As regards the question of subsidy
I admit at once that the subsidy in the
years after the last war was given without
any condition being attached thereto. The
obvious course then, and the proper course
now, is if a subsidy is being granted to
private enterprise it should be subject
to reasonable conditions. Those conditions,
in my judgment, should embody one to
the effect that the rent charged has a
bearing on the amount at which the house
would be sold.
I am concerned about this Bill because
of the fact that it seeks to establish what
I describe as a new management and an
unnecessary department. When I was
elected to this House in 1941 I was charged
with one particular job more than
Ml

another. It was to protest to the utmost
of my power against the excessive cost of
administration at Stormont. Here we
have in this Bill the formation of an
entirely new and expensive department
which, I submit, is completely and
entirely unnecessary. You have in every

suggest are capable of carrying out the
work in their various districts. These
local authorities are only entrusted with
houses up to a point where they can provide £5 per house per year out of the
rates. After that need is met the Trust
are to provide houses, and 100 per cent.
will be provided by the State. I suggest
there is no need for the Trust. If the
moneys that are to be spent on this new
and expensive department were given to
local authorities they could do the work.
They have the surveying and engineering
departments; they have all the facilities
without complicating matters with this
suggested Housing Trust. I suggest that
the proposed Housing Trust has not been
shown by the Minister to be necessary.
The Minister on another occasion said
-I am quoting his own words that local
bodies generally are efficient and well
equipped. Many of them, as I have just
stated, possess good engineering and surveying departments. Why not use those
departments to the full instead of adding
an unnecessary and new department to the
already overburdened and expensive departments that exist under this adminisstration.
It is not many years since the new
Minister of Home Affairs stated in the
course of a debate in this House, in which
he moved a vote of censure upon the
Government of the time, that this Government is the most expensive Government
in the world. I do not know how many
hon. Members are aware of the fact that
at the present time we have one civil
servant to every 160 of our population.
In spite of that we are going to add to
the existing extravagance by creating
what I suggest is something that is
absolutely and completely unnecessary-I
suggest to the Minister-I am speaking
with a desire not SO much to
destroy as to help that before he commits the country and this Parliament to a
Housing Trust he should seriously apply
himself to the question and see if the
purpose he has in mind could not be
accomplished without the necessity of providing this department with its officials.
I am speaking quite seriously this afternoon, and I am speaking from my
convictions. I am satisfied that we are
making a profound mistake in remedying
the housing position by the establishment
of a quite unnecessary and expensive
department. Before this Bill is finally
passed, the Minister should consider all
its implications and reflect upon whether,
in providing this Housing Trust, he is
not providing something which is going
to be in the same category as the Transport Board, which, but for the exigencies
of the war, would at the present moment
have been in a state of bankruptcy. I
throw out the suggestion to the Minister,
so that at the. last moment he may consider the implications of his proposal.
No matter how the voting on this Bill
may go, I will have the satisfaction, if
this Trust comes to its own inevitable
end, an end that will be a disastrous one,
of having it recorded that I uttered a
strong and emphatic protest against it in
this House.
My third suggestion is that this proposed Housing Trust has no counterpart
in previous housing experience, either in
Northern Ireland or across the water.
Reference has been made to the Scottish
Special Housing Association. I am not
sure whether the Minister has expressed
the view that the proposed Housing Trust
for Northern Ireland is based upon the
Special Housing Association provided in
Scotland. He is probably aware of certain facts, but if he is not, I think they
should be made known to the House.
First of all, the Scottish Special Housing
Association was an association designed
to operate in distressed areas only.
Secondly, that it was intended to act as
ancillary to the work of local authorities, and, thirdly-I think this is important
-it was designed not to compete with
local authorities, but was intended to
provide additional houses by the utilisation of what are known as non-traditional
materials. In other words, the local
authorities were to be free to go ahead
with the ordinary materials, such as
brick, that were available to them. The
efforts of the Special Housing Association
in Scotland were to be exercised to assist,
not so much by the utilisation of those
materials as by the use of non-traditional
materials. It was really designed to help

or across the water. I am not going to

I should like to make a plea for the
black-coated worker. I know a good deal

and throughout the country people who

That man is earning £4 10s per week,

£2 per week for rent. His need is as

per week. I want to make a sincere
plea here this afternoon. When we are
considering the ultimate occupants of
the houses which we hope to see erected
I trust that due consideration will be
given not so much to planning as to the
actual needs of the people in the country.
I wish to say a word or two about
temporary houses. I understand that
the Minister has stated that he has made
a request to the Imperial Government for
the provision of 10,000 Portal houses.
At £650 each that will involve an expenditure of £6,000,000 odd. Will that
be satisfactory even as a partial solution
of our difficulties here in Northern Ireland? I suggest that steel houses are
absolutely unsuitable in Northern Ireland. I would advise the Ministersince I have already offered one suggestion
he will not mind me offering another-to
investigate the method that has been
and is being adopted in the City of
Birmingham. There instead of providing temporary Portal houses they have
gone ahead with the ground floor storey
of a permanent house on a proper site.
With proper services the cost of the
initial portion of the house is less than
the cost of a Portal house.
The Minister has asked for suggestions.
I must confess that he has not shown very
much courtesy in the acceptance of any
suggestions. If he takes my suggestions
this afternoon in the spirit in which they
are made I suggest that before he commits
the country to an expenditure of
£6,000,000 by the provision of Portal
houses he should make some inquiries as
to the relative advantages of the scheme
which is at present operating in the
cities of Birmingham, Coventry and other
places across the water.
I have deliberately refrained from saying very much with regard to private
enterprise. Some months ago the Minister stated that the bulk of the war-time
housing programme would require to be

including the noble Lord-that private
enterprise should be brought in where it
I understand the Minister is not
opposed to the provision of houses by

taken by the noble Lord. It does not

Mr. McGURK: Being a member of a
rural and county council I must object

Ministry must be well aware that any increase in rates is not paid by the landlord, but by the tenant, under the Rent
Restriction Acts, and it is unreasonable
to ask the farmer to pay for the building
of new houses to bring Northern Ireland
up to the standard of housing in Great
Britain, a service to the community which
should entirely be paid out of the Imperial contribution.
I am of opinion that the building of
dwelling-houses is essential throughout
Northern Ireland. In my native county

not chargeable to the rates of local
authorities. As the time is getting on

I know there will be a war if the Minister

As I said before, I am much in favour

this point when we come to the final

The hon. Member went on to say:
What answer is there to that?-
(Official Report, 1st November, 1944,
vol. 27, col. 2101.)
There is, of course, a perfect answer to
that, that the rents and rates in Belfast
or in any other local authority where the
Trust operates will not go up as a result
of the Trust's operations, but, on the contrary, should tend in a downward direction because the local authority concerned
will receive rates from the houses built in
their area by the Trust, whereas the cost
of those houses to the local authority will
be nil.
The hon. Member for North Down,
who, I regret to say, is not in the House
now, said that the Trust, in his opinion,
was not in any way comparable with the
Scottish Housing Association. He stated
that when that association was first set up
it was established for operation in special
areas.
That is perfectly true, but the
extent of the operations of the Scottish
Housing Association have since been
widened, and it now covers housing in a
number of areas in Scotland which are
not by any means described as special
areas.
The object of setting up this Trust is
not that it should be in competition with
local authorities or with private enterprise, but that it should be complementary
to local authorities, and should step in to
assist them in areas, as the Bill says,
where the need is greatest. The object
in setting up this Trust is that it may
assist the local authorities in the areas
where the need is greatest, so that the
burden of providing the houses that are
required in those areas will not fall too
heavily on the ratepayers. In consequence, the Government are prepared to
pay to the Trust not only the amount of
the Exchequer contribution which they
will
pay to the local authorities, but also
the amount of the burden which will be
placed on the rates for the remaining
houses built by the local authorities themselves.

PETROL FOR A COUNTY DOWN
DENTIST.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That this House do now adjourn.'
(Sir Wilson Hungerford.)
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: I wish to
raise a question of which I have given
notice to the Minister of Health and Local
Government and to the right hon. Gentleman who has just taken his seat as Minister of Home Affairs. A case recently
arose in Downpatrick whereby a dental officer employed by the County Down Regional
Committee was prosecuted by the police
at the instigation of the Petrol Board or
Petrol Officer. The case came before the
Court. The dental officer used his car
to bring his equipment to Saul in order
to give dental treatment to the children
there. There is no bus or railway to the
place in question. The case was dismissed by the resident magistrate. In
doing so he used the most scathing remarks in regard to the prosecution having
been brought.
I wish to bring the sequel to the notice
of the Minister. The dental officer had
been treating children at Killyleagh, but
the job was not finished. Under instructions from the Down Regional Education
Committee he has now gone elsewhere.
Petrol for a Co. Down Dentist 7 NOVEMBER 1944
That has been brought about owing to the
fact that the petrol officer cut his allowance for the new quarter. Having prosecuted him and failed, he reduced his
allowance, and it was impossible for him
to carry out his duties in connection with
giving dental treatment to the children
in Killyleagh. He is now in Drumbo.
The petrol people suggested that he should
get up at 6-30 in the morning in order to
catch a bus, and that he should carry his
equipment in his hand. The situation is
impossible, and it is a damned scandal. I
would ask the Minister to look into this
case and see that justice is done.
Mr. MINFORD: I would like to say
that I think it is wrong that these dental
surgeons should be put to this expense,
and if the Minister of Health has any
control of health in Northern Ireland I
think he should make representations to
the petroleum officer, because what has
happened in Killyleagh is happening all
over Ulster. If the time has arrived
when the Petroleum Officer can dictate to
dental surgeons and medical men I think
the thing is absurd. I ask the Minister
of Health, with whom I have great
sympathy, to make representations that
these prosecutions should not occur and
that these dental surgeons should get
enough petrol. Not only in County Down,
but in County Antrim, they have made it
impossible for dental surgeons to attend
to cases, and the regional committees are
not able to get anyone to take their duties.
The children, who are the men and women
of to-morrow, are going to be destroyed,
because of the dictates of some of these
inspectors. I think it is time the Minister
of Health took a firm stand.
Mr. BEATTIE: I understand that the
school service is essential, and in England
I understand petrol allowance is given to
all school medical services, the dental
service being one of these. A supply is
given commensurate with the work that
the dental servant has got to carry on.
I
would like to ask the right hon. Gentleman is that not carried out in Northern
Ireland, and, if not, why? Before I sit
down I would like to ask the Prime
Minister whether he can state the order
of business to-morrow and the following
day, if any.

dentists. I know a dentist and
my advice

and if the facts are as stated the Government certainly would not stand for that
sort of treatment. We shall have to
make careful inquiries. I shall have a
consultation with my right hon. Friend
the Minister of Home Affairs and see if
something cannot be done to ease the
situation.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: Thank you
very much.
The PRIME MINISTER: In reply to
the hon. Member for Pottinger, tomorrow we shall have the continuation of
the Adjourned Debate. If he will ask
me about future business then I shall let
him know.
Question, "That this House do now
adjourn," put, and agreed to.
Adjourned accordingly at halfpast Five o'clock.

Debate on Amendment to Question

Which Amendment was, to leave out

of
Mr. MINFORD: When I received this
Bill, like many hon. Members, I had
some misapprehension and doubt, but
after the speech of the Minister
Health and Local Government, and also
the speeches of the Prime Minister and
the Minister of Finance, all doubts and
fears were removed from the minds of
those both inside this House and outside.
I was struck very forcibly by three things
in the Prime Minister's speech. The
first was that private enterprise would
have an opportunity of doing its quota in
regard to housing the people of Ulster;
the second was the statement that there
were materials available for building
houses-that was the first time I knew
that, and it was a big and pleasant surprise for hon. Members-and the third
was that this Bill is not going to be
rushed, that he was going to allow two
weeks to elapse before the Committee
stage, so that hon. Members on both
sides would have an opportunity if they
so desired of putting Amendments before
the House. That to me is a very fair
and democratic way of putting this Bill
before the House.
I sympathise with the Minister very
much, because he is undertaking a very
heavy duty and has shouldered a very
great burden. He has got to make up
the leeway that should have been made
up thirty years ago in regard to the
housing of our people, and in regard to
their health. I feel it my duty as a back
bencher to make a recommendation to the
House that he should get the unanimous
support of hon. Members on all sides of
the House in order that he may go out
with the courage and determination
which are required to tackle the great
problems he will have to solve. I have
the greatest confidence in him, because
he is sincere, and I feel that the House
to-day will give this Bill unanimous
support, because after his speech on the
Second Reading he left no doubts in the
mind of any hon. Member of this House
of Commons. There was, doubtless,
regular propaganda outside the House
with regard to private building, but all
those fears have been allayed.
I come now to the Bill. The Minister is willing and anxious that recommendations should be made to him on
the question of giving a grant each year
or paying a portion of the burden placed
upon the ratepayers of giving £11 10s
for a house of three rooms. I feel that
it would be much better if the Minister
did not go into details in regard to having houses built for two, three, or four
people. Houses should be built of a
standard size. I am speaking for the
rural authorities and the urban authorities, and one does not know what the cost
of building may be in the years that lie
ahead. It would solve the whole trouble
if the Government went 50-50 with the
local authorities. That would save any
quarrelling or quibbling about the
amount the Government were going to
bear.
In my opinion that would be a fair
way because the Minister would be taking half the burden off the local authorities. The local authorities then would
rise to their responsibilities as they
realise the time has come to put an end
Housing (No. 2) Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Minford]
to the bad housing conditions in Northern Ireland. I believe that our people
are worse housed than the people in any
other part of the United Kingdom, and
when I asked the. Minister of Finance
some time ago about withholding a few
millions from our annual contribution
to Great Britain, he said he could not
do it, but that he was going to get a
loan of six millions from the Imperial
Exchequer in order to make up the lag
that had taken place in regard to the
health of the people of our country and
put it on a par with that of Great
Britain. Housing and health are inseparable, and I feel that if the Minister
would make a statement to the House today to the effect that he is prepared to
go 50-50 in the expenses of building
these houses we would have a united
front by the local authorities.
The local authorities have to guard
their people in regard to the rates they
can pay. In this progressive age in
which we are living, we expect education
to reach a much higher standard than
before. That will involve further
taxation. Water is most essential in
all homes, and that will entail another
tax upon the people, as will also sewerage. All these things will mean a fairly
heavy rate. I have been in this House
fifteen years and I have. always said that it
is the duty of the Government to see that
the people are properly housed.
The Minister is assuming full responsibility for this programme. The Trust
is a thing which people look upon with a
certain amount of suspicion. I sympathise with the Minister, because some local
authorities in the past have not lived up
to their responsibilities, but if any local
authority try to evade their liabilities
the Trust will carry out their duties and
put the charge upon the rates. If the
Trust are to select sites, they should
not select the most favourable sites in
industrial areas like Ballyclare, Antrim,
Randalstown, or York Street, Muckamore. They are going to be in a much
better position than the rural authorities,
because they will build the houses in
order to suit the requirements of the
local people in scattered districts. We
cannot expect the houses to be built in
little villages, they must build the houses
in places where the workmen will be within
a reasonable distance from their work.
I suggest to the Minister that if it were
possible he might do without this Trust,
but if he must have it in the Bill then
I have no objection.
During the past five years it has been
the policy both of the Government and
the people to save money in order to win
the war and also to save all they can for
the post-war period. If we are going to
establish another Department which will
require heavy finance to carry it through
people will grumble and say that the
money could have been better spent on
housing. My position to-day is that I
do not care who builds the houses so long
as they are built, because housing in
Ulster to-day, as I said a moment or two
ago, is not an ornament to this Province.
I was delighted yesterday to hear the
hon. Member for South Armagh and
other hon. Members on the opposite side
of the house backing up this Bill, because
this morning I was amazed when I read
in the paper a letter or article by the
Archbishop of Westminster, in which he
said that this Government were treating
the Roman Catholics of Ulster the same
as the Jews were being treated in Poland.
That is an unfair statement. It should
not go unrefuted. It is the duty of the
Government to-day to allay the suspicion
which that article will create in Great
Britain. The Bill before the House is not
a party Measure. It would be wrong for
this House to let politics enter into the
question of housing. When I read that
article in the Belfast News-Letter I was
amazed that a man who never visited
Ulster should say what he did. As a
loyal Ulsterman I object to that statement. There is no foundation whatever
for it, because everyone here is treated
fairly and squarely. I think the Government should refute such a damnable and
scandalous allegation against a people who
during my career and that of the Government never attempted to persecute any
man because of his religion. We are
living in a free country, and no man is
denied his rights either civil or religious.
When this war is over-we pray that
victory may come soon-and our gallant
lads come home they will see that this
Government did not delay one moment in
regard to the building of houses. Why
should it? When these boys come home
they will want houses, because many of
their young brides are living with their
parents, while others are living in rooms.

would be a shame for a man in the eventide of his life to be moved from his house

many of
which would be trivial.

There is another point to which I should
like to draw the Minister's attention.
This Measure is described as providing
housing accommodation for the working
classes. The working classes have been
defined under a previous Act as people
earning 30s per week or less.
sequent Act the working classes are
defined as people earning 45s a week or

under 50s a week. Therefore, according

working classes, and I suggest that that
should be amended, and instead of working classes we should insert the words

do not intend to labour the matter any
further. If I might presume to advise
the Minister, I would say, get on with

Health Services.
MEMBERSHIP OF ADVISORY
COUNCIL.
1. Dr. LYLE asked the Minister of
Health and Local Government whether
he acted in accordance with the recommendation in paragraph 14 of the Report
of the Select Committee on Health
Services by appointing on his Advisory
Council a majority of medical men, and,
if not, can he state the reason why.
The MINISTER OF HEALTH AND
LOCAL GOVERNMENT (Mr. Grant):
There are nine medical men, one dentist,
one
pharmaceutical chemist, two nurses
and seven laymen on the Health Advisory
Council, which I have appointed.
Before taking action in this matter I
gave full consideration to the recommendation of the Select Committee on Health
Services in Northern Ireland, as contained
in paragraph 14 of their Report.
The hon. Member will observe that the
majority of the Council are members of
the medical profession or of the allied
professions of dentistry, pharmacy and
nursing. I have no doubt that he will
agree with me that I have been singularly
fortunate in obtaining the assistance of
eminent members of his profession and of
other persons with wide experience of the
many aspects of the health services of
Northern Ireland.

of the right hon. Gentleman, is it not a
fact that the recommendation in paragraph 14 of the Report of the Select
Committee stated definitely that the
majority of that Council, or Committee,
should be medical men?

Health and Local Government whether he
can
now state the intentions of the
Government regarding the proposed erection of a sanatorium in each County of
Northern Ireland.
Mr. GRANT: I am not aware that it
has been proposed to erect a sanatorium
in each county of Northern Ireland.
The Select Committee on Health
Services in Northern Ireland stated in
their Report that about 500 more beds
for tuberculosis patients should be provided, and that they were convinced that
two additional sanatoria were required.
an-

nounced those arrangements in this

GRANTS FOR TUBERCULOSIS
PATIENTS.
6. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Health and Local Government whether
the Government will extend the grants
for tuberculosis sufferers recently announced to all who are afflicted by the
disease.
Mr. GRANT: The scheme referred to
is not a pension scheme-it is a special
war-time scheme devised for the specific
purpose of encouraging people suffering
from pulmonary tuberculosis who would
benefit to leave their work and undergo
treatment.
I regret therefore that I am unable to
extend these exceptional provisions to
chronic cases, or diseases other than
pulmonary tuberculosis.

Alleged Persecution of Roman Catholics.
REPLY TO ARCHBISHOP OF
WESTMINSTER.
7. Mr. MINFORD asked the Prime
Minister whether his attention has been
called to a report which appeared in the
local Press on Wednesday, 8th November,
that the Archbishop of Westminster had
stated, "That Roman Catholics were
even in the present day being persecuted
in Northern Ireland," and, if what
steps the Government propose to take to
repudiate this shameful slander.
So,
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Mr. Warnock): I have been asked by
my right hon. Friend to reply.
I have read with profound regret the
report of a speech delivered by the Roman
Catholic Archbishop of Westminster on
the 7th October at a meeting in London
of the Council of Christians and Jews.
In the course of his remarks, after
protesting against the Nazi persecution of
his co-religionists in Germany and
Poland, he is reported to have used these
words:-
"And I need hardly mention the
persecution that is going on even at the
present day in Northern Ireland."
I regret that the Archbishop should
have made this accusation against the
Government and people of Northern Ireland, because I believe it to be completely untrue.
I do not desire to speak disrespectfully
of any high dignitary of any church, but
it is difficult to understand how he could
have permitted himself to make this
charge at such a gathering and in such
a context.
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Warnock]
If any answer to the Archbishop's
allegation was required it will be found
in the fact that since the establishment
of the Parliament of Northern Ireland
there has been abundant evidence of the
desire of a very large number of Roman
Catholics to leave Eire and come to live
in Northern Ireland, and the infiltration
has been constant and ever increasing.
Since the 1st January, 1940, no less
than 30,000 Eire citizens have applied
for permission to come to take
up
residence in our midst.
-
If the Archbishop had in mind the
fact that we faced with a threat from
the I.R.A. and in the interests of public
safety-had to intern a number of people,
I would draw attention to the fact that
in Catholic Eire the Government, faced
with danger from the same source, has
felt it necessary to take powers of internment far more drastic than any we
possess, and have exercised those powers
with a rigour unknown in Northern
Ireland.
The latest figures available to me show
that on the 31st August, 1942, 477 persons were interned in Eire.
I would venture to express the hope
that this unfortunate speech may quickly
be forgotten.
Mr. MINFORD: Is it not a fact that
the people coming in here from Eire are
seeking permission to stay in Northern
Ireland? Will the Government, in its
wisdom, see that these people coming in
from Eire to get positions do not get
them, but that the loyal people here get
them and thus save their standing in
queues at labour exchanges?
Mr. AGNEW: Is it not still a fact that
this is a Protestant Parliament for a
Protestant people?
Transport and Distribution of Fish.,
8. Mr. BROWN asked the Prime
Minister whether the considered statement, read out on his behalf in Parliament on 31st October by the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Commerce, regarding the waste of good
food on account of the unsatisfactory
shipping, transport and distributing
arrangements for Northern Ireland fish,
represents the views of the Government
and is in accordance with their policy
with regard to food production in general.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
FINANCE (Sir Wilson Hungerford): I
have been asked by my right hon. Friend
to reply. The answer to the question is
in the affirmative.
The hon. Member will appreciate that
to catch fish in quantities exceeding those
which can be transported in the limited
shipping space available, or absorbed in
the local market, must inevitably create
a difficult situation which it is only within
the power of the fishermen themselves to
control. Moreover, it will be apparent
to the hon. Member that not only is a
waste of food entailed, but also a depletion of the nation's fish stocks, and the
Government would, therefore, urge upon
the fishermen that restraint for which the
occasion calls.
Mr. BROWN: In view of the fact that
in this statement the Government have
told the fishermen that the only solution
of the problem would seem to be for the
fishermen to limit the landings of fish,
and have advised them to agree to voluntary limitation of landings, surely the
Parliamentary Secretary will agree that
in these serious times the fishermen are
entitled to more sensible advice from the
Government than this?
Lieut.-Colonel. PANTER: Is it not a
fact that the fishermen in Annalong and
Kilkeel, which places are in my constituency, will consider such a reply an
insult to their ordinary intelligence?
Mr. BROWN: Are we not going to
have any explanation of the fact that the
Government are advising the fishermen to
sabotage the food production effort?

is not in any danger.

Agriculture.
TILLAGE QUOTA.
9. Mr. BROWN asked the Prime
Minister whether he can state why the
Government have refused to agree to the
requests of a large number of Members
of Parliament, representing rural constituencies, county committees of agriculture, and others, for a reduction in the
tillage quota of Northern Ireland; and
whether the Government will put the
farmers in a position to act on the advice
tendered by the Government to the sea
fishermen so as to obviate the destruction
of good food in the agricultural industry."
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Rev. Robert Moore): I have been asked
by the Prime Minister to reply.
The answer is that every hundredweight of arable crop that can be grown
in this country will be badly needed. Our
livestock production which represents 80
per cent. of our agricultural income is,
and will be for a considerable time to
come, dependent upon it.
The last part of the question does not
arise as the Imperial Government has
undertaken to take all food that is produced at fixed prices.
Mr. BROWN: Would the Minister tell
us how the Government propose to have
it both ways inasmuch as they are telling
the fishermen to restrict their supplies
to avoid losses of fish, and then refuse to
give the farmers any relief whatever from
this excessive tillage quota which is causing grave loss of food in the agricultural
industry also?

DOWNPATRICK GRADING
STATION.
13. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he will investigate the conditions prevailing at Downpatrick Grading Station; whether the
arrangements for weighing of livestock are
suitable; whether it is a fact that casualties are common in and around this
station; whether in cases of injury livestock are taken to the abattoir, thus causing loss to the farmers concerned; and
whether he will look into this matter so
that livestock classified as casualties will
be paid for in full by the Department.
Rev. ROBERT MOORE: The conditions prevailing at Downpatrick Grading Centre are satisfactory for the working of the Meat and Livestock Scheme,
Abattoir as the result of accident or
injury occurring in the purchasing centre.
Casualty animals presented by farmers are
received at Downpatrick Abattoir and are
paid for according to the schedule of
prices laid down by the Ministry of Food.
Casualty animals receive a far better
price under the scheme than was the case
in pre-war days, when such animals were
practically a total loss to producers.
BARLEY PRICES.
14. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he can state the
fixed price for barley, according to
quality, and if below the standard what
is the barley used for and what price is
paid for it; what prices are offered by
merchants for barley below standard and
what is done with this barley when
bought; and whether the farmers are
satisfied with the prices offered for all
grades of barley.
Rev. ROBERT MOORE: Maximum
and minimum prices to growers for barley
have been fixed as follows:-Barley of
millable quality, maximum 25s per cwt.,
minimum 22s 6d per cwt.; barley of
potentially millable quality, minimum 20s
per cwt.
All these prices are net ex farm.
Parley may be disposed of only to the Port
Area Grain Committee or to merchants
who are approved buyers. Such buyers
may sell millable barley only to the Port
Area Grain Committee, and it is included
in rationed feeding stuffs pool.
When the barley is of such poor quality
that it is not purchased by the Port Area
Grain Committee the Ministry issues a
licence permitting the grower to use it for
feeding to his own stock.
Only 110 out 3,000 tons so far offered
this season have been refused by the Port
Area Grain Committee as unsuitable for
milling.

Houses Destroyed by Enemy Action.
CONDITIONS FOR REBUILDING.
Mr. DOWLING (by Private Notice)
asked the Minister of Health and Local
Government whether he is yet in a position
to make any statement about the rebuilding of houses in Northern Ireland which
have been destroyed by enemy action.
Mr. GRANT: I have very great
pleasure in telling the House that in consultation with the Ministry of Commerce
I am able to announce that owners of
houses in Northern Ireland which have
been totally destroyed by enemy action
may rebuild in the near future, provided
certain conditions are satisfied. The
general conditions are-
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Grant]
The houses must have been the subject
of an intimation (Form Val. 3 or Val. 4)
from the War Damage Commission that
on rebuilding the work will attract a cost
of works payment.
Licences for rebuilding will be issued
by the Ministry of Commerce as applications are received and approved by the
Ministry of Health and Local Government. The rate at which licences can be
issued will depend upon the supply
position from time to time.
In authorising rebuilding a preference
will be given in the case of (a) owners who
undertake to rebuild for their own use,
and (b) owners who agree to let the houses
to their original tenants at the original
rent, or, if the original tenant is not available, to let the house to a person who is
neither the owner nor tenant of a house.
No licence will be granted for any
house in respect of which the cost of rebuilding would exceed £1,500.
In addition to the building licence to
be issued by the Ministry of Commerce,
applicants will require to observe the local
building by-laws and Planning Acts and
Orders.
Where the preceding conditions have
been fulfilled the "proper cost" of rebuilding war-damaged houses will be
recoverable from the War Damage Commission. Owners are, however, advised
in their own interests to consult the
Commission in advance, under the new
arrangements announced by the Commission in the Press on the 13th November,
1944.
Applications for permission to rebuild
should be made in the first instance to the
Secretary, Ministry of Health and Local
Government, Stormont.
I am very grateful to the War Damage
Commission for their help in dealing with
this question and for the arrangements
which they have made to facilitate the
work.
I hope that owners who are affected will
make early application for permission to
rebuild. In doing so they can serve their
country by making an immediate contribution to our housing needs.

ORAL ANSWERS TO
QUESTIONS.
Labour.
DISABLED EX-SERVICE MEN.
1. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Labour whether he can state if it is
customary for labour exchanges to treat
ex-soldiers in receipt of full disability
pension as unfit for work, and if it is
usual to submit such ex-soldiers who have
served in the present war to the medical
referee in view of the Ministry of
Pensions award; whether it is proper for
the manager of the labour exchange to
submit an ex-soldier in receipt of full
disability to the medical referee and then,
after the doctor's decision, to issue disallowance to the man that he is incapable of work; whether he considers
that this is the proper treatment for our
ex-soldiers, and will he take the matter
up with the Armagh Exchange.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Midgley): In answer to the hon. Member's question, I may say that it is not
customary for employment exchanges to
treat an ex-Service man with full disability pension as unfit for work. It is
recognised that many such men are quite
capable of getting and retaining useful
employment and are entitled to benefit
when unemployed. But when, in particular cases, the insurance officer has
reason for doubting a man's physical
fitness, it is his obvious duty to refer
the matter to a medical referee. If, in
the opinion of the referee, the man is
capable of some kind of work, the insurance officer is better able to judge the
sort of employment suited for him and
to help him to find it.
If, however, the medical referee is of
opinion that the man is incapable of
work, the insurance officer must disallow
benefit because, as the hon. Member is
aware, the Unemployment Insurance
Acts prescribe that before a man can get
unemployment benefit he must prove that
he is capable of, and available for,
work.
If the claimant is dissatisfied with the
decision he has a right of appeal to the
court of referees.
Mr. BEATTIE: I should like to ask
the right hon. Gentleman if he will inform the House of the qualifications, if
any, of the insurance officer to decide.
whether a man with 100 per cent. disability is fit or unfit for any class of unemployment.
Mr. MIDGLEY: The insurance officer
does not decide. He only decides on the
face of the matter; it is then submitted
to a higher authority, and when it is submitted to the higher medical authority
the decision is given on the basis of the
knowledge then gained.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is it not a fact that
the right hon. Gentleman said that the
insurance officer decided whether the
man was fit or unfit? I asked what
qualifications he has to decide that
question.
Mr. MIDGLEY: The exact words I
used were these:

If, however, the medical referee is of

That is in accordance with the Regulations. The Unemployment Insurance
Fund prescribes that before a man can get
unemployment benefit he must prove that
he is capable of and available for work.
If, in the opinion of the medical referee,
not the insurance officer, he is incapable
of work the man has then the right of
appeal.

Mr. MIDGLEY: It would be a cryingout disgrace if the Ministry did treat
people in that way, but the Ministry do
not treat people in that way, and no

facts in relation to the particular case
which the hon. Member has in mind. He
asks, how does the insurance officer in the
first case reach the conclusion that the
man should be submitted to the medical
authority on the question of whether he
is capable of work. The insurance officer
arrives at that decision on the basis of his
experience of the man, not only in relation to offers of employment, but also in
relation to previous offers which had been
made to him.
We have the entire history of the case
the hon. Member has in mind, and nobody
-I say this without egotism-can be more
sympathetic towards ex-Service men than
I am prepared to be. This man
offered employment on several occasions.
He was offered various types of jobs, and
he refused to accept those offers of employment of various kinds. Also, he
was
asked for a transfer from Great Britain
to Northern Ireland on medical grounds.
It was presumed, therefore, that as he was
employed in England and asked for a
transfer from England because of his
medical condition, that medical condition
serious enough to warrant
investigation; and upon that investigation, plus the refusal of the man to accept
suitable employment, he was defined as
being outside the scope of the Regulations.

CONDITIONS IN WOOLLEN MILLS
2. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister
of Labour whether he will investigate the
conditions prevailing in woollen mills
in Northern Ireland in order to have
wage regulating machinery set up so
that better conditions will apply, and
whether, after investigation, he will
discuss the question of wage regulating
machinery with the particular union or
unions in order to have a trade board
similar to that operating in the textile
industry.
Mr. MIDGLEY: In reply to the hon.
Member, wages and conditions of workers
in certain woollen mills in Northern Ireland have been the subject of awards of
the National Arbitration Tribunal. No
disputes concerning the conditions of
workers generally in other mills have
been reported to my Department. In
the circumstances there would not appear
to be any ground for action on the lines
suggested by the hon. Member. If,
however, he can furnish me with evidence
of unsatisfactory conditions in the trade
I shall be pleased to give it careful consideration.
I am sure the hon. Member will
realise that I am always open to receive
representations with a view to the improvement, where necessary, of arrangements for the settlement of wages and
conditions of employment.

4.
REMAND HOME FOR GIRLS.
Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Home Affairs and Security whether the
Belfast Corporatión has acquired a suitable building for a remand home for girls,
and, if so, where is the home situated,
from whom was it purchased, and what
was the price paid.
Mr. WARNOCK: The Ministry of
Home Affairs on the 9th December, 1943,
acquired premises suitable for a remand
home for girls. The premises are situate
at Whiteabbey, Co. Antrim, and they
were purchased from the trustees of Henry
Grattan Pring, deceased, for £3,150.
The provision of such a home is the
responsibility of this Ministry, and not
the responsibility of the Belfast Corporation.
Fishing Industry.
LIMITATION OF CATCHES.
5. Mr. BROWN asked the Prime
Minister whether he can state if the advice
given on his behalf in Parliament on 31st
October last to the members of the Ulster
Sea Fishermen's Association to limit their
landings of fish was given with or without
knowledge of the fact that the industry
represented is at present working only to
about one quarter capacity.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
COMMERCE (Mr. Maginess): I have
been asked by my right hon. Friend to
reply.
I am aware that the boats have not
been fishing every day in the week. My
suggestion was not that they should fish
less frequently, but that they should
restrict their daily landings to the amount
which the cross-Channel steamers are permitted to carry, plus the demands of the
Northern Ireland market. By adopting
this suggestion the men would be able to
fish on every day when weather conditions
are favourable and the problem of surplus landings would be solved. For the
hon. Member's information I would add
that the amount of shipping space available would be more than adequate for our
requirements if the catches were evenly
spread over the fishing period.
Mr. BROWN: Owing to the unsatisfactory reply I wish to give notice that I
will raise this matter on the Adjournment.
TRANSPORTATION AND
DISTRIBUTION.
6. Mr. BROWN asked the Prime
Minister whether he can state the result
of the conference he recently had with the
members of the Ulster Sea Fishermen's
Association regarding the present unsatisfactory shipping, transport and distributing arrangements for Northern Ireland
fish.
Mr. MAGINESS: I have been asked
by my right hon. Friend to reply.
As the hon. Member was present he is,
of course, aware of what took place at
the meeting. As a result of the request
made by the representatives of the association, the Ministry of Food have now
agreed to receive a delegation from the
association in London, and I understand
that arrangements to this end are in progress. I am glad also to be able to inform
the hon. Member that, following representations made by my Ministry, the local
Timber Control authorities have arranged
for the immediate release of an additional
quantity of timber for the manufacture
of fish boxes, and that a contract for an
extra thousand has already been placed
and is now in hand.
Mr. BROWN: May I thank the Parliamentary Secretary for the small mercies
vouchsafed in his reply, and ask him to
get on with the matter? If he does he
will eventually succeed.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: Is the Parliamentary Secretary aware that quite
recently 1,200 boxes of fish were left on
the quayside owing to lack of shipping

FISH IMPORTED FROM GREAT
BRITAIN.
8. Mr. BROWN asked the Prime
Minister whether he can state why little
or no difficulty is being experienced in the
transport of fish from Great Britain to
Northern Ireland and why the present
difficulties in the transport of fish from
Northern Ireland to Great Britain apply
only to such transport from this side of
the Channel.
Mr. MAGINESS: I have been asked
by my right hon. Friend to reply.
a
The control of shipping and shipping
space rests with the Minister of War
Transport, and, therefore, the hon.
Member will not expect me to explain the
considerations underlying the allocation.
of shipping space for the transportation
of fish between Great Britain and Northern Ireland in either direction. For the
information of the hon. Member, however,
I would point out that, altogether apart
from the question of shipping space,
Scottish wholesale merchants are restricted
in the quantity of fish which they may
send to Northern Ireland during
specified period. In no circumstances,
therefore, can the quantity despatched by
the Scottish wholesale merchants exceed the
amount of shipping space available. On
the other hand Northern Ireland merchants are not restricted in the quantity
which they may send to Great Britain,
except in so far as the quantity is governed by the amount of shipping space
available, that is to say a maximum of 55
tons nightly. Obviously difficulties are
inevitable when the landings on a particular day provide a surplus of more than
55 tons in excess of local market requirements.
Mr. BROWN: In view of the fact that
the Parliamentary Secretary referred in a
previous reply to the Ministry of Food
and that he has now referred to the
Ministry of War Transport, will he make
arrangements for a similar conference to
be held with the Ministry of War Transport, or, alternatively, that a member of
the Ministry of War Transport should be
invited to attend this conference with the
Ministry of Food?
Mr. MAGINESS: I am sure that when
the hon. Member for South Down goes
with the deputation to London the
Ministry of Food will have such officials
present as may be deemed necessary.

suppose that in relation to the total crop
the losses in agricultural crops incurred
this year are any higher than those
suffered in bad pre-war harvest years,
and, if not, whether he can state how
this statement can be reconciled with the

The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE

The statement by one of my officers in

I cannot, therefore, see what there is

Mr. SPEAKER: The hon. Member

In any case a supplementary question
