be sent to
to fever hospitals elsewhere;
whether the Report of the Select Committee on Health Services stated that "the
evidence showed that so far as the city
of Londonderry was concerned the health
services were far behind those of other
parts of Northern Ireland," and what
action has been taken on the recommendation of this Committee that steps be taken
to see "that the existing state of affairs
is remedied at the earliest possible
moment."
The MINISTER OF HEALTH AND
LOCAL GOVERNMENT (Mr. Grant):
It would be an exaggeration to say that
epidemics of scarlet fever, diphtheria and
typhoid fever have been raging in the city
of Londonderry for the past two years.
There has been a minor epidemic of
scarlet fever in Londonderry since the
autumn of 1943, and unfortunately there
has not yet been the decline in the disease
which I would like to see. In the present
state of medical knowledge there are no
steps which can be taken by the Londonderry Corporation or by me to prevent
outbreaks of this disease. When it is
possible to improve housing conditions in
the city and to prevent overcrowding we
may hope for a reduction in the notifications. In the meantime, all that can be
done is for the medical profession to detect
infected persons as quickly as possible
and arrange for their segregation. I have
no reason to believe that any person has
neglected his duty in this matter.
There have been too many cases of
diphtheria in Londonderry. In the
summer of the year 1943 there was a sharp
rise in the number of cases notified, and
in the autumn of that year the number of
persons affected reached a total' at which
the use of the term "epidemic" was fully
justified.
After October, 1943, there was a steady
decline in the number of new notifications,
but it increased again in the spring of the
present year; the outbreak was, however,
less serious than in 1943. A reduction
was reported in the early summer, and
last week only one case was notified; in
the previous week there were four.
I am convinced that the incidence of
this disease could be very much lessened
if the population made a better response
to the efforts of the Londonderry Corporation to induce the public to take advantage of the free immunisation scheme.
There has been no epidemic of typhoid
fever in Londonderry during the last two
years. There were a few isolated cases,
but the ascertained source of infection in
the majority was many miles from
Londonderry. The six cases reported this

WAR-TIME
HOUSING POSITION.
12. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister
of Health and Local Government whether
he can state the present position in regard
to war-time houses authorised for erection
forthwith in November, 1943, and in
May, 1944.
Mr. GRANT: As the reply is rather
lengthy I propose, with the hon. Member's
consent, to circulate it in the Official
Report. The reply is supplemental to
the report which I circulated on the 10th
ultimo in response to a previous question
raised by him on this subject.
The following is the reply referred to:
Belfast: Agreement has been reached
between my Department and the Corporation regarding outstanding matters arising
out of the preliminary drawings submitted
in respect of the erection of the first batch
of 86 houses on the West Circular Road
site. My Department is now awaiting
submission of the final working drawings
and specifications.
Londonderry: I regret that I cannot
report any material progress by the
Londonderry Corporation as regards the
erection of the 250 war-time houses
allocated to the city. I understand that
discussions have been held between
representatives of the Corporation and the
Ministry of Commerce on the question of
materials. No drawings or other documents of any nature relating to the erection of the houses have, however, been
submitted to my Department.
Lisburn: The preparation of working
drawings and contract documents in respect of the war-time houses allocated
to Lisburn is proceeding satisfactorily.
Separate drawings in respect of the
engineering services are also being prepared.
Newry: Tenders have been received by
the council in respect. of the first 24
houses out of the total number of 100
houses allocated to the town, and are at
present under consideration. The council
has selected a site for the balance of the
houses, and has submitted a plan for the
Ministry's observations thereon.
Armagh I understand that the difficulties experienced over the selection of
suitable sites have been resolved and that
it should now be possible for the council
to make some material progress. The
work of designing the houses proposed to
be erected is, I gather, completed.
Newtownards: This council has also
experienced a certain amount of difficulty
over the question of a site. Arrangements have, however, now been made for
the acquisition of suitable land.
PRIME MINISTER'S ILLNESS.
Sympathy of the House.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Major
Sinclair): I am sure the House learned
with profound regret that the Prime.
Minister has been ordered by his doctors
to lie up for a time. Fortunately, it is
hoped that his illness will yield to treatment and that a few weeks will see him
back with us in full health. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) The Cabinet
and the House will miss his wise
guidance and wide grasp of
all the
interests of Northern Ireland. His illness is the direct outcome of the outpouring of his boundless energy and
driving force in all that appertains to
the interests of Northern Ireland, first
of all to ensure the maximum production
of industry in the war effort, and
secondly to ensure as far as possible that
in the post-war years we will have the
maximum employment in our Province.
I am sure I am speaking for both sides
of the House when I say we wish both
the Prime Minister and Lady Brooke a
speedy recovery from their illness.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)

with what the acting Prime Minister has
just said. I am sure that I am also
speaking for every Member of this
honourable House as well as those we
represent when I say that we deeply
regret the illness of the Prime Minister.
We extend to him our very sincere
sympathy, and we earnestly hope and

Major SINCLAIR: The financial proposals contained in the Resolutions before
the Committee are already set out in the
Bill and have been the subject of very
full discussion. In moving the Resolutions, however, I propose to take the
opportunity of explaining in
explaining in further
detail some of the financial aspects of the
Bill.
In speaking to the Second Reading, I
referred to a statement submitted to the
Belfast Corporation by a member of that
Council, and I described this statement
as misleading. At that time I had not
seen the Press report on which the statement was based. I now find that,
assuming the Press report to be correct
in its implications, the statement to
which I referred was made in all good
faith. Unfortunately for the Northern
Ireland Exchequer, the assumption taken
out of the Press report cannot be substantiated. It may be a picturesque and
quite valid journalistic method of expressing the Scottish position to state that
a
£50,000,000 or some such amount will
be expended on a ten or twelve years' programme of housing to be undertaken by
the Scottish Housing Association, but that
does not mean that this amount of money
is being earmarked now for payment out
of current revenue to the Secretary of
State for Scotland. The statement concluded that it did, and that, in consequence,
sum of £12,000,000 (presumably the Northern Ireland proportion
of £50,000,000 based on relative housing
needs) would be paid immediately, or as
soon as house construction began in
earnest, by the Imperial Exchequer to
the Northern Ireland Exchequer. I need
not follow the statement into the argument that, in that event, at the end of
forty years the Northern Ireland Exchequer would still have this £12,000,000
intact, because no such payment will, in
fact, be made. As I have said, I am
quite satisfied that the alderman in question in making his assertions did not
intend to mislead the Corporation or the
public, but said what he did in the
belief that it was indeed the true position.
It is, I think, self-evident that the
national income of Great Britain, and in
the same way of Northern Ireland, in the
post-war years will be subjected to a
heavy strain if it is to meet ordinary
current expenditure, which includes the
new national insurance proposals and
other day-to-day commitments which
have been or will be undertaken,
and that capital as distinct from
current expenditure (and by capital
expenditure I mean the provision of
houses, hospitals, water supplies and
other physical assets) will have to be
funded over a period of years. But
those who carry out these and other
essential works will expect to be paid
during the actual construction and on
its completion. In order to do this,
Government and local authorities will
have to borrow the capital sums required
and pay off their loans by annuities
(composed of interest and sinking fund)
charged against the actual revenue of the
years which comprise the term of the
loans. This is the principle which was
adopted in pre-war years, and indeed we
are carrying on our votes annuities in
connection with pre-war houses, which
amounted last year to almost a quarter
of a million pounds. It is also the
principle which will govern the pro-

In this connection, a point to which I
suggest insufficient attention has been
given in its application to the housing
schemes of local authorities-although, I
think, those immediately concerned are
sufficiently appreciative, indeed the chairman of the Estates Committee of Belfast
Corporation referred to it recently—is the
Government's action in reducing the local
loans borrowing rate to 3 per cent. in
parity with the rest of the United Kingdom. This is not only the lowest Government loans interest rate during the
existence of the Northern Ireland Government, but compares with a rate operative
over the whole Kingdom following the
last war of 6 per cent., or just double the
present rate, and we have to go back to
the year 1900 before reaching a period
when the rate of interest was as low in
Northern Ireland and the United Kingdom generally.
I think I should make it clear to the
Committee that it is the Government's
intention that the Housing Trust should
be run on sound financial lines. In other
words, the annual net cost to the Trust
of sinking fund and interest payments on
its capital borrowings, plus expenses of
administration, will determine the rents
to be charged, and as it is, of course,
intended that these should be kept as low
as may be possible, the exercise of a strict.
degree of economy in the Trust's finances
will be necessary. Hon. Members will
appreciate that it is far from being the
case, as has been suggested, that the Trust
will be given a blank cheque to proceed
with the provision of houses.
Further, it has already been emphasised
that the duties of the Trust will be
limited under the Bill to the provision
of working-class houses in those areas
where needs are most pressing, and I
should add that the programme of the
Trust will in general be limited to 25 per
cent. of the number of houses required.
I have no doubt whatever that experience
will show that local authorities will
purposes.
As there seems to be some misunderstanding about this question of the rate

Sir MILNE BARBOUR: I must say
I am very greatly relieved by what the
Minister of Finance has just told us.
But on the other hand I think we must
take the Bill as it stands and consider the
Clauses in the language in which they
are written, and in spite of what my
right hon. Friend has just said the Bill
does seem to be asking a blank cheque
from this House. There is one thing I
am sure of and that is that all of us in
this House are agreed in the desire that
houses should be provided as quickly as
possible. We are all agreed on that,
and we all have the greatest sympathy
either with those of our fellow citizens
who have been blitzed out of the houses
they previously occupied or with those of
our soldiers who have been abroad
and have not been able to look after the
housing of their families to the same
extent as those at home. We do wish
that their lot may be lightened to the
greatest extent possible.
But on previous occasions when housing Bills have been introduced in this
House there has been some regard to
the charge on the public purse. I remember in the olden days the arguments
that used to take place and the desire
for an estimate of the limit of expenditure. But in this Bill it seems to me that we
are somewhat reckless. There is no indication as to what upward limit on the
Trust should be imposed by this House.
There is no mention of rooms. Apparently the houses are defined as having

the size of these rooms?? There is no indication whatever as to the size of the

we talk of the contribution from the
public purse and from the local authorities. We fix these amounts, but then

up?
A lot of people object to private enterprise. I have no axe to grind. They
think that private enterprise is capitalism
and that it is a way of making money
out of the houses of the people. So it is
to a certain extent. They think that
houses built by the Trust is not private
enterprise and that no one makes money
out of the houses built by the Trust.
that respect they are completely wrong,
because it is capitalism no matter what
way you take it. If any three people are
going to build houses they have to get
money before they do anything, and the
only way money is to be got is by borrow-
In
ing it at interest, although you have
a foolish paragraph in the Schedule of the
Bill that there are going to be presents
given. Supposing the Trust borrows three
millions at 31 per cent., who are. they
going to borrow it from? They are going
to borrow it from people who have money
because nobody else can lend it.
The man
who lends £100,000 to the Trust has
nothing to do twice a year but put out his
hand for the interest and put it in his
pocket. No matter what way we look at
it it is capitalism. Therefore, there is
no point in that argument that you gain
by having the Trust.
A short time ago I was listening to a
lecture by a man for whom I have great
respect. He was an extremely welldressed man. You could read into his
lecture that people could do things without money. You could not go home on
a bus without money, nor could you go to
the dining-room without money. You
could go to it, but not to dine. My hon.
Friend (Mr. Agnew) brought forward
Russia to prove that. That lecturer was
about the best dressed man in the place,
and I was wondering if he got his clothes
for nothing, or whether the workmen who
wove the cloth in the mill worked for
nothing. As regards Russia, no one here
has more respect for Russia than I have.
That feeling has not been born in the last
four or five years. Russia raises loans.
We had in this country a Red Cross Fund
to assist Russia. It is all humbug that
you can do without money.
On another occasion I went to a committee meeting to raise money for a
certain object, and after devising ways
and means, somebody told us the money
was no use, it was only a token. That is.
all humbug. You could not do anything
without money. That is why my hon.
Friend (Mr. Agnew) has made many good
pleas in this House and elsewhere to get
better wages, that is to say, more money,
for people in industry. Yes, money is
valuable, and the man that squanders
money, either in a private or public
capacity, will have. none. If he squanders
it in his private capacity he may live to
regret it. If the public allow him to
squander it, they may live to regret it.
I have expressed my opinion on this Bill.
I certainly know the Bill is no good. The
Bill will not produce houses, and there is
nobody more anxious than I for it to
produce houses.

Major SINCLAIR: I should like, first
of all, to apologise to hon. Members if I
do not reply in detail to the various
remarks which they have made, because
in very many cases other hon. Members
referred to the same point. I think the
first point that seems to have loomed

them that the Bill gave the Trust a blank
cheque. Well, I should like to say that
the object of the provision that the
Treasury will meet any loss which may be
caused by the operations of the Trust is
not in order to provide the Trust with a
magnificent staff and add to the numbers
of civil servants. It is merely that the
operations of the Trust should not be
cramped by the fact that they have to be
absolutely certain in anything they do
that they do not run into debt. The
Trust has no other way of meeting any
debt. They would have no recourse to a
call upon the rates. But it is, as I said
when introducing the Money Resolution,
the intention of the Government that the
Trust should be run on sound, financial
lines, and that the loss should be as small
as possible. There is no desire on the
part of the Minister of Health or on the
part of the Government that the setting
up of the Housing Trust should mean the
setting up of another large Government
department. That side of the thing will
be very carefully watched.

Mr. NIXON: I shall take just a few

going to raise, but I am sure he will have

to refer to this subject of utility furniture which, according to the Press, the
Parliamentary Secretary was going round
inspecting. He inspected the premises
where the furniture is made. I believe in
a man understanding what he does. The
Parliamentary Secretary is a bachelor,
and I should like to be informed what he
knows about a cot, or what he knows
about a double bed. (Laughter.) I
should like to know his knowledge of these
subjects that he is investigating.
Here we are within one month of the
end of a leap year, and after that there.
is no hope for him. Time is flying fast
and his chance will soon be past, and instead of going about looking at utility
furniture, he should first put himself in
a position to be a judge of furniture, to
know what is required for a bedroom, for
a kitchen, for a scullery, or for any other
department of a married man's house.
What does he know of babies? What
does he know about a pram- —a high pram,
a low pram, a bassinette, or a double
pram? I say he knows nothing about
it.
Losses of Crops.
Mr. BROWN: I want to ask whether
the Government have got a reply to the
representations made to the British
Government in regard to the great and
grievous loss sustained by farmers in connection with the potato crop. I notice
that the Minister of Agriculture does not
consider it worth his while to remain here
to hear these matters raised. I protest
most strongly against the absence of the
Minister of Agriculture. It is most discourteous to the House. Time after time
I have endeavoured to raise this question,
but I cannot get the Minister here. It is
very important for him to catch his train,
but this is a very important matter for
the farmers who have sustained such great
and grievous losses. It is no small matter
for them. They cannot leave to catch a
train. We have a right to know at once
whether these representations the Government are alleged to have made to secure
compensation for the farmers of Northern Ireland have in fact been made, and
if they have the result of them. I think
we are entitled to compensation.
I was shocked to hear the Minister of
Finance tell us this afternoon that a sum
amounting to millions of pounds which
we all thought was a grant has turned out
now to be a loan. The conditions in regard to housing are totally different in
Northern Ireland from what they are in
Great Britain. Hundreds of thousands
of houses have been built across the
Channel during the war, but not one has
been erected here. I am not going to
labour that matter now, but the whole
position will have to be looked into. It
came as a great shock to me as well as to
other hon. Members to be told that what
we considered to be a grant was in reality
a loan. It is a very serious matter and
will cause hon. Members to reconsider
their attitude to this Housing Bill. We
should have definite information from the
Government before this matter is carried
any further in the House.

The MINISTER OF FINANCE

country. As hon. Members are aware,

which is being allowed for houses built
through the Trust. I should like to explain to the Committee that there is no
necessity to be nervous about the money
being forthcoming when it is required.
There is not the slightest doubt that, as
long as we keep in parity with Great
Britain, the money will be available for
building houses according to our relative.
needs.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: This Housing Trust is to last until 1947 for the
purpose of building houses, but what will
be the position of the Trust after 1947?
Is it going to continue building houses or
not? After 1947 the collection of rents
and all that sort of thing has to continue.
You are going to have two rent collecting
bodies. You are going to have the local
authorities collecting rents and you are
going to have the Trust, which ceases to
build in 1947, also collecting rents. This
could be equally well done by the local
authorities. It is considered by a good
many people that the Trust when it
ceases its function of building houses in
1947 in the various areas should hand
over the duty to the local authorities.
There would be no extra expenses incurred in rent collecting, and there would
be no necessity, in my opinion, for having all these people pensioned off. What
we have to bear in mind is that the local
authorities are composed of people elected
to do certain jobs. They are elected and
not nominated. It is a question whether
or not the local authorities get the same
financial assistance as the Trust gets. It
has been said—and the Minister himself
has mentioned it-that in the past local
authorities in some areas could not afford
to build houses because they would overburden the rates. To meet this difficulty
those areas need extra assistance. That
policy has not been adopted, and this
Money Resolution proposes to by-pass the
local authorities and to give preference
to the Trust.
There was one point which I raised
yesterday to which I did not get an
answer, that is that the Ministry can meet
any deficiency in any financial year.
Where the net annual expenditure of
the Trust is greater than the money coming in the Government are going to make
it up and put it on the Estimates. That
puts the Trust in a favourable position,
because the local authorities have to put
it on the rates. It seems to me that we
are going to have two sets of rents under
this system: we are going to have Housing Trust rents and we are going to have
local authorities' rents. Those two rents
will be operated by the gap of the
financial assistance given in addition to
the Housing Trust.
Yesterday I mentioned the fact I do

Act? All these things should be made
clear. If you want your Housing Trust
you must have your Money Resolution,
but all the points that have been raised
are for the purpose of the clarification of
the position. The sooner it is clarified the
sooner we will get on with the job of this
Bill.

I am only speaking for Belfast at the
The bigger the city would be

Dr. LYLE: The hon. Member for
Woodvale asked a question as to what
was to become of these two-roomed houses
when they ceased to be occupied, as they
will cease to be occupied. I think I can
give him an idea, judging from what
happened in the case of the building of
schools. There was a new school built
in the neighbourhood of Bready. The
local people wanted it made a certain
size. There was another school within
a mile or two which was to be closed down
in a few months. When they sent
their plans to Stormont the civil servants
and the Ministry of Education-I
presume it was the Ministry of Education-would not pass them. They said it
was too big; that there were too many
square feet. In the case of schools it is
square feet not cubic feet of space.
According to their calculation of measurement the children in many schools do not
get sufficient air space.
They were told that this school was
being built larger because the other school
was going to be closed within 12 months.
The Ministry replied, "No, you cannot
do it. We will not allow you to do it.
You have only got so many pupils."
The local authority had to build the
school as directed by the Ministry, and
in less than 12 months the other school
was closed. Subsequently they had to
put an addition to the new school which
cost three times as much as would the
extra cost of building on to the new
school when it was being originally
erected. I think you will find in the case
of the Housing Trust that the two-roomed
house which is not occupied will have to
have added to it one or two other apartments, and the cost of that house will
eventually be more than the cost of a
five or six-roomed house.
From the course of this debate, I think
the Government do not want local
authorities to build houses. They are
trying to prevent the local authorities
from building houses. They want to
throw the whole building programme into
the hands of the Housing Trust, and
when they find that local authorities will
not build houses, as they will not, they
will make a show of using their authority.
to compel them. But will they use that
authority? No, they will not. They
have never used their authority to compel
local authorities to do anything they
ought to have done in the case of health
administration. The Government have
always been afraid of the local authorities. They are still afraid of them.
They would not coerce one or two local
authorities. How, then, can the Government coerce hundreds of them? The
Government will come to this House and
say that the housing scheme was a
failure because the local authorities did
not do their duty. They will then ask
that the 25 per cent. limit, or whatever
the limit is, for the Housing Trust be
increased, and eventually the Trust will
gather the whole housing administration
into their own hands and we will have a
completely nationalised housing service in
Northern Ireland.

that Clause 4, as originally printed, has
formed part of the housing legislation in
Great Britain since 1936 and has, I am
informed, caused no administrative difficulty. At the same time I recognise that
there are two features about this Clause
which, on reflection, I am not sure should
find a place in our legislation. The first
is that in paragraph (a) the Clause as
drafted gives my Ministry power to withhold contributions due under this Bill in
respect of a local authority's default
under any part of the Housing Code.
The second point to which objection
might be taken is that the powers conferred by the Clause are exercisable by
my Department without any right of
appeal. The hon. and gallant Member
for East Down has drawn attention to this
feature of the Clause in the Amendment
which he has put down, suggesting that
action taken by the Ministry under this
Clause should be referable to an arbitrator acceptable to both the local authority
and the Ministry.
I am anxious first of all to remove from
the Clause the provision which enables me
to withhold grants under this Bill in respect of defaults arising out of other
housing legislation. I am also anxious
to meet the point put forward by the hon.
and gallant Member, but I do not think
that arbitration is the best solution.
In my view the correct course is so to
word the Clause as to give the local
authority the right to go before a court
of law if there is any dispute as to whether
or not the statutory conditions have been
observed. I am advised that the Clause,
as it will read in its amended form, fully
covers both these points.

This Clause creates rural councils as

Housing of the Working Classes Acts,
that is to say, the ordinary urban housing
code. In drafting the Bill, we had
thought that perhaps town commissioners

for the areas which they administer. But
the Association of Rural Councils drew
attention to the fact that these town commissioners had very limited powers of
raising money, and that they were not

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 23rd November, 1944.
The House met at Two of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
ORAL ANSWERS TO
QUESTIONS.
Tyrone and Fermanagh Mental Hospital.
1. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Health and Local Government whether he
can state why Tyrone and Fermanagh
Mental Hospital Committee refused to
spend £30 on the destruction of cockroaches which infest certain parts of the
institution; whether this Committee is
economising at the expense of the patients.
and staff; and whether he will have an
inspection carried out to see what can be
done in the matter.
The MINISTER OF HEALTH AND
LOCAL GOVERNMENT (Mr. Grant):
I have had inquiries made and understand
that many months ago the Tyrone and
Fermanagh Mental Hospital Committee
had under consideration the question of a
complaint regarding the numbers of
cockroaches in certain parts of the
hospital premises.
I am informed that the Hospital
Committee asked a certain firm for a
quotation for the making of special
arrangements to destroy cockroaches on
the premises and that a fee of thirty
guineas for services over a period of 12
months was quoted by that firm.
I understand also that in the meantime the inconvenience at the hospital
had been abated and that the committee
did not consider it essential to proceed
with the scheme, which would have cost
thirty guineas for 12 months.
I have not received any complaints on
this subject, but I feel certain that the
committee of this efficiently-run hospital
would at all times give due consideration
to the health and comfort of the patients
and staff, and would not decline to undertake any necessary work merely because
it involved the expenditure of a small
sum of money.
Mr. NIXON: Would the Minister
consider the advisability of sending down
a few packages of Keating's Powder?
(Laughter.)
Overtime for Agricultural work.
2. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he will look into
the question of payment of overtime to
labour gangs on agricultural work as dissatisfaction exists at the present time, as
no overtime is paid if gangs are rained off
for a part or a whole of other days, and
whether he will take up this matter with
the appropriate branch of his department and with the county agricultural
officers in Northern Ireland in order to
amend the regulations.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Rev. Robert Moore): I have looked into
the question of overtime to workers
employed under the harvesting labour
scheme. For the time being these
workers are engaged in agricultural work
and they are paid wages and overtime in
accordance with the rates determined by
the Agricultural Wages Board. These
rates provide for the payment of overtime only after a worker has completed 54
working hours in any week. They do not
provide for overtime payment on a daily
basis. The workers are paid wages at the
highest district rate irrespective of the
district in which they are working, and
are guaranteed full weekly wages provided they report for work every day,
even though, as the hon. Member is
aware, there are many days on which
adverse weather prevents any work being
done. I should add there are few instances in which overtime is worked.
Civil Service.

land; and whether the Minister will state

The MINISTER OF FINANCE
(Major Sinclair): The document to which
the hon. Member refers was not issued as
a circular by my Ministry to other
Departments, but is merely an office instruction sent to heads of branches of
the Ministry of Finance in response to a
request contained in a circular addressed
by the Ministry of Home Affairs to all
Government Departments-both of the
Imperial and of our own service-in
Northern Ireland.
The circular explains that persons in
the service of the Crown and resident in
Northern Ireland in the course of their
duty, who have removed to Northern Ireland from Eire or places abroad since
the 1st January, 1940, may be eligible
to be included in the electoral register
for Imperial elections now in course of
preparation, but that they can only
obtain electoral rights by presenting their
appropriate document of employment,
together with an identity card, at the
National Registration Office serving the
area in which they reside; and employing
Departments are therefore asked
bring this matter to the attention of the
persons concerned.
to
The Ministry's office instruction makes
provision for the future in so far as any
further personnel from the places indicated may enter the civil service of Northern Ireland. The Instruction was
signed by Mr. G. W. Schumacher, a
Principal in the Establishment Division
of my Ministry.
I may add that concurrent arrangements have been made by my Ministry for
the immediate removal from the elec
toral register of the names of any such
employees of the Ministry who lose their
electoral rights as a result of the cessation
of their employment. This also is in
accordance with a request made in the
Ministry of Home Affairs Circular to
which I have already referred.

other place outside the

Mr. WARNOCK: The situation in
Northern Ireland was such that it was
essential to retain in police employment
all available trained policemen, and in
general, therefore, members of the Royal
Ulster Constabulary could not be permitted to enlist.
Twenty members of the force who were
Army reservists were recalled to the
Colours after the outbreak of the war
and five other members of, the force were
allowed as an exceptional measure to
enlist voluntarily in the Fighting Services.

per five-roomed house would be transferred from the taxpayer to the ratepayer;
that is, of course, assuming that the local
authorities build the total number of
houses. If there were no Trust in
existence no houses could be built by it.
The special terms applicable to the
Trust do not and cannot be made to apply
to houses built by local authorities, provided we maintain parity with Great
Britain, as we propose to do. The
setting up of a Trust is a method by which
the taxpayer can contribute a greater
amount to the cost of the houses than is
the case at the present time. It is intended to relieve the ratepayer of an unnecessary and heavy burden. I want hon.
Members to appreciate that in moving
the rejection of this Clause they are in
reality voting for the transfer of £110.
for each five-roomed house from the taxpayer to the ratepayer.

question of housing is not, after all, going

the Government want local bodies to build
I am inclined to think they do not.

750 houses being built by the Corporation

Under the arrangement of £13 and £5

able to enter the field. If the Chancellor

should we take upon ourselves the building of houses before the British Treasury
decide what the subsidy should be? I
believe that if a grant in excess of £13

Trust. It is a question of keeping the

as possible.
If under this Bill local authorities do

If that were done there would be no

their duty. When the

Fermanagh Education Committee.
1. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Education whether he can state why two
ex-Service men were turned down by vote
and refused jobs as School Attendance
Officer by the County Fermanagh Education Committee; whether these ex-
Service men were eligible for this work;
whether he will sanction the appointment
made; whether he will remind the
County Fermanagh Education Committee
that they have a duty to perform to ex-
Service men; and whether he has seen
the observations made by a member of
the Committee who is Chairman of the
British Legion.
The MINISTER OF EDUCATION
(Lieut.-Colonel Hall-Thompson): My
Ministry has been informed that the
County Fermanagh Regional Education
Committee recently appointed a temporary school attendance officer in
part-time capacity to fill a vacancy
caused by death.
a
This appointment is not subject to the
approval of my Ministry, and I have no
information on the subject other than
that contained in the Press.
I might say that a letter was issued by
the Ministry of Health and Local Government to local authorities, including local
education authorities, asking them, when
making appointments, to give preference
to ex-Service candidates, other things
being equal, and suggesting that in
advertising vacancies a statement that
ex-Service candidates will be given preference should be embodied in the
advertisement.
A letter in similar terms has also been
issued by my Ministry to the managers
of all schools recognised by my Ministry.
I have not seen the observations made
by the member of the Committee who is
Chairman of the British Legion.
I would add that it is the earnest hope
of the Government that the claims of
ex-Service candidates for appointments
will as far as may be possible receive
favourable consideration.
Mr. AGNEW: Arising out of the right
hon. Gentleman's reply, would he be
good enough to send the circular to the
education committee of each county
instead of to the managers of schools?
Mental Hospital Staffs-Taylor Scheme.
2. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister
of Health and Local Government
whether he can state when the Taylor
Scheme will apply to Mental Hospital
Staffs in Northern Ireland; what is the
cause of the delay in bringing this Scheme
into operation; and whether any Mental
Hospital Committees have adopted the
Scheme.
The MINISTER OF HEALTH AND
LOCAL GOVERNMENT (Mr. Grant):
I am happy to inform the hon. Member
that after consultation with my right hon.
Friend, the Minister of Finance, I have
now been able to promise the mental
hospital authorities a 50 per cent.
Exchequer grant towards meeting the cost
of bringing the salaries of their nursing
staffs up to Scottish standards.
The grant will be available with effect
from the 1st November, 1944.
The arrangement is of a provisional
nature, since the Scottish Committee
which has been considering this whole
matter has not yet arrived at its conclusions. When that Committee finally
issues its recommendations, the question
of their application in Northern Ireland
will have to be considered.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Arising out of the
right hon. Gentleman's reply, is he aware
of the fact that the Tyrone and Fermanagh Mental Hospital have already
adopted the Taylor scale?
Mr. AGNEW: Hear, hear.

28 NOVEMBER 1944
Agriculture.
FLAX.
3. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he can state why flax
acreage payment was reduced; whether
this was done on instructions from the
Imperial Authorities; whether in view of
this reduction the price of scutched flax
will be raised to compensate farmers for
loss; whether it is a fact that foreign
flax will be introduced again to the detriment of the home grown article; and
whether he will make a definite statement
as to the future of agriculture in Northern
Ireland and what guarantees will be given
to the farming community.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Rev. Robert Moore): The acreage payment was introduced with the object of
inducing farmers to grow flax on certain
types of less suitable land on which, without the acreage payment, the grower ran
risk of financial loss. The Imperial
Government is now satisfied that sufficient
flax for war purposes can be obtained
without having recourse to the use of this
less suitable land.
With regard to the second part of the
question I would point out that the final
decision as to the price of flax is entirely
a matter for the Imperial Government.
The answer to the third part of the
question is in the negative.
As to the fourth part of the question
I have no official information but I would
assume that some flax will be available
on the Continant from now onward.
As far as the last part of the question is
concerned I have nothing to add to the
announcement made by the Imperial
Government guaranteeing the present
minimum prices for fat cattle and sheep
and milk until 1948.
POTATO CROP.
4. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he can state what
steps, if any, he has taken to secure compensation for the heavy losses sustained
by farmers by the failure of a very large
proportion of the potato crop in the
current season, and whether he has taken
any steps in the matter.
Rev. ROBERT MOORE: I would
refer the hon. Member to the reply which
I gave on 14th November to a similar
question by him.
Mr. BROWN: Can the Minister tell
us whether or not there have been any
developments in this matter since that
time, and has his attention been called
to the announcement made in Westminster
turning down his request?
Ministry of Finance-Signatures to
Letters.
5. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Finance whether he is aware of the fact
that great inconvenience is caused to the
public through the illegibility of the
signatures on letters signed by officials of
his Ministry; whether he will give instructions to his officials that the names
of the persons signing letters in his Department are to be typewritten under the
actual signature; and whether in view of
the importance of this matter he would
make it applicable to all Ministries.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Major
Sinclair): I sympathise with the hon.
Member's feelings in this matter, especially as I know from experience how inconvenient it is to receive a letter, no
matter from what source, where the name
of the writer cannot be readily deciphered.
I would point out, however, that in the
case of communications from Government
Departments inconvenience caused in the
way mentioned by the hon. Member is
minimised by the fact that the official
letter paper normally indicates that any
reply should be addressed to the Secretary
of the Department. Nevertheless
welcome the hon. Member's question and
am having the attention of the staff of
my Department drawn to the need for
due care in ensuring that the names of the
signatories of letters are readily legible to
the recipients either by signatures which
leave no doubt or in the manner which
the hon. Member has suggested.
I
Now that the matter has been raised,
I feel sure that Ministers responsible for
other Departments will consider the
advisability of taking similar action.
Mr. JOHNSTON: Should this question
not be addressed to the Minister of
Education?

the right hon. Gentleman, seeing he has
conceded the request of the hon. Member,

Council of Civil Liberties.

regarding the passages in that report

Major SINCLAIR: The answer to the

The Government of Northern Ireland,

Youth Welfare.
7. Mr. THOMAS CAMPBELL asked
the Minister of Finance whether the
Government at any time took steps to
implement the recommendation of a
Y.M.C.A. Committee on Youth Welfare,
that the Government should with the
instruments of propaganda now at its
disposal counteract the boycott of Catholic
youths seeking employment.
Major SINCLAIR: I am not aware
that any recommendation was put forward, as suggested by the hon. and
learned Member, by a Y.M.C.A. Committee on Youth Welfare. I understand,
however, that the statement referred to
was made by three members of the
National Council of Y.M.C.A.s, and was
not supported by other members of the
Council.
The matter was fully debated in the
House on the 1st October, 1940, when the
Minister of Labour of the day was able to
show that the alleged boycott of Roman
Catholic youths seeking employment was
entirely without foundation.
I regret that in this and the previous
question the hon. and learned Member
should have sought to raise matters which,
although already answered, are calculated
to create discord and interference with
our war effort.

Minister's Right to Answer Question.
MR. SPEAKER'S CONSIDERED
RULING.
Mr. SPEAKER: The hon. and learned
Member for Central has raised in writing
a point of order.
New Industries Bill-
Second Reading
28 NOVEMBER 1944
He asks whether a Minister is either
warranted or under an obligation to
answer a question on the Order Paper as
was done in this Session by the Minister
of Home Affairs and Security, who referred in terms of criticism to a public
speech in London of the Archbishop of
Westminster when the answer did not
relate to a further matter with which the
Minister was officially connected or to
proceedings pending in Parliament or to
any
affair of administration for which the
Minister was responsible.
This is my considered Ruling:
The Government of Northern Ireland
is responsible for law and order; this
includes the duty of ensuring that no
section of the population is oppressed: if
anyone states there is oppression, then
logically the Government has an obligation to answer a question on the subject
provided the Government does not consider it is against the public interest so
to do.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Can I raise a point
of Order?
Mr. SPEAKER: Certainly.
Mr. CAMPBELL: You are the arbiter,
of course, in a matter of this kind in the
House, and I follow your line of reasoning. Before you spoke I did have an
opinion to the
contrary-that
the
Minister was not at liberty to go outside
three specified courses. That is that he
could answer and refer to a matter for
which he was officially responsible, a
matter pending in Parliament, or to a
matter of administration for which he was
responsible. Until your ruling I thought
there was authoritative opinion in support
of my view and that it was confirmed by
the disallowance in the British House of
Commons of a question which stood on
the Order Paper on the statement of the
Archbishop of Westminster.
Mr. SPEAKER: I can assure the hon.
and learned Member that all these matters
receive very careful consideration.
ORDERS OF THE DAY.
NEW INDUSTRIES (DEVELOP-
MENT) BILL.
Order for Second Reading read.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF COM-
MERCE (Mr. Maginess): As hon. Members will have perceived, the purpose of
the Bill which is now in their hands is to
renew for a further period of two years
the powers conferred on the Ministry of
Commerce by the New Industries
(Development) Act, 1937. The extension
of these powers, granted by the Act of
1942, expires on the 31st December next,
and it is in these circumstances that I am
asking the House for a renewal.
Total war has brought with it the
almost total upheaval of industry. The
exigencies of war in Northern Ireland, as
in Great Britain, have caused our industries to flow into new and unaccustomed
channels. Our industrialists have had to
face many difficulties as a result of the
controls and restrictions necessitated by
total war, but it is fair to claim that they
have faced them courageously and successfully.
It has been my privilege during these
war years to visit many of our factories
and workshops, and I have been struck by
the way in which the managements have
tackled these problems. Often the work
they were called on to do was of a type
for which the existing machinery and tools
were unsuited, and to overcome such problems management and workers pooled
their energy, knowledge and resources.
The way in which our workers have reacted to the demands made upon them has
been inspiring, and is a good augury for
the future. Many tributes, generous but
deserved, have been paid to the skill and
adaptability of our workers here, both
male and female, by industrialists who
have commenced production here since the
war began.
Hon. Members will appreciate that the
powers conferred on my Ministry by the
New Industries (Development) Acts, 1937
and 1942, have necessarily passed somewhat into abeyance. Now the situation
is changing; final victory is assured, and
while there must be no relaxation of our
war effort, the problems of reconstruction
have been engaging our earnest attention.
To meet these problems measures more
comprehensive than that now before the
House will have to be considered. But
the war is not over and many of the
problems of peace have yet to become
clearly defined. I would not propose,
accordingly, to detain the House this
afternoon with a discussion of the larger
issues to which we must return on some
New Industries Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Maginess]
future occasion. I would merely indicate
that this is not a moment at which to let
fall from our hands any instrument which
may be of service in helping us to meet the
problems of the reconstruction and
diversification of industry when they come
It is, therefore, for this reason
upon us.
that this Bill renewing the terms of the
1942 Act is submitted to hon. Members.
I beg to move.

will never survive it. To-day we have

Let us review what has happened. Five
years ago, after a period of 21 years of
peace, Britain was onec more at war with
Germany. The Government of Great
Britain, ever mindful of the awful threat
of starvation in 1917 due to U-boat warfare and the very small margin by which
it was averted, once more called upon the
farmers to feed the nation in its hour of
dire peril. The Government tillage compaign had now come into operation and
has continued until to-day with an annual
increase in the acreage of arable land to
be ploughed, until it has now reached the
peak figure of approximately 50 per cent.
The farmers in Northern Ireland
accepted quite readily their part in this
heavy task, and have, with a mighty
effort, contributed to a large degree in
the maintenance of a healthy and ample
diet for the people of these islands. But
here we ask, is the present tillage campaign profitable? Is the present policy
wise, and prudent in so far as we farmers
in Northern Ireland are concerned, or to
the nation as a whole? We say no. First,

put into operation. The Ministry of

to all intents and purposes the agent of

together a mighty army of officials and,
armed with the powers granted or conferred on them by Acts of Parliament,
have become a power both above Parliament and the ordinary man. They have
become a power in the land which, in my

nation in 1917, never
again will

I have known the Minister of Agriculture all his life, and I know of nobody

Mr. LYONS: In discussing the Compulsory Tillage Order, we may well ask
ourselves why it was ever thought necessary to introduce such a measure of compulsion into Ulster agriculture, because it
must surely be realised that nowhere in
the world is there a more independent
type of individual than the farmer of this
Province. He is a man who works hard
frequently under primitive conditions,
primitive only because in many cases he
has never been sufficiently well off to lift

resents any attempts to drive him, and

is lost.
and we
Why, then, was it though necessary to
set the percentage of tillage as high as
45? I can well imagine the Minister of
Agriculture answering that question by
saying that it was necessary in order to
obtain the required food production
during war-time. That seems a very
reasonable and proper answer,
shall not quarrel about that. But what
we do find fault with is the method of
achieving that result. Let us carry our
minds back to the period of the last war,
and perhaps we can better understand
the situation. During that critical period
in our history the need for the production
of more foodstuffs was as great, if not in
fact, much greater, than to-day.
The Government of that time, in my
opinion very wisely, did not apply compulsory tillage. They did a much better
thing. They offered the farmer attractive
prices for all the farm produce which it
was necessary should be produced. The
result was that the nation was saved from
starvation; every ounce of food that could
be produced was produced, and we had an
era of prosperity not only in Northern
Ireland but all over the country, and in
England and Scotland as well. This era
of prosperity was not confined to farmers,
it was shared by all classes of the community, as always is the case when agriculture is prosperous.
When the war was over that situation
quickly changed. About 1921 the demand in Britain was for cheap food, and
there followed quite a spate of imported
food into the country from foreign
Reduction of Tillage Quota 28 NOVEMBER 1944
Reduction of Tillage Quota
countries. That immediately put the
home farmer into the background. Agriculture became a forgotten industry for
many years. But the story does not end
there. Industrialists very soon found that
with an impoverished rural population
they had no market for their goods, and
then followed the natural consequence,
depression at its worst.
Farmers who managed to hang on
during the depression did so with an
optimism that was not justified. They
saw the seeds of another war being broadcast in Europe and believed they would be
called on once more to save the situation.
That call duly arrived and found them
prepared to do their part to the utmost
of their ability. Prices of farm produce
were based on the minimum cost of production with the definite promise that any
statutory increase in costs would be offset with corresponding increases in prices.
However, as soon as it was seen that the
U-boat menace was overcome there came a
change of policy. I refer here particularly to
to the Imperial Parliament.
Vital promises were given a twist and
have not been honoured.
That irritating and irksome Compulsory
Tillage Order came into force compelling
farmers to plough up valuable permanent
grassland and also to cultivate land in big
areas which was not capable of producing
a profitable crop. All this, added to
serious shortages of labour and exceptionally severe weather conditions entailing
considerable extra work and loss of crops,
has served to make the costs of production
very much higher than they normally
should have been. Consequently, a great
many farmers find themselves in serious
difficulties.
Let me point out that the whole of
County Fermanagh was exempted from
the full application of the Compulsory
Tillage Order. In the past season the
result was that Fermanagh was the only
county in Northern Ireland which had an
excellent harvest and saved it well. In
the face of that result I suggest that the
reduction in the amount of tillage under
the Order could very well be applied to
all Northern Ireland. I consider that
this instance of Fermanagh's successful
harvest is proof that the Tillage Order as
at present enforced is defeating the very
purpose for which it was framed, that is,
the maintenance of the maximum food
production.
I shall now mention a few of the disabilities and vexatious restrictions with which
the farmers have to contend. Bad
weather has already been mentioned by
quite a number of speakers. We have
had three seasons of shocking harvest
weather. This is a thing which we do
not hold against the Minister of Agriculture because that is a matter over
which he has no control.
There are labour difficulties. While
certain hon. Members may consider that
labour is not a real difficulty I beg to
differ. If one is a farmer one will quickly
realise that it is a very genuine handicap to the maximum food production.
As well as being short in many districts
labour is, unfortunately, so organised in
certain areas that an additional hardship
is being imposed on farmers. I refer particularly to where my Friend, the hon.
Member for South Tyrone, comes fromthe Cookstown and Dungannon districts.
In those districts there are organised
labour gangs who call themselves
"boons."
These "boons" advertise in
the local Press offering their services to
any farmer who may require them. I
have seen these advertisements in the
Cookstown papers.
One such reads:
I am prepared to supply labour for
grass-seed time, flax time and harvest
time. Apply
—
These men offer to supply up to 70 men.
I submit that when the labour of a
district is organised in a gang such as that
there is no other labour to fall back upon.
That being so the farmer must employ the
"boons." I am informed on reliable
authority that the labour of these
"boons" may be obtained at a minimum
cost of £1 per day. While I have no
objection to labourers being adequately
compensated for their work, I do object
to farmers being exploited.
I have always maintained that at such
a time as this farm labour should be subsidised in some form. In a difficult season
it is impossible for farmers to carry on
satisfactorily. They have double the work
to do, and when the crop is saved they
find that it is not worth half what it
would be in a good season. One of our
troubles is the restriction placed upon the
use of tractors. Those who are engaged
in agriculture are aware that the tractor
has been introduced for the purpose of
taking the place of the horse. Undoubtedly it does part of the work that
Reduction of Tillage Quota HOUSE OF COMMONS
Reduction of Tillage Quota
[Mr. Lyons]
was formerly done by horses, but why, I
ask, should the tractor not be permitted
to do all the work formerly done by
horses? That is in connection with the
hauling of farm produce, and the domestic
requirements of the farmer. It is a nasty
and troublesome problem which one comes
up against in practically every district in
Northern Ireland. Owing to the operation of the Transport Board farmers are
not allowed to use their tractors for many
of the purposes for which they formerly
used their horses.
On the one hand, the farmers are being
pushed by the Ministry of Agriculture to
till 45 per cent. of their arable land, while
on the other hand they are up against
various restrictions which hamper and
impede their work. They are between the
devil and the deep sea. Their lot is not
to be envied. The Ministry have tried.
to meet the farmers-I am now referring
to the question of keeping the cost of production down-by giving acreage subsidies. While actually bringing more
money into the country and distributing
it amongst the farmers, these acreage subsidies this may seem surprising-do not
achieve the result which they were intended to achieve maximum production.
I should like to point out that in regard to the growing of flax the acreage
payment has a tendency to encourage
speculators into the business and also
others who know nothing about the
growing of flax. As a result of this
subsidy we have had the desired high acreage of flax without having the increased
production we should have had for the
amount of public money expended on the
scheme. Food production might be encouraged more by attractive prices than
a high tillage quota. I should like to
illustrate my point by referring to the
serious shortage of winter milk which
was much in evidence in the years before
the war. It was found necessary to do
something about the matter.
The production of winter milk had to be increased in order to meet the needs of the
people in Britain. I cannot give the
exact number of gallons exported each
winter from Northern Ireland to Scotland,
but I believe it is in the neighbourhood of
one million.
When the Ministry of Food wanted
milk production increased they did a
sensible thing. They did not adopt
compulsory methods because they knew
they would be futile; they advanced the
price to an attractive level and that had
the desired result. May I suggest to the
Minister of Agriculture that he should
reduce the compulsory quota and at the
same time bend his energies towards
securing better prices for farm produce.
If he did that the farmers would be
much happier, and the Minister would
then find that the reduced tillage would
not be taken advantage of.

to address the audience than anyone
here. What did Mr. Hudson say speaking about the probable position in the
supply of cattle feeding stuffs in Ireland
and the United Kingdom? He looked
around the audience and said: "I do
not see any probability in the lifetime of
any of the people here present of anything like the supply of feeding stuffs we
had been accustomed to."
It is all very easy to cry out about
more live stock, but how are we going
to support them if we do not grow the
stuff? Remember in spite of all the
complaints about the difficulty of this
harvest we had actually 59,000 acres less
cereals harvested this year than last year.
If we take barley, oats and other cereals we
had actually 59,000 acres less this year.
I am just afraid before next harvest is
reached a good many of our farmers will
feel the draught and the want of the
produce of those 59,000 acres we missed
this year.
I am perfectly satisfied on
giving this matter the closest consideration-I think I know the farming community and the farming situation
throughout the Six Counties as well as
hon. Members-and I am perfectly convinced I would not be acting the
farmers' friend to-day in Northern Ireland if I took any other decision than
the one I have taken.
Before I sit down I should just like
to say the general quota is 45 per cent.,
but there are exceptions. We have
excepted the whole of County Fermanagh,
and that was used as an argument for
a measure of relief in other districts. We
have drawn a line from Larne across
South Antrim away to Lough Neagh.
There they have the same tillage quota
as in County Fermanagh, 30 per cent.
I should like to say this further on this
question. There is not any comparison
between the definition of arable land that
my Ministry insists on and the farmers'
own definition. I hear some people complaining about the kind of land my
officials list in their schedule as arable
land. I know some of these farms that
have come on the market, and when it
came to the auctioneer saying how much
was arable land, it was very different to
what was put to my officials. I think I
have as capable an official at the head of
this whole section as any Ministry could
expect or wish to have, and it has been
the practice since I took over, and I am
sure before I took over, that wherever a
case of special hardship could be put up
it was not decided by the field officer nor
necessarily even by the county executive
officer. It goes right up to my Ministry
and in the last resort it comes to me.
So I do not think there is any excuse
at all for raising the question of oppressive administration. Where any farmer
is engaged in milk production he gets
special consideration. He may get exemption. There are many cases where we
would give that and in any case he gets
special consideration. I want to assure
the House that, apart from the milk producer, where there is any case that affects
the general condition of the land or anything of that kind that would seem to
warrant more sympathetic definition of
the quota I am always prepared to give

New Industries Bill
Housing (No. 2) Bill
29 NOVEMBER 1944
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Wednesday, 29th November, 1944.
The House met at Two of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
ORDERS OF THE DAY.
NEW INDUSTRIES (DEVELOP-
MENT) [MONEY].
Considered in Committee under Standing Order No. 65.
[Sir ROBERT LYNN in the Chair.]
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That for the purposes of any Act of the
present Session to amend the New
Industries (Development) Act (N.I.),
1937, by extending the period in which
the Ministry of Commerce may make
grants and recommend the making of
loans under that Act, it is expedient to
authorise the payment out of moneys
provided by Parliament of any increase
in the sums payable out of moneys
provided by Parliament under that Act
which is attributable to the passing of the
said Act of the present Session.".
(Governor's recommendation signified-
Major Sinclair.)
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Major
Sinclair): The proposed extension for two
further years of the New Industries (Development) Act, 1937, renders necessary
this Resolution to provide for the additional financial aid to industry which may,
as a result, be made available from public
funds. It is not proposed, however, to
remove the existing limit placed on the
aggregate of loans which will remain at
the present figure of £750,000. The
latest return shows that at 31st March,
1944, some £260,000 had been advanced
by way of loans, and though I know that
it is the hope of all of us that new indusstries will be established in increasing
numbers, thereby creating a firmer base
for our economic future, it is clear that
the available margin of loans facilities
will be likely to prove adequate in view
of the relatively short period of extension.
proposed. I beg to move.
Question put, and agreed to.
Resolution reported, and agreed to.
NEW INDUSTRIES (DEVELOP-
MENT) BILL.
Considered in Committee.'
[Sir ROBERT LYNN in the Chair.]
CLAUSE 1 (Extension of period for
the making of grants and loans), and 2
(Short title and citation), ordered to
stand part of the Bill.
TITLE agreed to.
Bill reported, without amendment, to
the House, and read the Third time.
Ordered, That the Clerk do carry, the
Bill to the Senate and desire their concurrence.

£2,000 a year men are to be included in

civil servants 8,000 strong.
I want to remind the Committee that
as recently as 1933 the total number of
civil servants was 2,179, while in September, 1923, the number was 1,007. We
have now roughly eight times that number.

The TEMPORARY CHAIRMAN
An elucidation was required on
The Trust shall be a body corporate

The ATTORNEY-GENERAL: A body
corporate may be more readily understood
by a series of illustrations. The Great
Northern Railway Co. is a body corporate; it is incorporated by special Act
of Parliament. It has perpetual succession and a common seal, and it is permitted to hold land in accordance with
the terms of the Act of Parliament incorporating it, that is to say, without a
licence from the Crown. There are many
thousands and thousands of limited
companies who are in precisely the same
position with a limitation in most cases
as to the amount of land they may hold,
and there is nothing novel or startling in
the principle whatever. There was an
objection of course at one time to mortmain-if I take the Committee back
several hundred years-mainly against
the acquisitive powers of the then Church
Committee.

it possible for the body corporate to hold
land for the purpose of its undertaking
without special licence from the Crown.
There is nothing novel about it. Indeed

CLAUSE 13 (General powers and
duties of the Trust.
(1) The Trust shall exercise their
powers and duties under this Act so as
to secure, in co-ordination with local
authorities, the provision of housing
accommodation for persons of the
working classes.
(2) Subject to the provisions of this
Act the Trust may, with the approval
of the Ministry, and shall, if so directed
by the Ministry, exercise all or any of
the powers specified in the First Schedule to this Act or otherwise conferred
on them by this Act.
(3) The Ministry may—
(a) make regulations as to the procedure of the Trust and generally as
to the manner in which the Trust
shall carry out their powers and
duties; and
(b) with the approval of the Ministry
of Finance, make regulations as to
the accounts to be kept by the
Trust, the form of such accounts
and the particulars to be contained
therein, and as to the records to be
kept by the Trust;
and the Trust shall act in accordance
with those regulations.
(4) The Trust shall, at such times as
the Ministry may direct, transmit
through the Ministry to the Comptroller and Auditor-General for Northern Ireland for examination in every
year accounts, in respect of the preceding financial year, in such form and
containing such particulars as may be
prescribed under paragraph (b) of the
last preceding sub-section. All such
accounts shall be duly vouched to the
satisfaction of the Comptroller and
Auditor-General, who shall certify and
report on the same, and copies of the
said accounts and of the reports thereon
shall be laid before Parliament as soon
as may be.

Bill in the spring of this year, and it was
generally agreed that the vesting order
procedure, as drawn up in 1934,
adequately safeguarded the interests of
the owner. The vesting order procedure provides for an appeal to the county
court on the question of value.
There is a Clause which at present forms
a proviso to sub-section 4, which provides
that before making a vesting order the
Ministry shall have regard to the effect
which the order would have on the user,
value, and amenities of lands in the
immediate neighbourhood of the land to
be acquired.
This provision was inserted during the
passage of the 1944 Bill and was then
accepted as a reasonable safeguard to impose upon the Ministry.
The suggestion which the hon. and
gallant Member makes is that an appeal
should lie to the county court about user,
value, and amenities.
The vesting order procedure deals very
fully and very fairly with the rights of
owners whose land is proposed to be taken
and with the compensation to be awarded.
The whole object of the vesting order
procedure is to hold a balance between the
legitimate interests of the land owner on

on the other.
This appeal procedure which the hon.
and gallant Member proposes is, in my

enabled to buy the house which they
Occupy. The Government is not in the
least opposed to tenant purchase, but it
should be clearly understood that at
present, while houses are in such short
supply, it is desirable to have sufficient
houses to rent before allowing them to go

houses have an entirely artificial famine
value; it would be difficult to approve any
scheme of tenant purchase which would
not lead to serious abuse.

house one week, whether on direct or hire
purchase, and sell his interest in it the
next week at a sum reflecting not its
actual value, but its scarcity value under
present conditions. On the other hand,

a permanent nature, and there is no

of hon. Members by providing machinery

schemes. Even without amendment the

actual wording of the. Amendment is

or on deferred terms, and long lease, and
I am satisfied that it covers all these
points.

the first instance I say the Imperial

If those houses were knocked down by

you will not build very much if you do

that it was the Government's intention

Lord GLENTORAN: There is one
question that is worrying me about the
financial aspect of this scheme, and that
is the question of the Imperial Contribution. If we run into a very heavy
debt as a result of building these houses,
as we are almost bound to if the Trust
is a success, what is going to be the
position? Has the Minister of Finance
had any conversations with the Imperial
Treasury with reference to our Contribution, because it was originally laid
down in the Government of Ireland Act,
1920, that all our Contributions to the
Imperial Government were to be settled
by the Colwyn Committee. Later that
was changed, and they were to be decided
by a committee of financial experts in
London. They have always been very
careful, and I remember that when my
right hon. Friend was Minister of
Finance he was brought up on a matter
of this kind. They have always taken
very great care to see that we went step
by step with them. It occurs to me that
if the Imperial Government do not introduce a Bill similar to our Housing
Bill, or if we incur any considerable debt,
they will not allow us to deduct it from
our Contribution, and it will be a special
debt that will have to be shouldered by
the people of Ulster.
That is a point
that has never been raised during the
passage of this Bill, but it is a very
important one, as I am sure the Minister
of Finance will agree.
Major SINCLAIR: Just to ease the mind
of the noble Lord, I should say that the
whole of the provisions in this Bill were
thoroughly discussed with the Imperial
Treasury, and they fully understand
their implications. The position of the
Trust here is exactly the same as that of
the Trust in Scotland. In the case of
the Housing Association of Scotland, if
it cannot balance its accounts the
Treasury will make good the difference,
and they are going to treat us in
exactly the same way as Scotland. I do
appreciate that there is the danger the
noble Lord mentioned, and that is a
point I shall have to watch particularly
carefully.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 30th November, 1944.
The House met at Two of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
ORAL ANSWER TO
QUESTION.
Housing.
the.
BUILDING MATERIALS.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON asked
Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry
of Commerce whether he can state if
materials are available to build the 1,500
houses allotted under the Housing (No. 1)
Act, and the number of houses for which
materials are available over and above
this number.
The
PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
COMMERCE (Mr. Maginess): The
answer to the first part of the question is
in the affirmative.
With regard to the second part,
materials are not at present available for
houses above this number, but, as the
housing programme develops appropriate
representations will be made to the
Imperial Departments concerned.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON : Can the
Parliamentary Secretary explain to the
House why it is necessary to move the
suspension of Standing Orders so as to
curtail discussion on the Housing (No. 2)
Bill when there is no material to build
houses?

if from this House we were to send a

Churchill, congratulating him on attaining his 70th birthday. With the permission of the House, I would ask Mr.
Speaker to send a telegram to that effect.

years of comfort and ease, and Mr.
Churchill has not been sailing through
peaceful waters. I happened to be a
member of the Churchill party at one
time, that was the old Liberal party.

are you a member of now? (Laughter.)

of the Labour party, because it seems by

one time and support Labour now you

valuable service in the nation's interest.
But I want now to get to this seventieth
birthday. I remember the right hon.
Gentleman's party meeting Mr. Churchill
in a very hostile manner in this city——

CLAUSE 23 (Provision as to management of housing accommodation).
(1) With a view to securing the
proper and efficient management of
any housing accommodation provided
by a local authority under the. Housing
Act (Northern Ireland), 1944, or this
Act, or provided by the Trust under

number of persons who may be

in the selection of tenants
occupiers of such accommodation;

Ministry may require to be included in any agreement under
which any person is permitted to
Occupy or use any such accommodation; and
(d) such other matters as the Ministry
may consider necessary or expedient.
(2) It shall be the duty of the local
authority or of the Trust, as the case
may be, to manage any such housing
accommodation as aforesaid in accordance with any regulations made under
this section.

Sir NORMAN STRONGE: I beg to
move this Amendment which is standing
in my name and that of others, and I
am quite sure the Minister will accept
it. I think everybody is anxious that
everything possible should be done for
our ex-Service men. I have heard it said
that this may be cutting across the 1920
Act, but this is not a special scheme for
ex-Service men. I would like hon. Members to realise, as I think they do, that
all ex-Service men who have gone from
this country are volunteers. They have
gone away while others have stayed at
home, and I would like them to realise
that when they come home again there
will be houses for them to live in.
Therefore I hope the Committee will
accept the Amendment. Large numbers
of these young men have sacrificed their
lives, and we hope their widows will be
enabled to get some of these houses.
Lieut.-Colonel PANTER: I rise to support the Amendment moved by my hon.
and gallant comrade, the Member for
Mid Armagh. I do so because I am convinced, after a considerable number of
years experience, that promises made to
Service men and Service women are not
generally implemented. We may remember the slogan, "A country fit for heroes
to live in," and the bitter disillusionment
and privations that faced and pursued our
fighting men after the last war. It was
said that this was mainly due to the
inadequate arrangements that had been
made for their return to civil life, and it
is now intimated that past errors will be
rectified in a demobilisotion plan shortly
to be announced.
Be that as it may, I am convinced that
a specific assurance should be given by
the Minister of Health and Local Government that a distinct preference-not
necessarily a priority-must be granted to
ex-Service applicants from Ulster for
tenancies, and that it will be obligatory
upon the Housing Trust, and all local
authorities concerned, to make service in
His Majesty's Forces the principal consideration in any scheme of lettings. The
Minister has, I understand, already
promised that he will ask local authorities
tc give special consideration to ex-Service
applicants, but, whilst I appreciate the
Minister's intention, I am of the opinion
that such a vital matter should not be left
to a mere request.
Priorities can, and will, I expect, be
dealt with in Statutory Regulations, but I
want to see an explicit instruction introduced in this Bill, and surely such a
demand is warranted. The men and
women who have been voluntarily engaged in the defence of British homes
should surely have a first claim to establish
homes of their own on their return from
our far-flung battlefields. Even to-day
the British Legion are receiving daily requests from ex-Service men's families
pleading for accommodation, and one can
see endless trouble and difficulties unless
some definite provision is now made in the
Bill.
It may be argued that a prior claim
exists for those persons who have lost their
homes as a result of enemy air raids, but
this applies almost solely to Belfast, and
I do not think that any ex-Service man
wishes to deprive such people of a house.
On the contrary, he merely wants a
definite assurance, fortified by legislative
authority, that his claims to a house should
receive a high degree of preference. Many
thousands of our young lads are away,

who would begrudge them their just reward. Let us then show them our

approval in this Bill that there will be
after this war preferential houses for
Ulster heroes to live in.

Lord GLENTORAN: Yes. I beg to
move to leave out the Clause. I do so
because I think it is redundant. These.
are all new houses, and therefore I do not
see how they will need rent restriction.
It seems to me that to say that these
people are to do without the benefit of
the Rent Restrictions Act makes it appear
that they are to do without something
which ordinary people have given to
them, that is the protection of the courts.
As these are new houses, I do not see that
they come within the ambit of the. Rent
Restrictions Act, and, therefore, I think
