Mr. GRANT: The noble Lord always
makes everything look so simple when he
rises, as he has just done in this instance,
that he requires careful watching, because.
there is something very dangerous in his
suggestion.
The Government must resist this
Amendment. I have already explained,
in the course of my speech on the Second
Reading of the Bill, some of the reasons
why it was considered necessary to
exempt these houses from the operation
of the Rent Restrictions Acts. In Great
Britain, no houses which have been built
by local authorities have ever been subject
to the Rent Restrictions Acts. In
Northern Ireland, houses built by local
authorities in the rural areas under the
Labourers Acts have similarly been
exempted from the, operation of the Rent
Restrictions Acts.
The safeguarding of the tenants from
having to pay exorbitant rents is, in the
Government's opinion, better secured by
the requirement that the rents shall be
subject to Government approval rather
than that the tenants should be left to
the operation of the Rent Restrictions
Acts. It should be borne in mind that
the Rent Restrictions Acts do not in any
way control the rents of new houses,
except in so far as the tenant can prove
that these rents are excessive, in relation
to the value of the house, but, in calculating this value, no account can be taken
of the controlled rents of similar surrounding property.
Moreover, it must be remembered that
public bodies are in a very different
position to private landlords. Public
bodies must select their tenants in regard
to the need of the people concerned for
houses, rather than in regard to their
desirability as tenants. A private landlord can select as his tenants people whom,
from his knowledge of their circumstances, he feels he can rely upon to pay
their rent regularly and to behave in every
way as good tenants. Public bodies must
select their tenants for other reasons, and
on that account they should be placed in
a
more favourable position than the
private landlord to obtain possession of
their houses from unsatisfactory tenants.
The essential point is that the rents as
I have stated must be approved by the
Government, and the Government must
answer to this House for the actions of
the local authorities and the Trust.
For these and many other reasons the
Government must resist this Amendment.
It is well within the knowledge of many
Members of this Committee that there
are certain areas in the city of Belfast
where houses were built, and it is
also well known what would happen if
certain people got into them under the

having stood up.

and I want a vote.
The Committee divided: Ayes 19;

Therefore I want the Committee to consider the implications involved in this matter. The first thing I

effect. All regulations made under this

remind the Committee that in this matter
of regulations we have not the protection

You, Mr. Beattie, as a Member of the
Imperial Parliament, are aware that there
is a Select Committee of the Imperial
House to examine these regulations. It
is an unpaid Committee, which is the sort
I advocate. In Great Britain, therefore,
they have greater protection than we
have. And that is not the only safeguard
we have not got. They have at Westminster a Select Committee on Public
Expenditure. Further, this Select Committee examines and reports to the House.
Of course we have not got such a committee here.
I will only say in conclusion that the
public will certainly brook no further
delay on the part of Parliament in dealing with this matter of the undue growth
and domination of bureaucracy. They
will grant no further respite to this House
if it is to have public esteem in tackling
this serious problem. The scales are
rapidly falling from their eyes. Therefore, I say there is no use talking about
mounting bureaucracy and mounting
expense and mounting squandermania if
we do not do something about it. This
alteration which I wish to make in the

Mr. GRANT: I beg to move, at the
end of sub-clause (1) to add the following
words:-
"workers" includes all person working
for wages; persons not working for
wages but working at some trade or
handicraft without employing others
except members of their own families;
and persons whose income in any case
does not exceed an average of eight
pounds a week; and includes the
families of of such persons who may
any
be residing with them.
As hon. Members are aware, I promised
to try to find a form of words to bring
the wording of this Bill more closely into
conformity with modern ideas in so far
as the term "working classes" was concerned. The suggestion was made that
we might adopt the phrase "the people,"
but it would be impossible to achieve a
definition of this term narrow enough to
exclude from the benefits of subsidised
housing those who were quite well enough
off to provide houses for themselves.
After a good deal of thought I selected
the word "workers" instead of the words
"working classes, " and as hon. Members
will see from the Amendment which
stands in my name, I have simplified the
definition and brought it up to date. It
now means that houses built under this
Bill may be let to anyone who works for
wages and to any self-employed people
who do not employ others outside their
own families. Outside these two main
classes, houses may also be made available to persons whose income does not
exceed an average of £8 per week, which
is approximately the present limit for
compulsory insurance under the National
Insurance Acts.
I should like to explain that the
Amendments consequential upon the
passing of this Amendment will have to
be put in on the Report Stage in so far as
those Amendments relate to the first 27
Clauses of the Bill, and I will see that
the appropriate Amendments are put
down for consideration on report. In
the remainder of the Bill, including the
Title, it will be possible to make the
Amendments as we go along. I beg to
move.

FIRST SCHEDULE (Powers of the
Northern Ireland Housing Trust).
1. To construct new houses, hostels
or flats for the accommodation of
persons of the working classes in urban
and rural districts, and to acquire
alter, enlarge, improve or repair houses
or building for the purposes of such
accommodation.
2. To construct, acquire alter,
enlarge, improve or repair any temporary buildings which may be, or may
be made, suitable for residential purposes.
3. To provide fixtures, fittings and
furniture in houses or other buildings
acquired by the Trust or under their
control, and to sell, let, lend or hire
such fixtures, fittings or furniture on
such terms and conditions as to payment or otherwise as the Trust may
think fit.
4. To manage any housing accommodation provided by or otherwise under
the control of the Trust and to promote
the welfare and comfort of the tenants
or occupiers thereof.
5. To develop land; to lay out
streets, roads and open spaces; to hand
over to the local authority any streets
or roads when completed.
6. Subject to the approval of the
Ministry of Finance, to borrow or
raise money for the purposes of the
Trust or any of them.
7. To invest such moneys as are not
immediately required for the purposes
of the Trust in securities in which
trustees are by law authorised to invest.
8. To undertake and execute any
lawful trust which has for its object
the furtherance of the provision of
housing accommodation for persons of
the working classes in Northern Ireland or any other object similar or
incidental to any purposes of the Trust.
9. To accept gifts and donations.
10. To establish and support, or aid
in the establishment or support of,
charitable or benevolent associations or
institutions connected with the provision of housing accommodation for
the working classes or with objects
ancillary to such provision.

Section twentyfour.
These are purely consequential Amendments arising out of the decision to give
the entire housing powers in the areas
administered by town commissioners to
rural councils, and to change the
definition of the persons for whom houses
may be provided under the Bill.
The effect of this particular Amendment is to repeal the power under which
town commissioners became housing
authorities under Part 3 of the Act of
1890, and also to deal with the question
of their expenses and borrowing powers.
The effect of the latter two alterations is

Bee Pest Bill [S.]—
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
Bill, with Amendments and an Amendment to the Title, reported to the House.
As amended, to be considered on Tuesday next, and to be printed.
BEE PEST PREVENTION BILL
[SENATE].
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Rev. Robert Moore): This Bill is being
brought forward at the instigation of the
bee-keepers and their association. The
last Bill dealing with matters of this
kind, I think, is dated 1908 and is entirely out of date. It only provided for
the, destruction of stocks of bees that were
found to be diseased, and the only disease
that it covered was the disease known as
foul brood. Since then other diseases
have appeared on the horizon, and for
some of these the treatment is quite satisfactory, and this Bill is intended and is
drafted to cover not only foul brood, but
ocarine and other diseases which may
emerge in future..
There are two main principles involved
in the Bill. The first is in Clause 2,
which introduces compulsory registration
of all bee-keepers. We propose to take
that step, if the House is agreeable, for
this reason, that up to now, when
disease broke out in a district, we did
not know who the bee-keepers in that
district were, and the disease spread
sometimes from a stock that nobody knew
anything about. The harm was done, and
it spread over a comparatively wide area
before the source of the trouble was found
at all. Under the Bill, it is proposed
that all bee-keepers should register. A
question was raised as to the right of the
Ministry to refuse registration to a particular bee-keeper or particular stocks of
bees in certain circumstances, and that
position has been safeguarded by introducing the right of appeal-
Notice taken that ten Members were
not present; House counted, and ten
Members being present
Rev. ROBERT MOORE: I was saying that we tried to meet the objection
which was raised to the Bill in its draft
form, namely, that my Ministry could
refuse to register bee-keepers in certain
circumstances. We have introduced a
new Clause to give such bee-keepers the
right of appeal against refusal, and also
against revocation. The other outstanding principle in the Bill is that which is
covered by Clause 3, and which takes
power to set up a compensation fund, so
that where stocks of bees have to be
destroyed, these shall not be a total loss
to the owners and that it shall be possible
to pay in part compensation for the bees
and appliances that are destroyed in the
interests of the. health of bees in the community. The compensation fund will be
partly derived from the registration fee
collected from bee-keepers. No definite
figure is set out in the Bill, but we have
had discussions with the Bee-keepers'
Association on the point, and it is thought
that about 1s per stock will be ample to
cover the cost. As to the amount of compensation that will be paid out of the
fund, that also is not set out in the Bill.
It is a matter of some difficulty to assess
the value of a diseased stock of bees, and
the Bill sets out that the basis of compensation will be arrived at by the
Ministry, after consultation with the
Bee-keepers' Association.
I
The rest of the Bill really contains
empowering or enforcement Clauses and
I think they are self-explanatory.
would just say in closing that my Ministry
is interested in bee-keeping not so much
as an industry in itself, but because of
the growing industry, and from the pollination point of view. At the present
time the industry is languishing because
of disease and because we had no proper
power to control that disease. The power
proposed in this Bill will, I think,
achieve that end. We have been
promised the co-operation of the Beekeepers' Association, and I think with
that we can make a success of this
I'beg to move.
measure.

Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: May I say
at the outset that I am considerably surprised that this Bill has been brought up
at this stage. I got no notice that this
Bill would be dealt with to-day. I think
the Government are going back to the old
practice they used before. That will not
work. Members ought to be given notice
when these Bills are coming on. I did
get notice that this afternoon's work was
to be the Housing Bill. I did not bring
with me my Bee Pest Bill or the correspondence I have had with various people
Bee Pest Bill [S.]—

30 NOVEMBER 1944
about it, and I am at a considerable disadvantage. I object to the Government
advancing things like this at this late
hour. It is not fair to private Members,
who have tried to make themselves
acquainted with the Bill. I was told the
Bill was coming on on Tuesday and, as I
say it is grossly unfair to private
Members. I say quite frankly these
things can be done, but they cannot be
done for ever. That was what broke the
last Government.
Having said that let me now say that
the Bill is desirable from the point of
view of bee-keepers. There is a great deal
of disease among bees. I think that has
probably been due to lack of proper feeding. I have been in communication with
the Bee-keepers' Association and I understand this Bill is welcomed by that body.
It has now 1,100 members, with branches
in every county. They agree to the
registration of bee-keepers and the inspection of stocks, but there is one snag and
the Minister knows it well. People interested in bees take out certificates from
the Bee-keepers' Association after passing an examination. I have it, however,
in writing from the president of the
association that the people who know less
about bees are the officials of the Ministry.
They know damn all about them; they
are absolutely ignorant. Inspectors go
round for the purpose of curing certain
diseases by treatment, but they are the
very people who are spreading the disease.
That is in writing from the Bee-keepers'
Association. They want competent people
to deal with this matter. The officials of
the Ministry have little scientific knowledge and the thing will fall to the
ground unless the Minister gives an
undertaking that these officials will learn
their job.
Another complaint is that when the
inspectors visit one house they tell the
people they must destroy their bees, and
when they visit another they tell them
not to destroy them. The Bee-keepers'
Association say that the inspectors of the
Ministry are not efficient. Inefficient
people are going about telling efficient
people how to do their work. Is that
common-sense? I have not been given
an opportunity of bringing along the
correspondence I had with various people
about this matter owing to the fact that
the Bill has been rushed upon us this

"involuntarily acquired."
When people find a swarm of bees they

When hon. Members take an interest in
the Bills to be presented to this House
they should be given an opportunity of
putting their views properly before the

was not to be taken until Tuesday next,
but it is being rushed through the House
this afternoon. That does not give hon.
Members a chance of doing justice to
themselves or to the Bill.
The bee-keepers are anxious that only
efficient inspectors will be appointed.
They do not want inefficient people. I
was told the other day that there are
7,314 people employed by the Government. This Bill will mean additional
staff, unless the inspectors are already in
existence. I complained about so many
people being employed by the Government. The bee-kepers want this Bill,
but they are anxious to see efficient
inspectors appointed.

3. Mr. JOHN BAILEY asked
Minister of Agriculture whether he can
state what steps have been taken by his
Ministry to open an artificial insemination station in Northern Ireland.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Rev. Robert Moore): The Ministry has
given full consideration to the establishment of an artificial insemination station
for live stock in Northern Ireland.
Legislation will be necessary in order to
confer powers of control on my Ministry,
and such legislation is at present under
consideration.
EX-SERVICE MEN AND WORK ON
LAND.
4. Mr. JOHN BAILEY asked the
Minister of Agriculture whether he can
state if any plan is in preparation by his
Ministry to train ex-Service men after
the war for work on the land, thereby
giving these men who want to farm a
chance to do so.
Rev. ROBERT MOORE: No arrangements have yet been made by my Ministry for the training of ex-Service men
after the war for work on the land. The
hon. Member will appreciate that this is
primarily a matter for the Imperial
Government, but discussions are taking
place with the Departments concerned.
Ulster Savings Certificates.
5. Mr. LYONS (for Mrs. Parker)
asked the Minister of Finance whether
he can state what percentage, if any,
of the money invested in Ulster Savings
Certificates, since the outbreak of war
has been withdrawn.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE
(Major Sinclair): The total sum invested
in Ulster Savings Certificates between
22nd November, 1939, being the date
of the inauguration of the National Savings Campaign, and 30th November, 1944,
was £19,384,844. Repayments during the
same period amounted to £1,886,535,
representing 9.73 per cent. of the total
sum invested, and as the interest on
repayments amounted to approximately
£48,500, the moneys withdrawn have on
the average been invested for an
appreciable time. Moreover, the hon.
Member will appreciate that, as rather
more than 90 per cent. of the sum invested
still remains with the Government, the
Voluntary Savings Movement has made a
notable and continuing contribution to
Ulster's war effort.
Mr. NIXON: With regard to the
Minister's statement about the amount
withdrawn, is it not a fact that if people
want to withdraw their money they have
a right to do so, and is it not a further
fact that anyone who has not a private
income may be compelled to withdraw it?
Lough Beg Flooding.
6. Mr. LYONS (for Mrs. Parker)
asked the Minister of Finance whether he
is aware that large areas of good grazing
land on the shores of Lough Beg have
been subject to severe flooding during the
past eighteen months, and whether he can
explain these disappointing results, in
view of the expert's forecast that Lough
Neagh and Lough Beg would remain at
summer level after the completion of the
Bann drainage scheme.
Major SINCLAIR: The answer to the
first part of the hon. Member's question
Oral Answers

is in the negative. The latter part

Eire Taxi-Cabs in Northern Ireland.
12. Mr. JOHN BAILEY asked the
Minister of Home Affairs and Security
whether he can state if it is a fact that
taxi-car owners residing in the Irish
Free State are not restricted with regard
to distances which their cars travel for
hire in Northern Ireland and, if so,
whether this competition is fair to
Northern Ireland taxi-cab owners who are
confined to a 10-mile limit; and whether
both Free State and Northern Ireland
cars are using petrol supplied by Great
Britain.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Mr. Warnock): The Control of Motor
Fuel Order which limits the distance
travelled by taxi-cabs in Northern Ireland
does not of course apply to Eire or to
any petrol supplied in Eire. There is no
limit therefore to the distance covered by
an Eire taxi-cab in Northern Ireland,
where it has been hired in Eire and is
using Eire petrol.
I fail to see how any question of competition with Northern Ireland taxi-cab
owners arises as Eire taxi-cabs cannot
stand or ply for hire in Northern Ireland.
I do not know whether Eire is supplied
with petrol from Great Britain or not.
Mr. NIXON: With regard to the
scarcity of petrol here, does the Minister
know that if a traveller gets off the train
at a railway station in Eire there are cabs
waiting and that he can take them for
practically as long a distance as he likes?
If so, why do we not get a little more
petrol here?

WRITTEN ANSWERS.
Downpatrick Grading Station.
Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he can state the
number of casualty animals in the past 12
months at Downpatrick Grading Station,
and why is there a fixed price for such
animals as none existed pre-war; and
whether the retail price of casualty
animals sold as beef is cheaper to the consumer as the owners receive less than that
paid for non-casualty grades.
Rev. ROBERT MOORE: Seven cattle
and
seven sheep were bought on а
casualty basis at Downpatrick Purchasing Centre during the past 12 months,
but in every case the animals came into
the casualty class before arrival at the
centre.
The hon. Member is, of course, aware
that no fixed prices for fat stock of any
description existed until the introduction
of the Meat and Live Stock Scheme in
January, 1940. Before that date, therefore, casualty animals were sold by producers for what they would fetch to
whomsoever would buy them.
Carcases of casualty animals are now
graded after slaughter, paid for at their
appropriate price, sold to the trade at the
prices fixed for their grades, and if of
retail quality sold to the public at the
specified retail prices.

BALLYCASTLE
SCAVENGING,
WATER AND SEWERAGE.
Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Health and Local Government whether
he can state what action Ballycastle
U.D.C. have taken to comply with the
report issued on 23-5-44 by the Ministry's
medical inspectors dealing with scavenging, water supply and sewerage; and
whether this U.D.C. are keeping in touch
with requirements and needs of the people
and are willing to adopt the Ministry's
report as mentioned.
Mr. GRANT: The Ballycastle Urban
District Council have indicated their intention to adopt a domestic scavenging
scheme when conditions permit.
The council have already sent samples
of water for analysis as suggested by the
Ministry's medical inspector, and have
instructed their engineer to proceed with
the preparation of a scheme for augmenting the supply.
As regards sewerage facilities, the
Ministry's medical inspector made various
suggestions for improvements to be undertaken when increased supplies of materials
become available and when the town planning scheme is being formulated. The
council are awaiting the report of the
town planning officer.
So far as I am aware the rural district
council are alive to their responsibilities,
and are prepared to undertake, in so far
as the war situation allows them, the
improvements which have been suggested.
Tynane Brick Yard, Dungannon.

Labour whether he will investigate the

Messrs. Kellys, Tynane Brick Yard, near

Bee Pest [Money]

HOUSE OF COMMONS
in
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Midgley): In reply to the hon. Member,
I am informed that the rate of wages
the brick yard mentioned is 1s 2d per
hour for a 511-hour week, plus a weekly
bonus of 8s 6d. This approximates to
the average district rate in the industry.
My Department has received no complaint
on behalf of those engaged in this industry
in the district, but as the hon. Member
is aware the procedure of the Conditions
of Employment and National Arbitration
Order is available to deal with matters of
this kind if reported in the appropriate
way.
With regard to the disallowance of unemployment benefit claims the hon.
Member knows that if a person refuses
suitable employment his benefit must be
stopped; but whether the employment is
suitable or not depends upon the particular circumstances in each case. There
is always a right of appeal from the
decision of the insurance officer to the
court of referees if the person concerned
thinks that the disallowance is unfair.

Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That for the purposes of any Act of the
present Session To provide for the prevention of the spreading of pests or
diseases among bees and for purposes connected with the matters aforesaid," it is
expedient to authorisesums
(1) the payment out of moneys provided by Parliament of the
necessary for meeting, to the extent
specified in the said Act, any deficiency
occurring in the Compensation Fund
established under the said Act.
(2) A charge upon the Consolidated
Fund in respect of the sums to be
issued thereout under the said Act by
the Ministry of Finance to the said
Compensation Fund for meeting_any
claims against the Compensation Fund
for which no moneys standing to the
credit of the Compensation Fund are

Major SINCLAIR: The Resolution
before the Committee is largely selfexplanatory. Hon. Members will be
aware that the Compensation Fund to be
established under the Bee Pest Prevention Bill will be fed from registration
fees to be paid by bee-keepers. My right
hon. Friend has already explained that
the fee payable in each case will be of
modest dimensions, and it is expected
that in the early years outgoings from the
fund by way of compensation for destroyed stocks and appliances may exceed
the income of the fund derived from
fees. It is proposed, therefore, that any
deficiency which may arise will be met
to some extent from the Exchequer, and
that such Exchequer grant will normally
be limited either to half the total of the
compensation paid in the year in question or £500, whichever is the lesser. In
any year where the deficiency in the fund
exceeds £500, the Exchequer will provide
advances, but such advances will require
to be repaid by the fund in future years,
even though such a development may
connote an increase in the fees payable
by bee-keepers. It is proposed, however,
that in exceptional circumstances the
Ministry of Finance may approve an
arrangement under
excess deficiences shall be permanently defrayed
from public funds. I beg to move.

FOOD AND FLAX PRODUCTION.
Mr. BROWN: I beg to move,
That in the opinion of this House the
Government's policy regarding food and
flax production calls for immediate and
comprehensive review, particularly in
regard to the need for vigorous representations to secure compensation for
farmers who have sustained heavy
losses as a result of the failure of a
large portion of the potato, flax and
other crops in the present season.
2671 Food and Flax Production

5 DECEMBER 1944
Food and Flax Production
I want to refer briefly to the question
of flax. Since I came to the House I
have been handed an Amendment standing in the name of the noble Lord the
Member for Bloomfield, and in order to
secure unanimity in the interests of agriculture, which I believe will be achieved
through that Amendment, I formally
move my Motion. The noble Lord
is a warm and sincere friend of the
farmers.
In the meantime I want to put one or
two facts before the House to prove that
the reduction in the flax subsidy is a very
serious matter, and a matter of which this
House is bound to take notice. I think
I can best express the views of the
farmers in this connection by reading
from a leading article in the Farmers'
Journal, the leading journal for the
farmers of Ulster, for the month of
December. It states:
During the past month farmers in
Northern Ireland have seen the first
flicker of the red light. In the twinkling of an eye it was recognised by
farmers throughout the length and
breadth of the Province as heralding
the first signs of a dangerous and difficult period for the industry.
Like a bolt from the blue came the
announcement from the Ministry of
Supply, through the Northern Ireland
Ministry of Agriculture, that the
acreage payment for the 1945 flax crop
would be reduced by 50 per cent., i.e.,
to £5. True it undoubtedly is that for
some of the major outputs of the farm,
viz., milk and fat stock, there is a price
guarantee which will extend to midsummer, 1948; but the signal which
has now been given in the matter of
flax is a foretaste of what is likely to
happen ultimately to acreage payments.
The U.F.U. Executive Committee lost
no time in expressing in a very vigorous
manner exactly what the farmer in the
Province thinks about the whole
matter. Costs of production have
been mounting up steadily since the
war started, and are still climbing.
Whether wages have reached the peak
no one can be certain; but could anyone in his senses visualise the costs of
producing an acre of flax in 1945 being
less than it was in 1944? It would
appear that to the Ministry of Supply
all that is to count for nothing.
Enough and more to meet requirements has been produced, and the
farmers are to be left to take charge of
the baby. That is the immediate and
definite reaction to this announcement
by every flax grower in the country,
and to suggest otherwise would be to
ignore facts. To clamp down on
prices-
Mr. DEPUTY SPEAKER: It is out
of order to read newspaper articles in this
House. The hon. Member might give the
House a summary of what is contained in
the article.
Mr. ELLIOTT: But do you understand

Mr. DEPUTY SPEAKER: That does

To clamp down on prices without any

terribly harsh, crude and unbusinesslike way of limiting production. It is
a method not entirely unknown to the
Civil Service of exercising power, but
without accepting responsibility-a
method which had its beginning about
the time when men lived in caves and
exercised authority not by reason, but
by brute force.
I am not going to develop that any
further. Those are the views of the
farmers of Ulster as expressed in the
Farmers' Journal regarding this reduction in the acreage payments for flax.

now that flax growing is to be thrown to

wonder whether that aspect of the question has been taken into consideration.
What has happened in regard to flax will
undoubtedly reduce employment on the

Food and Flax Production
HOUSE OF COMMONS

[Mr. Brown]
I have raised, by means of questions
and otherwise, the question of the securing of compensation for farmers for the
very serious losses they have sustained.
We know that tens of thousands of tons
of potatoes still lie rotting in the fields,
and the losses to farmers will be very
grievous. It was suggested in a previous
debate that something was asked for the
farmer here which was not asked across
the water. That argument cannot be
advanced now because the farmers of
England and Wales and Scotland are also
asking for compensation in the same
manner as the Ulster farmers are doing.
I suggest that we in Ulster have a special
claim for compensation; in fact we have
a much greater claim than the farmers
across the water. The majority of our
farms are small. The size of the average
farm in Ulster is less than the size of the
average farm across the water. Everybody knows that across the Channel they
can go in for a system of mass production,
as it were, by adopting mechanisation and
other means which we cannot adopt here
owing to the small size of our farms.
Furthermore, in regard to the price of
potatoes, it has been stated time after
time in this House that the growers are
not getting anything like. the prices they
get in Great Britain, that the average
is £2 a ton less than the average the producers are receiving in England, Scotland, and Wales. Ulster producers
should get the same prices for their
potatoes as are paid to the producers
across the Channel. I have asked for that
time after time, in this House, and so far
as I am concerned, I will go on asking
until something is done. But I believe
the noble Lord will be able to deal with
that question effectively. The farmers
here have a case for compensation, and a
better case than the farmers across the
water in consequence, of the facts I have
pointed out, and also because they are
getting on an average £2 a ton less than
the farmers there.
I want to refer to the fact that the
Minister of Agriculture spoke in this
House a week ago about a certain quantity of oats that we were geting from
Scotland. He suggested that if the
change were made in the tillage quota,
vengeance would be wreaked upon us and
the oats withdrawn. Let me remind the
Minister that he did not give anything
like a complete picture. He gave only a
very small part, and I suggest a misleading part, of the picture. When he
talked of getting those oats from Scotland,
he seemed to forget the fact that they
came for the purpose of feeding our cattle.
They came to produce beef and other
meat to be sent back across the water.
I want to see everything possible sent
across the Channel to help the war effort.
I am glad this is so, but it should not be
forgotten that the bulk of those oats
was used to produce beef and other meat
for people across the water.
We also produce more milk for the children in schools
in Scotland than the children in schools
in Ulster are getting. The Minister
should have brought out those facts, but
he did not bring them out. We send
20,000 gallons every night to Scotland,
and that results in the children in Scotland getting a larger quantity of milk
in their schools than our children in
Ulster get. I do not intend to develop
that side of the picture.
Then the fertility of the soil was mentioned. There has been a great loss in
fertility, and in many cases farms have
been ruined, but I leave this matter also
to be developed at greater length by the
noble Lord, who is an expert. He
handed in his Amendment, and I received
it before I came into the. House. I think
it will achieve, in a different form of
words, what I want to achieve. So that
the House may be unanimous in the interests of the. farmers, I will in advance
say that I accept the Amendment to be
moved by the noble Lord, which he tells
me has been brought forward in a most,
friendly manner. Of course, I accept it
knowing that he is a very warm and
sincere friend of the farmer.
I shall have no hesitation whatever,
when the time comes, in falling in with
this Amendment so that the matter may
be unanimous and something be done to
help the farmers in the. really serious and
grievous plight in which they find themselves to-day. I am not exaggerating the
thing one bit when I say that I hope
the House will come to a unanimous
decision on behalf of the farmers.
On behalf of the farmers we are asking
for nothing but fair play and justice in
this matter. It is really a business
transaction. The price of potatoes has
been fixed, and as the noble Lord well
knows the average yield of ware potatoes

That man's experience is the experience

you will see the serious plight he is in.
He is faced with terrible loss-to him an
absolutely staggering loss. I think it is
unfair of the Ministry to come along and

failed owing to circumstances over which
he had no control. It was good seed

Lord GLENTORAN: I rise to propose

"this House recognises the abnormal

I propose this Amendment for two
reasons. The first reason is that I think
it is against the interests of the farmers
that an Amendment should be carried by
a narrow majority, because it gives a
wrong impression. Agriculture is our
principal industry. It
It is really our
national industry, and, therefore, I think
that matters of agriculture being of such
importance should have the support of

bring forward.
The second reason I move this Amendment is this: that I honestly believe that
the Minister and the Ministry are doing
their best in difficult times. They are
wrestling with the season just in the same
way as the smallest farmer in Ulster is
wrestling with the season; for this has
been the worst harvest in the memory of
man. I say the worst harvest, because
although it is well into December we are
still trying to save the harvest. Anyone
who knows anything about farming will
understand what that means to an ordinary farmer. Big farms, with capital
behind them, were still struggling to get
their grain in in the month of November,
and their potatoes are still in the ground
in thousands and thousands of acres.
I should like the House just for a
moment to consider what the farmer is up
against. I should like to say that the
Government have lost very little.
We
have got most of it in, at the expense of
the farmer, not of the Government,
because in order to bring the crops in
and get them into the house we have
employed outside labour continuously.
We could not have saved our harvest if
it had not been for voluntary labour.
Voluntary labour has been the saving of
us.
But voluntary labour is somewhat
of a misnomer because voluntary labour
costs us something like a shilling an hour.
I should like to say something about the
farmers' wives and families. Again and
again we have brought out 25 men and
they have to have dinner and tea, and

That is not the whole story. Nothing

Every farm in Ulster to-day is just a

This time it is the Ministry of Agriculture.
We have not only this year to think of,

Naturally he is very hard on those who
are here to help him.
*
There was one other important point
raised by my hon. Friend-the taking
away of the £5 subsidy for flax. There

an extraordinary effect on the mentality

fellows are at it again. They threw us

I should like to say a word or two about

been mentioned. It is not in any way
the responsibility of the Minister. The
£5 subsidy has been taken off by the
Ministry of Supply. I have never found
the Ministry of Supply to have any policy
whatever. They are out for what they
can get, and when they get what they
want they throw the people who got it for
them to the dogs. I want to inform my
industrial friends that the same thing
will happen in industry.
Why have they flung the farmers on
one side? Because they have found that
there is 50,000 tons of flax in Belgium.
There has also been a movement in regard
to taking flax from Russia. Therefore
they do not want much home-grown flax.
They would not have dared to do the
same thing with labour.
If the wages
of people in industry were going to be
cut there would be negotiation after

be arrived at, but so far as the wretched
farmers are concerned it is a clear cut.
When the Minister was faced with the

of better quality than flax grown under a
subsidy per acre. I say that although I
was responsible for the subsidy.
wanted quantity and I got it, but in the

compete with our competitors. When
I
they cut off the subsidy they should have

Question, "That the words proposed to

Question, "That those words be there

Resolved: That this House recognises
the abnormal losses suffered this season by
growers of main crop potatoes, is further
of opinion that even with normal yields
the present prices of main crop potatoes
are too low, and, while recognising that
prices are solely a matter for the British
Government, supports the Minister of
Agriculture in his efforts to obtain
satisfactory solution of this urgent
problem.

office of chairman of the Newtownards
Rural District Council, but it is open to
any person to have the matter determined by instituting legal proceedings

were invited by his Ministry for the erection of a new building or buildings at

were

Sinclair): Yes, Sir. Tenders

new building, but in view of the decision
not to proceed with the scheme at present,
the tenders were returned to the conractors unopened.

CLAUSE (Contribution to local
authorities in respect of provision of housing accommodation).

pursuance of a housing scheme approved
by the Ministry of Health and Local
Government (in this Act referred to as
"the Ministry"), provided housing accommodation for persons of the working
classes, the Ministry shall, subject to
the provisions of this Part of this Act,
pay to such authority, in respect of each
new house completed by them before
the first day of October, nineteen
hundred and forty-seven, forty successive annual contributions, the amount
of which shall be calculated in accordance with the following provisions of
this section.

Mr. GRANT: I beg to move at the end
of sub-clause (3) to add the following
words:
"Provided that no contribution shall
be paid to the Trust under this subsection unless the Ministry is satisfied
that the Trust are carrying out their
powers and duties in such a manner as
to ensure that the expenditure incurred
by the Trust (other than expenditure
for purposes of experiment or research
directed by the Ministry), and the
rents charged in respect of accommodation provided by the Trust, correspond
as nearly as may be to those which are
normally incurred and charged by local
authorities in respect of houses provided under this Act."
This Amendment is designed to meet
some of the misgivings expressed by
right hon. and hon. Members during the
debates on the Committee stage. It is
designed to ensure that the Trust, before
it can claim the deficiency contributions
provided for in this Clause, must satisfy
the Ministry that in general its operations
have been conducted in a normal and
reasonably economical manner. The
Trust will not be able, for instance, to
build palaces and charge very small rents
for them. They must cut their coat
according to their cloth just in the same
way as the local authorities will naturally
do.
My right hon. Friend the Minister of
Finance and myself have had considerable
difficulty in designing a provision which,
whilst not having the effect of unduly.
cramping the style of the Trust, will
impose the sort of sensible restriction on
their actions which he and I, no less than
the hon. Members who have spoken on
this Clause, would wish. In view of the
present uncertainity with regard to the
eventual subsidy amounts, and the programme which the Trust may be asked to
undertake, it is not possible to put in the
Bill any direct limit in figures or in time;
but I hope that right hon. and hon.
Members will accept the Amendment
which has been put down in the Government's name as an indication that, at any
rate, the Trust will not be allowed to
adopt methods of unfair competition with
local authorities.
Sir MILNE BARBOUR: As one who
criticised this Clause on the Committee
stage of the Bill, I should like to take
this opportunity of thanking the Minister of Health and Local Government and
his Colleagues, not only for their willingness to meet the criticism which I and
other Members expressed, but also for

Lieut.-Colonel
GORDON: I should

on introducing this Amendment, which
is designed to put a stop to undue extravagance. It will meet the purpose
very well. It is a business Amendment
to deal with a very open door.
I congratulate the Minister on having met the
wishes of the House in connection with
this matter.
Lord GLENTORAN: Whilst I join
in congratulating the Minister I should
also like to congratulate the Members of
this House for impressing upon the Minister that an Amendment was necessary.
Without the Amendment the House
would have had very little say in regard
to the amount of money that could be
thrown away if it were desired to do so.
I think this Amendment will improve
the Bill, and I am grateful for it. It
shows the value of having on the floor of
the House a full discussion on very important matters.
*

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 14th December, 1944.
The House met at Two of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
ORAL ANSWERS TO
QUESTIONS.
White Paper on Educational
Reconstruction.
VOLUNTARY SCHOOLS.
1. Mr. THOMAS CAMPBELL asked
the Minister of Education whether the
Government project the denial of all concessions under their Educational Reconstruction Scheme to voluntary schools
under individual management (of which
the great majority are Catholic) unless
the principle of individual management
of the schools is abandoned; whether he
is aware that this principle has been the
keystone of the Catholic
Catholic elementary
school system in Ireland from time immemorial; whether the pupils in the
Catholic voluntary schools are about 38
per cent. of the elementary pupils of this
area; whether this project is part of a
persistent Government manoeuvre to get
complete control of the Catholic schools;
and whether he realises that such a
crowning injustice to these schools will be
vehemently resented and resisted by the
Catholics of Northern Ireland.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Major
Sinclair): I have been asked by my right
hon. Friend to reply. I should like to
apologise for his absence which is due to
stress of weather encountered when coming over from England. The proposals
contained in the White Paper on Educational Reconstruction will, I hope, be
debated by Parliament shortly after the
resumption in January next. In the
meantime I do not think we should
anticipate the debate.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Does the right hon.
Gentleman or the Minister of Education
expect the Catholics in Northern Ireland
to settle a great question by a great
surrender?
SELECTION OF TEACHERS.
2. Mr. THOMAS CAMPBELL asked
the Minister of Education whether the
selection of teachers for the provided and
transferred schools first by the school
management committee and secondly by
the education committee from the management committee's short list has led to
widespread abuses, and if he will indicate
what forms the abuses have taken.
Major SINCLAIR: The answer to the
first part of the hon. and learned Member's question is in the affirmative; and
in reply to the second part of his question
the abuses referred to are, in the main,
canvassing. Attention is drawn to the
existence of these abuses in paragraph 63
of the White Paper on Educational
Reconstruction, and it is also suggested
in that paragraph that the existing system
of selection should be reviewed.

Mr. CAMPBELL: Can the right hon.
Gentleman say whether the canvassing
he referred to in his answer has led to
inefficient teachers being appointed to the
detriment of efficient teachers, and
whether the appointments under the
individual voluntary school system are
altogether clear and free from this
parasitic growth?
Major SINCLAIR: In reply to the
first part of the supplementary question,
I cannot admit that.

UNIVERSITY OF IOWA
3 1858 029 298 753

Wednesday, 26th April, 1944,
three prison officers came into my cell
to search it, and they also told me to
strip. The names of the men concerned are, Prison Officers-
I am not going to give the names of
the three men, but I am going to call
Vote on Account
Vote on Account
14 MARCH 1945
It
The
them Prison Officers A. B. and C.
right hon. Gentleman can have this brief.
The names are mentioned in it, but I am
not prepared to mention them in public,
because I would not risk any man's livelihood that way.
The cell which I was in was very hard
to keep clean as the dust from the coal
heap and the exercise yard continually
blows through the cell window, so
when you wash your plate in the morning it is coated with dust at dinner
time. The officers came into my cell at
dinner time. Officer A said to me that
my plate was very dirty. I said I
would use it. He then said, "Half of
you fellows must have been reared in a
pigsty. Did you live like this outside!
You must have been reared like pigs.'
At this I said, "I am sure I was better
reared than you. As soon as I had
said this he wheeled round and struck
me twice on each side of the face with
the back of his hand. Although the
blows hurt me at the time they did not
mark me. On the following Friday I
complained to the Board of Visitors
about the incident, but they would not
believe it. They said as I was not
marked they could not believe it.
""
""
I was a member of one of these Boards
of Justices. A lot can be concealed from
one of those Boards, and a lot was concealed. The reason I am not a member
now is because I brought to light things
that are now concealed, and I agree with
these things that have been stated by this
man who has signed his name to them.
They happened, and they are happening
inside the prison. That is only one
incident. I could give you another
incident where it says,
A warder called Mr. B approached
me and ordered me to strip off my
entire clothing. As this was the first
occasion on which I had received such
an order I naturally refused to obey
it, as I deemed it rather humiliating to
have to strip under such circumstances.
Upon my refusal to take off my clothes
Mr. A said to me, "We will soon see
about that." He immediately grasped
me by the waistcoat and pulled it off
my back. He then threw me down on
my back on a mattress which was lying
on an iron bedstead about three feet
from the ground.. In the process of
doing so he had managed to pull my
shirt up to my head. In this position
he then pressed his knee into my chest
and pulled the shirt completely off me.
After that he pulled me from the bed
to the ground, holding me by the feet
in doing so, with the result that my
back hit the concrete floor in falling.
He then trailed me by both feet along
the ground, at the same time pulling
the trousers off me, and whilst doing so
he also kicked me on the left side. After
this both men left the cell leaving me
completely naked. I may mention that
Officers B and C did not in any way
take part in the assault. I was then
locked up in my cell until the following
day. When at 12 o'clock I was paraded
before the medical officer, who examined
me, the marks were on me,
but
nevertheless no action was taken.
Is that conduct that we can condone ?
Can we justly say that we are doing the
right and proper thing in passing money
for the payment of people who act in a
manner such as I have read out? I say
no. It would not be tolerated in Britain.
It would not be tolerated in any country
in the world. I want the Committee to

that the form of government for Ireland
should be an Irish Workers' Republic, as

Let me make a comparison between the

and what powers they could use. There

a new orientation has been introduced

right and justice irrespective of whether

I am prepared to say that many men

sent to the House of Lords.
I want to say that prison medical officers
are perhaps just like all other medical
officers-they accept decisions in reports
from persons who are perhaps concerned
in those reports. I think that a review
of the medical officers in the prisons might
be worth while. I would also say that if
the health of these men and women, who
are interned or who are prisoners because
of political actions, deteriorates in any
respect, I think a change is called for in
the medical service, a service which is set
up for the purpose of looking after the
health and strength of the men while they
are incarcerated. I know that the food
in the jail is anything but good. I have
seen the food and I have tasted it. I
have watched it being cooked, and I must
say that I cannot recommend it. Over a
period of four months, while I was there,
the cooking and the serving of the food
improved considerably, but I understand
that they have now gone back to their
former condition.
It is badly cooked and served in dirty
vessels. Searching of the cells usually
takes place before dinner and supper,
and the warders hands are anything but
clean after searching dirty and sweaty
clothing and mattresses, yet they will
leave such searching and commence to
serve out the food without bothering to
wash their hands. We must object to a
Vote on Account to people who are so
careless about the health of others that
they would start to handle food with
hands that have been used to search
things that are likely to be covered with
many millions of germs and other
dangerous things. Surely, there should
be some little consideration for the health
of these interned people, and surely the
warders should at least wash their hands
before doing this work. More hygienic
methods could be introduced into the
prison service so far as the food is concerned.
In England and Scotland there are 26
dishes served up to the prisoners every
month. The same used to apply in Northern Ireland when it was under the
Imperial Authorities. In Belfast there
are six different dishes in the year.
Surely the medical officer should realise
that he is responsible to those men, and
that all men cannot take the same dish.
There are men interned in Belfast, because of political convictions, who should
not on medical grounds be taking some of
the food provided, but they have to take
it, because if they did not they would not
get anything else. Here is a quotation
from the Report of the Scottish and
English Prisons: "There are twenty-six
different diets in any one month," but in
Northern Ireland there are only six diets
which prisoners can have in any one year.
Another question I want to raise is
that these prisoners are entitled to
liberty and they are entitled to
letters and to visits. For the first year
a prisoner is allowed one letter and a
visit once every three months. On these
occasions only certain relatives are
allowed to visit. The decision as to whom
they shall be rests with the police. One
man is allowed to visit his son but is
prevented from visiting his brother.
Physical contact between the visitor and
the prisoner is not allowed, not even a
shake of the hands being permitted.
Public events are not allowed to be discussed by the visitor and the prisoner,
and the visitor must confine himself to
personal affairs.

These visits last for twenty minutes
under the supervision of the warder, who
sits between the visitor and the prisoner.

conditions. Why are those strict and
rigid regulations applied to Northern
Ireland and not applied elsewhere?

girls who in the excitement of war conditions go astray. There are many such.
There have been many committals in the
Belfast courts of young people of that
description, and I have stressed very
strongly that there should be a remand
home for girls of that type to put them
on their feet again and to save them
from the danger and destruction towards
which they might be heading under war
conditions. I should like to know if the
Minister has taken any steps in the direction of providing a home for each of the
main denominations here in the North of
Ireland where the girls would be under
tutelage and wise control that would lead
into ways of straightforward and virtuous
conduct.
Coming to the Ministry of Health and
Local Government, I have spoken very
little on the question of housing, but I
feel deeply about it. I say that we are
making no headway whatever in regard
to the housing of the people of Northern
Ireland; we are not making an inch of
headway. The problem is just as great
to-day as it was 20 years ago, graver, as
the hon. Member for Antrim says.
People are living in hovels. In Belfast
within a stone's throw of Royal Avenue
people are living in shocking conditions.
Children are living in streets in which
they can hardly ever see sunshine. And
we are doing nothing. We are making
speeches, and as far as the public are
concerned the whole thing is I was going
to say a downright shame.
We know that dwellings are selling at
very high prices. A very small, decent
dwelling-house will cost about £900, the
rent will be in the region of £1 a week
and there will be rates in addition. How
is a working man to pay that? How is
he to get the money to provide also rates
and taxes? The cost of building has gone
up until it is from 50 per cent. to 100
per cent more than it was pre-war and the
prices of houses have gone up in the same
ratio, if not higher. There is one way it
might be partially solved-if out of the
£30,000,000 a year the Government
are contributing to the Imperial
Exchequer they held something for the
construction of housing in Northern Ireland. They might hold £3,000,000,
£4,000,000, or £5,000,000 for that purpose and that might go a good way towards the solving of the housing problem.
But they will not do that because of their
Imperialistic ideals. Their eyes are on
Greenland, Newfoundland, or the
Antipodes, and not on their neighbours or
on their own slum surroundings.

We have heard a great deal about full
employment coming after the war.
are told that we are in for a beautiful
paradise after the war. Every man is to
be happy, every man is to have a home;
this is to be a place where heroes can
live. All is going to be grand in the
garden when the war ends. Does any man
with the least knowledge of history or
with the least common sense believe one
scintilla of those promises? It is all
moonshine. The Prime Minister said some
time ago that he and his colleagues, mark
you, his colleagues, those six gentlemen
sitting in a row like Christy Minstrels, had
reduced the unemployed in Northern
Ireland from 60,000 to 15,000. Does the
Prime Minister believe that himself? I
know he is capable of drawing a long
bow when it suits. He apparently believes
that when you draw a long bow you should
draw it to its full stretch, to breaking
point. He can gull some of the people
of Northern Ireland all the time, but he
cannot gull the whole of the people of
Northern Ireland at all, even part of the
time. He asked his supporters to believe
that he and his Cabinet colleagues had
reduced the unemployment figures from
60,000 to 15,000. He had no more to do
with that than the Three Tailors of
Tooley Street. It would be like Mrs.
Partington who tried to brush back the
waves of the Atlantic with a broomstick.
I say he is drawing a long bow.
At the end of the war-I say this with
great earnestness and with great fear and
Vote on Account

apprehension-we will be faced with a
tidal wave of unemployment. There
never was a war yet which did not leave
the people drenched in poverty, hunger
and want. This is the greatest of all
wars, the most widespread of all wars,
the most destructive of human life and
property, and does any intelligent person
believe for one moment that we are in for
a golden paradise at the end of it when
so much has been blown into the air and
so much sunk to the depths of the sea?
The Prime Minister did not reduce the
unemployment figures. His colleagues
did not reduce the unemployment figures;
it was the war and the war only. The
war gave the people munition work. It
put men and women into the munition
factories and it took men into the armed
Forces and large contingents of women
also.
Of the entire population of these islands
something like 22 million people, roughly
50 per cent. of the entire population, are
engaged on active service or in the different
war factories. That is what gave employment, and that is what reduced the
figures in Northern Ireland. With the
slackening of work in the factories the
unemployment figures are creeping up
and up.
There are not now 15,000; they
are now at least 21,000. Does the Prime
Minister take credit for the increase from
15,000 to 21,000? Mark you, 21,000 is
a higher figure than the entire unemployed
in all Scotland. Scotland, with a population three times our own, and with an
area far and away larger than ours, has
fewer unemployed than we have in
Northern Ireland with our model Government, which can reduce figures by a mere
turn of the wheel. We have now 21,000.
What will the figure be at the end of the
war?

Mr. WARNOCK:
As I said a very
wide field was covered on some matters.
Some of the matters were of importance
and I want to deal with them.
the first matter dealt with by the hon.
Member for Pottinger related to the
police service and prisons, and almost
inevitably it centred round the position
of internees in the main in Belfast
Prison. Reference was made to the
Secret Service in this country and postal
censorship. It is very unforunate that
these things should be necessary in any
community, but they have been forced
upon this Government by circumstances
beyond their control and by circumstances
not of their own seeking.
Ever since the constitutional position
of Northern Ireland was established some
25 years ago we, unfortunately, had in
the country a body of people who were
bitterly opposed to its Constitution and
who sought by every means in their power
to destroy it. I think the first duty of
any Government is to defend its constitutional position. The attacks which
were made upon the Government of Northern Ireland were characterised by a
violence and severity which is almost unknown in any civilised community. They
were met and they were defeated by firm,
resolute, but, I believe absolutely fair
government.
It is suggested that at the present time
there are a number of persons deprived
of their liberty in Northern Ireland by
reason of their political views. Certainly
I would be no party to any such proceedings. When a man holds particular
political views and is prepared to advance
those political views in a constitutional
manner he will get the fullest and
greatest liberty to do so; but when, in
order to force upon the community views
which are destructive of the Constitution
under which we operate, he seeks to have
recourse to violence in order to destroy
that Constitution, then the Government
is not only entitled but absolutely bound,
in defence of its Constitution, to take
measures to put an end to those insurgent
or revolutionary ideas. The Government
of this country has done it firmly, resolutely and fairly. Speaking as the
Minister responsible for the maintenance
of law and order in this country, the
policy of firm, resolute and fair government will, so far as I am concerned, be
maintained so long as the threat to our
Constitution exists.
It was suggested by the hon. and
learned Member for Central Belfast that
the internment of certain persons who
constitute a threat to the security of this
country is due to partition It is a very
interesting argument, but it has not the
merit of truth. Partition does not
operate in Eire in the same way. The
latest figure I have of the number of
people who are interned in Eire as constituting a danger to the Government of
that country is 477. We have nothing
like so many as that; in actual fact the
number in Northern Ireland is 232. The
last figure which I have from Eire is 477,
almost double the number of persons
whom we have interned in this country.
The conditions of internment there are
vastly more rigorous than those in operation in this country.

The hon. Member went on to speak of

When you go round the country and see

Something, even of a temporary nature,

A good house goes a long way towards

Government he undertakes to pay it back
in instalments over a period of two years.

months it is not right, when a man sells

be deducted from the cheque he should
receive. There is a time specified in the
contract and that should be adhered to.

saw the other day where Mr. Hudson
said it would take £200,000,000 to

implements and other articles necessary

three years,
make them repayable over

such as I have mentioned should be
made.
